I'm not a huge fan of games where you try to explore an environment and solve puzzles while being constantly pursued by an unkillable stalker. Fortunately Soma is not that sort of game. Exploration and puzzle solving is largely kept separate from the hide-and-seek/stalker sections, and the game's autosave feature acts as a kind of warning that you might be approaching something that could kill you.
So, as a horror game Soma is kind of an odd one. The mechanics of the game neuter the threat of the monsters, but the environment is still fascinating and creepy to explore. Also the story is excellent and thought-provoking, and more than enough to drive you towards the end. Also worth mentioning is that the story does not try to be purposefully obtuse. Characters ask the questions you want them to ask, say the things they should be saying, and by the end you have the answers you want.
10 hours long too. Thats a good length for a game that throws up so few obstacles.

An hour in and you'll get stock at a village where you'll be boxed in with no clear objectives on how to proceed.
What a waste, the game seemed promising but this is a game breaker for me and therefore I cannot recommend this title to anyone. Do *NOT* waste your time nor money on this.

Here's what it looks like:
Released and developed by the Russian fellow Носков Сергей, 35MM is a game about 2 men who are making a journey across some unknown lands after a global epidemic-apocalypse has occured. They start off in this forest, where the user has to collect items to pass certain obstacles. Later on the game develops and there are events such as being chased etc.
There is no real crafting in this game. It is a journey/adventure type of experience. The atmosphere is very well done, and it is not a laggy game by any means. There are a few issues users may have with making it full screen.
When you initially start the game, everything is in Russian so you will have to change the options to English yourself. It's in the settings menu, which is near the top. The first option is to start your game. There ARE english subtitles in the game, however they're not the best. They're good enough to be understandable for native English speakers though.
The key to this game is how immersive it is. Rummaging through houses and encounters are what engage the user into progressing to the next part. The atmosphere in the game is what makes this game.
Something annoying you may find is the progression of your partner. He is quite slow and will walk, however that gives you time to rummage through the area of houses and things, but make sure that you don't lose him!
Another annoying thing you may encounter is the lack of instruction at some parts. You may become lost or not know what button to press so here:
TAB opens inventory, the numbers displayed in your book show what to press for what item. ESCAPE simply brings up the menu, E interacts with objects and that's pretty much it.
If you start the game with no events occuring, i.e the opening scene doesn't show, restart your game because the rest of your game won't work very well.
Overall I am enjoying it so far and I think I am about halfway through the game. I have to work tomorrow so I will update when I have completed the game a little later!
EDIT: The game has multiple endings depending on what you interact with and what you do, it has quicktime events, a gun fight, and much more! A WORKING interesting game to say the least. I would recommend it for those who like immersive games with surprises.

2011 saw the release of 'Rock Ages', a hybrid of ball racing and tower defense.  It was a very different concept; battling historical and mythlogical figures throughout the ages of human history with a giant boulder and assorted defenses on obstacle course-styled maps. Throw in some Monty Python-esq comedy and many a pop culture reference. It was not only different; it was brilliant too.
Fast foward six years into 2017 and we have yet another brilliant release. This time, we have the sequel, 'Rock of Ages 2: Bigger and Boulder.'
Rock of Ages 2: Bigger and Boulder takes the concept and finer qualities of the original game and refines them, while introducing many new features. The level design at each of the battle locations is now more clever. Better varied for layout and uniqueness, they are also aesthetically appropriate for the cast of characters and famous artworks which are your opponents. One example I had to reallly appreciate was the surrealist style of Salvador Dali, brought to life whilst fighting the Burning Giraffe. Another thing worthy of appreciation is the requirement of now having to choose what boulders and defenses to equip before battle; the arsenal consisting of many toys returning from Rock of Ages as well as new ones. This adds a welcome invitation to strategy and experimentation, which you will have to do a fair amount of at the various locations. This applies to both singleplayer and the new two vs two online multiplayer modes. Finally, it is hard not to laugh and smile at the wackiness of the game's cinematics and boss fights. There is no shortage of the Monty Python-esq comedy or the pop culture references. How many will you recognize?
All in all, I believe this is a sequel done right and a damn memorable one of that! Rock of Ages 2: Bigger and Boulder earns a well deserved spot in what I feel should be a list of 'Video games of 2017 you must play.'

High quality action rpg fun with a lot of nostalgia tossed in aswell. There really isn't enough I can say about this game, the multiplayer is crafted perfectly, with drop in/out features enemy difficulty increasing with each additional player not just increases in attributes but additional skills for bosses etc.
Very indepth character leveling, allows you to create and mold your hero as you please, so you can find your perfect build. The story mode is probably about 50 percent complete, by the time i reached the end i was really yearning for more. There are tons of collectibles and several mini games including pets. Perfect game for the kind of person that loves additional content after the story, especially those who enjoy some grinding.
For those tired of playing in the story, there is a very well crafted arcade mode that is of course also multiplayer and has almost infinite replayability.
The real seller with this game though is the combat, which takes you back to old school SNES 2D top-down games like Link to the past and Secrets of Mana, but it is so much more then that. Once you find a build you enjoy whether you're just sitting back grinding enemies or facing the highest difficulty challenges, time just flies by.
As you can tell I highly recommend this game. There is a demo available which definitely gives you enough of a taste of the game to understand my high praise.

This is my Review of Star Wolves 3: Civil War.
SW3:CW is a non-direct Sequel to SW2 which... had its flaws.
You start the game off and get instantly Asked what kind of Skill-Tree you want to follow, note that this is a Permanent selection, each of the Tree's is balanced out enough, but still there "Rocket Salvo" which when Skilled to max extent, will not only let your Pilots shoot rockets at an INSANE rate, but it also affects Big Guns/Small Guns and other types of Weaponry.
Which makes the game very Easy in fact, you can take down several Battleships in just a couple of Seconds with the right Weapons, not even including Modded Weapons. (Full Plasma + Endgame Rocket Salvo = Ez Win).
But as the Difficulty of the game rises as you go further down the Storyline that doesn't matter most of the time, but theres still the side effect that you feel like a Superhero at endgame.
Many People are talking about how Linear this game, and... yes. it is, but what can you expect some small group of Ex-Modders is able to do?, and yes. The Development Team of this Game is a Group of EX Modders, please take that into consideration when you (reader) also want to make an Review of this Game, you can't go too harsh on em.
OVERALL PRO'S & CONTRA'S OF THE GAME -----------------------
PRO:
-Fun and Challanging Game if you have Played Star Wolves 1 and are familiar with this Style of Gameplay
-Neat and Quite Useful "Realtime Pause" Feature, which reminds of Baldurs Gate
-Easy Moddability, which lets you almost change every Aspect of the Game, from Weapon PFX/SFX to Whole new Sectors with Systems, although it could have been a bit more, the unlocked files in the game data folders are doing its job.
-Although not so active anymore, still has a very Friendly Community and the people over at 1C Company Forums in the SW Thread are always willing to help
-Due to a wide array of Available Weapons & Rockets this game allows the Player many Tactical Choices
-OK Graphics
-HIdden Stashes & Eastereggs to find.
CONTRA:
Uses LUA4.1 which is severely Outdated, even for a 2010 Game (Since LUA5.0 was available at that time)
-Outdated Engine and Poor Optimization, this game goes down to the knees everytime there is a Scripted huge fight going on (Several of the Ending Fights often go down to 20-15 FPS because of that)
-Balancing Problems (Example: Rocket Salvo 4)
-A Bit of boredom in Freetime: This game has made an attempt to fill the universe by increasing Random events and random encounter by a huge percentage than it was in the last game, but they will get boring quickly since most of the time it is the same thing over and over again, there is only very little stuff todo if you are Freeroaming and not grinding Missions
-Although the game got patched on the usual occasion, the are still Story breaking bugs present in the game, but they are not consistent, they will often happen at random due to the Script Code not being able to keep up with what a Player has done or not done
-VERY Limited Freedom: This game has you on the Leash, I mean it almost literally, there are extremely many occasions where you as the Player need to do what the Mission and Story tells you EXACTLY or the Game will Blow your Ship up and tell you its Game Over.
As Much as I like and Love this game, there are far more Negative things in it than Positive, but I would still Recommend it, I don't know why, but this game is just too much fun sometimes.
One Last Note: If you are New to this Game and would like to try it out, heres a ProTip: Save. SAVE OFTEN. SAVE EXTREMELY OFTEN, because the game will eventually get the jump on you and RNG will take you out. and also: Go to the 1C Forums and try out some Mods for the Game, its worth it.

This is a gem of a flight simulator. It is highly atmospheric and the aircraft all have a good individual feel to them. It is a lot of fun and conveys a great sense of the air conflict over the trenches of the First World War. The free-to-play version comes with 3 great aircraft, although there is a bit of a learning curve to get started.
is a flight-simulator for the First World War. The atmospheric is great and the graphics are lovely, albeait a little dated now. There is a good selection of aircraft and a reasonable range of multiplayer servers and scenarios to keep you enthralled. The base game is free-to-play, and there are two ways to purchase add-ons: either through Steam (with DLCs) or the Rise of Flight Store (with individual items). You cannot mix the two methods (I went with the Steam option).
It is not an arcade game, but should be treated as a serious simulator. As such, there are a lot of keys to map, and a lots of things to learn. We often see newcomers turn up and have trouble figuring out how to start their aeroplane or take off (tip: search on the Internet for videos on getting started in
).
The setting is compelling and there are a range of weathers, times of day, maps and settings. Targets are many and varied and there is a great selection of aircraft to fly against, from bombers to scouts to seaplanes. The aircraft seem fragile and occasional gun jams, mechanical failures and a rough feel enhance the title. This is the only sim where I've managed to suspend disbelief and truly feel in the environment.
There are some flaws (see the cautions above), but these are minor compared to the many features offered by the rest of the sim. In total, if you purchase all the modules, it can be pretty expensive. But you can either be selective (like me) or wait for sales or discounts. One recommended DLC for those who go with the Steam version is the
, as it adds the English Channel Map (excellent) and a great selection of fine aircraft.
Despite its age and somewhat confusing purchase model, this is nonetheless a worthy simulator and comes highly recommended.

This game could be amazing. It has so much potential. The combat mechanics are incredible, with a pretty high skill ceiling making it competitive and fun. Here's the issue though: the matchmaking is terrible. You will come in at level one, and get matched with people who way outskill you. This on it's own can be fine, especially if you like a big challenge, but more often than not, you are killed in ways that leave you angry and frustrated.
The matchmaking has potential to be fixed in time, it is a relatively new title after all, but one thing that can't be fixed is the toxic community. When you play, the majority of your experience with players will be toxic behavior paired with toxic chat. Yes there are community members who aren't toxic, and you will see them fairly regularly, but if I had to make a guess, I would say that about 75% of the community is toxic on some level, while the other 25% aren't, and after playing them, win or loss, you feel fairly satisfied with the experience. In fact, if the community weren't so toxic, the broken matchmaking wouldn't even be much of an issue, since you would have an enjoyable duel with decent members of the community.
My recommendation:
Wait to buy this game until matchmaking is fixed, or the game goes on sale, as right now it is not worth $60 for a multiplayer heavy experience. I was gifted the game, so I don't feel too bad about it, but if I had paid for it I would be sorely disapointed.

For anyone getting bad FPS in the game, I found a fix...at least it works for me.
I have an r9 380 strix 4gb, thought it was my gpu, but it is not.
It has more to do with how this game sees CPU cores and how it chooses to use them. I have 24 cores, well really what I have is 24 threads spread over 12 real cores of which those 12 real cores are split to two separate physical processor dies of 6 cores each.
I run a dual processor XEON workstation.
In order to get this game and subnautica to play correctly i have to go into task manager details and set core affinity for this games .exe file. I set it to the first 4 cores. It works about the same with 3 cores but not with 2 cores. So there you have it.
It's odd that all my other games run fine but the 2 water games I play need to be told to only use 3 or 4 cores. I have even split the 4 cores in between the 2 different physical cpu's to each run 2 cores for the game and surprisingly ran just as good as when the 4 cores were on the same die.
That was striking as you'd expect a difference when the data does not have to travel so far in between physical dies.
I am one of the 0.01% who game on a xeon so i guess it's whatever. Wish win10 knew how to handle processes better.

Do not buy this game now. If you're interested, consider purchasing it way later, especially at a lower price.
Mechanically, you are punished for attacking. Guard Break / throws, moves meant to open an opponent up or counter block-heavy opponents, is used as a free-win button - although the counter window is already small, you can't counter Guard Break if you're dodging or have been parried, or sometimes tried to throw your own guard break to defend from theirs. Guard Break makes sense to counter a dodge, but dodging is the only way out of getting hit by many character's many unblockable moves, most of which can recover and score a free un-counterable grab on you before you can even finish. Many characters have combo chains that can kill you in one go. Environmental hazards are way too numerous - normally in a fighting game, they're great positioning hazards to either bait or punish your opponent against a wall, but in this game they're unavoidable. The levels are good size, but the fighting arenas are embarrassingly small. and a throw (into one of the gratuitously placed environmental hazards or any nearby wall) is instant death, which cheapens the entire duel given the simplicity of getting a throw. Gear scores make for some crazy builds, but instead of opening up new tools for players and interesting counter-play, they simply lock lesser powered players out of play, usually placing lower-leveled players against max level players with crazy damage, revenge builds, or my personal hated throw distance - which usually ends a fight in one combo/hit. Basically, fighting games require an opponent to make multiple mistakes in order for you to win - this game needs you to make only one, and the higher-leveled, unblockable-stacking characters will always have the upper hand.
I am expecting to see some character balancing down the line (in lengthly seasons), but I believe this game needs a massive overhaul before I'll consider playing it again.
This is a good contender to the fighting game, neat concept, and a hell of a lot of fun to get started on. Casually, you will rage by the constant shut-down by stronger leveled players. Hardcore, you will abuse the Guard Break mechanic, never throw the first hit, and be locked down to play only one or two characters to have a fighting chance. Knowing this, this game is no longer fun - getting crushed or when doing well. Set it down, wait for the devs to work on it a bit, wait for a major price drop if you're still interested in hopping in.

On the plus side, the weapons are far less overpowered this time around, and the modified Quake engine allows for far more complex level design, on top of a 3D look that hasn't aged perfectly, but still is more pleasing to the eye than enemies that look like they're made from cardboard. They also played it up as much more of an RPG this time around, giving each class a set of visible stats that automatically level up when you've gained enough experience points from killing enemies, giving you an incentive to fight rather than just run past everything. The puzzles are also largely improved, most having solutions that don't require you to activate some unknown wall or something. No, this game will tell you, and you'll probably be able to figure it out without a guide.
On the negative side, the Quake engine. While it's good to look at and everything, you'll have to do a bit of tweaking to get the resolution accurate, set mouse controls, and all that stuff, and it all has to be done manually. It's not a huge complaint, but it's just a quick pain that you have to go through whenever you install the game.
Even if you weren't a fan of the previous games, I'd suggest giving this one a go.

This was a negative review changed to positive.  Read on for why.
The game is definitely worth playing, and therefore I recommend you get the game and add the DLC modules to your wish list.  When a sale comes, load up and go fly.  It's all the IL-2 quality in a game for WWI planes.
The only real downside after playing this game for many hours now is the lack of really good AI in the career (offline) mode on either side of the front.  Even if you can get your fellow flightmates to get into the mix, they will fire off all their ammo and do some pretty redonkitarded maneuvering trying to get shots off - so they waste their entire ammo load shooting up the sky.  Or they will shoot you if you get in the mix.  Or ram you out of the sky as you're closing for a shot.  As a result, you can fly for weeks and weeks in a squadron and be the only one scoring kills.  Enemy AI is no better, as they don't "see" you at all until you close to within .30km.  Because of this, you can fly up under a formation of 5 enemy alone, and creep up slowly and pick them off one at a time.  The others, well within 1km of the action, never seem to notice one of their friends getting shredded right below.  They never react as a flight or coordinate in their response.  This is kind of sad, considering they managed a better AI in the 1990 Red Baron game, where you could even tell when you were going up against an ace, and sometimes even which one.
Otherwise, it's great fun and everything you'd want in a WWI sim.

SOMA has several weaknesses - the puzzles found in the game not only are rare but also disappointingly easy for something that calls itself a horror adventure, the monsters tend to be more annoying rather than horrifying, and you spend the better part of the game simply walking from A to B while the gamer sputters forth its narrative.
It is this narrative and the atmosphere created by it, however, that really make the game shine. What starts out as a more or less regular visit to a doctor quickly turns into a biomechanical underwater nightmare that repeatedly questions the philosophical concept of the self and what constitutes as a human, anyway.
Long story short, SOMA basically is a glorified walking simulator, but unlike most other games in that category, this title actually has a story engaging enough to let you forgive its rather lacking pure gameplay. Those looking for a pure horror game that constantly keeps your heart pounding may be disappointed, however.

Rock of Ages is the sequel to the original Rock of Ages and is created by ACE Team. It is like no other game with it combing strategy, racing and action all into one game that can be fun or frustrating for others. It contains an expansive story mode, which you can also do in co-op mode, a local 1v1 co-op battle and an online mode in which you can verse other people in this interesting game. All this comes at a cost of $15, which could stop people from buying the game, but it does have many features going for it.
The gameplay of this game is unique compared to any other game I’ve played, it uses strategy and preplanning and then a fast race where you must break through the enemy’s defences while trying to get to the castle door before the opponent.
The pre-race stage is quite simple. Before you start the war, you select a certain number of traps or defences and then after every race you get a certain amount of money. With that money, you must strategically place walls, traps and other things to either slow down the enemy’s boulder or destroy it completely. Meanwhile the enemy is downing the same thing in the aim to slow or destroy your boulder. This part is quite simple and sometimes the traps you place can be avoided but it is a crucial part of the game, even though it isn’t the most fun part. I found I often either ran out of money or finished my defences way before I could race.
The racing part is the best part of the game, with it having fun moments when you get break through walls or dodge traps or when you have too much speed and are thrown off the edge of the map. The controls for this part of the game are super easy to use which allows you to focus on the fast-paced gameplay. As well as trying to dodge the traps placed by the enemy you also have to try and smash into the castle door before them, especially if the castle door is on low health, and the first person to beak the door and kill the leader wins the game. This part of the game is defiantly the most riveting, and I can tell the developers put a lot of effort into it.
The story in this game is expansive, with it having different castles to attack all around a map of Europe. It also contains tons of different leaders and a little back story/cutscene for each of them. All the characters are based off historical figures and a lot of the times, the cutscenes and the ways the characters are portrayed can be quite entertaining. When attacking all the castles it has the gameplay but it doesn’t become repetitive with it having different map layouts and different styles and themes, which often changed according to the enemy character or the location in which the castle your fighting is. Even if you just bought this game for the story you could have many hours of fun and  frustration.
The graphics of this game aren’t really anything new except for the 2D depictions of the characters which are often humorous. It mainly uses normal 3D models which are well done, but aren’t anything substantial. Lucky this game distracts you from the on pare graphics with the gameplay making the graphics not necessary to make this a fun game.
The sound design in the game is well done, using some great intense music and good sound effects for the characters, cutscene and defences. It always has some sound play even if it’s just the boulder rolling through the map it fills the ‘quiet’ parts of the game.

Very slow paced game. I don't normally mind a game being slow paced, but this is just painfully slow.  After almost 24 hours on easy, I still haven't gotten past the fourth objective, or at least I think it was the fourth one. After setting up your base and getting things running, slowly, you have to collect plans for a doomsday device, which I assume you will later build. There are three of these devices, each one has three parts that you have to collect, so nine total. I can only find six, two of each. The objective says that you can find them on the world map through missions, which is how I got these six, by doing research on the map, which I have done on every place on the map and haven't found anything, or from Agents coming to your base. I have captured several Agents and Super Agents and tortured them several times, never find anything. I have no clue how you are supposed to get any of the remaining three doomsday plans, and there are no hints other than what is in the objective of "from the map missions, map research, from Agents."
Another problem is that you constantly have enemy forces coming to your base and sabataging/ destroying everything they see. Even some of your own henchmen will do massive damage to your base when fighting the enemy. Trying to repair all of the damage and then build new things takes way too long and is very boring, preventing you from doing much of anything else.
The only way to make money is to steal from countries on the world map, where your units are constantly being killed off and you then have to wait for more units to train. Something that really irritated me is that you can build a hotel and casino as a cover operation, which is expensive to get started, but you do not make any money from that. Those buildings are strictly to keep tourists out of your evil lair.
I think 20 hours is more than enough to say I gave the game a try. It is almost fun, but they really did a terrible job on it.
***Update***
I put a few more hours into the game. The final 3 plans for the doomsday device were on random enemies, but none of the ones that were marked as "Agents" or "Super Agents." There is no identifying mark on the enemies that have the plans, you have to click on every single one to see if they are holding it, then kill them.
So! plans gathered, 2 million dollars saved up as part of a mission objective, now to move to a bigger island. Yay! Except...
When leaving your first island you must give the order for your minions to evacuate the island, with a warning that they will grab "as much as they can" (which apparently means "only artifacts"), and that once your Evil Genius arrives at one of the 2 ports anyone and anything left behind is lost. Naturally it sounds like your Evil Genius should wait in the base until everything is cleared out, so that's what I did. Bad choice.
As soon as you sound the alarm 2 things happen:
1) your minions grab any artifacts that they can and move to one of 2 ports, and this cannot be stopped, altered, or overriden in any way.
2) Enemyy forces swarm your base and begin killing your now defenseless minions, who will not fight back and cannot be ordered to do anything other than head straight into enemy fire on their way to the ports. Fun fact: there are 3 branches of training for your minions, with 3 levels of training. New minions can only be trained by other minions of a higher level in that branch. So if the enemy kills all of your high ranking military units, for example, then you cannot train any more of them on the next island until you go back through the tedious process of capturing more of that unit on the world map to learn their secrets.
Following the warning not to send your Evil Genius to the port until the base was empty means that your Evil Genius is now completely defenseless and must hide from and evade the enemy swarm that now has free run of your base. This results in yet another long and tedius process.
Now, provided that you made it you your new base alive, you may think you get to have fun and can avoid any logistical problems you had with your first base. No. Imagine a big triangle on this big new base of yours, each of the 3 points representing the 2 ports that your workers must go to to buy construction supplies, and the 3rd point being your treasury, where your workers must go to first to get the money to go to the port to buy the supplies. These 3 locations are as far from eachother as possible, resulting in a lot of unnessecary travel time to build anything. Also, you have no control over which port your workers go to, so when I built the entrance to my new base near the airport, my minions chose to travel to the seaport for supplies. It literally took over 5 minutes just to build the door to my base.
Another "fun" thing here is that all of those valuable artifacts that you collected and transported from your first base are now sitting around outside, ready to be stolen by enemies, and there is nothing you can do to stop them because almost all of your minions were killed when trying to leave the first island.
Long story short, it took over 2 hours to get my new base running, by which time several artifacts had been stolen and the last of my skilled mininos had been killed. I was out of money (apparently the 2 million was not enough, and I hadn't even built a lavish base, just the basics), and enemy units were all over the island because it took 2 hours to build. Essentially you are worse off than when you started the first island because back then the enemies were not coming after you as hard as they are now.
Again, terrible game, do not buy it even if it is 90% off. Don't even waste your time if it is free.

I'm not a huge fan of games where you try to explore an environment and solve puzzles while being constantly pursued by an unkillable stalker. Fortunately Soma is not that sort of game. Exploration and puzzle solving is largely kept separate from the hide-and-seek/stalker sections, and the game's autosave feature acts as a kind of warning that you might be approaching something that could kill you.
So, as a horror game Soma is kind of an odd one. The mechanics of the game neuter the threat of the monsters, but the environment is still fascinating and creepy to explore. Also the story is excellent and thought-provoking, and more than enough to drive you towards the end. Also worth mentioning is that the story does not try to be purposefully obtuse. Characters ask the questions you want them to ask, say the things they should be saying, and by the end you have the answers you want.
10 hours long too. Thats a good length for a game that throws up so few obstacles.

While the game isn't terrible, it has grossly overrated user-reviews. With user-reviews in the 80%+ range, I expected it to at least be a short, but decent rpg story. After finishing it, I don't think it's worth it even at a deeply discounted sale price. I would struggle to say it even deserves the 61% metacritic score it has. At full-price it's an absolute rip-off.
The game is pretty short (finished it in 9 hours) and it has no real replayability - but I expected that going in based on the consensus from reviews. It's still a negative but wasn't a surprise.
What was a surprise was how absolute garbage the story and characters were, which are heavily praised by many users. The story, the characters, the setting, the dialoge... all of it is TERRIBLE - all the way to the end. There are some poor attempts to add some depth to the characters, but everything ends up very cheesy, the story is driven with no real sensible motives, and it all falls flat.
Lots of games have very bad characters and story, but that was the leading element of praise from the community that led me to purchase the game and try it out and ended up being the most disappointing aspect of the entire game.
As far as the game mechanics, while the camera and combat can be a bit finicky at times, I didn't find them to be huge issues. The physics-based combat system is a pretty cool idea, but ended up being rather unsatisfying. This had nothing to do with the technical implementation, but was more the result of the balance of skills, regular attacks, terrain, etc. (Regular attacks do very little damage, enemy count is high, and special attack cooldowns are low - this results in gameplay of constantly pausing, tabbing through the characters and queueing up special cleave attacks every few seconds. The movement skills were largely ineffective, though fun to use.) Overall the combat mechanics are a bit of a wash - novel and sometimes fun, but ultimately unsatisfying.
The overmap travel mode seemed impressive at first, but quickly became boring. You move from node to node and occasionally have some dialogue options. There are consequences to choices here, though you never really feel them and nothing is ever thrown into the mix to make it more interesting.
Lastly, there really isn't much RPG meat on the game's bones. There is no customization, almost no itemization (1 very limited item slot per character for a charm or potion), and very little character development (on average, a choice between 2 skills every other level). You can only use a portion of your party and each party member can only use a portion of their skills, so it wasn't uncommon to go through several areas and character levels, with no changes to the lineup of characters/skill i was using. Often times there just wasn't any reason to ever switch, unless the game forced you to by killing someone off, etc. I tried to pair up some characters and skills for interesting combos, but they were never effective - using tankier characters with a power attack (which is usually their starting skill) and using it every few seconds was almost always better.
There were some positives to the game - the voice acting and visuals were pretty good and some parts felt like they were just a step away from being really interesting, but at the end of the day, it's a bad RPG with a bad story/characters.

The game has a couple bugs and its share of flaws, but it's the only space sim I've seen like this. The game revolves around carrier mechanics and your survival doesn't depend on your ship anywhere near as much as your fighter pilots. In practice it's a squad based tactical RTS with RPG elements and limited open world exploration.
The fighter mechanics are what set this game apart, since no other space sim to my knowledge does anything like it. The combat itself is very deep, weapon fire is done in real time so a shot only hits if it connects (anyone who's played the new x-com and compared its combat to the original will know exactly what I mean). This can be misleading since piloting skills in the skill tree make it seem like it's a chance to ignore damage like on other games but it actually upgrades the pilots AI so they manually avoid incoming fire.
The game also features a lot of meaningful choices in the story and it takes several playthroughs to see everything, and get every pilot and capital ship.
This game has left an itch no other game has managed to scratch since. It's a shame the original team that made the series went bust.

Based off of the original quake engine, Hexen II is quite stunning in both it's technical aspects and its overall appeal as a game. Continuing where the original Hexen left-off, this game adds some twist in the medival storyline, expands the Hexen universe, and provides us gamers with an easily digestable narrative. Gameplay-wise Hexen II puts an emphasis on ranged combat, but melee combat also feels very satisfying (seeming as you can decapitate and quarter your foes once they're down). The leveling system isn't robust, but because the game is more action-oriented the RPG elements are more of an addition rather than a main attraction. The wide variety of enemies and open world compliments the different classes to play as, and substantially increases the replayablility. Overall if you're on the fence about getting this classical masterpiece or if you seem vaguely interested in the vintage fps genre, GET IT!! You won't regret this purchase.

A great many people have ripped this game apart because of it's payment method. Frankly, I like it. I owned RoF years ago, standalone (non-steam) and even though my laptop BARELY ran it, it stuck with me. When I saw that it was available on steam as a free-to-try, I knew I had to see what it would do on my brand new custom gaming PC. I am ok with the idea of trying a somewhat neutered full version of a game, and then paying for the modules I want.
Yeah, when compared to the old days of IL-2, Combat Flight Sim, and the Jane's simulations, where you pay for the full program up front, and get all the content - no questions asked it seems a bit ridiculous. But to me, I see a major quality difference in a program like this. I paid $25 for the Channel Battle add-on, that seemed to bring the free version up to par with what would have been the in-store box edition years ago...that I paid i think $40 for. The planes really feel like what I would expect from them, judging from what I have read. I think that in todays simming age, so much more attention is paid to each individual aircraft, instead of a select few...I remember Microsoft Flight Sim 98, the first one to include virtual cockpits. The cessna 172s, and a couple others had it...but the boeing was a literal grey cardboard cutout you sat behind with NO gauges or anything. That was what your hard earned money got you. In ROF, you pay for each plane, but from what I can tell, they give the same thought and attention to detail to each plane in the lineup, so you get same type of experience in each seat.
I like it, If you like the IL-2 installments, you'll like it too.

This game is one of those small gems that you love despite its flaws.
You have to approach Nether, not with progression in mind (get to level 30 ASAP then get all the guns and money!), but with adventure.
The world is beautiful and I had little trouble getting into the bleak survival feel with the thousands of small touches that went into the visual design. The gunplay is forgiving, yet responsive, and feels skillful yet easy. It absolutely nails the tension between players and the environment. I'm enjoying slowly sneaking around, exploring every nook and cranny to be rewarded with either loot, or some tucked away miniature nightmare scene, complete with grisly corpses seated at a dinner table.
There are lots of things to do like package runs, scavenging for supplies, hunting mobs/players, getting hunted by mobs/players, missions of opportunity, 8 optional factions that can control pvp objectives in the world, and more.
However there are some glaring flaws in Nether. Occasionally you see someone hacking, but they tend to hang out at the main safezone as that's where most people are. The water is terrible on most accounts, though it does look pretty in places. The sound of water splashing is 300,000,000 times louder than any other noise. I tend to find myself avoiding the water, not that there's anything in it.
The game occasionally crashes (once every 3 hours or so), though it does automatically detect, and generate crash reports (no idea if it's actually helping). There is also some occasional server lag, and the server count is dwindling.
The game looks to have been designed well, but rushed out due to budget constraints, but the core is definitely there. It is definitely playable, mostly pretty, and I am definitely having a blast.
Once more: It's not a game where your levels matter. Levelling gives you perks which you can look at as a reward for staying alive so long. You also have an account level which has rewards that persist through death. At any time a level one can find a pistol and kill you and suddenly get all your gear. It's a survival game FIRST. RPG SECOND. Play to live and survive in the hostile world, as a simulation of what you would actually do, and you'll have fun.
I'm not paid to do this review or anything I just love this game ind it feels like it is on life support and It really deserves a second look.
... and if my review doesn't sell it, watch Markiplier play it. That sold me.
(also note the cool turn of karma at the end of the second one)

Sometimes when a game is based off of a book (series), it runs the risk of appealing only to its previously-installed fanbase.  The Dwarves isn't quite one of those, but I have the distinct feeling I would have enjoyed it a lot more if I had read the series.
You play as Tungdil, a dwarf raised by a human magus to love books as much as blacksmithing, and are initially tasked with delivering some loaned items back to their owner, another mage months away.  From this humble beginning, you are embroiled in a plot to destroy the world, and reconnecting with your dwarven heritage is the only way to thwart this threat, because of course it is.
Don't get me wrong, the writing is the high point of The Dwarves, and it is excellently voice-acted.  However, there's no getting around that the epic storyline crams itself into roughly 8-12 hours of play if you do all the sidequests.  Although the world map is large, most of the nodes do nothing, or provide random bits of narration that do little to flesh out the world or its implied lore.  Ancient and colossal dwarven cities are relegated to considerably less exploratory space than even Dragon Age's versions of them.
You get the feeling early on that the game is going to be more open-ended and RPG-like than it winds up being.  There's simply no time to soak it in, and since there are no random encounters, no gear to acquire, and nothing else to see except for a handful of tiny zones in the game, there's no reason to. Many resolutions amount to nothing, such as a character leaving, or a group of people "allying" themselves to you, towns being saved, and so on.  You get the feeling you're setting up stories, cutscenes, even diplomatic foundations for something bigger, and you simply never hear of these elements again.
Combat is mostly about strategically positioning your heroes so that they don't hit each other with the abilities you should be spamming until everything is dead, and battling an infuriating camera.  The only variations on this objective are to quickly - very quickly - do something specific, such as killing a specific target (like a god*amn teleporting Alfar), or to simply escort the entire party from point A to B.  Eventually, you are given many characters in the party that you can swap in for these battles, but the truth is the variety is pretty much wasted on the game.  I found the generic combat to be the most rewarding, because the variations have no mercy and are totally linear.  If you don't do them right away, you're going to fail.  No complex formations, very little environmental integration, not even time to enjoy the ork blood on your axe.
And so, the game that starts off full of promise winds up being.... okay.  The ending arrives unceremoniously tacked-on, and with sequel-bait to boot.  Is it worth 40 dollars?  No, of course not, you'd either have to be insane or (possibly) a fan of the book series.  But if you're just an RPG nerd who likes dwarves, 15 dollars should be what you're waiting for.

This game is kind of a cross between Homeworld, IWar2 and Blackguards. The spaceship mechanics are almost a direct copy of Homeworld. The game is an open world with a central storyline like IWar2. It is a party-based RPG with a focus on tactics like Blackguards, my favorite genre.
The story and dialogue are pretty good. There are multiple branching paths and different endings. The English translation is sometimes rough, but not too bad. I like the combat, ships and itemization. No real complaints here.
The main aspect this game failed at is the open world. The star systems are pretty boring, and there's not much to look at. They're all pretty much identical, though there is the occasional weapons cache hidden away in a remote sector. IWar2 had much better exploration. Luckily, the game lets you skip most of the exploration and proceed directly to the next story location. So it didn't bother me a whole lot.
Overall, I liked this game and would recommend it to people who like Homeworld and RPGs.

In one word, The Darkness II is a gem. From beginning to end this game just continuously impressed me and constantly engaged me in a way that a shooter just hasn’t been able to in a long time.
I would like to start with the weaknesses of the game, but I’m having trouble pointing out any. I found the melee attack using the darkness was a bit finicky, however by the halfway point in the campaign I had adjusted to the way it works. I still found it a bit obnoxious that your view would be put completely out of whack after using the tentacle, but honestly the rest of the experience was so wonderful I’m having a hard time even bringing myself to complain about it.
I never played The Darkness (shame on me) so it was awesomely welcome to have an option to see “Previously on The Darkness” before starting up the campaign. While it was clearly intended just to remind players where they left off, it did a good enough job highlighting the plot points of the previous game that I didn’t feel lost jumping into the second game.
Following the recap, the first thing that struck me was the art style. I knew nothing about the game going in, I was expecting a generic shooter with the equally generic HD graphics but what I got was a spectacularly gorgeous cross between a comic book and cel shading. Everything from the guns and the effects down to the wrinkles in a characters brow was cohesive and beautiful.
In typical shooter fashion they drop you into action as quickly as possible; however, between the theme and dark tone of the game, the back story I was presented with, the introductory dialogue and the dialogue presented in the initial gun fight, I found myself actually emotionally engaged with my character. It was absolutely wonderful! This fantastic writing and story carried through the entire game, at one point towards the end of the game I was asked to make a certain choice and I could not believe how difficult it was. I actually had to pause the game and walk away from it for a while before actually committing to a path. There are very few games out there I can say that about.
One of the other extremely strong points of this game is the AI companion, the Darkling. His writing is hilarious, crude and an exceptional juxtaposition to the very grim story being told. Arguably more important, however, is that his functionality and intelligence is flawless. He is never a burden, in fact he’s actually quite helpful, and there was never once an issue with him being stuck running against a wall trying to get to the next area.
The Darkness II is a twisted psychological thriller and I loved every minute of it. The number of times I got chills at a revelation or had to pause to think about what was actually going on was incredible. I would recommend this game to any one of my friends in a heartbeat.

TLDR - If you liked Star Wars the Force Unleashed 1, you should enjoy part 2. The game is much shorter but takes up much less of your hard drive space, and you may actually want to replay it, unlike its predecessor. - 7.5/10
*Spoilers for first game*
The Force Unleased 2 continues the adventures of Darth Vader’s former apprentice Starkiller who actually died at the end of the first game if you chose the “light side” ending. If you chose the dark side ending, well, you were in a whole new timeline that directly contradicts the Star Wars movies.  In part 2, you awaken in captivity and are told by Vader that you’re actually a clone of the original Starkiller, kind of like Milla Jovovich’s character in the Resident Evil movies. Basically Vader’s making a bunch of super powered clones so when one dies in training, he’ll just wake up another one. Fortunately for you, this clone is actually as powerful as the original Starkiller and can kick some♥♥♥♥♥with his dual lightsabres (twice as many as in the first game).
Just like The Force Unleased 1, the game is played in the third person perspective with your main attacks being quick swings with your laser swords and your ranged attacks being force powers. There have been some refinements to the gameplay system so the sword attacks seem to flow better compared to the first game, both in combat and the way you upgrade your skills. You no longer have to navigate a long list of sword attacks that you need to buy one by one. Now you upgrade your sword skill just like any other force power and it automatically improves your sword combos. Speaking of upgrades, the game now uses a visible “experience” system where you can actually see how many points you have to buy skills with (similar to Darksiders). You don’t “level up” in the game, you just buy upgrades with the experience you earn. There are holocrons (treasures) hidden around the levels just like the first game that contain things like bonus experience and different upgrade crystals for your lightsabres.
Most of the enemies you face are Imperial stormtroopers though there are a few new big dudes and annoying spider bots. Just like the first game, the large enemies have a ton of health if you try to slice them to death, but after you’ve done significant damage, you have the opportunity to kill them via quick-time events. You definitely should take advantage of this because unlike the first game, most of the big guys don’t get “stunned” by your force lightning. Overall though, I think you’ll find the game easier than part 1 because of a new auto-heal system where you can regen most of the life you just lost if you don’t take damage for a few seconds.
Pros:
+Hack and slash adventure in the Star Wars universe. The story is actually pretty short (lengthened by long battles) but it is decent. Most of the characters from the first game return in case you’re emotionally invested in any of them.
+ The game is simplified compared to Force Unleashed 1, which is a good thing because part 1 was unnecessarily complex in some parts (such as the upgrade system). It also seems to be better optimized for the PC and doesn’t have so many damn loading screens. I played both games with mouse + keyboard by the way.
Cons:
-It’s nice to have challenging boss battles, but some of these fights are a pain because of how long they are, especially at the end. The boss has a ton of health and you can only chip away about a millimeter from their life bar at a time. And that’s if he’s not blocking all your shots. It’s not like he’s throwing out cool attacks either, just the same stuff repeated a few dozen times.
-The game is very short compared to the first Force Unleashed, about half as long actually. And since this isn’t a Game of the Year (Force Unleashed 1 was “Ultimate Sith Edition” with included DLCs) there aren’t as many extras this time around.
Overall the game is fun and you can beat it in a day if you want to sit down for 6 hours. There isn’t too much variety in skill paths, although I didn’t have enough points to buy everything by the end of the game. If I want to focus on “force persuasion” I’ll have to play the game again, which I probably will in the future.

As it stands, Shark Attack Deathmatch 2 doesn’t quite cut the mustard when you compare it to Depth. There are various problems that plague this game in its current state, which include a distinct lack of gameplay modes, very few players on the servers, and a fairly basic and unimaginative execution of the underwater first-person shooter genre.
The main issue was that having played Depth – a game of almost unimaginable tension that is created and maintained with a clever combination of high-quality sound effects, intelligent map design, and graphics that truly reflect the claustrophobic nature of the murky depths of the ocean floor – this game struggles to compete against it. Though the underwater graphics look great, the scenery itself is rather bland and the environments too well-lit to create any sense of mystery or instil the fear of the unknown in the way that Depth manages with ease. It may be worth waiting for the game’s full roster of features to become available, but its lack of maps, game modes, players, tension, and distinguishing features make this one of the lower-intensity shark attack games here that are on the market right now.

I am writing this review after having just rage quit a couple of hours in. However I feel as though I have seen enough of this game in order to effectively speak about the quality of the game because most of the powers are unlocked at the beginning of the game and if the first game was anything to go off of, the combat won't take a drastic change 5 more hours in. And combat is the focus here really.
Lets talk about the pros:
- Despite the fact that I was playing on keyboard, the combat (for the most part) is relatively smooth and flows nicely.
- Very Scenic. Beautiful level design
- Collectables. Early on they just leave some out in the open to let you know they are there but those few entice you to look for the rest. They are all neat little this that are either cosmetic or change your stats somehow. Nicely done
- Adequately challeging. Yes you are a walking tank and it isn't that difficult on the normal difficulty but enemies still do enough damage that you must pay attention in order to not die. That and based off of the normal difficulty, hard mode would actually be hard.
Now lets talk cons:
- The story is rubbish. I mean, you're playing FU2. What did you expect?
- Remember when we had silent protagonists? This game made me miss those days.
- While the combat flows very well, there is no personal style. The game gives a wide list of abilities to use but then forces you to use specific one to kill certain enemies (i.e. Jetpack troopers you must kill with lightning. Apparently they have developed the ability to dodge any attack ever. Lightning is the cure) and this is a huge detriment to personal style. Yes you can upgrade anything you want but it means nothing because you are always going to need every ability for at least one scenario. This make combat tedious very quickly
- checkpoints
- The AI is bad. Normally this is a complaint about coperative AI but not today. I spent a solid 5 min trying to go up an elevator before giving up to look for collectables only to find that the game had spawned two enemies on two corners of the map and they didnt want to attack me so i inevitably couldnt progress.
- This isn't a huge deal but whenever I would change my lightsaber I would click "back" on the screen and it would tab me out of the game. Easy fix was just to use the escape key to go back. Kind of nit-picky but just something that should have been taken care of is all.
All in all it isn't a terrible game. Actually, i will probably finish it over time. However I am torn as far as my recomendation for this game. Despite all the flaws it has the potential for a lot of fun. Yet, I will not recommend this. Only because it displays nothing note worthy that hasn't been seen before in better games. If you've got money to blow then go ahead and get this game. But if you are on a budget, honestly, you could do better.

I haven't really written a review before, but I hope this helps the developers or at least anyone who might be interested in purchasing this game. I remember playing a little of the original game back on the Xbox 360 as an Xbox Live Indie Game. I remember it being one of the better looking Xbox Indie games, but I also remember gameplay being just alright overall. I really liked the concept of an FPS where you fight sharks in some manner and then Depth came out. I recently started playing that as well and in short I'm really satisfied with it. It's probably the best shark game we'll ever get or at least from a multiplayer standpoint. That being said what do I think of this sequel now that Depth is already established you may ask. Well to be honest for $3 I really enjoyed it. No I don't think it's nearly as good as Depth, but it doesn't need to be. However if it does turn out to be better than Depth or just as good later on then I would be more than happy to praise this game and recommend it to whomever I can.
VISUALS: Right now, I believe the developers have created a very stable foundation to build upon. Visually the game looks very appealing. Definitely a vast improvement over the first game. Perhaps it may not have the best graphics, but many of the animals' character models are in a way realistically  animated and rendered nicely. The divers not so much. The controls are smooth. Many of the physics like shooting a speargun or swimming as a shark feel quite natural and easy to get used to.
THE MULTIPLAYER: The main DEATHMATCH MODE is fun for a little while. It is basically divers vs divers with some npc sharks thrown in to attack the players as they kill each other. I do like how you can get points by killing sharks, but you get more points by killing players. However I hope you'll be able to kill more animals than just sharks in future updates, but only lethal animals should give the players points if they kill them.
For me the best mode is the PREDATOR MODE which is very similar to Megalodon Hunt in Depth. First divers start the match by killing each other. The first diver to kill someone gets to become a Great White Shark until another player kills them and then they become the shark. Depth definitely has the better shark gameplay, but this game does cleverly separate it's gameplay style by having a first person view from within the shark's mouth instead of it being third person like it is in Depth. This is very similar to playing as an Alien in the AVP games. A very cool concept which also limits the player's vision as the shark. This is a good thing however. In my opinion the shark is overpowered enough as it is already. It's able to kill a player with just 2 heavy bite attacks. Don't get me wrong, the shark should be overpowered. The problem I have is the shark is like a giant bullet sponge or spear sponge in this case. It takes a lot of hits to kill the shark and by the time you kill it you've probably died like 14 times. To fix this, divers should start off with the chaingun instead of the speargun. Then replace all the chaingun pickups on the map with more ammo or flash grenades. This way divers will only die 4 or 5 times and have the chance to go on a man eating rampage themselves before the match ends. Often times one decent shark player will be the shark the whole match with an overwhelming victory. I mean it's easier to kill a player as a giant 40ft Megalodon in Depth than it is to kill a player as a 25ft Great White in this game. For me it was at least.
Lastly then there's SURVIVOR MODE, which has divers hunting as many NPC sharks as they can before the timer runs out. Sometimes sharks will attack you or sometimes they just ignore you unless you attack them. I like how the sharks are sometimes aggressive in Deathmatch Mode, but for Survivor Mode in my opinion all the sharks should constantly be trying to eat you. Then you progressively wipe out each wave from there. Survivor Mode feels less like a survivor/survival/horde mode and more like a miniature timed underwater hunting simulator. It isn't bad by any means, but that is what it feels currently at least.
OVERALL FIRST IMPRESSIONS: For $3 I easily got my money's worth out of this title and more. Right now perhaps it's not the next Depth, but it could be or something bigger. I'm really curious to see where the developers decide to go from here and very much look forward to it. I would love to see new playable sharks, more indigenous animals, more weapons, and definitely more game modes whether it's polishing the existing ones or creating all new ones. Maybe throw in a Megalodon, Dunkleosteus, and maybe even a crocodile or two. Somewhat joking, but maybe even a Sharktopus. If you're looking for a good time with your friends involving sharks or you just want to scare someone with a phobia of sharks and Depth is too expensive this is a pretty good alternative.

This is the best WW1 flight sim that I have encountered. Period. The flight and damage models are impeccible, with little holes getting blown through wings with them beautifuly getting ripped off after you shoot some supports. The game models CEM (Complex Engine Management) where you have to worry about the temperature, RPM, oil, and raidiator to keep your plane flying. This alone would be enough for me to buy this game at a 50$ price tag and be happy with singleplayer campaigns.
But that's not all. It has created campaigns sure, but there are also dynamic careers. You pick what date you want to start, what plane, with what squadron, all in accurate historical detail. The missions are layed out wonderfully to me, where each "day" in game has multiple sorties. Sometimes you take part in just one, or all, or even none. The missions range from various patrols, recon, and escort missions to name a few.
The missions are even pretty realistic. Sometimes you have a mission where nothing happens at all. And yes, it is boring, but I like that more than always knowing theres going to be some action.

Having played this game since 2011 before it came to Steam, and before it was even free-to-play, I think it’s a great WW1 aviation simulator and really no other games come even remotely close to rendering this period of aviation in the way that Rise of Flight does.
When the game first released there was the typical optimization issues and ‘will my pc run it question’. But now through refinements and as hardware has moved on it does play really well and I encountered no issues personally as of writing this (Game runs fine for me on Windows 10).
There is close to 40 aircraft included in the game consisting of fighters, recon, bombers and attack planes. Three of these can use without purchasing (
,
and
, which are all single seater biplane fighters). These can be modified with different weapons, additional cockpit gauges and paint schemes that all varies from plane to plane.
The flight models are really well done, and makes for a really challenging experience on realistic simulation settings, and equally satisfying when you manage to shoot down an opposing aircraft, or even just survive a sortie. As learning curves go, these are some of the hardest planes to fly, but a really interesting period of aviation.
The game being currently 'Free-to-play', which means you can install the game and fly a few well-known aircraft without even having to purchase anything. There is around 35 additonal planes you can own with various purchases - but these are not required to enjoy the game unless you specifically wish to fly them. Planes you don't own will show up fine in Missions and you can play people online okay as-well.  Overall I don't consider current prices that expensive, when you compare to other Flight Simulators these are a lot cheaper and you could likely buy several aircraft for the less than you would of spent on a non free-to-play title. This does let you pay for the content you actually want, rather than paying full price for the base game, then having to buy addons on top.
The multiplayer used is not through Steam, however to simply join via in-game seemed quite straight forward and was quickly in the air flying missions, you can also host via in-game easy enough. A dedicated server on the other hand, while included is not that straight forward on how to even set it up and after long winded searches with mere snippets of information I was unable to test this.
In quick missions this is where you can setup quick engagements of a few types and specify a number of parameters easily for quick instant action gameplay for up to 30 aircraft. You are able to define the aircraft of 3 friendly and 3 enemy flights, including their formation (and number of aircraft in the formation), paint scheme, weapons and skill level. In some locations you can also choose to start on the ground and scramble start as enemy approach.
This mode is a good way to test the ability of your chosen aircraft, as you can choose to go against any aircraft you wish, including ones you haven’t purchased.
There is a few scripted missions included that will work with 2 of the included free aircraft (SPAD 13.C1 and Albatros D.Va), as well as a training campaign. There is a mission editor external to the game.
The career mode is a dynamic campaign but quite restricted without purchasing more aircraft. This is simply down to the fact most squadrons would change aircraft several time during the war and you would need all these planes for when they are each used.
If you have all the required aircraft for the squadron you wish to join (which could be French, German, Belgian or British), then career mode is a great game-mode that will offer countless hours of interest (and to be quite honest, is the main reason I play this so much).
So if interesting in WW1 aviation, or are simply interested in aviation in general and want to take on a new challenge, then Rise of Flight is recommended. Given its free to play, there is not much to loose by trying it and there is quite a bit of content included to keep you busy.
Vast selection of detailed WW1 aircraft with modifications
Realistic Flight models
Dynamic Campaign (Career)
Free-to-play (Additional aircraft purchasable seperately)
Non-steam multiplayer (easily playable, but without clear dedicated server setup procedure)

So, after reading the top review of this game, I figured I should make my own. Now, this is a flight simulator. The feeling of flight is fantastic, your canvas and wood planes shake and rock about as the wind buffets your machine around all over the place. Every plane is modelled fantastically and the wings literally bend under weight or if they collide with something, brackets snap and bullets will go through both wings if shot at the right angle.
This isn't Warthunder, or World of Warplanes. This is a simulator. Meant to simulate world war one planes to a detail that is as close to reality as possible without being the real thing. Because of this, getting blueprints and performance statistics for each and every aircraft that they add, costs money. It also requires a lot of time and devotion to get their simulated aircraft to a degree of realism that is unbeatable by any other Great War flight sim.
My only complaint about it is that I don't have the money to spend on them myself, but the few packs that I do have I love, and I've played this game before it arrived to steam. As far as games go this day, this companies business model is fantastic, and a lot of the regulars of this game would likely agree with me wholeheartedly.

The Dwarves is a mostly linear, squad-based, action/strategy/rpg, top down hack and slash; see definition of "mouthful" for more information. The story apparently follows that of the narrative of the titular book series, which I've never picked up.
As for gameplay, it takes place in two parts. First off, you'll be controlling a large super-mario esque world map, picking where you want to go, micromanaging food and events as they pop up. Secondly, when the need for combat arives, you'll load in to a map (all of which seem designed around each specific encounted so there is little repetition) and bury axes in faces until said faces stop screaming.
The graphics are crisp, and I ran into few issues with a upper-mid range pc. The character designs are quaint, possibly inspired by the author's description. They are just unique enough to be a breath of fresh air, while still familiar enough to keep my disbelief in check.
The sound is meaty and satisfying. The music keeps your blood pumping when it needs to be, and brings you down when things get serious and/or somber. However, as with many games, character voice lines during combat can get repetitive.
The whole game clocked in at about 8 hours for me which is by far one of the more dissappointing notes on the game. While I'd agree that all stories need an end, I couldn't help but want for more when it was all said and done.
As such, my final verdict on the game is as follows. It's a great game with a reasonably unique style of gameplay and art direction. However, given the shortness of the game, I can't recommend it for it's full price of $40. $30 is a distinct possibility, anything below $20 is a steal.

Mario Kart levels of fun.
How fun can a game about rolling boulders be? Actually, pretty fun. You're trying to hit the enemies castle's gate with as much speed and as much structural integrity of you bolder as you can, while the enemy is trying the same with yours. You hinder each other by strategical placing traps while you wait your the next boulder. Add to that a Monty Python-esk animation humor, funny cutscenes and so on.
The other relevant mode is racing against up to 3 other players while the traps are placed by a neutral AI. This might sound like a dump racing game and it's surely simple, but quite genius in that regard. The leading player is the one who most likely gets hit by the traps and has to clear them out, organically allowing the others to catch up, which puts Rock of Ages 2 amongst the top racing games on PC.
Several tracks, unlockable traps and boulders, including cubes - several historical avatar characters, rock-paint jobs (including Wilson from Cast-Away) are making the experience really round - pun intended.
It also has a field of view slider, which goes up to 110.
I actually don't have anything negative to say, the game knows what it is, executes that perfectly and doesn't pretend to be anything else.

Now I want to be 100% honest with you, guys - this game has some flaws. Some minor and unfortunately some major as well. Like in all previous games this one also has somewhat weird and uncomfortable controls, it will take time to get used to it. It can get very frustrating and hard when you realize that some missions spawn endless waves of enemies until you run out of skills, ideas and rockets (or at least until you figure out what you are supposed to do) or find out that during some quests you may encounter a scripted auto-deaths just because "Middle finger for gamers not playing our games as we want them to". There is ZERO voice acting in english version, you have to read every single line of dialogue. The AI - while singificantly improved than in previous games - is still buggy (occasionally you will see both allies and enemies entering a "U spin me round" state - small ships start spinning very quickly and moving in one direction until then hit something or die). And let's end this list by the biggest flaw of this game: extremely poor optimization on Windows 7. My computer was built one year ago as a "Ridiculous machine" and it can play newest games in full HD and 60 fps, but Star Wolves 3 can occasionally drop from 60 to 30 fps for absolutely no reason or even to 10-15 if there are large battles with dozens of ships on the screen. It seems that my graphics card is not even spinning up it's fans while my CPU is working it's butt off to make this game running, no idea why. Tried many things, nothing worked. You have to live with it.
So as you can see, you have to forgive this game A LOT. But I still think it's good and it has a lot to offer for it's price. Why you may ask? Well, let me give you the fast version:
It's entertaining, it has a decent non-linear plot with a mystery and some enjoyable twists. It has graphics that - while not stunning - often can surprise you with some great images and big explosions with rich particle effects. It has a dangerous open world consumed with civil war, with many systems to explore. It gives the player many options and possibilities, hundreds of items, ships and other equipment while still managing to keep things simple. You can go to abandoned systems and fight in maps filled with literally hundreds of pirates, then after all that hard work collect a stash hidden inside an asteroid with a blinking light on it, sell it for a ton of cash, give escape pods with pirates to star patrol and get even more money as a reward - then buy some colorful lasers, hard hitting plasma guns and tremendously powerful torpedos and head to the border sector in order to fight aliens with ridiculously durable shields. Or try to beat an entire fleet of berserkers - sentient machines, that rely on hundreds of small, poorly armored bots with extremely hard hitting weapons. What, you think that "quality over quantity" is always right? Well, it's not. You will learn that the hard way. When you finally become a space badass with a big mothership and strong, reliable team, you can then try to attack MSF's or NESF's warehouses which have latest, experimental equipment, but will immediately spawn a fleet of dreadnoughts to protect them. Go to no-man's land (space?) and visit a smuggler's station if you want to buy missiles based on alien tech, and then wipe out an entire wing of fighters with just a single one of these lethal gems.
I could go like that for hours. There is so much to do in this game. Every time I find something new. Something awesome. Even easter eggs - chek out the description of a X244 system in Border Sector. Very Dead Space-ish, I tell you :) So far I've put 160 hours into this game and I keep coming back to it when there's nothing new to play. It's just a really fun and solid game, what else can I say. If you like space strategies, give it a try. Who knows, you might have a lot of fun too.

I only have three real gripes with the game.
Firstly, and most importantly: the game ends on a cliffhanger, and a sequel is entirely unconfirmed. One can hope that there is one in development, but it's equally probable that The Darkness III is an "HL3 confirmed!" situation.
Secondly, the gameplay feels good, but isn't exactly mind-blowing. The game isn't long enough for you to unlock all of the different skills in the available skilltrees, so you never really get to experience all the different powers in one playthrough. The gunplay is satisfying, but repetetive. The Darkness powers are awesome, but repetetive. The game is around six hours long, and thank god for it.
Thirdly, and most importantly, the game has some hardcore vsync bugs. If vsync is turned off (as I like it,) you can sometimes get stuck in vents. If this happens, you just flick it on and off, of course, but having to go through menus just to pass through a door is obnoxious to say the least.
All things considered, buy this game on sale for six dollars like I did. It's more than worth the six hours you'll get out of it, and you'll thoroughly enjoy them. The game may not blow you away, but you'll have fun nonetheless.
Final Score: 7.5/10
Letter Grade: C
Verdict: Worth slightly more than a "Venti Caramel Frappucino, extra caramel, and make it snappy, I have places to be in my pathetic, meaningless existence full of poor patronage and fake milkshakey coffee."
