If hacking through hordes of zombies, dousing the screen with blood, and levelling up your undead-murdering character in an open world sounds like a good time, Dead Island Riptide would be the perfect game for you, had it not taken every flaw from the first game and multiplied it by three.
Set after the events of Dead Island, you play as one of five characters--each with unique traits and bad stereotypes--battling through Oceanic beaches and jungles in an effort to escape becoming a walking corpse’s dinner. During your 12 or so hours in the main campaign, you’ll meet a wide roster of characters who’ll offer you quests in return for cash and weapon modifications. Interactions with said characters comprise the bulk of the game’s generic plot, and although Riptide takes an occasional break from the zombie-slashing to acquaint you with them in awkwardly animated cutscenes, any emotional impact that could be made is lost due to an overall lack of substantial character development. Trust me, the game does try to inject some meaning into itself, especially when a major character gets their throat ripped open in super-dramatic slow motion, but when these events occurred I was devoid of any response other than, “Hurry up so I can get back to killing.”
But story hardly matters when there are zombies to fight, and fortunately, Riptide continues the satisfying job its prequel did. With a near-endless variety of weapons, each of which can be upgraded, diving into groups of undead only to emerge with limbs dangling from your appendages is just too much damn fun. Meaty sound effects and visual variety in the common infected help stave off initial repetition, as do some awesome takedowns you’ll earn when you reach the higher levels. RPG elements allow you to customise the progression path of your character—in theory making repeated playthroughs worth your time --so that come the end of the game, your character will be so muscled with power-ups that any brawl you encounter, big or small, will become a gore-rich affair in seconds. It all adds up to a good time. If going solo gets dull, the drop-in co-op is still there, staying as chaotic and team-driven as before.
So, the game looks, sounds, and feels good. Must have really ironed out the problems Dead Island had, right? Ha. If only.
Chief among the laundry list of problems is the dreadful stamina system. Inherited from its prequel, Riptide’s characters are reliant on stamina to run, fight, and execute their decaying attackers. An understandable mechanic, in order to keep the game challenging. This wouldn’t be a problem if stamina didn’t deplete so quickly and take several times as long to recharge. Without stamina, you can’t fight, nor run away, and this is a problem that really spreads its excrement-covered wings in Riptide. Enemies now are way stronger, faster, and take far more of a punch before meeting their long-overdue end. Several times did the slow-as-hell stamina bar get my behind handed to me, and although there are virtually no consequences to death (you respawn 5 seconds later with a slight monetary penalty), it does become a point of frustration around the fifth time it happens. Add to that regular hit-detection problems (particularly with kicks) and zombies who spawn right behind you in areas you rightly assumed were clear, you get difficulty spikes that occur from rubbish design instead of genuine challenge.
Take note, game developers. Challenge should come from interesting levels and enemies; not from throwing six super-fast, super-strong bullet sponges at me who’ll take nothing short of an atomic bomb to fell. This is a source of frustration that persists from start to finish, no matter how potent your arsenal is, and it is unacceptable that even a game like Dark Souls does a much better job of scaling its difficulty than Riptide.
Of course, we can’t forget the bugs, of which there are enough to make Garry's Incident seem like a polished title. Zombies launching into the air and getting caught in environments is a common sight, as is audio cutting out when too many sound effects emit at once. The waypoint system now only works when it feels like it, and the general design of Palanai is so inconsistent with the map that you can be forgiven for pursuing an outlined shortcut only to realise that it can’t be traversed at all, no matter how much jumping or crouching you do. Add to that extremely repetitive quests that demand constant backtracking, you get a game that clearly had to feed off the creative leftovers from its far cleaner predecessor.
Awesome as it feels to drive an electric-powered machete into the chest of some hungry zombie, any fun you have with Riptide will be counterbalanced by frustrating combat, an anaemic plot, shoddy game world, boring missions, and a lack of polish so blatant it’s a wonder the game doesn’t fog up your screen the instant you load it. With or without company, Riptide varies from being a solid zombie slice-em-up to an annoying saga of busywork. Whether you should buy it depends on your ability to accept it for what it is: a vastly inferior product to its prequel that carries over most of the good things but doesn’t try to fix any of the flaws. If more Dead Island with a slippery surface sounds okay to you, check it out next time it’s on sale.

Cats Make You Smarter is a casual match-two memory game, which, as the title implies, is all about cats. All the different tiles you have to match are drawings of cats, and each cat has its own name, plus a small quote about cats.
The game presents five different gamemodes, although they're all played in pretty much the same way as the traditional game: you turn a tile around, and then try to match it to another tile. What the new gamemodes do, however, is add extra layers of difficulty, by making the pieces switch places after missing a few times, or giving you less time to match them. Also, if you want to add an extra challenge, you can also increase the amount of tiles required to match, up until five.
The background music is relaxing, which is a plus for a game like this. After all, this feels like a game you could play after a long day just to relax a bit.
Well, I don't feel like I have anything more to say. If you love cats, and memory games, then this game might just be for you. I recommend it.

EA Summary: Really polished encounters, controls, and a ton of fun.  Currently low on content (about 6-7 hours to do all main quests and side quests).  While I recommend this game, it is NOT worth $15 at this stage (9/1/2015).
Detailed Pro's:
The encounters (11/10!) in this game are incredibly well tuned and the clear highlight of this game.  There's no healing that I'm aware of, which means you will be challenged to learn each of these encounters as you die many, many times, similar to Super Meatboy or Dark Souls.  Like Meatboy, you will respawn instantly, and like dark souls, being greedy never pays off; slow and steady wins the race.
The world is also quite nice with beautiful pixel graphics.  I would describe the dialogue as 14-year-old humor that harps on many RPG tropes.  The writers clearly have a sense of humor, which is nice.  The (side)quests are about a 4/10, really only designed to have you revisit old areas.  Some of them have unique bosses, those are cool.
The gameplay is also about 8/10, very tight controls.  I really only played 2H with a few extra spells, but the game will allow you to play archer, sword n board, 2h, or a mage in any/all of 4 magic schools.  Plus, there are support spells that help both melee and caster.  The spells seem really weak at low level but quite good once "leveled up."  Points can be re-allocated for gold, which is great because you can try something for a price.
Cons: Not much content yet, but it is still a solid stable and polished beta build.  If they keep creating more of the same, this game will be a fantastic modern version of its predecessors like Secret of Mana/Evermore, Link 2 tha Past and others.

This game..... This game.
Where shall I begin?
Let's start with the story!..... It's Awful. Some how they made it worse than the first game.
I'll refrain from spoilers but it really wouldn't matter since it'll take you the same amount of time to read this review as it will to complete the game. It's no longer than a 6 hour game with about 3-4 hours of that being gameplay the rest devoted to cutscenes and quicktime events. (I wouldn't care about the cutscenes if there was an actual good story to go along with them)
The gameplay is basically the same as the first game. The only real improvements are mind trick and force rage. Mind trick allows you to turn enemies onto your side for a short period of time. (Or, if there's no else to kill, they'll commit suicide by jumping off a ledge or leaping into a sheild) Force Rage allows you to become the insane, saber-weilding, limb-chopping, force-throwing, Jedi you deserve to be!..... For a short period of time.
But other than that it's just a copy and paste of the first games mechanics.
One thing I actually really liked were the better boss battles. The first game simply had you fighting other Jedi or the occasional rancor. This game has you battling giant arachnid-like robots, Giant ships shooting at you whilst going at breakneck speeds on a tram, and my personal favorite. Skydiving after a 50ft tall, 4 limbed monster called the Gorog.
Which brings up another thing I moderately enjoyed. Skydiving segments!..... To bad those only happen three times in the game. It's just you falling through the sky dodging objects and force pushing tie fighters out of your way. It may not sound like to much but I actually really enjoyed those moments.
All-in-all this game isn't the worst game ever. It has it's moments that make you forget that you only have 3 more hours left in a game you just started. I'm giving it a down grade based primarily on these three facts
1: The price. (Do NOT I repeat NOT buy this game at full price. Only buy it when it's on sale and if you liked the first game)
2: The amount of content ( Like I said about 4 hours worth)
3: The first one is MUCH Better. I would strongly suggest to go and buy the first one, play it, like it (Or not) and buy this one when it's on sale for 6 bucks...... Actually, 6 bucks might be a bit to high.

This game is NOT Pay-2-Win in any way you can buy guns and armor faster yes but the perks of these guns and armor is no better then if you where you unlock it by grinding first.
These gold guns and armor give you big bonuses to silver or exp lvling mostly which again is not going to make you better then anyone else.
As of build 30a
The guns still need some more balance.
Shotgun is super OP as they do 120 dps and you can basically fire a round as fast as you can click making it a mid range killer when it should be only good up to 35 meters / close quarters for defense.
With the Shotguns they should still shoot a lot slower then how fast they shoot now.
Starting snipers should be a 2 shot kill unless above chest and then you should get a bleed out of 15hp which you dont.
Snipers with scopes should be a 1 shot kill above chest and a 1 shot bleed to death under chest which they are not.
SMGs have a small clip but with good accuaracy you can use it as a mid range assault rifle which sucks.
SMGs should have a big damage drop after 20 meters.
Assault rifles I think over all are pretty balanced but still have a bit to much recoil, after the first2-3 shots the gun is a mess to control.
On the AKM the crosshair is so flush that its almost hard to aim with down sight, they need to have the barrel crosshair stick out a little higher.
I have only used 1 pistol so far but I have it fully upgraded and it seems super weak all the time.
Pistols should do 30 dps but with small armor damage.
All Gernades are extremely OP! when you ge to lvl 15+ everyone will have a nade and at that point most these people are good at throwing them as well. Nades do 200 damage and with a blast radius of 10meters which for me is always a instant death.
nades should be around 120 dps and at a blast radius of 6 meters IMO.
The last thing I have to bring up is the SERVERS.
If you are from North America and you play on NA servers you will get connecion errors popping up on your sceen and even get a disconnect at times.
If you want the best experience play or the EU SERVERS.
My ping tells me I am at 160 most the time but I feel no lag when im in a EU server.
I get no connection issues in a EU server.
The worse thing I run into maybe 1 or 2 times a day is a hacker on the EU servers but it's no that bad.

The Isle is a very impressive game thus far, with mostly-functional features and beautiful shaders. I've noticed that lots of players seem to have bought this for the sandbox aspect, but personally, I loved the idea of a hardcore, progression-based survival game from the very beginning. Although I don't often play that genre, I felt like supporting its continued development.
When it comes to creature quality, this game's nailed it. Each model looks fantastic, with textures that feel alive, and animations that are (usually) very believable. Some complain about the lack of feathers on certain species, but I think they look just fine as they are.
Gameplay seems very solid; you start off with a lowly carnivore or herbivore, and progress up to a more powerful animal. Dying in the process resets the cycle, making it challenging and rewarding to keep yourself out of harm's way. Nesting allows players to raise young (player-controlled) and speed up a friend's progression.
(Progression gameplay may be obsolete.)
The community can be rough at times, and certain behaviors are frowned upon. I however have not yet had any personal issues with other people. Sadly, however, I've seen aggressive behavior from the lead developer towards other, smaller devs and their similar games. This honestly isn't ideal.
Overall, I like this game and its concepts; it was quite entertaining just to play on a test map, by myself, and check out the playables. As someone who has not played multiplayer often, I can't entirely decide on that aspect of gameplay.

Shark Attack Deathmatch 2 is the pinnacle of good game design. It has more depth than any game I have ever played and is certain to become the next youtube hit! Lighthouse Games have always had the reputation of being one of the top AAA developers and once again they have proven themselves! Shark Attack Deathmatch 2 has a gripping story and some of the best writing I have ever seen in a game, blowing classics like The Last of Us and any telltale game out of the park. There is a multitude of shark themed choices to choose from throughout the game all of which will impact what kind of characters you meet a long the way. The game has 7 endings, all of which are well thought out and incredibly enjoyable to achieve. I don't think a game has ever made me cry as much as Shark Attack Deathmatch 2, The amount of depth and thought that has gone into the ove 120hr long campaign really shows. Many developers often recieve criticism for open world games however this game nails it and provides a vibrant, fun filled world with a ludicrus amount of quests, tasks, and fish to do and meet.
Visually, Shark Attack Deathmatch 2 is on par with games like The Witcher 3. You can see every single piece of detail on the sharks, from his scars to his deep blue eyes. This game is truly beautiful and the colour pallete brings every piece of sea life and plant life to the forefront!
This game is certain to be the next hit and I can not recommend it enough. Defiinitely get it before it goes out of early access as this game is a once in a lifetime opportunity and must be gotten. :-) 10/10

And of course, the servers. Per to per connections while working well enough, don't work enough to make it viable. Often you are presented with a loading icon In game when someone leaves a match, and even more often after the icon the game is put back in time seconds. The cosemetics in the game are great and so are the executions, but its obvious they were designed to make the player to want to buy them with real world cash. Obtaining something like and execution is no where near impossible, doing the daily orders will get you there in no time. And it feels rewarding to use the execution you worked so hard to get on an enemy you demolished.
Overall, For Honor is a great game that needs work, which seems to be the theme for most ubisoft games.

Normally I don't really like walking simulators, but this one certainly stands out.
The restriction of "doing stuff" (e.g. shooting things like in ego-shooters, invetory stuff and skills like in rpg's) was something I didn't really miss at all. That's usually the characteristic of a walking simulator: it uses the media "video game" to transport a story and sets the focus on it by diminishing action and abilities - and still the game lets you explore, gives you time to build up a detailed atmosphere and motivates you to be active - I wasn't bored a single second (like in many other walking simulators).
Sure, if you just want to get a pure SciFi Horror game, this may be nothing for you. There are better Horror games and better SciFi games out there. As I already mentioned this game just uses some elements of those genres to transport the story - and it does it more than good imo.
The only real downside that's worth to mention is the price. 20€ would be fair in my opinion.
The story is deep and thoughtful. There have been some moments were I thought "Ok, I know whats gonna happen next" - and even if I was right it came different somehow. The story managed it in a good way to maintain the suspense, I had to keep playing - it's like reading a good book where you simply can't stop reading.
The topic is very philosophical and... well... utopic or dystopic, depends on you - but definitly good stuff to think about and discuss.
This will get topical in the future, if it is not already.

Fun and appealing. A worthy successor of the original title. Instead of moving through the ages we now follow Atlas and the Boulder on a map of Europe and Middle East through a variety of different levels representing different art styles spanning from Ancient Greek to Dali-like modernism sprinkled with cartoon-ish and totally historically-accurate humour, and an awesome soundtrack.
The principle stays the same, 'boulder' phase where we control a giant rock to crush the gates and defenses of the enemy, and  'defense' phase where we build up our own defenses in the hope that the enemy rock doesn`t reach our gates. Now, however, we are presented with a choice of what boulder(s) and defense mechanisms (or animals) to fit into our inventory before the start of the level.
My only concern, is that the single-player campaign feels a bit short: doing only the war levels you can finish it in about 5 hours. There are other activities, like time trials or obstacle courses, but they utilise the same maps. Haven`t tried out multiplayer so far.
Overall, highly recommended if you liked the first one, or you always felt like Monty Python cartoons deserved to be mimicked in a 2017 indie tower defense/boulder rolling simulator.

There are, of course, more games where you play an evil overlord (hello, Overlord!). There are also, of course, more games that focus on building an underground lair as an evil overlord (hello, Dungeon Keeper!). But there is, so far, only one Evil Genius. A must-play for all would-be criminal masterminds seeking world domination.
Amazingly, Evil Genius still looks fresh 12 years after its first release - mainly due to its cartoon-like graphics and wacky sense of humour. It's not a particularly hard game to learn; it's not even particularly hard to master as long as you remember to pace yourself a little. Perhaps most importantly, it's a game where actually winning is only part of the challenge. After all, why would you try to rush towards victory when there's so many deliciously vicious ways of dealing with your opponents (and the occasional disloyal minion) to think of? And remember, if things do take a turn for the worse, it's not your fault - it's just that you're surrounded by incompetent fools!
Unfortunately, a minor expansion pack (the World Somination Kit), including an extra henchman, is not included in the Steam release - but it is still available online, so don't forget to grab that one, too.

Never Alone isn't just any old platformer; it's an atmospheric adventure.
You're thrown into the role of a little girl on a quest to non-violently avenge and protect her village. You've got your trusty bola, your adorable fox, and your mad platforming skills. There's a beautiful world to explore as you progress through the game, but an even more beautiful culture to learn about as you overcome obstacles and discover secrets.
The scenery and graphics are phenominal! When I saw that sheen on some ice in the foreground I was hit with an immediate sense of awe. The wind, snow, water, trees, use of blur on elements in the background which directly affect elements in the foreground—everything was done just
well!
The premise for the game allows for the puzzles to be
interesting and very reverent toward the culture Never Alone is trying to represent. None feel cheap or lazy, but there are some minor bugs that can sometimes cause you to believe you aren't on the right track, when, in reality, you were actually a step away from the solution.
The storytelling is extremely well done! There are so few games that really put your journey into perspective like this game has. It makes you realize just how far you've progressed, making the ending all the more rewarding.
Never Alone is an example of how to create a telling experience without sacrificing the integrity of technical expectations from modern video games. It provides genuinely enjoyable platforming while making you ponder and admire the world, story, and culture it's established and portrayed throughout your adventure.
Kudos to anyone to finds this game in their library.

Even though Cats Make You Smarter! is little more than five modes of pairs, for what it wants to deliver, it's good. It's clearly a game for cat lovers, not only because of the pictures and sounds, but through miscellaneous quotes in conjunction with the cats' depiction that more or less refer to the peculiarities of a domestic cat's existence.
The portraits on the cards are drawn in various different caricature styles. Whether they are appealing is entirely a matter of taste, but they undoubtedly capture the cats' unique characteristics. The unobtrusive elevator music in the background makes it easy to concentrate and the distinct cat noises on successful matches are cute and rewarding.
Cats Make You Smarter! offers five game modes of which four are a variation of memory and one is more of a test of pattern recognition, since the actual cards are already flipped in this mode. Suffice it to say, players with memory like a sieve will have a hard time, but may be able to improve upon it.
My only gripe with this game is that there's no perfect window of opportunity to read the well-chosen quotes. Other than that, Cats Make You Smarter! is entirely satisfactory.

Although this game is short in the terms of gameplay, it tells a very emotive story. I literally found myself on the verge of tears in many parts of the story as well as hearing the response of the other character when the character you are controlling inexplicitly dies from whatever happens, weither by accident or design.. The narrator's voice is rather calming when telling the story of the Girl whom left her village to find the source of the blizzards and befriends an arctic fox. It is a platformer in its own sense as many of the puzzle need both the girl and the fox to complete. While the replay value is very low once you complete the game, it is a beautiful story that is worth playing over and over. Each level is beautifully constructed and while being emotive you can feel the overall emotions of each level, such as cursing vehemently while running from a hungry polar bear with a taste for little girl/arctic fox, to shivering out of empathy each time an an arctic wind kicks up and you need to dig in to keep from being blown back. This game is a must-have for every game collection even if you only ever play through it one time. It even has unlockable videos that teach about the lore and living of the Iñupiat people that help make this folk tale come alive.

This is an extremely promising 2D ARPG early access game that I absolutely adore. It is by no means close to being finished but it has an incredibly solid foundation. The first thing I need to mention is the art style is phenomenal and the game has one of my favorite soundtracks of any game out there. As I'm writing this review, my character is in the Flying Fortress just so I can listen to the music. The music gives me Final Fantasy vibes that I love. Let me also mention that the art in this game is awesome. The game is full of color and it's a beautiful game to look at.
In terms of gameplay, there are many choices to be made. There are skill sets for 1H or 2H weapons and the magic is divided into fire, ice, earth, and air (which should be called lightning...). There are no classes so you can mix and match between all of these sets (For example, you can be a 2H user that also specializes in ice spells. If you freeze an enemy, you are guarenteed your next physical attack to crit).
So far, there are 2 dungeons in the game that both have very strong themes and art styles. There is not a single part of this game I dread going through. I loved Tales of Symphonia but I HATED some of those dungeons/temples (especially the sewers, oh god). Let me also mention that the second dungeon has a mechanic involving changing seasons that I have never seen before in any game. Watching the whole room change colors is quite the thing to see. My only issue with the dungeons are that they are too short. I WANT MORE.
-There are 6 notable bosses in this game and they are all designed very well each offering very different strategies to conquer them.
-Each type of enemy has a small chance to drop a card which gives your character small permanent bonuses (5% discount at shops, Atk/MAtk/Def buffs, AtkSpd and CastSpd buffs, etc)
-"Farming" is very easy in this game. If you kill a group of enemies, stick around for about 2 more minutes fighting enemies and the spawn rate at that location will increase like crazy. There's a room in the toy factory that will spawn endless amounts of presents for you to kill repeatedly. I probably did it for a solid 30-45 minutes and it was great!
-This game also features Arcade mode which is essentially a rogue-like version of the game. It's pretty darn hard but fun I suppose. I haven't played it enough for the purpose of this review though.
I'm looking forward to seeing more updates for this game. Not sure if you want to buy it yet? No biggie, PLAY THE DEMO!
Thanks for reading! I will update this review once more updates come out.

Just beat the game. Contains spoilers for Darkness 1 and 2.
The first one I liked alot, although I had a hard time getting around the city with the train station being the main safe zone before heading out on a mission. I eventually figured it all out so I felt accomplished when I did and got far into the game. Now that it's gone, in the Darkness II, I felt a bit cheated out of my previous experience. The main redeeming factor about DII is the STORY.
So, I don't mind the "go in a straight line to complete the game" just as long as the story kept it's charm. What's with the fact that I can't just pull out the Darkness whenever I feel like it anymore? The reason it's gone is because Jackie is always in situations where he definitely needs it, or definitely does not need it, all due to that linear gameplay. I miss changing on command, not to mention multiple minions. Although the one is this game is funny so it's kind of sad when he dies. (I see what you did there. Good job. All the feels.)
The whole time, I felt the whole "you're in a hospital" thing has been done before but I would have prefered more of the mindgames that happened in Darkness 1, where you actually go back in time and feel less like you're on earth and more like you might actually be in Hell. My favorite part in the first one was where you actually have to fight the darkness, or rather that you do not. (Took me a very long time to realize that, that scene was trippy. Took me 30 minutes to realize that Jenny literally gives you the answer over the Darkness laughing at you while you're shooting bullets. "Fighting him makes him stronger, stop fighting him!") Well in this game you actually go to Hell.... and it's not as impressive as I thought it might be. "Hey Jackie, look you're in Hell, where do you possibly go? Oh nevermind. Just follow the relatively straight line."
Eh...
Darkness III or whatever the next title may be, should there be another, should give the freedom back to the player to tackle problems at his own leisure. I'd appreciate more threatening places to go when you're not walking around the city.  The first one put you in the middle of a war with no explanation. The first one put you in a fight against the darkness. This one..... you get a schitzo-hospital and a "you're having a delusion" storyline.... eh.... been done before. I just saw that done on one of my Charmed DVD'S
The art style is good, although reminds me a bit too much of Borderlands. I haven't played Borderlands, but Darkness II looks ALMOST too cell shaded. Not sure what they were going for there... but... it looks alright running on my slightly above low budget gaming pc. The opening scene "previously on the Darkness" confused me because I wouldn't figure out if I had incorrect settings because the way the characters face was lit was just.... ugly. Tried to fix it, later realized that it's just the art style. Oh boy.
Story though. That story, that voice acting. I forgive the game for everything for just having a DAMN good story and DAMN good voice acting. I don't even care. I still Love it. Just do better next time! I feel this one tried to improve where it didn't need improvements. but I think it went the right route with upgrading your abilities rather than your minions.

Normally I don't really like walking simulators, but this one certainly stands out.
The restriction of "doing stuff" (e.g. shooting things like in ego-shooters, invetory stuff and skills like in rpg's) was something I didn't really miss at all. That's usually the characteristic of a walking simulator: it uses the media "video game" to transport a story and sets the focus on it by diminishing action and abilities - and still the game lets you explore, gives you time to build up a detailed atmosphere and motivates you to be active - I wasn't bored a single second (like in many other walking simulators).
Sure, if you just want to get a pure SciFi Horror game, this may be nothing for you. There are better Horror games and better SciFi games out there. As I already mentioned this game just uses some elements of those genres to transport the story - and it does it more than good imo.
The only real downside that's worth to mention is the price. 20€ would be fair in my opinion.
The story is deep and thoughtful. There have been some moments were I thought "Ok, I know whats gonna happen next" - and even if I was right it came different somehow. The story managed it in a good way to maintain the suspense, I had to keep playing - it's like reading a good book where you simply can't stop reading.

An AMAZING game if You are the kind of person that appreciated a GOOD story and interesting world. Based on series of novels it already had a very rich world to base on, so it should be a eal treat for any fantasy lovers. In many ways it reminded me of Banner Saga in terms of how you navigate the map, manage your "party" (or more, a pool of characters in your group that you can make your party of) and deal with your choices in some situations. And YES, some choices matter, even if they don't turn the whole game upside down, they do give you that sense of impact on your story, which is just GREAT!
There are some awesome easter eggs (like the festival sidequest that you will have to finish yourself! :P) and the main story is just as good. The art style is more than enjoyable and the soundtrack is just great. Every part of the game, every leter is voice acted, so for all people who are a "more TV than books person", there should be no issues at all there. Characters are interesting and fun, even if I would wish to dig deeper into their personalities and backstory.
Of course aside from all the good stuff there is also some negatives. First of all the camera is farfrom perfect. It's NOT LOCKED as many reviewers calim, it just sometimes makes you wait for it to stop "sliding" from one character to naother before it lets you rotate and zoom. It gets stuck on geometry sometimes, but in the end there is always a way to position it just right and it's more a matter of getting used to it. Another thing is the character movement. They ... well ... they don't just muve, they float. If you make your party move to press on a single target, they will slide all over the place and can fall into random holes, so it's much better to actually play the game as it's designed and issue individual orders to each party member constantly switching between them and using their abilities.
In the end I'd say it's a solid 9 out of 10 for people who play RPG games for the story and a good 7 out of 10 for those, who just like to slash their way trhough an RPG (you savages!).

I didn't read the books, but I always felt like it would be interesting to me, so when I heard there would be a game about it, I had to have it.
The game is made by a pretty small german studio called King Art Games and you have to bear that in mind. They aren't as big as other studios and therefore cannot compete with AAA games. This far they basically only made the "The Book of unwritten Tales" series.
Does that mean the game is bad? Absolutely not. But it feels like the story and universe should have been in an open world 100+ hours game. Instead it is in a 10 hours + level game where the voyage itself is shown on a map where you can only choose different paths from given choices. All in all, the game feels like a Pen and Paper with a lot of narration and a lot of fighting, a good story, but little else. The few side quest you have are badly written and you can't get a picture of the situation before deciding on what you want to do, because once you say "I'll do that once I know more" the game won't let you get back - rendering the side quest useless. The main story however is good and entertaining - just not long enough.
I played the game in the german version and the voice acting is outstanding. Next to every role is perfect.
The fighting is fun, challenging and over all good. Different characters give you different fighting options, wich is nice. So there is nothing to complain here.
Since the game is made by a german studio you will find a lot of references to Germany, like for example to the festival Wacken - wich is fun, if you get them.
All in all, i recommend the game. It is a fun way to spend a weekend - if you like listening to a story rather then exploring the game world like you do e.g. in Skyrim.

Never Alone is a simple platform game, which tells the story of one girl and her fox trying to find the source of a blizzard that is threatening her village & her people. Throughout the game, which takes about 2 to 2.5 hours to go from start to finish, the player will also be exposed to other bits of folk lore, from the Little People (a group of mischievous, super strong humanoids), Manslayer (a person who puts their greed and selfish desires before the community), Sky People, nature spirits, and more.
At times controls can feel stiff and there are a few moments where you will miss a jump or fall off a ledge due to this. Had they put in a little more work towards this, I think the game would have been much more rewarding to players and less frustrating.
I think the art-style of the game was a very good choice. Cut scenes also mix in animated tribal art and figures, which help keep the tone and mood throughout the game. Living in the praries of Canada, we get our fair share of blizzards and wind storms, and Never Alone does a good job depicting the blizzard in the game in both animation and sound.
One of the things few mention about this game is that it also has mini-documentaries which are unlocked as you go through the game. There are 24 in total, lasting only a couple minutes each, and can be played in the middle of a game when you unlock one, or after through the main menu. I found playing these short documentaries during the game actually added to it, as they would have something to do with the lore of the level you were in. Some of these documentaries are about the lore of the indiginous people (such as about the Sky People), while others were more practical (like how skin of the cariboo from different seasons were used for specific clothing).
In the end, not only does one finish Never Alone feeling like they were just told a good story, but one also walks away feeling as though they have learned something.

Never Alone(Kisima Ingitchuna) is a pretty interesting game, but it did have a few things that got on my nerves. However, the positives way outweigh the negatives for me. A recommendation to anyone who likes story-based platformers!
The Positives:
-Unlike what I expected, Never Alone dives into the culture of the Inupiat very well, so it does a good job in getting you sucked into it and enjoying it. Aside from the fact that the entire game is built upon one of their myths(which, if you're a myth fan, a definite recommendation there), it incorporates pieces of it in the game itself with the artwork, sounds, and short videos of Cultural Insight. I can only think of one other game that got me interested in the culture, myths, and beliefs of the people as well as Never Alone did, and that was Okami. I would say Okami was immersive, so this game must be too! And it seems to prove this point as I found myself hungry, only AFTER I had beaten the game, despite having been hungry before. So note to future players, make sure you can sit down for long periods of time before playing this.
-At the mention of artwork, it is very well done. Not only is it vibrant(though a bit on the greyscale side for a lot of the gameplay), the models and animations are smooth and don't have any nicks or strange clipping errors to ruin them. Everything blends together quite nicely, allowing you to become more immersed in the world as you play it.
-The story is an interesting one. Even though there are parts where it's mostly gameplay, you don't feel detached, or forget what you have learned so far. It also goes along at an easy pace, so you can play through as you want without being forced into a pace. I'm trying not to spoil anything here, but it also concludes in a way I didn't expect it to-a definite plus! I think anyone who likes games based upon their stories can agree that a predictable story is a boring one that they would not want to revisit again. I would say that this story is far from boring.
-For a game that seems like it would go a lot faster and smoother as multiplayer, it can be played solo without any problems(except for one I ran into, see below). You can easily switch between who you play, and the controls don't change so drastically that you have moments of confusion, especially if you need to act quickly. Though I played through only on singleplayer, I can imagine that Never Alone would be a great game to play with a friend or sibling.
-You get to play as a fox!! What's not great about that?
The Negatives:
I had very few negatives while I was playing Never Alone, which is why I recommend this game. But they should still be taken note of.
-Several times I have died because one of the characters didn't move out of the way/pull themselves up quick enough/go the opposite direction they were told to go in/etc., and I saw this being synced up to the animations. It's a wild guess, but I'd say that the movements were loosely based on the animation times, so if say a pull-self-up animation  hadn't finished playing, but you were telling the game to walk forward, it would pause to let the first animation finish, then execute the command. Luckily a lot of the animations appear to be short enough that this isn't too big of a problem, and that tactic does make everything move smoother and look nicer and more natural, adding believability to the game, but I was still irritated by the many times I died because it failed to pull itself up in time, or it hesitated before jumping out of the way. This odd hesitance was my biggest issue with Never Alone, and it seemed to persist no matter how I adjusted my settings to see if it was an FPS problem. However, if you go slow with this game, it does a little better, even during the moments where you need quicker reactions.
-Despite the update that made the companion AI smarter, I still had instances where the companion would follow me and end up dead, or try to jump and miss. However, these moments were few, and I've only had two parts during gameplay where it was an actual bug, making this game relatively bug-free. This AI issue would be completely avoided in multiplayer, of course, so if you encounter it too, maybe try and find someone to play the other character with you?
-Spoiler alert, this game... has quite a bit of running in it. So don't expect any glorious battles or anything. But for a game that has very few moments in it where you do fight, it is incredibly well-done. I can't imagine being a developer and making a game like this with no battles, so they definitely hit the nail on the head with this one! My only problem with the many "flee!" moments is that every time it happened I felt like I was doing the same tedious thing over and over(run in this direction, avoid obstacle, etc.), but that might be because I enjoy the fighting aspects of games. If you don't care for such aspects, I absolutely think you'll enjoy this game!
-This isn't much of a negative, more of a pleading complaint. I liked this game, and became so immersed with it that when it ended, it left me wanting more. It's not that the conclusion isn't good-it's that it's a good game! I really wish it was longer, because I finished it so quickly, but it did brighten up my day even if it was all it lasted for. In short, this game is fantastic towards new players, even if it doesn't have much replay value.
Never Alone is pretty linear, is short, and it doesn't have very many puzzles in it. It is definitely built more for the story. Because most of its aspects are simple, it is easy to get into, yet keeping your interest peaked as you play through it. Even if you don't want to watch the Cultural Insights, I definitely think this game is worth its price, and it's worth being in any story-based game lover's library.

**This review is coming from a pure single-player experience** (there is multiplayer)
I have done all of the story mode content there is to do at this time, minus collectibles, as of version 0.600amigo.
Pros:
-Fun combat, lots of skills and perks. You can respec for a doable in-game fee. Smooth and fluid animation.
-Multiplayer, which I did not try out. This can be done in the story mode and arcade mode.
-The environments are awesome, the character artwork could be better, and the music is good, but nothing I see myself humming to.
-Many cameos from other video games. Zelda, RE4, Honeydew, to name a few.
-There's a stable version and a "frontline" version. Pretty self explanatory. The latter has more frequent updates (every few weeks) the former every month or two, from my understanding.
Cons:
-The amount of monsters you have to kill and the many hours it takes to get a drop does not line up with an items rarity most of the time. It is not unheard of to spend 4-8 hours killing the same monster all to get a drop that is probably not better than what you already have JUST so you can work towards 100% completion. This is never a requirement, but the cards you can get in particular offer small permanent bonuses, and it can take you anywhere from 30 minutes to 8 hours to find the one that you want.
-It's short. But the game's not done yet. The current story can be done in about 4-6 hours. Getting collectibles could get you another 10-20 hours, depending on your luck. Question is, do you want those mostly mediocre drops bad enough to spend all that time?
-Arcade mode as a single player is quite a challenge. I usually opt for the harder options in video games like Kingdom Hearts on Critical but this mode is hard from the get go if you are alone. I would like to see some scaling in difficulty to make it more doable (maybe there already is, and I just suck.) But if you're looking for a challenge, you've got it here. An option to turn down the difficulty would be nice though.
These problems can be easily remedied with time, however. The creators are friendly and interactive with their community, and they post frequent updates.
So the question is, do I recommend this game? Is it worth the current price of $15.00?
Yes it is. For the amount of playtime I got out of it, for the potential of what it can become, and for the multiplayer, which I didn't even touch, which is sure to add many hours. If nothing else, follow this game. Come back to it later. For an avid RPG fan, this is a game to watch out for.

It doesn't take you long to be pulled into the story. The Darkness 2 does a great job of immersing you into the feelings and thoughts of the main character, which is a rarity in modern day gaming. Often you are very disconected from the story and the emotions of the characters. Lately, the only other game I have played that did such a great job of pulling you in, emotionally, was BioShock Infinite.
Beyond the story, which while nothing especially impressive, what is there is enough and is well orcestrated. The most impressive feat is the game's ability to put you in the shoes of the main character and really doubt what is real and what is not real (in the game).
The gameplay is top notch though and if you enjoy shooters where you run from one area to the next and have to clear all the waves of enemies, then this is a game for you. The gunplay is fun and has impact and the tentacles are well implemented so that they are not overpowered and yet are still very fun and exciting to use.
I found myself using primarily guns but definitely had to use my powers frequently to stay in the fight. I was glad though that the powers did not dominate the gameplay so that you simply use the powers when you feel the need and are not forced to constantly use the powers. In some games where you have powers they dominate the other gameplay mechanics to the point that you find yourself only using the powers and nothing else. Fortunately, this is not the case in the Darkness 2.
The graphics are not impressive or special, but they make up for what they lack in the style, which once you've played the game to completion the style will make sense. A lot of people were surprised when they first revealed the first gameplay video of The Darkness 2 because of the art style they had used. But there is a definite reason for it and it only further helps immerse you into the world of confusion that the main character is living in.
The soundtrack is great and the voice work is top quality. All in all, it is a very fun game with a decent story that manages to pull you in and leaves you desiring more.
Would definitely recommend giving this game a spin! It is a great purchase and a great experience to play through once or even twice! In addition there are even some co-op missions to further the experience, so if you have a friend to play it with it will add a few more hours of quality gameplay.

Each week, Marsh Davies stalks through the reality-warping anomaly of Early Access and comes back with any stories he can find and/or gets turned inside out by a pocket of non-euclidean space. This week’s precious artifact is free-to-play online shooter Survarium, in which the remnants of humanity tussle over abandoned radar stations and chemical plants, long reclaimed by nature (and other, less natural phenomena). It’s to Survarium’s credit that I want to play a lot more of it. Alas, after a handful of hours, the game data corrupts and subsequent attempts at reinstallation are consistently halted by a recursive nightmare of error messages which can only be broken by pouring a half-pint of lamb’s blood onto my keyboard and calling forth the hissing spirit of Task Manager to devour the process in question. Survarium is not a finished game, then. But, being supported by a somewhat unalluring muddle of microtransactable trousers and gasmasks, neither has it cost me a penny. All the same, after this brief encounter, I am left wondering: how much less unfinished is this since Jim looked at it a year ago?

The Darkness II is, unlike what the description says, is a triple-wield shooter based on the comic book series. Triple-wield because you actually only have the choice of using your tentacles, and two slots for guns in your hands. Nevertheless, the keyboard controls are actually not bad as I was expecting it to be cumbersome, to have three weapons in your hands at the same time.
As you progress through the game, you will unlock new abilities and "talents", as they call it, that either passively improve your weapons or present new ways of killing off enemies. For the first playthrough, which you should be focusing on the story first anyway, there's no worry of getting too overpowered as it's hard to unlock everything before the end of the game.
Speaking of the story, the writing is alright and the plot revolves around the themes of Love and Revenge, despite  the fact that it may seem cliched. In short, you are a mafia boss who lost his girlfriend and can't get over her, so you decided to take revenge after your foes managed to interrupt your dinner (how rude!).
All in all, I would recommend this game if you like being a mafia boss. No, seriously.
(And of course, to live out your fantasies of having demonic powers with a vengeance - and possibly a dead girlfriend.)
P.S. Could be a gore-fest! :)

-Nice graphics for it's age
-Incredibly satisfying shooting/combat
-Very nice and interesting story
-Great music aswell as great sounds for the weapons

Cons:
-Very short story

-Lack of approaches (yes, you can choose your weapons but there is no stealth AT ALL)
CONCLUSION: In my opinion, it's not worth it's €29,99 price, but if you can pick it up at 80% off it's definitely a great experience! One of the top games I have recently played.

I absolutely love this game...although without the very helpful "how to play the first few missions" FAQ I most likely would have lost interest and uninstalled the game before I got far enough into the game to enjoy it.
It is not a space sim, it's an RPG. If you played Freelancer and X3 and decided that what you really want it for those games to play as an RPG with squad-based real-time-with-pause gameplay, you might get something like Star Wolves 3.  Character progression is somewhat limited, the plot is linear, but with branches, and there's a large world out there but you won't be interacting it in a freeform manner.
The writing is excellent and the characters have personality. The English translation was done in a rough "literal translation" style, which butchers English grammar something awful but leaves the flavor of the characters intact. If you've spent any amount of time on the Internet, this is not so shocking... I played the game with the feeling that this is a group of pilots brought together by chance, none of whom speaks English natively but who are using it as a common language, and that fits pretty well with the game world . If this bugs you, you'll hate the game. I really had no problems with it--a rough translation of good writing is infinitely preferable to a lot of the native-English bad games I've played. If the voices used in the ending movies are any indication, the game was significantly improved by the omission of English language audio. :)
I'm not so much reviewing as I am just rambling on about what I think of the translation, am I? I'll summarize: After 50-odd hours of play, I feel like the game ended too soon, and I'm ready to restart it and take a different career path. I am sad that the sequel/followup was cancelled. Highly recommended, but follow the FAQ for the first few missions.

It is well worth it to spend a few bucks and enjoy a great little game and story, as well as exapnd your cultural perspective. Wonderful and beautiful.

You know what I love? The tropical islands of the Pacific. Clear waters where you can see the bottom of the bay, warm temperatures year-round, palm trees, and the whole atmosphere.
So here I am trekking across the frozen wilderness of Alaska.
Never Alone is a puzzle platformer (think LIMBO) based on the Inupiaq story of Kunuuksaaayuka, originally about a boy (a girl here) named Nuna  who investigates the mysterious unending blizzards that are plaguing her village and threatening her community. Along the way, she'll tangle with polar bears, leprechaun-esque creatures called Little People, a dangerous being called the Manslayer, and the aurora (no, seriously). She's not alone, as she has an arctic fox friend, who can scale walls, wall jump, crawl under tight spaces, and most importantly, aid in the use of spirits for platforming. Nuna isn't completely worthless, as she gains a weapon called a Bola she can use to destroy obstacles, can climb ropes and ladders, and...yeah, the fox is certainly more interesting to play as.
The scenery is great, as long as you can take tons of snow and ice. It does a great job creating the feeling of a desolate frozen wasteland. The Inupiaq art style is brought in with story segments shown in basic cutscenes (with an Inupiaq narrator with subs), as well as the animal spirits that help you on your travels. Also of note are Cultural Insights, live-action videos of Inupiaq Eskimos who tell of their culture and way of life (you'll need to find and view all of them for achievements).
There are a few downsides. The game is short. I 100%'d it in about 4 hours, but LIMBO was about the same length. Also, the game can get glitchy, especially in a long climbing segment near the end of the game.
Overall, it's a good platformer with an insight into a culture that few talk about and is usually brushed aside as "Eskimos, ice fishing, and igloos". It's certainly worth checking out.

I'm a sucker for cultured games. By this, I mean that I love when a dev team has done good, thorough research and highlighted a game with rich streaks of culture. If you enjoyed the mythology behind Year Walk, you'll love this game. It doubles as a documentary of sorts, with unlockable video blurbs about the Inupiaq culture the game is based off of. I love the various art styles and the elderly, throaty voice narrating the tale is downright outstanding! The music during the chase scenes is intense as well! There is a two-player option in which someone can control your travel companion, otherwise it's up to you to control him!
My only complaint is that the controls seem a little clonky, so some of the more meticulous puzzles can take some time to solve. Once you get the mechanics down, the rest is just timing it right. Overall, I enjoyed my experience with the game and got all available achievements pretty easily. I would play it again just for giggles!
I would call this a side-scrolling adventure/puzzle game with some deep cultural flair. I would compare it to Year Walk and Child of Light (minus the lore and combat system). If you're looking for an action/combat game, or don't enjoy good plot lines (this game is based off of a folk tale), this game probably isn't for you.

As of right now, I am unsure if I love or hate The Isle. I'm still going to recomend it because the game stands well and has earned my respect, but keep this review in mind when thinking about buying the game.
The Isle is a beautiful game. The designs of the landscapes are great with excellent lighting and effects. There are little to no visual oddities that take away from the immersion. The animations are also fantastic. Each dinosaur has his own animations, each altered personally for him and little is reused between the different types. They have their own sounds and each a different sound for the different communications such as 'friendly vocalization,' 'aggressive vocalization,' 'long-range call,' and so much more that only adds to the realism this game is trying so hard to produce. The minimalist U.I. is effective and out of the way as to not take the player's view away from the visuals too often aside from when the dinosaur needs to eat, to drink, or to rest for a moment and regain energy lost while sprinting. Each bar, either of hunger, thirst, or energy, needs to be managed similarly to human survival situations. You shouldn't waste energy on sprinting everywhere you go, for example, if you are a lone herbivore under threat of being hunted in an area frequented by predators. You need to save that energy for when you must run away. You can regain lost energy by walking or faster by lying down. That said, this is a slower-paced, survival game, so those looking for a fast, in the moment game, I'd wait and see where the dev. team is headed, first. Humans were mentioned in the past and we are currently unsure of if they will be added or how they will opperate.
Now, the most problems I have ever had with this game have been with the user interaction. The Isle's multiplayer is the reason I bought the game in the first place and I truely believed that I would be getting into something where I could play close with other players in herds or hunting parties that carried on realistically as dinosaurs might once have. That isn't what I got, however. What I got was a beautiful game with large maps in which finding other players was a very difficult task and one constantly hindered by hunters who aimed at new-spawns for their food. Each time, I'd respawn in different locations. I tried to remedy this by joining multiple steam groups with their own servers that told me they could help me to have fun and play the game like I had originally wanted to. This was more or less a lie. The progression system is in place to stop players from playing the stronger dinosaurs right away and ruining everyone else's good time on survival servers. (sandbox servers just have everyone deathmatching.) The problem with this progression system is that everyone else in the community is always ahead of you in progression due to the fact that these communities are die-hard players that only play this game. They are always a higher-ranked dinosaur and no one wants to play with the smaller, starter dinosaurs, not even other starter dinosaurs. In spite of the communities' best efforts, I found myself stuggling to have fun in this game and it's appeal lessened and lessened. I had watched countless videos, read many reviews, and yet, The Isle was NOT what I expected it to be.
Now, this game is good. Not great, but good. The Dev. team is putting a great deal of work into the game and I will give credit where credit is due. However, as the game stands, I DO recommend buying it, but I caution you: Whatever you expect it to be like, it's not like that. This game is hard to read through other people's eyes. You need to get it yourself to see how you'll enjoy it. If you don't, then refunding it is always an option.

I don't need 100+ hours to review a survival game about walking around hunting or standing around eating plants. It doesn't take long to get what he game is about, so stop acting like I'm missing some big, spiritual thing by not playing this game religiously. I still recommended the game, so I'm not hurting the developers and I simply put in my own opinions while asking others to draw induvidual conclusions based on their tastes. I didn't personally enjoy the game, so I'm not going to play it any more than I'd like to. I meant to write out a review around the time I hit 1,000 hours but never got around to it so here you go. I bought the Isle May 2016 and I got exactly what I paid for. An early access game that allows you to survive as either a carnivore or herbivore dinosaur. That alone made it a one of a kind experience. At the time of purchase the game seemed worth $20. Where the game is now a year later I'd definitely say it's worth its price. I've gotten my money's worth from the Isle and more. The game continues to grow at a reasonable pace and I look forward to the many changes to come.
Is the Isle for you?
As long as you understand the game is in early access. There will be bugs, there will be missing mechanics, there will be drastic changes. You aren't paying for a final product, you are paying for a game in the making.
As of right now there are 27 playable dinosaurs and many maps to explore. Expect to die a lot. Just pick yourself back up and learn from your mistakes. You have the option to play a few different modes.
1) Sandbox: You have access to all 27 playable dinosaurs. You're free to do whatever you want according to the server's rules. Interact with other players, explore, hunt, hide. I highly recommend sandbox for new players getting to know the game.
2) Progression: I wouldn't recommend progression for new players. You start out at the bottom of the food chain and have to work your way up to the top by gaining progression points. Herbivores gain these points by eating certain plants as well as passively gaining 1 point per minute. Carnivores can only gain 1 pp per minute. If you're already familiar with the game then work your way up by joining a server with low pp requirements. For the ultimate challenge there are vanilla/growth servers.

It is fun to unleashed the force: stormtroopers are in air, AT-Ats get fed up with their own rockets and Vader is a nervous Sith Lord. The con of this game is that it doesn’t last long.
This game is high quality. The cinematics are better than the movies, the art style is gorgeous, everyone looks better(except for Juno) your force power are higher and in turn, the havoc you’ll create. The story is simple and there are some very discreet subplots(the biggest one is unlocked in the challenges). Some people have reported bugs, but they have submitted fixes as well. I for one didn’t have a problem with this game. Except for one thing. It was too short. It was like sex with someone really hot, one a day when you’re so full of energy and into it, but for a reason, it’s so short it will strike you like the Death Star.
A good question would be: “Is the game worth buying if it’s short?”. I’ll tell you what this game has and it will be your choice if you’ll take it or leave it.
Fans of its prequel will notice that old moves are still there, many unlocked from the start. You have the typical force powers: force push, force lightning, force repulse, saber throw and a new one: mind trick. They all feel powerful when used, they’re designed to be enjoyed rather than used tactically. Whether you push, stun, impale them or make them commit suicide, it’s still the same, you are unstoppable. However, they are more detailed than you can see at first glance. Mind trick makes troopers attack the others or jump to their deaths in a humorous way, lighting will overheat the jet of a trooper, resulting in his flying around without control to an explosive end. Also new to the series, there is the body dismemberment, making the sword combat more satisfying. Having two lightsabers instead of one make the protagonist to fight in a more agile and aggressive way.  Force fury is an ability that amplifies your power for a limited time. In that stance, enemies are pulverized by your power. The game itself is not hard. Unleashed mode will present something that could have been old school challenge, but gaining full health whenever checkpoints are reloaded simplifies things too much. Skydiving is fun and has its place, there are three sequences anyway. The QTE’s are the type that can be failed, but most are optional, boss battles being the only ones that require them.  Boss battles themselves are well designed, as there are multiple stages with key moments that make the real differences. The gameplay itself is one of the best.
The story is incomplete. Even if it doesn’t show, reading the novel(which proves the story’s potential) proves how much more there was to say. Even if you go through Kamino, Cato Nemoida, Dagobah, aboard a big rebel ship called the “Salvation” that will later engage in a space battle and facing Vader on your return to Kamino, it’s not enough. What is there is spectacular, but the canon end makes way for a sequel that will never be made.
In the story, you are the clone of Starkiller who inspired the creation of the rebellion. You are made stronger than the original to suit Vader’s more demanding commands.  As you retained the memories of the original, you’ll find yourself fighting the empire and looking forward for reuniting with your old love. This time around, Starkiller is the hunted one, but he has enough power to face whatever Vader is throwing at him. However he is delayed and at the end, Vader proves he can make him do his bidding.
Vader is portrayed as the menace he is in the books: manipulative and hard to take down.  He has the intellect from the original trilogy and the fighting skills from the prequel trilogy.
There are two endings, the light side one where the rebellion earns a major victory because of you and the dark side one, where you die, Vader stands victorious, with the perfect dark side clone at his side.
If you want to spend more time in the game, there are several challenges that make you use your force powers in certain ways, there are all kinds of outfits and skins to unlock(and they are worth it), holocrons to collect for getting new saber crystals(that change the sabers color and add an effect in combat), cinematics revolving around the dark clone subplot and that’s about it. If you look for more of the lore, there is a databank and concept art available.
It’s a well designed game, high quality, but low quantity. Star Wars fans and gamers in general(casual and hardcore) should buy this if they have the money to spare.

In one word, Star Wolves 3 was a disappointment.
Full disclosure, I went into the game not knowing what specific sub-genre of space simulation Star Wolves was, but I have a soft spot for anything space themed and that love spans many genres.
After booting the game, I was immediately both enamored and jarred by the graphical fidelity of the game. Many would say it was dreadful, but it immediately reminded me of my first time launching Freelancer way back in the early 2000’s. I maxed out the graphics, got my settings all nice and balanced and started up a new single player campaign. Immediately I was struck with a wall of text followed by an absolutely chaotic character creation screen. Again, in a way this was almost charming, I loved plenty of titles with worse openings than this. After putting together my character I was treated to a Freelancer-esque cutscene which did the job visually, gave very little in the way of context or plot creation. Next thing I knew I was sitting in space. That was it. After figuring out how to work the camera, I looked around only to see a huge asteroid sitting off in the distance. 15 minutes and a consultation with the control settings menu later I figured out how to move the ship, so I do. I travel about 10 feet “forward” and a huge fleet jumps in and some guy is threatening me over the radio. Next thing I know, he opens fire and I’m space debris with the very first volley. Game over. I’m taken back to the start screen.
I honestly don’t remember the last time a game has made me sit back in my chair and say aloud “Excuse me?”
I don’t like judging games by first impressions, I would have missed out on innumerable gems by doing so, but Star Wolves 3 has nothing to offer me that would redeem such a first impression.

Kisima Ingitchuna, or Never Alone is a platforming game about a young girl and her spirit fox friend.  Girl and Vulpine must work together to navigate tricky environments, escape from some enemies and defeat others.  Levels are interspersed with story cutscenes and narration, and there are so many cultural 'tidbits' tossed into the game you could even justify it as educational, though the education never gets in the way of the actual game. With smooth visuals and fairly clever design, as well as an interesting story, this game has a lot going for it.
That said, the game does have a few flaws.  Control, I would say, is it's biggest.  I played single-player with a keyboard, so how it would fare with a controller or a second player I cannot say. But there were times when the game simply did not seem to respond to my keystrokes, usually in the worst possible places, leading to my imminent death or frustration. In some areas of the game, having to rapid switch my control from Fox to Girl and back again required almost insane split-second timing, and really didnt add to the fun for me.
Lastly, though its mostly in the tidbits, there is a somewhat preachy and blame-y undercurrent to the game.  Climate change is introduced as a story element, and I note that 'The big bad' of the game looks suspiciously light-skinned. Though probably intended as a means to bring awareness, there is a faint whiff of 'We're very one-with-nature and you are not, you have to deal with the problem you caused, its not our fault.'  Which can seem a little hypocritical when paired with pictures of gasoline powered snow-mobiles, stories with cellphones in them, and mentions of whale hunting.
All in all though, I actually enjoyed this game and recommend it to everyone.

The following is based mostly on single player campaign at the highest difficulty.
Sniper Elite V2 sounds like an ideal sequel: bigger, prettier and more polished. Unfortunately it flushes a good basic sniping mechanic complemented by a delightful x-ray death animation system down the drain with horrendous design decisions like scripted enemies teleporting out of nowhere and lack of manual saving. Better place your bets on the sequels.
+Graphics have aged pretty well and the game seems mostly well optimized. Lack of borderless window support is a pain though
+On a decent SSD at least there are almost no loading times except when starting the game
+In terms of production quality sounds and music are fine work
+Depicts war torn areas reasonably well in the game's own limited context
+Good sniping mechanics
+X-ray killshots remain entertaining throughout the campaign
-No manual saving. Did I say no manual saving? There is no manual saving
-Only one checkpoint "save slot" that is used badly and far too sparsely. The game has no qualms about saving in the middle of a fight which may force you to restart a whole mission
-Scripted enemy spawning out of nowhere. This is a running theme throughout the game that becomes predictable after a few missions.
-Forced combat: no matter how stealthily you manage to get through one phase of a mission, the game can still throw a bunch of enemies in your face fully aware of your location
-The game is very linear with usually only one path to follow in any area which doesn't really fit with the whole sniper theme, Then again the whole gameplay feels more suited for some kind of commando or saboteur game rather than a sniper game
-Sniper duels are boring. As enemy snipers can spawn out of nowhere you tend to detect them by getting hit first. Then you wait for a moment to heal and try to return fire. Rinse and repeat
-In some missions enemy snipers are utterly infallible and will shoot you with perfect accuracy and no detection or preparation lag of any kind, leading to very tedious gameplay
-The player's weapon accuracy is laughably bad while enemies can hit you almost always no matter the distance or weapon. The silenced pistol is particularily inaccurate even at almost point blank range.
-Hit detection is appalling at times. I lost count how many times I saw a bullet shot at someones face impact on a wall behind them instead
-Absurd stealth mechanics. You either move soundlessly in a crouch (except when falling even a few centimeters, that makes huge noise) or then you run like a rampaging elephant which the enemies can easily hear. Oddly the enemies themselves hardly ever make any footstep sounds...
-Some inexplicable framerate drops in simple cutscenes

I'm not sure how to describe how much I love this game without sounding like I'm overstating it's charm, beauty, or overall amazing-ness. It tells a story in such a wonderful and refreshing fashion that I found myself getting choked up at various points thoroughout the game, both at appropriate times for the story, and also for simply how gorgeous the gameplay animation was at times. This game is immersive, beautiful, and ... educational. I can't recommend it highly enough. It also features a brilliant multi-player co-op feature that blends seamlessly into the game, so if you have a friend over, or want to show this story to anyone else, gamer or otherwise, they can join in very easily. Moreover, if you decide to play single player, there is no loss in gameplay at all, it is equally amazing as both single and multi-player. Absolutely everyone should play this game at least once in their life.

The gameplay has moments that shine and show the potential this game had to be great, but Ubisoft and the development teams incompetance and failure to acknowledge the problems in this game has killed the community as players became frustrated and left. To their credit, they have released patches and tried to address some of the issues in this game, but it is far too late for the majority of people who purchased this game.
At launch this game had a playerbase of 50-thousand. Now it is about 3 and a half thousand. In a few more months, I expect this game to not be relavant anymore and will only be remembered as a failure, if at all.
The problems with this game are:
P2P connection will constantly disconnect you from matches.
Matchmaking is not balanced at all because there isn't a large enough playerbase to create balanced teams. The majority of players who have not left this game are highleveled and have a high gear score. You also need to reach Reputation Level 3 and grind for steel which is used to buy armor and weapons, then pay more steel to upgrade them to their highest level. If you do not do this, you will lose consistantly. Alternativly you could purchase steel with real life money with ingame microtransactions.
If you do get into a match, you have the choice of playing 3 game types which always devolve into a moshpit, worsened by a unbalanced and unfair; gear system, hero unique feats, and revenge mode. The winning team is always the team lucky enough to have everyone connect and not be replaced by idiotic bots, stay connected throughout the match, the team with the highest leveled players, or the team with the highest gear stats for their heros.
The other two gametypes are 1v1 and 2v2. Your gear score and feats are not used in these gametypes, but these matches are also unbalanced from a low playerbase.

It's a trainwreck of errors that ruin an otherwise perfectly good game.
Where to start? Perhaps with the fact that you're charged real money to have a female character. Besides flipping the bird to all you ladies out there, you need to pony up cash to buy anything resembling permanence or customization. The game's defenders will argue that you get all sorts of freebies. They fail to take into account that some of us would like to put together a character from something other than random pieces of garbage strewn about from randomized packs.
Gameplay? Spectacular - once you get past the horrifically overpowered heroes. Don't see them yet? Probably because they're rank-restricted (so only the best people get to crush you). Unless you want to pay cash. Funny how that works. In all honesty, the gameplay is mostly fantastic, save for a few caveats. If you're caught blocking, you're screwed, as the other guy can attack you without any delay, leaving you with no option to fight back. This is a ridiculous failure for a fighting game. The other issue is the sheer number of crowd-control effects that rip away control from your character and, more frustratingly, forcibly reposition your character, often into a pit. How is that fun?
Oh yeah, overpowered heroes. They're out there, the best players have them, and you really don't have much of a hope against them. Expect to be comboed for half your health before falling off the stage, no matter what you do. Game balance was clearly an afterthought for the developers.
This could have been good. Why is the cash portion so forced? Why can't they balance the game properly?
