As much as I would love to give this game a great review, I can't.
Pros:  Amazing combat system.  Gameplay is  a lot of fun, and very much skill based.  The classes are fairly well balanced, and each feels unique.  Customization allows you to make your character stand out, especially in the prestige ranks.
Cons:  Peer to Peer networking solution makes for an extremely poor user experience.   I can't overstate this enough, Ubisoft, to save a buck, ruined the user experience of this game.  It could have been a AAA title, but instead, it feels like a cheap crowd funded failure.  For a $60-100 game, this is absolutely unacceptable.    Connection issues plague the game.  I would say ~25% of the games I play end up with one or more players being sent back to the lobby.  There's no way to re-connect to a game.
The story, while fun (due to the combat system) is shallow and very short, with very little attention given to the story itself.  It's really just a tutorial for the different classes.
The multiplayer "war" is poorly done.   It could have a lot more depth.   There's no real reason to involve yourself in the war.  Just play the game modes you want.
Team balancing is non-existent.  You can be on a team with 3 bots, as a level 0 character, against a full pre-made team of prestige 5+ players.  In Ubi's defense, the team selection is done prior to the character selection.
Game modes are pretty much all the same, with minor differences.  It's either a cap & hold game, or an elimination.
Conclusion:   This game could have been great, but Ubi either has a terrible User Experience designer, or none at all.  While the gameplay is alot of fun, the implementation is terrible, and shows they cut corners dramatically.

One of the most unique titles in the series, and one of the most important, if not THE most important if you care about the series plot. I won't give plot details away, but I will say that Overture is a very important chapter in the series, and you should definitelty play it to fully understand where the series is now.
Overall, I love this game, it's weird, but it's fun. Definitely worth trying out at the very least.

My time on record for the Steam version will likely look pretty meager, but I logged a good number of hours into it in its original Xbox360 incarnation. Reviewing the basic game itself, I can happily recommend it. Easily one of the most underrated exclusives that ever graced the 360. It earned bad-to-mediocre reviews back then, but I think that was mainly because people either didn't quite understand what the game was supposed to be, or they were old Guilty Gear fans who were disappointed that they'd been given a stylish action/real-time strategy hybrid instead of another sidescrolling fighter. I think if people give it another look nowadays, they'll be able to appreciate it more as the wildly original, solidly-made actioner that it really is. Possibly even more so by having it on Steam, where the community is more open to these kinds of experimental sidesteps.
And man oh man, dat soundtrack. Some of my favorite tracks from the entire Guilty Gear franchise, and this series is full of some of the best metal-based music in gaming.
All of that being said, It has to be mentioned that at the time of this posting, there are absolutely no graphics options to adjust, which is extremely disappointing. The game runs in a windowed 720p format which can't be altered in any way. Honestly, what's the point of even porting a game to PC if you can't pretty it up using the superior power of one's gaming rig? I was expecting that I'd be able to up the resolution, maybe improve the textures and all that... but as it is now, the port provides absolutely no way to do this.
Hopefully some kind of patch is applied at a later date, providing extra options to make the most of playing it on PC. Otherwise... you may as well just go play the 360 version.
So as a game, it's great, and I do recommend it. But as a PC port of an almost decade-old game, it could really use a bit of patching on the part of the devs.
Oh, and you can't invert the look controls. Just another thing to mention. An option for it is present, but it can't be changed. Kind of odd.

BeamNG.drive is a soft-body physics simulation game developed by the BeamNG company and first released in 2013. As someone who’s a fan of simulation games, particularly physics simulations, I got my hands on BeamNG.drive as soon as I heard about it. Upon playing the game, I was immediately impressed with the accuracy and detail of the crashes as the game boasts a real-time, soft-body dynamic physics structure using algorithms for physics calculations in real-time. The result is stunning car crashes upon interactions with various objects and other landscape obstacles.
One of the first things that I want to point out with BeamNG.drive is that, as of writing, this game is still considered “early access” which means it is still technically in development. As of right now, there are two modes available – Freeroam and Scenarios. For the most part, most people find themselves playing in freeroam as this is where you have the freedom to customize and experiment with the game, its maps and vehicles.
One of the most impressive aspects of this game aside from the realistic real-time physics and crashes is the graphical elements and beauty of the maps and vehicle designs. It’s apparent that great care and detail has gone into the design of all included vehicles and maps. Every element of the maps can interact with the vehicles allowing you to take your vehicle anywhere on the map and crash it. Even as parts fly and vehicles tumble, you’ll be impressed with the way they interact with objects on the map, oftentimes pleasantly unexpectedly.
For those of you like me who enjoy a good physics sandbox game and realistic car crashes, BeamNG is the game for you! The beauty and level of detail put into this game combined with the incredible real-time physics engine will leave you impressed and with hours and hours of entertainment. Look for this game to continue to evolve as it has been over the past few years with the developer providing full support and many updates. It is well worth the $20 for Early Access and can be purchased direct from the developer or through Steam.
If you're looking for a short-ish medium length shooter with a good story, and don't mind a little darker humor. Look no further.

Not only did I grapple with decisions about who would be useful to free versus who was too integral to my roster to let go of, those decisions were further complicated by my feelings about who I thought most deserved to be freed. Lost Saga is an arena fighter that doesn't do a lot of things right. A lot of these fall under accessibility, mechanics, customization, latency and as a personal matter, sound.
Part 1, Latency:
As far as the latency goes, if you're in the East Coast, then you will suffer a lot in this game even if you're gifted with FiOS or Google Fiber because of a mix of either deprecated and underpowered servers, or they're located far far away in a country that prevents data going through right. What I mean by this is that hitboxes and frames are two very important things for a fighting game. You need to figure out how big or how small the hitboxes are, and then you need to figure out the "frame time" of each attack. The hitboxes are the main problem for this situation. A lot of times, your hitboxes and your opponent's hitboxes will keep resizing or be somewhere away from the character model. This is a really bad problem when you're playing as a small hitbox Hero like Graffiti or Werewolf. Frames aren't as bad, especially when you can block and see the extra frames from a Hero like Death Knight, but it's a huge problem when you're guarding against D`artagnan, because you can't tell where that one "counter frame" is. What I mean by counter frame is the frame you can start your counter at to give yourself the edge. Seeing how popular D'artagnan is, it's even harder to fight unless you cheese yourself. Small games like these were originally made to only handle a small country like South Korea, Philipines, Singapore or Japan. For China, they create a million different servers inside two main servers. So unless you're a big publisher like Nexon or Tencent, you would have a hard time trying to find good servers to support a game like this. Other action-packed games such as LaTale, GetAmped 2, SD Gundam Online and GunZ also suffered from these problems because either the servers were too weak, had a deprecated protocol or too far away.
Part 2, Accessing the game and their mechanics:
Lost Saga has got to have the most stickiest controls I have ever used in a fighting game. A lot of times, you will have problems trying to do good attacks and combos. All you can honestly do is defend yourself with zoning and approach when they mess up. If you do a rushdown playstyle, you're going to punish yourself hard because the mechanics and controls are so stiff, you will not be able to properly do a good rushdown. Overheading is also a problem. What overheading is is when you attack someone from the air behind them. The only way you can get passed this is if your moveset has a divekick in it, which brings me to accessibility. You have a 10 hour option and a 2 hour option with free money. As you fight and have all those heroes, their time depletes despite the fact you never really bought them out to the field. Say I am playing Authur and I have Graffiti, Paladin and Werewolf active. When I am playing Authur and play nothing but Authur, the other three Heroes' playtime remaining will decrease, despite the fact you never swiched into them. This requires you to continously spend money on them to extend their playtime and if you're desperate, shell out or be lucky to find offers that aren't credit score or insurance related to get Permanent variants of them.
Part 3, How come I can't be a cute girl or have those equips?
Customizing your heroes in Lost Saga require you to shell out money or get lucky with boxes. This is where the game really falls apart. In GetAmped 2, Splash Fighters and Rumble Fighter, I honestly don't remember gear, weapon or accessory upgrading mechanics that breaks the game. What do I mean by this? You're able to try and roll for epic variants of standard Hero gear, or original gear to put on your hero. This breaks the game as you're also able to upgrade them to a point where you can one-shot newbies. Say if there's a mirror match between the two, one is vanilla and the other is decked out. The decked out one would obviously win, even if he's a bad player compared to the "novice". Being the little girl is a huge selling point in MMOs nowadays, so if you put them behind a paywall, you're pretty much either having them ditch your game or have them shell out five bucks just to be a girl for one hero.
There's also the general sound of the game. A lot of the voices and sound effects have little to no quality in them. The soundtrack is also not memorable whatsoever outside of the lobby theme and for fighting games, hype from the astetics and action are huge factors to keep a person playing, outside of giving cash shop items for free like crack, and then expecting them to get more with offers or their cards.

Although I recommend this game, I do so cautiously. I purchased this game as part of a bundle and played it immediately after Force Unleased I. The game looks significantly better, and is much less buggy than its predecessor. Hurling baddies across the galaxy is a lot of fun and the force powers work much better in this game than they did before. That being said, there are still a lot of really strange bugs that can hamper gameplay at various times. I had to restart one level because the auto-sequence wouldn't initiate due to one of the troopers getting stuck in a wall. I couldn't eliminate him and the sequence couldn't play out.
There are a ton of fun moments in this game. You'll fight giant monsters, use the force in powerful ways and say 'wow' more than once. That being said, the game is highly repetitive. Unlike the first game, there is little variety. For example, in the Force Unleashed, you can trigger a QTE to eliminate certain foes. There was more than one animation for these baddies because I'm sure the developers wanted things to feel fresh. Unfortunately, that variety was not carried over to this game. You fight the same guys over and over again and QTE them to the same animations over and over. It becomes boring and lackluster. SOMA is a well executed athmospheric sci-fi horror narrative. The game has an impressive setting dealing with consciousness in a post-apocalyptic setting ("soma" is Latin for body, which refers to the plot of the game).
The game is set in a facility on the bottom of the ocean in which you wake up one day, no clue what is going on. You unravel the story piece by piece while you follow instructions from a voice on the radio.
The atmosphere of the game is spot on. The story is interesting and left me empty. The visual style is perfectly executed.
As a horror game, it lacks the elements that made Penumbra and Amnesia terrifying. Instead, it focuses more on atmosphere and relies less on gameplay elements - it is a narrative game. Knowing this, I wasn't disappointed at all by the lack of tense gameplay moments or monsters. It was the facility that created the true tension at times.

Horrible controls, terrible graphic glitches (If you see weird glitches with your subtitles and menus you need to force enable vertical refresh in your graphics card control panel), and almost non-existent plot. My time would have been better spent doing other stuff, like Reddit.

DISCLAIMER: I have played singleplayer, but not multiplayer nor co-op though I watched a few gameplay videos. If you want to know more about them go watch Youtube videos or read other reviews.
Rock of Ages 2 is a sequel to Rock of Ages, which was released in 2011. The point was to destroy the enemy castle door with a big boulder. The opponent also has a boulder and both of you need to build defences while the boulder is being built by each side. It's a race to who is the first one to destroy castle door and killing the opponent. Rock of Ages 2 is pretty much the same, but refined.
Refinements include:
- Having an option to choose boulder to use. They have different strengths and weaknesses, so be strategic
- You can customize your flag, units colors and boulder which game will show in every match you are in.
- Banks are now required to be built near mines, which generate extra income.
- Boulder doesn't have three layers anymore and now it does damage (to castle door) based on health alone and shows damage number.
- You can finally build a proper wall instead of separate towers.
- There are less defence options, but they do have more variation, giving you more options for different strategies.
The game otherwise is very similar, but it's not a bad thing. As matter of fact, it's a very good thing considering that it doesn't add any unnecessary changes that completely change the game. It's just....refined. It's the gameplay and style you already liked.
Art-style, humour and soundtrack are still the best elements just as in Rock of Ages. Graphics look fantastic and are reminiscent of actual historic art and paintings. Just look at the screenshots in this game's front page. The game does look exactly like that, so I can confirm that there are no bullshots.
Rock of Ages 2 has more music, and every stage has it's own score. They are redesigned and remixed from classical music scores intending to sound more action centered and a bit twisted. If someone really finds classical music boring and too slow, they should listen the soundtrack of this game.
The game overall doesn't make any sense in terms of character actions and story. As many have said, it's suppose to be very monty python like with 2D cardboard characters. Cutscenes show historical figures doing something bizarre (the jokes usually tend to reflect something they did, but not always) You most of the time have no real reason to fight these figures, but who cares honestly. Cutscene's main point is to make you laugh and find excuses to fight these guys. If cutscenes don't make you laugh, I advice to skip this game and play something else.
Technical side; Rock of Ages 2 performs really well. I don't really have an amazing specs in my computer, but I can run Rock of Ages 2 with ultra settings. Only major frame drops I noticed were in volcano level and sometimes when psychics went crazy. I rarely find a game nowadays that looks great and performs well. Usually just it's one way or the other.
There are few flaws. Sometimes bot seems to have unfair advantage as it seems to do more damage to gate despite it having exact same stats and speed. At early stage of single player campaign, the bot has more defences and boulders that are locked for you. They most likely made it the way it is to balance the game, but it still can be slightly annoying.
Boss fights were major flaw in first Rock of Ages and yet devs didn't fix this in Rock of Ages 2. You cannot lose them (to my knowledge) because you just respawn when boulder is destroyed and bosses don't really do their 100%. Most of the attacks you can dodge so easily and only slight challenge I encountered was with Sphinx because it could destroy your boulder with one attack and even that was easy. Boss fights are suppose to be really challenging or atleast more difficult than standard stages. Bot offers more challenge even in normal difficulty than bosses, which really speaks for itself. Also, why show the weak point when you could just give indirect hint. In thinker fight they did that (though honestly they did show that in in-game cutscene for some reason), so why even show weak point in cutscene. Most players would've figure that out after multiple tries. This honestly gives me an impression that the game thinks players are morons.
Rock of Ages 2 is unfortunately short game and it takes 3-4 hours to complete the single player campaign. Single player honestly offers the best parts. As much content is has, like multiplayer and some game modes, I have no interest with playing multiplayer or co-op with randoms due to my social anxiety. I don't have any friends who own this game, which makes multiplayer aspect pointless for me. Also there isn't (online) co-op for single player campaign, which is just a minor thing, but still unfortunate.
There are some other minor things. Sometimes when you and jump and fall off, you are placed on the opposite side instead of the point from where you jumped. A.I is most of the time good, but sometimes it does weird things when it's controlling the boulder.
Yet, I should say that with it's low price and fun single player campaign, I was sadisfied with the final product. There are no microtransactions or season passes. If you liked the original game, you should definitely buy Rock of Ages 2. For new comers, I would highly recommend buying a bundle which include both games.

Never Alone has you playing as a small girl, Nuna, who quickly friends a Artic Fox and the both of them go on an adventure to find out what's causing a blizzard. You control both characters (co-op is an option though), whomever you control will follow the other one though sometimes the AI isn't the best in keeping up with the other character but that's not too hard to fix. The Fox is fast, can run up walls and jump further than Nuna, allowing him access to high areas to help Nuna proceed. Nuna quickly gets equiped with a Bola to break shards of glass and open pathways. The interplay between the characters is well done and never getting tiring. Puzzle elements are light, all in the form of platforming and getting to the next area so you should never get stuck or frustrated. If you're looking for something with a challenge this isn't it.
The greatest part about the game are the video interviews you unlock by finding Owls, all these Owls are usually in your way so you can't miss them. The videos unlocked are members of the Iñupiaq detailing their ways of life, philosophies, the fear of climate change and different stories handed down generation to generation. The latter usually ties directly into the gameplay itself as most of all of the concepts in the game are a traditional story applied to the game. It's only a small look into the culture of the Iñupiaq but it's incredible interesting!
If you're looking for an quick and easy game to enjoy with beautiful visuals you can't do much better than Never Alone.

The bullet physics are cool looking, but they fall short of real-life ranges hashed out on the scopes... The bullet drops about two feet every hundred yards on 'realistic' settings, and the game railroads you into one track. No using alleyways, ditches, burned out buildings randomly: there is -one- path, with maybe one/two buildings and -one- accessable pathway through it/them.
Not to mention, first mission I tried to use an alleyway to advance, turns out it wasn't mapped and I fell through the world to my death.
3/10: good premise, looks good, but falls short on ballistics, stealth, ammunition, supplies, variety, strategy, etc.

I've been a big fan of Supergiant's previous titles and can honestly say this is their best game yet.
The unique art style and evocative soundtracks that have been the hallmark of Supergiant's previous IPs are here in abundance, along with a roster of fantastically realized characters (exiles) that genuinely invest you in their story.
There's a very strong RPG element tp Pyre, much more so than in Transistor or Bastion. You're given ample opportunities to chat to your fellow exiles, giving you a bit of downtown between the fast and frantic 'Rites' that make up the primary gameplay element of Pyre. When done badly, these kind of tangential subplots can be at best laborious and at worst skip-worthy. That's not the case here. Each character has their own set of excentricities and motivations that, while perhaps a little derivative, are involving and immersive. This, coupled with the heavy emphasis on choices (and in turn consequences), leads to some genuinely trying decisions that will have you agonizing.
All this is to say nothing of the gameplay.
The vasts majority of the game is split into two parts. The first is a point and click explorer where you make your way to various landmarks dictated by your gift for reading celestial allignments. The art style really shines through during this section of the game. The world is visually stunning in a very unique way and the fantastical world building that accompanies it is top notch.
The second part of the game is based around 'rites' where your triumvirate faces off against another in a game of, what is essentially, second-world fantasy basketball. While the idea may seem overly simplistic, the gameplay is subtley addictive (and pretty tricky when you ratchet up the difficulty). Each of your exiles have a specific set of skills that allows them to shine in certain situations. As well as this, each character can gain new skills and abilities through 'Enlightenment', which is essentially a talent system that can be improved via experience points.
All in all, this game is well worth a purchase. Without doubt one of my favourite titles of 2017.

I installed the game with very low expectations after seeing many negative reviews. And I must say, I was pleasantly surprised.
After 3 days of heavy playing (24hours+):
+ At first glance, the game tries to be one of the "realistic shooters", however it does not go over the top to forget that it is a game after all. It's still extremely easy to die, but there are ways to regain full health. Aiming through ironsights can be annyoing at first but it's a matter learning how to use it. There are no arrows pointing at enemies, nicks or whatever - so you need to rely on your own perception and finding best vantage point or safest routes to objecties.
+ Playing from central europe, I had decent ping to EU and RU servers. Felt no lags whatsoever.
+ Very fair buisness model. Haven't spend a buck, still kicked butts. You are able to buy faster progression, cosmetics and some guns - all of which can be also obtained from random drops after each match. What is more, the hard currency guns aren't really better than the normal ones.
+ Nice map variety. 9 maps, each can be played in three modes. Some are quite open-space, some are more CQB oriented, some are typical post-apocalyptic city landscapes, some have more industrial vibe, some are rural villages.
+ Weather system. It's a detail, but very nice and actually affects gameplay by changing visibility.
- Game crashed 3 times so far, and I believe this to be the biggest issue with the game. It's not often, but it happens.
- There is no prone stance, which annoys the hell out of me. I mean - why the hell not?
- Some graphical elements of the game could use some polish - especially animations.
I eagerly await the moment when the game leaves early access
Edit post 0.30 patch: Animations improved, so one less cons for me.

Obviously it's still early in it's life, and while not quite early access you might get that vibe from it. Still, for $40 I've now gotten over 40 hours of gameplay at the time of writing this, so I obviously have gotten my moneys worth. I've payed $60 for single player games that last 12 solid hours and been happy, this game has provided me with a lot of entertainment and I can say I'll spend at least another 40 hours with friends in game.
Now, for the game itself, it's a ton of fun with friends. All my friends bought it so I consistantly have 8 player private matches, but I still have fun playing with random people online. I would not recommend this game to someone who doesn't at least have 1 regular friend to play with, 3-4 is recommended, and 8 is ideal.
As of now there are only 3 maps, and while they are similar they never feel like the exact same map, and I'm sure lots more are on the way. Classic Camp Crystal Lake is the best of the bunch. Almost all the counselor are fun and different enough for various play styles, and the EXP and perk system keeps things interesting, however most of the counselors all have the same voice (all males sound the same, females have a little but more variety). The Jasons are all varied, but whichever you pick, you're still Jason.
The server issues and game bugs are hard to ignore, but nothing encountered so far has made me regret my purchase or made the game outright unfun. The only thing that can make the game unfun are the random players who troll by betraying or geting themselves killed and losing you points, but most of the comunity so far has been pretty good.
If you're on the fence I say if you have a regular group of friends, its' easily worth the $40, if not, grab it when it's on sale for around $20. If you have never seen the movies, watch a few before you buy, you'll be glad you did, and look up the band "The Jasons" and show them some support!

Ok, so as many players already said this is a VN/sports combination. Having read that made me not want to buy the game. But i thought i'd trust this company after giving me such an immersive experience with transistor and buy the game anyway. I thought, even if i don't like it, i will have supported their next project. So it's win win. And i'm glad i trusted them.
It's not "sports". I mean i understand why they would classify it as such, but it felt more like an arena. I can't explain much without spoiling it for new players, so i'll stop here. I can write quite a list of differences between a sports game and this game, but let's just say it's "sports" but it will never feel like that. And i hate VNs. But after having finished it once, i'm more than eager to go play it again on the unlocked difficulty.
I think this is the problem with writing a review for this game. I find myself dodging spoilers left and right trying to get new players to get it, because my unspoiled experience was so unique and immersive.
The best quality of this game is its immersion. You will NEVER feel the game didn't record your actions, nor that your actions didn't matter. Every character is fleshed out, has his/her own backstory, and the dialogues always matter. Yes, i can't say it's not a VN. But usually VNs have so much information you just don't care about. Here, everything matters so much, and influences your choices, that you can't but read on. Treat it like an interactive book - most of it is understanding the world, the people in it and their motives, and deciding what you'll do next and why. This is why the "matches" have so much importance. Because you know who is fighting and why. The characters stop being tools to your victory, they are their own masters, what they want from you is your coordination (well, and special ability, without spoiling anything again.). Gameplay-wise, that is not to say they will act on their own, no, you do control their every move. What i mean is what it feels like. Because the whole game is about what it makes you feel. That's why i would put it under the "story rich" category much more than the sports one. I don't know, i wouldn't have included the sports one at all, it's right to be there, but it's very misleading.
Anyway, many people have already talked about the graphics' style, so there's no point in going on about it too much here, suffice to say i love it, i wasn't expecting still images to have so much life in them, the devs are really smart about this. What i will talk about though is the music. They had already impressed me with transistor, so i was expecting to be impressed here also. The feeling is similar to that of transistor, with the difference that now every different character/team/situation has his/her own theme. When you encounter bloodthirsty characters, when you speak to wraiths who have spent tens of your lifetimes, when you look at the stars, when you do anything the music is there to make sure you ARE doing that which you're doing. So don't mute.
Before i go on to sum it all up, i must say i am biased. I love this company and i want to support it. If you were overly excited with the company's other titles, loving their work will work to make the game better in your head. Sadly, i can't say what the game would look like if i had never seen its other title(s).
So to sum it all up. This is more of an interactive book with gameplay elements. If you skip dialogues in your games then this game isn't for you. Your very name even suggests you are supposed to read a lot and, even, that that's the best quality about you. This aspect of the game covers more than half of the game. However it would never work as a book, because what matters here is that you make most of the choices. Again, i don't want to spoil it, so i'll just say the position you find yourself in is not always fun. You carry a heavy burden and the game makes sure you feel that.
Because of the extreme meaning your every decision, action or match has, the game heightens your immersion to another level, where you don't care that you spend most of your time reading, and you find yourself thinking carefully of your next reply or move.
The music is amazing. The graphics' style is unique.
The RPG elements are there and, although many people said the chars' skills don't do much, i found that they do a lot. A char who's maxed out is usually extremely potent in a match, although it's your strategy that wins it. I loved that.
Now, i have one bad thing to say. All matches are real-time. I don't know how they would work if they were turn-based, but because of the fact that i don't own a high-end pc (you wouldn't need one, but mine is pretty low-end) and because the matches feel more like actual matches when compared to something like chess, i would prefer them to be turn-based. I think there are a lot of strategies wasted in how fast you have to react to everything. HOWEVER i believe the reason they went that route was to balance action with reading, of which, like we've already established, there's a lot.
So, that's all. The game's price is very low, even when it's not on sales, so you don't lose anything for buying and trying it.
Just remember, if you're not a reader, the game isn't for you.

There's a lot going with Pyre, but in a great way. It is a bit of a light sports game, with a skill tree leveling system to accompany its RPG-style story. Single-player is a fun experience, but is a bit too intense for my tastes to do another playthrough (there are multiple character endings based on the choices you make). There is a Versus multiplayer mode (local/offline) where you can go against another person or the AI (on separate teams).
It follows the similar "silent hero protagonist" found in Transistor and Bastion, but goes a different route for the hero's journey. Bastion was survival in a post-apocalyptic setting, and Transistor somewhat brings about the apocalypse (or hurried the pace along, depends on your view).
Pyre doesn't use the apocalypse theme as much as the other two, choosing instead to focus attention on the economic/social/political class system of a society. This game's core theme is about hope, and it is hard not to get emotionally invested with the story and its outcome.

So I actually wanted to take some time to review this game because I feel it deserves it.  First off I would like to state this is an RPGmaker title and gameplay wise it plays like Phantasy Star/FF series.   For an RPGmaker game I have been truly impressed.
It has your standard leveling up system but with a few different things that change it from the original formula.  For example you get skill points through gaining levels, completing side quests/main quests and monster nodes which you can collect in dungeon areas.   You use the skill points to learn various abilities for each person in your party.   Also there are 9 skills and 3 passives for each character in your party and each skill can have be leveled 1 to 5.  So with one character in my party I focused on her fire spells and dark magic, yet if I wanted to I could have went Lightning/Frost or the many other combos which are possible with her.   I personally feel you can choose any skills and make it through the game.(healing magic is a must though!)
The story is alright.   There are some actual parts where I was really into it; taking this base over or defending a castle(Trying not to spoil anything there)   What I do like is that alot of the dialoge feels mature and well written.   Except with some of the characters. They seem like the average comedy relief anime people which to me felt generic.   Other then that it is pretty solid I'd say.
The graphics are your classic SNES era or equivalent.   I personally like old games since they old a nostalgic charm over me.   Overall I would recommend this to any person who enjoys a good JRPG.

SOMA is a well executed athmospheric sci-fi horror narrative. The game has an impressive setting dealing with consciousness in a post-apocalyptic setting ("soma" is Latin for body, which refers to the plot of the game).
The game is set in a facility on the bottom of the ocean in which you wake up one day, no clue what is going on. You unravel the story piece by piece while you follow instructions from a voice on the radio.
The atmosphere of the game is spot on. The story is interesting and left me empty. The visual style is perfectly executed.
As a horror game, it lacks the elements that made Penumbra and Amnesia terrifying. Instead, it focuses more on atmosphere and relies less on gameplay elements - it is a narrative game. Knowing this, I wasn't disappointed at all by the lack of tense gameplay moments or monsters. It was the facility that created the true tension at times.

The game is so good.
Gameplay:
The battle system is well done, and makes you want to fight the enemies instead of retreating (because if you want to run you'll have some consequences) and you'll never see yourself pressing attack and attack over and over, overall the battles were engaging and tatical.
On the otherhand, outside of the battles were these mazes... and I will say the first few 'dungeons' they were pretty fun and challenging to get around and find the correct ways, but as the game progresses through these dungeons they just keep getting worst and more repeated... I found myself towards the end of the game with this scenario, "I found the exit, oh wait but where's the quest item!?". I felt towards the end of the game, the dungeons were rushed and almost had no sense of directions. I won't lie, but I just walked to random area till I eventually got to an exit.
Side quests were very well worth. The leveling/equiping system was very exciting and fun to play around on which build I wanted on each character.
**Gameplay - 7/10**
Graphics/Audio:
Audio was pretty good, I really didn't listen to it most of the time, but I do believe they had the same sound track for almost every dungeon(I may be wrong). Battle music were alright, nothing memorable although, but nothing to complain about.
Graphics were pretty good, the mapping they did in this game was top-notch, not sure if they used parallaxing at all, and if they didn't I applaud them. I thought the maps were really well done, espically the towns for their simplistic layout and directions (knowing where things are).
**Graphics/Audio - 8/10**
Story:
The story was ehh... I mean it seemed pretty cliche at some moments, but I think if you were to play a cliche rpg, this game would be the one. I say that there were SOME cliche moments, but those were only SOME moments, overall the story of the game was compelling and dynamic, but I did feel the character development was sometimes at a lost, also I did feel there were some questions to be asked. The story was decent, nothing memorable or different, but I mean it was still a great story.
Dialogue was GREAT, very good. Funny moments were funny, serious moments were serious. You could tell by the dialogue and I think the creator did a great job taking words and creating a tone with it. Very well done.
**Story - 7/10**
Overall the game was pretty well done. Dialogue really helped set the tone of the game which helped the somewhat cliche story and characters. Battles were very tatical and engaging, as well as for the quest. The game does some things that are just incredible, but does some things that are just straight out annoying, which killed my experience with the game and the story.
In the end although, I would recommend this game for any RPG fans.
**Overall - 7.5/10**

-A leveling system to access content, which gives the game an end goal to access certain characters.
-Jason's executions
Cons:
-3 DAMN MAPS TO PLAY ON! There is only 3 maps to play on when there was a plethora of areas Jason ventured to across all movies.
-Max level is roughly 100 but you stop earning anything of value at level 31 (that is when you stop earning characters).  From here all you will earn is different colored clothing for the Camp Counselors.
-The Glitches that allow for either instant death from Jason without him performing an execution, or simply the glitches that make the Counselors invincible and cannot die.
-Playing without friends is highly ill-advised because there is no regional play.  I live in the Center of North America, literally withing 500 miles of the geographical center of NA and I still connect to Russian, Chinese, Japanese, Bulgarian, and the French more than I do English speakers at all hours of the day.j
-COMMUNICATION is attrocious.  Without people using the radios in game to communicate the location of jason or vehicle parts you will find yourself dead more times than not.
Overall its a solid game that you can have fun with  your friends, and if you're lucky you will find some same language people that are willing to communicate and have fun with you.  I will admint that you have a 1 in 8 chance of being Jason, and honestly thats the only time I have fun when I am playing solo, even if you have the "preference of spawning in as jason" it will normally choose someone else.

They have announced a single player and the addition of more content, but when that will actually happen is unknown.
Is it a must buy, no.  Its a fun time killer, but do not expect any wow moments because the executions quickly lose their effect on you and the reactions you give will become more and more tame the more you are executed.

This game is worth at best 1£/hour. Seeing as it clocks in at 4 hours in a fairly avarage run, I'd say avoid it like the plague.
Usability:
This is also because it has numerous issues running properly on my win 7. To actually get it to start you need to change the compability settings of you .exe, an .exe which you must first download online if you actually want to play your figther game at 60fps instead of 30. Add to that the long, unskippable start up movies (which you can fix with another download).  Of course you also have some random crashes ( i counted 4) during playtime, and a few glitches while plaing. All in all it's not a very good port. Though i will say it actually does present graphical options, unlike it's predesessor.
Combat:
The gameplay is very much the same as one. You have you're similar attacks, lightsaber throwing, litghtning firing and normal saber combat basically. Where it changes is in the speed of combat. Your dash ability from 1 has a shorter cooldown, you wield 2 lightsabers instead of one, which basically means you hit faster, but you're comboing abilities are if anything increased. Unlike the 1st installment, you have little ability to change hit quickly, so you mostly end up doing a quick few slahes on normal enemies, and spam the normal 4 hit combo on more tough ones.
There are two new installments. Those are mindtricks, the ability to turn a weak enemy to your side, and rage. Mindtricks replace the sheild from 1, but offers little useability to make up for this. Since you dispose of enemies so quickly, and the effect last such a short time, it barely sees any use. Rage on the other hand works as you would expect. you kill enemies, build up ragem, and get a damage boast for a short amount of time on use. All in all it is an allright mechanic, if a bit underused.
Tha min issue with the combat lies in it's overreliance of quick time events. Any enemy stronger than your common lightsaber uer or stormtrooper is finished using the same qte, with minor variations in buttons. This means since you have the same animations and enemies throughout the game, you end up repeating it for atleast 50 times over the course of playing. Add to that the stronger focus in bossfights. where earilier the main combat was indeed swordplay and force use, with qte's being used as finishers, here almost the entirety of the bossfights are qtes.
Upgrades:
As in 1, you have your lightsaber upgrades. These are colloected as holocrons, which are fairly easy to find as you progress through the game. They are cosmetic and gameplay effects rolled into one, where you can pick one crystal for ech saber, having effectssuch as drain health,
You also have your powerupgrades as in 1. In 2 these are instead "streamlined" or perhaphaps simplu dumbed down, into one page. Previously you could upgrade your powers, your combos and your player strenghts (hp, energy etc9 with different points earned by lvling up and completing challanges. Here you get all your points based on enemy death (as in bulletstrom). Your upgrade all your swordplay (damage, combos) in one, and the rest upgrades your indivudual forcepowers. The problem with this way is you loose the sense of progression of 1. Since you have all the useful combos from a fully upgraded jedi from 1, you dont actually receive any interesting new combos with upgrades. This leads to all upgrades essentialy being damage buffs, something which isnt very exciting for a quick, combo based combat.
Aesthetics:
Immidiatley you can see they put a lot of effort into making this a beautiful game. The scale of the eniroments, and graphical fidelity are much better than 1, and are enjoyable throughout the game. The only gripe i have is that they removed the enemy healthbars, making fairly difficult to know the damage required to actually bring down enemies.
Story:
This game picks up a year or so after 1, and it follows a supposed clone of good old Starkiller. He keeps his old memories, and becomes obsessed with finding the (very) brief love interest of 1. That's it. That's the story. You find Kota from 1, assualt the cloning facility you were created, and fight Vader. Game over. This in a game where half the time (atleast) is spent in qte's and cutscenes. Needless to say it doesn't offer enough.
Conclusion:
It feels like this game was horribly rushed. The potential lies to have the game stretch atleast another 4 hours, both story wise and gameplay. If nothing else they could have reused enviroments and enemies from 1, albeit graphically updated. As it is, the game ends up feeling like watching an anime, as the game grabs every possibility to wrestle control away from the player at every turn. The little combat there is isn't varied and enjoyable enough to carry the game either, mainly taking place inside corridors and buldings, inlike the vast fauna of felucia in 1 or burning buldings from the wookies homeland. In other words, dont play this game. It isn't worht the wait for the download.

Lost Saga is not a game I would recommend at first if someone asked. Too many issues that make players quit playing: Unstable servers, major emphasis on pay to win, and a not so friendly community, just to name a few. Yet there is a reason I keep coming back and that is LS's mechanics.
Lost Saga's mechanics rank up there with the best games out now, AAA and Indy alike.
First there a hundreds of characters/heroes/mercenaries with specific skills and moveset. The movements and skills of these characters are easy to grasp and even the more complicated ones can be mastered with time.
Second LS has this "gear drop" ability, where the armors can be knocked of characters and can be used by opponents. It's hard to describe in words, so play the game to find out :D.
Third Lost Saga has a hero for everyone. Are you someone who likes to fight close range, mid range, or far range? There's a hero for you and with the ability to mix and match gears you can create a hero set/style specific to you and works only for you.
Lost Saga is not a perfect game, yet if you find a group of friends to play with and take time to learn and master your heroes, the experience will be mostly positive. Lol

Ok. Ths is my absolute favorite game. Period. This was a hundred thousand times better than Amnesia in my opinion. The atmospohere of Amnesia was captivating -- Who doesn't love exploring creepy castles? However, the story was really dumb, and fell apart towards the end. People who consider Amnesia the flagship of Frictional Games were probably just so young that everything scared them that much. I disagreed with them vehemently because of the story. I just couldn't handle it, and I felt like it ruined the game.
This? BOTH creepy, frightening, and fantastic story! To the people who say that the creepiness ruined a "Sci-Fi game," shut the f*** up. This was obviously a horror game before everything, and this was not a way to "brag going all 'Hey! We made Amnesia!' People like you seriously need to get the hell off the review system. What is the genre of this game? HORROR. You were sorely mistaken if you thought this was supposed to be anything else. I can refer you to thousands of other Sci-Fi titles like this without the horror.
Stay away. These horror games are few and far in between. People like you need to GTFO and don't even dare give Frictional Games any ideas. Just play ANY other dumb Sci-Fi game, seriously. Don't ruin it for people like me who actively seek out horror games with good stories. Anyway .I digress. The ending of this game was a little bit sad, but anyone could have seen it coming from a mile away. Simon, though, definitely did not, which is why I don't really sympathize with him. He was an idiot who irritated me for the most part.
The puzzles were incredily reminiscent of Amnesia, which I seriously loved. There is nothing like trying to solve a puzzle while being stalked by some creepy monster. The concepts and ideas in this game are just revolutionary. Please, Frictional Games, continue trying new genres and ideas. This completely blew me away. Frictional Games is officially my all-time favorite game developing company, and I'm going to look for more games made by these people. To everyone reading my ramble of a review, what are you even doing?
If you like horror at all, get this! I'm not usually a big fan of Sci-Fi, but this was executed so well. Much like Amnesia, you wake up in the middle of a weird place without absolutely any  knowledge of what is going on. You have to progress further in the game to piece together the story, and whle in Amnesia it was just absurd and contradictory for the most part, in this game there were absolutely no contradictions. Everything was connected flawlessly! All the characters were consistent, and felt very realistic and concrete.
Buy this game already! It's a steal at 10.99 dollars.

So what a lot of reviewers seem to be missing (probably from not playing very much) is that you can easily rack up enough money with a temporary character to get another 2 or 10 hours on that character. The beginning quests give you a ton to start with as well.
Basically the game works on leasing characters (time is in-battle not real time) and in terms of costs while it might be hard to save up a lot of money for other items and have a lot of time on a lot of characters left they give plenty of money (I have combined over 50 hours of play and still enough money to buy some cosmetics).
It's free to play so not surprisingly some characters (maybe 1/5th of them?) are premium (cost real money) as well as the option to buy a character permanently which as I mentioned isn't really needed at all it's just nice to have. Almost all of the cosmetics can be bought with in-game currency as you level up but if you don't want to wait you can use real money to buy them at any point.
Gameplay-wise it's pretty fun, nothing amazing but it's lighthearted not something I'd consider competitive. There can be some lag issues but I'd say most of the time it's not more than a minor issue.
Overall I'd say try it for maybe an hour or two and see if you like it, try the different modes (prisoner is fun). For free it's a pretty decent game.

This was a hard review to write - it's a hard game not to like, the art style is beautiful and it provides a fascinating insight into an indigienous people/culture that may soon be lost to the world. If you ever want a game you can point at when people claim games can't be art, serve no other purpose than mindless entertainment or violance - this is the game to point them at.
It's a genuinely moving at times, albeit mainly through the video segments that you unlock along the way. The story its self is interesting but for me this game's soul is driven by it's exploration of story telling through games, and opening up access to a culture you would otherwise move through life knowing nothing about.
That said, the game its self is far from flawless. The difficulty curve on the puzzles is random, and the controls at times are clunky. The most frustrating part, to the point that it becomes a distraction, is the companion AI. Some basic puzzles are made more challenging, and some hard puzzles made almost impossible by a random and sporadicly moving AI. The secondary challenge at times being where could you wedge your companion so they can't run off a ledge, or float off so the platform you're stood on dissapears beneath you.
As a medium, and as a piece of engaging storytelling this is pretty expectional and should not be over looked for it does and the message it carries. As a game it is solid, but challenging due to development flaws rather than the core concept. However, do not let that put you off...this is well worth having in your collection and will be 3 hours well spent.

The game is mostly a visual novel with a 3v3 basketball-like game punctuated throughout. The story is good, I found it to be quite poignant. The gameplay is different from most other stuff and I respect the devs for going with their own vision over something easier to implement.
The gameplay can be challenging if you just try to rush your way through it, some thought is required. I played through on normal and could certainly see the game get very demanding on high difficulties.
There is an amazing visual style which was kind of expected due to the past two games these devs have made. Depending on choices you make you may end up visiting the same places often yet they never get tiring to look at.
The best part for me was easily the characters. In most rpgs or games of this sort there is usually a character to two that you just can't get yourself to like so you avoid them, either in combat or in the social side.
Here all characters have a usefulness so I found myself often switching them out. Also even one character who I originally found annoying I came to sympathise with more as the game went on.
I still had my favourites of course but some choices the game presents became difficult because of how evenly I felt for most of the characters.

Review so far in its current state, solid 6.5 out of 10.
Pros:
-Being Jason is the highlight of this game.
-The maps are large and allow for diverse play as Jason and the Counselors.
-A leveling system to access content, which gives the game an end goal to access certain characters.
-Jason's executions
Cons:
-3 DAMN MAPS TO PLAY ON! There is only 3 maps to play on when there was a plethora of areas Jason ventured to across all movies.
-Max level is roughly 100 but you stop earning anything of value at level 31 (that is when you stop earning characters).  From here all you will earn is different colored clothing for the Camp Counselors.
-The Glitches that allow for either instant death from Jason without him performing an execution, or simply the glitches that make the Counselors invincible and cannot die.
-Playing without friends is highly ill-advised because there is no regional play.  I live in the Center of North America, literally withing 500 miles of the geographical center of NA and I still connect to Russian, Chinese, Japanese, Bulgarian, and the French more than I do English speakers at all hours of the day.j
-COMMUNICATION is attrocious.  Without people using the radios in game to communicate the location of jason or vehicle parts you will find yourself dead more times than not.
Overall its a solid game that you can have fun with  your friends, and if you're lucky you will find some same language people that are willing to communicate and have fun with you.  I will admint that you have a 1 in 8 chance of being Jason, and honestly thats the only time I have fun when I am playing solo, even if you have the "preference of spawning in as jason" it will normally choose someone else.
The game certainly isn't worth $40 when you can unlock all the content easily within a solid day of play and when the game is clearly still considered "early access".  If this game had a price point of $25-30 it would feel almost justified, but the games clear lack of content in its current form with all of its issues it does not deserve a $40 dollar price point.
They have announced a single player and the addition of more content, but when that will actually happen is unknown.
Is it a must buy, no.  Its a fun time killer, but do not expect any wow moments because the executions quickly lose their effect on you and the reactions you give will become more and more tame the more you are executed.

Great sim, not for lightweight mouse click/ kill pilots (although mouse flying works just fine in RoF). I have played the non steam version of ROF on and off since it was released years ago. IF you like real flight SIMS (example: IL 2) and like or love WWWI era areoplanes/games/sims (example: Red Baron) you will like or love this game. If you want to be the baddest pilot on the block in a weekend you will hate this title,   lol.  Now I enjoy and play  WOT, WOWS , War Thunder, AW etc, just becasue you like, or think you are competitive in an arena shooter does not equate to being any good at all or enjoying a flight sim. They are not the same thing at all those arena games are for the most part "dumbed down" and  are MADE  and constanlty changed to be appealing to the broadest section of potential online gamers as possible. Even War Thunder in simulator mode is no sim not even close. World of Tanks, World of Warships , Armored Warfare, World of Warplanes (ha!) none of those are. They are all fun  GAMES, I love to play them also, but they are not simulators. That's just a fact.   So just becasue you like or think WG or WT are great  does not mean you will like Rise of Flight it is a SIM , not  an arena fps shooter dressed up to look like a simulator. If you require instant gratification ala WOT or WOWS , WT. And you do not like spending time learning to actually fly your virtual A/C, and then spend more time learning to fight said A/C then you will not like this title.  As for as the DLC if you dont like the game you dont have to buy the DLC . As a matter of fact you should not by ANY DLC untill you know you like the sim or not, you get 3 fighters for free now.That it a LOT of hours of flying time to decide if you can even handle RoF. And you can do pretty much anything you like. If you have RoF long enough to master one of those three airplanes then you might want to start buying DLC and you do not need to get all the DLC maybe two or three tops and you can fight the whole airwar in europe. There are some wonderful guides to what DLC you need to get for what you want to do.  RoF is defninelty not for everybody and it is not an arena mode FPS game like WoT , etc. It is however a nice old school combat sim and I like it quite a lot.

To start off this review, I'll say that I Kickstarted this game because I liked Battle Worlds: Kronos, also by King Art Games. BW:K was a competent enough game, but this isn't, sadly.
The positives is that it looks and sounds gorgeous. The graphics are great(graphics, but not so much the animation at all times...), the effects look nice, the music is excellent, and that's about where the good things stop. Because while it looks and sounds great, The Dwarves just plays like garbage. Supposedly this was tested but apparently no one listened to the testers. So let's get into the gripes and issues I have with this game.
Firstly, the story, you're going to quickly realize that it's extremely generic. Like... I don't think I could even write something this generic on purpose. The entire WORLD is, in fact, really generic. Like someone passed Lord of the Rings through the washer until all the colours were worn out. The dialogue and characters are generally passable and believable, though, despite being super generic, no one was really badly executed to the point of grating on my nerves. But one issue is that the game tosses like a dozen character threads at you, and they all get like... two dialogues each to round them out, excepting the ones you have with you from the start.
You get some dialogue options at times, mostly while exploring the world, and sometimes they matter a little, sometimes they don't matter at all, and sometimes they just make you look at the screen in disbelief. Because the result is just "and then everyone died" and you have to reload. Why even give me this choice, then? Give me a super hard battle or somethign if I did something stupid. Not just "dead." Or when the game gives you a choice, then goes "PSYCH, IT WAS ACTUALLY THE OTHER WAY AROUND." Kill this NPC? Or don't kill this NPC? Well, whichever you pick, the game reverses your actions with no hint that it's so. Just kind of a little "♥♥♥♥ you for having agency" from the writers.
Now, that's my issues with the story. Let's get into the gameplay. Because it's actually worse there.
The basic gameplay is that it's pausable-to-give-orders realtime squad combat. Fundamentally not a bad idea, but hard to pull off, and King Art Games definitely aren't the people who can do it.
For instance, most of your attacks are area attacks, they don't target a given enemy. And with everyone sprinting around, it often means that your attacks will completely miss anyone mobile. On top of that, the targeting indicators are hugely misleading and sometimes you won't hit someone who lights up, while you'll kill or halfway kill a bunch of friends that weren't indicated at all. There are also some issues where if you activate another skill while one is winding down, it'll cash in the AP's used to activate the skill but not actually activate it.
Also the whole gamut of usual design issues where a ton of skills are useless. And, for instance, the ranged characters seem to love to run into melee to attack with their ranged weapons. Why? Characters can't path past each other(they'll get into this little dance or just stand still) or past enemies, so unless they've got the "leap far" skill they tend to get very easily bogged down(the AI is generally pretty bad for your characters, you have to micromanage EVERYTHING or they'll happily sit around eating arrows to the face and picking their nose). Generally obfuscated design. "Don't let your characters get surrounded!" says the hint message. Why, though? Do back attacks and flanking attacks do extra damage? Should I be making use of that? Or is it just because more enemies can hit me at once that way? Why did one of my characters lose half his health almost as soon as the mission started? Was it a special enemy attack? Did he get winged by the ability I just used? I have no clue. Why are these three enemies indicated with huge big indicators like boss enemies usually are? Well they're unique enemies that're blowing horns instead of fighting, but is there some reason why I want to kill them? The game never says!
The camera's also horrendous, it's always tied to characters, meaning that giving orders far away is hell, or on a couple of maps, finding the last couple of enemies you need to kill is painful. The camera also has EXTREMELY limited zoom out and loves to get into fights with the level geometry, fights that the camera usually uses. Speaking of which, at times I've seen enemies clip through walls to instantly die, or get knocked into pits, then just keep sliding slowly across the ground until they reach the other side and get up.
Levels also never indicate whether more enemies arriving are reinforcements from off camera or an infinite supply or enemies, so you never know whether you should beeline for your objective while avoiding fights, or whether you can take your time and murder enemies to give yourself a decent chance of actually accomplishing it. On top of that, you're burdened with something around a dozen PC's, but you're only ever allowed to take FOUR of them into battle. It makes sense from the perspective of "our combat is already a goddamn mess and our controls are garbage, with a dozen characters, it'd be total madness" but it's never explained, and except for one situation, your other characters just vanish. They're not in the background having a pretend fight with NPC's or something else that'd be believable.
Other baffling design decisions is the fact that most characters end up having five active skills, but can only carry three of them with them into combat. I could understand this if there was a massive list that needed limiting. But really? Why not just give me two more icons? It wouldn't take up a lot of space.
In general, just imagine the developers always making the design decision that looks better, but works worse... and then executing it kind of poorly and probably ignoring tester complaints about poor execution. Which actually reminds me of the funniest animation bug in the game, something you'd really think they'd have caught: At one point you're meant to dramatically say farewell to an NPC, complete with a final, hearty handshake... but for me, the timing and facing was off, so it looked like my main character brutally snubbed the poor guy when he was being left to his fate. I was already very little invested in the game's storyline, but that just completely broke all immersion.
Ultimately this is the sort of game that should really just have been turn-based in some fashion, that's about the only reliable way to execute this sort of game well. Sure, it doesn't look as flashy or as cinematic, but it gives you controls and UI that actually function better, 99% of the time.
So, uh, don't buy this. Some of the issues they can patch out if they give a damn, but there are so many fundamental things that should've been caught at the alpha or pre-alpha level, in the very design phase, even before any testers got involved.

I really enjoyed playing Dwarves and it kept me engaged. I measure the success of a game by how many times my wife is yelling at me to get off the computer and spend time with the kids.
I'm an original kickstarter backer and supported it because I like RPG games. I thought this game was worth my money and backing.
Positives:
- Good story. I've never read the books so I don't know if it follows the books or not. But I like the way the story was told in the game.
- Fun tactical abilities, that make you feel powerful
- Traversing the map and having encounters through dialog was a unique and fun.
- Gameplay was fun with some minor frustrations
- Characters were fun and interesting.
- Interesting bad guys.
- Gameplay length perhaps could have been longer, but it was close to being right for me.
- Large selection of unique companions. I tended to use the same companions, so perhaps for certain battles, they could have made it mandatory to use certain companions on certain missions.
- Difficulty was between moderate and hard throughout the game. Would have like opportunities between battles to use potions to heal injuries.
Cons:
- Need a game manual. Halfway through the game I finally figured out how to use potions, and how to access other abilities from leveling up.
- Provisions are kind of useless. A first, I didn't explore everything I could explore because I worried about running out of provisions. Provisions, are basically only used to heal character injuries and nothing else. Kind of a weak mechanic.
- Sometimes you finish one battle and are immediatley thrown into another battle. I would have liked an opportunity to save my game.
- Potions can only be used if you equip one potion per character just before battle. For the most part potions were useless to me, since I preferred to use a talisman and not a potion during battle.
- You can't use potions outside of battle to heal injuries, instead you have to have provisions and walk around to use the provisions to heal the injury.
- There is a silly limitation on the number of skills you can use before a battle. What is the point of leveling up, gaining new skills, if you can't use all the skills in battle. Instead you have to choose only 3. Didn't like this mechanic at all.
- Some battles, it was not clear you had to hunt down Horn Blowing Orcs in order to thin out the herd.
- A few minor bugs during the game. When selecting new abilities after leveling up, earned abilities would be greyed out. Hitting the reset button allowed me to access and select the earned abilities.
Cheers

1) If you haven't played this you really, really should.
2) It's scary as heck at times but worth dealing with the frights to see the ending.
3) You have choices and they matter.
4) If you look in the mirrors be prepared to deal with the beginning of a huge existential crisis and a complete reassessment of what your life means. Or whether it has any meaning at all.
5) Take your time. I took screen-caps of all the signs in the game. Theres plenty to look at in-game, not much to collect but you should take the time to pick up the photos and pieces of paper, they all contribute to the mindblowing back-story.
6) If it's really too much for you, got to the Steam Workshop and grab Wuss Mode. The WAU critters can't hurt you with Wuss Mode, so you can walk around with your torch on, throw things at them, jump up and down, whatever you like. I replayed on Wuss Mode so I could look at all the stuff I missed the first time. Well worth it. And far less scary but still hecking scary; but in a philosophical way moreso than just pure heartpounding frights.
7) Elements remind me of Aliens (as in the 2nd movie in the franchise), Bioshock, Dead Space, Doom 3 (2004). If you like any of those games, or any of Frictionals other titles, you should play this. Honestly, if you liked the complexity of the moral dilemmas in Life Is Strange and other Telltale games, you'll enjoy what this has to offer.
8) When you're done with the game go watch Transitions on Frictionals YouTube channel. Don't bother watching it first, you won't have a clue what's going on.

I never finished Amnesia.
The biggest problem with the first title I thought was the constant pressure you experience. SOMA gives you some time to breathe, to take in the story and atmosphere in between different chapters.
The gameplay is okay, less challenging than Amnesia but still enjoyable. It's less of a horror game than its predecessor but conveys the setting in a better way. Puzzles are fairly simple, more putting the adversaries in between them than making them challenging on their own.
The story is well paced and engaging, even if it draws from a lot of well known cliches. In the end the story and immersion is why you play SOMA. It's nothing groundbreaking but it does what it sets out to very well.
Unlike a lot of other games you'll end up caring about the people and events that happen around you and the choices you make, even if they might not have a large impact.
Huge credit to the voice actors, easily one of the best performances in recent years (Jared Zeus should get more work).
A negative is that probably some of the details of the setting could've been expanded on, SOMA builds a very interesting world but in the end you're still in the dark about what it looks like, which might be intended.
tl;dr
Buy the game. Finish it in a weekend and congratulate yourself on playing one of the best horror/sci-fi games out there. Probably worth a replay in the future.

Lost Saga is... okay.  It plays alright, with A, S, and D keys acting as combo buttons, with A as jump, S as guard and D as attack, and different combinations of those three keys (A+D, S+D, for example), activates one of four unique skills for each hero.  There are a LOT of heroes in this game, including a few licensed ones, the only problem is they are all locked behind a paywall.  You CAN access heroes free as random drops or by obtaining or purchasing an item with in-game currency that grants you permanent access to a new hero from a short, random list.  However, all other hero purchases with the in-game currency called GP are rentals that las for 2, 4, and 10 hours.  This is rather disappointing because the few heroes I played are fun, but the fact that I either have to pay, re-rent or rely on luck to keep playing them is just a shame.
Lost Saga is lobby-based, so fans of games like DFO will feel comfortable here.  Once you've selected your desired mission or PVP event, you enter a lobby to wait for more players or you can enter a dungeon solor by locking out other players with a password or by using the matuchmaking options.  From there, things are pretty straightforward.  You fight trash mobs, you defeat mini-bosses or towers and doing so turns those into towers for your side, attacking enemies or spawing AI allies to aid you in combat.  It's not a bad idea and it works well.  The gameplay is frenetic, forcing you to think fast, but can mostly be won by simply spamming attack and the occasional powerful skill when it's not on cooldown.  Once you beat the boss, you get a random reward based on performance and then are dropped back into the lobby.  This system isn't as well polished here as it is in other lobby-based MMO's, but the dungeons are much faster, so it doesn't feel so grindy, at least not at first.
A final and minor gripe is the constant pop up balloons from quests and help dialogues that plague the start of this game.    You will click through twenty or more little reward and dialogue balloons just from completing the most pedestrian of tasks, and it gets old.  The writing, which attempts to be clever, is bad and the presentation is just lazy, as all of this dialogue is just pasted on a yellow or blue popup.

Ladies and gentlemen, public school boards and teachers, THIS is how you get people interested in learning about different cultures. This game brilliantly excels at what the public education system in North America ultimately fails to do.
If you live in North America, I know you definitely spent at least 9 years of your public education focussing on Indigenous cultures. In all honesty, the specific focus of "social studies" class didn't change from first grade to ninth (I believe tenth through twelfth focused a lot more on politics and world affairs); it was boring, preachy, repetitive, and about as unengaging as a class can get. Until I tried playing this game, I had a bit of a preconception that all attempts to teach Native American cultures would end up being snooze-a-thons. I didn't even ask why it had to be that way. There is absolutely nothing boring about this game. Not once did I find myself thinking "Will you shut up? No one cares!" In fact, I found myself intentionally seeking out the little documentary-like video clips to watch, and trying to make sure I didn't miss one bit of information from this game.
Outside of that, the main characters are the most loveable cuties in the whole wide world. If you see reviews complaining about the AI being dumb, they were probably written before the patch (and not updated). There is a two-player co-op mode, but for those of us who hate social interaction, rejoice in the not-terrible AI. There are still a few issues, but that's totally okay, it doesn't make the game unplayable or too rage-enducing. That said, some of the controls are so finicky I just about quit. I would recommend stepping away for a bit if you can't get a specific part or going on youtube for the solution (some of them aren't really that obvious).
All in all, a wonderfully executed concept, fun gameplay (albeit with annoying puzzles at some points), and touching story.

Playing Never Alone (Kisima Ingitchuna) felt to me like stepping into a folk tale: not just reading it, but actually experiencing and overcoming the obstacles that the heroes face in that story. It's an actual folk tale, not just one made up for the game. Even better, it comes with deep context. I wasn't just avoiding green ghosts while platforming, I was hiding from the Northern Lights and the ghost children that wanted to play football with my head.
This game is probably most enjoyable for in-between gamers. Hardcore players might get frustrated that the characters won't turn on a dime, and very casual players will likely find the last few chapters frustratingly hard. If you're in the middle, and enjoy story, learning about culture, atmosphere, and animation detail, Never Alone (Kisima Ingitchuna) is a great experience. Personally, I think it's worth playing even you you never make it through to the end.
Second to playing the beautiful white fox, I found the "cultural insights" to be one of my favorite features of the game. I love collecting things in a game, and trying to find every single owl was a great reason to explore the game's settings thoroughly. Some of the insight videos were like mini documentaries, telling me things about how this native culture exists in the modern day. Many of the videos were stories: life and death experiences that had happened to the tellers or their family. Almost all provided depth and background to the game: I learned the traditions of the Northern Lights, I really felt the abandoned landscape of King Island, I saw how the art of the cut scenes came from on the style of real-world scrimshaw, and I got to hear several other traditional stories. I strongly suggest not waiting until the end of the game to watch the insights you unlock.

There will be parallels made to Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past. And this would be a fair comparison. But it's also a much different experience. It introduces more contemporary RPG elements and does so in a fluid way. It's loaded with side quests. The world is more fleshed-out with... flesh. NPC flesh. The skill system feels great, allowing you to build your character as you see fit. Hurl meteors while wielding a big sword? Go for it. Plink at enemies with a bow and arrow while hiding behind a pet? You can do that too.
Aside from gameplay, the art is beautiful. Very colorful, and the atmosphere is top-notch. The sound design is also great, and the music fits the environment, supporting but not distracting from the game.
Despite these good points, this is still early access. I'm enjoying what I've seen so far, and what I've seen is polished, but it will need a lot of content to fulfill the promise I see in it. Whether or not that's delivered on is to be seen. But if it is, I have a feeling it will be one of those gems people will keep playing for years.
