Ok so I have been questioning whether or not I should do a review for this game and I hae decided why not. So let us get one thing straight, this game is still pretty good but it was so much better. Back when it was in Alpha it was a strong game with a lot of potential. The concept was good, the mechanics i.e. looting, crafting where all good, the nether (the main enemy) was and still is a good idea. So why then does it feel now that it is unfinished, glitchy, buggy and too some degree just a broken game full of people killing each other.
This game has become less about killing or surviving against the nether and more hunting other players down and killing them again and again and again. Some players in this game, dont want to fight, instead they want to do what made Nether good; loot, craft, survive and so on. The game makes not attempt to ensure that it doesnt become a cluster of death. The nether are barely in it now, it is literally whoever has the biggest gun wins, and in truth that doesnt appeal to me.
Should you buy and play Nether? I would say no, dont buy this game, really dont, it is frustrating on a few levels. The mechanics are still there just not emphasised enough, the concept of the ganme; survive, pits you against players more than it does the nether (this is usually done in a situation when you get shot at repeatedly without knowing where your shooter is OR when you have a lot of stuff or no stuff). The game just feels rushed and broken. It WAS good, really it was. It could still be good but because of the rushed nature of its development from Alpha to release it still has a lot of broken parts to fix.

Play time: About 6 hours for campaign
The Darkness 2 is based on a popular comic book that I haven’t read, and the first Darkness game never made it to Steam/PC. Fortunately, I found the story strong enough to stand alone so I didn’t feel like I was missing any important backstory. There’s a “previously on the Darkness” cutscene that you can watch upon starting a new game, and there’s actually some “talking head” scenes between game chapters where the protagonist Jackie talks to the player as if he’s narrating his autobiography, so you should be caught up pretty quick.
You play Jackie Estacado, a kind of Mafia boss who has sworn off using the Darkness, a demonic entity that inhabits his body and gives him superhuman powers at the cost of his soul. Too bad for Jackie, a powerful mysterious group comes to town determined to reclaim the Darkness, which they used to be caretakers for. Since the Darkness can only be given up willingly, the only way for them to get it back is by turning Jackie’s life upside down and torturing him into giving it up. This means war.
The Darkness 2 is a first person shooter with the gimmick of having 2 Darkness tentacles that you can use to grab objects or slash at enemies with. You can also dual wield many one handed guns, so essentially you have 4 limbs to kill people with (2 guns + 2 tentacles). The Darkness also gives you a few powers that you unlock through purchasing in darkness “shrines” found throughout the world. You get dark essence by killing enemies and finding special artifacts, then spend the essence at the shrines on skills and upgrades. It’s not an open world game, you just find the shrines all over the place along the way. There are 4 skill trees to spend your essence in, but you won’t find enough essence in one playthrough to purchase everything. You’ll need to use the New Game + option and grind for more essence.
One of the key game elements is the need to destroy light sources (lamps, street lights, etc.) since bright lights will inhibit the Darkness, causing your screen to lens flare out and go black and white. Your powers and Darkness tentacles are also disabled when this happens so if you’re playing one of the higher difficulty levels you need to snipe out lights before you get too close. The Darkness 2 uses a regenerating health system like Gears of War or any of the Modern Warfare games so if you’re taking too much damage, get behind something for a few seconds to recover.
Pros:
+Excellent story with some twisted enemy bosses. The boss battles aren’t spectacular, but you’ll probably really hate those dudes by the time you get to fight them.
+Pretty good graphics, which kind of remind me of the Borderlands games but with more detail. There are a number of death animations for various ways that you can use the Darkness to execute weakened enemies. The tentacle arm executions can be gruesome.
+The game has a long co-op campaign called Vendettas, though I have only tried a few of the missions (they run parallel to the single player campaign with 4 new characters). The Vendetta missions have their own bosses and you can build up character specific skill trees with dark essence gathered in multiplayer games.
Cons:
-There are a ton of characters and even though I’ve played through the game twice, I only know the names of 3-4 of them. I’m sure most of them were in the first game so they’re just making appearances in part 2. They aren’t all that important though, so no sweat.
-The game is very short at under 6 hours for your first playthrough, but this doesn’t include the Vendetta campaign. It means you probably need a co-op partner to get the full experience. For your second/third playthrough (with all your maxed out powers) if you skip the cutscenes you can probably finish the single player campaign in less than 5 hours.
All in all, the Darkness 2 is a great game and well worth the low price you can find it at. It was even in the $1 tier of a Humble Bundle a few months back so you can probably get it cheap. The game’s highlight is the single player story, and you probably won’t find many people playing multiplayer nowadays.

Game: Star Wars: The Force Unleashed II
Format: PC
Released: 0ctober 2010
With the recent advent of Humble Bundles or at least to me they are newish I decided to buy to star wars bundle. In said bundle I received overall a total of 12 star wars games, I won't bore you with the list but that is a lot of star wars.  The game I want to draw attention to here is Star Wars: The Force Unleashed II.
Now  personally I loved the first game other than the levels on Felucia it was a genuinely stellar game. It made you feel powerful, like a real force user out for revenge. The second one? Not so much. It's good and I enjoyed my time with it but my biggest issue is time. I completed the game quit out looked and steam and there it was. FOUR hours of game play from start to finish. Granted I was running through it on medium difficulty but even so should a sequel to a game that had a solid 8-10 story with a♥♥♥♥♥♥tonne of DLC released after the fact last FOUR ♥♥♥♥ing hours? No is the answer to that question. I'll save that rant for later though let's talk about the good first shall we?
Graphics
It was a beautiful game when it first released back in October 2010 and it really does still stand up 4 years later. Weather effects, clothing moving in high winds, the motion capture is genuinely stellar it really shines through. Environments are fantastic and true to the movies, there are really very few games that get as visually close to delivering a star wars experience like Force Unleashed II. The flip side to this is artifacting everywhere all the time. graphical glitches were many and if this were a longer game maybe it would count as less but after FOUR hours there are just far too many graphic glitches. Another thing that ties into that is absolutely no V-syncing options at all and it's constantly stuck at 30FPS no matter the hardware configuration.
Game Play/Mechanics
This is another place where I feel the game before was a better example of how to do things.  It had a better level system,  It had the better skill upgrades In the prequel you gain experience, level up, earn talent spheres, and the spend them on abilities. combos, and skills. in the sequel every time you break something or someone you gain force points which you then spend on the 6 skills open to you. This is literally it. you gain minor other bonuses from different Light Saber crystals but it's so insignificant its barely even worth mentioning. The fighting is much the same but with a severe lack of combos (of which there are only about 20 as opposed to the amount from game number one) really limits the flashy combat and pulls you away from feeling like you are a stupidly powerful Jedi/Sith. No real puzzle elements or alternate paths and that really doesn't help it's case of FOUR hours.
Sound
This will be a real short one. It sounds like Star Wars. biggest point to note here is like the prequel Mr James Earl Jones returns as the voice of Darth Vader. Voice acting is actually very well don across the board but then again you only ever hear about 5 characters actually speak. whodathunkit?
Replayability
NOPE. FOUR hours. FOUR hours. On a harder difficulty I might've gone a whopping 5 hours. some challenges await after completing the game and what DLC was released when pulled from sale for whatever reason. Once this game is finished there is NO reason to EVER come back to it.
Story
You play as the clone of Starkiller for game numero uno on a quest for revenge and to save the one he loves. awww isn't that cute? isn't it also the most generic thing ever? I won't rant too much here I did enjoy it even for its generic seen it before storyline the voice acting really helped me trundle through the story. Much like the first game(noticing a theme yet?) you will be required to fight Darth Vader. this is the highlight of any of the bosses but I felt even that may have dragged on a bit too long.
Okay rant time. Lucas Arts all you had to do was make the first game again make it look prettier and everyone would have been so happy with the end product but no, like every other developer you decide that you should change one of the fundamentally greatest things from the first game. The progression for Starkiller. you took what made that game great and just♥♥♥♥♥♥all over it with number 2(see what I did there?) I really wish that you had just copy pasted for number 2 and considering that  because of Disney we won't get number 3 there are so many things you left unanswered. is he Starkiller prime? is he just a clone like all the rest? If he is a clone why can he use the force? There is a real simple solution to all of this. DONT MAKE IT FOUR ♥♥♥♥ING HOURS! another 4-6 hours and you could have told the rest of star killers story and fans would have been happy but now all I have is an empty pit of unanswered questions and disappointment for series that could have been so much more.

Landscape
Dinosaurs/Buildings in the distance
Bushes/Dinosaur food

Pvp would be very fun if the bodies wouldn't stack, and have a time limits as to when they start to "rot" into the ground. This would also make the game more challenging and fun for all players.

Bites marks more around the legs and the neck
Scratches on the sides or tails
Bruises on areas where the bone sticks out more
Scars leftover from battle, light and barely noticable unless you look closely.

Never Alone is a cultural art/game/story platformer.  The game is based
on a story from the natives of Northern Alaska, passed down through video game
format.  Overall the game runs smoothly, with a beautiful atmosphere conveyed
through visually appealing graphics.
The game is rich with traditional Northern Alaskan culture, with beautiful
visuals and music that captures the atmosphere perfectly.  There are also 'cultural
insights'; little clips you can unlock throughout the game that sheds some
light onto the native community and culture.
The platforming element of the game is done well.  As this game is
available to be played co-op, the challenges are scaled up to make it
challenging enough for two, so  playing the game as a single player can be
even more challenging.  You sometimes need to switch between the main
character and the companion, which does necessitate going slightly slower
in order to go back and forth between characters.
The game has a unique atmosphere, and while it is challenging, I didn't
find it to be repetitive or unfair.  The balance between usage of mechanics and
length of the game was done very well.  The atmosphere, story, and environment are woven together in an artistic, well done way, making this a game that
is easy to recommend.

Admittedly, I went into this game not knowing much about it at all, which is somewhat rare for me in this day and age. I did this because I felt I didn't need to know much about the game, my very first impression from the trailer and a youtube video sold me on the spot. And I can say, roughly 9 hours into the game as of this review, that my first impression was spot on. If you enjoy the classic action RPGs of the 1990's and early 2000's, such as Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past, Illusion of Gaia, or (obviously) Secret of Mana, then this game is for you and is well worth your time, money, and intrigue.
From my perspective, this game offers 4 distinct areas of interest that define the experience:
I will be covering all 4, explaining my experiences and impressions of each.
While a bit lacking in the engaging story aspect, Secret of Grindea's (SoG) Story Mode offers something many RPGs have failed to have for a while now: the elegance of simplicity. Many modern titles have an obsession with creating a novel's worth of narrative. Cutscene after cutscene, wall of text after wall of text, the experience of these titles are moreso about the story and presentation of it than the actual game.
SoG takes the short and simple approach, where it gives enough story and narrative to provide context and motivation, but is spaced well enough where it does not feel like a chore to read through it all (having the option to skip cutscenes helps too). Not to say that the story isn't interesting, though. While simple and somewhat of a parady of other RPGs, many of the characters are likeable in their own right and their clever interactions are both entertaining and humurous. It's clear a lot of heart was put into the devolpment of this game from all of the silly and minor references to other games and characters.
Putting aside the storytelling aspect of SoG, there's quite a bit of content packed into what is currently available (game is still in beta as of this review). From collectables, to crafting, to minigames, puzzles, Zelda-esque dungeons, side quests, arena challenges, and engaging and replayable boss fights, there's a lot to do. But my favorite aspects are the inclusion of a genuinely difficult hard mode that can be toggled on or off at any time and the ability to customize the look of your character in the form of hats and accessories (that override the look of your currently equipped armor).
To review:
Pros:
Cons:
Arguably, this is where most of your time will go. This mode is SoG's roguelike feature, where you attempt to progress as far as you can through a serious of increasingly challenging rooms and obstacles on a single life. Much in the way of other roguelikes (such as Rogue Legacy), you have the ability the make succeeding runs easier in the form of unlocking perks. These are unlocked via a currency you obtain randomly as a drop and from completing quests and achievments.
The farther you go and the better you do, the more points you will recieve. After each death, your points are tallied up and added to your total score across all games. After certain thresholds have been met, you will revieve rewards, such as cosmetics (hats and accessories), more NPCs to interact with, and more buildings/decorations for your hub. There is also a global leaderboard for the mode, so if you're into that sort of thing you can sate your fancy here.
As for the actual content of the mode, it's challenging but rewarding. Like any other roguelikes, there are a lot of elements of randomness involved. The dungeon layout, challenges in each room, and the loot you get are all up to chance. However, this works as the combat system is based on skill moreso than raw stats. You will get farther in the dungeon because you got better rather than because you got some good luck on your drops. You find that you are excited to get as far as you can as that shows just how much better you got at the game more than anything else.
Pros:
Cons:
While I have no personal experience with this feature myself, I have seen examples of this in videos and streams. From what I have seen, multiplayer is fairly smooth and simple to do. Multiplayer is available for both Story Mode and Arcade Mode, so if you have a group of friends you can enjoy all aspects of the game together with up to 4 people.
Be that as it may, it's not perfect. Currently, there is no option to play with your friends locally. You will need to connect to each other through different computers, and each person will need to have a copy. Additionally, it lacks some quality of life functions such as being able to join someone from your friends list. And, as one would expect from online play, there can exist some connection issues and bugs (although I've yet to see any).
Pros:
Cons:
An RPG needs to have some form of progression, and SoG does it with it's ability system. What makes this one stand out from the rest is its simplicity and its lack of restrictions. There are no skill trees, no level/stat requirements, you just choose the skills you like and roll with it. And so much is added to this game because of it.
There are a varity of skills that appeal to all forms of play, be it aggressive, defensive, evasive, melee, range, single target, AoE, Burst, DoT, etc. And given the lack of restrictions on obtaining skills, you can create a massive amount of different and interesting builds. Want to be an aggressive and fast melee striker? Go for it. Want to be a long-ranged magic nuker? Sure! Want to combine both melee and magic for a hybrid spellsword? That's cool too.
Additionally, a lot of the skills from different branches work well together. For instance, Static shock is a spell that will do additionally damage very time you hit with a physcial attack. You can restore charges for this skill from using physical skills or doing perfect guards, meaning this skill can be used in all kinds of builds, both offensive and defensive.
While I would argue a need for more skills, the simplicity of the current design is also appealing and useful. While some talents prove to be more useful than others, many of the skills have their uses and can work well given the right circumsances.
In the end, what gives this game a lot of replayability, both in Story Mode and in Arcade Mode, is the progression system and the appeal of trying out new builds and tactics.

TL;DR: The game is basically an un-needed “expansion” to the first game (aka. the mechanics/graphics are pretty much the same with an additional story) and is not particularly fun.
I played and loved the first Force Unleashed and so had hope - even though the majority of reviews were bad - that this game would still be good. From a technical standpoint, the fighting and force use are still there from the first game, but the gameplay and level design are just inferior in every way.
Here is the differences between the this game and the first from a gameplay perspective.
Level Design: Levels are really long and repetitive. Each level has "puzzles" that seemed incredibly forced - almost like the designers said, “This is a game about the force, I guess we need to add some puzzles that use it, but we don’t have time to do more than about 5 types of them, so lets just try and reuse them over and over and over again.” There are basically no “secrets” or reasons to explore.
Level Variety: There are essentially 3 environments that you play in, 2 of those environments you play twice for a total of about 5 levels.
Bosses: There is really only 1 boss and he is not nearly as fun as any of the first games' bosses. There are 2 other “bosses” but they are more like quick time events.
Enemies: I counted roughly 10 different enemies in the entire game. So be prepared to kill lots of stormtroopers and their variations.
Story: Pretty bad. It adds pretty much nothing to the Star Wars universe and builds no extra connection with any of the characters from the first game.
Length: Each level is about an hour and a half long. So the game comes to about… 6 hours.
So no, I don’t recommend this game, even if you consider it an “expansion.” It is just not fun, and really does not bring any of the fun back from the first Force Unleashed. In fact, this game basically feels incomplete/rushed in about every area. Pretty disappointing that all the bad reviews were right :(
+The force and fighting style is still there, just a little bit more polished.
-No real good boss fights
-Level Design is horrible
-The game adds nothing in way of substatial lore to the Star Wars Universe
-This game was flat out not fun
-Game felt rushed/unfinished
-6 hours of gameplay?

I actually have been playing this series in an odd order. I completed SE3 first, then SE1 (Wasn't into it with it first came out, but recently became fond of it, probably after seeing what they did to it with V2 and 3), and now am wading through SE2. I liked SE3 quite a bit, it was a lot of fun, but my main gripe with it was the braindead AI and broken stealth mechanics. Which still exists here. But the upside was that SE2 was a bit more of a playground, and the AI were slightly more aggressive.
So in Sniper Elite V2, you obviously play as a sniper, but you don't really feel like one at all. It just feels like it's on rails to me. Most often, the best thing to do when you see enemies is to just sit and one spot and shoot all of them. Yeah, even with the difficulty and realism settings on max. You don't even have to be good at it, honestly, just wait for your health to come back and pop out to rapid-fire snipe them until it hits them. Though there is a lot of reward to get headshots and vital shots without the diamond aim assist. With the aim assist you just get to feel badass.
But sitting in one place for five minutes is bad, right? No, the AI (even at the highest difficulty) don't really do anything that forces you to move. You never need to set up traps like they show you in the tutorial, you'll barely get any good chances to use them. They lack the ability to perform fire-and-movement tactics, or flanking maneuvers, and grenades are easily dealt with by walking backwards. Just inch your gun out from behind cover to where nobody can shoot you, but you can shoot them. That's it. If they get too close you can just use iron sights on your rifle, or throw a grenade (they won't run away from them). All of the submachine guns are worthless (you're more likely to die using them than you are killing anyone with them). I haven't tried any pistol except for the Welrod, with its gloriously inaccurate 6-round magazine, so if they are any good I am unaware of it. Welrod is nice though. Even if you fail the miserable stealth system, just shoot them three times in a row with the welrod to kill, and no matter how much yelling they make, it won't attract anyone. It just stunlocks them. Actually, it doesn't seem like ANYTHING the AI says influences their fellow soldiers. Their speech is just empty, like only you can hear it.
Speaking of stealth, it's simple. Don't be seen, don't be heard. Well, often times falling a short distance (maybe a foot off of some object, this is a normal thing when proceeding through the level) will cause some horrendous noise that alerts enemies half a block away from you, causing them all to walk around awkwardly shouting "I know you're here, sniper!!" "Sniper no sniping!!" "What was that!? A sniper?!". Yet shooting someone that is just a foot away from someone facing the opposite direction, having them scream and gasp and fall to the ground, will not alert them...this is exactly the problem I had experienced in SE3, and I get this crap in almost every level.
Another thing, which is kind of interesting, is that there are some environmental noises that can mask your gunshot. But..it doesn't really make sense. Your gunshot is only masked if YOU are in range of the object that masks your noise. An enemy could be by a noise source and hear everything going on. But if you stand by a noise source and a bullet whizzes right past their face, they aren't going to notice a thing. Nope. Not even if it hits the wall right beside them.
One time, I think it was the third level, in the underground factory or whatever it was, I had a big firefight on one of the big hallways. Of course all I had to do was crouch behind a table and shoot all six of those nazis. Despite all of their hollering and return fire, I walk into one of the side corridors, not even 10 meters away from a dead nazi, and there's a guy just peacefully walking along as if he didn't notice a thing.
So basically, I don't know what anyone was expecting from these sequels. But I was coming to this hoping for an awesome, gritty, realistic, stealth-sniping game, and if you want that you can give SE1 a try, it's not great but it's good (really dated, might not be an issue for other gamers). What I got was more like a light gun shooter. This game could've been great, but everything about how the AI reacts to the player made it go all wrong. SE3 is better, but still has the same problems. And I'll probably get SE4 too just because it's supposed to be even more sandboxy.

I’ll admit up front, my understanding of American history and our secession from the British is lacking. I suppose my teenage and collegiate studies into key events, people, and issues is limited to dudes throwing crates of tea off a boat, and some guy riding a horse through Massachusetts, screaming, “the British are coming!”
One of the things I love about board gaming, and in this instance, a digital replication of it, is you can learn about various historical scenarios, all the while trouncing your foolish opponent into the ground for leaving Boston open to a naval assault.
1775: Rebellion opens up with a dramatic FMV, featuring a misty, forested countryside. Soon, troops from both sides of the war are aiming down their barrels, and firing off-screen. This sets the stage, albeit a little more dramatic than the actual gameplay.
1775: Rebellion plays up to four, with two teams, the British (red and yellow) and the Americans (blue and white). One can control both of their factions, or split up the work between two players a side. One can also choose between three different scenarios: the 1775 short game, the full 1775 game, and The Battle for Quebec (the advanced variant). Each has specific setup differences and slightly different rule changes and card additions to complete the gameplay experience.
The game board focuses on the new American colonies, and has a smattering of red, blue, white, and yellow figures all over it. The Americans have a strong hold on the New York and Boston coastline, while the British are slowly establishing themselves south of that, but completely dominating in Canada and the northern “states”. In addition there are Native Americans on the board, but later on, the French will assist the Americans, and German Hessians will come to the aid of the British. Lots of warfare. Lots of conflict. Better yet, these troops can pop up at various places you thought you had complete control of.
The game is played until all have played a truce card from their hands, or at the end of the last round. Turn order is decided randomly. Throughout your turn, you might be able to play special cards, based on what stage of turn you are on. With your hand of three cards, you must first place recruits and fled units onto cities you own. Then you must move a number of troops X spaces, all depending on your card.
You can only move your own colored armies, but you can pick up the troops of your teammate along the way. These movements typically will either help to reinforce key locations on the board, or more likely, initiate combat with an enemy you land on.
Combat is simple, with each color soldier having specific balance to the values on their individual dice. Some roll more kills, and some have more ability to retreat from combat, or reposition themselves to hold ground better. Each instance is last man standing, so ideally you brought enough men to the fight to mostly guarantee success.
Once you’ve controlled all zones located inside a colony, you are given a control chit. The team who has more control chits at the end of the game are declared winners.
This digital translation is an impeccable production of the original tabletop game, even though I say that with a few caveats.
It changes no mechanics. It faithfully reproduces the aesthetic of the original game. Cubes are replaced with figurine soldiers who march hopefully around the battlefield. Cards can be examined more closely. The dice roll around, slowly clomp into each other, even precariously toppling onto a die face resulting in either heartbreak, or total domination. This hearkens back to the all-important dice roll in the film Jumanji, as you pray for the roll to destroy your last enemy before they have another chance to counter.
Even the game box sits up in the corner of the screen, as if you just gathered around the table with some friends to simulate historical rebellion together. Visually, HexWar has flawlessly implemented the feel of 1775: Rebellion. Even including sound effects of gunfire, marching, and special abilities. These are the stars of 1775.
One wonderful addition to the 1775 gameplay is saving your game. It is easy to drop a game, save, and come back later to finish it. Games will play quick against AI, so it’s up to you to remember unit placement, and what strategy you were implementing.
As a beta tester for 1775, I saw great things, and strange things. First of all, I rather prefered the original score for the game. It has since been replaced with a very MIDI-sounding orchestral bit that doesn’t do the game justice. In all reality, one would feel more atmospheric if they played Revolutionary War tunes from Spotify and muted the in-game music. It just feels forced and strange.
Hexwar has made great strides to simplify the combat presentation, and help players to better understand where to click on the UI and how to initiate combat and movement. Combat plays out with units in the middle of the screen, surrounded by dialog boxes detailing how many of each unit are in the fight. When you need to roll or decide where to lose units, it is evident where to click, and when you need to. I appreciate this UI, and while I think it is a little messy, it does a fine job.
Choosing where to group your armies is weird. You grab giant, chunky squares to decide how many stay and how many leave. It feels mostly responsive, but is still a tad clunky.
Like I mentioned, most of these are nitpicky, but my least favorite function in this game is the camera movement. I don’t need silky smooth zoom and pans, but when an enemy moves their units around, the camera jumps to and fro, like a puppy towards the ball that two kids are tossing back and forth. It’s disorienting. I know the goal of this camera move is to focus the player on where the opponent is positioning, but it sometimes ends up more confusing as certain spaces light up, yet I’m still confused why the camera moved where it did.
Another nitpick on camera is how jumpy it feels while you navigate the map. Luckily it’s not a huge board, and you generally want a bird’s-eye view anyway. Simple clicks can pop the map around a bit, so I suppose it feels sensitive, especially on higher sensitivity mouse settings.
One other note is: either I don’t grasp the strategy to 1775, or the AI really isn’t very smart. I don’t understand the appeal to placing 14 yellow units on one space, only to never move them the entirety of the game. Of course, it didn’t matter because they max at three dice a combat roll, but I moved in with 7 dice to roll per engagement. They melted, and partly to my own good die rolls, but I can’t help but wonder why the AI turtles at times.
If you are looking for multiplayer, it is here, and works fine. Some will love play-by-email, but I’m too impatient for such a thing. By creating a Hexwar account, you will be notified when your opponent finishes their turn. I would rather have a live-hosted game where I can communicate quickly back and forth with my opponent, trash-talking and what not.
Technical strangeness aside, I find this digital adaptation of one of my favorite historical games to be good and interesting. Yes, there are some odd things about the execution, but the pristine gameplay and attention to aesthetic detail excuse those things for me.
+ Absolutely faithful adaptation of the board game presentation and mechanics
+ AI games play quickly
+ Interesting integration of animation and presentation of figures on the board
- AI makes questionable strategic decisions
- Play by email isn’t the most ideal multiplayer solution

I didn't play the boardgame so I can't vouch for how close of an adaptation this is. That being said, I won my first playthrough as continental army/patriots on default difficulty and I enjoyed the game.
Interesting game mechanics - turns are random every round and your turn consists of 3 phases - reinforce -> move -> battle. You draw 3 random cards at the beginning of your turn and play them during one of the three phases depending what the card is. Sometimes the French/Hessians will show up to reinforce you, sometimes you will pull a warship movement enabling you to hit your opponent from any coast, and sometimes you won't get a movement at all. In my opinion this randomness makes you think on your feet and makes the game pretty enjoyable.
I was worried this would be too much like Risk and it really isn't. It's fairly unique.

Okay so let me first explain what you're getting into, if you haven't played this yet.
You are one of the many survivors that survived an apocalypse. You're angry at the world and band together with random people to kill the other angry people that banded together. So far so good. After the apocalypse something called "The Forest" swoops in and throws "anomalys" all over your junk. Hmm... ok. You go to random places and kill people for.... I dunno really, let's say just because you can.
The actual gameplay isn't much different from any other FPS game, you spawn, you shoot, you kill, you die. And unlike most FPS's bullets kill, fast. The big difference are the anomalys all over your junk, at the very beginning when you do your tutorial they will kill you. You have no chance of destroying them, you'll have to join a specific faction. Well actually there are 2 factions that can deal with them.
You start with 4 weapons at the very beginning; a pistol which doesn't do jacksquat, a SMG, a hunting rifle, and a carbine. I chose the SMG for my first battle and thought I start wrecking people. Now the game itself is quite well made, looks really good. The maps feel big with lots of hiding and sniping places. Now I start the battle and find some unsuspecting sucker and I start rat-a-tat-tating away, killed him, done. Not a second later I got sniped by a carbine of which I neatly get to see in the kill-cam that shows me my last seconds, neat. A little more into the battle I realised that the SMG is kind of bad but still good enough to kill people if they didn't see me or didn't expect me. The overly used weapon that was stopping me in my tracks were the carbines. Apparently the devs thought it'd be super nice to have people start out with a one-hit killing machine that is the carbine, headshot, bodyshot, no matter. one shot, one kill.
Now if the shot didn't outright kill the person they will be bleeding and if they didn't bring a bandage or didn't use it in that second they had left they would die. mercilessly. Oh but don't think these killing machines were for mid to long range only, these weapons of destruction can easily be used at close range too.
Now this is just the first battle where you have absolutely no armor or gear to help you survive. 2 factions offer armor that would give you more time to react on the bleeding when you get shot. However they have absolutely no defence against these anomalys that are spawning in your face, not just in your face though, often they spawn in key locations such as safe routes or sniping area's. You can definatly survive if you ran, but you will have at least 50% less health which is incredibly annoying and putting you on a disadvantage. The starting bandage also doesn't really help you recover from that. So let's say you want to remove these overly annoying anomaly's... Well you'd have to join one of the other 2 factions which offer little armor against other people but let you survive and kill off anomaly's... and when you try to destroy one... well... I think you got one hit killed again by a carbine... *kill-cam* yup, he was waiting for you.
Obviously to be -not- annoyed you'd need teamwork between all the factions in one team, rarely is there ever teamwork.
A little further in the game I noticed that there is no overall gear to buy at all, you need to unlock them at your faction. Great. Also after every game you have a chance on some gear/money/items and you really only get 1 chance, if RNG has never been on your side, well... for a small sum of real money you can try again. Sometimes the loot you get is so damaged that you can't really wear it unless you repair it, but it'll take 12 hours. Or repair it immediatly for gold/real money...
TL;DR / The List
Pros
+Beautifull aesthetics
+Nice/Real looking guns that actually hurt
+Variety in roles to play
+Various game modes
+Great sound
+Killcam
Cons
-Only one character model
-One hit killing weapons
-A lot depends on teamwork
-Anomalys can wreck your face
-Bleeding... why would you even have this?*
-long wait times before getting into a game
-bad matchmaking, pitching high levels against lows.
-quite a bit of pay-to-have items
-lots of in your face carrot on a stick moves to make you throw your money away
-It's a russian game**
-no balance
notes:
*Sure bleeding makes the game realistic but nobody is really waiting to die from a shot and would normally kill them but didn't but will still kill you cuz you didn't press 3 in time.
**Call me whatever you want but the rusky's are where most of the aimbots/hackers/scriptkiddies come from. And the game oh so happens to have underpar anti-cheat. Want to appeal to the masses? At the very least have a spoken english tutorial, the translation on the vids are just plain dumb.

Go and buy the game when it's on sale for around 20$.

Lost Saga is a great game.
It has that unique feel to it that no other game can even hope to obtain.
With an ever growing roster of heroes to choose from, it shouldn't be hard to find a hero that works for you. From the iconic characters of franchises such as KoF, BlazBlue, Guilty Gear, Samurai Shodown, God of High School, etc to characters like the Legendary King Arthur, Robin Hood, Hong Gil Dong (Staff Master). Lost Saga offers over 60+ characters to play as and enjoy. Theres a hero for everyone out there! A common complaint is that the game is 'p2w' however that really is not the case whatsoever. With the major system update, the NA quests have been brought to the original prizes of the mother game. Newcomers to Lost Saga can expect 2 free permanent heroes of their choice using 'permanent basic scrolls' relatively early on for playing the game. The events award players a variety of style items, gears, and other in-game items. The log-in system utilized in Lost Saga awards player for logging in daily and theres even a special prize for logging in for 5/10/15/20/25 days. With plenty of game modes, tons of customization, this game certainly has something for everyone. However, no publisher is perfect the game does have its latency issues, text problems, and other errors that other games experience from time to time. Most major problems are resolved in a timely manner. For fans of fighting games, you've found your haven. Come to Lost Saga, and experience for yourself why we play 'on another level'. Give the game a decent try, and you'll see it can be quite fun :D

Frictional Games continues strong with their atmospheric horror survival genre with SOMA. If you've played Amnesia, then the mechanics will be familiar to you. The core concept of "encountering a monster->hide, evade and distract monster->escape the area" are well founded and play very well. It was nice that there was more than one type of monster, which shakes up the encounters quite a bit. Overall, the mechanics are pretty standard and they have them well-rounded at this point.
The surrounding story and environment complete the package. There is much more detail in the environments than their previous games and the underwater facility feels more than just a setting, it feels alive and has purpose. The outside areas where you walk on the ocean floor are excellent and feel very genuine. They're not anything to write home about compared to some games (ie. Bioshock) but it held its own. I would have to point out that from a level design perspective, some areas were over-cluttered as I did become stuck trying to figure out where to go or what to do in certain parts. Stronger cues would have been helpful in these spots and some I felt were unecessary obstacles that didn't really add to the gameplay.
The story itself was one of their strongest yet. It dealt with interesting moral dilemas and although I felt the character did not quite ask the right questions, overall I felt I had gained some insight by the end of the game.
Best title from Frictional Games so far. I look eagerly look forward to their next production.

If the best level in an action game is the one where there is no fighting at all,just walking and cinematics...it says a lot about the game, doesn't it.
The Force Unleashed II is a lazy cash grab sequel that shouldn't have been made. Apart from a few moments, and all of them are non-combat related, it is a bland,boring and short game.
The story is...well not much of a story. It somehow feels empty, no structure, no twists, no anything. The only potential twist they could have done is more of a hint that leaves it up to you to think about it, but it's not one of those mindblowing things you wrap your head around for days. In this case, it is up to a minute. And then you're back to cursing Lucas for deciding to make this game.
The combat is the same as in the previous game, but somehow you are even more overpowered, and with the regenerating health and the ridiculously overpowered force lightning, you will just breeze through the game. Oh wait, you won't. Because it is filled with too many QTEs. Almost everything is a QTE. Every other door requires you to mash a button in order to open it. And the prompts are scattered to the sides of the screen so you have to look everywhere just to see them, and it doesn't help that they are small and easily blend with the surrondings.
The level and boss design are just lazy and atrocius. In the first game, levels did happen on same planets, but those were outdoor areas and they did bother to make them look interesting visually. Here there is a lot of backtracking through monotonous corridors and hallways, just wishing for the game to end. Bosses come down to silly QTEs followed by sillier button mashing with no patterns or anything. The final level+boss are especially frustrating, with the former consisting of a single needlessly long and generic platforming section...copied twice more. And that one section consists of a single platform copied ten times or so. And the boss is just a bunch of waves of enemies followed by button mashing...followed by a long QTE which ends with you having to mash the Q button for some 10s or so. And the game is ridiculously short even with the backtracking and level copy-pasting, and can be easily beaten in about 2-3 hours tops.
If I would have to choose anything good about the game...it would be the Dagobah level, mentioned at the beginning of this review.No fighting at all, just great ambient,atmosphere and cutscenes. Two more nice moments, both without fighting...and that would be it. Voice actors did the best they could, and did a pretty good job if I might say, but they can't do anything for the bland writing for an even blander story.
This is a game that definitely shouldn't have been made, and you shouldn't waste your time and money on it. If you are still interested in the story, might as well go to YT and watch all the cinematics (and maybe levels)...it might even be more enjoyable than playing the game itself.

Review is thumbs down for game balance issues -- I ran into a boss fight where the boss had a healing ability, and so did one of its minions, and they were able to outpace my ability to deal damage, rendering all of my opponents effectively invulnerable and immortal -- so I eventually had to flee the fight.  I tried to rest, and was immediately beset by another group of monsters -- who also had a healer who could also keep up with my ability to deal damage.  After several tries, I eventually managed to flee and escape the adventure.
It feels like there are a lot more complicated details and numbers than there need to be, and like the numbers/details that are there aren't balanced against eachother in a coherent way.  It also feels like the game is very broad and scattered -- I'm supposed to care about the stats, skill trees, and equipment of several dozen adventurers who level up once every few minutes, simultaneously?  While monsters invade, quests happen, crafting things, and balancing town reputation?  Rather than having you focus on one very complicated thing, or thirty very simple things, it wants you to concentrate on thirty very complicated things -- it doesn't scale well, and has problems guiding the player's expectations and experience.  Generally, simplification, polish, and balance would do it a world of good.
Check the steam discussion forums before deciding whether or not to buy it.  Check out the problems people tend to have, and the mods' responses to those problems, and follow your heart.

So I just finished Never Alone, which is more or less an Inupiat (one of the northern Alaska/Canada native cultural groups) fable set around some light platforming.
The fable part is cool as hell. Absolutely wonderful art and audio direction paired with Inupiat-language subtitled narration is transportive in a way that actually deserves the word. I grew up in the northern plains of the US (Minnesota) and the feel of cold, winter, and blizzards are conveyed in Never Alone in a way that I've never experienced in a game before. It's worth the ($15) price of admission for that alone.
The platforming, on the other hand, ranges from "reasonable" in the dead-easy first two-thirds of the game to "unbearably janky" in the final three sequences. I made it through thanks to a checkpoint system that would be generous to a fault in a game with mechanics that aren't actively offensive, but I would have gladly hit an autoplay button to experience the story and the ambiance so as not to have to suffer through the awful gameplay in those later sections.
That said, I'd recommend playing it through rather than watching it on YouTube if only to enjoy the production values and to be put into the story a little more, at least in the early sections. Plus you unlock "cultural insights" which are slickly produced live-action segments that illustrate some fashion of Inupiat culture, history, lifestyle, and suchlike.
It's not long (~6 hours it took me, maybe?) and best enjoyed with a co-op partner (switching characters during timed-platforming sections is one of the larger issues with the gameplay, though it's not quite as irritating as the unresponsive movement and janky collision).
Definitely recommended, though I can't fathom the universe in which this gets a 10/10.

TL:DR - Never Alone (Kisima Ingitchuna) is a beautifully done, artistic piece of Iñupiat culture. (Pros/Cons Below)
Never Alone is best played with two people, but still plays very well solo since many of the puzzles only require one character to do something at a time, and the ai controlling the other character is intelligent (for the most part). The dynamic between the two characters is worth mentioning, since both have different but complimentary playstyles; the fox being more nimple at climbing or crawling through small spaces, whereas the girl can climb ladders, move objects, or use her weapon to break ice.
In addition, Never Alone shares the Iñupiat culture in a tasteful and powerful way. Short cultural videos - that display the beautiful alaskan landscape, and the lifestyle of the Iñupiat people - can be unlocked in-game by encountering lore owls. The gameplay/storyline itself is also rich with Iñupiat folklore; such as spirits helping you traverse perilous terrain or dwarf-like characters causing mischief.
All in all a beautifully done game which is not only fun to play, but teaches you something in the process.
------------------------------------------------------------
------------------------------------------------------------
PROS:
----------
- Smart & intense gameplay
+ Interesting and moderately difficult puzzles
+ Occasional fast-paced action sequences
+ Minor map exploration elements
- Great for co-op
- Stunning visuals
- In-depth cultural experience
CONS:
----------
- Occasional gameplay/graphical glitches
- Short storyline

Review ( as of 7/23/15)
Secrets of Grindea is a great throwback to the ARPG genre and takes heavy influence from a lot of games from the SNES era of RPGs. The game is played from a top-down perspective and combat is done in real-time, comparable to Secret of Mana and 2D Legend of Zelda games. If you like the combat in those games you'll probably enjoy Secrets of Grindea.
The skill and customization options in the game are very unique in how much freedom the game gives you as a player. The game gives you several options as far as play styles, but you can mix and match the skills as you desire and create a unique playstyle and skill set for yourself. You're also given 2 cosmetic item slots for your characters to customize your hat and/or face accessory so that you can look good, but keep the stats of much better items instead.
The Pixel art is great, everything looks vibrant and is very reminiscent of the SNES era, but at the same time has a very modern feel. The Music is fits well, and is exactly what you'd expect from most RPGs. The humor and references are great, if you've played a lot of RPGs, you'll really appreciate the games' dialogue and subtle nods to other franchises.
The Arcade mode adds great replayability to the game by adding a roguelike element in randomly generated areas and starting from the beginning if you die, great for those looking for a challenge and wanting more of the game.
Did I mention the game supports (Online) Multiplayer? It does, this game can be even more fun with friends! You can go through the Story Mode or Arcade together and this only adds to the game's merits. Local Co-Op is currently unsupported unfortunately.
At the time of writing this review, the game is in early access and incomplete and Story Mode is a bit short, but I strongly suggest trying out the demo and trying the game for yourself. If you like it, you'll probably enjoy what the full game offers now and in the future.

I played the first Shark Attack Deathmatch on xbox and a friend saw this sequel and bought it for me. Getting back into it, I forgot just how stressful, in a good way, this game is. There are few games that get genuine audible responses from me while I play. I am ashamed to admit I have yelped in sudden terror several times.  There has not been a much more frightening experience than finishing off a bull shark with a harpoon to the head, letting out half a sigh of relief because I escaped with my life in tact, only to have a great white come out of the murky depths and chomp. Murdered by a shark.
The beauty of this game is it's simplicity and delivery. It doesn't promise you anything more than what it is and really delivers on what it promises. A fun, scary, deathmatch where you get to shoot harpoons at your friends while simultaneously avoiding underwater living nightmares. I am a fan of the survival mode too.
For five bucks? That's a big win.
Upset with early access games? Me too. This game is solid, relatively bug free, and easy to play. The devs are all over the bug fixes too with patch notes easily accesible from the menu. (Not something you see everyday). This is definitely on the positive side of early access and doesn't feel like a QA test but more like an actual game.
The only problem I have is that not enough people own it, so now that this review is over. Instead of that cheeseburger, spend the five dollars on a fantastic and unnerving experience that you can play and enjoy. Then, make your friends play and watch them squirm.

Star Wars: The Force Unleashed II, a 3rd person hack and slash platformer with QTE's (quick time events), and a lot of button mashing.
Now that the i have that out the way I will delve a little deeper **MAY CONTAIN SPOILERS**.
This game is very short, taking me around 4 hours 30 minutes to complete with the 'Light Side' ending. The story is nothing amazing, you are apparantly cloned by Darth Vader who used dna from "Starkiller" of the first game and you are apparantly defective due to the flashbacks you have which are memories from Starkiller's past life, one of the flashbacks reveals the female pilot, Juno from the previous game (who you fall in love with) and you decide to go searching for her  and you kick some♥♥♥♥♥along the way, thats about it so dont expect anything epic.
Gameplay is good, but again like the first one its nothing special, another devil may cry hack and slash platformer with an anorexic leveling up system. Some people said its repetetive and it can be, but they also complain saying its the same attacks and QTE's over, and over again, and i know why, button mashing. Instead of timing your attacks to allow variations in your combos and QTE's people are just mashing buttons, I found that timing my attacks and combining force powers in with them resulted in some brilliant combos and finishers and i thoroughly enjoyed doing so for the entire game. The QTE's at first were the same repeated over and over, until i realised they changed depending on how you messed up the enemy, throwing objects at an enemy to start the QTE gave a different result compared to using force lightning to bring up the QTE which resulted in another finishing move, so each QTE to me was different unless it was a mini-boss those were the same. The platfroming side of the game is a big improvement over the first game, its more refined and felt responsive and fluid plus I didnt find myself falling off/out of the level due to poor game mechanics like I did in the first game. So, overall gameplay I found it better, but shorter than the first game.
The graphics, that definitive question everyone wants to know, does it look good? YES! it looks nice in 1080p with all settings on max, but has very few graphical options which is nothing new for console ports, it run smooth on my pc with me only having issues with the video cutscenes pausing and crashing the game at first which turned out to be a compatability issue with windows 8.1, but easily fixed by setting compatability to Windows 7. The cutscenes i noticed varied in quality through out the game some being clear then others being blocky, but nothig major.
The sound is your typical Star Wars soundtrack always good and what we expect to hear when playing a Star Wars game, but i personally prefered the soundtrack from the first game it felt more dramatic for some reason.
Controls, I used a Xbox 360 controller which worked fine no issues at all (it is a console port so thats to be expected) I have read that people say the Keyboard+Mouse is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ to play this game with, but each to their own i say.
The game overall was fun to play I really did enjoy it, and im a full on gamer who plays everything and anything and reading the reviews for this game anyone would of thought it was garbage heap material, but its not as bad as people make it out to be. If you have played the first game its the same gameplay just refined and shortened with better visuals and little to no story. It could do with being longer and having more depth not only in storyline but actual character customisation. Its worth playing if you have played the first one but dont pay full price for this try get it in a sale or now from
, Its more like an expansion pack for the first game due to the shortness of and the only thing to make you play it again is the challenge mode and alternate endings (load your save chose alternate option, done). Im gonna give this game a 7/10 I liked it, plenty of epic moments just too short.

I'm about 2.4 hours into the game thus far but already i can absolutely recommend this to any true star wars fan. In the beginning there wasn't anything just Darkness and void.. and that's the way the Darkness liked it.
I'll start off with saying I never played The Darkness ( first game ) but 2 was a wonderful experience. At first glance (and possibly a first few minutes of playing) the game seems like a quick comic book styled lame action game but its actually really in depth, and quite fun to play.
Overall the story is excellent and often times I found myself quite engaged with the plot. I will admit the demonic themes of the game were slightly concerning at first but I eventually found myself quite enjoying the way everything was portrayed. The main character Jackie might be a little shallow, 2d or cardbordish but the game's in between levels cutscenes where Jackie reveals his past make him a more rounded character.. and so it evens out in my opinion. The main female of the game, though not overly present (usually in flashbacks or cutscenes) is easily lovable and the developers did a good job showing the relationship between her and the main character in a way that is almost real and life-like. A lot of the minor characters are well voiced and fleshed out for how little they show up and any lack of detail I experience could be blamed on me not knowing the source material or having played the first game. Finally the ending was actually quite good and I look forward to a Darkness III.
Gameplay is intense, overly graphic at times and extremely fun. You (as the host of the Darkness which is essentially a crazy powerful demonic personification of the dark) use your powers (which come in the form of two demon head tentacle like things) to pick up, throw, tear apart and eventually eat your enemies. Its nastier than it sounds but oh so fun. After picking up an enemy you are given 1 - 4 execution techniques (they give different buffs like more ammo or a shield but all share the same ...12 ish animations) to brutally dismember your foes.
The gunplay is pretty standard but the overall pacing of the game seems faster. enemies are not all that hard to kill but there are a lot of them. You are given a wide variety of guns although a lot of them play the same way. Pistols, SMGs, 2 handed rifles and shotguns make up the arsenal that you'll have available. They are all fun and great though perhaps a little generic. Since you have demon arms to pick up people with you obviously have two hands to use for shooting. Dual weapons are great to play with and mix up a lot of the variety for the combat.
There is a good upgrade system...which basically functions as kill someone in a cool way and eat thier heart to gain XP which you spend on upgrading your powers to let you fire bullets through walls and make black holes to clear entire rooms of enemies. Its great.
There is a multiplayer 4player co-op but its kinda lame in comparison to the main story. Its basically a bunch of survival arenas. The 4 characters are great personality wise and the story is like a behind the scenes of the main plot but the characters gameplay is just Jackie (the main story character) just dumbed down. You don't get the cool tentacle demon arms but instead get a special weapon exclusive to the character. Its still fun but its surely not the main draw for the game.
Finally its not all that hard of a game to get 100% achievements on. If that matters to you. The game isn't overly long and especially not if you skip story and blast through everyone with the upgrades on newgame+ but it will still take you probably 3 playthroughs of the main game to get everything. The co-op achievements can be done solo too so you don't have to be social to 100% the game.
Overall this game is totally worth getting and if it looks even remotely interesting to you I would recommend picking it up. Its not the best FPS I have ever played but the story and the attention to detail really make up for the average gameplay. The Darkness 2 is addicting and worth a good chunk of your time.

This is a phenomenal game. I beat it a few days ago and it’s still sort of sinking in how great it was. It’s a return to eminence for a company that never really stopped being excellent.
Pyre is a story-driven game that hinges around 3-on-3 sports-like encounters called the “Rites”. It presents its story in a Fire Emblem/visual novel style, where you get a self-insert character in the narrative to talk to everyone with. For a game that presents itself in this style to work, the characters you interact with have to be good. On this front, Pyre exceeds all expectations. The characters in this game are extraordinarily compelling and well written. I loved most of them the second they crossed my screen, and I found myself growing to love the others as I experienced their arcs and watched them grow, themselves.
The story, and by extension the world it takes place in, is beautiful in its desolation. Supergiant is a developer that takes complete executive control of all the tiny pieces that make up a gaming experience, and then uses them to wrap you up in the story they want to tell. Everything, from the in-game banter to the UI buttons, is meticulously placed to enhance the story’s themes of hope and perseverance in the face of adversity. I was completely engaged from beginning to end, with one small exception about a third of the way through the game. Basically, the characters I was growing to love took a back seat to the main plot that hadn’t been fully hashed out yet. Even so, I’m willing to let that section slide, as there is a very good reason for the narrative shift, and it wasn’t long before the game hooked me back in to the expanding main plot.
The main playable portion of the game is the much-discussed “sportsball” game of the Rites. I enjoyed this part of the game, although I will admit, not at first. Not because it wasn’t fun, but because I didn’t feel like I was truly in control of what I was doing. The Rites are framed as performances; with consequences if you fail that go beyond “restart this Rite from the beginning”. It took a while to get my bearings enough to where I felt like I was playing well enough to earn my keep. Towards the end of the game, after I had mastered the characters and built strategies around them, I enjoyed the Rites quite a bit.
Oh, and the soundtrack. Good god, the soundtrack. It’s so beautiful it makes me ache. It winds all around and through the narrative like a satin scarf through a hoop. Plus, it pulls the regular Supergiant tricks where it punches you with a heartrending vocal performance at just the right moment, and all you can do is stop playing, close your eyes, and listen. I’ve loved all of the other game’s soundtracks, and I think that this is Darren Korb’s best work by far.
Honestly, it’s probably just Supergiant’s best game so far. I loved Bastion for its soundtrack, gameplay, and the interesting way it told its narrative. I liked Transistor, though I could never really get grips on its story or its gameplay because it wouldn’t slow down and let me get my bearings before it was over. But Pyre took its time, gave me a host of excellent characters to love, gave me space to get invested in the beautiful world it presented, and gave me an experience that reached out and healed scars I didn’t even know I had. I strongly recommend this game.
(Oh, and Supergiant? If you want more of my money, make a Ti’zo plushie. I’ll buy, like, ten.)

Fighting games are scare on PC, and Lost Saga combines elements of Smash Bros. (colorful cartoony graphics, with up to 8v8 player brawls).
The game covers your standard fighting archetypes (Melee, Ranged, Magic) + "Support" which can be a mixture of any of those. There's also characters from popular Console Fighting Games and Manga (King of Fighters, BlazBlue, Guilty Gear, God of High School, "Priest" etc.)
There's some RPG elements mixed in as well, you have Stats you can allocate towards a build of your choice and you gain them by leveling up.
You can customize the look of your character, and recolor / reskin gears. You're also able to switch out any of your equipped items (aside from the weapon) to further yet make Character's your own.
There's also Guilds, the ability to spectate matches, there's "Faction Battle" which is just a seperate PvP mode where players under [X Faction Name] fight against players of [X Faction Name] for "Faction Points" that reward you with in game $, and help your Guild appear more dominant.
If you like fighting games, or PvP in any shape or form then this game is definitely worth trying out. I've met some interesting people on here, and it's definitely worth some SSD / Hard Drive space!

I purchased this game knowing absolutely nothing about it, or even the lore or novels for that matter. The visuals and desire to play a new RPG based in a medieval setting was what initially attracted me to this one. The first few hours of gameplay were actually very enjoyable, however the last 30-40% of the game became a bit old and I found myself longing for it to just be over. From that point of view, the game delivered... considering that total gametime from start to finish was only about 13-14 hours. Following is a list of likes/dislikes:
LIKED
- Pleasing graphics and attention to detail in the animations.. for example when picking up an object in the world it doesn't just magically appear in your backpack... instead you actually see the character pick up the object and wield it in the game world
- Voice acting was absolutely stunning - probably some of the best in any game I've ever played
- Lore was extremely compelling and dialog options were interesting. The designers kept the dialog choices relevant to the situation and didn't include pages and pages of unnecessary dialog just as filler.
- Interesting mix of combat style using MOBA style actions combined with Dragon Age style pause/command issue.
DISLIKED
- Control was very clunky. In particular achieving a camera angle to properly assess the battlefield is impossuble when your character is near a wall, as the game doesn't let the camera pass through the wall to see further. In other words you are locked into an overhead view in this situation.
- Game was far too short for the price. Total gametime for me start to finish was about 13-14 hours playing somewhat casually.
- Provisions system is flawed. I didn't run out of provisions once during the game, and it felt like more of a chore than adding anything meaningful to the game.
- Items/loot: Virtually non-existent. There is oppotunity to buy various potions or talismans at times, however these are quite "boring" and add very little to the gameplay
- Zero replayability as the storyline is fixed.
- World map initially gave the sense of an open world, however you quickly realize that most of the map "nodes" are empty and the map simply serves as a point and click method to get from one story point to the next.
- Quest log was very poorly implemented. Very little detail/background on the quests was provided, and it's not clear why the log is even necessary as there are actually very few side quests and there is only really one main quest / destination at any given time which is marked quite clearly on the world map.
- At the time of my playthrough (1st week of release), there were still several bugs in the game, although none of them were showstoppers. I.E. consuming a health potion doesn't always heal the character, etc.
TLDR; An interesting story, well presented, but poorly implemented with no replayability. Pick it up on sale and expect 10 - 15 hours of playtime.

T.l.d.r. This is a tough review to make. While I do recommend this game, it comes with a lot of caveats. For someone who is a fan of great fantasy worlds and of course dwarves, I do think this is a must play, but I would suggest waiting for a few patches first. The game has a lot of heart and soul behind it, but it is a very rough gem, so be sure you can stomach all those rough spots before you buy.  For anyone else, fans of action-rpg’s especially, I think you should probably put this on your list and wait for a price drop.
A bit more in depth: Full disclosure, I am a KS backer. The game was made with a small budget by a small team, I know a lot of people think that isn’t an excuse, but for me it is, because I think they did a very good job for a first attempt at this kind of game with what little they had, but I will admit that the game might be a little to ambitious for it’s own good.
The game has 2 phases: one is the map on which you travel in a very similar way to FTL, as in from point to point, having encounters that you must resolve either by conversations or combat; the other phase is the combat itself, that takes you to a top down view just like in any party based action-rpg.
Pros of the game:
-Great story and characters
-Great music(cought*Blind Guardian*cough) and sound
-A unique take on the CRPG/actionRPG combat system. I loved the combat system, it is a real time action-rpg system with a pause option like Dragon age O, Tyranny etc but with a twist. Your characters don’t have any crazy spells or bombastic abilities, the ones they have are very simple, but they have a lot of weight behind them and they can displace the enemies in different ways. The same goes for your characters. Unlike in other games where you are locked into a position when you are attacked in melee, here if your characters stand close to each other they can push back the enemy line with their sheer momentum while moving and its super fun to smash through them and execute different combos with this system.
-Decent length, about 10-13 hours
And now some negative aspects:
-By far the greatest sin of this game, like many other KS games, is the lack of polish, especially in the final part of the game. It starts very strong but at the end you can see the game is very much unfinished, because of the glaring problems like missing sounds, a missing final battle, almost no conversations with your main antagonists that were built very well until that point etc
-While the combat is refreshing it comes with a cost. As you can imagine a game of this budget doesn’t have the animation quality required for such an ambitious system. A lot of the pushing that I talked about above merely slides the enemies out of your way for a brief time and so it doesn’t have the visual impact you would hope. Also you have a lot of weirdness with some attacks have very long ranges, even though the weapons would never reach that far in the hands of a Dwarf.
-Combat lacks variety in the number of different encounters, the number of enemy types and you abilities as well
-While you are given quite a few choices to make, they have little value
-All combat encounters are scripted, meaning that the game itself is very linear. That also kills any kind of replayability.
-Other minor glitches and bugs
Overall, as a fan of Dwarves and their lore I was pleased with what a got and enjoyed my time. The game does show that a lot of love was put into it, even if it is rough as hell at times. I for one would gladly back another Dwarves game, but I would certainly expect a lot more from that one and I hope the devs get as much experience as possible from making this, because the potential is huge.

The Dwarves, the newest game from THQ Nordic is... quite the peculiar thing. The game revolves around an amazing story, full of twists and mysteries (instead of the opposite), tactical combat which is a mixture of Pillars of Eternity, DOTA and Starcraft 2. Crazy explanation, isn't it? It has the real-time + pause option of Pillars of Eternity (and thus, sadly, the "I don't have anyone around me, so I'm gonna do nothing while my friends are dying" AI), the Click + QWE skill combat sytem from DOTA and the 1-2-3-4 hero selection + micromanagement from Starcraft, which makes it easy to get into The Dwarves for fans of these games.
The GOOD:
1.  It is a game that revolves around the story, instead of the opposite. As such, the story is way more compelling and interesting. It is by far the strongest thing about this game, and by many accounts, worth the admission price alone. I, myself, was captivated by it.
2. The art style does the fantasy theme justice and never lets off.
3. The soundtrack is amazing. Blind Guardian made a great theme for the game.
4. The game provides some choices that do affect the gameplay to a certain extent, which is always nice to see.
5. Skill threes (albeit minimalistic) add to the replayability of the game.
6. The 11 playable characters add a lot to the game, allowing you tomix and match parties that would best suit your tactics.
7. The tactical combat is really good, and is making good use of the terrain. For each battle, you get to select up to 4 characters and equip them with a single item - be it a trinket that boosts something, or a potion. You can also send enemies flying into pits or other places where there will meet their inevitable death at the bottom in many satisfying ways. I felt a good amount of challenge on normal. Next playthough goes on a higher difficulty, absolutely.
8. You can easily do a few play-throughs, spanning about 25-30 hours, unless you are a crazy completionist and want to do everything on the first go.
And now, the BAD... and it is a lot.
1. The game is overpriced for its length. It took me just above 9 hours to finish it, and as I usually judge my gameplay time by Euros per Hour, 10 Hours for 40 euros is quite the rip-off.
2. You will fight orcs of various statures and sizes (yes, including ogres, which makes it all the more Lord of the Ring-y) and the occasional Älfar boss. So much for enemy variety... well isn't that a huge turn-off for many people.
3. The fact that the AI is relatively stupid, doesn't really help the game. You really need to channel your inner Starcraft 2 spirit and micromanage as best you can. Thank God you can pause in this game...
4. Sometimes it feels like you can go to a specific point on the tactical map, but you can't because the grid of the game doesn't allow you. This causes tons of frustrations in combat and while exploring towns.
5. WHY THE HELL do I lose the battle when one of my guys falls down from a 1-2 meter high ledge (and breaks his/her neck I guess), when an orc just shrugs it off and takes barely any damage?! Enough said.
6. Pretty much every battle has its tactical quirks, and while it can be a good thing, it may also lend to a good amount of frustration before you win it and/or find the best team to complete it.
7. There are characters that are obviously better than others... Which really destroys immersion and makes you pick them till the end of the game, in order to make battles easier.
8. While it looks like you have a huge map, little happens on it apart from random encounters (with orcs, duh) and the occasional lore segment. As such, it feels like a streamlined choose your own adventure game book...
9. I wish there were more ways to complete a tactical combat than "Kill all enemies", "Get all characters to the end of the level", or "Kill a certain NPC". While these three are sort of kind of enough, there could have been more outcomes. Why not get someone captured if he/she doesn't manage to get away on time and rescue them later?
10. Choices matter or only a few occasions (to gain a companion for example), which always makes me question why give us, gamers, choices when the outcome will be similar.
11. Even though you have many Points of Interest to traverse, ultimately you are forced through bottlenecks in order to progress the game.
12. There could have been way more side missions, lore segments and battles. The potential for those is there, the developers just didn't put more effort into the game...
Conclusion:
I am recommending this game to crazy Lord of the Rings fans or to everyone when it hits 50% or more off, in order to merit its purchase price. The captivating story and the tactical combat are very strong selling points of this game, but they are largely overshadowed by the lack of enemy variety and the small amount of side activities to do. I enjoyed myself thoroughly, and while the BAD outweighs the GOOD by quite a few points, I can't discard the fact that I was very much into the game, and I was so captivated by it. As such, it gets my thumbs up - but if you are on the fence about The Dwarves, wait until it goes on sale.
