I am a dwarf fanatic.  If a game allows me to play as a dwarf, I do. If it doesn't, then I think long and hard about whether I should play a game with such a glaring oversight.  So, when I learned about the development of a game called "The Dwarves" I was ecstatic.  I also love RPGs and tactical games.  What I'm saying is: I am the target market for this game.  All the developer had to do was make an easy layup.
I am sad to report that they have failed.  Which is not to say that it's terrible in every way- I just can't recommend it universally.  Here's the lowdown:
1. Combat
You control a party of 1-4 characters against a horde of weaker enemies, and sometimes one or two stronger enemies as well.  You pause the game and issue commands. Each character has 1-3 active abilities (usage limited by stamina) and an item (usage limited by cooldown) that they can use.  If they don't have an ability queued, they will autoattack nearby enemies for insignificant damage.
This might sound okay in theory, and I commend the developer for taking a risk and trying something different, but in execution, it's a terrible compromise between an action-rpg like diablo and a traditional crpg like baldur's gate.  You don't get the fun of pressing a button and seeing something awesome happen, but you also have very limited tactical depth because you have access to few abilities, many of which amount to "do more damage" or "move over here".
The best aspect of combat is the physics.  Although buggy sometimes, knocking a wave of orcs off a cliff with your giant dwarven hammer can be very satisfying.
2. The World Map
Getting from point A to point B is not a great experience.  You are presented with a board game map with many interconnected nodes, and you move your piece between them.  Sometimes this movement will result in some dialogue between party members, or an interaction with a town. And sometimes you will be presented with choices.  The right combination of choices will continue the story, and the wrong combination will kill you. Just restart and select choice 3 instead of choice 2! THRILLING GAMEPLAY.
3. The Narrator
This game is not an RPG - it's telling you a story, and you are along for the ride.  An overbearing narrator constantly chimes in, telling you what your character thinks and feels.  There is no room to imagine that you are free in the world, to explore and make choices that impact it.  The narrator's voice also has a nails-on-chalkboard effect on me, personally, although I have gotten used to it as I've played more.
4. Characters and Story
This is where the game truly shines.  The voice acting is good, the story is well executed, the cut scenes looks great.  In fact, it's an extremely impressive achievement for a small developer.  If you like fantasy settings and are up for playing through a good tale, then this might be worth buying for that reason alone.
---
Conclusion: it's a flawed game, but there are silver linings in the clouds.  If I was rating this on a 5 point scale, I'd give it a 2.5.  I think it's worth picking up for some players, at some price points. Just proceed with caution.

Well written & creepily atmospheric sci-fi walking simulator which raises philosophical questions about what it means to be human. Oh, and there are some survival horror bits included, though I'm not sure why...
Pros:
* Unique underwater post-apocalyptic environment
* Great story, the two main characters and their viewpoints are very well written and acted.
* Great sound design, the underwater setting is captured really well.
* Pretty good length (Took me 10 hours to complete)
Cons... well... "Proto-Cons"... they're more like minor niggles really:

The game is currently unbalanced, favoring Jason over the counselors. I understand that Jason is a supernatural being who needs to feel threatening and the game certainly does a good job of that. However, Jason's abilty to "teleport" anywhere on the map roughly every 30 seconds is certainly overpowered. Coupled with his Shift power, which he can instantly perform a grab action after doing, allows for Jason to easily persue and kill the counselors. There are items that help combat Jason such as the pocket knife and the firecrackers and the game also emphasizes teamwork and sticking together to stay alive. However, if Jason discovers your location early in the game before you can aquire any of these tools or finding another player then you are pretty much left defenseless. I played all the way through this game, and I want my 2 hours of my life back.
At first glance, this game seemed like an empty world, devoid of anything interesting, filled with nothing but the simplest of puzzles. I assumed that it could only get better.
I was wrong.
The story was cliche and delivered pretty much exclusively through (bad) narration. Travelng between objectives? Here's an ex-machina that you don't even get to control! Picked up all the gems in an area? We're just gonna take any extras you have on you, so you need to do the same thing again in the next area! End up at a laser puzzle where you need to rotate mirrors to reflect a beam to a certain point? Well, we'll do that one 5 times, and have the solution just be "press every button once" for all 5 of them.
The gameplay is bland and uninspired. You start the game being able to jump, double jump, and pick things up to throw. You end the game with this same set of moves. The double jump is broken, sometimes allowing triple or quadruple jumps when you press against a wall, and sometimes ceasing to exist with no reason or warning given to the player. Throwing things is almost exlusively limited to the bosses who are as bland and uninspiring as the gameplay. On top of all that, the few times there are sections of gameplay that are different, such as sliding down a hill or riding in a minecart, there's no explanation of what controls do what. The middling air control only serves to disillusion the player into thinking that there's some kind of air movement, when in fact you will find your poor robot simply falling inelegantly.
There are 5 areas, which all share almost identical gameplay. Upon arriving, you nee to collect X amount of gems in order to open a door or something. You usually also need to find some item or a key in order to progress. Repeat this cycle until there's a boss fight. Throw rocks at the boss until it dies. Press every mirror button once to reflect the beam where it goes. Endure cutscene. Repeat. There's very little variation.
The bosses had some potential. All of them could be tweaked a little, turning them into an actual engaging experience. Unfortunately, that isn't the case. There's a giant worm that you throw rocks at. A giant gorilla you throw rocks at. A giant octopus that you solve a "puzzle" (that's actually just a copy of what you did in the previous area, just with a giant octopus in it) and it just leaves. There's a giant frog where the fight is just Scarecrow from the Arkham games. There's a dragon that's just a series of quick time events that fail you if you have incorrect timing, but also don't show you the timing in any way. The finale is a fight against a giant robot. You just throw rocks at it.
The art style doesn't help this pile of dung. I will happily play a game with terrible gameplay and a terrible story if it's nice to look at. Scrap Garden isn't nice to look at. If I wanted everything that wasn't directly in front of my face to be so blurry its unrecognizable, I'd take off my glasses. There's no setting that I saw to extend the field of view. Even when loaded, the textures are muddy, enemies don't even come close to being the same art style, and every animation is stiff and jarring. Almost every cutscene is an assault on the senses, the animations not matching up with what is happening, the dialouge filled with grammatical mistakes and nonesense blabbering, the main character doing an R2-D2 impression, the works.
I recieved this game via a humble bundle, and thus will not be requesting a refund. That being said, I still feel like I should be paid for whatever kind of torture this experience was. I would not reccomend playing this if you got it for free.

If the game is not working (as with me) and you get the OpenAL32.dll is missing error,
Here is what you can do:
1. Go to the Steam folder where your installed games are (Steam/SteamApps/common/stealthinc)
2. The the game folder should include another folder called _CommonRedist. Double click that.
3. In that folder you find the OpenAL folder double click that aswell.
4. In that you find the 2.0.7.0 folder. Go in there.
5. Now you find the oalinst.exe
7. Double click that Data and it automatically installs the missing .dll file that you need.
8. You should be able to play the game now :3

Ok, I will admit I was not very impressed at first when I bought wayyyy back. However... I decided to play again... I have to say AMAZING progress. Its much more robust than it was at launch, dinosaur models have been updated and I love each one of them, in fact I am moving this game up on my radar again. Its playable now, but obviously far from done.
As a dinosaur fan I really recommend it to those that also like these creatures, especially with the nesting component. I didn't know anyone in the community, but it was quick to find a crew and get started. Nesting is when one baby is controlled by another player, this essentially allows the new player to "skip progression". So I was nowhere near unlocking an Allosaurus, yet I accepted an invite and became another players offspring, dinamically growing until adulthood (it takes about 2 hours to fully grow, but you can save progress and come back later if needed). Our pack (one adult, juvenile and 2 infants) did get slaughtered by one mean Rex, but it was awesome all the same, despite how sad it ended. lol.
There are 2 modes, I recommend progresssion (need to survive to unlock better dinos) over sandbox (every creature is unlocked). But sandbox could let you learn the handling of each dinosaur, like how fast it can move, how long it takes to starve or thirst and so on, then when you do get them on progression you are not as lost as you would be otherwise thus avoiding learning the "hard way".
My main grudge is dedicated hosting, it could be better with tooltips explaining each check mark, if you are acostumed to editing .ini files than you are fine, but for the average user the game doesn't help much. Also, the "supplied" maps, Test and Pillar of creation, are not playable right now, so you will end=up going to community servers since they have the playable maps, which can be a pitty for those trying to get the feel before getting hunted or becoming the hunter.
This game can be tough, but I can see it is easy to master once you understand which fights to avoid and which ones to persue, pay attention and learn from mistakes and surely you will rise on top now and then.
Again, if you like dinosaurs, this game is very enjoyable, just go with a mindset that you could lose all your progress if killed, accept that and start again, eventually you will be an apex too.

is a 2.5D puzzle platformer based around Alaska Native stories and culture. You play as Nuna, a young Alaska Native girl, and Fox, her four-legged vulpine friend (I call him Pat) as they journey across the tundra and ice floes of Alaska in their quest to uncover the source of the savage blizzards that are threatening their very existance.
As previously mentioned, the game is a 2.5D platformer, by which I mean it takes place on a 2D plane with backgrounds in full 3D. It can be played in local co-op, with one player controlling Nuna and the other handling Fox, or single-player with the player switching between the characters at the touch of a button.
The puzzles are not too difficult, though they do take a few tries to get right, and they use the environment well. Each character has their own set of skills that you uncover as you progress through the game. Nuna can push heavy objects and throw a magical bola to destroy ice barriers, while Fox can scramble up high walls, perform wall jumps and get the spirits of the land to help you out.
The game has some AI problems, with the character you're not controlling sometimes doing some stupid things like casually hopping off a platform or forgetting to brace in the wind. These problems were apparently worse at launch and a patch has since addressed some of the issues, but it is not perfect. The platforming also feels a little bit heavy, which makes sense when you consider the characters are not superbeings. I prefer platforming to be more dynamic, but this is just personal taste. Nuna's bola is also awkward to aim when using a controller, since you have to tilt the right thumbstick away from and then towards your target. I didn't play with mouse and keyboard, but the game apparently works just fine with them.
runs on the Unity engine, so it should run just fine on any system. Its a lovely-looking game, with glistening ice and whirling snow bringing the harsh landscape to life, aided by good-quality textures. Animation quality is somewhat lacking, but the character models have a pleasingly cartoony look to them and fur is pretty well rendered on Nuna's coat and Fox's body.
Cutscenes between stages are animated in a traditional native art style, which made me think of shadow puppet plays. While I respect what they were trying to achieve, I ultimately thought that these looked a lot worse than the game itself, and actually detatched me from the experience. I think the cutscenes would have been better had they been done in the game engine but, again, this is down to personal preference.
The narrator delivers the story in his native tongue (I don't know what it's called, forgive my ignorance) with a voice that seems to carry the wisdom of thousands of years. It is not reactive in the way that
was, but does a good job of giving relevance to your actions and progress. The music grants the game a feeling of loneliness and isolation that makes me think of the Phendrana Drifts zone in the Gamecube classic
, and the howling winds of the blizzards are brilliantly realised. You can almost feel the biting cold as each gust of wind threatens to send you flying over an edge or aides you in crossing a wide chasm.
is a lovely game. It is only a couple of hours long, yet it seems to be just the right length; not outstaying its welcome but not leaving the player gagging for more. The AI could have done with just a little more tweaking and a couple of glitches could be fixed (there were a couple of times when I clipped through a wall or across a gap), but the experience of the game is one to savour. There are several videos that give you some insight into the Alaska Native culture, which you can view ingame after finding them (I recommend you wait until you've finished the game before viewing them). Overall,
is by no means perfect, but is a heartwarming tale, ideal for the cold winter nights ahead.

SOMA is really good (best) sci-fi horror game. Events in this game happen under Atlantic ocean where things have gone pretty wrong as well as things have gone wrong in land too. You play this game as Simon Jarrett trying to survive in Pathos-II facility. This game and it's story will really stick with you for some time. It is amazing experience for anyone who likes horror and sci-fi themed games.
You have to run away from different monsters and hide so they can't catch you. There are many monsters in soma and they behave differently. Story in soma is mind-blowing and just amazing, I can not even find words for how well it has been made. It really makes you think what it means to be human. Gameplay works also really well. Graphics are just amazing. Underwater worlds look so nice as well as things inside Pathos-II.
In soma you don't have inventory, you just carry a thing named omnitool that gives you acces to different places. That makes this games gameplay simple and you can just focus on the game and its story. You are also given few puzzles, some of wich are a bit hard and some relatively easy to get trough. I personally loved all of them. Gameplay is simple in other ways too, you do not have to combat, only hide and sometimes... run. You can pick up stuff from floors and throw them to make noise for distracting enemies and use doors etc. Enemies in soma are really well made. They are pretty scary, others not so much but others are really scary. You are also given options in some parts of the story, like kill a robot to get power for a door etc. All the things mentioned above make this game a really good experience. Last but not least, yes this game manages to be scary as well.
Personally this was one of the best games I have ever played in my life. I only wish it was longer, it was over so fast ;_; I played 14 hours to finish this game, It's long enough, but still I need more games like this or sequel/prequel to this. My rating for this game 10/10.

Shark Attack Deathmatch 2 is a sequel to Shark Attack Deathmatch, an indie game on the Xbox 360. I have played both games and to whoever is reading this review I can tell you that Shark Attack Deathmatch 2 is worth your money and time. However, that does not mean Shark Attack Deathmatch 2 is not without its flaws. I will start off by naming the positives about the game.
+ The graphics are absolutely amazing for an indie game and I am extremely impressed with what can be done by just a 2 man team. The water effects in particular look incredible and even better than some modern day AAA titles we see today.
+ The AI for the sharks is quite smart and often will catch you off guard. The Black Tipped Mako Sharks in Predator which assist the player controlled Great White Shark are actually quite scary since they cannot do a whole lot of damage but they can and will throw off your aim. I cannot count how many times I have been lining up the perfect shot to get on my friend who was playing as the great white and then suddenly like an anime loli little sister the Black Tipped Mako Sharks come out of nowhere and screws over my aim.
+The player customization is another positive about the game that I did not see anyone else talking about. There are a bunch of different colors and you can also change the shade of the color as well. Colors aren’t the only thing however; you can also change your skin color (TRIGGERED) and your wet suit design and flipper design (there is a total of 20 different wet suit designs and 23 different flipper designs).
+The Developers are some of the best I have ever met (actually they are the only game developers I have ever met) although I have only spoken to one of them that being jonesjonesie
Unfortunately I must move on to the negatives and there are a few of them.
- The lack of story, lore, and overall content of the game. There is a huge amount of potential for a story that is packed full of lore. The biggest lack of content in my opinion is the very few weapons. There are only 4 weapons in the game. The spear gun, the chain gun, the diver’s knife, and the flash bang grenade. A good example of the lack of lore and story is the level called “Tsunami”, which takes place in the flooded streets of New York City and features the torn off head of Lady Liberty at the top of the map which spawns many questions. How did it get there? Why did the water rise? Why did the water not recede? What caused the tsunami? Why are we under water hunting sharks? Why are the sharks so aggressive?
-Little to no community exists for this game. I tried searching for any open games and could not find any. Although this complaint is not really the game’s fault since the only way to get a bigger community is to have more people play the game and as mentioned up above with the positives, this is not a bad game.
-The constant need to keep grabbing oxygen. I find it rather annoying how fast your oxygen and stamina depletes and how often you must replenish it. I have died countless times from drowning and I understand in a real like SCUBA situation drowning is a real and serious threat but your oxygen only last about 3-4 minutes .
Over all I enjoyed Shark Attack Deathmatch 2 even if it does have some faults and this review is not technically complete since it is still in early access so I have plans to come and update it in the future when it leaves early access. I only hope that day will come.
That’s why I believe this game deserves a temporary score of 7/10

I was very skeptical of this game at first, reading reviews about this game being glitchy, not fun, and the servers were dead.
After buying it and playing it for my self, I can say that this is one of my favorite games of all time, me being a large fan of dinosaurs.
Yes, I have only played for 11 hours in total (as of this review), but my point still stands.
The game is entirely multiplayer. There are 2 modes as of the review, Survival, and Sandbox. Survival is a gamemode where you start out as a low-tier dino (carnivore or herbivore), and progress your way up to the higher tiers with pp (progression points.) I haven't played much of this gamemode (as it's not really my style), and it does need some polishing up before it can be as good as possible, but it is fun and offers a challenge. The other gamemode is sandbox. This gamemode is where there is no progression, and you can play as any dino you want without needing to progress or level up. It's basically a free mode where you can run around and do things that you want, and roleplay and things like that.

Challenging.

All in all, this game will not be forgotten by me. It is very, very good, and keeps improving with every update!

A sequel to the 2012 Xbox 360 indie game of the same name, without the "2" in the title. Shark Attack Deathmatch 2 is a rather lackluster underwater FPS that becomes dull quickly.
The game takes place entirely in the ocean, which is a welcome change since not many games have this setting. Initially, this creates a tense and fearful atmosphere; which is then shortly nullified when you realize how easy it is to kill sharks, even moreso after the radar update that allows you to see all enemies at all times. You strafe around them or swim up to dodge the pattern of attack every single one has; which is to charge at you in a straight line. Afterwards, you shoot them in the rear with one of two projectile weapons available. Repeat this only twice for littler ones, and maybe six or seven on larger ones.
Three game modes are offered; Survival, FFA, and Predator. Survival can be played alone or with one online partner, and consists of a 15 minute session of killing as many sharks as possible. As stated earlier, the AI is a bore and this gamemode is ultimately passable. FFA is slightly more exciting, seeing as you not only have to fight sharks but also enemy divers. However, this also becomes uninteresting after a short time, because there's not much to PvP combat besides who can lead their shots better. Movement and item control matter very little, and take note the online population is almost nonexistent as well. Initially predator mode didn't work, but recently it functioned as planned. This is the game mode I had the most fun with, seeing as the bland AI issue is somewhat remedied with one player being able to use the shark. However, there are very little people playing, so a proper 4 diver team against one shark is hard to come by.
The graphics and visuals are actually quite nice for an early access title, but that does not excuse the rest of the game. There's also a decent variety in sharks, but sadly they all have the same behavior so they feel like model swaps more than anything. As far as the musical department goes, the title screen theme is a royalty free track I've heard before (This is the only example I can find as of right now:
), and the other only piece of music that plays is a generic Jaws-esque "horror" track when a shark is hunting you.
Compared to the first game, there are more maps, enemies, weapons, as well as diver customization, but overall the game doesn't stand very well on its own with such a basic combat formula. As of now with 7 hours into it, I feel as if I've already exhausted this game and more. I would imagine people who dislike replaying would get an hour or two maximum out of this. I highly recommend buying this on at least a 50% sale if you absolutely have to own this title, for whatever reason that may be.
8/2/16 edit: Developer contacted me and Predator mode worked

Overall a very fun game. The combat is complex enough to be able to make an entire game out of, with plenty of tutorials and tips given by the game that teach players almost everything they need to know in order to succeed. Maybe not in ultra high levels, but low to relatively high, it'll teach pretty much everything. The animations are all very good, the graphics and art style of the game are great, and the classes each feel unique yet balanced enough with the mechanics in the game to make it so that one isn't so blatantly overpowered that nothing will ever win against it, at least in 1v1 and 2v2 where gear stats don't matter at all. There are only 4 major problems with the game as far as I can tell.
The first is as you've probably heard at this point, the servers. Specifically the lack of any and instead using peer to peer matchmaking. As of now this means there's almost no penalty for just quitting out of a losing game and sending literally everyone back to the main menu, as well as fairly long times to set up a match. This ultimately means waiting 3 or 4 minutes while it hopefully connects you to a game where you can easily have any of the 2-8 players quit and send everyone back for another session of waiting for matchmaking. Ultimately this is the biggest and most talked about problem because its such an issue it overshadows all the others.
The second is kind of obvious for an online game, but the salt of other players is fairly high. I've only played a few online matches at this point, but as far as I can tell its pretty bad since half of them had very angry players in chat. For example, I was playing a 4v4 against bots to finish a quest the game gives you. So I killed the bot it spawned me near and went to look to help my other teammates. One was getting his♥♥♥♥♥handed to him, so I run over to him and help him. But he didn't see it that way and claimed I was "kill stealing." Keep in mind this is against bots, kills ultimately don't matter outside of the end result of win vs loss, and he was getting the crap beaten out of him by fairly mediocre AI. I thought he might be joking so I went to help out again as he was getting mauled, and he kept typing "♥♥♥♥ YOU" in all caps over and over. He quit the match shortly after (if it wasn't against bots we would've been sent back to the main menu but instead he was replaced by a bot until another player could join). This was only my third or fourth match in this game, low level and against bots, and its been that bad already, which seems worrisome for higher levels against real players with bigger stakes.
The third is the story mode. There really isn't much of one. There doesn't need to be necessarily, since games like overwatch don't even have a story mode and yet are good enough by multiplayer and character design themselves to get players interested in lore and whatnot, but this one has one and outside of being a tutorial is overall bland. The plot is utterly boring, and most of the levels are just fighting hordes of bots that can admittedly be very challenging especially on higher levels like "realistic." Speaking of, realistic mode is so difficult because it ups the AI's abilities to being able to parry nearly every attack, defend against everything else, and takes away your UI that you've been relying on up to this point to inform you of where to block and attack. This can be useful for helping you prepare against certain characters' abilities in other modes, but outside of that is utterly pointless save for a few cosmetics and achievements for beating the game on that difficulty. However outside of "realistic" mode, the story mode is laughably easy, with "hard" being a breeze to go through. My first time playing it I chose hard mode and expected to get wrecked, only to find that it was far too easy outside a couple more difficult levels of the game that were infuriating on realisitc.
The 4th is more of a personal gripe, but I haven't found any way to set up a 1v1 against a friend. I tried to find one but there wasn't any way as far as I can see in the menu for 1v1 to do so, and there doesn't appear to be a custom match option, which is very dissapointing. I was hoping to show my friend some tips and tricks that the tutorials in-game only briefly touch on, and had no chance to.
Like I've said, its very fun. But at the same time the issues I've listed are definitely important to consider. If there was a "wait and see" or neutral recommendation, I'd probably be more likely to hit that, but overall the game is good enough and the issues I've had have been small enough, that I feel comfortable recommending it.

Finished Sniper Elite V2. Took me exactly 8 hours according to in-game statistics actually. A bit sooner than I expected but just the right time. It was getting tedious.
It's a third-person shooter with a clear focus on long-range sniping, set in the last days of World War II. You play as a generic American sniper with the mission to eliminate five German rocket scientists before they can escape to Soviet Russia. This is it. This is the amount and depth of the story and characters. I don't remember a single name of the scientists or high-ranking German officers. I don't even remember my own name or if it was ever told. You could call it shallow, a backdrop or just not a focus of the devs which is fine because Sniper Elite V2 feels like a budget production, so it's natural for it to be lacking in visuals, polish and presentation in general.
They did however put enough focus on what matters, the actual sniping. It is simply fun. What also makes it stand out is the gratuitous, excessive violence of the slow-motion x-ray kill-cam. It never got not satisfying to watch organs, skulls, gonads and bones get shredded.
The game's structure is very straightforward with corridor-like maps that leave little room for different approaches. This surprised me as sniping could be done in a more open map design. It's not a detriment to the game though. This way missions take not too long and avert becoming tedious hunts. Besides your sniper rifle you also have a submachine gun and a pistol which will be used not as often. This is a good thing since close-quarters combat is lacking.
On that front I feel the need to advise against a stealth playstyle. The mechanics are just not well implemented and the results are frustrating and unsatisfying. Once I abandoned stealth after the first few missions, my enjoyment with the game increased significantly. I feel the devs knew this as well, since there are no missions which have stealth requirements which is odd since there are stealth mechanics like carrying corpses, timing shots to ambient noise, visibility markers etc. They just don't work well on top of a lack of manual saving and bad, bad AI. As an action shooter it is a fun time.
I do recommend giving this a try. Just leave any expectations of story at the door and prepare for a glorious shooting gallery.

Evil Genius is an excellent, if old game that is not without its flaws. Players are the Evil Genius, leader of the evil organisation that is planning world domination. The evil genius builds their evil lair, on their evil island. He brings in evil minions to do nefarious deeds and generally just manages the organisation's island lair. And he's evil.
You begin by building your base, designing corridors and rooms and placing the neccesary furniture in them. A place for work, a place to let minions relax and recover, a power plant. And then you gradually unlock more rooms and more items, expanding more and more until you've outgrown the small first island. But that will be a while.
During your growth, you're going to deal with agents of the forces of good, investigating your base for wrongdoing, and sabotaging, stealing, or outright assualting you. And for you to defeat them there are varying kinds of traps, misdirection, and just plainly having them taken care of by a minion with a gun(Or indeed, multiple minions)
The basic gameplay is solid, and while it has a few annoyances in the minion and agent AI, it is still very enjoyable. Base building tickles all the right spots for those who want to be creative, and managing your evil base is even immersive in some ways as you get to be the big boss cartoon villain for a change. It provides you with every tool you may need to feel like you're in charge, with systems that are neither too complex, nor too simple to enjoy.
The graphics may be a little out of date, but they are still perfectly fine in most cases. It is true that characters viewed up close don't look as shiny as they may be able to with today's graphics, but when zoomed out and inspecting your lair you will not notice much of this, with an artstyle that matches the game's theme. It remains even today a nice sight to see the corridors and rooms with your minions walking around in them.
Sound design is well done, with the music being the best fit for the theme that I could imagine. All other sounds are very much what one expects of them, clean and clear so you can tell what's going on, and the only sound that becomes annoying is your blaring alarm. When you're dealing with a base under attack, you're going to want to keep the alarm on. But your ears will want it off after a while because it is loud and repetitive. More reason to finish off those intruders then!
The game happens to also be laden with humour, as after all, you are a cartoon style villain of sufficient evilness, I highly recommend taking a look at interogations and reading the fluff text of your nefarious deeds on the world screen, almost every part of the game fits seamlessly into the others, with a unified theme that never seems to fail or fall apart except for technical reasons.
But then, there are issues too. As there are always issues with games that will lessen your enjoyment. Luckily for Evil Genius, these issues are few. Specifically, they are twofold, though other flaws exist.
Super agents, and the AI.
The AI is the simplest to find, and simplest to complain about. It is incredibly simple, and even without resistance it will not go deep into your base, or pose a threat to your evil genius avatar. A little planning and you will always be safe, though you may lose all your minions as they too don't think about things. You will see a horde of minions happily run into an attacking army to repair the door that is being broken down, or to use a fire extinquisher on an item that is still being actively attacked.
The agent AI is not much better. For the 'forces of good' they are remarkably bloodthirsty, with some super agents and soldiers shooting everything that moves on sight. They will enter a hotel and shoot all the valets, bomb the tourists' bedrooms, and declare their mission a success. They will destroy a cardboard target and explode the pressure plate triggering it, then get injured by their own explosion and go on alert because they took damage. The AI is, sadly, incredibly simple and completely incapable of making sense or anything resembling planning.
That said, it is still functional, though the killing spree and indiscriminate destruction these agents cause will be most annoying as you can not tell a few highly trained minions to sit back, thus almost guarranteeing that you will be spending the next 30 minutes recovering from AI sillyness. And recovering is a slow thing, as everything is expensive, and income is low.
As for the super agents, I won't spoil them. But I will say the complete anticlimax that is the final super agent is a shame. Instead of an interesting ability like the other agents, the only thing this one has is boosted stats and an interface screw. The best way to deal with his ability is to pause the game and fix what he messed up, which can take a while with bigger bases, and manually set everything back to normal.
In the end, there is a lot I can say about Evil Genius, but even with its flaws it remains a very solid game capable of hours of enjoyment, unique and interesting with all the right things to make you feel like you are, indeed, the evil genius.

Gameplay in The Dwarves is the aspect of this game I am going to really dissect. Since this is essentially an action role playing game, gameplay is very important. Due to the fact that the game was set up to be a semi open world on top of that, even more emphasis needed to be placed on this aspect of the game.
The core element of The Dwarves is combat. Yes, there is a bit of exploration, and the map screen by which your party travels along linear paths is simplistic and mostly functional, but the actual areas which open up for all encounters and exploration are the bread and butter of this game.
On the map screen, you see an overview of the available world. Your party is represented by a simple icon, and all stop points on the map are placed along lines as large dots or specific icons (like town or merchant icons for example). You select one of the dots on the line(s) nearest you, and your party moves there. Rinse and repeat until you either encounter something or someone OR arrive at an actual destination, be it a town, ruin, or enemy encampment. At that point, you exit the map screen and enter the area with an isometric overview of a 3-D world with either your selected party members or your entire party depending on whether there is a battle to be had or not. You can then explore the limited area found within and/or battle your way through.
As your party grows, your options grow accordingly, but for each battle, you are allowed only Tungsdil and up to three other party members. Your choice will be balanced by each party member’s skills and, especially later on, by the amount of injuries they have accrued. Injuries are healed while camping as long as you have food available, but some battles are sequenced and happen one after another, which doesn’t afford you that opportunity. As far as the battles themselves, you can freely switch between your four chosen party members, pause the game at will to issue commands, and move them about as needed. They all have default actions which they will perform when not executing a battle order. Combat is resolved simply by pointing a character at an enemy. Party members will automatically attack whatever enemy is nearest, so you aren’t required to aim or anything like that, except when using special abilities, almost all of which have an area of effect (excluding buff abilities which are generally centered and focused on the individual character) and will require some staging to maximize their benefit.
Battles will all have objectives, which might be as simple as killing all enemies while having at least one party member still active by the end or as complex as closing portals and/or escaping a map with all party members still up and about. Rather than die, your party members simply get knocked out when they run out of health, except for the battles where all party members must survive. In those battles, being knocked out is equal to death and failure, and you will have to redo the battle if that happens. If everybody gets knocked out, regardless of your objective, the result is the same. Fortunately, you can manually save anywhere outside of a battle, and autosaves happen before all major events as well.
In my opinion, everything I mentioned above was quite enjoyable. In fact, despite the various difficulty levels being a bit more difficult than their contemporaries, I found the actual gameplay in The Dwarves to be engaging. Unfortunately, there are so many issues plaguing this game that an otherwise excellent experience was rendered frustrating and eventually game breaking.
Sequenced battles: There are points where you will fight consecutive battles in this game. There is no rest between, and you will want to swap out party members who have accrued injuries for fresh members, or simply members better suited to the specific battle requirements or layout. The first issue is that you can never swap out Tungsdil. This is an issue since he also accrues injuries. By the third battle, he might have as many as 8 or 10 injuries, and these impact his starting health, which for all intents and purposes means he will likely be starting a battle already at death’s door.
However, an even larger issue is a bug that I kept experiencing which didn’t allow me to swap out all three other party members without freezing the game. I’m not the only person who experienced this, and ignored bug reports for this issue can be found here
and here
. This issue was dismissed by the developer as being false despite actual evidence to the contrary.
Other notable bugs include times where your cursor wont stop on a map icon (which forces you to click repeatedly when near the icon in hopes of it registering), plenty of framerate and stuttering issues, heavy lag at points, actual video card overheating and what seems like a mild memory leak, game crashes, audio lapses, clipping and accidental teleportation (which is what I call it when you clip something and the game miraculously teleports you somewhere otherwise inaccessible on the map which forces you to reload the game), and so on.
These issues are made worse by the fact that they were all reported pre-release and ignored. In fact, on the day of release, all bug reports on The Dwarves Steam discussion page were removed by the developer, which is one of the shadier acts I’ve seen, especially in light of the $39.99 price tag attached to the game (the forum has now been repopulated with discussions of course). The first bug report link I listed above is actually my query regarding this. The developers’ response as seen below:
julian.strzoda [developer] Dec 2 @ 2:24am

"Since the last BETA version on Steam, we fixed tons of bugs.
We already have some successfull playthroughs by hardcore streamers and they had none of those bugs.
If they are not fixed in your version, check the system files – and do not use your old savegames!
Otherwise, of course, we are happy if you report them as fast as possible so we can adress them."
While dismissive, at least Julian said they would address the issues as they are reported. The problem is that they haven’t actually been addressing them. Based on my own reporting of bugs on the now removed pre-release bug reports, PC issues have been ignored for more than two weeks. This makes sense in context when you consider that most games see the majority of their sales in the first week.
While the gameplay is genuinely fun in The Dwarves, the unacceptable amount of post release bugs, all of which ignored so far, has me rating gameplay as a 2.5 out of 10. This could be salvaged and redeemed with actual patches and better communication, at which point I would revise my score to a 7 out of 10, which would reflect my view of the gameplay without such heavy bug saturation.

BeamN.drive beats most car games. it's not really a game but more like a test on what the game engine can do.

i played it on a better PC instead.
the game might not be as beautiful as some AAA games, but on unltra it's pretty great looking. dents on cars might look odd from some directions, but from a far it looks great.
pros:
you can modify cars allot. using the parts menu you can easily make a old beater sedan into a sleeper drag racer within 2 minutes. no advanced confusing settings like in other simulatiomn games, the parts are more or less listed as ''base, race, rally, offroad''
great physics overall: (duh) beamNG is more or less a  demo to test the game engine, which is a groundbraking advanced experimental engine.
realistic car physics: if you look closely, you can see the parts of the suspension move and turn when you go over bumps, if you damage your radiator, the coolant will gradually overheat and evaporate, then the cars engine gets progressivly worse until it goes boom and the car stopps. the tires bend and deform over the road surface. if you drift, then you'll see the tires bend and twist. if you go offroading, you will see the rocks shape the tires over it, or when you do a dragrace you'll see the wheels expand when they turn.
cons:
high hardware needed. just so you know, the menu is going to take a larger toll on weak PCs, if you start the game and see that the menu lag, then test the game itself as it might run better than the menu instead of instantlly deinstalling.

If you ever needed a "monitor benchmark" game, Pyre has come to your rescue. One hour into the game and I can already tell it's a work of art; not only due to its lush and gorgeous usage of colors, tasteful UI and animations, changing instrumentation and very dynamic sound range (you'll have to turn your speakers up for this one, but the bass alone is completely worth it), subtle rumble effects (even on a 360 joypad), polished presentation and writing...
The game may not be as long as Bastion or Transistor, but it might as well be Supergiant's finest work to date. It's polished to death, and even though the Rites (sports) part of it may be its less stellar side, it's still a fun and engaging mechanic. Storytelling follows a very Fire Emblem-esque formula, in which you interact with characters and choose which ones get more or less screen time, which affects the story's outcome. As another reviewer on the interwebs bluntly stated, it's "NBA Jam having a child with a lush Visual Novel".
Liked Supergiant's games so far? Get it. Never played them? Try it. Transistor still is my least favorite from them, but this may top Bastion. I'm eager to play more.

The Dwarves is a simple game. It tells a dark, yet hopeful story that compels the player to finish it, and it doesn't punish the player by taking dozens of hours to finish, either.
If the game were any longer, I can foresee that the combat and gameplay that really drives the game wouldn't have held up forever. It would've gotten boring and repetitive, as the combat really isn't as deep as combat in other similar isometric RPGs. It is fun watching hordes of orcs be kicked around, but it isn't exactly thrilling or gripping.
The questing is minimal, primarily focusing on the main storyline. There are side quests, but the only interesting one to me was the quest to pass the Blind Guardian statue (eponymous of the band, of course) and enact the festival of Wackenstein. Let's be honest, the only reason I bought into this game's Kickstarter was because of Blind Guardian. I'd followed the game before then, but only really became interested when I watched the developer update video of them demoing the game to the band, and them confirming they'd take part in it. Call me shallow, but it's the truth.
However, the game itself turned out remarkably better than I'd expected. I enjoyed my time with it, and I enjoyed the influence my favorite band had in the game, and I do recommend picking it up for a reasonable price if you enjoy action RPGs with a commendable story and likable characters.

Dead Island: Riptide Definitive Edition is a great game in my opinion. I'm seeing many reviews saying that there's more bugs than the last game and many graphical issues, but I haven't seen any of those yet. I have had a crashing issue but I verified the integrity of my game cache and that fixed the problem, although the crashes were on multiplayer and I haven't been on multiplayer since I did that. I never played the original, but once I heard it was an open world zombie apocalypse game I just had to try it out.
- Controller support (I prefer playing this game with a controller, it just feels better IMO)
- Great graphics (even though I have them set to medium to balance graphics and performance)
- Fun combat mechanics
- Variety of characters to choose from, all with different advantages with certain fight styles (ex. some Logan is good with throwing stuff, I believe Purna is good with firearms, etc.)
- There's not a lot of bugs in this game (at least I haven't seen any) (more in cons)
- Money isn't difficult to get and you can use it to make your weapons do much more damage, repair them, buy more, etc.
- When you're in the main story and you want to have a break (by that I mean a break from the story), you can do some side missions or just walk around and kill zombies.
- The only bug I've come by so far is sometimes blood appears white, beige, and silver
- If you hit X (interact button on controller) more than one while putting down a barricade you'll pick it back up over and over again which gets annoying
- I've seen a crashing bug in multiplayer but I think I fixed it (mentioned this above)
- There's no way to cancel missions where you're defending against a horde, so if you're having trouble or you weren't prepared you're forced to do the mission anyway no matter how many times you fail
In conclusion, Dead Island: Riptide Definitive Edition is a great game for those who enjoy zombie apocalypse games, and open world games.

In a single sentence: if you remove the monsters, and added in more puzzles, it becomes more like the Talos Principle - heavy on the undergraduate first-year philosophical warblings and light on the actual story development or characterization.
All in all, I was immensely disappointed. So many glowing reviews, so much praise...look, you'll like it at least for the atmosphere and the set design. It's a truly beautiful game.
But don't expect the story to be revelationary or, indeed, interesting beyond any other simple FP(S) survival horror - this game is more like Doom3 than anything else - some scares, some running around finding story bits and pieces, and a premise that is explained to you at the start, that never changes.
I was thinking (hoping) it would be more like Silent Hill, Deep Space, even J.U.L.I.A or Myst.
The Park, Silent Hill 3 (any of them really), or Alan Wake do 'atmospheric horror with deep, unexpected, unusual and immersive story' far better than SOMA.
If you want a similar 'walk around and learn an effed up story' but without the monsters, you'd be better going with Gone Home and others.
Also note that your choices have no impact on the story.
Now, yes, people are likely to claim that what you do influences how you 'intepret' the story blah blah, except there's really no interpretation to be had: it's a linear story that delivers exactly what it promises - don't expect any twists, any unusual or thought-provoking insights (other than the simple Cartesian premise 'I think therefore I exist' which is repeatedly hammered into you throughout the game), or anything deeper beyond being scared, everybody meaning exactly what they say, and characters that don't change or grow.

This game means well, but it is plagued by problems. It is not a puzzle game, except in the sense that clicking 5 buttons in order or finding a key to open a door is a puzzle. The sound design is off, many of the textures are samey giving no depth to the scene and the lighting is simplistic. Some of the sounds can be jarring, and some of the music that starts as eerie becomes repetitive. Every time you collect an item, which you'll be doing a lot to meet gateway values where you need X items to progress, the game control lags and you may not end up facing the way you wanted. I quit at the first boss who clearly you have to get to hurt himself as part of his animation, but the animation isn't possible to influence by the player's actions. The dialogue has grammatical errors that can be a little startling, and the robots are given emotion but not voiced by actors who portray emotion. Much of the level design is one way navigation, open mazes or simple platforming - there never feels like there is purpose to an action. There are enemies, wherin combat involves jumping on them, but double jumping in the air finds the enemy scurrying under your feet awaiting their doom.... that is if you can double jump because sometimes this power is taken away from you, and if you can see the enemies when the environment gets in the camera's way. The story is a classic trope of a machine that wakes after the robot apocolypse, but there are no characters (at least at the start) who you are particularly worried about dying.
Overall it doesn't quite look, sound, feel or play very well. Maybe it has a marvelous onward story and opens into a puzzle masterpiece but I simply can't wait around for 10 minutes for an enemy to kill himself via random spawn animations. It has good intentions but I don't feel that they are quite realised. If you can put up with the control lag and you love pure platforming with very little combat you might get some time out of it. It is rather crash bandicooty but it doesn't live up to the level design, art style, controls or animations of that game.

This isn't so much a horror game as much as it is a story that leads (rather than forces) the player to ask questions about their own existence, perception, and understanding of what it means to be who we are.
Soma is the greek word for "body" and that certainly plays a large role in this story as you try to answer the age-old question of Monism vs Dualism. Are we a body with a soul/spirit/consciousness? Or are we completely physical and there is nothing beyond that to who we are?
It's a fun and engaging story, well made and thought-provoking. The puzzles are entertaining and feel relevant rather than minigames. The character development is believable and doesn't seem forced. Absolutely worth every penny.

This game has had a rocky road. For a bit the game was $1, then free... as the dev was having issues with the end product.
That having been said I've followed the game for some time, and one day grabbed a copy just on a whim. The game is pretty simplistic in its concept... you create parties of adventurers that you send out on 'adventures'. So far it fulfills the requirement based on name.
Now lets be honest here:
Pros:
- Has a silly story. Nothing well written, but it's still funny. Almost has a bit of an engrish style of writing, and alot of the encounters have 'pop-ups' that make zero sense such as 'release or give money' yet... the results typically are so bizarre and have nothing to do with the choice you make (Either you get gear or a fight breaks out).
- Lots of options, and you can have some interesting parties.
- LOOT! If you thought Borderlands has too much loot, then this game will do the same essentially. Bizagillonillion...s.... of gears. Issue here is much like MMO gear... lots of combinations make little to no sense.
Cons:
-Essentially everything I mentioned above is also a con here folks. This game is poorly written, so don't expect to understand 90% of the stuff going on here. Stats are not really explained very well, and gear builds become hard to determine, as are skill boosts vs gear choices at times. There is ALOT of trial and error to figure out what works for what class.
- The Dev has done weird things when it comes to the future. The DLC that was released is actually a bit of fun (Endless tower with epic gear isn't a bad thing, and it's cheap to boot!), but there has been talk about rebooting the graphics engine... or say the gameplay... but yet nothing solid has come from it.
I'd say if you wanted to give it a go, definitely do. The Dev has been involved with the community... but at the same time be aware this is definitely not an amazing game. It can be fun to laugh at the story/dialogue, but the menu is counter intuitive at times and mid dungeon crawl... some of it makes zero sense whatsoever. Accept that, and get the game on sale... and you should have a bit of fun.

I had fun with Adventurer Manager (AM). It reminded me a lot of Darkest Dungeon, but AM is a lot lighter for if you don't feel like the dark and sometimes depressing tone you get with Darkest Dungeon. It scratched a gaming itch I'd had for a while, and it was quite fun. The tone's deliberately lighthearted and funny, so it worked great for me as a follow-up to having just finished playing something much more serious.
It's complex in that you can make a lot of choices (e.g. which of your adventurers to send to university and what they'll each study when they're there; equipment choices; how to put your party together / what talents to give them; and so on), but it's not overly *complicated*.
It is a little clunky in places, with some of the UI being a little less usable than other bits. But all in all, I found I could work out the UI if needed, and given it's an indie game I somewhat anitipate dealing with the fact that not everything is slick yet.
One thing I'd like to see is some work going into your overall list of adventurers. Not very long into the game, I had about 12 adventurers. I found it tedious to click through them all one at a time to find the one I wanted, and this was not helped by the fact that I found the adventurers hard to distinguish sometimes (please can we have some names that are different to the rest  and not one letter different from many other names -- yes, I know I could rename them, but I was playing this to chill and I take hours to name one character). So, if we could perhaps have tabs on the adventurers list box? Either to see adventurers split up by their class (one tab = one class), or a tab for each and every adventurer (which might get a bit unusable if you have a lot of adventurers, of course). Or some kind of filtering options on the list of adventurers. Basically, devs, please play with different options so that I don't just have to scroll through them one at a time.
Would I recommend this game? Yes.
Do I expect to go back to it? Yes, at some point.
*Do not* go into it expecting miracles. It aims to be fun, light-hearted, and at its core, a manager-style game. The adventuring itself is very basic and old school, so if you go into it expecting it to be hugely innovative you're going to be disappointed. But if you want to micromanage adventurers in order to save the kingdom, give this one a punt.
(Last note: devs, when I tried this game I was hoping it would be like the garrison sub game in WoW, which I really liked but am not going to login to WoW just for that. AM sort of was, but it really wasn't quite there. I think the questing was the main thing. I liked sending teams of carefully selected adventurers (with different traits) off and then having them return with shinies sometime later, while that also levelled them up -- I don't really want to be doing the dungeons manually. I don't know if you want to take this comment on board and think about going in that direction a bit more -- some people did really like garrisons).

In Stealth Inc. 2 the player controls a quality assurance clone, created for the purpose of testing products in dangerous situations and intended to be disposable. After surviving a test meant to kill them, the clone becomes aware of their nature and breaks loose into the facility, where they discover other trapped clones and an employee determined to kill them in service of a high productivity rating.
To free the other clones and escape the PTI Complex, the player must traverse six zones where products are being tested. Each contains test chambers, progressively complex environmental puzzle stages focused on a different product. Test chambers are completed by accessing one or more terminals which open a path to the exit, while avoiding death by way of traps including mines, lasers, whirring blades, and the constantly shifting walls of the facility.
That last one is a favorite of the game. Stealth Inc. 2 frequently employs traps which are unforseeable, mostly by crushing the player with walls and usually mocking them after doing so with pithy text. It's a game where level memorization is fundamental to play, an element reinforced by the rank-based scoring system which grades on completion time, number of deaths and the number of times spotted by enemies. While it does occasionally feel a bit mean-spirited, regular checkpoints within a test chamber usually mean that little ground is actually lost when it happens, softening the blow.
The first zone, a testing area for night-vision goggles from which the player initially escapes into the larger facility, introduces basic elements common throughout the remainder of the game. The player's clone can run, jump, and cling to certain ledges, while encountering environmental objects (like pressure switches, force fields, and infrared beams), enemy turrets and robots, and the simple lighting system which determines how visible the clone is.
Zones after this introduction each provide an additional piece of equipment around which all test chambers in the zone will revolve. The products vary in their range of function and the simplest objects generally provide the broadest possibilities. The Inflate-A-Mate, a small device which may be thrown and then enlarged remotely to become a rectangular block, is the most utilitarian by far. It can function as a weight for buttons, a platform for climbing or standing on, a wedge to stop moving walls, and a barrier to block lasers or create shadows. It can even be thrown over enemies and expanded mid-flight to crush them or provide a boost for high jumps.
The other gadgets may not have as much range, but they have enough to justify ten stages in which to explore them, at least. The "Me Too" lets the player create a second clone, with both clones responding simultaneously to commands and allowing for one to be killed without consequence. A pair of teleporter beacons enables instant relocation for both the player and enemy robots, while a portable light illuminates paths and activates special switches.
The least interesting of the gadgets, the "Jack Boy," allows the player to assume control of robots, provided they can sneak up on them and successfully time the use of the device. And while it's fun to control the enemies, the very fact that the robots are the only element the gadget interacts with gives it limited application. It doesn't take long to realize that for an entire zone you will tag the back of at least one robot per test chamber because that's all your gadget does.
It's forgivable, especially as there is clever level design at work. Determining the proper approach to clearing a test chamber, where to throw gadgets and what objects to interact with first, is an enjoyable process if you don't mind the occasional bit of trial-and-error learning. A few stages verge on maddening in their difficulty, but these are rare and Stealth Inc. 2 is a moderate challenge, though total completion will require thorough and riskier exploration of stages to free hidden clones.
Completing the eight required test chambers in a zone rewards the player with that zone's gadget for use in the facility overworld, necessary to enter the next zone and providing ways to reach collectible items and bonus test chambers. Completing zones also opens up the facility to provide easier access between previously explored areas and aid in the hunt for these extras.
The previous Stealth Inc. had no such overworld; levels were instead selected from a menu. The addition does give the game a greater sense of cohesion by minimizing interruption of play and serves the sparse plot with more opportunities for taunting from the scientist (the necessity of which is questionable), but not much more than that. Moving from one door to the next is rarely compelling. There are few enemies and those that exist present little to no challenge, making these passages mostly consist of stuff to clamber over on the way to something worthwhile.
It seems like the overworld should be fun, too. As the player accumulates more of the gadgets, the potential is there for complex puzzles requiring the use of multiple items. The way equipment works winds up limiting a lot of that potential, as only one tool can be in the field at a time anc changing tools returns any thrown objects.
Stealth Inc. 2 is by no means a bad 2D puzzle platformer, but it doesn't stand out in a genre which has had some impressive entries in the past year. Attempts to improve the experience of its predecessor by adding an overworld feel more like padding than an increase in scope and many of its levels necessitate foreknowledge to complete them successfully. Still, there are pleasures to be found in discovering the many facets of the tools and the puzzles do an admirable job of squeezing out their individual potential in clever ways.

Never Alone is the type of game that makes me loathe the Steam review system.  A simple yes or no for a game does little to explain how strong of a yes or no you're really giving the game.  Butwhen it comes down to it, the bottom line is that I can recommend this game and here's why:
This is one of those truly unique games that does something new and should be rewarded for the efforts in spite of it's short comings.  I'm not normally a "list" guy, but I think it will suit this review well; so here's a list of pros and cons about this game.
Pro:
* The game has a truly unique story that tells the tale of a traditional Inuit legend.
* The game's visuals stand out, whether it be the gameplay graphics or the animated story segments in between chapters.
* You can really get a sense of how much passion the developers put into this project; they really wanted to share their history and culture with people and found a unique way to do it via gaming media.
* There's the option of playing co-op locally.  I didn't play co-op at all, opting for a single player experience, however, from what I could tell while using the switching mechanic to play solo, the game should work well in co-op and the story pulls you in so that you can really bond and share an experience with whomever you play it with.
* The unlockable cultural insights vignettes are really well done and enjoyable.  They keep things short and to the point where you're given enough to be interested but left wanting more.
* As a single player experience, there were some really nicely designed sections that proved to be challenging and rewarding.
Cons:
* Those well done unlockable cultural insights are locked away behind the collectible system in the game.  Most are easy to find and the chapter select menu gives you a count of how many you've found in a chapter.  As I wanted to know more and more about the Inuit and found myself unable to do so until I found more collectibles, I was slightly irritated.
* There are some really unfair sections of the game as well as some sections where the goal/objective is rather obtuse/unclear.  I had quite a number of deaths I felt were unfair.
* The game is pretty short... you can probably knock it out in an afternoon, especially if you're playing co-op.  And after you've found all the cultural insights, there's not a lot of replay value here.
So overall, I give this game a yes, as I believe the experience provided is greater than the sum of it's successes and failures.

TL/DR;
Pros
- Spiritual successor to older ARPG titles (Secret of Mana/Star Tropics/A Link to the Past)
- Solid build customization and choices that change gameplay a lot
- Responsive Controls, Xbox controller works fine off the hop with zero third party software necessary
- Good Humor
- Good Multiplayer Experience and Customization
- Decent Musical Score
- Fairly difficult compared to modern games (Tough but fair, it's not quite "Nintendo Hard" but close)
Cons
- Default keybindings can be hard on hands, probably want a controller unless you want to custom keybind.
- Menu slightly unintuitive at first
- Crafting doesn't seem to be covered at all in the first few hours or so
- Game is incomplete, some areas not accessable even early on, does not impact current gameplay though.
It's pretty decent, only have 3 hours in so far though.
Like it says on the tin it definitely captures the spirit of Secret of Mana/A Link to the Past/Star Tropics. However it also adds in some nice new shiny features, the biggest one being build customization. I guess the closest comparison on the build system would be something like Skyrim or Kingdoms of Amular: Reckoning (as in non linear, pick whatever you want but there's still progression within each).
The controls are responsive however being an old goat I got hand cramps after the first hour and switched to Xbox 360 controller and enjoyed it a lot more after that (could still probably be solved with some manual rebinding). It's a little quirky to get used to the menu controls being that it behaves exactly like an old SNES title (no mouse, nested menus button press down and back up).
The dialogue is pretty funny, it has a lot of fourth wall humor often poking fun at itself and the genre. So far the score is decent but I'm only a few hours in.
I got a few friends to buy it and we've been playing together and having a blast, the steam integration makes this super easy. You can choose whether to scale the leveling or not which seems nice but hasn't actually been tested by me yet, we're all pretty low level so I didn't see the point. Also loot options can be customized I didn't bother though as round robin seemed to work, the nice thing is it seems that if you haven't got a chest yet in story mode and another player opens it up you still get it. It doesn't seem to scale the enemies much in 2 player, so you can sort of cheese some content by ressurecting a downed player, but you have to time it properly so I guess it's not the end of the world. Oh and other than that, there's no healing in the game beyond picking up a certain drop (sort of like old Mega-Man games).
I was nervous buying on early access but feel that this genre was worth the investment, we don't see many and I was pleasently suprised by the quality of this early access and the decent amount of difficulty in the game, you'll probably die quite a bit, but it's pretty fair. So yeah would recommend.
EDIT: After playing with 3 the difficulty does indeed scale, though perhaps not enough I removed the con from the list.

I originally found this game interesting because I had recently played Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons and Limbo some time ago.  I found that they struck me in unique ways.  Interesting and not overly challenging (since I am terrible at most platformers), and loaded with a story that I can really get behind.
Never Alone strikes a different mark from the other games I compare it to.  It's not as emotionally striking as Brothers, nor is it as dark as Limbo.  Rather, it's exactly what you find in the description.  History and culture blend as one to tell a story that is both close to home and filled with imagination and wonder.  Throughout, the story has compelling twists and tense moments.
That said, I prefer the games I've played before.  Strictly from a gameplay standpoint, the game gets a bit clumsy and repetitive.  There were times I found myself baffled or frustrated by the controls (playing on a keyboard may be my problem) and occasionally not sure of my next step.  I also felt that the end was cut short.
I digress, for all the negative thoughts I have are forgotten in the storytelling and opportunities to learn about a culture I wouldn't know about otherwise.  Plus, as I mentioned before, I'm not good at most games requiring coordination.
I would consider this game to be a work of art for the way it portrays a fairy tale and it's significance to the culture.  The videos detailing the cultural tropes you see are fascinating to myself, simply because I love stories.
I highly recommend the game for curious learners.

The best stories are the ones that stick with you, and the story of Simon Jarrett and his journey through the underwater Pathos-II facility has definitely stuck with me. I finished SOMA several days ago, yet I still find my thoughts drifting back to this fantastic game and to Simon.
The gameplay is pretty simple: sneak around the enemies to complete various objectives and uncover the truth of what is happening and why, solve a few puzzles (usually to unlock doors or activate certain mechanisms), and tear through the corridors in a mad panic when the situation demands it.  There is no combat, therefore Simon depends entirely on stealth, distraction and speed.
I didn't find the enemies particularly scary but their very existence is certainly unsettling.  Making your way around them without triggering an attack can be tricky at first but once you understand their mechanics, progress can be made rather quickly.  And speaking of enemy AI, it's important to note that while each enemy type varies to a degree in terms of what you can and cannot get away with while evading them, they all share one trait: acute hearing.
The various compounds that comprise Pathos-II are dark and foreboding.  The oppressive atmosphere grows heavier as you travel deeper into the Atlantic Ocean.  The feeling of complete isolation is tangible, even when you're not technically alone. All of the above, combined with maze-like areas to explore and enemies that stalk you relentlessly, enable SOMA to keep your senses on edge and your emotions raw.
The storyline is where SOMA truly shines; the premise plays on our most basic instinct: survival.  The feelings of desperation and loneliness steadily increased as I progressed through the game.  There were moments when I sat looking at my screen, considering some new revelation or choice Simon was facing, with a lump in my throat and tears in my eyes.  The feels are real and they linger.
SOMA asks terrifying questions that are difficult to answer.

Now, I know what you may be thinking: "Ok, so the title is badly chosen, so what?". Well, so the buyer has some expectations, and this game is far from them. The Dwarves is a decent game, following the German novel "Die Zwerge". As a kickstarter backer I might say that I'm a bit biased, having played the beta, but now that it is released, I feel that I can now finally write down my thoughts based on the retail version.
FIrst off, it does feel a bit like Blackguards, or a mix of that with The Dark Eye / Drakensang games, but not to the depth of either. It is simpler, but for good (design) reasons.
Pros:
- The game is lovingly crafted, the characters are genuinely different
- Visually, the game is stunning (playing it on 4k @ ~ 55-60fps)
- The soundtrack is well done, and sets the mood fine. Though I would have liked a bit more variety, especially in battles
- Gameplay wise, the game plays well with keyboard + mouse, or gamepad (I preferred the latter)
- The world map is huge, and you can easily spend a bit longer going through the side quests
- Both the German and English voice-overs are well done and feel "right".
Cons:
- While there are many characters that can join your journey, only a handful feel fleshed out. While this is fine for the main characters in the cut-scenes, it does however feel more like the others are cannon fodder / not worth playing with
- I experienced regular crashes, either after battles or during travelling / transitions. So I would suggest you save often, and you make multiple saves
- Saving isn't very good. Occasionally it would claim saves are corrupt if I save over them (they all load fine however), and when you think you're saving at a certain location, it seems to save your progress based on the last area you visited, not depending on where you are on the world map. This can lead to frustrations, especially if you are an achievement hunter or if you want to try different dialogues in a conversation and don't want to do the whole world map trek again!
- It has little replay value, due to the fact that your decisions (apart from on a few characters) are not really affecting the story. If you do not bother with sidequests, then I would strongly suggest you level up characters early, to make it easier for you later.
- Some of the battles are a mess, where the only objective is to kill everything and just pray that nothing will happen to your main character. This could have been made more engaging (not simpler, but more varied, I mean) by changing objectives or by not throwing as many foes as you can at the screen, but trying to get the player to engage a bit more into tactics or strategies (especially since the help text constantly suggests to press X for pausing the fight - if I'm honest, I only ever used that 4 or 5 times throughout the game).
All in all, I did enjoy my time with the game, even though saving and crashes were quite frustrating, but if you are looking for a Blackguards or Drakensang type game, then give it a whirl, but just don't expect the same depth as those games. If you read the book (either in English or German), then it would be a nice addendum / virtualisation of it, and it might be more fun that way.
