I generally avoid writing reviews for games, but after checking out this game's store game based on the name change to "Rise of Flight United" rather than "Rise of Flight", I saw this game's rating has plummetted since I played it 9ish months ago. How can this be? Based upon reading the reviews, a bunch of people installed the game now that it's free and proceeded to trash it with negative reviews, which I guess is understandable considering that this game appeals to a niche audience. If you're the type of person that enjoys a high-fidelity, historical flight sim that demands a joystick and patience, this game is for you. If you can appreciate that to play the game without any computer assistance you need to learn how to monitor your engine's fuel mixture, this game is for you. If the career mode, in which you follow your own pilot (replete with a nice narrative via his biography) throughout the war as you rack up victories and medals and eventually command your own squadron, this game is for you. If you're going to install this game because you see that it's free, there's a good chance it isn't for you. Please try it; that's why the devs made it free. In the free version you can access the game in full and decide whether or not its a right fit for you. If it isn't, just move on. But don't be like justmeman117, who after less than two hours gave it a negative review and ranted for at least that long about the game's marketing.
Of course, that said, this game really does have ♥♥♥♥♥♥ marketing, and I regret sinking so much money into the steam version. Last year I spent probably $70 on the paid game and stupid dlc packs which left me with a mish mash of campaigns, planes, and dumb crap like streamers for my plane and coloured scarves for my pilot, when all the while the game could be downloaded free on
. To add insult to injury, you used to be able to buy all the game's content for $50 via their website, an option that's no longer available. If you're reading this, I suggest you refrain from playing or paying via steam for this game and go straight to the source.
Of course, despite all that this game is still fantastic, and it scratches an itch and serves a niche like no other game. Flying above the French countryside is beautiful, looking down at no-man's land from the clouds is an impresive experience, and combat is  visceral, intense, and incredibly rewarding. Probably the most dramatic, nail-biting episode in any video game I've ever played was my epic duel with a French Ace in career mode, and my triumphal yell upon scoring my first kill was deafening. One of my all time favorites, and don't let the torrent of pouty reviewers dissuade you if you think this is your sort of game. Just try it; it's free! Sort of...

Make a que system, where every round you play gets you points toward being Jason (except for the people who dont want to be him) that way EVERYONE can have a fair chance and we don't get the same person playing Jason 3 times in a row!
This game also punishes you for trying to save your friends, basically if you team kill you lose 1,000 points. Adventure Manager is an RPG/management sim developed by Vigilant Addiction Studios for the PC and Mac.
The evil illusionist Miraj has slain the king and queen and has taken over the kingdom of Adventuria. The player is the sole heir to the royal family and must restore order by recruiting adventurers and sending them on quests.
How many times have we taken up sword and shield and stormed a dungeon in the name of loot? How many dark corridors have been plumbed looking for chests? How many monsters have we fought? How many stats and skill points have we agonised over, wondering if we made the right choice? But have you ever thought it would be sort of cool to act as a manager to the people who go delving into those dungeons? Probably not, but that’s exactly what the developers of Adventurer Manager thought.
You take on the role of the sole heir to the King or Queen of Adventuria, and your goal is to build up a small army of adventurers whom you can dispatch at will to tackle quests and retake the land from the evil Miraj. Despite the name of the game  you’ll actually participate in the questing often, taking a group of four heroes into deep dungeons while other parties partake in their own objectives. The first step is to go through the limited customisation options to create your wannabe ruler, a somewhat pointless step since you’ll see very little of them throughout the game.
So, go go go there with your best crews and give it a try Adventure managers !!!

I've had this game high on my wishlist for a good long while.
And, finally being able to load it up, it looks exactly like my kind of game-
An amusing dungeon romp with classic turn-based party play, using an action timer system [ie, performing x action creates y delay before that character can take their next action].
Dungeon exploration, loot gathering, town management simulation.. it just seems quite fun.
A vast pity, then, that I'm unable to play it.
That is to say:
The graphic quality is abysmal.
I'm not referring to subjective preference toward pixelated graphics- I'm a JRPG nut, I play my share of pixel-heavy games.
Rather, the very low quality of pixelated graphics, even at the highest graphic settings, is so painful and hard to focus on that it induced a migraine within 10 minutes of play.
And it's clearly not a graphic issue, since it extends even to the text within the game, which is so grainy and distorted that, for me, it's nearly unreadable.
Rather, the pixelation gives the impression of a game designed for 640x graphic resolution, that isn't upscaling properly- except, I tried it with 640x, and it's still unreadable. Moreso, even- the game downscales TERRIBLY, and goes from painful to read and view to impossible to.
This game seems quite fun, and if the graphics are ever smoothed out, I'd gladly repurchase it and give it another go.
But, no matter how I might want to play the game, right now I simply, functionally cannot.
So if you'll excuse me, I've some painkillers to pop..
PS: Let us adjust sound settings before completing the first tutorial mission. I couldn't find a way to do so [as the settings menu is locked until you've completed the mission], and it was rather annoying. :X

I really wanted to like this game. But unfortunately there just doesn't seem to be any real gameplay.
Has anyone played the little, now old, kid's educational game Wolf Quest before? (Just me? OK.) It's quite a bit like that game. Both games have basic survival mechanics that have the potential to be fun: The Isle has Hunger, Thirst, and Fatigue. However, Wolf Quest (at least single player) and The Isle consist of traveling for hours in large, beautiful, immersive, but completely empty, maps, with nothing to interact with.
I mostly played Survival Mode on The Isle, as I wasn't sure what was courteous in Sandbox mode (it seemed that people were mostly chatting/hanging out on those maps). Both modes had extremely empty maps, and I barely ever saw anyone, even after hours of playing, even where there being between 20-40 people in a map. There were players by the water in Sandbox mode, but they just seemed to be hanging out. And nobody in Survival mode.
This makes the game impossible for carnivores - and for herbivores, a horrible grind.
You start off as weak dinosaurs and earn points to progress to bigger, stronger ones. I like this mechanic, but all you can do as a carnivore is wander around aimlessly until you starve to death, as there is nothing to hunt. Sometimes you can run into a carcass, but come on, what's the point of role playing a hunter if you can't hunt?
As a herbivore you can at least earn points by eating plants, which are readily available. However this makes the game consist solely of grinding your way through plants for hours, until even I, a carnivore fan, finally got a bit attached to my little herbivore after a few progressions to a mid-tier herbivore. So what happens after you spend hours seeing nothing, doing nothing, but aiming at the screen and tapping E hundreds of times?
You finally see your first dinosaur besides the 3 apex predators by the waterhole, and it's a mid-tier carnivore, and there is nothing you can do. As I had so lazily eaten plants without a care in the world, a mid-tier carnivore can bleed you out in a hit or two, and you're done for. And somehow, you can't seem to do the same to them back, despite being a Pachycephalosaurus (the bone-headed head-butt machine). The first tier "tacos," I get. It's frustrating though to be unable to defend yourself though later. Can't run, can't fight. Hours of "progress" down the toilet, and you then have to start over from scratch.
I don't think this would be a problem at all if the gameplay was faster and more concentrated: faster progression, and faster dying. The big worlds are lovely, but so lonely and barren I think making them smaller (and therefore forcing players into the same space) would be better. It would also help develop packs and herds. Also, more AI dinos, especially to serve as prey for carnivores so they don't starve.
Again, as a carnivore, I never saw any prey. I thought maybe I was looking in the wrong places. But as a herbivore, I was able to leisurly enjoy giant plant spawn locations without seeing other herbivores. Even patches of plants BY THE WATERHOLE, which I would think should be the most action-packed area, with dumb thirsty and greedy herbivores, and crouching carnivores waiting in ambush. But nope, no one.
I was hoping The Isle could at least be a relaxing nature exploration game, but since it has so much grind and so harsh a punishment when you finally achieve some kind of progress, I can't really play it as that either.
A suggestion besides a smaller map would also be a scent system (one was actually in Wolf Quest!), through defecation or by leaving a scent trail where you walk. Scent marking would allow dinosaurs to establish territories, help carnivores track prey, and help prey steer clear of danger.
As for the positives, the maps are gorgeous, the textures are gorgeous, the animations are gorgeous, and the sounds are gorgeous. This game is serious nature porn. I'll check back later, and I really hope this game improves, because it's quite the experience roaming richly textured maps as a dinosaur so beautiful and skillfully created, and occasionally hearing the exotic calls of other dinos off in the distance.

Stealth Inc 2: A Game of Clones is a 2D stealth Platformer with heavy focus on puzzle platforming.
The gameplay is very solid. Every chapter you get a new gadget that you have to test in at least 8 test chambers. This switches up the gameplay pretty frequently but not too fast, since in those chambers you can only use that one specific gadget so things dont get too clustered. In the hub world tho, after completing the testing you recieve the tested gadget and can (and often have to) use it in the hub world to get to the next area. Also, the gadgets are all different and have unique uses, delievering a game experience that doesn't get dull and entertained me until the end and even further. The stealth is also well made and easy to use with a bar that shows your visibility. You often need to hide in the shadows to take out or sneak around your enemies and especially in the boss levels (which are awesome), you have to manipulate and use the shadows in order to progress.
The story is nice.
is maybe not the best story, but the narative is done very well. The antagonist's words are being projected onto the walls as you progress through the level which is a nice alternative way of making him "speak" (there is no voice acting). I also like how he speaks to you, as he switches between sarcastic, caring and hate, aswell as making fun of you when dying in hilarious ways.
The aesthetics is nothing special. Cute characters in an acceptable looking world. It won't give you eye cancer but it is certaintly not an eye candy but since it is a 2D scroller you don't expect the best graphics.
The controls are are semi-good. The movement is very responsive and accurate but the throwing of gadgets (what you go a lot) is sometimes frustrating. Even in fullscreen mode, my mouse (I have a triple monitor setup) when onto another screen, resulting in the game being unfocuses and me having to click onto my main screen again. Disabling your other monitors might fix it. But even without this, the aiming is hard since you can't see where your mouse cursor is and the movement of the camera can mess with your throws.
From a technicals side I only had the problem I mentioned in the controls with a multi monitor setup. No framedrops or crashes but I heard some had a .dll problem that has working fixes in the guides and reviews. The optionsmenu is a bit limited but offers everything you need: Resolution, fullscreen, a bit AA, rebindable controls for keyboard and controller, brightness, as well as two volume sliders. Also, I runs at 60 FPS at default. Some say it runs poorly on their system but I can't say that about mine (i3570 + GTX 660).
I also comes with a level editor which contains some very challenging levels and allows for infinite new content.
Overall, Stealth Inc 2: A Game of Clones is a very well made stealth platformer with good, challenging puzzles that doesn't get dull thanks to new game elements that are frequently added. If you either like puzzles, stealth or platformers or need in gerenal a good game, definitely go for it.

Hey there.  I'm a Depth fanatic.  But I'm a shark fanatic too.  I would love to have another awesome shark game to play around with.  But I don't recommend this one in the state it's in.  I'm hoping it'll improve over time.
First of all I would like to point out the irritating, unprofessional matters.  I suppose the developers are just sensitive.  But there is literally a thread stickied in the forums labelled "this or depth."  That in itself is a recipe for disaster.  Like the developers are encouraging flaming -- which is the only thing that comes out of threads like that.  I find it unprofessional and frankly, disappointing.  That's not the worst thing though.  If you go into the main menu after launching SADM2, there is a button you can press that will send out messages to 10 people on your friendlist, without your permission, asking them to play the game.  That right there just pisses me off.  That is completely unprofessional and a♥♥♥♥♥♥move for advertisement.
Moving on.  While I haven't played much, I think I've played enough.  Had some friends help me learn, wasn't too hard to pick up.  Unfortunately the gameplay right off the bat was exceedingly boring.  I swam around a town for about 5 minutes, saw a few AI sharks here and there, but never saw the Great White player or any other divers.  It was really slow gameplay, and I never had any sense of fear, or being hunted.  I finally found a chain gun, and soon after found the shark, shot everything I had, then got eaten.  Not really sure where the exciting part was supposed to be in all of that.  It's not like I had any chance of getting away from the shark, you just shoot and hope it dies before it eats you, and that only lasts about 20 seconds.  And if it does get you, you just respawn and do the same thing.
We moved on to another gamemode.  It was divers vs divers, with a shark AI.  I was very disappointed about the AI.  You can easily dodge its attack, then go to its tail and stab it.  Then it swims away, comes back and you repeat.  It's not even worth wasting your ammo on it.  The diver vs diver gameplay was pretty fun for a little while.  It was fun having to predict where the diver would be and lead the shot, since the spears travel so slowly.  But it did become boring after a while with such a small selection of weapons, and the shark AI was just a nuisance that interrupted us every now and then.  It actually became frustrating when my friends started using the knife.  There is no sense of distance in this game when it comes to CQC.  If they look 10 feet away from you, they will still be able to knife you to death.  That, combined with the great effectiveness of the knife makes it a really annoying weapon.  Why do you even need the spear gun?  Easier to just dodge someones spears and then stab them.
Finally, the graphics and ambiance.  The textures and ambient creatures are really nice.  There's a large variety of fish which really makes the game feel alive.  I'm just not a fan of the disorienting water effects.  It makes me feel like I'm a drunk diver.  It'd probably give me nausia if I played it too long, which is really rare for me.  The sounds are also disappointing.  The breathing is very immersion-breaking, and it sounds very stock.  Otherwise, nice job in the visuals.
That's all from me.  But... I just want to put this out there.  Look around at all these reviews.  Look at their hours.  90% of these people have just 2 hours in the game, and have never returned.  Doesn't that say something in itself?

Let me start off by saying if you think this game doesn't have grinding in it...then seek help. There are people who care about you and don't wish to see you go down this path (not me per se, we've only just met. But I'm sure there are people who love you very much. Like your grandmother or that neighbor with the nice rack. Anyway, I'm going off topic here).
Secrets of Grindea is a tongue-in-cheek RPG that draws heavily on the nostalgia of games like Secrets of Mana, Zelda: Link to the Past, and Illusion of Gaia. The sprite animations and colorful backgrounds mimic classic 16-bit games and go well with the fluidity of combat. NPCs are prevalent in towns and in the overworld to the point where the world does not feel empty and that their character is not some lone warrior living on a planet full of monsters (though that sounds like an awesome game idea. Dibs). Each area has its own unique feel that you will hopefully enjoy because the aforementioned grinding will have you staying in one area killing the same enemies for drops.
The combat is extremely straight forward where your basic attack is spamming one button or having a charged skill where you hold and release one button. Let me go on record to say that I do not think this is a bad thing. Sure, you won't be chaining attacks that culminate in your wooden sword hitting with the power of a tactical nuclear device, but you will be unlocking and upgrading skills that define the way you, the player, wish to play. The skills are limited (for now I hope) to a 1 handed skill set, 2 handed skill set, and a magic skill set. The player is able to mix and match these skills however he or she wants and has the option to refund some or all of the skill points that were spent by spending gold (this is done in the menu rather than with an NPC). There is a bow the player can get from a sidequest but so far doesn't have a dedicated set of skills to leveling up the damage.
The story is pretty straightforward for an RPG of the era it emulates: You are a guy or gal that wakes up, is handing a magical bag that can hold anything without weight restrictions and are sent out to become a renowned member of the "Collectors". It seems, from the start, that these "Collectors" are a bunch of people that go out and collect cool, rare things. It is all very prestigious. And dangerous. And sexy. Seriously, so far every NPC that isn't a Collector is jealous of you. Normally one would have to buy seven sports cars and have an attractive life mate to get that kind of recognition. This game hands that to you right off the bat (Disclaimer: The developers of this game will NOT buy you cars nor introduce you to hot people for a hook up).
My main concern with the game is that it seems too short and I say that knowing full well that not all the features in the game have been implemented; this is not the reason that I feel the game is too short. The in-game journal keeps a record of all the enemies in the game and what they drop when killed. Enemies you haven't killed yet appear in the journal as silhouettes. Upon counting (yes, I did a math) I found that there are only about thirty (30) enemies total in the game including boss enemies. This, in my opinion, is a low number which may make gamers shy away from the game. An increase in not just the number of potential enemies but different types of enemies will add more variety to the grinding while still keeping the player's interest high. I eagerly await the areas that have not yet been implemented to the game.
Now, I'm not going to end this review by giving the game a number based off of 5 nor 10 nor 325745456415 (<--- not sure what this number is. It just punched my Numpad to come up with something ridiculous). I will end this review with just a few simple words:
I enjoy this game.
I hope you enjoy it too.

Not too sure what to write here so heres a recipe for Pancakes instead
Ingredients:
1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
3 tablespoons sugar
1 tablespoon baking powder
1/4 teaspoon salt
1/8 teaspoon freshly ground nutmeg
2 large eggs, at room temperature
1 1/4 cups milk, at room temperature
1/2 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
3 tablespoons unsalted butter, plus more as needed
Now to make it
1. In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, and nutmeg.
2. In another bowl, beat the eggs and then whisk in the milk and vanilla.
3. Melt the butter in a large cast iron skillet or griddle over medium heat.
4. Whisk the butter into the milk mixture. Add the wet ingredients to the flour mixture, and whisk until a thick batter is just formed
5. Keeping the skillet at medium heat, ladle about 1/4 cup of the batter onto the skillet, to make a pancake. Make 1 or 2 more pancakes, taking care to keep them evenly spaced apart. Cook, until bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, and the undersides are golden brown, about 2 minutes. Flip with a spatula and cook about 1 minute more on the second side. Serve immediately or transfer to a platter and cover loosely with foil to keep warm. Repeat with the remaining batter, adding more butter to the skillet as needed.
6. Procedure for adding fruit to pancakes: Once the bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, scatter the surface with sliced or diced fruit, or chocolate chips, nuts, etc. Flip with a spatula and cook for 1 minute more, being careful not to burn toppings.

by E-Line Media is a Jump 'n' Run Puzzle Adventure about a hunter girl from a small native tribe in Alaska, that has to save said tribe. Artwork and Animation are by any means exceptional good. The games offers a lot of short clips to give insight into the culture of the native tribes (and the dangers their people have been facing). Especially if momentum is the key to solve those puzzles.
tl;dr: It's not the new Limbo, though it's cute and interesting. Buy if cheap (or as a present)

Right off the bat, I want to give a big thank you to Ubisoft for the free weekend, because I now finally had the chance to play Rainbow Six Siege. A game that was met with mixed reviews at launch, rightfully so, since there were so many problems with the game, and unfortunately it turned away a lot of potential players away, like me. Jump forward to 2017 - the game is not only polished now, but the amount of content it has is just amazing! Huge props to the developers for continually adding new stuff to the game, because I strongly believe that R6S is one of the best tactical shooters I have ever played!
With the little time I have spent playing the game, I found myself blown away at how atmospheric both the combat and the strategy aspect of Rainbow Six Siege really are. I mean this is coming from someone who is not the least bit interested in Counter Strike. In fact, R6S only solidifies how much of a mindless and inferior product CS:GO is. The amount of fun I've had so far surpasses any other tactical shooter on the market that I've come across.
Expect to die a lot. This is a pretty realistic game and very much requires you to plan out your attack, or, in others cases, defense against the enemy team. In that sense, it can become quite the competitive game, where each squad is trying to outsmart the other and it becomes this tense and surreal moment when you get pined down, leaving you to adapt and figure out a way to counter back.
The destructible environments are a key aspect of the game since they pretty much allow you to turn the tide of a situation and overcome it. Granted not everything can be destroyed, in fact, it feels archaic by it's design, but it is also understandable since there needs to be some balance in order to have a healthy competition. I have to admit, breaching through a wall with an explosive, followed by a flash bang is so satisfying and is probably the most awesome parts of the game.
Now, I have to address the multiplayer since this is what most people want out of the game. So far it has been a mixed bag, granted this is during a free weekend, I found most players to be competent, but also slightly toxic in their approach. I guess it's unavoidable at this point. There will be people who are more casual and others who will be aggressively competitive. However, if you have friends or manage to find friendly players in-game, make sure you play with them, allowing for a vastly superior experience. I honestly think that is how the game is meant to be played.
One last thing. There is a lot of debate on what version of the game you should purchase. I could write a short book about this topic, but the easy answer lies with you. Are you the type of person to grind for their loot? (in this case we are talking about characters and cosmetics) Or are you the type of person that wants most, if not all, of the loot at once? Whatever version you choose know that you are getting all the content either way.
Overall, I believe Rainbow Six Siege to be one of the better Ubisoft games out there. If you love tactical action, if you love strategy, if you love shooters, if you love having fun with friends then by all means give this game a chance. Thank you!

There is no honor in a game called For Honor.
Buyer beware, if you're looking for an intense dueling game, you've found it. The 1v1 mode is one of the best melee combat games I've ever seen. Unfortunately, I cannot recommend any other part of this game.
The matchmaking system is entirely skewed towards high-level players and makes entry-level play as enjoyable as shaving with a cheese grater. The skill-based balance found in the duel mode is thrown out the window in favor of gear-based stat boosts and a revenge mechanic that gives players a boost to health, damage, and defense. With the right set of gear, players can earn the revenge mode when fighting one on one. Not that you'll find yourself fighting one on one in the larger game modes. More often than not you'll find yourself running from two or three opponents who, unless you have the gear to survive it, make the game a respawn screen simulator.
Unless you're looking for a sparsely populated dueling mode, I'd give this game a pass. At least until the matchmaking system is fixed.
And, as I'm sure the other reviews have pointed out, the peer to peer matchmaking system is abysmal.

This game is not a bad game, and its built on a solid premise, but theres quite a bit that the other reviewers do not tell about. So please read this knowing that it only means to highlight some things about the game.
First off, this is a sniping sim played through a third person shooter lense, but it is not "Realistic" its "Arcade" The most you can have is wind and gravity, for many gamers this is much more than their normal sniping experience, but it is still very watered down. The game plays in one of two ways, either its "Stealth mode" where you get a little indicator that bombs are falling and can cover the sound of your shooting, or you basically play zombie survival with enemy soldiers, every ten feet a new wave comes. Its not very sniper-y, youll spend most of the game in the streets of Germany, where no one with half a brain would stick around (as in no sneaking into buildings or picking your path, the game forces it on you)
Another important point is there is almost no sniper versus sniper strategy. You die in two shots from an enemy sniper, so poke your head out, take the shot, learn where they are, wait 15 seconds for your health to come back, peek back out and empty your clip in their direction. If theres more than one sniper, youll die in the two shots and have to restart the spot hoping that the random sniper spawn changes. The enemy snipers also spawn at predetermined times, so you cannot look through your scope at the next area looking for enemies, you literally HAVE to walk in and get shot at to find them in almost every situation.
Again, the game is not bad, its a great sniper game for people who think basic wind and gravity are "Hard". The story also is not bad, it's a ww2 setting so it's hard to stand out but it manages to keep ones attention.
Overall, it's good for a few hours of fun. The sniping, especially in the stealth portions, is fun, and the killcam part makes it more exciting to get crazy kills like Richochets or long distance headshots. That being said, the distances you shoot at with the rifles you use, in reality, would have very little if any bullet drop.The longest shot i took thus far was about 5 blocks away.
Review is still positive because what the game promises is there, and it is fun! But keep in mind what you are buying, this is not a hardcore snipers game, this is an arcade style ww2 shooter. When the game wants you to be stealthy, it lets you know, when it doesnt, you dont have the choice to be.
The graphics might not be great but it's still one of my favourite games of all time.

Quite possibly the shortest game I've ever played (I clocked in just about five hours). Force Unleashed II is very obviously a mere afterthought to its predecessor, with a campaign that without the long stretches of repetitive combat would make a fine piece of DLC, but is fairly laughable as a standalone game. The plot feels cut down to the bone marrow, with major plot points and character beats hand-waved in a way that hints ever so meekly at the epicness that could have been. Starkiller's bond to Vader could make for an explosive, compelling relationship, but we only ever see Vader briefly in the beginning and for the final boss confrontation at the end. We're to understand Starkiller is haunted by his former master throughout, but the dark lord's presence is all but forgotten after the initial escape from the cloning labs on Kamino. In general, the sometimes comically unhinged Starkiller is a completely unrelatable protagonist. Apparently his love for Captain Juno Eclipse, with whom he shared a shy kiss before plunging into the depths of the Death Star at the end of the original, has grown to such obsessive proportions that he turns his back on the rebellion he helped kickstart. Juno herself is even more of a non-entity than previously. She barely gets any lines and exist only as a lazy plot device to keep Starkiller moving along.

Beautiful story, terrible game.
If you are a dwarf-maniac you should play this game. Otherwise you can totally give it a pass, or wait for a discount.
Pros:
- DWARVES!!
- More Dwarves!
- The twins Boïndil and Boëndal in particular <3
- Awesome storytelling
- Engaging story (even though it's your standard fantasy cliche)
- Interesting and memorable characters
- Beautiful graphics (both gameplay and cutscenes)
- Great animations
- Beautiful (if somewhat limited) soundtrack
- Voice acting is top notch
- All in all the game rings all the right dwarfish bells, if you're into the setting
- Innovative combat system...
Cons:
- ... which is a total mess
- Terrible AI and messy collision detection turn combat into a chore of micromanaging and pausing every 2 seconds
- More often than not your heroes will get in the way and block each other's pathways, or even worse - fall off a cliff on their own
- Friendly fire makes it so your companions are more likely to die due to their own skills rather than the actual enemy
- Each and every encounter boils down to getting some aggro, then hugging the wall with your entire crew, wearing the enemy down wave after wave
- The combat is mainly physics-based, so all of the above flaws make it virtually unplayable (I switched to Easy mid-game, even though I enjoy a good challenge and usually pick the hardest possible difficulty)
- Overall the combat feels like babysitting a group of four clumsy infants (taking great care so that they don't hurt each other) rather than controlling a fellowship of mighty warriors
- It's very linear. The huge overland map seems pointless as there's very little actual adventuring
- The itemization and character customization are very limited, it's a small con though as I understand this is not what this game is about
- The final battle is a joke. *SPOILER AHEAD* You literally have to walk 5 meters to the nearest staircase, watch a series of cutscenes, then click on the main antagonist once and he dies. After a series of rather difficult encounters I was done with the main boss after app. 10 seconds. WTF?
- The ending feels rushed
- The loading screens are too frequent and too long
- There's a multitude of minor glitches and bugs
- The interface works against you. There's no 'select all' option. There's no way to pan the camera whilst in combat. There's no button mapping whatsoever. There are these huge and ugly health bars attached to your characters which you cannot disable (even though all HP and AP are listed on the side of the screen).
- The stability of the game is outrageous - it crashes a lot, both on the overland map and during encounters
- The game overall feels unpolished and unfinished. It felt like an early beta rather than finished product
This game could have been so much more. The potential and the idea behind the combat system were great but outside of the beautiful storytelling the overall execution was weak and rushed. It is a great tribute to the Dwarf lore but sadly it's little more than just that. Maybe after a patch or two it gets better but it's unlikely seeing as the developer has already moved on to another project.
Storytelling: 9/10
Presentation: 8/10
Gameplay: 3/10
Verdict: 6/10
I still enjoyed it and I do recommend it, especially if you're a fan of either the books or the Dwarf-race in general. I'm not so sure I'd have bought it now though (Kickstarter backer here). It's got Dwarves and the storytelling is superb, the game that follows is mediocre and unfinished. Take from that what you will.

Do you remember Dungeon Keeper? You know, before EA f#cking made a sh#tty phone version, KILLED IT FOR GOOD, AND THREW THE CORPSE INTO A MOTHERF#CKING GRINDER, TO THEN SERVE YOU IT'S ORGANS ON A PIZZA? Well, games like that still exist. And this one is a great example, mixing most of the good stuff from Dungeon Keeper to (I sh#t you not) the Austin Powers movies. Yeah... It sure as hell is a random f#cking mix. As usual, I will start with the stuff the game doesn't go right:
First of all, the game only offers a story mode, with 3 humans to select for your main character. That's dissapointing, there's no Freeplay mode, there's no multiplayer, NOTHING. It also only has 2 islands, unlocking the second one midway the story. The lack of content is a real shame, as it could've help make this game stand out and live longer.
The second thing are the bosses. Later on, completely hilariously broken characters with start invading your island. However, this offers a really harsh challenge: You need money to keep your base up, however getting money will get you negative attention. Getting negative attention will make more people go to your island. The more people blowing stuff and killing your minions, the more money you'll need to keep up with everything. Is a never-ending death cycle that will probably end once you're out of the game for good.
The last thing I'll comment uppon is that the game hasn't aged well on performance. There's people who have issues setting the resolution to the game to a number that's actually good for them, and stuff like that.
All of that being said, what's left is a really good strategy game, which also has quite the amounts of comedy.
The biggest standout on this game has to be the designs, animations and graphics. THIS is a great example of cell shaded graphics well put to use. The animations for characters fit perfectly with the cartoony style and FOR F#CK SAKE, THIS GAME HAS THE BEST LOOKING MENUS I'VE SEEN. I'M NOT KIDDING.
The music and voices are also quite good, fitting perfectly with your role of a generic overly evil dude who wants to screw over everyone ellse.
The characters themselves are also quite entertaining, as you can unlock henchmen who are all parodies of a movie. Jules Winnfield from Pulp Fiction? You got it. A Russian Rambo/Arnold? You bet. There's even a ♥♥♥♥ing Ronin that reminds me of The Last Samurai, tons of stuff to choose. This hilarity also goes to the world map and events, were most stuff is just pure gold (until your troops are taken prisoners, that is).
The game also lets you fill the base with deadly and stupid looking traps, and set them to trigger on different ways. The best part about it is watching some of your staff trigger them as well by accident because their intelligence dropped to low, although that might suck as you'll have to get new ones. You can also interrogate people in some hilarious ways, some even being parodies, like using a GIANT F#CKING LASER ON HIM LIKE IF HE WAS JAMES BOND.
Do I recommend this game? If you enjoy strategy games AND like games such as Dungeon Keeper, then I seriously wonder why don't you have it already. It's a really good game, and fun to play. However if you're not a fan of base-managing games, then that might turn your boner off.
TL:DR Edition: Dungeon Keeper mets any Humour-based movie that parodies James Bond and similar stuff. Fun game, although a bit challenging at times. Get it on sale if you like that sort of stuff, totally worth it.

DISCLAIMER:
I've kickstarted this game, tested it when it was in its early stages and I've read the books years ago, so my opinion will be different from a fresh newcomer, no matter how much I try to be objective.
Over all I'd give it a 7/10. I'm happy this game has been made because it's unique and it might've never happend without a kickstarter, it's a solid foundation for future sequels or DLC, but it also has its problems. The story and the D&D like narration is interesting and accurate to the books.
You're looking at around 8 to 10 hours of story, told through nice voice acting, good cinematics and interesting characters, in a world that, for once, focuses on the Dwarves. Also, don't buy this game expecting an RPG, it's not, no matter how much the studio markets it as a such. It's a Fantasy Adventure with an RTS combat system focused on single individuals fighting large groups of enemies.
The combat is unique, the closest things you can find to it is the Dinasty Warriors series, but it's not even a good comparison anyway since the Destiny series is focused on the over the top action.
Mind you, unique doesn't mean flawless.
Would I reccomand this game? Not to everyone, it's a niche title but if you're looking for an adventure out of ordinary, with a combat system just as unique and the price tag seems fair to you for an 8 to 10 hours enjoyable campaign, sure go for it. If not, get it on a sale and after a few patches so they can fix the combat bugs. Like a certein actor refusing to cast the animation for his pocket flamethrower, making it uncontrollable.
In the end, the greatest strenght of The Dwarves is definetivly not its polish or long campaign, but rather the passion you can see they poured into this odd project, the cinematics are treat for exemple, even tough they seem to be a bit too fast, and the audio team could've done a better job at times. It's a rough gem in need of improvements. But for a game on limited budget, I'd say it's good enough for me.

So at time of this review I've got about 71 hours and finished the main story.  I could have probably finished it a good 10-20 hours ago actually but was doing some extra grinding for achievements instead of continuing the quest line.
Anyways, Adventurer Manager feels more like a Darkest Dungeon lite (or casual I guess) then say a guild manager or something of the like.  You recruit various heroes to create parties with and can either send them into dungeons to control manually (the primary portion of the game) or send on auto adventures to grind levels and accumulate gold/gear (secondary).  There are a vast number of classes and races to mix and match with so you can optimize (or not) as much as you wish...provided you unlock the other classes in each race.
If you liked adventuring in Darkest Dungeon than I feel like you may like the manual part of this game too.  It's nowhere near as complex as DD with the stress mechanic and moving rows and the like, but you still have to consider your parties endurance as each encounter saps some of it.  The mixture of classes, races, and genders all contribute to possible party bonuses as well so there's that part to consider if you like a lot of customization control.  Each encounter in a manual dungeon counts as a hour tick for the auto adventures (and the world in general), the game pretty much directs you in this path instead of just idly grinding adventures in the auto adventures....otherwise it auto sacks towns and screws with the allegiance levels.  Ouch.
Speaking of customization....there's plenty of it.  Each level gives you 5 stat points to distribute as you wish, 1 skill point to go into a skill that you want (provided you have the levels for each tier), and the look for your king and any party member is customizable as well (cosmetic yes, but it's there).  You can reroll the stat points and skill points at any time on the world map without penalty so you can adjust how each party member is used, well, indefinitely.
Doing quests for towns builds their allegiance with you, and allegiance is built as you use races corresponding to those towns in your party.  The higher the allegiance level the other classes you can hire of that race, the better shops are to you, and a few other benefits.  And yes, there is grinding throughout all of this to accomplish these level ups.  In the mean time you can build up your castle to give your parties more benefits, train your party members in the university for more buffs, and work with the crafting with the blacksmith in case the shops, drops, and gambling don't keep you going (and they may not).
I haven't tried Ironman (permadeath) mode, which could have sucked as I lost all but my main cleric in one early dungeon run and had a few deaths much later on.   I'll continue to sink some more time into this from time to time as I work on the last achievements I want to get.  Perhaps I'll pick up the Endless Tower DLC if I want to do those achievements too...but that's just more grinding as it is.
In any case, I really enjoyed the time spent going through it as the dialogue of the quest givers as well as the choice encounters in the dungeons (I have a few screenshots of those) livened things up through the grinding.  The added ambient sounds made it a bit more interesting in each area and while the music didn't grab me as much as other games it didn't put me off at all.
And yes, the UI and merchant areas are a bit...clunky I'll give it that.  I personally didn't find it enough to put me off the game though.  Just something I learned to manuever around.
So yeah, pick up the game if you'd like to spent time every so often running a group of 4 in a dungeon and going after the various bosses it sends you at (and go after them again and again as you may need to for levels and gear).  Not an idler if you're thinking it's that, but I found the game relaxing and enjoyable anyways.

Nether is, obviously, still a work in progress, but I would hold off on getting it if I were you.  Most of the gameplay consists of getting completely dissoriented and unbearably lost until somebody one-shots you from out of nowhere. On top of all of this, upon death, you lose all of your non-aparrel items and a good chunk of cash, plus all of your player levels and skill points. Not too sure what to write here so heres a recipe for Pancakes instead
Ingredients:
1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
3 tablespoons sugar
1 tablespoon baking powder
1/4 teaspoon salt
1/8 teaspoon freshly ground nutmeg
2 large eggs, at room temperature
1 1/4 cups milk, at room temperature
1/2 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
3 tablespoons unsalted butter, plus more as needed
Now to make it
1. In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, and nutmeg.
2. In another bowl, beat the eggs and then whisk in the milk and vanilla.
3. Melt the butter in a large cast iron skillet or griddle over medium heat.
4. Whisk the butter into the milk mixture. Add the wet ingredients to the flour mixture, and whisk until a thick batter is just formed
5. Keeping the skillet at medium heat, ladle about 1/4 cup of the batter onto the skillet, to make a pancake. Make 1 or 2 more pancakes, taking care to keep them evenly spaced apart. Cook, until bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, and the undersides are golden brown, about 2 minutes. Flip with a spatula and cook about 1 minute more on the second side. Serve immediately or transfer to a platter and cover loosely with foil to keep warm. Repeat with the remaining batter, adding more butter to the skillet as needed.
6. Procedure for adding fruit to pancakes: Once the bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, scatter the surface with sliced or diced fruit, or chocolate chips, nuts, etc. Flip with a spatula and cook for 1 minute more, being careful not to burn toppings.

Scrap Garden is a fun little platformer that reminds me a lot of early 3D platformers. The gameplay is fun even if it is a little too straightforward at times. Basically you jump between platforms collecting objects in order to proceed to the next part of the level. What makes Scrap Garden stand out is the game's world/characters. The game is so cute/charming that I think the whole family can enjoy the game.
The two issues I had with the game come down to difficulty and length. Scrap Garden is probably one of the easiest platformers that I have ever played. There really aren't any hard platforming sections, the enemies are easy to kill, and the puzzles are really straightforward. If you have ever played a platformer you shouldn't have any troubles with completing Scrap Garden. The difficulty leads to the game being quite short at only 2-2.5 hours.
My recommendation for Scrap Garden comes down to how much you like platformers and how important length and difficulty are to you. If you like platformers I think you will enjoy Scrap Garden. If you want a challenge though you won't get one from Scrap Garden. If you don't mind that the game is easy and short though I think you will enjoy your time with Scrap Garden.

I think Never Alone will be one of the Indie gems of 2014.  Fans of story-rich games and /or platformers should find something to like here.
The story, while on its own interesting, is heightened by its connection to the Iñupiat people and their culture.  The short videos you unlock as you progress strengthen that connection and transform the game into a quasi-documentary.  It’s clear the devs intended the game and videos to be viewed simultaneously and make it very easy to do so while in game.
The gameplay and platforming is ok, not great.  There is certainly some originality in the use of the fox, animal spirits and the wind/blizzard.  The controls are good enough to get by but aren’t always as tight you need them to be, particularly in the faster areas of the game.  But those were few and I never got stuck on any area for longer than a couple of minutes.
All in all, I’d recommend.  It’s a short game, 3-4 hrs, but feels like you get more out of it than the relatively low time investment would suggest.  And I found the graphics and art direction to be gorgeous.  It’s bleak, colorful when it needs to be, and you’ll feel a chill as you trudge through the snow and blizzard.

**UPDATE** Still THE BEST Story game I have ever played. I literally recommend it to everyone that is wanting a story game.
After getting 100% on it, I should probably make a review of it.
The Darkness 2 is an extremely violent FPS with a storyline that twists and turns and gives you even more addiction at the end game. This is one of the better storylines that I have ever played and it gives you all the feels in all the right ways. You get joy, revenge, sadness, vengance, longing, and all those other characteristics to be able to relate with everyone in the game.
The Darkness was an interesting concept because it isn't a voice that is just narrating you or such. It is a part of you and influences you. It doesn't tell you to go here or there, it screams at you that your will obey it and it taunts you with a lost soul it controls.
The boss fights in the game are pretty solid, the bosses have enough mobility to where you can't just stand there and shoot at them in one direction. They move a lot and most of the time you have to be moving as well.
The light concept is very well done and brings more aspects of thinking ahead and getting priorities out (especially in the harder difficulties). If you are under a light source your screen goes white where you can barely see and being in the light removes your powers and any buffs that you have acquired that only apply when you are in the dark. So when a van comes crushing through towards you, you should probably shoot out the headlights first before trying to fend off the enemies.
The execution moves are super brutal. There are 4 different executions that you can do and each results in a different buff and also a different execution style. You can either use the execution to restore health, restore ammo, gain a demonic riot shield, or shorten you skills timers. Each I believe have 3 different executions resulting in 12 total executions which all have their own amount of brutality for anyone to enjoy.
There is enough of a talent tree to make you play more than one run through and probably just move on to Don difficulty at that point. You can do New Game+ to keep all your talents and such, which makes a considerable amount of Don difficulty pretty easy, but bosses still can be hard to beat.
I know that some people didn't really like the graphics of the game, but I believe they probably made them that way because of the Borderlands series, both are made by 2K games, so I think that is what they did, but in my own opinion I love the graphics as do I love Borderlands, so it was enjoyable for me.
The NPCs in the game all have a certain human flair to them where they aren't just NPCs, you can relate to them easily and they become much more than just NPCs.
You collect relics throughout the game that will give you essence (which is gained by killing people, getting relics, and is used to buy talents) and they aren't that hard to find. Some are easy to miss but generally you won't have problems finding them.
The weapon selection through the game is pretty small, but they made it for a good reason. There aren't any snipers or rocket launchers or big weapons like that, no grenades either (unless you count throwing propane tanks XD ). with the smaller weapons, you can either weild one at a time, or dual weild. The choices are for single shots: Desert Eagle, Cobra, and M9. The choices are for automatics: UMP5, MP7, and Micro UZI. The choices are for the main weapon: Carbine (M16 Burst Fire), AK47, Sawed Off Shotgun, Model 1887 (?), and a Stiker.
The powers you have through the game is also limited, but they are super powerful so it doesn't really matter at that point honestly. You have two activated abilities, The Swarm and Gun Channeling. The Swarm goes out and swarms around people effectively stunning them (and sometimes even killing them), you can get upgrades for it to last longer, recharge faster and affect more enemies. Gun Channgeling gives you infinite ammo and super powered shots for a limited time. The upgrades consits of longer lasting, faster recharge, auto shooting towards targets and shooting through walls. So as you can tell, turning a corridor full of enemies you can just activate both and blow through them both in two seconds.
I didn't really find any bugs in the game. The only real problem I had is that sometimes the screen goes a little blurry, like the beginning of being of barely stepping in light and it just causes some depth of view problems. It doesn't really last long if it happens, but it can and when you are trying to fight people it messes with your vision a bit.
So all in all to say: 10/10 hands down. Would love to have harder achievements though.

To start off, I did not buy the game, but rather, I received a key to help provide feedback on the game and its flaws and features. With that being said, I can't write all too much about this game, (this is for the time being of course, I'll make an update once I familiarize myself with this game a bit more)  but I can say that this game certainly has the potential to become something great. I was iffy about how this game would run on my toaster laptop (Intel HD Graphics and i3, ew, I know) and honestly, I didn't think it would do too great. To my dismay, I was actually quite surprised, I tested the game on how it ran on all the different settings and even on the highest setting the game wasn't horrifically unplayable. As with pretty much all games, the game ran smoothest on the lowest settings, but it still shocks me that it wasn't as bad as I thought it would be on the highest. The game is obviously very well optimized and if you have a low end PC, don't be too skeptical about trying out this game just because you think it won't run, if it can run on my PC, it should be able to do so on yours too. One thing though, while it isn't really a problem, graphics can't be manually input. What I mean by this is that you can't change shadow, texture, and enviroment detail to your liking manually one by one as you can with most games. This isn't really a problem, but it would still be nice to see advanced graphics settings added in the future, considering how everyone is different and likes to balance their games to their likings. Apart from the graphics, the sounds are pretty nice too and add a nice feel to the game. From what I have seen so far, gameplay seems fun and simple to pick up, although playing the game solo isn't the most fun, the game certainly seems to be much better with others. Now, while what I'm about to say isn't about the game itself, it is probably just as equally important. One thing that isn't rare to see nowadays in the gaming community is the vast amount of early access titles that have been stuck in early access for a while, and will probably stay there for an even longer while of time due to lack of effort associated with devs working on the game. One thing I can say for a fact is that with this game, you won't have to deal with that. The devs constantly work on Shark Attack Deathmatch 2 and actually encourage you giving your thoughts on their product, whether it's good or bad. Not only does this show that the devs care about what you think, but it shows that they are willing to change the flaws to make the game shine. The devs working on this game not only listen to their fans to figure out what they should fix, but they go the full mile and actually go ahead and try their best to fix said things. Now, should you pick up this game? The answer is yes. The game has a great dev team that listens to its playerbase, is very well optimized for an early access game (especially one that looks as nice as this one), and is only 5 dollars. If the work being done continues, there is nothing but a bright future ahead for this game.

Pyre is a fantastic game by Supergiant, the creators of indie hits Bastion and Transistor.
Unlike their previous games, Pyre seems to be heavily overlooked by the general public, regardless of it's highly praised reviews, I personally feel as though the general public's idea of the game and lack of a competitive multiplayer aspect is what hurt the game and overrides Pyre's critical acclaim by the games media.
Pyre is a pseudo sports title with RPG elements, and like the previous titles, minimal voice acting (i.e; one voice actor, Narrator from Bastion, Transistor Blade and the Judge from this game). Character interactions are played out in almost a visual novel interaction, with simlish like mumbles and phrases that lead a character's line of dialogue.
Based on who's advice you follow between fights, usually leads to you getting a chance to interact with character's and uncovering why they were exiled into the Downside. The interactions are fantastic and incredibly well written and thought provoking. The game is a slow burn of intrigue, a lot of world building and phrases that are cleverly explained by a cursor highlighting system. It's nowhere near say, Final Fantasy 13's Fal'cie/La'cie/Coccoon etc; confusion. Supergiant does an excellent job of it's explainations and making the writing inviting and easily digestible.
Without spoiling too much, the game's stakes and overall plot really open up toward the end of the game's first "Season". The game asks you to make difficult decisions regarding the cast, and does an fantastic job of making you care about each memeber of the group, which makes some of the choices excrutiatingly difficult. On the note of the difficulty, the game features three base diffiulty modes, as well as the ability to alter them to the player's will for bonus XP like their previous titles, a feature that is frankly welcomed in today's hand holding gaming landscape.
The story is arguably the strongest of Supergiant's trilogy of oddities, which is saying a lot. Supergiant continue to push themselves and take risks that pay off each time. Bastion was a safe bet with it's ARPG style, Transitor takes a more tactical approach, changing up their pace, rather than sticking to the genre which put them on the map, and they further push themselves with a genre that is quite frankly difficult to pinpoint.

Pyre is my game of the year for 2017 and it excites me for where Supergiant decides to take their amazing art direction, storytelling and gameplay next.

Whilst it says 28.8 hours on record, outside of steam I have ploughed an insane amount of hours in, and I still absolutely love it! I love the humour, the missions, the difficulty at times and the creativeness it allows.
I wish there was steam workshop support, and I wish there was a sequel... maybe there will be one day.
All in all it's a steal at £6.99. A++++

The overall level of all your characters combined determines who you are matched with, despite which character you might want to use. If you have an overal level of 10, but want to use a brand new character (level 0), you could be matched with a player using a level 10 character. This matchmaking system encourages players to use one character and not diversify, which leads to a lot of games encountering the same 4 or 5 characters all using the same tactics, despite the players being completely different. It gets pretty stale after a while of playing the same character, and fighting the same characters. Trying a new character is very difficult unless you decide to fight bots, but you earn less experience.
Conclusion: Its a brand new game. The little bits and pieces work great, but probably the most important parts aren't quite polished yet. However, this tends to be common. I have a feeling that Ubisoft will try to fix some of these issues (maybe by allowing you to select your character before entering matchmaking, and then matching players based on the chosen character's level rather than the player's overall level). I feel that if you want a game that looks awesome and feel satisfying when you beat someone or win a game, but are prepared for some quirks and issues, then its a good buy.

Pyre is a game that is half sports-ball and half visual novel, brought to you by the makers of Bastion and Transistor. Unlike the previous two, the game has a fairly open-ended story. Without revealing any spoilers, the art, the music, and the ending makes it worth getting through the few grindy bits.
Minor spoilers to describe the game; you start by meeting your team, and you start learning about them and the world, while simultaneously establishing who you, the player, are. Soon you enter a game, which feels almost like NBA Jam, if each member of the Chicago Bulls had special abilities. Once you finish the battle, win or lose, you're thrown back into the visual novel, and you start to learn more about the world you're in. Rinse and repeat.
The game throws enough curves in, with new characters, new mechanics, new challenges, and it constantly ramps up so it almost never gets boring. I say almost, because towards the end, I was reaching a point where I was ready for the game to be finished, and I felt I was just grinding through the last bits to complete it. But the payoff of seeing what happens to everyone, the credits, the music, it is just so flawlessly executed. If you played Bastion or Transistor, expect that level of music and fanfare all the way through.
What is there to say about a Supergiant Games game? The art is lovely and the presentation is delightful. The characters are compelling, ally and enemy both. The world is interesting to learn about as you play. The gameplay is not completely original, but it's different and interesting enough to remain enjoyable until the end, with some options for replayability for those who wish to. And I can't say enough good things about the music. My mind was blown when I realized that a certain battle had different tracks depending on who the competitors were, AND it changed based on who was winning at the time. I have yet to see another game or another company make something like this.

Judgement:
Pyre is the best thing to come out of Supergiant Games’ door, and the best game to come out in 2017. Seriously, its phenomenal. It’s also an acquired taste. The main section of gameplay, the basketball like fights for freedom called Rites, are these weird bits of gameplay that quite a few people took issue with, and understandably so. For a while I thought they were difficult to control, poorly balanced, and sometimes just felt like a hinderance to the story’s progression, but after a while I warmed up to them. I don’t have anything concrete gameplay wise for this, but more on the story side. To me, the Rites are your way of becoming part of the narrative. Player agency in Pyre is off the charts, and the way that the game rolls with your performance really ties you into the world in a tangible way. Save-scumming and generally trying to fight the game to get the “best ending” will only ruin the experience. Pyre shines brightest when you suffer a terrible defeat, or pull a daring victory that you thought impossible five minutes before. Watching the games story twist under your influence and getting to spend time with the lovable members of the Nightwings were the best things I did in gaming this year, even considering the amazing sense of wanderlust I experienced with BotW.
Pyre is my game of the year for much the same reason that I loved Doki Doki Literature Club. It’s unique, a bit strange, and a benefit to the medium. So many games, Visual Novels especially, have this problem where they really don’t need to be a video game, and could perform fine as an Anime or TV show. Pyre is an absolute exception to this idea. It’s defining trait, outside of its phenomenal visuals, writing, and music, is its willingness to let the player matter. You define what happens next, not by endless dialogue options, but by trying your best in the face of overwhelming challenge. By daring to live up to the legacy of the Eight-Scribes, and to Return in Glory, if you find yourself able.
Soundtrack:
Link: On Steam, or
Now I’m no stranger to hyperbole, but know that I’m not trying to exaggerate when I say this:
This is taking into account Supergiant’s phenomenal soundtracks to both Bastion and Transistor. Pyre’s soundtrack is beyond amazing. Darren Korb and Ashley Barrett just keep doing this, making the best soundtrack in a game ever, and then next time around they just get even better. Bastion’s music was phenomenal, Transistor’s was groundbreaking, and Pyre is just indescribably amazing and diverse. It really gets room to explore different styles with themes matching each group you face in the rights, making the soundtrack a wonderfully full-bodied album, with songs ranging from somber lute pieces to heavy metal, and never missing a stride in-between. It’s effortlessly stylish, and just ♥♥♥♥in great.
The music is astounding, and made even better by hearing it organically, so take my word for it, and don’t listen to any of it until you play the game. If you, the casual Reader, are still unconvinced, give just this song a gander, then get your wallet out stat.
This is one of the early Rite songs, so listening to it early shouldn’t spoil much of the fun. Still, I absolutely recommend just playing the game before listening.
And def buy the soundtrack. Get the bundle, buy it on Bandcamp, I don’t care, just give these people money for this. Seriously. This is the kind of quality product that deserves to be financially supported. Supergiant Games is only around 12 people, and they’re making some of the best games and music the industry has ever seen.
Alright, for the rest of this, let’s just jump into my ramble that I so dearly love to do:
Now’s probably the best time to mention that there are no explicit fail states in Pyre. When you lose in a battle, the game moves forward, and the standings on the Religious Basketball Extravaganza leaderboard get updated to match the outcome of any given match. By the time you get to Liberation Rites (fights to free a member from exile) the game really shows that it means that. If you lose a Liberation Rite the opposition gets to send someone free instead of you, creating real ramifications for your performance. It’s a flexible narrative done right, twisting not by direct dialogue choices, but instead bending based on your actual contribution to the team.
This flexibility works best when your objective isn’t to “get the best ending”. My first playthrough, my main goal was to play the game perfectly, and not fail any of the Rites. Because of this, I restarted a few Rites, and generally fought the game for control, not wanting to increase the difficulty for fear of failure. By the end of my first playthrough, I realized that wasn’t really the point of the whole experience, and my method was honestly a disservice to what Supergiant intended.
Pyre is first and foremost a story, and it’s one that you have a place in. Your skill at the game and your willingness to take risks, directly factor into your place within the narrative. The game shines brightest when you’re challenging a triumvirate better than you, facing an actual challenge, where the outcome could go either way. Most other games, screwing up means you restart, and your agency as a player has no tangible impact on the narrative. In Pyre, screwing up can cost a person their freedom, permanently. The only Rite I fumbled in my first playthrough was halfway through the game, and the defeat was staggering. My favorite character was denied their freedom by my lack of skill, and that impact made me feel like an integral part of the story in a way that I haven’t seen before.
People like to tout games where “everything you do matters!” like the QTE’s in Telltale games are going to make anything different by screwing up and dying. Quantic Dream games and Until Dawn get closer to this promise, but there’s still plenty of decisions in those that don’t matter at all.
Pyre is the closest I’ve seen someone come to fulfilling that promise. Since each Rite has a tangible impact on the games narrative, all the prep work you put in before a Rite has an impact on the story, in a once removed kind of way. Even small incremental stat bonuses and the upgrades you give members of the Nightwings have an impact on the story of Pyre, since they can be the things that sway a Rite in your favor. Similarly, the choice of Titan Stars (Pyre’s organic difficulty system) you activate for any given Rite levies the same impact. This level of consequence for your actions really helps to immerse you in the game world, and goes to show that immersion isn’t about graphics or endless sandboxes, its about making the player feel like part of the world.
I’ll be honest, I had very low expectations for Pyre. I didn’t pre-order it like I did Transistor, as the whole Rites aspect scared me off. I’ve never liked sports games, so seeing Supergiant tackle a genre I hate had me concerned that the final product wouldn’t be up to snuff. At the end of the day, I’ve never been so wrong about a game. Supergiant has made a customer for life of me, and the fact that they’ve gone 3 for 3 on their releases is something everyone should be taking notice of.
In summary, I love this game, and the aspect of player agency is really what sells it for me. The fact that the player has so much sway over the game helps to elevate it above near everything else I played in the last 12 months. The world needs more games like Pyre, and more devs like Supergiant.

8.5/10. Every Supergiant game is an experience worth paying for. Just be aware that Pyre is NOT an action RPG and definitely NOT a spiritual successor to the previous games. It is, however, definitely still a Supergiant game, so you can expect relatively simple gameplay but with incredible detail, endearing characters and an amazing narrative.
Pyre introduces you to characters, both allies and enemies, that you'll eventually begin to care about. And then you'll be given the choice of giving them a good or bad ending. But giving them the good ending also means saying good bye forever. It turns RPG farewell scenes into a literal in-game ritual. The great music score and art style gives every good bye an appropriately melancholic feeling.
However, hope is never lost. The game encourages the player to continue the story regardless if they win or lose a match, and the story will progress no matter what. No matter the outcome, the ending results in different shades of "mostly good" but always with a sense of optimism.  That being said, I found myself deleting the game pretty soon after I beat it and researching online for the endings I missed, because the gameplay itself wasn't thrilling enough for me to go for a replay.
Great game, worth the full price.

Edit: Okay, fine. A serious review.
This one's mixed to me; I'd give it a thumbs sideways if I could. For the sake of this review, it will be marked as positive however, as at least the game was fun-ish.
I've finished the original Dead Island three times on consoles, and wanted to try something new, so I picked up this game. At the start, it does a lot right and a lot wrong. And going further into the game, these rights and wrongs increase in severity.
The rights:
-Visuals are amazing. Not cutting edge or fantastic, but truly an improvement.
-Most of the bugs have been fixed from the original, as far as I can tell.
-Decent atmosphere, not as good as the first Dead Island, but still something significant.
-Entertaining if you can stomach fetch quests. (More on that later)
-It didn't forget it was an RPG, and there are minor elements to it.
-No frame drops on computers that aren't loq-budget. (Not optimized for laptops)
-The new maps are nicely done.
The mixed:
-Gameplay. Fetch quests, the main quests can literally be streamlined with little consequence, and it gets boring after some time, but is fun as long as you're doing something.
-Combat is a bit clonky and pretty much the same. Spam M1 and occasionally press Z or M2.
-The new party system was useless to me, and I never picked it up.
-The new special infected are okay. The wrestler (Tank-y) is hard as balls to kill and the screamer (Distracting) is annoying. The grenaider is a nice touch, although rare.
The bad:
-Story. Awful. So, you're immune to the virus, survive a boat crash,
-The general logic of this game.
-Fetch quests are a good 65% of all the quests in the game, and get annoying when you want to do something else.
-The loot system. Even in level 3 crates, I find myself getting uncommons.
-Multiplayer is dead.
If you're a fan, or wait for a sale, get it. Otherwise, unless you want it, just do more research or get Dead Island's definitive edition.

To be honest, this game feels like a super streamlined version of the first sniper elite. The missions are more like sniping wave arenas than levels where you could tactically or stealthily get through. The AI has super vision and can easily spot and  shoot you from a mile away with their machine guns before you can take them out with your sniper rifle.
X-Ray cam looks really good.
Levels feel more like cramped corridors and if you want to take a stealthy approach, you're in for a broken stealth system that hates you.
Also, you can't save manually. Yup! you need to reach certain checkpoints in order to save your progress and that is just plain silly and frustrating in a game where trial and error and trying alternate paths is key.
The DLC is crap if you want to stick to single player (kill hitler is short and uninspired, haven't tried the rest) but I think this game would shine better as a multiplayer sniping arena. So if you're craving for some exciting sniper deathmatches, this may be the game and DLC for you. If you want to play singleplayer only, I'd say skip this watered down sequel altogether. may look great but it's too "Arcade"y and severely watered down for my expectations of the series.
