For a Early Access game this is highly impressive. For one the amount of effort and polish here is staggering. Spritework is very detailed and charming and the animations are top notch all around. NPCs don't just sit around, they walk, talk, sneeze, cough, sigh, eat some chicken, work and more. They are all doing something and each one feels unique and goes a long way to draw you into the game world.
The gameplay is very tight and responsive. You have a robust amount of options when it comes to combat style thanks to weapon skills and various schools of magic. Specialize or mix and match, its all up to you and the game encourages it. The option to buy back level up points is a nice feature if not pricey.
The game also has tons of great design choices. Puzzle challenges let you rewind various steps of the puzzle. Pushed a block in the wrong space? No problem, step on a tile to undo it without having to reset the whole thing. And that feature is nice cause these puzzles can rack your brain on occasion. When it comes to crafting you can pin recipes your working on to your hud so you can know what you need at all times. Tons of smart game design on display here.
And not to mention the games Arcade mode which honestly could have been a whole game by itself. Its a permadeath roguelike style experience which asks you to go into randomly generated dungeons to rack up as many points as possible in one run by not only clearing rooms but being smart and quick about it. These points go towards improving your hub town. You can also find special rare items you can cash in for permanent perks that carry over from character to character. Also this whole game has 4 PLAYER ONLINE CO-OP! For Story AND Arcade mode with various features that go with that too like competitive minigames.
My mind is blown that this is a Early Access game cause good lord its already far acceded its asking price for me. Get a copy or two for your buddies and enjoy some good old fashioned action RPG goodness. ^^

This game is 4 years old now, and I believe it is time for a new review. My standards for review scores are 10 starting points, and -1 point for everything done wrong. Before I continue, I need to state that I am not biased towards any particular gaming company or extended universe/lore. I review the game as it should be reviewed -- as a time waster. Things done right in this game are below:
Great Graphics
Lightsaber Combat and Force Powers Done Right
Many Customization Options (Including several costumes [Just for aesthetics] and many lightsaber crystals which give you different upgrades)
The game has done a good job with capturing the atmosphere of the environments, especially Kamino
Things done wrong are below:
The Story is atrocious, no debate. And with the story being a major point of any game, an extra point is taken off. -2 points.
The player character is a mix of blandness and unoriginality, however, at times, you can feel like an indestructible god, choosing who lives and who dies which provides a fun experience. Not enough to keep a point, however, so -1 point.
Finally, Quick Time Events (QTE's) are abundant, and repetitive. -1 more point.
The final score for this game is: 6/10. While being a good Star Wars game, it still has enough flaws to put it at an average rating. In my opinion, if you haven't gotten this game yet, get it. Frankenstein: Master of Death is a nice Hidden Object game. It is quite representative of the whole genre without weird experimentations and if this is what you are looking for it can be enjoyable.
It is, however, ridiculously easy.
While puzzles thoughout the whole genre are often quite simplistic (find star shaped object to put into star shaped lock and progress to next room) this games really exaggerates. You often find the key objects right next to the locks or just repeatedly use your crowbar/screwdriver/metal gauntlet? to solve puzzles on sight. The progression is also extremely linear. The mini-games are super simple too, for example in the typical rotating disc game the discs move all independently. Finally also the hidden-object scenes are too easy. The scenes are drawn up-close and all objects are huge and clearly contrasted. The mini-games in the hidden-object scenes are sweet although not challenging. The challenge seems appropriate for children, although the story is too dark.
On the bright side the artwork is very pleasant and I somehow enjoyed the fast pace. I still cannot really recommend it as there is an abundance of better games in this genre out there.

Man do I love this game, it does everything right! But at the same time it leaves me wanting so much more.
The good:
(And boy is there alot of good.)
-Rewarding fluid combat that makes attacks feel impactful
-Stunningly beautiful and just lovely to look at
-Amazing choice for voice actors with even side or background characters being fully done
-A very fun way to play an RPG in terms of traveling, very D&D like
-The narration is perfect, it feels like someone is reading an epic sega to you
-The story, oh boy the story! Twists, development, ups, downs and comedy it's got it all and well written!
-A Real feeling of under-dog progression from the main character
-Diverse wonderful characters from all races in the game
-Very viable for multiple play throughs, do all the things! Learn from your mistakes!
-Knocking enemies off cliffs does exactly that, say goodbye to invisible walls!
-Fun character interactions as the story progresses, it feels natural and unforced.
-Four hero party system feels very well balanced and slightly Tales like
-It's actually hard on hard mode... imagine that!
-Gold is a resource not a second thought, use it well it's limited!
-Dwarves!
The not so good/not so bad:
-Food mechanic during travel is a really nice idea, but with how harsh it gets when your party grows it feels like you're being punished for exporing
-Cutscenes while beautiful and amazing can be accidentally skipped with a mouse button press, no way to re-watch them without having a save just before or replaying the game.
-Battles are fun, I went looking for everyfight I could, but you lose yourself onscreen quite easily and this can get you into a heap of strategic trouble.
-Not enough orc hordes on the overworld map! To repeat my point I like the combat in this game, I crave it, but there simply isn't enough threat outside of the scenarios.
The bad:
-Slippery enemies, and I don't mean small or fast ones those are fine, I mean the type that slide across the floor while your heroes push them off a cliff... then follow them.
-GET OUT OF MY WAY! You'll find the main character gets stuck on... everything, during combat it's your team and during movement it's corners of terrain and npc's.
-The inventory screen is very lacking and you can very easily lose track of equipment at items during what is basically the set up phase.
-The story is so good why can't I have more? Seriously I completed the game in about six-ish hours doing every side quest I could find.
-A few of the heroes are just lack luster versions of other heroes with equal or less damage and more often than not less health.
-The very few dwarven cities you do get to walk around in never actually feel like cities, just very decorated hallways with clear "don't go here" guards.
-Not enough side or optional quests. I know we're rushing to save the world and all but lets be real, rpg's are all about those side quests.
-Level cap at ten for every character with limits to three spells or abilities, this is just nitpicky for me really but playing through it I felt like combat would flow even nicer if I could string together a lovely combo.
All in all I really do love this game and if anyone were to ask meif they should get it I'd answer yes. The downsides to this game are easily forgotten as you get engrossed in the world and story and the positives really make themselves known without ever feeling obnoxious.

Before you decide to purchase this you should realize one thing.  This isn't a game.  This program is basically a glorified Tech Demo that shows you what the BeamNG crew's physic engine is capable of.
The landscapes are beautiful, the crash physics are awesome, but the program itself is nothing but a large sandbox for testing the engine's capabilities.  You load up an area, load up a vehicle, and drive around.  That's it.  That's really all there is.  You can drop in objects and other vehicles, even add some AI so you can "race" against another vehcile, but it still remains just a glorified tech demo.
Aside from crashing into things, playing with the AI, and testing the physics, there really isn’t much else to do here.  Honestly I got bored after the first 30 minutes but decided to press on for another 30 just to be sure I was good and bored.  I will admit, the first few times you completely wreck a vehicle it's really amusing, but the novelty wears off REALLY fast.  Personally I was hoping this program might have been something along the lines of "Flatout 2", a racing game with awesome crash physics, but no.  The AI here is really basic so don't expect much.
After an hour I decided to refund the product before I lost the capability to do so.  I really can't recommend this program without it actually showing signs of being something more than a tech demo.

I think the team behind this game is very talented and has executed their vision exceptionally. My main beefs are witih their vision.
Pros:
* I run 21:9 3440 x 1440 and the game immediately picked up the setting and ran with it. A+
* The story telling is grand.
* The lore is wonderful.
* The visuals are so pretty.
* The responsiveness is there.
Why the downvote?
Cons:
* The combat is clunky and unrewarding. For me, combat is primary. I feel like the devs started with a premise and this premise was a bad starting position that led to bad conclusions. This premise was probably something along the lines of "let's have a party-based combat system centered around collision physics". It sounds awesome, but the reality is dull and disconnected.
* The introductory fight is a really bad intro. You dominate that fight, which is misleading. Subsequent fights are much harder. I felt like it didn't matter what I did during the intro fight.
* White damage is abysmally low compared to special attacks. The disparity is far too great. This requires pausing the game relentlessly to run a tactical special for each party member every 1.5 seconds. Unlike the intro fight, this is so far the opposite, that it felt oppressive. I had to nuance every single move. There wasn't a moment where I felt like I could kick♥♥♥♥♥ not even in a small way.
* The physical collisions felt like they got in the way more than they added to the experience. Friendlies trying to path around one another failed all the time, even when there was room! Managing physical collisions and movement is great when you just have one character to manipulate (think Counter-strike). This was just a chore in this game.
* Loot, gearing, and character growth were very shallow. Don't expect the game to shine in these areas.
* The camera always center-focused on the selected party member. This was aggravating when trying to view the battle field. There is no camera pan during combat.
* Combat felt like homework to get throguh so I could get back to the story.
* Targeting misfires regularly. Sometimes I would pause the game, but a specific enemy would not be target-able. I would then unpause and pause immediately, and then I can target said enemy.
* The world map is just a digitized mini figure that you move around like a chess piece. If an encounter "pops", you go to battle. This model can work, but the world map is actually very small when you realize you can only move to and from specific points of interest on the map. There is no free roam of any kind. That said, the integrated story-telling on the world map was just awesome...so good. I would be so forgiving of the encounter-based combat if combat was actually fun.

Supergiant Games do it once again. They deliver a completely fresh gaming experience while making the most out of their known strengths with gorgeous graphics, an award-worthy soundtrack, and excellent storytelling.
The greatest hurdle for players will be their own genre expectations. Pyre combines the experience of a visual novel with breakneck paced action sports interludes, peppered with RPG elements. This lead to some players expecting a different experience from what they got, and leaving disappointedly.  For those who stay however, Pyre soon reveals itself as an incredibly innovative, diverse, and rich experience.
The visual novel/world exploration portion guides you through a beautiful fantasy world peppered with unique characters. Other than Supergiants' previous games, Pyre makes use of a huge cast of factions and characters. Necessarily this means less narration and more text focus. The dialogue is kept fast and interesting enough to appeal even to those who wouldn't be all that convinced to play a visual novel.
The second core mechanic is a lighting fast 3v3 sports game called the "rites", which is somewhat of a fantasy battle basketball. Surprisingly for such an innovative game mode, it turns out to be immaculately designed. It is easy to get into, and every character offers wildly different options for their team. These can be further diversified through a simple yet enormously impactful skill tree and an item slot.
These mechanics may appear disconnected at first, but the designers managed to blend them together seamlessly. Your dialogue and exploration choices will influence which team members you can field in the rites, find new items for them, or strenghten or weaken them. The much more impressive mechanic however works the other way around, as the story branches out by your success or failure in the rites. Rather than forcing you to replay a rite until victory, losing a rite has significant impact on the story development and makes for greatly memorable moments. Together with the many other choices, this leads to myriads of possible outcomes that will all reflect to the story, and ultimately the ending.
For those who have their reservations based on genre expectations, I can only recommend to give it a shot. Everyone else can expect a lovely experience. Pyre also has great potential as a gateway for casual players.

Evil Genius was a hard one to review, but alas, I've finally done it, and I can say that I'm quite impressed. I first played this a couple of years ago but didn't really like it back then. I thought, since its sitting in my library, I'll give it another go. It has turned out a lot better than I thought it would. You play as an evil mastermind, tasked at building your own base and gaining noteriety around the globe by completing devious missions. Basically being a James Bond villian. If base building is your thing then yes I would recommend this!
Evil Genius is a base building game, where you play as one of three different evil masterminds and attain noteriety across the globe by completing missions. If you've played games like Dungeon Keeper, this will be very familiar to you. You are first placed on an island, with a few tasks to complete. You are also given a huge mountain. This is where you build your base. You are given a selection of rooms to begin with plus gaining more the more tasks you complete. Pretty much simple right?
Obviously, for the kind of game it is, your camera is set from above so you can manage your base easily. The game isn't as simple as it seems. Plenty of things can happen at any given time such as blackouts, attacks, e.t.c. The game gives you tutorials on how to do things when they're needed so in some ways the game does hold your hand. As I mentioned before, there are three different leaders to choose from, all of which, are different in their own ways. But no matter which one, you always start on the same island. People who are familiar to these kind of games will find it easy. Newcomers won't find it hard to adapt.
Being a game from 2004, the graphics, of course, are a little bit outdated, but that didn't bother me at all, and it shouldn't bother you. Everything is clear to understand, and there're different graphics options to fit your PC, some of which might make the game look better for you anyway. As of the design, I can say that the island you start on is a bit plain in terms of detail, but that doesn't really matter since you're trying to build a base anyway. The rooms are interesting and can have added detail anyway. It's one of those games that doesn't try to be lazy when making it.
Again, for people unfamiliar to these kind of games, they might struggle on where to find things. Like I said earlier, there are tutorials on how to do things, but not everything. Sometimes the game leaves you to try and find out where things are and what they do. At some points I did struggle on finding my way through things, but again, you adapt. In terms of settings though, I never had a problem, nor should other people.
- Interesting James Bond feel
- Unique Idea
- Plenty of entertainment
- Sinister soundtrack :D
- The game is quite humorous at times.
- Can be confusing at times
- Sometimes left at points where you have no idea what to do
Evil Genius is one of those games that doesn't look amazing, but when actually played, suprises you. The idea of the game is what intruiged me the most. Playing as an evil mastermind that made you feel like a villain of James Bond is excellent in my opinion. Although sometimes confusing, Evil Genius makes up for it with It's excellent features and the enjoyment of annoying other countries. :D Worth buying if you like these kind of games, or want to get into them.
Final Verdict - 8/10.

Welp, review time.
It's an interesting game, and I think it has a lot of potential, but in its current state it may fall under your expectations. The UI is kind of unfriendly, the amount of grinding you need to do may be too much for some people, plus sometimes it's hard to keep track of what all those dummies need in terms of gear (especially if you have more than twenty four adventurers). And speaking of dummies - you won't be attached to any of your adventurers since all of them are just different skins with a bunch of different abilities. To be honest, I think it's a wasted opportunity. Some sort of relationship system would make things much more interesting and fun.
On the plus side, AM is actually a pretty good time-skipper. Moreover, the writing in this game is a lot of fun, too! Elven Elders and Jester never failed to make me smile. And, as I already said, AM has potential, so if devs will take the right road, this game will become a pretty interesting and "stable" title.
To sum everything up, AM got my interest, I do like and recommend it as a time-skipper, but if you're looking for something stronger gameplay-wise, then this game isn't for you. In its current state, of course.
So, here are some suggestions/ideas:
1.Do something about the UI (especially in the shops) because it's a bit bulky and unintuitive.
2.Rework the salvaging system. Make a single "scrap pile" for all colours of equipment instead of separate piles for each one. Salvaging white and green equipment is pretty much useless right now.
3.I'd like to see more developed adventurers. Would be awesome if you could implement some sort of perks/traits system like in Darkest Dungeon.
4.Again, more interactivity between characters. Some sort of relationship system that would affect how adventurers perform in dungeons. Since AM has an Ironman feature with permadeath for adventurers, I want them to actually matter.
5.Auto-equiping gear. This will make the whole "is my dummies' gear up to date?" thing A LOT easier. You already have the "Suggested gear" as a filter option, so why not to make an option that will allow adventurers to gear up according to the filters I've set? I have three parties for auto-adventuring and keeping thier gearscores up to "date" isn't really fun. And don't forget that I need to keep an eye for my main party's equipment.

Ok, I´ve read a bunch of reviews now, some negative and some positive, but nothing said there have swayed me in my opinion:
THIS IS AN AWESOME GAME!
Got it as a present from my brother and have played it immensely since then! It IS hard to survive as a counselor when hunted by Jason, and if one of the counselors who gets killed happens to carry an important item, lets say the fuse or the car keys, it gets even harder, especially if they get killed in the wilderness. Sure, the items that they carried will be found scattered around their corpses, but they are tiny and easily overlooked. This means that sometimes counselors are running around on a wild goosechase with VERY little chance of actually finding said objects.
With that said, it is SUPPOSED to be hard to survive as a counselor against Jason! In the movies he´s an unstoppable force and few has seen him and survived. This is mostly true in the game also. I would hate to see Jason nerfed since this is a horror game, and anything but a strong, fearsome Jason would make a counselor survival quickly loose importance. The feeling when I survive a match despite being hunted by Jason is absolutely unbeatable!
IMPLEMENTED GAME FEATURES
The way the music works in the game is wonderful since the actual game mechanic (to announce for counselors that Jason is closing in on them) is hidden. No flashing tokens or anything that takes away from the feeling. Player health is also well integrated: No bars that tells you how wounded a counselor is, just how fast they move, the movement animations (and how their clothes are soaked in blood). Also, fear is simulated in unvolontary gasps of horror that Jason can hear, unability to see the small player map, loss of colors, decreased visuals to simulate tunnel vision, trickier movement control etc. Spooky! Combat is tricky. It is fairly easy for counselors to miss their target and they might accidently drop their weapons, or the wepons might brake. I love it! The counselors aren´t supposed to be brave action heroes and their adrenaline spikes, making them clumsy! As said earlier; this is a horror game, and lack of control over the situation is a MAIN part of this. If combat were easier, it would ruin the feeling of "Better to run" that is so important for the right atmosphere.
WHAT´S NOT IN THE GAME
A typical feature that isn´t in the game is Jason´s habit of rigging murdered victims in places and ways where the living counselors would find them for maximum terror effect.
Also, in this game, the counselors are aware of the danger from the start of the game session, while in the movies, Jason often goes to great lenght not to be seen by more then the ones he is actually killing, keeping the others in a false security while picking them off, one by one. This, however, would be a totally different gameplay where, for example, unaware counselors would get points for doing wonderfully stupid counselor stuff like getting cold beer in the cellar, taking a bath in Crystal lake alone, snogging each other in abandoned cabins, hiking in the woods, showering etc. until the truth gets uncovered, while Jason would get more points the longer he´s not triggering the public panic. Oh well...

Disclaimer here:  I'm new to Frictional games.  I have not played a single one of their games (they're in my Steam library-- I'll get to them one day! :D).  This review is based on Soma alone so there are no comparsions to any other Frictional Games developed/produced games.
The environement of Soma is completely immersive.  The audio aspects are oustanding. When combined with superb use of lighting (or lack of), a completely believable and immersive atmosphere is created.  Soma is DRIPPING with 'atmosphere' from start to finish.  The atmosphere is TENSE once the storyline really kicks off.   It does contain a few 'jump scares' but they are few and far between and done well.  When it's all put togthere, Soma gets under your skin in ways few games ever do.  You'll be thinking, as I did, about your experience/gameplay for days afterward.
The story quality is quite good.  You'll need to be patient as it's drip fed to you as you progress through the game.  If you're the impatient type, this will will drive you crazy as said patience is paramount.  Important ideas such such as 'what does it mean to be human, are humans  and robots equal (and more) are core story elememts.  They will make you sit back and think hard.
Puzzles are found throughout the game.  I liked them as they hit the sweet spot of being neither too hard nor too easy.  You will more often than not simply overthink them as the solution is staring you clearly in the face,    The creatures of Soma are done very well.  Almost all the time, you'll not see them clearly.  In my opinion. The Dev team nailed this point.  With monsters, the less you see is oftentime the scarier they are.  They understood that your mind makes the scariest monsters (they're just there to give you a little help ).
The voice acting is quite good; specifically the two main characters of character of Catherine Chun and David Munshi,  Some people might find David to be a bit mundane (I had no problem).
Soma isn't perfect as oftentime you are oftentime 'dropped' into situations where you literally have no clue what to do, where to go or simply what can be done next.  Again, be patient; you will figure it out.  The game can get a bit repititous in regards to the puzzle solving or eluding of 'monsters'.  This point is, admittedly, a bit nitpicky as I easily overlooked it in regards to many superb aspects of Soma.  A HUD, mini-map or a simple nudge in the right direction would be have been most welcome.  Oftentimes I simply wandered around until I stumbled upon 'what to do next'.  This, momentarily, killed the atmosphere and left me frustrated.  I understand why the Dev team didn't include such things (see Alien: Isolation) but I feel they could have done something to help you out (a hint system of sorts?).
You need to pay attention to everything because in Soma, the 'devil is in the details'.  Don't rush through the game; enjoy it and always take take note of your surroundings.
There is a glitch near the end of the game <no spoilers here>.  I'm not sure if it has been patched out but you'll know when/if you encounter it.  You simply reload an earlier savepoint and avoid it.  Simple.
The regular price is $30.00 which I feel is a bit too much as the game isn't overly long (it's not short either); a better price would have been $20.00 to $25.00. <C'est la vie!>
Summary:
Soma does have some issues but the good/great aspects of it GREATLY outweigh the lesses ones.  I bought Soma at a 20% discount.  The best compliment I can give Soma is that  I would have gladly paid full price for it.  Grab it on sale, grab it at full price, it matters not.  You will get your money's worth and then some.  Enjoy!!

Considering the amount of effort the devs have put into working with the community to make this game better, I feel obligated to update this review, if only to say that the game has gotten better with the recent patches.
I still don't feel comfortable recommending this game yet, but I think it's only another patch before that changes.
It started out well. The bantering gurads on the title screen, and the tongue in cheek reference to Star Wars gave a glimpse at the humor to come. Then that annoying Jester showed up, and I understood why people hated that stupid paperclip in Microsoft Office.
The game has a unique sense of humor, and solid gameplay mechanics. It gets repetitive fairly quickly, but I could see it appealing to both casual players and hardcore number crunchers alike. Unfortunately, there are too many little things wrong. It makes the game feel unfinished, like a it's a port of a mobile app instead of being built to run on the desktop. On the positive side, the devs are engaged and seem commited to continually updating the game.
As much as I dislike the Jester, my biggest issue with the game is really the UI. None of the interfaces are intuitive, nor are the elements of the UI consistent. The shop gives you a "Buy" button, but no "Sell" button. Some dialogs can be dismissed by clicking on the background, others have to be closed using the "X" button. Audio settings aren't available while in a manual dungeon. There's no audio or visual feedback that to confirm you hired an adventurer. In fact while there's a lot of audio elements (some of which are quite annoying), there is very little in the way of audio feedback (button clicks, notification sounds, etc).
Then there's "Fast forward". Maybe you're waiting for an auto adventure to complete, your adventurers need rest, or they're training at the university. You can use fast forward until they're done, but this increases the risk of invasion. If you don't have any free adventurers to take on a manual dungeon crawl, you'll have to fast forward. It will stop automatically if an invasion occurs, but ironically not for any of those other things that are the entire reason you use fast forward in the first place. There is a notification, but you won't see it if you're in the shop, or otherwise not on the world map screen. This isn't a criticism of the ability to fast forward as much as it is a criticism of how useless the UI is in managing it.

Scrap Garden
3D Platformer
Egidijus Bachur, Alexey Davydov
Flazm
is a 3D platformer developed by Egidijus Bachur and Alexey Davydov and published by Flazm.
The game is set in a world with only robots living in it. You play as Canny, a lonely robot, who awakens in a post-apocalyptic world to find all other robots shut down and seized up. What happened to the City? Why did all robots stop moving? Did anyone survive except him? Little rusty Canny has to do all he can to find answers to these questions... and try to fix it all.
The story isn't really all that charming and interesting: while it starts out as a small version of Wall-E, it quickly turns into your typical "find-x-object-to-save-the-world" storyline without bringing anything new to the table.
Made with the Unity engine, the game's graphics are okay: the character models are mostly fine, the enemies are very repetitive (only two types for area) and the environments are varied but without anything interesting to look at.
The game is a 3D platformer that thankfully controls very well. But the real problem is how repetitive and not engaging it is: in every area you start out by collecting red gems to open a door that leads you to a small puzzle area (pick up objects or jump on a couple of buttons) to then face a boss that is killed by either throwing rocks at him or by following a straight path while avoid his attacks.
Your only buttons are (double)jump and pick up/throw objects, and good luck trying to aim: most of them times you will throw an object off screen since Canny hasn't fully turned around. This got quite annoying, and it made the game not as fun as it could have been.
The game is very, very easy: you one-hit kill any enemy by jumping on them, and the puzzles are (hopefully) designed with children in mind. The bosses don't require that much strategy, but the semi-final boss had a quick-time event that felt bugged, and it took me 16 times to manage to beat him. Now that ain't good, and I hope they fix the margin of error on it.
The soundtrack is pretty mediocre, and the sound effects are fine. The small amount of voice acting that is in the game is decent at best.
The game lasts around 2 hours, but you can replay it to find hidden objects that can be used to access a secret on a website. Otherwise, I will never play this game again.
Overall, the game is well done, but it unfortunately becomes very boring very quickly and it is way too short. Recommended when sale.

I really wanted to like this. After reading the reviews I really thought I’d like it. This seemed to be exactly  my kind of game, having liked the likes of Ico, Brothers, Limbo…
And at first I did. It looks beautiful and charming, the plot is engaging enough and I liked the characters.
Unfortunately the execution is lacking in other areas. In their defense, the developpers made it hard for themselves, with 2 characters to control, blizzard constantly messing with your movements, and many chase situations requiring fast reaction. It could either be a great game, or a very frustrating one. I'm sad to say it's the latter.
Movements are floaty and awkward. Momentum doesn't exist whenever wind is involved (when the wind stops you just stop) but does for certain moving platforms. It's pretty hard to predict where you're going to land, and there's almost no air control, making some areas very hard for no good reason. Many animations have a crazy recovery time for a platformer. The AI sometimes messes up in frustrating and unfair ways.
All of these elements combine to make a very frustrating game. As much as I wanted to enjoy the plot, and the atmosphere, the gameplay ruined it for me.

Never Alone (Kisima Ingitchuna) is a beautiful and emotional little game about a girl and a fox trying to find the cause of a blizzard that is threatening their world. The game is based on Alaskan Inuit folklore and conveys part of the culture with short documentaries that can be found throughout the game. These short films are a very novel and interesting way to make the player think about man's place in nature, and what we are doing to the world around  us.
Gameplay is a mix of puzzle platforming and some tricky timing/running. It does get a bit frustrating at times, and at certain parts there is a lot trial-and-error. But it never gets to the point of getting irritating.
Midway through the main gameplay gets a pretty big change and this is really beautifully implemented.
The winter landscape in the game is lovely, and the game does a good job of conveying the feeling being in a cold and dangerous world. The game is short, about five hours to finish and find all the collectibles, but very much worth the money for the enjoyment, and the wonderfully shot documentary shorts about Inuit culture is almost worth the price alone.

First of all, this is one of the most adorable games I have ever played. Everything about our little robot protagonist and the world he lives in makes me smile (Well, except maybe the spiders… but that’s beside the point). There is a ton of charm and atmosphere packed into this game, from the lonely piano music and quaint voiceovers to the number of fun (and sometimes destructible) details the developers put into the environment.
Scrap Garden is a simple, light-hearted platformer (with the occasional puzzle element) that does what it sets out to do very well. It reminds me a lot of 3D platforming games I played as a kid. The gameplay elements are varied… each chapter plays around with a different mechanic or two; there is a little bit of everything. Some are quite fun, others a little frustrating. It keeps things fresh regardless.
The game recommends using a gamepad (I used an Xbox 360 controller). The controls were simple and straightforward besides the occasionally wonky camera and double jump. Performance also seemed pretty good. I play on a cheap laptop with integrated graphics and it ran flawlessly on low settings and occasionally stuttered on medium. And despite playing on lower settings, the game still looks great. I ran into a few small graphical glitches and experienced a crash in a particular area, but the developers seem very responsive and good about getting out hotfixes.
Scrap Garden is on the shorter side and is not a particularly difficult game (I still died plenty of times), so if you are looking for a challenge, it might not be for you. However,  if you or your kid wants to relax and spend a couple of hours casually hopping around trying to help a little robot save the world… this fun little game might do the trick.

Basically, this is a cute little game. It's short, it's not too challenging, and it has a nice storyline.
First, some drawbacks (for me personally):

-  I must say the voice acting was a bit iffy -- but it was also entertaining to listen to (perhaps unintentionally). The English grammar was also a bit odd at times, but I imagine that wouldn't bother most people.
- The storyline lost me sometimes, though I don't know if that's because of an issue with the way it was written, with a hazy storyline in general, or my own inattentiveness.
- The puzzles weren't very challenging, so I would've liked a bit more in that regard (but this level of difficulty would probably be great for kids).
- The controls using a mouse and keyboard were a tad frustrating at times but not impossible.
- I felt like there was little incentive to collect more red crystals than required, and it was a bit disappointing to see all the crystals I collected get used up in each level even when I had more than necessary. Maybe there is an incentive to collect more that I'm just not aware of.
Things I liked:
- It felt really personal. This is why I like indie games. They give you a glimpse into the creators' minds and imaginations, and that really came across in this game. It certainly has a unique feeling to it, despite being (I imagine) inspired by a variety of similar kid-friendly puzzle games.
- The music is really nice and pleasant to listen to; it added to the overall feeling of the game as relaxing and sort of magical in a melancholic way.
- The game world is pretty to look at.
- Canny is quite adorable and I really liked its R2-D2-esque way of communicating.
- There are moments of odd and unexpected humour in the game that made me laugh out loud. It's an inoffensive and slightly absurd humour that perhaps appeals most to the young at heart.
- The game felt a bit old school in some ways. It reminded me of when I used to play games as a kid in the 1990s. I'm not sure how to articulate what specifically about the game made it come across that way, but it was both nostalgic and refreshing.
Anyway, it's a pretty nice game, and I'm glad I played it. If you think you appreciate similar things to me in an indie game, go ahead and try it out!

Recommended - with a few caveats.
Version reviewed: Rise of Flight - Channel Battles Edition
At the time of writing this sim is selling on Steam for £8.99, and the DLC between £4.79 and £6.89.  I'm willing to buy DLC of this quality at this price (in fact I've bought the lot).  When compared to £15 I just paid for the FSX Spitfire I think the Rise of Flight DLC represents good value; at full price, however, I'm not so sure.  All flight sims seem to have adopted the DLC model, with DCS World typically charging 30 quid for theirs.  They should all be put against a wall and shot.
The DRM and registration is a pain, and I don't think it's made clear quite how to do this properly.  On first registering the game you're taken to the ROF website to create an account, and (if I remember correctly) you're given an activation key - but this activation key is for the demo version, and you also have to paste in your Steam purchase key as well or you do not get the Channel Battles Edition (I spent quite a while swearing and cursing about what thieves these guys were until I worked this bit out).  Likewise with the DLC, all you get from Steam is an activation key which must be entered before anything will work.
The graphics and detail are gorgeous on a half decent machine (mine's two years old, so state of the art isn't required), but to set things up you need to launch a separate settings.exe file hidden away in SteamApps\common\Rise of Flight 2.0\bin_game\release\.
As for the game itself, where it's good it's absolutely outstanding, and where it isn't so good it really is cr@p.  The learning curve is steep.  Those early planes were awful, and real pigs to control.  This is reflected in the flight models, and even getting the damned things off the ground is a challenge.  If you want to jump straight into dogfights without learning how to work these things you won't last long; you'll tear your wings off or spin into the ground or, maybe, get shot down.  If you're not willing to spend time learning this game then think carefully before buying it, you might be better buying something else.  On the other hand, if you do stick with it, the first time you successfully take off, complete a few circuits and land safely is a real buzz.  This sim creates a feeling of actually being in the air better than any other I've played.
Where it's not so good is the mission and career selection, which all seems very muddled.  And while the the aircraft modelling is excellent, the character modelling is the worst I've seen for years, with voice acting so atrocious I winced the first time I heard it.
Overall then: if you think you'd enjoy a challenging flight sim, and if it's at the right price, you should buy it.  Otherwise go to the ROF website and download the demo before spending any money.
Now I'm off to have another go at getting that damned bomber off the ground...

This is a really fun flight sim.
This is a game where you can jack up the realism settings to maximum and still have a good time. All the annoying boring parts of flightsims, like propeller feathering, fuel mixture, radiator settings, radar calibration, complicated start up sequences? None of those have been invented yet.
Neither have parachutes.
On top of that, WW1 dogfights are in many ways even more fun than dogfights in WW2 aircraft. The planes are slower, more agile, and more fragile, so you can't just dive in from fifty million feet and wipe someone out before they have a chance to respond. You can try it, but your wings will snap off when you pull up. Engagements are terrifyingly close, and collision is always a very real threat, or option, depending on how much of a maniac you are.
Dogfights also last a lot longer. The planes are reasonably tough by virtue of effectively being large kites. If you don't hit the engine or the pilot, you won't do much more than superficial damage. Most of the planes carry plenty of bullets, too, so you'll get at least one extended dogfight per mission even if you waste ammunition.
The demo version, available on the website, lets your friends fly two very good planes for free, or occupy any gunner position in any aircraft, so you can get your friends to play with you even if they're broke and don't own a joystick. It's a generous move that makes up for the irritating DLC model used for the rest of the game.

The Dwarves (also known as "Die Zwerge") is a tactical-based RPG based on the novel series written by German author, Markus Heitz.
Story and plot premise:
The series takes place in the fictional fantasy realm of Girdlegard. The humans, whose primary deity is the goddess Palandiell, have seven kingdoms in the land, some of which house enclaves of magi who train famuli apprentices. The elves, who revere Sitalia, hide their kingdom of Alandur between the borders of two human kingdoms, Gauragar and Tabain. The dwarves, however, built their kingdoms around the mountain barriers of Girdlegard. Vraccas, their deity, ordered the dwarves to defend Girdlegard from orcs, ogres, and alfar (dark elves), all of which worship the dark god, Tion.
The story's main protagonist is a Tungdil Bolofar, a young (relatively speaking) dwarf who has never met one of his own kind. As a baby, he was discovered by goblins and sold to the magus Lot-Ionan. Living among the humans of Idoslane, Tungdil grew up to be a learned scholar, but he was completely naive to the world outside of the magical vaults he lived in.
One day, Lot-Ionan gives Tungdil the opportunity to go out into the world and see it for himself. Giving him a rucksack of magical items and a gentle shove out the door, Lot-Ionan tells Tungdil to deliver the items to his former apprentice, Goren. Meanwhile, other forces are at play. The magical barrier protecting Girdlegard from The Perished Land is weakening, and the orcs of Toboribor are rallying behind new leaders. What is a simple delivery job spirals into a quest to save Girdlegard...
Gameplay:
The gameplay of the Dwarves can be best described as a "tactical RPG". With 15 playable characters, you are given control of a party of 4 who must work together to fight off hordes of enemies. Each party member has unique abilities to use in tandem with others. Players can pause the game any time they choose in order to give new orders to the party. Characters will earn experience points and level up, and players will choose what skills they learn.
Each character has their own playstyle. For example, Boindil is a "speedy berserker" that moves and attacks quickly. His brother, Boendal, is a slower-moving warrior who can take a beating and is effective at crow control. Djerun is the slowest moving character in Tungdil's gang, but his attacks pack a heavy punch. Rodario has the abilities to feign death, convince enemies to fight for him and even physically mimic their appearances.
When players aren't fighting or in a specific area, they are travelling through Girdlegard on a world map. Tungdil's party, as well as other parties, are visualized as board pieces, moving through the waypoints one-by-one. Sometimes players will run into merchants, allies, or orc warbands. Even more, players can intercept orc warbands ransacking a settlement to save the villagers for rewards and experience points.
As someone who backed the game and beta tested it almost a year ago, I can conclude that King Art games polished game mechanics and removed a multitude of game bugs. However, players will still sometimes struggle with camera angles, and allied AI can be a bit stupid at times. For example, if you're helping villagers fight off an orc warband, they will sometimes deliberately walk in the way of ability AoE and get themselves killed. Additionally, moving through the world map can be a bit exhausing at times when players are literally forced to move waypoint by waypoint to get to the other side of the continent.
In conclusion, The Dwarves will be a treat for those who enjoy RPGs with dialogue and are able to tolerate slight mechanical frustrations.

I'm just playing for 2 hours, still I can say it's one of the best game I played in a while.
As the name "Grindea" already implies, the gameplay is kind of grindy, but in a very innovative way.
Every monster you can find in the world of Grindea has a few possible drops, which can be gathered to craft new equipment or sold to make money and therefore buy new equipment. These drops are listed in some kind of codex but unless you find them, they are blackened out. Besides that there are also very rare cards which drop only once and improves your characters abilities permanently. These two features provide a lot of motivation randomly hunting monsters for their loot while following the main storyline on the side. It's almost a pokemon-like feeling where you try to complete your pokedex.
As I said, I haven't played much, but till now the story is pretty basic stuff. Starting in a small village, doing a test to finally become whatsoever and heading out to great adventures. This is not necessarily a bad point, because you still keep track of the story, even if you skip some dialogues. The dialogues on the other side are quite funny and self-ironic. They make fun of some very stale RPG-cliches, like the bottomless bag of the game's main character.
The main story holds up with some big boss battles, which are more or less challenging, depending on how much you grind on the side. If a boss can drop unique loot, the battle can also be repeated at any time. As far as I discovered, the game also provides some side-activities like fishing or treasure-hunting.
The game's skill system allow to spend an active skillpoint in melee, magic or supportive and a passive skillpoint in general, melee or magic on each levelup. There are some skills that aren't implemented yet, because the game is still in early access. Nevertheless there are plenty available skills which can be combined freely. Every skill can be charged up to unleash a more powerful attack, which variates based on the amount of skillpoints put into a single skill. All in all the skill-system provides a wide range of different gaming-styles.
Also, there is an arcade mode, where you have only one life to conquer a randomly generated world. Everytime you die, you start all over again in a newly generated world. But there are some unlockable permanent advantages.
Summary: Buy the game! Also I'm sorry for possible language mistakes.

Despite its many flaws I really like the game after about 50h of play.
PROS:
The grafics are detailed and animations are smooth. I havent seen many grafical glitches.
The single player campaign was short but enjoyable und introduces you to all the classes, but I wouldnt recommend buying it only for the campaign.
For someone who has never really played 2d or 3d fighting games before the combat mechanics are fun to learn but hard to master. The games has a few tutorials explaining all the moves, but you need to watch some guides on Youtube to master your class. The classes look pretty balanced to me at least at the lower to mid levels of play.
I rarely feel cheated when I get killed and most times its my own fault. After a loss I allways try for a rematch to get better and nothing is more satisfying to finaly beat someone after you have lost to them a few times.
Also I havent seen any cheaters or hackers (at least I couldnt tell). Most people are friendly in 1v1 or at least dont insult you, but in 4v4/Dominion there is more flaming/insulting.
CONS:
I mainly play 1v1 so some of the problems dont affect me as much as those who play 4v4.
The biggest problem is the connection. Dropping out of games happens often enough to be anoying but at least for me wasnt a dealbreaker. They just released a patch to fix some of the errors so we will see if it improves stability.
Finding a 1v1 match takes a bit long depending on how many people are playing, but 4v4 and Dominion matches take way to long to find and way to long to get startet. This is where the p2p is the problem I think. If they dont want to offer servers ( and I dont think they ever will) they should allow private servers like in other multiplayer games.
Another problem is the matchmaking system in 1v1. I constantly play against people many levels below me. Thats why I have a >80% winrate in 1v1. Its nice for me but bashing people who just bought the game or are trying out a new class gets boring pretty quickly. On the other hand im not forced to get better because I rarely play against people of equal or higher level and learning to get better is one of the best things for me in the game.
The microtransactions dont bother me that much but still are bad for the game and only another way to make money of people. Most of the things you can buy are cosmetics/different animations but you also can upgrade your gear with the ingame currency (steel). But in 1v1 matches gear has no effect, so if you want to just rely on your skill play 1v1. You can get steel through 4 ways without paying: playing the campaign (but only 1 time), finishing the tutorials (also only 1 time), finishing quest which refresh daily, or just by playing matches. But if you want all the emotes/skins/animations you will have to play hundreds of hours... which is just a way to make you buy steel.
All in all im still enjoying the game and hope that they will improve whats wrong with the game.

Why should you play this game? The immersion and the story! The dwarves is probably the best game on dwarves and bringing them to life with their habits and culture that I have ever played. It is also one of the best story telling RPGs I have seen ,as the story seems to evolve quickly, has  interesting characters, an immersive world, takes unexpected turns every now and then and still manages to not get overly complicated and confusing.
All dialogue has voiceover and there is a great narrator. Also the music is excellent, helping create the awesome atmosphere in the game. And, oh yeah, Blind Guardian!
What you should be aware of when deciding if to buy the game:
Combat is simple for an RPG with only a handful of skills per character, so it plays rather quick even though pausing to issue orders every few seconds is a must. The collision system used to make positioning more strategic in the game can become annoying from time to time as characters sometimes block each otehr of run into each others AOE attacks. Most fights have objectives rather than just being "kill everyone", which gives it a bit of variation. Objectives get a bit repetetive after some time though.
The same thing goes for the other elements in the game mechanics: traveling on the world map is turn based and all locations are marked neatly on the map, which makes it easy to travel but also doesn't provide any chance for real exploration. There is no inventory management, as you can only equip a talisman / item per character and that is it, so no armor / weapons. The leveling system is also very simplified. Every two levels you reach, you chose one of two skills. Thats it, no complex skilltree, no stats to raise, no nothing. A bit more variety would have been nice.
All that being said, the games focus on the story really works well for me and I can hardly wait to continue my journey with Tungdil.

I think this game is fantastic, but let me be up front about it. If you only like visually stunning graphics, this is not for you. If you are a fan of content then keep reading. I am an old school gamer that started with pong. I have been through most of the systems over the years and RPG's are my favorite genre. It has never been about the graphics in an RPG though, it's about the content. I like to be able to equip several things on my character, have a multitude of magical variations, crafting, skills and a large selection of stats with a leveling system. This game has all of that. Graphics, it does not. It is a very cartoonish overview world map with point and click to travel to each destination. The graphics in town are even worse.  The dungeons and battles are very similar to the original Final Fantasy.
You play a ruler of a kingdom that must hire adventurers to defeat an evil wizard. You can hire a multitude of adventurers but must use them in parties of 4 to battle. There is an auto adventure option which is what makes the sim aspect of the game, but you do not have to do this. You must build repore with other races and gain quests from them. You are able to perform quests over and over and this allows for grinding levels, money and crafting  materials. There is also a lot of humor in the game. The bio's on you adventures are set up in a "mad-libs" sort of fashion with a basic background with random words inserted. There is a fun basic crafting system for any of the items you can eqiup. This game is not as in depth with story line and content that you would find in Skyrim for example, but it is a very fun game that you can walk away from and come back to over and over again.

Hoo hah, prowling Steam for some five dollar fun? Make a stop here, lower your expectations and just go with the flow! Adventure Manager is a sweet turn based RPG where you recruit strangers to forward your campaign as a ruler. Surely Sir Kurt whom wields the dagger you gave him will save the day? He seems to be pretty stabby with it, so surely those cave spiders will lay vanquished in no time at all.
So what's good? Well, apart from the jester's occasional witty rhyme (a welcome sight!) there's quite a bit to do. Train your recruits to master the quests you undertake, recruit more to help further your cause, build a castle to support your kingdom, and perhaps expore the lush world you intend to rule? Of course as a ruler, there's no need for you to be doing any fighting. Just uh... stand back and let the barbarian do the dirty work. The cleric you hired yesterday should keep him alive, right?
And now, what's not so good. Battles seem to drag out quite a fair bit early on due to missing a fair bit, scarce gear and generally underleveled characters. The grind is fun to an extent, but sometimes watching your barbarian swing his club at a zombie and miss a few times in a row takes a little bit from it. Sure, maybe my "barbarian" is a little rusty at his job. But never imagined a zombie being swift to dodge a swing. Suppose I'll just blame that hasty random number generator, but the machine is simply doing its job. Also I don't think the "gamble" tab is explained at all in the game. Am I missing something? Probably.
After the early stages of the game, the pace picks up and things get real. But the gruelling curve can be a little hard to embrace. And I'll say it again, for five bucks, what do you really want? I'll admit, I picked this up at a steal (I really do feel bad for that...) and it looks like the developer is more than happy to listen to players. So yes, you're getting your money's worth from this game. I do recommend it for that sweet sweet single player diversion.

The dwarves is a fantasy game centered around dwarves (obviously), focused on story and tactical combat against large hordes of enemies (mainly orcs, but also humans etc), and overcoming them. The game is based upon a number of books by german author Markus Heitz, which, after playing through the whole game in one marathon sitting (13 hours or so), has inspired me to go out and buy the books and immerse myself further (fantastic world).
When playing I found myself repeatedly playing further when I should have been done for the day, up until the ending. The game has side quests, but none that ever detract from the main story.
I felt like I was on an epic adventure, with some awesome companions, whose characters all come to life with the consistently brilliant voice acting. You will spend your time travelling around on the beautiful world map, every now and then interrupted by isometric oldschool (pausable) combat with up to 4 characters.
I thoroughly enjoyed the game, although it does have some minor kinks such as characters (happened two times for me) not moving, not a huge deal for me, as I could fire up an autosave without any major loss of progress.
The Dwarves is an approachable game that most RPG-fans will appreciate. Its no Skyrim, but neither is it trying to be. Focus is on story and challenging combat. If you love dwarves and/or games like Baldurs Gate, Pillars of Eternity and such, you will definitely have a blast, and you owe it to yourself to check this one out!
+ Fantastic Story
+ No "Kill 20 Rabbits" Side Quests, while side quests do occur they are interesting!
+ Great Voice Acting (English), including a narrator, pretty much everything is actually read out
+ Great Art Direction (Characters look great, and environments are beautiful)
+ Large World (massive world map)
+ Fairly Challenging without being punishing
+ Tactical combat (pausable) with massive hordes of enemies vs your 3-4 characters
+ Great Music, also has some Blind Guardian!!
- AI and Pathfinding could use some work and occasional character freezing in the tactical combat (will hopefully be fixed)
- Limited Strategic Options in tactical combat (stances etc)
- Friendly Fire, while adding to the challenge, forced several reloads when a character was tossed into abilities

I'm usually not a fan of typical fantasy fare, and actually actively despise the Heitz novels. But this game is excellent. It is very "german" in its sensibilities, by which I mean that players of the Dark Eye (Realms of Arkania) series will recognize certain tropes and mechanics, but mostly that it is very narratively oriented.
The game is basically split in three modes - the world map, where the player decides which path to travel and has choose your own adventure-esque encounters; the area map, where the player moves around and interacts with items in a Baldur's Gate-like fashion but which are overall more designed like areas in a point and click adventure; and the combat, which happens on the area map, but is a more action-focused affair that makes heavy use of knockback effects (yes, your characters can fall or even rush to their death if you're not careful) but is straightforward enough to be fun.
Special honorable mention goes to the very fair save system. Yes, some CYOA sequences can actually kill you, but from what I have seen so far, you get a pretty fair chance to try again without having to backtrack too much.
If you don't mind a very trope-heavy setting and like grand RPGs, I'd definitely recommend checking this one out.

Having been impressed with Bastion and Transistor, I was naturally inclined to pick up Supergiant Games's latest game: Pyre.
The best way I can describe this is it's a sports RPG (OK please don't leave just hear me out). You control a team of three (each with different stats and abilities) and fight another trio over a glowy ball and try to run it or throw it into the other team's "goal". Sounds simple, but it's deceptively complex. Things like terrain, equippable items, and more can drastically alter a match's outcome.
The Rites (as the sport is called) is what moves the plot forward. To give a short premise, playing the sportball allows you and your friends (the people you recruit to use on your teams) to eventually gain freedom from the hellscape you've all been banished to. The lore can get a bit too much at times, but it's an interesting narrative nonetheless. An interesting thing to point out, however, is that even losing in the Rites progresses the story. It doesn't feel like a punishment because, despite your loss, the narrative moves forward. In fact, losing certain games can create interesting story/character development situations.
I think what I like the most, however, is the characters. They're more than just these people you control to pass the ball. You actually get a sense of who they are, why they were banished, and why they desire freedom. Not to divulge too much on how the story goes, but you will reach a point in the game where you feel conflicted about their respective fates. Interacting with them also directly impacts how you fare in the Rites. Sometimes they get buffs or debuffs depending how conversations go. Even how you traverse the world (e.g. what paths you take) affects them in a similar fashion. And speaking of the world, it feels like a massive world. The wide array of environments, complemented by how pretty this game looks, makes traveling between Rites a pleasant experience.
Along with a gorgeous art style, superb music (once again by Darren Korb), and the ability to play multiplayer (or just a casual match with a CPU opponent), it looks like Supergiant Games has another crown jewel on their hands. This game is the total package and is worth checking out, even those with an aversion to sports games (come on just give it a chance pleeeeeease).

The presentation, the presentation is none other than awe-inspiring. The gorgeous 2D art is standard for Supergiant. What
standard for Supergiant Games is the
. -- Don't get me wrong, their past games, Bastion and Transistor both had amazing music -- But to have an amazing soundtrack that
? That's a whole new level.
Oh, by the way, the
! -- Avoiding spoilers in general, this isn't a linear story like the previous two Supergiant Games (where Bastion gave you a couple of choices, but only towards the ending. Which members of the party you level up, which opponents you choose to challenge for the Rites once that choice becomes available -- All can have an effect on the story, leading to an ending that, while mostly told via Obsidian-style still images and narration (with added text), feels like the culmination of all your choices, making you feel that all the time spent was worth it.
And now I realise I didn't mention the gameplay. It is also very good! I wouldn't give this game any awards on gameplay alone, but it is

And also affects their Enlightenment (experience level), which defines which party members may or may not be set free.
Basically, I blazed (lel, I funny) through Pyre in like, a month. And it still easily stole a spot among my top 20 games ever. So, absolutely pick it up, yeah. :L

I don't write game reviews. Who has time? Then suddenly, there is Soma.
While looking around on Steam, I happened to come across this sleeper. Looking at the trailers and pics of the game, I was taken by the sharp graphics...and that was about it.  I had a general idea of what the game play would be so, I did what we all do, throw it on the wishlist and think about it later. Four months later, to be percise, it goes on sale and, after a 10 plus gig download(it took me two days), boom I own it.
I urge you to read both points.
The bad points first:
Game was too short. I completed it in 12 hours.  For ten gigs, this should of been at least 20 hours.
Possibility of getting stuck(unable to move) in some spots. I never got stuck but I can see where some spots can.
Very minor texture glitches. You have to look very hard to find them.
More puzzles/interaction. Most of the story you are along for the ride.
Good points:
Incredible once in a lifetime story:
I have played a lot of games, but this by far I was the most immersed in. I felt vest in the characters and some of the choices I had to make pulled at my heart as well as my morality. It made my question what it means to be human. It made me feel sad, desperate, happy, determined, angry, and scared out of my mind. This game will frighten you and more than a dozen times I had an "Oh s**t or holy f**K" moment. If you like being frightened, then this is better than any horror movie you could watch.
Spectacular graphics:
In some games, there are parts which are graphically beautiful. The whole game was like that. Details
and logical, reasoned design made me feel that I was there, at the bottom of the sea. I was there.
Wanting:
While playing, I kept wanting more. Never sated. I needed to see what the next area brought, what more story I would encounter, how it all ends. Metaphorically, I felt this game was like a lover. Warm in it's embrace, secure in it's presence and happy, whatever happened. Then the end and feeling, jilted(it's the only way to describe it) because my lover left me.
I played a lot of games, and Soma isn't a game at all. It's an experience.

It hurts me for simply owning this title in my library, even if it was for free. Steam quality control at its best.
DO NOT BUY THIS!

First of all, Never alone is a relatively short game. I started playing it completely blind (knew nothing except for a trailer) and enjoyed every second of it, and it's well worth it's price. I wish I could just erase my memories and play it blind again.
Without spoiling, all I can say is that the storytelling is just awesome, especially since it is told in the native language of the Iñupiat. It really adds an unique touch to it. Some kind of cutsenes show parts of the story you are experiencing in a beautiful way which reminds me a bit of Journey. In the end you'll learn where said story is based on. I loved the fact that it's one of the last things you'll learn. Like it sums up everything. The little insight videos you can unlock every now and then really add to the atmosphere and the game. It's like a documentary, but better. I've learned a whole lot out of this game and some insights even surprised me. The scenes and music chosen for those videos were really beautiful. They made me even tear up at some parts.
The gameplay itself is great. I used a controller and it worked fine. I'd actually recommend a controller over the keyboard, it seems a lot easier this way.  The game runs really smooth, the graphics itself are just BEAUTIFUL and I love the overall atmosphere. It can create a creepy, cold, beautiful or whatsoever feeling. It's great.
I ran into some bugs every now and then, like glitching through the platforms, but I can't complain in any way. I don't know about the co-op, but I can see it working well. No framedrops, no nothing. Everything was fine.
Some parts can get a bit frustrating because you have to be fast and basically switch between the characters frequently. But it's not that bad, it took me a few tries to figure out the right way. The only negative point at those parts would be the sounds of the howling wind. It's reeaaally loud sometimes and I got a headache of it for hearing it over and over. You can set the volume lower though, so that's probably a flaw on my end.
I suppose it can get a bit boring for some people though. It didn't for me, just wanted to point that out.~
Conclusion: So.. overall this will definetely be one of my favorite games from now on. It can't beat e.g. Journey and To The Moon for me, but it is a masterpiece in itself and I'd buy it again without a doubt if I had to. With it's great narration and graphics, it feels just like getting told a story in a way that makes everything come to life around you. It's almost magical. It CAN get a bit frustrating at some points, but that's completely fine. It's a game after all, it is supposed to be challenging, even if it's just for a short amount of time. If you're even thinking about getting the game, then go get it! It's really not that expensive compared to other (worse) games and you'll even gain something out of it.
tl;dr: Beautiful, interactive documentary. Awesome graphics and gameplay and a great story. Well worth it's price. Would recommend everyone to at least give it a try.

First off:
BE CAREFUL WHERE YOU PLACE YOUR CONFERENCE TABLE
If you move or delete it at any point after building it but before Objective 2 is totally complete, you'll glitch your savegame and be unable to proceed.
That being said, this game is phenomenal.  Pretty forgiving early on, with a difficulty arc both graceful and satisfying that really gets much tougher later.  The graphics are of course dated, but as is the hallmark of many truly great games it doesn't matter.  The fun comes from the game, and the graphics are there to help you keep track.
It is often compared to the Dungeoun Keeper series, which is fair.  I played me some Dungeon Keeper 2 back in the day, when mice had balls and input devices were not even hot-swappable, let alone wireless.  Despite the relative technological desolation of those dark ages, I remember that being a pretty awesome game.  Still, I cannot adequately describe how much happier I am to be a sinister plotting megalomaniac bent on world domination.
Many of the reviews here already break the game down by pros and cons, etc, so I'm just going to say highly recommended, and even when not on sale it's pretty cheap.  Take a spiritual journey to 2004 with Elixir Studios and get in touch with your inner despicable villian.
Extra Endorsement: I experienced the glitch with the conference table on my very first playthrough of the game, and found out about it on the internet after being stuck for hours unable to complete Objective 2.  20ish hours into the game, my whole save became worthless.  Without any hesitation, I calmly opened the menu and clicked "New Game".  For me, that means this game = digital crack.

Well, that TL;DR is basically explaining you the whole concept of the game: it's a first-person shooter (feels something like a bit slower version of Call of Duty) in Stalker-ish post-apocalyptic universe. You're playing as a survivor in three (as of July, 2015) fast-paced game modes -- Team Deathmatch (or basically "kill 'em all"), Research (where you capture zones and gain points) and some other one, I didn't get to play it yet (it's probably something like Capture The Flag). One match usually continues for 10-15 minutes, in all of the three modes.
Graphics look a bit outdated, so don't expect Battlefield 4 in here. Though, stability is game's strong suit -- it gives 60 fps on a relatively old PC, easily.
I've started playing the game when it was out of beta (after it was released on Steam, didn't play it before), so I have no idea what bugs are people talking about. I did encounter one bug with the scoreboard not showing that one time, but that was it -- one small bug in 3 hours of gameplay. Game looks really smooth and even kind of polished, for v0.29 (which means that it's not fully developed, as I see it).
It's not a pay-to-win type of F2P shooter (like the new Ghost Recon) -- new equipment won't make you invulnerable. It would make you a little bit more stronger and you'll look cooler, but that is it.
Game balance is something to discuss, yet I've just started playing (got 3 hours in, like I said, at the time of writing the review), so I don't know what happens next. Hopefully, balance stays around the same in the later versions (no weapons are currently dominating the battlefield, nothing's too imbalanced).
- - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
I like the game progress -- even though the gameplay itself is getting repetitive really fast (like in every other online shooter, as you well know), but the unlocks, factions, achievements and missions are all giving you the reason to stay and play "just one more round".
I have to remind everyone, that the game is not fully released yet, it's still in Early Access -- this implies that a lot of stuff might change later on, so I might change my mind about the game later. Yet, now I'll gladly go and play it some more.

Shark Attack Deathmatch 2 is an easy-to-pick-up-on first person shooter.
You are placed in an eerie environment, from the selection of 5 or 6 maps. When you die, you lose points, when you get kills, you gain points. If you are playing deathmatch, those points allow you to rank up. If you are playing survival (which can also be co-op), you can use it to try to beat your high score.
Different sharks are worth different points because some take more hits and/or bite harder. On online deathmatch, the focus is killing each other for points, along with sharks coming to kill you. However, you can toggle sharks on or off in deathmatch. Deathmatch lobbies allow 2-8 players.
The gameplay and graphics are beautiful, but it will has one fatal flaw. Almost no one plays it.
There are never any available online games. You have to host them yourself, and if you are lucky, another player joins. This really deteriorates from the idea that this is supposed to be a competitive FPS against other players.
In all, I enjoy this game. Deathmatch and survival are fun, the AI is great, really nothing to complain about other than the size of the fan base.
This used to cost $10. For the price of $5, it is absolutely worth it.

Overall, The Darkness 2 is a good game, but it has a variety of frustrating details that make the game much less fun, and generall my willingness to pay attention to the story.
1. Controls - There are several boss fights as well as a bunch of ordinary encounters that require you to quickly move out of the way or dodge something. The problem is that you move like a pregnant boat. This isn't really that much worse than a lot of first person shooter games, but those games don't want you to dodge.
2. Nonsense - You can run through the game getting blasted by shotguns and machine guns and survive. I don't have a problem with this. After all, in the context of the story you should be able to. The problem is that whenever the story wants you for some reason a quick flash or lights or a shotgun blast put you on the ground unable to move.
3. Lights - I really do like the mechanic that you can't use any of your powers in the light--that is the way that it is in the comic after all--but that game randomly desides that some lights can't be destroyed. So, you spend a great deal of the game destroying one light after another only to be held up in the level by a light with a metal grate over it. Annoying.
4. Story - The story deviates significantly from the comic, but that isn't necessarily a bad thing. There are however two main problems with how the story is told in this game. First, there are a greate deal of boring dialogue that you have to pay attention to, to have any understanding of what is happening in the story. This becomes grating. Second, the story relys very heavily on common tropes. Vengence for the murder of your girlfriend. Vengence for *spoiler*'s murder. A dark broodin man of violence, fighting his inner demons. It's been done.

"Sniper Elite V2" is a lean, mean, nicely executed example of what it is to build a game around a single, excellent mechanic.
The game basically functions by asking the question: "Okay, we've got a guy with a scoped rifle. What are the various situations we can put him in that play into the usage of that rifle in different ways?"
And so, you get into a series of encounters that test your handling of the various tradeoffs. Keep your heart-rate down, and you can use "Focus Time" to see exactly where your bullet is going to go. That sounds great, and it is, but you won't be able to use that trick all the time. Sometimes you'll have to scope-in and pull the trigger based on just your basic reckoning, especially when the pressure builds and a lot of opponents are trying to get a piece of you.
The environments in "V2" aren't exactly enormous, but they are both generous and multi-pathed. The experience IS focused, so that the developers can guide you through various problems to solve, but there do seem to be a large number of solutions to most of those problems.
My guess is that, at least partially because of this focus, the game is very short. the developers at Rebellion play their hand, and then stop when they run out of cards. Thus, they avoid the whole problem of creating an interminable slog through doing the same thing over and over.
In terms of complaints, I only really have two.
The first is that this offering is actually something of a step down from "Nazi Zombie Army." Obviously, the setting genres are different, and "Zombie" can get away with all sorts of craziness that a period-piece can't, but "Zombie" also showed just how much variety could be created. "Sniper" doesn't do everything it could with environments and enemy types, which could have extended the game and created more "epic scale" setpieces.
My second minor gripe is that the pre-mission interface doesn't really explain itself very well. I actually got about halfway through the whole shebang before I realized that you could go edit your loadout. The "diamond" buttons just don't do the job of advertising that there's more available to you than simply starting the mission.
...but those are just little zingers in the end. "V2" does well with what it has, and doesn't overstay its welcome. I'd buy it again - and I'm pretty sure I'll enjoy "Sniper Elite 3" when I get my hands on it.
