Secrets of Grindea is an action RPG that hones many aspects from RPGs that I know and love. I will be going into a lot of detail about the game and why I love it so much, so hold on to your seats!
Gameplay
The game has a story mode and an Arcade Mode. The story mode is currently unfinished (along with the Arcade Mode), but the game currently boasts a lot of sidequests and collectables along with the story. I have managed to collect almost all of the cards (the rarest collectables in the game, one unique to all normal enemies) as of the 15th of July and I continue to collect even more in the future when I have the time and patience to do so! The game features many sidequests, puzzles and hidden items to find and collect, which required thinking and pure potential in your combatting skills. Currently, the game is very difficult in its Arcade Mode and Hard Mode of the story.
Arcade Mode is the true challenge of the game and the main feature that people will come back to after beating the story. Similar to many roguelike indie games such as The Binding of Isaac and many more titles, the game offers a mode that offers permanent death and restarting all over again upon death, which will truly test your skills. Many of the enemies are buffed up versions of monsters seen in the later parts of the story, beefed up bosses from the story mode and some completely unique enemies that are not (yet) available in the story mode. For anybody who likes roguelike games, this is for you! This also is a good option to play the game without the story being spoiled for yourself if you would like to play the story from the beginning until the end with no interuptions!
For you bustling people with many friends, both modes offer multiplayer aspects, but more people doesn't come with no risk. More players often means newer moves (at least in the story mode) and higher enemy HP, that truly will test your skill instead of making the game a breeze.
Soundtrack
The soundtrack of the game isn't extremely special, but the music fits the game very well and really creates the mood of the game. Often faster-paced/more upbeat versions of the songs in the story mode are used in Arcade Mode corresponding to the area that they are found in. The music is definitely highly atmospheric and I definitely reccomend the soundtrack for any outer-game listening purposes!
Design/Artwork
The art of the game is very detailed and is drawn to a great extent. All of the places in the game are drawn in photoshop and in good detail. Sprites and other things are done seperately but the game blends in and really feels alive. Many of the animations used in the game are done very well and the artwork to follow the characters are also done to perfection. The game is crisp and looks good all the time!
Overall Rating
I think this game is possibly my favourite game I've played in a very very long time, and the game isn't even finished yet. I would definitely reccomend this game to anybody who wants a good game!

Thus far, Adventure Manager has been a lot of fun for me.  But I tend to enjoy games that require a bit of a grind and a head for numbers, and boy does this game deliver on both sides!
All stages thus far (except the invasion stage, which I will discuss briefly later) require your party to have an average gear score of a certain number, which it uses as a difficulty level.  Getting your party up to snuff is not really easy to do most of the time, and will require multiple trips through a dungeon to get there.  Further, once you start dabbling in crafting, everything becomes a bit more of a cake walk, and then the grind shifts to finding gear to have crafting materials, and running dungeons over and over for that.
The one difference is the Invasion level, which randomly pops up through the course of your adventuring.  I really think that this level needs to be better announced rather than just a red flashing text in the upper right corner of the screen.  Half the time, I'm running a dungeon and don't even see it blinking because I'm pouring over stats, or trying to keep my party alive through spell caster's volleys of multiple hundreds of damage.  Anyway, the invasion level is always "tailored" to your party's gear score, providing a decent challenge with a boss at the end.  The end boss has thus far been a more improved version of a boss you'd beaten in a previous dungeon, with updated versions of their unique gear as well.
Abilities of the classes are fun and flavourful, but I felt like many of the abilities could be removed from the game, or changed in a more meaningful way.  Most of the time, I just go for the damaging abilities because everything else seems really ineffective.  Yeah, an increased critical buff is nice, but when it takes a round away from my damage class to activate, only lasts two rounds, and only affects one person...it seems useless to me.  Some abilities I would LOVE to have affect multiple party members.  Especially a heal spell (the closest thing I've gotten to a heal spell was after I unlocked a special class, and even then it was a heal over time.)
Also some stats I feel could be better utilized for certain bonuses.  For example, Strength only increases melee damage, and does nothing for your chance to block like it does in some games.  No direct stat (Strength, Dexterity, etc.) increases your parry chance or your riposte chance, even by a fraction of a percent.  Nor does anything seem to affect your Dual Wield percentage, even though you can pretty much make most classes dual wield.
Some weapon types should also have their own identity with little bonuses as a basic to the weapon.  Many have the same damage range, so it makes no sense to really use more than one type of weapon.  Hammers increasing your chance to stun, for example, would be a wonderful way to add some flare to classes who have abilities that can stun, and make them a little more viable.
All in all, I'd give the game a 7 out of 10.  It's a fun ride, but I don't know that it has the power to keep people interested in it long enough to beat it, especially with it's difficulty and grindiness. Many of the complaints I have are personal wants for the game, and really don't detract from the overall experience of the game.  I would recommend it to RPG fans,  but it certainly requires an investment of time to play.

Well, what can I say? It is unique, solid, and uncontested. Shedding Bastion and Transistor's narration-driven story heavy action combat games, Pyre is an adventure that is half fantasy sports, half compelling visual novel. The sports portion is at worst solid for what it wants to do and at best amazing albeit only so in bursts, combining Supergiant's penchant for playstyle agency with an all new genre sure to overwhelm your senses but be gentle enough to get to grips with in time. The visual novel portion is enhanced both by compelling characters and an infinitely branching story depending on your win/loss rate in the rites. The ending you get isn't so much one of a set of results, but a spectrum dictated by the state of every character you come across by the end of the game. Each player's run is unique to them based on their choices and performance.
Conversely, that coupled with the length of the game means that going back to replay it for a personal re-run probably won't be in the cards for you, since you'll all be burnt out and won't be chipping away at much else to see. But for that one run you'll be in some major afterglow. Pyre is nothing you've seen before and definitely solid despite being a fresh new genre and having nothing to iterate on before it... even if it is basically basketball.

As long as you keep in mind this is a work in progress, *stupidly cheap price* and WILL give you a metric gazillion-tonne of fun, you won't complain. I've had hours of enjoyment out of it, and I have no doubt it's a game I'll be coming back to for a long time to come.
The little flaws? Well:
1. It'd be nice for the game to pause when an attackable invasion force appears. It seems to pause a couple of times to warn me about continued use of the fast forward button, but then suddenly an invasion appears, sacks a town then disappears in what seems like a few seconds. That's mildly irritating.
2. An auto-assign option for core stats when a hero levels, based on their class, would be a good addition. It's nice in early stages of the game to assign stats when you have a handful of adventurers, but after a while when you've got a full compliment, it's mildly iritating.
3. Minor menu options you wish were there/more obvious, blah blah blah. Lot of games guilty of this to some degree. Mildly irritating.
Having said this, the best way I can think of describing this game is potentially like some kind of fantasy-RPG-Master-of-Orion-2 hybrid. For anyone that can't remember the beeps and chirps of 56k modems, that means it's good. *Real* good.

Hello, I don't know the best way of getting this review started, since I'm just a ordinary gamer who lives in Brazil, but I'll try to do my best, so let's go!
First of all, in Pyre you lead a band of exiles, striving to achieve freedom back to the Commonwealth through the Rites, that play a very important paper within the game's plot. This game is a pretty different type of RPG than what we were used to see from Supergiant Games, with their previous games, Bastion and Transistor, respectively. Pyre completely abandons the old formula used in its predecessors, which consists basically in a isometric action/real-time/turn-based RPG, containing an amazing narrator present during the whole game and really tied with the plot. These characteristics have been replaced with visual novel elements, a much more detailed and deep history (that will most likely make you cry or spill some tears at the very least) and, the most noticeable change, a "slower" pace of the campaign (not a bad thing, but I had some difficulties about getting used to it). Also with an outstanding art direction (by Jen Zee) and a perfectly fitting original soundtrack (by Darren Korb, with vocals by Ashley Lynn Barrett and also Darren Korb). That's how I would describe Pyre in a summarized way.
Now, the reason that you clicked on "read more", a more detailed point of view:
The campaign, which is the longest ever made by Supergiant Games (so far), is extremely well written, entirely created by Greg Kasavin alone (as stated by Pyre's IMDb webpage). It really keeps the player engaged on the game, also making the player eager to know how it's going to unwind. The problem that I personally have with it though, is the fact that it takes a pretty longer amount of time to experience the volume of dialogs, that even though are really well made, make the game feel more slow and less dynamic. I mean, that varies from person to person, at first I felt not so much comfortable with it, since I don’t have much time to play videogames, because of school resposibilities. After some time, as I had previosly stated, I got used with this different approach for the game’s campain. I have nothing to complain about its quality and extreme depth.
The art! Supergiant Games proves again their originality with breathtaking environments that are completely different from one another inside the game itself, and also something 100% original after their previous games. The credit goes to Jen Zee, and her amazing work! Every place of the Downside feels truly original, organic and stunning!
The music! Darren Korb and Ashley Lynn Barrett again did an extraordinary job! The original soundtrack is totally fitting to the game’s theme, and also to the characters that you meet along the journey. The songs are excellent and really pleasant to listen. If you play this game, I highly recommend to buy Pyre’s Original Soundtrack, on Steam it comes with two extra albums (The Black Mandolin and The White Lute).
Also, Pyre contains multiple endings and I’ll leave it at that, in order to not to spoil the game. An amazing detail about this is that the ending song has several variations that correspond to YOUR campaign outcome.
So, as a Supergiant Games fan, I my verdict about this masterpiece is: BUY THE GAME! IT IS WORTH EVERY PENNY!
My final opinion sincerly consists that Pyre is not just a videogame, it’s an original and unique experience. A 0-10 number is just not enough to describe it. Thank you for reading up to this point. Have a great day! I hope that this review has helped you make up your mind about the decision to buy this awesome game. :D

Originally released in 2008 for the Xbox 360 and PS3; Baja: Edge of Control reviewed fairly well but was overlooked by the general gaming public. Now, nine years later, we see it it come back around for a second lap, remastered and on PC, and while I enjoyed my time with it, it did consistently remind me jut how far the racing genre has come in nearly a decade.
With this being an HD remaster, let's start off with graphics. Does the game have the bleeding edge of graphical fidelity, letting you see every single grain of sand on its rather massive maps? No. What it is is a fairly respectable graphical clean up of a fairly old game. It doesn't knock your socks off, but its cleaned up enough that when played in 1080p it looks fine.
My only real problem with the graphics, besides a sheer lack of graphic options in general, is there's a fair bit of detail pop in. Signs in the distance will appear and trees suddenly gain a lot more detail as you get near them, for example. Nothing too bad but I would have liked to seen a smoother transition between different levels of detail in the game world.
As for gameplay, there's a lot to cover. The game has eight different classes of cars and trucks, going from little Baja Bugs all the way up to Trophy Trucks and nine different environments. The maps in this game are simply huge and events range from short little circuit races to several hour Baja rallies. If you're able to deal with some rather aged design choices and love off road racing then the game does offer a lot master.
Now, I mentioned that the game consistently reminded me how far the racing genre has come. This is mostly with how the game handles some things rather clumsily by today's standards and has some rather old design choices that just haven't aged that well.
For example, in order to unlock a fair amount of the content in the game you have to go through career mode, fairly common racing games. However, it uses a binary, easy or hard, difficulty setting and there's a great deal of difference between these two settings. This setting not only controls the game's AI drivers, but also which physics system the game uses. On easy, it uses arcade physics, which makes the cars drive straighter and bounce far less, while hard cranks up both the AI's skill and gives the simulation physics system with the added difficulty that entails. This makes for a great discrepancy between the two options where I found easy far too easy for me on most races, but hard a bit too much to jump into because of the changes with the driving physics. With practice I'm sure it is doable but when the quick race has the options physics modeling and AI driver skillseparate, as well as a gradient on the AI driver skill, it is a bit galling to not have any middle ground between these two extremes.
Something else that annoyed me with the AI is that they appear to be glued to the road.  If they have tires on the road they will not deviate from their chosen racing line no matter how much you bump, rub, or grind on them. This makes the game feel like the AI just isn't playing by the same rules the player is, because they aren't. They don't have to contend with a rather slick, sandy road. Also, the AI loves to bump the player out of the way and they can do so with hardly any risk to themselves in the process. A very old game design choice that just has not aged well at all.
Finally, there's the game multiplayer. On release, I simply wasn't able to get a match what so ever. Granted, I usually play at off peak hours for my timezone, but there's not that many players out there in general. So, if you're looking for on-line racing and you're not bringing your own friends then you'll be sorely disappointed. Baja does offer four player split screen for local play, which does make it a good candidate for LAN parties. So, it does have that going for it and may be worth checking out for your next local get together.
Although I was rather hard on the game, then again I'm rather hard on most games, I did enjoy my time with Baja: Edge of Control HD. While there isn't much in the way of competition in the genre, and it stands pretty much alone for Baja racing, it still is a pretty decent arcady sim racer. If you're able to overlook some rather old design choices, and a bit of a clunky UI, you'll find a lot of bang for your buck with Baja: Edge of Control HD and it is will worth checking out.

Basically, metaphysics 101. It's really not as deep as some people make it out to be. It talks about what makes you 'you'. Whether you're actually 'you', or if you're only 'you' in your body.

Once you lose them they'll usually linger far too long and force you to sit there and wait for them to move. There's some puzzles, but nothing mind blowing.
One thing I really hated about the game is the way the character reacts. You'll get a couple choices throughout the game, and depending on what you pick, your character will react completely inappropriately. (i.e. You chose to do X, then your character gets really mad because he did X.) If you give choices to the player, you can't have the character get mad about it. If you want the character to think a certain way, you can't allow the player to interject their opinion.
If for some reason you want a story heavy horror game, I guess grab it on sale. But I wouldn't really recommend it.

The best part about this game is that there is absolutely no shame in cheating. Remember San Andreas? Remember how the game was 100% more fun when you were spawning hyrdras and ♥♥♥♥ing♥♥♥♥♥♥up? This game is kind of like that. Playing without cheats is a good genuine challenge regardless but it's ok to do some good ol' guilt free money cheats because freedom to build the base of your dreams is half of the fun. (Actually it's probably 90% of the fun; the other 10% is making examples the minions that displease you by shooting them / stabbing them in the neck with a curvy dagger /  burning a hole in them with a cigarette).
The art style is an overstylised...... early 80's?That reflects the whole OTT spy genre that was happening with James Bond and the whole USSR vs America with all of the inbetween cultural stereotypes thrown in like the ridiculously overdone accents for the respective world regions and a lot of the time this makes for some great satirical comedy.
The one downside for me is that there are definitely a few things that can use rebalancing but luckily somewhere on the interwebs there's a unnofficial patch that fixes a wide variety of minute but overall rebalancing aspects. I've had some fairly rare texture glitches and sometimes the agent models turn into inpromptu contortionists acts but frankly it doesn't even seem that out of place in a game that's main artistic drive is to completely overstylise the era.
9/10

I'm a sensible gamer. I know there are faults with this game but I also know it's in alpha. I'm excited to see where this game ends up. I wasn't playing The Isle when it came out, so I don't remember eating trees or any other map except for v3, so you may take what I have to say with a grain of salt. However, I have had some amazing moments in this game. I have also had some extremely boring moments in this game. (Sounds a lot like life?)
Someone referred to this game being boiled down to a 'beautiful chatroom'. I have experienced this. I reached Shantungosaurus after a few days of gameplay and honestly, right now, there isn't much reason to play massive herbivores. You find a bunch of Shantys, eat at a field, drink some water, and walk around while chatting. Maybe someone lays down a nest and you all hatch babies. There is a low danger aspect as a Shant. The same applies to the Puerta, which I have also heard being referred to the 'Walking Simulator'. (Nothing can kill a Puerta outright at this time. It has no natural enemies, which leads me to my most important point.)
Whenever I meet another herbivore in game (I mostly play herbivore) I try to let them know that massive high tier herbivores are cool and all, but with no natural predators (besides mega packs of apex), they get boring really fast. The real fun is had in the mid-tiers. Some examples;
I was playing as a Maiasaurus (Aladar from the movie Dinosaur) near the center of the map at a lake. I had just finished eating and drinking so I decided to rest in some brush to avoid detection. Night came and there I sat. I was looking at my phone, talking on Discord, when I looked up at my screen. A Gigantosaurus (sp) had crept right past me and had not seen me, which was amazing. Then there was another...and another. I knew I had to get out of the area fast. So I stood up and took off. This led to an insane chase which felt like minutes of heart pounding terror. Thankfully the Maia is pretty quick on its feet and I crested a hill and doubled back and sat and watched as the Gigas looked around dumbfounded.
These moments of extreme, heart-pounding fear are what keep me coming back. You don't get these moments of fear as a top tier herbivore (my herd was surrounded by 4 gigas the other day, lead to a battle that lasted 30 minutes, that was intense but those are few and far between for top tier herbs)
So if you do buy the game, do not even focus on endgame. There is no endgame right now. The endgame of The Isle is Chat Simulator, Lawnmowing Simulator, or Walking Simulator. The real fun lies in the mid-tier dinosaurs where the danger is palpable and the fear is real. I would recommend it right now as I feel I have had enough fun to justify $20. Would I pay more than $20 knowing what is inside the game? Nope. Not at all. As of right now, this is a $20 game that I would recommend. Get your fear on.

It explores themes such as loneliness, isolation, life vs survival, humanity, concept of Selfness, among others (without giving anything away). I thought this game was amazing. It engaged me on both a cerebral and emotional level. After i finished it, I just sat and let it's story sink in. I would recommend this game to anyone who appreciates deep, poignant storytelling; rich visuals; tense, frightening atmosphere; and engaging character development. If any of these things appeals to you, you will not regret buying this game.
I would honestly even recommend this game at full price. On sale, it's a no-brainer. BUY IT.

This game is like a lower-quality version of the very first Mortal Combat ever, which wasn't exactly a prime fighting game itself. The combat is incredibly rudimentary, there is a samey quality to the characters, jump-kicking hurls you about 75% across the screen, and the special attacks do stupidly insane amounts of damage for just charging up an energy blast for a second.
Honestly, this is the kind of game that looks like a fan game put together in Flash by somebody who likes video games, but not necessarily somebody who knows how to make them. Nothing about the game is very... professional. I understand it's "indie", but many indie games have a quality about them that really shows you that the developer(s) knew what he/she/they were doing. This game does not.
This game is playable on Newgrounds for free, so if you're buying it here on Steam just to get 4/8 of the trading cards, you'd be better off just buying the cards from the marketplace because you will save money that way (you don't have to own a game to craft a badge). It's just not an interesting game at all. Even if you wanted it for the story mode, which I don't know why you'd want a fighting game for a story mode... but if you did, this game's story is really lame too. I hate to say "why play ___ when you can play ___" because comparing two games isn't always good practice in reviewing, but in this game's case, I just wouldn't play it over any other fighting game for any unique reason of its own. It has no draw to me.

I rate this game Very, Very Positive. I acknowledge it's lackluster racing wheel support and thanks to previous reviewers' "head's up" I was not at all surprised when my old MS FFB Sidewinder wheel wasn't recognised during controller set up. Howevever, the controller I used (XBox gamepad) worked flawlessly. In fact, I would say the lack of racing wheel support is now a non-issue for Baja:EoC...I don't believe I said that...especially since I HATE the lack of fine control in steering when I use a gamepad. I was able to weave through opponents with precision. Very surprising. Gameplay is exciting and realistic...the AI opponents have a temper and I don't get away with much during a heated race. Multiplayer (split screen) worked without an issue. The black line (bug?) cutting off your upper field of view when in cockpit, as mentioned by another reviewer, is still there, but I switched to another view without an issue. If it's a bug, they need to fix it. Graphics are clean and crisp, framerate with a GTX970 hovers around 120fps with all the bells and whistles on "high". Sound is great and allows me to hear when an opponent is catching up and on what side of me he is on.
Overall, as a fan of Mickey Thompson(R) and his spectacular off-road events, I would say, "Drop whatever you are doing and buy it".
Parting thoughts: Baja:EoC is the best off-roading game I have played. Controller (or lack of) support is a non-issue; and believe me, I would have returned it, if I couldn't control it. Any off-roader worth his/her salt will enjoy it. You can play it on one PC with friends. AI is smart, but they believe in "an eye for an eye". No crashes in 17.4 hours on my PC.
EDIT: With over 30 hours in this game, I feel I must double-down on my review after a whole lot of races (solo). This game really satisfies my off-road racing bug, with the majority of races won and lost by a margin of mere "feet" (or meters). My opponents definitely have a temper and will use the track to their advantage. Is the bug regarding the partial black screen gone? I haven't noticed it for a few days, now. My only complaint would be, when changing views from external to the cockpit (driver 1st person), the sound of the engine is way louder than from the outside view...either raise the sound externally or bring the cockpit noise down a wee bit. That's the only thing I can think of...not a deal breaker, at all. The driveable area is mind-boggling...I can drive to points far into the horizon...kudos to all that were involved in creating this game. Thank you.
In closing...I'll say it again...any off-road enthusiast worth his or her salt needs to experience this game. You can always return it, but I bet you won't after a few races. Take a trophy truck out for a test drive...listen to the engine and watch it eat up the road/track/trail.

Well about this game, lets start with the pro's. Since the first Star Wars the Force Unleashed the combat has massively improved. Starkiller is not only wielding two lightsabers but his powers have majorly increased. For me this was a really good thing, beacause I always wanted to see what starkiller is cable off, and in this game you experience the force at its maximum. Another thing I liked was the upgraded graphics. For its time, SWTFU 2 looked amazing and it still does on PC. Finally, the gameplay was also updated with loads of new moves and a very impressive engine. Nevertheless, SWTFU 2 suffers from a lot of problems. Let's start with the story. The story from the first game was interesting, quite comlicated and offered us a lot of lore. In this game however, the story lacks charater, polish, and doesn't make sense at some moments. This is a big flaw for me, as I enjoy Star Wars games for their story, and SWTFU 2 fails to deliver this at a passable level. Then there is the lenght. I completed the Campaign in a mere 5 hours. 5 ♥♥♥♥ING HOURS. For 29,99 I expected more than pretty graphics and a few costumes. Another HUGE flaw was the easy as balls and forgetable boss battle with, you guessed it, Dark Pops. Overal does this game not what a sequel should do. The campaign is shorter, the story is duller and hard to follow and the price is too high. Lucasarts did a lot of work on the outside (graphics, moveset and engine) that they completly forgot the ambiance, the vibe and the overal experience. A Star Wars game should give the player a memorable experiece instead of a shiny, polygon physics demo. That's why I recommend that you play the first one, buy the ultimate sith edition, and let this one pass.

It feels awesome to patrol the air high over no man's land, eyes flicking between guages and the open sky, knowing that a lapse in concentration on either could mean death. You spot a plane, check your compass, his heading could mean enemy or friendly, dive to gain speed, he's spotted you, you're zoomed in as much as possible, wind is blasting your ears, muffling the spluttering engine. Sights are on him, heart's pumping, check for stoppage in the machine guns, trigger set, here we go, aaaaaand it's a friendly. Wave off, Never mind
The game itself is fantastic, great flight model. Multiplayer that has population (for now) and doesnt babysit you. It forces you to respect your engine and airspeed, windage, ammunition and fuel load. Most flight sims do this, but only in RoF have i managed to play a good multiplayer match that doesn't hold your hand.

One-hour review: Boy is this game ever pretty.  The core idea of "hey let's teach our kids about our culture by making a video game" is neat and I'm happy to support that.  I'm liking the Lost Vikings kind of thing, and if you have a controller you can even play co-op with the girl and fox.  They are pretty darn cute, and hey, walljumping fox.  There's a lot of cultural background videos that are pretty cool.
Downsides: It's a little glitchy once in a while, especially the partner AI is not good at not dying.  This isn't so bad because you don't lose anything if you die and the checkpoints are close together, but it is a little frustrating.  I've started to think of the critter as Derpfox no matter how cool he is.
I feel like I'm about halfway through the game after one hour, but the cultural videos seem like they are a big part of the experience and I haven't watched many.  Maybe think of this as an interactive cultural exhibit: you're paying for that, not for a huge amount of gameplay.
I'd rate this highly. I've learned a lot from this game and it has brought myself and my friends many hours of fun!

Wow... There are so many things going through my head as I finished my playthrough of Never Alone. The biggest one is how the idea of this game was born out of the want to educate people about Native Alaskan culture. Upper One Games, brought into existence, through E-Line Media and Cook Inlet Tribal Council, have managed to produce an amazing and captivating game through stories from a culture most of us don't understand.
The first thing to discuss is the art style of Never Alone. Everything from character models to the environments are spectacular. Granted, the cutscenes sometimes took a bit of that sparkle away from the game, but the art while playing is downright gorgeous. I caught myself many times with my mouth wide open and eyes dried up from hardly blinking. The animations help ground you in the game. They are smooth and seamless, yet the characters have weight to their movements, immersing me further into the game. Environments are dynamic and interactive. Riding on trees through the forest, running away from polar bears, and climbing large animated objects give the game an action packed feel.
If I were to rate each section of the game serparately, the mechanics might have been rated the lowest. This is not to say the mechanics are bad, but everything else was on another level. The two character puzzle solving mechanic is brilliant, yet I don't think they took it far enough. Most puzzles in the game are one note and very straight forward. I felt like they could have expanded on the difficulty of the puzzles at some point, perhaps requiring more back tracking or more steps in certain puzzles to accomplish that. The game mechanics overall were good though, using the two characters simultaneously to solve puzzles, very interesting platforming, and dynamic environments that require the player to react accordingly. If Upper One Games is going to release a sequel to Never Alone, they need to develop more intricate puzzles.
Speaking of a two character puzzle solving team, the lack of character development for Nuna and the fox were actually very positive choices. Even though I'm an almost thirty year old white male, I could easily put myself in Nuna's shoes and feel like I'm the little girl trying to save my village. Sometimes no character development is the best choice for a game and its immersion. I felt a natural bond between the two characters, a friendship that evolves over the game. Words don't have to be spoken between Nuna and the fox, but the bond naturally develops as the player uses both characters to work out puzzles, giving a strong feeling of comradery.
Never Alone does a great job progressing the story. There are not many moments where I felt that I wasn't making progress towards something. The story is quick paced, including multiple nemeses, which provide smaller subset stories to the overall story arch.
Last but certainly not least is the sound quality in Never Alone. The music and ambient sound is what ties the whole game together. Upper One Games does a great job at setting the mood for whatever is happening on the screen with not just the visual quality but also the audio.
Congratulations to Upper One Games, for being the first Native American development company, and for nailing their first project. Hopefully we will see more high quality games coming from this company, albiet maybe a tad bit longer next time eh? :) Overall, you should definitely play this game, it finishes around 3 - 4 hours which might make the price too steep for the hours you will get out of the game. I gaurantee that those few hours will be a blast though.

Now, before indulging any further into ridiculous so-called "reviews" of this game from hardcore zombie game p*ssies that doesn't go into detail (no offense). I'll give you my version, including... let's just say EVERYTHING ELSE than gameplay too.
At start, the games registration was a pain in the butt, I waited 2 days for the registration to go through for my account. But after that, I got into the world, spawned inside the safezone. There was no tutorial, no friends, nothing to lose. So I did what I usually do in survival horror games: Into the wild!
After 10 minutes I find myself on the ground with a rifle-bullet through my head, which is where most people give up. But f*ck most people! I thought to myself and thought that would be a bad orgie, ANYWAYS! I respawned, went out again, found guns, ammo, food, drink and I killed Humans, Nethers and Demons. and yes, I made sure the humans were hostile first. for example by asking in chat and not getting a response after stalking them for 5 minutes. Or they shot first.
I went back to safezone and throw some extra guns and ammo into my stash (aka global inventory) and I had a good career start as a survivalist. I also played with some friends later on, which was amazing too. Group survival, killing Nethers, hunting humans. All the more fun with a group of friends, as long as you remember one of the golden survival rules: Don't trust anyone you don't have on skype or teamspeak. -Or other voice communication device.
----------
Now for judging:
Graphics: 7/10 -a bit over-glossy water, some weird grass-patches on pavement. But everything is clear and nothing is over the top or under the bottom.
Level design: 10/10 -Very nice world, lots of buildings are open, lots of multi-level buildings, good for sniping, hiding, ambushes, hunting and scavenging.
Atmosphere: 8/10 -Very eerie and semi-scary. Works well with both humans and nethers being enemies or friends. Trusting the right or wrong people? Is there a nether around the corner? you may never know.
Gameplay: 9/10 -Yes, I like the gameplay. Even if I died at the start, I still came back and I got to experience all the awesome things of leveling up, getting skills and abilities, gathering loot for the sweet tooth and racking up kills. This is one of the only PVP and PVE games that I actually enjoy, due to it NOT being zombies, there's fewer hackers than most other survival horror games (atleast to my observation, I don't have statistics on it.)
-The shooting works perfect, aiming and reloading, never experienced a single flaw, maybe except for the little variety, but the balance is very good.
-The melee system works very nice, if you use your first skill in the melee skill tree that let's you block, you won't regret it. It will block weak nethers attacks so you recieve much less damage and no, it does NOT block bullets. You control a human, not a ninja. (to the observation ninjas are above humans.)
-The health, food and drink elements are well-implemented, though simple, they work as they're supposed to.
Overall: 8/10 -Yes, I really like Nether for what it is and how well it's done. It's a Survival Horror game. (no sh*t.) but it's so well done compared to other survival horror games out there. Yes, you WILL get killed, but seriously, try and name a PVP Survival Horror game that hasn't killed you... yeah? thought so. Oh? Really? Then don't use hacks, silly b*tch~<3
----------
Also... I played since early access, everything else than the cheapest price just adds cosmetics and easier access to some melee weapons which you can get in the wild in... under 10 minutes if you're lucky, so no need to waste money, it isn't pay to win.
Back then, in Early access there was ONLY ONE SAFEZONE, BUT! They have added more since then, the playable area has doubled since early access and the loot is in containers now rather than lying on the ground, which I like a lot.
Oh, and it's easy to gather teammates, just write in chat on the server and get some skype names or get together for some voicechatting. THEN you can trust them a bit more than down the barrel of your 12 gauge...

See this small game as a chunk of interactive folklore. A small, fireside tale of limited scope but great appeal.
The gameplay is nice and smooth, and both the co-op and single player - where you'll switch between both controllable characters - are implemented well. The visuals are top notch and for me carried most of the attraction. The tilt-shift depth of field, the muted colour palette, the subtle lighting: they all complement each other well. There's many a wow moment there, even if this is a short experience. If you're looking for extended gameplay, this is not your fix. I completed the game in little over three hours. For me, that's fine. I like it when games don't overstay their welcome, or go for artificial extension.
If you're looking for challenging, innovative gameplay, or if you're expecting a prolonged experience: this game offers neither. What it does offer is rich and rewarding, but that is mostly by proxy of setting and design aesthetic. And if you like those, you're sure to like the documentary-style bits of film describing the Iñupiaq way of life and this people's cultural heritage. You discover these bits of background in-game. I found all but one in my single play-through without really looking.
In conclusion: this was a welcome dip in Iñupiaq culture and folklore. If you're interested in that, and don't mind a little puzzle platforming along the way, plunge right in.
EDIT: a lot of reviewers mention a less-than-perfect partner AI. In fact, I didn't perceive it as such. Quite possibly because I still have quite a low opinion of most in-game AI I've encountered, I immediately assumed that during the single player experience, you're supposed to continuously flick back and forth between characters. In fact, I found it one of the more fun gameplay mechanics to keep switching as quickly as possible. When there was a gap to be jumped, I jumped with one character first, flicked to the other mid-jump, jumped again, and flicked back before landing. Try it out. You'll not only encounter much fewer of these glitches, but you'll have some more fun along the way.

I really like Adventurer Manager.  I am of the generation who saw the Nintendo Entertainment System (NES) come out when I was a kid in the mid-1980s and fell in love with video games since.  Without fully realizing it, I was waiting for Final Fantasy to come out in 1991.  Once that game came to America, it pushed every button in my video game life (pun intended).  I knew then that I was a turn-based role-playing game (RPG) fan, and all I ever wanted since then was basically just Final Fantasy with more depth.
Adventurer Manager reminds me of those days when I first discovered Final Fantasy: the graphics, music, and play style.  Adventurer Manager also fulfills my desire to have "Final Fantasy Plus" - extensions of the game concepts that use modern programming languages to enable greater customization, etc.  I really think that the developer of Adventurer Manager did a great job with a concise presentation of classic turn-based RPG elements and a fluid game concept.  While Adventurer Manager comes off as an homage to the late 80s and early 90s RPGs, it still goes one step further in areas like item crafting (not hard to do and somewhat rewarding), user decisions when leveling characters (stat allocation and special ability augmentation), and making questing be fair (two difficulty levels, Energy restoration after each fight, resurrecting dead characters after the quest, etc.).
I also read here on Steam that the developer is going to update the graphics and a few other features (including the "Auto Adventuring," which is similar to Final Fantasy Tactics, if you've ever played that game).  I am hoping that not too much of the current Adventurer Manager system will be altered, though.  However, as odd as it may sound, I do seem to have some faith in this developer's decisions, as I read elsewhere how they tweeked some initial elements of the game to result in what we have now.  Also, the developer has made a game with great attention to detail - you can tell it's been play-tested and optimized.  (For example, filtering item lists for individual characters, saving party formations for easy deployment, etc.)
To close, Adventurer Manager is a game that I will be spending very many hours on.  Yes, it is easy to pick up and play and learn how to optimize, and soon you will get the hang of how things are handled.  You may even get into a groove that some non-appreciative folks might call "tedious" or "monotonous."  But for fans of the genre like me, it's more like "doing work" so that you can build the "perfect cleric" or whatnot.  It's like investing the time and effort to have things go a certain way so that you can bask at your end accomplishment.  In other words, playing a game like Adventurer Manager has had me pondering the future possibilities, which I love to do.  So I guess this is a speculator's game.  :P  Nevertheless, for me, the ability to auto-adventure and the ability to create new characters and level them through re-playable quests/levels is the kind of "work" that I enjoy performing.
I've put in about 30 hours of game time in about 7 days of owning Adventurer Manager, and I have found myself succumbing to the same issues I did as a kid.  Things like arriving late for dinner, rushing to meet an appointment, etc.  So I have appreciated both the nostalgia that Adventurer Manager has invoked within me as well as the genre itself, which I love dearly.  So I'd actually like to thank the developer for keeping something like this project alive, and I hope more will support him.  Adventurer Manager is the game I would make if I had completed my degree in computer science instead of changing it.  And I paid $5 for this game on sale.  I highly recommend that you do the same, and keep your eye out for other games from this developer.  This is the kind of stuff that guys like me want more of.  :)

DISCLAIMER: "Mr Scum, you have zero playtime on this! How can you make a balanced judgement?"
20 years of practice outside steam, plus modded engines for the game.
Doom. It is the master and the grandfather of all FPS games. The first? No, but by far the most important without a doubt. Describing what Doom is at this point in time seems moot as, alongside Mario and a series like Warcraft or Pokemon, even if you don't play games you will likely have heard of it at some point in your life.
Like the aforementioned Mario in the first few games, Doom's real strength is its pure gameplay. As daft as that may sound bear in mind Doom was made back in a time before cut-scenes were really viable and in engine ones looked abysmal. There is lore, and there is even an ongoing story as the series progresses, but that is mainly a page of text at the end of each chapter describing the interim between worlds. Regardless of that you can just jump in and start without any major fanfare, you hit new game and select the difficulty, BAM you are in control and can start shooting stuff in about 2 seconds (difficulty dependent). A flaw here for newer players here may be the fact there is zero tutorial  as this was made in the days of paper manuals, but if you quickly read up on the controls before-hand there will be not much in terms of learning what to do. Once you get the basic movement down in the first 5 seconds you are set for the remainder of the game, such is the simple brilliance that is Doom.
It cant be ignored that the game, at over 20 years old, is rather rough looking even in comparison to something released 2 years after. If I remember correctly the highest resolution you can play at is 480p with a good chunk of the screen taken up by your inventory. The graphics are grainy and animation is simple, but this is a game designed for systems with 8MB of RAM. Once you can get past the technical restrictions on the game in that manner there is a really fine game inside, very finely balanced with the weapon loadouts and enemy attack patterns. Granted the first chapter these days is stupidly easy, but once you get to chapter 4 "thy flesh consumed" things are a lot different. One thing that will never age with Doom however is the superb level design and the layouts of everything. John Romero may have fallen from grace in later years, but his levels in the first Doom are works that are still viable as good layouts to this day. Granted they are very abstract at what they are trying to depict (I honestly have no idea what they are supposed to represent half the time) but in terms of scaling difficulty with a learning curve they are rather good.
It must be mentioned however that the afore mentioned Thy Flesh Consumed sits outside of this glowing praise slightly. It has its moments, but generally just feels like Romero made the maps for people who like punching themselves in the face.
Regardless of the above gushing, I would say for a modern player Doom is indeed slightly archaic and just rather aged. It is without doubt something you should play at least once and for those who cannot tolerate its aged engine there are some fantastic solutions in possibly one of Gaming's deepest rabbit holes: Mods.
In 1997 iD software released the source code for Doom, meaning anyone could come along and edit the game to their pleasure. The result was a huge number of legacy engines that have been released over the years allowing Doom to be played on just about any OS one can think of. The game even had a damned Amiga version made! With modern systems providing not only better optimised OS and hardware absurd in comparison to the original system's requirements modern engines have been made that will allow you to use mouse-look, have WASD movement and update the resolution so as to accommodate even the latest 4k monitors. Many have crossover with each other, but generally there will be something out there for everyone.
For a general good overall engine, GZDoom covers most bases, but has some odd issues purists may take umbrage with (usually very small things that the majority will not notice).
For a multiplayer focused but still generally very stable across the board engine, Zandronum is there. My personal choice.
For people who want to try just the regular old doom but with better animation, there is apparently Smooth Doom. I have not tried this myself, so I cannot comment on it fully.
For people who ABSOLUTELY WANT THE PURIST OLD EXPERIANCE AND ONLY THAT! Chocolate Doom will cover you.
So with all this legacy, you can now experience the first few chapters of both Doom and Doom II with little to no issues. The original Doom can be played through in about 6 or so hours perhaps (I can polish it off in about 2 and a half, but that is with LOTS of practice) and Doom II, being slightly longer, can probably be done in about 10 to 14 hours. So about 20 or so hours of play time at least. Aside from nuts like me who religiously play the game about once a month, that seems like good value, and I guess that is about as far as it goes? Again, wrong thanks to the modding community.
Doom is endless, Doom modding is endless.
When it comes to .WAD and MegaWADs Doom is possibly one of the greatest examples of a bottomless pit when it comes to how deep one can descend into a modding scene. If there is the old Rule 34 where if you can think of it there is porn of it, Doom would have a similar rule. If you can think of it, someone has made a Doom mod about it. Wars? Which one? The Second World War? Vietnam? The Gulf War (both)? The American Revolutionary war? Knights in Armour? Naturally there are mods for them. SPOOKY JUMPSCARE GAMES? Its a given. Sonic the Hedgehog and Mario? Well, yes you thought of them. Absurd memes? Of course there are, memes are the internet's lifeblood. RACIST MEMES? Sure Moonman. Doom is so Rule 34 in its logic toward mods that there are even Rule 34 mods, and I'm being serious. Look up HDoom (or don't).
Quite possibly the most famous Mod is the infamous Brutal Doom, essentially making it into the silly OTT violent chaos that people in the 90s made it out to be on the news. Its not very Doom like and changes almost all the core mechanics, but it is still very playable, coming with its own campaign to boot. If one wants to see its legacy, look no further than the latest DOOM (or Doom 4), a game mostly inspired by that silly gore mod. While Brutal Doom does have a bad rep with some people, it is certainly worth playing at least once. Even if you do skip it, you should at least try the glorious Brutal Doom 64, an update of the Nintendo 64 version with some fantastic subtle changes which, ironically enough for a 1998 game, was my favourite shooter of 2016.
So if you are ever bored of new games and want something that not only can stand as a history lesson but also be in itself the basis for an almost endless amount of content, Doom is one of the most important games ever released. Go and try it, and face your DOOM!

A fun, funny, and challenging game with plenty of gameplay elements to keep you occupied Evil Genius is a unique simulator. Taking control of this genius and his minions is fun but challenging. Players must keep in mind that while they are trying to opperate their base, minions will do their own thing. Your sort of at the mercy of these guys in some cases. This is where you might find a little flaw in the game. Sometimes minions won't do things as fast as you want or react to an intruder unless you tag or notify them. I had a tourist end up in my freezer. This guy walked right past a hallway full of minions and ended up in the freezer. Not to mention as I was locking the tourist up, investigators came in and started taking pictures. So be prepared for incompetence from minions. However, it does add to the challenge so I wouldn't completely call this a problem.
While I'm technically still new to this game, I will say this game keeps me well entertained. From building to managing my minions on the world map, there's so much to do. Placing traps is also quite fun. Just make sure you get traps placed at the main entrance early. This may save you from having idiots trapped in your freezer. Just don't go too willy nilly on things you may not need right away. I had to start over after I accidentally wasted money on stuff I didn't need at that moment. Also, pay VERY close attention to how you use and distribute your minions. This is a crucial resource for making your lair run as smooth as possible. Keep this in mind when senting minions out into the world to do your bidding.
Overall, This game is simple and just challenging enough that you will not get bored with it.

Great first impression, been after a endurance offroad racer for a while. As a avid fan of Dirt Rally and RBR something like this is a nice compliment to the homologated rallying scene.
I wanted a pad game, I dig out my G27 for the aforementioned titles of course, and it plays great. The seemingly awkward looking controls actually feel pretty natural, making use of the right stick as the gear shift. It took maybe... 30 seconds to get the feel of that? Will need to give the wheel a spin.
The various buggies feel like they have a decent weight, and playing on simulation physics with full damage is great fun. Definitely the only way to play: put up the realism settings and cater the AI to your needs, and have at it. Don't expect RBR/DR level of physics here, but it feels decent all the same.
Tracks are great. Expansive, variable, ready to bite you in the rear end at a moments notice. You'll need to have a care if you're playing as "real" as possible, engine management and limiting/negating damage as much as possible will be key to making decent headway. Don't expect to be able to "learn" these tracks, unless you have a damn GPS system in your head.
Sure there a couple of bugs that need fixing, and maybe some tweaks to be made (keeping your default/preferred view would be a nice one), but for that Motorstorm like feel, on huge tracks, with damage management and decent enough driving physics that put some "simulations" to shame (looking at you, Dirt 4), Baja nails it.

Very sleek visuals with a nice concept behind it.  The character, like the gameplay, is somewhat uninteresting, but if you give it time, the game wins you over with some creative puzzle challenges involving quick movement, strategic thought, and stealth.
This game was fun for a time, but it quickly became tedious to play.  Perhaps a person with a greater aptitude for platformers than myself would enjoy the challenge, but this game does not offer the same slick moves found in games like Super Meat Boy and simply punishes the player for wanting to explore at all.  For example, if you are curious what's at the bottom of a pit where the door is closed, you jump down there, but then, you realize it's a dead end and have to restart the level from the beginning rather than simply a redo like when you die.  If you die, it seems smart enough to simply place you back at the last checkpoint, so why not just give us a suicide/redo button?
Overall, it's a good 2D stealth platforming game with a professional quality presentation.  It should offer well over the 93 minutes I played if you want to continue through the tougher challenges, but if you're like me, it's just too much challenge and not enough fun.  The character is somewhat lovable but ultimately bland and uninteresting.  That said, it's well worth the asking price, especially for a game I got in a low-priced bundle deal, because it offers a very high quality stealth puzzle experience.  Worth delving into even if you only get an hour out of it.

I am writing this review to spread awareness to other people who are looking at getting this game. This game is completely different than what is advertised.

You don't really see too many games with those tags together in one sentence, and I have to give Supergiant some props for the creativity. I'm all for developers trying out new things and innovating, but this game just didn't feel right. It felt like it had all the right elements but it couldn't execute.
Pyre is 10% gameplay, 10% traveling, and 80% reading text.
Now, this isn't necessarily a bad thing. There are a plethora of good VN games out there who can balance text and gameplay well. However, I personally felt that Pyre fell short. Majority of the text is filler one-liners and useless information. I consistently felt like the balance between gameplay and reading was extremely off, and found myself really only playing the game for the aesthetics and the inevitably repetitive glorified soccer gameplay.
Pyre does have its pros though. The best parts of the game were the characters, artstyle, and music by a long shot. Each character felt unique, had their own story, and their own unique abilities/movesets to be used in the Rites. Every single scene is eye candy to the max and is incredible to look at. The music is top notch and fits extremely well into the game. Not to mention, a visual novel sports game is an interesting new take in the RPG genre. This game is definitely unique to say the least.
However I can't recommend this game because of the latter alone. Unless you are the type of person who enjoys extremely text-heavy visual novels accompanied with very minimal gameplay, then I don't recommend this game. I ultimately found myself only enjoying 10% of Pyre, and I can't recommend it because of that.

Final Slam 2 is, to put it quite frankly, an abomination of a game. It falls below poorly designed shovelware into something that feels like an insult to other games in the genre. As a fighting game it fails on a fundamental level with a horribly shallow pool of moves, awful controls (which includes a complete lack of gamepad support), and broken systems that make fights feel entirely reliant on luck. Every aspect of the game, from the tutorial to simply the menu navigation, manages to be far more convoluted and confusing than it should ever be, making something as simple as changing the screen resolution unintuitive.
The art design has the dubious honor of being possibly the worst of any retail game I've yet seen, with horrendous character designs, blurry textures, an inadmissible lack of detail in every scene, and horrendous animations that can hardly be called as such. It's like MS Paint got exceedingly drunk, and this is the aftermath that it threw up the next morning. The over the top and misogynistic dialog from the story mode is just the last nail in a terribly constructed coffin.
If it was possibly to revoke my copy of Final Slam 2, I'd gladly take the chance to never have to glance at it again in my library. It's one of the worst games I've had the displeasure of playing on Steam, and I shudder to think that people are actually paying for something that would compare unfavorably to the average flash game. Fantastic mix of arcade racing with sim details. Sort of a thinking man's racer.
It's main draw from other racers is the almost openworld nature of the circuits and tracks, circuits spanning 2-4 miles. The average circuit race has your multiple lap head-to-head. 5-8 minute rallies. And my favorite, the 1-4 hour Baja races.
Normally that would sound dreadful. But it features a wear&tear damage system. You have to manage how you drive throughout a race.
Brake too much and you might wear them out before the end of the race. Clutch kick too often and eventually lose acceleration power.
Drive too aggressively with powerslides, high RPM, and lots of jumps and bumps, and your suspension, tires, and engine can each be victim. All the types progressively worsening the performance of your car in different ways. Forcing you to stop to use your limited spare wheels, or call in a chopper for system repairs.
But, if you have a preferred driving style, you spend your credits on upgrading the parts most affected by the style, and fine tuning the various parts of the vehicle.
Steering wheels are supported, but force feedback is lacking even constant resistance, making it really hard to steer. It's very much designed around a controller, and shouldn't be played without one.
Watch out for this one in sales. It's current 30€ tag is way too high for anyone but those who immediately know they're in the niche for it.
I should also add that this isn't a great PC port feature-wise. It uses a custom launcher to set all the PC specific settings, and it has at least at launch had issues working. But once the actual game starts I've noticed no issues. And 120 fps no problem.

Seeing as I knew the game was in Early Access, and that I really enjoyed my time spent on the game at first. I continued to give it more tries without just giving up. But it wasn't fun anymore. Every match I got dropped in, I stood no chance. I'd rather spend my time on a shooter that is more balanced, than deal with getting killed constantly until I'm high enough level to unlock the same equipment. I'm using WWII era equipment going against people using modern weaponry.
TL;DR    Fun game at first. Quickly became unbalanced; unfair matchmaking.

Disclaimer: I haven't played the former The Darkness, so i didn't know anything about the plot before starting with this one.
But for the most part, i felt like the plot wasn't really well developed. In fact, the gameplay is very linear, for most of the game (i might say, aside of a few short "missions", things get more complicated in the last quarter of the game), quite corridor-like.
The characters are truly well done, slightly less so the voicing part, which is good but not ideal (Bioshock Infinite comes to mind).
Theorically you have your guns and the Darkness power. In practice, you get to find a limited amount of bullets along the way (not much of a choice). Lucky enough, the Darkness works really well in combat, makes for a lot of gore but that's not something the game lacks in the plot itself, either. During combat, you gain essence, which in turn allows you to buy Talents for both your shooting and darkness skills. Actually, there are so many of them that you will hardly ever max out 2 out of the 4 skill trees (could be a balance, though).
There are some parts that feel "rushed" and overall the game could've benefitted of more care for detail, some places don't have a strong "mark" on them, funny enough literally everything gets better in the last chapters, with the last chapter being quite impressive for several reasons (you get to play with some truly nice weaponry and the feeling could be that of a modern "Quake" or "Doom" idea).
Visually, the game looks about "functional", the cell-shaded graphics are fine, but i'd bet it's a trick done for performance issues on consoles rather than being a visual feature that makes real sense. The game could've probably benefitted of a realistic graphic (which proved good on the previous game), maybe that could have improved the game atmosphere.
Last but not least, bugs: i had a lot of CTD errors with this game, and precisely only cinematics started. It didn't happen every single time, but i had to re-play several parts because of this.
7,5/10 - about average,could've been better. But the last part is quite intriguing, it's a short experience you can get over with in about 6-7 hours. Worth playing (if you got some patience).

Full Video Review -
Never Alone tells the story of an Iñupiat girl Nuna who while out finds herself stuck in an eternal blizzard. She is saved by an Arctic fox who then becomes her companion. They both then set off to find the source of the eternal blizzard meeting friends and foes along the way to try and save their way of life.
Nearly 40 Alaska Native elders, storytellers and community members contributed to the development of the game. The story of the game combines different folklore tales of the Alaskan natives and produces some wonderful, atmospheric storytelling. The game is narrated by a native elder who speaks in their native language throughout. The whole narration is very well done and due to the fact that the narrator is speaking in the native language it not only adds a degree of gravitas to the story but also a sense of atmosphere.
Graphically the game looks great. The Arctic setting looks great its mix of black, blues and whites all make for a very eye pleasing vivid look. The game visually reminds me of a cross between Brothers and child of light at times. The mixture of the 3d and 2d works really well and the effects such as lighting, snow winds and more look good and provide great atmosphere. The soundtrack of the game is also wonderfully composed and adds to the ambiance of the various situations and story points throughout.
In terms of game play you must use both Nuna and the fox to accomplish different tasks in order to progress. Similar to Brothers, Nuna and the fox both have different roles. Nuna can climb ladders and ropes, move heavy obstacles, and throw her bola at targets. Where as the fox fit through small areas, scramble up walls, jump to great heights and can control spirits that come to help you. In single player you can seamlessly switch between the two at any time allowing you adapt to any given situation or puzzle.
You can use either use mouse and keyboard or a controller to play the game. The game has clear been designed with the joysticks of a controller in mind particularly throwing Nuna's Bola and so I would recommend using one if you have one.
As you go through the eight chapters in the game you'll come across a variety of puzzles and your run of the mill platforming to take care off. Usually you'll need to you both characters abilities to overcome hurdles such as moving a crate with Nuna so the fox can jump, then run up a wall to the throw a rope down so Nuna can climb up. As the game progresses Nuna and the fox will gain some other abilities such as Nuna's bola which is a throwing weapon that Nuna can use to break objects among other things.
The puzzles in the game are done fairly well and all work well in the arctic setting. The folklore adds really colorful elements and characters to the game such as spirits who help to traverse land. Like in any puzzle platformer, as you progress the puzzles become more difficult however theres nothing that requires more than a couple of tries to get right. Should you find yourself dying the game has a regular checkpoint system denoted by owls along the levels.
As well as the single player, you also have drop in co op which works really well. Having a friend control either Nuna or the Fox can not only be fun but also allow you to progress much faster and smoother. However you will require a spare controller to play co-op..
While the Never Alone hits the right marks in terms of looks, atmosphere and story it does currently have a number of issues. Firstly something that hopefully the developers will try and iron out as soon as possible is the sheer amount of bugs in the game. In several major places in the game I found a couple of bugs that hampered my progress briefly and I had to restart from a checkpoint to continue.
At one part in the game I was getting chased by a polar bear until you reach an ice bridge. Now whats supposed to happen is the bear steps on the bridge and falls into the water which triggers a water spirit to carry Nuna and the fox across the water. However on several occasions this scene bugged and the bear wouldn't step on the bridge causing the ice just to break apart and causing me to die over and over until it after on reset the bug was no longer present.
Another issue is in the single player mode only. Because you can only control one character at a time the other follows. Sadly if your in danger say for example someone is throwing rocks at you the non controlled character sometimes forgets to move and dies which can get annoying.
One of the great aims of the game is to educate people on the culture of Alaskan natives. They have done this by putting insights which you unlock through playing. Insights are short videos which you can watch anytime that explain different parts of the culture. It was a great way to implement this in the game and some of the short videos contain really interesting information.
As a whole Never Alone is very well produced. While it does have some minor hiccups along the way. It is a beautiful, atmospheric puzzle platformer that not only allows you to traverse beautifully crafted Arctic environments. But its a video game about sharing and ultimately celebrating a culture. Not only does the game provide entertainment but it harnesses to some degree the mediums other potentials such as education.

Half-life 2 can be surprisingly fun to play with a friend! None of the levels feel too cramped, and there's often just the right amount of difficulty to support two or more players. However, I thought the difficulty was a little high at times, making it more of a challenge than it should be to get past an area. Also, the games occasionally isn't very well optimized for more than one player. For example, only a single one-seated jeep would be spawned in a couple of the coastal levels, which means you have to spawn in others for the extra players.

Lets start by saying what this game is.
It's a beautifully, culture enriched casual platformer that has an immersive story that will captivate you or your children.  I'm personally not a big platformer player but after seeing the trailers I was hooked.
The story told by the narrator is one that you would tell to a child.  One that helps show a child courage and dedication.  But let there be no mistake, this is for adults too.  There were a few moments were i had to hold by my feels from tearing up.
What's great about this game for me was that every time i felt like i reached a point of, 'I've had enough of platforming', there would be a cut scene with some story.  It was a great break for me and really helped the game flow fluidly.
What this game is not, it is not for the hardcore gamer.  While there are a few moments where the game is frustrating without a second player, the platformer game is extremely casual.  The game is meant to immerse you in the story, not have difficulty settings in game play.
I do highly recommend that you play this with two people.  The second half of the game when one person would play as the boy fox is extremely difficult by yourself.  At times it's really frustrating as the AI does what it wants and screws you over.  This is all I can say without giving anything away.
If you're interested in the game play, I Lets Played the whole game.

The best game a gearhead could buy.  Seriously.
You like car wreckin'?  I like car wreckin'.  I like BeamNG cause it's literally car wreckin' (virtually).  The developers have some super aspirations with game modes, scenarios, challenges, etc and I dig that.  But it's a great engine for wreckin' cars.  I loaded a mod someone online made and it lets you COMPLETELY customize engines and transmission gear ratios.  They don't have a horsepower slider, you have to understand torque rpm relationships and how that's applied to the tires through the transmission/clutch.  Yesterday I decided to change the gear ratio on gears 2 & 3 just for fun after I added a turbo AND supercharger to the engine and set he max RPM's to 9000 and the upper shift limit to 9000 RPM.  I had to switch out the tires for drag racing versions cause the stock tires just peeled out nonstop.  After I got traction and hit second gear, the car wouldn't shift past that and while I was looking at the tachometer to see where it was and why it wasn't shifting, the engine seized.  When I looked at the messages, it showed I had destroyed the valvetrain and melted the piston rings.  Sure, it was just text telling me this, you don't SEE it.  But all that stuff is simulated.  You can give your car so much torque and tweak gear ratios that you can literally shred your tires.  If you want a car game that lets you wreck stuff REALISTICALLY this is it.  I have Wreckfest but I don't really play it much anymore after really digging into BeamNG.  The game is supposedly hitting full release in the next 6-8 months with a big update due after Christmas 2017.  It's Dec 8th right now and I'm super stoked.  Best $25 I've ever spent on a game!

Observations and other musings...
You pay a lot for little!
Yes, it is a very good flight sim: one of the best I have tried.  However, the price point for the base game gives you only the basics and then you have to dish out a heck of a lot of money just for some basic enhancements... like planes that should have been available from the start!.
On the Steam December 2014 sale, the game wason for 60% off, which means the base game and the DLC will still cost you about $120...OMG on sale!  For that kind of money I should be able to have every piece of kit that flew in the sky in the First World War!
Now get this, if $120 at 60% off doesn't satisfy your need to open your wallet, just remember, the undiscounted price is $55 for the game plus $240 for DLC!  These guys are as greedy as the guys that develop and market the DCS World sim.
So, if you really want to experience a good WW1 flight sim, then get it while it's on sale, because that kind of money would be better spent on something more enriching than wasting your time on a computer, like taking your love for a romantic getaway… ;-)
Now, I appreciate good quality software development.  I always look for historically accurate depictions of warfare.  I really love it when these two factors come together.  This game system is a rare breed that achieves this in a fairly good way.  The flight dynamics are great.  The planes beautiful.  The adversaries deadly.  It’s a pretty good game!
But I will be ♥♥♥♥ed if I dish out that kind of money for DLC.  I will wait for a better product with more reasonable price model.

I do like this game. I like it far more than dead by daylight. However, there are good and bad things about this game.

-graphics- are surprisingly good, the facial animations are funny and the models are all good looking.

cons

Overall I do enjoy this game. It has a great concept and I do have some fun.
Edit: recent patch has improved bug problems a bit. there are still bugs but not as frequent which is greatly appreciated. - Typical story, but hilarious dialog, fun characters and environmental/discovery-based story telling makes it a great experience.
- Super deep and rewarding combat system with a plethora of skills and mechanics to master such as the perfect guard.
- Enemies and bosses attack differently between normal and hard mode, as well as single or multiplayer
- Skill charging makes it so you have almost 3 different skills at your disposal despite leveling only one skill.
- Loads of side quests, mini games and discoveries to be found.
- Multiplayer with up to 4 players that is super smooth gameplay-wise. Connection is also easy via Steam friend list.
- Gorgeous pixel art that contains many little details to make the game world feel alive.
- Music fits each area very well and does not overstay its welcome at all.
- Arcade (roguelite) mode adds a ton of replayability. Beating it is hard enough, the side roguelite quests and high score chasing allows infinite replayability.
Cons:
- Non-hosts may experience lag, which ruins the multiplayer experience [case-by-case basis]
- Would be nice for some skills to interact with each other more for multiplayer mayhem [Earth spike wall + Smash?]
