First impressions are that its a fun little game.  Its a cross between Diablo and a JRPG.  Diablo in the form of random loot drops with randomly generated stats and crafting, JRPG in the sense of combat and questing.  The humor is off-the-wall random to the point that quests details are randomly determined without any sense; Go defeat the 32 mice and recover the 56 bales of hay; find the 15 merchants and dispatch the 82 legions of spoons.
The one mechanical difference between this game and other JRPG types is that you can create up to 12 different adventuring parties and have 3-4 of those parties go on seperate adventures simultaneously while the others rest up or train at the university; thus you manage your adventures (roll credits).
The story is just an excuse plot to make you go kill random things in random dungeons and goes so far as to poke fun at the entire JRPG/fantasy genre.
If the random humor is the up side, then the down side is the micro-management.  if you have 12 parties with 4 members each, then you have 48 heroes to level up, choose skills for, assign gear to and send to school (wow, did I just inherit 48 children?).  Eventually you will develop a pattern that works for you, but, about 60% of my game time is spent managing my parties and only about 40% is spent grinding the dungeons.
If you want a simple rogue-like/JRPG experience with some satyrical humor give it a go; just don't expect it to be GOTY.

For Honor is a difficult one. It’s one of those love and hate cases. The gameplay itself is fantastic. It has this really great and innovative combat system that very much reminds me of Dark Souls PvP, it has a very similar feeling. You really need to focus on your enemy, on what he does, how he reacts to your moves and how he prefers to attack you. Does he like to use his kick attack quite often? Then, adapt. Evade kick with a side step and follow that up with a light attack. Get the timing right, and get it right quickly, or the fight will be over soon. For Honor is a game about reading your enemy, about learning combos and when to perform them. It’s about patience, mashing buttons won’t get you anywhere. After 30 hours it still isn’t boring, easily the best duelling experience since Dark Souls.
Of course, it all gets a little crazy in the 4v4 modes, like Elimination, or the most favored mode right now – Dominion. The duelling aspect is still there, but rarely will you actually finish a fair fight against the enemy. People often quit duels in order to escape to a safer place and maybe regenerate some health. Often other players interfere, so you end up in a 1v2 or 1v3 situation. It’s a frantic back and forth, a fight for spawn tickets or control zones. It is a lot of fun, but there is not that much honor to be found here. Which is why I generally prefer 1v1 and 2v2. If I lose, it is my fault, and mine alone, if I succeed in a 2v2, I will stand there and watch the duel between my ally and the enemy and will not interfere. I will wait for them to finish, and if the enemy is victorious, only then will I approach him. This game is called For Honor, after all!
So, why did I say it’s a difficult one? You can probably guess by now that I really enjoy this game. Well, the main problem with it is the connectivity issues everyone has right now. Ubisoft decided to use P2P technology, which unfortunately results in several problems. Sometimes you will need several attempts to even join a game. Once you’re in a match, it is very possible that the game simply throws you out for no apparent reason. If someone else leaves, the game can get stuck in an endless loop where it tries to reconfigure the network session over and over again, which is especially common on the 4v4 modes. Ubisoft really needs to address these issues soon.

Charming, fun, vibrant and addicting - this is one great RPG!
In this world you are a Collector, someone who explores and adventures across the world in search of rare loot and items of power! Every enemy in the game has at least one rare "drop" to collect so this really is a game for players who love to collect/farm/grind! There is also a crafting system that can *GASP* actually make powerful and useful gear!
The combat gives off vibes of Secret of Mana but its much less rigid and limited than the old school RPGs of yore are. You can choose freely amongst 1h melee with shield, 2h melee and 4 schools of magic (Fire, Earth, Ice and Air). You invest skill points into whatever skill you desire and then the combat becomes an awesome weave of offense and defense as you bust out your skills in real-time!
Boss battles are great and plentiful as well! Really, this is a great action oriented RPG with a major emphasis on its addicting collection system (GRINDea, get it? :P) Usually "grinding" is looked poorly upon but honestly its quite addicting in this game and every enemy and boss can be beaten without taking a single point of damage so ultimately you don't actually have to grind - if you're really good!

A solid and thoroughly enjoyable puzzle platformer that's admittedly more about not getting murdered by robots and laser traps than being stealthy.
The basic elements of the game like the controls, the visuals and the audio are all well polished and fully functional. The puzzles demand a combination of good reflexes, observational skills and a small amount of strategic thought (good planning will mostly just make your finish time faster). Gadgets that you acquire as you progress through the game switch up the experience at an adequate pace and each level is unique and more-or-less interesting in some way. I very much liked the Metroid-vania aspect of the game, actually. Being able to explore and mess around with the gadgets in the sandbox-ish enviroment of what is basically the game's overworld is actually quite fun. The overworld also has multi-gadget puzzles that with their more open-ended nature give more variety to the gameplay and have a nice change of pace in comparison to the puzzles in the levels, aka the "tests". That variety is a welcome addition for me, even if brings with it the fact that a fair amount of playtime will be spent just running around the overworld instead of solving puzzles (perhaps a teleportation system like the ones in some Zelda games, such as Majora's Mask, could remedy this). The techno-industrial style of the game is pretty slick, too, and I really like the soundtrack and the visual aesthetics.
My biggest gripes with the game are:
As a whole, the game was a lot of fun and I would definitely recommend it (and the original, Stealth ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Deluxe) to anyone that likes a fairly challenging puzzle platformer that's just a bit more action-oriented and exploration-focused than the usual.

Do you really need information about this game? Do people seriously not know what Doom is?
Okay fine. Story is that some sinister corporation decided to start screwing around with teleporters and accidentally opened a portal to Hell. You, a nameless space marine, have to fight hell's demons off and save Earth.
Gameplay: Start level with gun in hand, collect items, kill enemies, find the exit. Make sure to be observant for secrets.
Now, the experience you get playing this game depends on what you play it with, if you want the purest most 90s experience possible, DOSBOX (Which comes pre-installed with the game upon steam installation) will do the job. But if you want a more modular and arguably playable experience playing this game, I would suggest you try a source port. Doom's source code was released in 1997 so people have been making ports for a long time.
The one everyone will tell you to use is g/zDoom. And with good reason, it's the most modular and most compatible with different operating systems. For those looking for a slightly more modern yet still 90s feeling experience, try it's predecessor, zDoom. Doom had a very popular deathmatch mode, if you want to experience this deathmatch mode today, try Zandronum and Doomseeker.
To run a source port, after installing the game, Right click on the game, go to "Properties", "Local Files", "Browse Local Files" and it should open the game's directory. Rename DOSBOX to DOSBOXBACKUP, Extract all files relating to your source port into the directory using something like WinRAR, go to the source port's .exe and rename it "DOSBOX" You should now have the ability to run your source port through steam! Usually source ports give you the choice of which game to run upon running them, so make sure to select the correct one.
Mods? I suggest you beat the game using no mods to start off, or maybe just Smooth Doom. But this game does have a very dedicated modding community, and most mods you find will work for Doom 2 as well.

Genre - 3rd Person melee duels
I bought this full price, which I don't often do nowadays. However, after playing the Beta I was surprised how much I enjoyed this game.
There is a single player campaign with over 15 levels. These can be played on three difficulty settings. I have been through on normal and hard.
The multiplayer modes are a 1 on 1 duel, a 4 on 4 scrap and a 4 on 4 control point mode called Dominion.
There are 12 warrior types to choose and they are all varied enough to add a lot of re-playability. From the fat boy Samurai to the stabby Peacekeeper.
Fights involve blocking in three directions and light or heavy attacks in the same. However, each class has a special move and 4 traits they can use once they are earned. I find the combat system natural and fluid. To be honest this is the main part of the game. If you don't like this, you won't like it.
There are enough maps to keep each game varied. Orders are also given earning bonus steel that will encourage you to try all modes. The ai can be used or will jump in when someone rage quits or crashes.
There is an over-arching battle map, which relies on one of the three factions you chose at the start Samurais, Vikings or Knights. Each game allows you to help the war effort.
There are a few criticisms. The AI NPCS that fight in some of the modes are weak and remind me of the foes in Dynasty Warriors. These are to make a battle feel but this really needs to be expanded by my points to fight over and new units. There are war machines and archers in single player, so why not multi.
Also I am getting a few crashes such as returning to world map. A few games have crashed me out too. It relies on Uplay being installed and run through.
This is my casual game of choice at the moment and I keep coming back for quick and enjoyable battles.
Just don't try Dark Souls after as you will get horribly killed when you keep holding left trigger to enter a stance!

Leaving this as a negative review for the moment, I may change it depending on future UI and game updates.
Major cons, personally-
- Tonnes of grinding- as stated, they intend for us to grind a party most of the time we play.
(this is not a manager game, this is a repetative dungeon crawler game at that point)
- The dungeons are bland even the first time they are played through (let alone the 10th), and while the story is quirky and kinda fun like Knights of Pen and Paper, there is not nearly as much of it, and it feels lackluster in parts.
- The tutorial is incomplete, never once mentioning the huge importance of reforging weapons.
(This seems to be a core mechanic, and for it to be left as an "advantage" for the players that go read the forum and know that it is a core mechanic... seems a little, eh, not good?)
(Will have to replay but I also don't believe it warns the player to use the fast forward VERY sparingly.)
- The invasions are very very very steep learning curves with a craptonne of luck involved in surviving without RNG blessings.  Invasions also need to be sought out and clicked on the map, without it ever really telling the player about them (tutorial issue or much clearer identification, possibly a different color or pulsing aura?)
Overall, the generally clunky interface is not made up for with in game humor or the spark that makes indie games appealing, and the lack of really engaging, well, anything about the grinding, makes it a frustrating mess to me personally.
I can put up with a little grind for a fun story, and the reward of another new one liner or groanworthy pun every few minor tedius tasks (what made me spend so much time and money on Knights of Pen and Paper) can make up for a myriad of sins.
Even discounting the mix up between what I thought the game was, and some shaky wording from what I remember (something about avoiding grinding.) the lack of sufficient little QUESTS makes this game a meh at absolute best for me.  Give us new bits of text, or, even better, new dungeon options or variety, and it would make grinding less of a chore or job. (Something I do NOT do for fun. As it stand I put this on the same tier as scrubbing a floor or cleaning the fridge in a dorm.)
The autoplay mechanic will definately salvage that, because I do not need to be bored to tears grinding the same exact layouts of 4 or 5 dungeons near endlessly to advance to the next dungeon... and do the same thing again there.
But as it stands? This makes it a negative review still, and a strong "Buyer really needs to be aware before buying" situation.

The game is a nice concept and return to the old school RPGs.
There is a decent sized world to explore, but the nature of the progression system makes the game extremely linear.
I enjoy some grinding, but I feel that early on in a game it shouldn't just be a grind fest.
The pace of the game is relatively slow, as each battle (if fighting at the appropriate level) is a bit slow.
It made me favor running with two mages in the rear of the party for maximized damage.
The fact that the rear two members of your party cannot engage in melee combat makes the party composition a bit restrictive.
The leveling system does indeed have all the D&D based stats that one would desire and the items are numerous.
The issue I have is the extreme monotany of scroling through all of your many many characters to see who has leveled and to adjust their stats accordingly.
This would be no problem if you had less than 10 characters to deal with, but remembering your build for each of the numerous characters is quite tedious (I probably have 28 or so and you are allowed many more than that).
The story is irrelevant, but it's not supposed to be the focus of the game. The mood is intentionally silly, which is fine.
I liked the randomly generated bio for the characters, but the code determining the details is a bit lacking.
Basically they are set up like mad libs where certain nouns and activities are filled in with a random choice from their designed library of content. This is fine, but you end up seeing the same wonky descriptions over and over again (sometimes twice in a sentence) and there is little regard for logic.
I've logged 6 hours so far and it feels like I haven't gotten much done besides having a large group of characters and having cleared the same dungeons multiple times.
I have spent a lot of the in-game money upgrading characters and your castle, but this feels largely unrewarding and tedious as well.
If the game cost under $5, then I would revise this to a recommend. I paid $7.50 during a deal week and even that seems a bit expensive.

Baja, Baja, Baja, Baja, mushroom, mushroom!
What an interesting game.
Here, I'm analysing the game based on the current racing game landscape. I never played this back in the day, so I have no nostalgia factor here.
PROS:
- Reminds me of the Motorstorm days
- Some of the best car - environment physics interactions I've seen in a game
- Wide variety of vehicles
- Upgrading system that isn't too detailed, but is detailed enough to be interesting
- Tuning and upgrading that has a meaningful effect on car handling (different people will have preferences, there is no 'best' tuning setup)
- Complex parts damage simulation, from the radiator to the oil pan
- Can call a helicopter to come repair you on long-distance races
- AI that makes mistakes in a believable manner
- HD texture work adds a ton of atmosphere
- Three hour long race across all the maps in the game combined
- Have to fight with the car to keep it on track (if you're used to road racing like I am, you have to re-learn how to appraise corners and jumps)
- Local split screen, online multiplayer
- Cheatcodes, because fun is more important than achievements
- Can shove small buggies around when driving a big truck
CONS:
- Mediocre visual damage model (no dirt/mud on car, no denting)
- Some of the worst car - car physics interactions I've seen in a game (if you bump into another car, you can get locked into drifting TOWARDS the other car until you clip through it) [EDIT: This happened to me lot more with the first two vehicle classes than it does the later ones]
- Terrible sound mixing (volume of car engine is insanely loud when in hoodcam)
- Very dated music
- Awful keyboard control mapping (once you remap the controls so that you can play the game, navigating the menus is a nightmare)
- Strange, jarring holdovers from arcade racing (for example, when you cut a corner, you don't get docked time like you do in real life - you get reset onto the track)
- AI can get so obsessed with its own racing line that it absolutely refuses to overtake you, and just bumps you up the butt until you crash
- This is probably the biggest one for me: You cannot damage your car to the point where it stops working. 200km/h into a tree? Whoops, flat tire.
This game is, essentially, a more grounded Motorstorm 1 with far better environmental interactions, and far worse car to car contact. It's really growing on me, but you have to be a specific sort of person to find the diamond in the rough. Get it on sale for USD$20 or less. Or maybe $23, like it is at the time of this review.
EDIT: Here's a couple of things I've found. 1) The '160 vehicles' thing is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. The game counts each different vehicle paintjob as a vehicle. There's still a nice variety of vehicles, though. 2) It only gets more fun the further in you progress. If you're like me, and you just want to race without the stress of needing to come first to progress the career, just input 'SHOWTIME' into the top right of the configuration tool. Bam! Unlock everything.

Final Slam II is a fighting game originally made in Flash. And as a Newgrounds submission Final Slam II is pretty decent, but unfortunately it doesn't hold up compared to other independently developed fighting games, especially those released on Steam. Final Slam II goes for the simple with it comes to combat. You use WASD and GHJ (no gamepad support which is typical for Flash games) to control your fighter but the way fighters move, jump and punch seems very much unnatural, like a combination of the original Street Fighter and the original Virtua Fighter. As to be expected there is a story mode (a cliched and confusing one) in addition to a tournament mode.
The best thing that Final Slam II has going for it is the character creation system. Using a large variety of body parts, colors and a few sizes you can create your own fighter with special moves, stances, poses, and voice chosen by you. Unfortunately this is also one of the game's biggest flaws because all the characters already in the game were created this way, and use the same "custom mannequin" creation method. There's no expression or animation outside the movement and rotation of body parts and it gives you this strange feeling that you're playing with jointed paper dolls instead of martial arts masters. On top of this is the fact that the only difference between male and female fighters is the large set of boobs pasted onto the male torso.
I've played a lot of fighting games in my lifetime from Street Fighter, most games on the Neo Geo and Skullgirls to more obscure titles like Yatagarasu and MONSTER and in my opinion the quality of this game does not merit the price. If you want to try the game for yourself before paying, you need only head to Newgrounds and play Final Slam II there for free. The only real difference between the paid version on Steam and the free version is the full Story mode, a Season mode and more custom fighter slots.
You can find much better fighting games on Steam. Not recommended.

I'm on my fifth playthrough right now and so thoroughly over the game I have to review it negatively.
Sure, Frankenstein manages a good sort of a story and the puzzles are not your usual artifex-mundi-esque stuff. However, while at least in the hard mode the puzzles seem complex on the first glance, they are extremely easy to solve.
The atmosphere and 'feel' of the game is generally good. The weaker moments are thanks to cutscenes that don't really add anything to the story nor atmosphere and two notable failures in representing the era (VW Beetle and a plane).
The game's biggest failings come from the design. Playing this requires constant back-and-forth. You move 4 screens forward, the same 4 back, same 4 forward in quick succession. Nothing seems to be in the same or the next room. All the locks (and there are plenty) are in the 'find an item that fits here' style, usually requiring three such items. When you're looking for 4 sets of 3 random badges, it's not fun. The UI gets constantly in the way, especially in the HOS where it is not uncommon to have items under the UI buttons (like the hint button!). I like that you have an inventory full of stuff, but I have to question the design choices when you have 4 items with a blade but need to find a fifth to cut something.
On top of all that you get a lot of bugs and glitches. F.e. the HOS have nice little minigames, but on two separate playthroughs they have glitched in a way that I could not proceed forcing a restart of the whole game.
If I weren't an obsessive completionist, I would have given up on this game at least three playthrough attempts ago.

To review this game is to review it in two parts.
: An amazing adventure akin to the days of Secret of Mana, Sword of Mana and Seiken Densetsu 3. Quick swordplay with an oldschool-meets-polish aesthetic that's filled with charm. Combat is quick paced and - with over 20 skills and spells with multiple charge levels, along with 30 talents - more or less unique for every character made. Every attack, skill and spell feels as if it has weight behind it for a thoroughly satisfying brawl through hordes of monsters and challenging bosses.
The story is serious at times, tongue in cheek in others without outright resorting to cheese. There's plenty of side-quests, mini-games and collectables, but contrary to the name no grinding appears to be necessary. The shield is as relevant to the gameplay as the sword is, every attack can be blocked if you know the exact timing, reminding me of the days of 'Timed Hits' from Super Mario RPG and Final Fantasy 8.
The music is beautiful, the characters well written to make you love or hate them, I can't say enough good things about Story Mode. The only shame is it's incomplete, but between pet taming, treasure hunting, fishing, card collecting, playing with 4 player online co-op and duking it out in the arena, there's more than enough content to keep me busy between updates.
: All the rules from Story Mode no longer apply, Arcade Mode feels like an entirely different game. Less Secret of Mana, more Binding of Isaac. You start in an empty plain and delve within a randomized roguelike-esque labyrinth. Each room is different every time, filled with traps and all manners of enemies or bosses not present in Story Mode. HP is precious, mastery of skills, spells and shielding is required.
Arcade Mode is perfect for sinking endless hours into as you try to go deeper and deeper into the labyrinth, gaining points and essence to level up and expand your town, unlock new NPCs to aid you, take on quests for rare and unique loot not found anywhere else. Skills and spells are best experimented with in here to see which build suits you best. With friends it's harder, but with 4 people on screen the monsters barely stand a chance once you hit your groove. The online leaderboards for Arcade Mode help to give it even more replay value by trying to do better than your friends or complete strangers to try and hit #1.
If you have any doubts whatsoever, try the demo. With an hour of Story Mode gameplay, several hours of Arcade Mode and co-op bundled into the demo, it's a great teaser for what to expect moving forward.
: Opt into 'Frontline' by selecting SoG in your library if you want quicker updates. The normal version receives slower updates, but your experience in the game will be much smoother.

+ Enemy variety forces you to change tactics.
Cons:
- "Avoid/destroy enviornmental lights, they hurt you" gets old and dissorienting really quickly. Your screen is often blurred trying to find a light to shoot, disabiling your darkness powers and letting enemies tear you apart while it happens.
- The mafia tone to the story is horridly stereotypical. Good thing it shifts to the supernatural pretty quickly.
- Some enemies are annoying or blatantly unfair. Flashbang throwers, whip-carriers that steal your guns, shield carriers.
- Some actions can conflict due to the same button being used for them. The E key eats enemy's hearts to replishing your HP, but also picks up guns. I've swapped plenty of guns on accident and died because I didn't get my health pickup.
- Too short. Main campaign took me 5 hours on second hardest difficulty.
- "Vendetta" missions do not use Jackie. They're co-op missions with a new crew of marauders, but you'll miss a lot of Jackie's abilities.
^ Cons are nit-picky for the most part, but some really tear you out from the action too much. This game is worth buying if just for the main campaign alone, but know how short it is. Too unique and too fun to dismiss.

First of all, your search for the ultimate car game/simulator ends RIGHT HERE and RIGHT NOW.
I'm serious. No other simulator in history has ever been as realistic as BeamNG.drive. In fact, once this sim gets popular, it could even be used in driving schools! The cars handle, perform, and DEform EXACTLY like their real life counterparts. Behind each car is a revolutionary system of nodes and beams that calculates the deformation of the car's body at 2000 times a second! Not only that, but the windows crack and shatter, and pretty much every part from the headlights to the tailpipes to the fenders to the engine can break off like they would in real life.
This is a long, in-depth review, to give you the best idea of what this is.
This is an awesome simulator! You can do anything you want with cars, trucks, boats, planes, and drive/fly them as well as smash them, crash them, and drop boulders on them (Yes, I'm not kidding). There are also numerous props you can play with such as a car shredder (two rollers close together that you can drive through) and many others in the official game. There is even a fidget spinner mod that you can DESTROY cars with. And, if you want you can put that 3 foot tall spoiler on your old Honda! The base game comes with 13 maps (aka terrains) to explore, and they range from 1 square kilometer to 4 square kilometers (there is a 16 square kilometer map coming). The developers do, however make them seem much bigger despite their real size. There is also an infinite grid map which is completely flat and empty and the ground is nothing more than a grid. In addition, there are maps created by the community that can be as big as ~350 square kilometers. Once BeamNG's engine gets optimized to the point we can have open world maps, we will start seeing even larger maps.
Here are the vehicles included with BeamNG.
Also in the base game are 20 fictional vehicles (as of last review update) based off of real-life vehicles, which are FULLY customizable in almost every aspect. In addition to in-depth customization, you also get about 10 preset configurations (trims) for every car. You can choose the one you like the most and then add/remove/change the parts on that trim to make it JUST the way you want. Here is the vehicle list:
Anyway, enough about the content. Let's get into the gameplay and physics.
Although for now there is no Career mode, this simulator is still very fun to play. There are scenarios, and they are usually coordinated time trials on a specific course on a specific terrain. Sometimes it is just for fun, like jumping a van off a ramp and landing unscathed.
And the physics, they will not get any better than this. BeamNG is the most realistic and detailed vehicle simulator to date. It simulates the behavior of vehicles from the glass breaking to the hubcaps falling off to the engine block melting. BeamNG uses a unique system for ultra-realistic vehicle behavior that yields a unique gaming experience each time. It uses beams (BEAMng) and nodes to simulate each and every part independently. The nodes connect all of the thousands of beams together, and the beams can deform, bend, and break. There are no predefined damage models. The node and beam system calculates the damage on any one section of the car. For example, if you slide past a wall in a Need For Speed game, with the front facing it slightly more than the back, the windows will probably shatter and then there will be paint scratches on random places of the car. Let's slide past that same wall in BeamNG. The mirror fell off and there is a dent in the front bumper EXACTLY where the car contacted the wall. Also a hubcap most likely fell off if the car had plastic rims.
If all that isn't enough, there is a big community on the BeamNG forums cranking out mods frequently. There are well over 200 vehicles/vehicle mods to download and well over 200 extra maps to download from the mod repository alone.
And, finally, let's talk customization. Let's take the D-15 for example. For this single vehicle, you can customize the paint job (color/decals), the tow hitch, the type of engine (I6 or 2 tiers of V8s), supercharger, lights, color, bumper type and color, suspension, body, and even the light bar to name a few. So the bottom line is, this game offers more customization options than any other driving game currently on the market. Even NFS Underground 2.
Also, in the 0.10 update, each kind of engine (inline 4, v6, etc) has its own sound!
I hope this review was helpful to any new BeamNG players. Enjoy this wonderful game!

I honestly felt as though I could have written this review within the first few minutes of playing this game, but ultimately I decided to wait. There is just something so attractive about games that give you solid fundementals (a fun metaphor for mechanics). The thing that makes games like GTA fun isn't the fact that you can do "anything" (within the confines of that game), but rather that the developers have spent the time, effort and resources to create consistent fundementals for which the game is based around that make the limitations of "anything" seem far more distant. Make a cutscene where a car crashes realistically and you'll keep me interested for a minute; create the fundementals for such scenarios to occur naturally as a consistent part of the game and I could spend years coming up with different things to do.
BeamNG doesn't use any flashy storylines, characters or Hollywood pizazz to keep you playing. In reality the vanilla game doesn't even really offer that much content. What BeamNG does do however is provide you with some of the most (if not the most) realistic softbody physics (fundementals) to ever grace this unworthy earth. If a games' appeal and playability is a combination of the number of items, areas and things to do in the game then most games simply add up these values. BeamNG, on the other hand, takes the factorial of each number and multiples them together. If you decided to add mods then get ready for some really complex infinite series as the sum never converges and neither does the amount of things to do in the game.
I don't think I will ever run out of fun things to do in this game, the developers are constantly rolling out new updates and the mod community is out of this world. If you thought Rigs of Rods was the be all and end all of softbody physics, wait till you see what is has grown up to become. Cannot praise this game enough 10/10.

I have played this game since the early stages of development, and all I got to say is that it only got worse, and worse.
Pros
- Lots of chances to micro manage things.
- LOTS of loot to sort through, makes you feel rich.
- Good variation of classes to build parties from
- Sems to be a lot of content to go through (though you will have to repeat some things)
Cons
- Not a very good UI.  You have to click to access and exit everything.  Hitting esc will only cause problems trying to clear your screen.  Can be confusing when youre trying to leave a shop that doesnt have a door or when an NPC's hit box is bugged out.
- Dungeons can be long and boring.  Some groups of mobs ahve taken me over 5 mins to kill because they dont seem to run out of energy, so they all heal one another over and over and over.
- Your own kingdom doesnt seem to matter aside from a passive bonus here and there.
- Remember the micro management and loot?  You can have up to 48 heroes.  You need to personally gear, choose stats, and skills for all of them.  Every time they level, or they can't do anything new.
- Loot is unfortunately randomized with no way to salvage it.  Example, scepters are cleric only, cleric wants wisdom, focus, maybe consitution.  You can roll a Mythic sceptre with strength, intellect, and dexterity.  The salvage and crafting system has felt really lack luster too so far unfortunately.

This is not a perfect game. I'm leaning towards recommending it for fans of shooters who like sniping things. There is an element of stealth in the game as well, and experienced stealth players will likely end up breaking some necks and headshotting with the Welrod. However, do not expect this to be a Hitman-esque assassination game because it isn't. You will not be able to remain hidden. Sometimes you'll just have to make some noise and spray with your Tommy Gun. It isn't even a choice at times.
I do not like multiplayer shooters. This review only covers the singleplayer portion of the game.
-------------------------------------
-------------------------------------
► Control- Gameplay- Graphics- and Audio options are adequate for a PC game.
► Mouse smoothing and acceleration can be disabled and unfiltered mouse input is very precise.
► You have holds and toggles for various actions like aiming, holding your breath and using your binoculars.
► Ingame field of view is wide enough for a desktop PC.
► The game's controls are smooth and responsive for the most part.
► Features that might annoy people, such as the constant slow-mo bullet cam for kills, or motion blur can be disabled.
► Weapons use different ammo. You can't just refill your Tommy Gun's .45 ACP magazine with 9x19mm from an MP40 or 7.62x25mm from a PPsH.
► German characters speak German and Russian Characters speak Russian. Player can turn on subtitles to understand them.
► The game has pointless collectibles scattered throughout the levels, but fortunately nothing is locked behind collecting them.
► Crouch isn't insta-stealth and standing up isn't insta-detection. As long as you move quietly out of sight, you can stay undetected even upright.
▼ Restrictive tutorial locks you out of basic gameplay functions to teach you specific things. It doesn't reflect real gameplay, and doesn't even give the player the proper opportunity to practice shooting.
▼ Some contextual controls cause issues. Searching bodies for supplies and switching your weapon for something on the ground is bound to the same key.
▼ Levels are way too linear and basically have just one way of completing them. The player is funneled past a few easy stealth sections into situations where the only option is to get into a firefight and kill everyone to proceed down the narrow corridors of streets.
▼ Bullet drop is insanely exaggerated. Probably caused by the smallish levels. Also, there could have been a practice level that would allow the player to associate the leading of a shot with distances, movements, and altitude differences.
▼ The noise cover that allows the player to snipe in silence is inconsistent. For example, a church bell or an explosion can completely obscure a nearby .30-06 gunshot, but a loud alarm combined with a battery of AA fire can't conceal footsteps.
▼ Sniper enemies are supernaturally perceptive at extreme ranges even though they're not looking through their scopes when casually guarding their positions.
▼ In some situations, sniper enemies can instantly detect you through completely opaque obstacles, like a thick cloud of smoke, through which the player has no chance of seeing.
▼ Over-the-shoulder camera angle obscures one side of the screen, and aiming exacerbates the problem. This can lead to situations where the player can't shoot an attacking enemy even when standing directly in his line of sight. A third person camera should be situated behind the character, like in Max Payne or Hitman.
▼ The player's health regeneration is too fast for a game where combat is not the primary focus. However the shortcomings of the level design seem to require the player to have a system to survive against insurmountable odds.
▼ Despite the game's decent ballistics, bullets have no penetration through walls. You can however shoot through multiple enemies.
▼ Volume settings do not affect intro splash movie. RIP headphone users.
▲ It's a war game with a basic set of missions where your objective is to help your side win. There is no contrived dramatic storytelling with deep characters or love interests. Despite its linearity, in its core it's a game, not a movie.
▲ The slow-motion x-ray bullet cam is fantastic and gory, and seeing skulls and jaws being shattered, with mangled bullets popping through exploding eyeballs, tumbling through the air with a stream of arterial spray... it basically never gets old. It's the absolute highlight of this game.
▲ Several specific parts of levels are pretty clever and let you experiment with different covert tactics. Heavy bombardment, ringing church bells or thunder clapping help you make your shots without raising the alarm.
▲ Instead of a modern tedious upgrade system, your character periodically picks up a better sniper rifle to use for his missions.
▲ Your SMG is a last-resort short range combat weapon for dealing with immediate threats and your silent side-arm is a bolt-action inaccurate piece of garbage. You have no perfect universal weapon. You need to git gud and be careful with everything you do.
TL;DR: If you want shooting, this is for you. If you want sneaking, perhaps not so much. Just a little. The game doesn't have much to it but what it does works pretty well.

Supergiant has successfully created a game where it is extremely difficult to tell what the optimal playstyle is.  The gameplay is so unique that past gaming experience does not confer much advantage. Further adding to the puzzle is the sheer number combinations of teams that can specialize in wildly different ways.  Pyre is an exceedingly complex and deep game if you take the time to master its systems, yet is also very approachable.
Such potential for strategy in a game can be wasted if the AI does not utilize it well.  Thankfully, the AI is quite superb for most of the game.  On the hardest difficulties, the computer is quick to punish player mistakes and take advantage of openings.  There are only a few isolated instances which the AI was obviously not programmed to deal with well (namely, the lava map with environmental hazards, and the Sap character type), and it ends up making very strange or poor decisions.  Overall, for Supergiant's first attempt at creating a real opponent AI, their work is largely commendable.
Lastly, whether the game be too difficult or easy for you, there are a plethora of difficulty modifiers for you to choose from, either in the campaign or to even the scales between you and your Pyremates.  Supergiant has always excelled in their modular difficulty options, and Pyre fares just as well as Transistor in this regard.  Difficulty for supergiant is never about bland number changes, but rather about changing the way that game plays, introducing greater complexity and challenge.

Great simulation of early warplanes.
Graphics and sounds are good.
Flight model and aircraft simulation are very accurate and detailed.
There is plenty of variation and things to do and there are multiple customization options for planes.
Multiplayer especially has very cool features such as sharing same aircraft: a friend can be the gunner while you are flying the plane. Especially with the Felixstowe "flying boat" you take off from water, have buddies as gunners while going on a bombing missions: there really are very few simulation supporting that kind of interaction.
Keep in mind that these planes are not easy to fly, especially not in combat.
The engines are not powerful and amount of lift from the rudimentary wings is not a lot.
Simulation is accurate representation of the early era of flight and for people interesting in flying biplanes this definitely is worth it to buy.
So keep above points in mind when deciding if this is for you.
Recommended for fans of WWI planes and flight sim fans in general.

Probably my favorite game as a kid was Knights of the Sky, a WW1 flight sim on DOS. I played that game for hours on end, day after day. Nothing like flying around and dueling with enemies in three dimentions. Getting within 50 meters trying to put a hole in their engine. Great times. RoF comes back to the awesomeness of those deadly duels above the trenches of WW1, and does it modern justice with awesome flight models that take realistic damage, and great physics to the point where flying in 10m/s winds is a hell of a chore.
Although the game gets exponentially more fun the more realistic you set the simulation, you can simplify the physics to make things like wind no longer a factor, and you can add gauges to your hud which will also tell you the limits you can push your plane at the current moment, and finally you can add icons so you don't have to manually spot the planes against the horizon or down over the trenches. This can be exceptionally useful for new players to the flight sim genre, expecially of the hardcore WW1 variety. There is a reason there's the saying "any landing you can walk away from is a good landing".
There are currently about 30 different airplanes (almost a 50/50 split, but the Entente do have a handle more to choose from). Most of the planes fly completely differently, its usually not just "oh the Fokker D.VII is all around better than the Fokker Dr.1". The D.VII might be more of a standard all around fighter with fairly high specs, while the Dr.1 tends to buck like a horse at the rodeo. But in the hands of an Ace the Dr.1 can be a terrifying aircraft. Werner Voss took on 7 S.E.5a planes on his own with a Dr.1 shooting down two and damaging all of the other five. There are some vast differences in how each plane flies, giving each easily 100 hours of replayability if not more.
One of the biggest attractions of this game is the career mode, which given WW1's unique setting of largely unchanging front lines allows for random missions for your fictional pilot to fly, rather than pre-scripted storyline missions like most WW2 flying sims. Getting random missions to patrol behind enemy lines, scramble to intercept recon/bomber planes, attacking balloons, etc. just helps keep the game fresh as you fly your pilot into the history books trying to catch up to Richthofen's score. Take it from me, I've played 100 hours and I haven't even tackled the other half of the game yet, multiplayer.
I can't really review multiplayer as I haven't played it at all yet. But watching some videos, it's not just shoot down enemy planes. Rather you have objectives, photograph facilities, bomb tanks, destroy AI flights, etc. to earn points to bring victory to your side; all the while keeping your eyes to sky, watching for other players who are much better pilots than the AI and who are ready to swoop down on you.
To get all of the dlc, it costs quite a pretty penny. But it is so worth it in my opinion. There is nothing like starting up another mission in your career, climbing up to 2km, spotting an enemy a kilometer below you and swooping down on them, hoping you don't destroy your engine in the process or rip off you own wings coming out of your dive. This game runs the gamut from relaxing flight among the clouds to adrenaline pumping dog fights were you don't even know if your pilot is gonna live to keep flying. If you have any interest in dogfighting, this is hands down the best game on market for it.

Some times when using an item set to open a puzzle specifically, the sound effects audio would ignore your audio settings. Minor annoyance, but becareful if you use a headset. I also have an achievement that wont give credit (for watching all cutscenes and dialogue), but I havent tried playing again to earn it.
Overall, Id recommend it. Item set collecting got old after awhile, with a couple minor bugs, but the story was more than good enough to keep going to the end.

To review this game is to review it in two parts.
: An amazing adventure akin to the days of Secret of Mana, Sword of Mana and Seiken Densetsu 3. Quick swordplay with an oldschool-meets-polish aesthetic that's filled with charm. Combat is quick paced and - with over 20 skills and spells with multiple charge levels, along with 30 talents - more or less unique for every character made. Every attack, skill and spell feels as if it has weight behind it for a thoroughly satisfying brawl through hordes of monsters and challenging bosses.
The story is serious at times, tongue in cheek in others without outright resorting to cheese. There's plenty of side-quests, mini-games and collectables, but contrary to the name no grinding appears to be necessary. The shield is as relevant to the gameplay as the sword is, every attack can be blocked if you know the exact timing, reminding me of the days of 'Timed Hits' from Super Mario RPG and Final Fantasy 8.
The music is beautiful, the characters well written to make you love or hate them, I can't say enough good things about Story Mode. The only shame is it's incomplete, but between pet taming, treasure hunting, fishing, card collecting, playing with 4 player online co-op and duking it out in the arena, there's more than enough content to keep me busy between updates.
: All the rules from Story Mode no longer apply, Arcade Mode feels like an entirely different game. Less Secret of Mana, more Binding of Isaac. You start in an empty plain and delve within a randomized roguelike-esque labyrinth. Each room is different every time, filled with traps and all manners of enemies or bosses not present in Story Mode. HP is precious, mastery of skills, spells and shielding is required.
Arcade Mode is perfect for sinking endless hours into as you try to go deeper and deeper into the labyrinth, gaining points and essence to level up and expand your town, unlock new NPCs to aid you, take on quests for rare and unique loot not found anywhere else. Skills and spells are best experimented with in here to see which build suits you best. With friends it's harder, but with 4 people on screen the monsters barely stand a chance once you hit your groove. The online leaderboards for Arcade Mode help to give it even more replay value by trying to do better than your friends or complete strangers to try and hit #1.
If you have any doubts whatsoever, try the demo. With an hour of Story Mode gameplay, several hours of Arcade Mode and co-op bundled into the demo, it's a great teaser for what to expect moving forward.
: Opt into 'Frontline' by selecting SoG in your library if you want quicker updates. The normal version receives slower updates, but your experience in the game will be much smoother.

Pyre is an excellent and unique game from Supergiant with an awesome story and characters to hold the game together.
Pyre is a mixture of a text based adventure game and sports game. In it you have a pilgrim style quest to gain freedom from the downside and must take 3 of 8 characters into a match against other pilgrims for the chance of freedom.
The game involves taking a star and either throwing or sacrificing a character with the ball into the opponents pyre and the game is won when the other team has lost all there hit points.  Players can be banished for a short time by stepping into a other players presence which can be fired at the opponents but cannot be used when the player holds the star and when you sacrifice yourself to the other users pyre you are banished until someone else has scored.
Ultimately this is a fun if simple gameplay which makes up a large portion of the game. Each of the different characters have a different setup and play style although I felt that the characters weren't created equally and usually preferred using the faster characters over the slow ones. Still each character has they uses and the story actively encourages using all your characters.
The biggest straight of this game is the characters. Each has their unique back story, motives and wants and each have their own relationships and clashes with all other characters whom you encounter including other pilgrim teams. The game also has a great reversal of the team sacrifice. Normally when you lose a team mate it is due to death but in this case it is due to the character achieving freedom but it also means losing them. Ultimately it is the character who stay who are making the sacrifice especially when it becomes obvious later on that not everyone is making it out of the downside.
The story is pretty well built but takes second stage to the characters and acts more of a back drop to progress the characters through there development and relationships. That's not a big problem as the characters are the best part of the game. Never the less I wish that they continued with the pilgrimage travelling which you do in the first cycle of the rite where the next few rights were travelled through using a balloon.
As always the artistic style of this game is beautiful with a great mixture of colour and a mesmerizing soundtrack it is well worth a listen to as a separate entity.
Ultimately Pyre is a beautiful and unique game from supergiant which I'd highly recommend anyone to play.

Survarium seems like an interesting game. With long rounds, intense and often brutal combat and extremely long waiting times, it is something good but not quite great.
Match making takes roughly 3-7 minutes a pop (in my experience), often resulting in me growing bored and leaving. For someone who has done a grand total of three matches so far, that isn't a way to keep me playing.
Graphics are good, in my opinion. Nothing state of the art, but my eyes don't bleed and they seem rather pleasing to the eye. The fidelity helps, especially on the larger maps, because of flora cover and all that.
Combat is also quite fast paced in the regards that a single round can put you down. Using a Mosin Nagant, you can take out most people - including those armed with SMGs - faster than they can take you out. Weapons are loud, have recoil and feel somewhat like guns. Not exactly Red Orchestra, but luckily not Counterstrike either.
The game also seems to have an extensive store. You can purchase a lot with real money - and I mean a lot. But from what I've seen, all purchases seem to be a case of 'skip the fun' or 'skip the grind' or whatever you want to call it. Custom weapons are hardly OP uber death lasers, especially when the starting weapons already are.
Matches also take a damn long time. You can wait nearly ten minutes to get into a match, then the match itself will last ten minutes or more. Very few players fighting, yet the number of kills or points require to win often imitate what you'd expect of much larger matches with many more players.
So yeah, game is interesting. It's balanced and premium players don't get a gameplay advantage, so to speak. You pay if you want your character to look 'cooler' or you just want to max out your character with little grinding.
But as I said, matchmaking is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥ It's slow and takes a long time to find a game. You can sit in the queue with (apparently) 500 odd other players, yet no is found for a long while. At least it's free - if I paid so much as a single penny for it, I wouldn't be happy because it is virtually unplayable.

DOOM is often credited as the best game ever made. This is true. But, true on a deeper level than usually discussed. DOOM itself was a groundbreaking game in its day. If nothing more was done than releasing the game, that alone would have forever secured it in the pages of computer gaming history forever.
What is less often noted in reviews of DOOM is that it’s so much more than just a single game. ID Software intended DOOM to be able to be modded from the beginning. That’s why it’s WAD files are designed as they are. So that resources could be replaced and the game could be ever-expanded.
More than that, once the commercial viability of DOOM had ran its course, the source code to the engine itself was liberated under the GNU GPL; making it Free Software. Everyone who knew how to code could now tare into the very heart and soul of the software that brought DOOM to life and make it into whatever they wanted it to be.
In doing this, ID Software had made DOOM eternal. More than just swapping out map layouts, audio, and visuals; people could mod the very engine itself; as well as eventually write mods for the engine to run within the game. This was made possible because people could mod the engine. They were able to implement a scripting language within DOOM that modders could then use to add things like new enemies, weapons, and much, much more.
What this all means is that when you step into the esteemed halls of DOOM, you’re not just getting a game. You’re getting so much more. You’re getting full access to an entire engine. Couple that with the Free Software programs that have been made to edit DOOM; and you have a full software development suit.
The DOOM modding community is alive and well. It creates amazing game after game. Note I said games, not just levels or mere mods. All sorts of games. It’s been nearly twenty four years and I am still finding entire games people have created for the DOOM engine. Some new, some old; all fun.
There are people who have made it their passion to mod DOOM. They try every idea imaginable for the first person shooter genre and beyond. It is a development platform that has a massive array and tools and community support. Never have I seen a more accessible entry into making your own game in 3D space.
And, if you used only your own content, the game is yours; as the license does give you that. GPL work can be sold for a profit legally. (Note, the original DOOM wad files can not be used in this way. You have to make your own stuff or start off with the FREEDOOM wad files.)
All that said, DOOM is more than a game. It is a platform of limitless potential to the budding map maker, coder, and modder. It is the definition of ease of access, yet the very wellspring of the experimental in gaming.
Time and time again, I have seen DOOM mods that I have enjoyed more than AAA releases. I have also seen DOOM mods that have re-made AAA releases with better game play.
I will describe just a small smattering of what can be done with DOOM.
Want to play something new forever? Why not try Oblige? It’s a Free Software program that uses procedural generation to create new levels for DOOM. With this program, you’ll always have more maps to play.
Try Slade and Doom Builder to create your own maps manually. They are detailed level design tools that allow for editing in 2D and 3D. Slade can edit far more than just maps.
Want to explore deep learning? There is a DOOM engine plugin for creating Bots to play DOOM. There is even a competition that you can enter; both are called ViZDoom.
Want a great arcade shooter? Try Reelism Gold. Every game is a slot machine that rolls three mods and you try to get the most points before you die.
Want to play a bloody gory DOOM with new weapons, vehicles, and new demon attacks? Try BRUTAL DOOM.
This is the value of liberating a game engine under the GNU GPL. It allows the community to rally behind the game and make it into so much more than just one game. It allows people to make the software their own and truly make new, revolutionary, and fun things with it.
I often wonder why more of the game industry hasn’t fallowed the ID Software model. Proprietary first, then Free Software once the commercial value of the engine has ran its course. It’s the ethical thing to do. It wasn’t just the technological leaps forward that made these engines and these games so valuable to the public. It was that ID Software gave these innovations to the public. In so doing, they changed the way the public saw the software they gamed with. Software was no longer a black box that just made the game work. Software was now an open door to creativity that a community could bond together over. That’s what made ID Software games so special; more than anything else.
I also wait, in hope, that ID Software itself will continue to fallow this model. We’re still waiting for the ID Tech 5 release under the GNU GPL.
That said, ID Software has no one there that originally started the company; and Carmack was known for really pushing for the source code releases under the GNU GPL. Many have told me that with him gone; we’ll likely never see another source code release from ID. I don’t want to agree with them too quickly. But, I think they’re likely right. Were the source code releases ID’s tradition, or Carmack’s tradition? Only time will tell.
I hope ID keeps this tradition. I also hope other software development companions fallow this model. That said, we’ll always have DOOM. The original DOOM. Which, twenty four years later, is still alive and well with its modding community. A truly infinite game that is forever growing.

I usually don't really like horror-themed games that much, nor do I really write any reviews to the games I played, but as one of my friends suggested me to try it out, I did, and I really think this game is more than worth a review.
Never before made me a game think about life itself that much. The story was superb, the atmosphere dark, yet very varied. Even though there weren't many "enemies" in this game, you still felt like someone would always follow you, every step you take. I think I've never been more focused in a game than before, I didn't want to stop playing. Once you start with this game, you'll want to finish it in one go (which could indeed be possible given the lengh of the story). But what impressed me most about this game, was that you didn't have to "run through it". There are many open rooms you can go in and explore, open drawers, look into the bins... Every room in the game tells it's own story, and I could've just stood in a room, looking around for an hour, thinking about what might have happened here.
Another great thing is, that the soryline actually suprised me like every time something happened. This is not a game where you know or can guess what'll happen. This is how a game should be!
To sum it up: This game is a piece of art. It's what I'd call "a perfect game". As many other reviews already said, the Music is great, the visuals are great, and the story will make you cry and keep your mind occupied for the next few days. The only thing I'd like to see the next time is a longer story. But I prefer quality over quantity so I'm fine with how it is.

This is the best Dungeon-Keeper-style game since the original! Set in a world reminiscent of a 1970's James Bond and all its comical evil personalities (with maybe the cartoony touch of The Incredibles thrown in), and this time YOU'RE THE VILLIAN.
Construct your island's evil base a la Dungeon Keeper with well-designed and very comical traps and torture devices (nothing even PG-13 here if you're concerned about violence/gore). To reiterate for those unfamiliar with Dungeon Keeper: this is a base-design game. It's about minion management and base construction, done better than any other game I've played.
Attention to detail is great; game mechanics are great; everything in the game has a great personality, down to your hordes of your minions (the animations are par excellence). The graphics are "dated" but there's been a recent resurgence of cartoony retro-style game art themes, as such this could easily pose as a new gorgeous indie release.
Bottom line: if you enjoy this genre even a bit, you will enjoy it more than ever with this game.

I was directed here by the lead artist, and gave him some advice on what to improve.
He was friendly. Jonesjones or something?
Anyways, back on topic.
I'll give this game a moderate score. Nothing negative I wouldn't expect, you know? Nothing ground-breaking, and not fully developed like Depth, but it's a start.
First topic, first impression.
I started out with a random lobby, because I didn't mind where it began. Within seconds, I was in a lobby. Brownie point.
So I see the sharks, minding their own business. It was a Great White, actually. To be honest... It was intimidating, yes, but not spooky like snorkelling chills I usually get when I'm next to a trash can of teeth and death. It just lumbered around aimlessly, even when I shot it. It was like punching one of those aluminum baloons in wal-mart; it's attack was so slow that there was absolutely no way it could deal damage. I knifed it to death with jonesjones watching lol.
Then I see that someone died, and checked out the game size. It was just the two of us, plus jones. Jones basically just popping around here and there like anyone would do in their own made world. I felt a ping of envy there.
"Deathmatch" seemed so unfair due to the fact there's a gattling gun box sitting in the open that can be defended easily by a guy with a gattling gun. I felt bad for the other player, so I just stopped the massacre and declared a truce. He obliged, then we just jammed out to "Ocean Man" while pretending we were riding the ♥♥♥♥ing great white.
I mentioned it to jones that the AI needed improvement, and reccommended he play "Stranded Deep" to get that creepy vibe that game gave you when you were being stalked. He said he'd check it out.  I also mentioned that there isn't a "turn your head, then your spear follows you" type thing you would be more likely to do, but I'm sure they may implement that later?  Also, a panicked reloading animation would be nice.  I just imagine the diver swinging his head around to view the environment before even having the gun near ready to shoot, then take like 3 seconds to actually prep a decent shot.
He left immediately after, so I left as well. I checked out all the lobbies, and it turned out that the other guy and I were the only players on. Nobody is playing this game? That sucks. Reviews seem decent.
So I decided to take his advice and play "Survival."
This is where I could see the negative sides of the AI, big time.
First one I noticed were no indications of where things were. I panicked trying to find the ammo box.
Secondly, the sharks don't have a sense of tactics. They just lumber in circles around you until they hope to catch you by surprise, which includes basically swimming slowly and biting too soon, which causes you to just Disney bounce off of their nose. I may have played with that for a few minutes.
Thirdly. Makos are pretty much the only thing that make me check my surroundings, since they just charge you head on.
Fourth, the sharks don't follow you that easily. For a guy wearing flippers, you are RIDICULOUSLY fast, faster than anything in the game I've crossed. I mean, I've fed makos, and those f*ckers can disappear with your arm before you know what time it is.

Another "Shark vs Human" catagory. After playing for a few minutes, I can already tell there isn't much point of revisiting this one. Fairly one sided gameplay with the scales being tipped in favor of the predators far too much.
As for realism this game has beautiful graphics (while you can look around before dying at the hands of or should I say 'teeth' of some player controled terminator with fins.)
Sharks of different species unrealistically pack together. Such as blacktip and great whites. With how much damage it takes to kill one shark you start wondering if they found a sunken ship that had both Quad Damage, and the Invulnerability sphere.
The lack of an effective startup weapon only leaves me to believe that every diver in the game is psychotic. Better to have made a game about hunting lions with a olive fork.
Before you say "You can get other weapons" yes, there are other weapons you can pick up, but, only if you can get to them before losing an appendage to serrated teeth or the air in your supply ("'tank'? Might as well be a inflated trash bag with a straw.) running out in three to four minutes.
No spectator mode so you can't get a sense of how to play before offering yourself up as chum. Single player has no real goal except to survive as long as possible before dying either from lack of air or being "Murdered by a shark, although it's not really "murder". Maybe you'll actually get to kill a great white before running so low on ammo you can't kill a sea slug with whats left.
Overall this game looks great but needs ALOT of work. I wouldn't suggest buying it unless it's on sale or that they patch it to even out the game play.
Of course this is just my opinion. Yu may buy it anyway and think it's great, but it's your risk.

Although, I have only played this game for around 5 hours, (I definitely plan on playing more) I can already say that i would recommend it to almost anyone that has a PC that is able to run it.
Being able to see a small, big, fast, or slow car smash into another vehicle or maybe just a wall, and then having the ability to rewind time and watch all the chaos in slow-motion, is nothing but pure satisfaction and happiness in my opinion.
Although destruction is definitely one of this game’s strong points, it isn't the only thing that makes this game so great.
There are many, many mods that you can choose between, including; Vehicle mods, Maps, Graphics mods and more.
Once you have found a car, modded or not, you can choose a map from around the world or in a fictional place that you want to drive around in, and let me tell you. There are very few things as relaxing as taking a maybe 15 min break from everything and just driving around in your rally car, race car, truck, van, whatever. Just the relaxing and fun experience of taking a drive on the roads of nature or somewhere else is absolutely something this game has nailed. You don't have to worry about missions or anything. Just. Drive.
Then there are also missions if you're the type that wants a bit more action. There are many different missions or as it is called in the game; Scenarios.
Scenarios are different types of short or long, missions that you can choose to do. Some of these missions are easy and some of them are tough. Some of them take a long time to complete and some of them can be done in under a minute. Ex. The police chases. You play as a cop car, and you have to drive fast, and use your driving abilities to maneuver the roads, catch up with, and stop the "villain" before he gets to his target. These missions are relatively easy and can be done in under a minute, most of the time.
Then you have the campaign.
Now, I haven't played the campaign a lot so I can't really tell you lots about it, but if I’m correct, it is very similar to free roam, in the sense that you can drive wherever you want, and do what you want. The difference is that in campaign, there will be big, glowing circles placed around the map, for you to park in and start a mission. When you start a mission a cutscene will appear (Which you can skip if you want) and then you will be able to start playing. Since I have only played the campaign for a very short time, that is mostly what i know about it, but I recommend you to buy the game and see for yourself what it's all about.

Just so I'm clear, this game wasn't horrible.
It wasn't bad...It was decent. I'm normally very easily pleased with games like these but this one wasn't all that great.
Pros: I loved the cutscenes. They were very well animated, the sound effects were great, and the voice acting was alright.
The art style in the game was very well done. Visually, the game was eery, and while daytime atmospheres don't really work well with me in a horror style game, this one actually had me spooked quite a bit.
Cons: First of all, the music was very unsettling to me. Throughout the entire game there was this jarring music that never settled even the most peaceful areas of the game. The game sound effects were average and the hint button didn't always help both in visuals and in direction (which is an odd thing to critique but it still bugged me).
The puzzles led me back and forth everywhere. While I liked the concept of being able to use the same item multiple times (because in other games it never made sense to me to find a useful item and then discard it after one use), I hated the idea of having to go to multiple spots all over the game. The puzzles themselves were easy but not really worth solving since whenever one puzzle/key item opens up something, I just get another item to either complete a set or to open up another area with yet again another collectible to find. Most of the objects I'm looking for are just keys and others are missing items/items that make no sense realistically.
There are also quite a few glitches in the game, and one that struck me in particular was the one toward the end where I was able to go into the basement without even unlocking it and it confused me royally.
Excluding the finding keys/items and going back and forth throughout the game looking for generally the same thing, the few puzzles that make actually make sense in the game make it a very short game. The cutscenes were very worth it, but the gameplay....not so much. It would have made a very good short film, though.

Goodness this was unexpected! Stealth Inc 2 is a sequel that does a great job standing on its own two stubby feet and distancing itself from its predescesor. But loses a bit of its identity (slightly) in the process.
To start, Stealth Inc 2 (or Sneaky ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ 2 if you want to call it that) mirrors the beginning of the original but adds a few twists along the way. Soon enough you're loose in the killer facility to do whatever little stubby clones do. The relationship between your cloned companion and your caretaker who was prideful enough to unleash you in the first place mirrors that of Chell against GLaDOS from Portal, but goes on a bit longer to great effect. And for the most part this drives the game as he conspires against you, providing a number of the game's challenges (and again, great dialogue, not as hillarious but still filled with snark and a ton of fun).
In a number of twists, Stealth Inc 2 is seperated between test chambers and exploring the facility. In test chambers you can rescue clones and learn how to utilize intreguing gadgets, all of which were optional unlockables in the first game. After eight levels with this gadget, you get to toss it around in the facility to help you maneuver and get to other test chambers along with picking up various collectables. While the facility itself is incredibly linear, it becomes a puzzle in its own right later in the game and feels much more open than it actually is. That said, there's no easy way around the facility minus creating shortcuts and it gets incredibly confusing to navigate as time goes on and you open up more of the facility. If you're looking for secret test chambers or collectables, navigation is often times more tedius than rewarding. Really a warping system of some sort or even an improved more detailed map would have made things a lot better.
However, Stealth Inc 2 (appropriately) focuses on the gadgets more than its original core gameplay this time around. While it keeps it from feeling like an expansion pack, there are a lot of moments where I felt like it could have still been utilized rather than put to the side as much as it had. Again, I feel like it was a smart choice to focus on these gadgets, but it severely weakened its original selling point.
Despite that, Stealth Inc 2 is still a lot of fun to play, but it's highly recommended to play the original first. There's a fair bit going on and understanding and perfecting the core game can make it easier to navigate this time around. Overall, a solid recommendation.

First, this "bad" review is only for the Steam version of this game that I really enjoyed playing when it first came out, something like 18 years ago. Exploration has also been simplified, in a brainless and boring way. To be fair, I didn't experience any of the bugs or save issues that were reported by some other players.
That being said, I still like the atmosphere and story of the game which always makes me want to read "Dracula" again. Gameplay is very simple and rather smooth, and the game aged well for a pre-2000s game, with decent animation and cinematics.
In conclusion, you can consider buying it on sales or in a bundle if you're nostalgic of the game or are curious of a short and simplified old classic. If you're allergic to old point-and-clickers / graphics or look for brain-teasing enigmas, I'd advise you to ignore it.

Evil Genius is a base-building strategy game, similar to Dungeon Keeper.
You play as a malevolent mastermind during the cold-war era, with the sole aim of taking over the world.
As with all plotting masterminds circa 1970, you have a secret base built within a mountain on a tropical island, and of course, what evil genius is complete without his evil henchmen? These fellas are under your total command and do all dirty work you task them with. You start off by hiring basic henchmen, which carry out menial tasks such as construction or basic room staffing. These henchmen then branch into three different paths: military; science; and social. These paths each have four henchmen types each, ranging from basic guards, to valets, and mad scientists.
Henchmen aren't the only things you'll find in your evil lair. There's a variety of room types to be constructed, from barracks for the men to sleep, or security rooms to manage CCTV cameras and hold prisoners. Your base requires power, and your staff have many stats (needs) that must be met. By building each type of room you can meet the demands of your ever growing lair. As you progress, more rooms and various objects for rooms can be researched via your science minions, allowing more depth to your base as well as better ways to meet the ever growing needs of your minions.
Finally, no evil lair is complete without traps. Throughout your campaign for world dominance, you're bound to draw the attention of various justice forces. From agents who snoop for incriminating evidence, to burglars trying to steal back ill-gotten gains, building traps can have all kinds of nasty effects on intruding spies. From simple pressure pads and toxic gas, to wind corridors of death, the game offers a wide selection of traps with endless customisation for you to build the ultimate defence against intruders.
Outside of your lair, hotels can be built on your island. Pesky tourists want to visit, and in order to keep them busy these establishments can be constructed to help prevent them wandering into your base. Social minions such as valets will man your hotels, and ensure tourists remain outside the base. Hotels can have a variety of recreational objects for tourists to pass time.
Away from your island is the rest of the world. Accessed via the world map, you can deploy your henchmen all over the world to perform multiple nefarious acts. From stealing money, to plotting schemes. Henchmen can also be deployed on missions in each region to build notoriety, as well as steal priceless artifacts, or even research that can be used for new objects and rooms.
The game itself, in the spirit of most similar British games made in its time, has a strong sense of humour. These moments show in the little things, such as your evil genius gloating over agents locked in your prison cells, or torture scenes consisting of the torturer smoking a cigarette, whilst the unfortunate agent being interrogated begs for a puff.
Visually, the game has aged amazingly well. Though the game was released in 2004, the clean and sleek aesthetic has allowed the game to remain as beautiful as it was at release. A rare accomplishment for many older games. Evil Genius visually competes with a lot of games released today.
Overall, if you're looking for a base-building game, look no further than Evil Genius. This game is both incredibly fun and absolutely stunning, whilst having plenty of depth and an amazing sense of humour. The game only offers a campaign mode, but will easily keep you playing for around 50 hours or more. If you find yourself wanting more, there are sandbox mods available for you to just freely build the ultimate evil lair.
A brilliant game, even by today's standards, and one of the best PC games to have ever been released.
