This game is basically a LEGO game + Oceanhorn. Its cute and shiny and a decent premise. 4 characters all with their own unique ways to traverse the map and get through puzzles. I figure that I had played the Trine series and an absurd amount of LEGO games, so I would enjoy this game, but no. This game suffers from two absolutely fatal flaws: bad direction/map systems and lack of permanence. You have to get EVERY character to each checkpoint individually, they don't work as a unit and pretty much nothing you do on each character helps the other characters make it to the next checkpoint. So it just feels like you're pointlessly having to run each part of the map 4x for no good reason, just because the door at the end needs to have a mage blast, fist punch, and door crawled through by your digger dude and the psychic's animal pal. And every time you run through it, any enemies you killed along the way have respawned and all things you opened up are now closed again. Nearing the end of the game, their directions become pointlessly vague, so you just have to wander around looking for buttons to push, but you can't just waltz through the backtracking areas because remember all the enemies and blockages are still there, so you have to literally complete each puzzle area to explore around in your search. Its so flipping frustrating, especially since you already have no idea where you're supposed to go and now they make it hard to get anywhere. Then when you finally do find where you need to go, you will need one of the characters specifically to open the door or whatever, so now you have to get them ALL the way to where you are on whatever character you made the maze through with. But since every hero is different in how they get places, you have to take a completely different map route and it takes you forever to figure out how to get from Point A to Point B because everything you learned about pathing on Character 1 is meaningless for Character 2.
Overall, it just made me more and more annoyed and even though I was reaching the end, I just Alt F4ed and uninstalled because it wasn't worth my time anymore. I was stuck and not happy about it. Would not recommend.

It is important to take into account that I'm reviewing this game from a grown up's point of view. The milage can be completely different for younger people.
The core gameplay and feel of the game is nice. Not great but not bad either. The game unfortunately has few flaws that ruin the game for me (see the Cons).
Overall rating: 6
Pros
+ The 4 characters feel significantly different both in combat and in puzzles.
+ The controls feel responsive and clear.
Cons
- The idea of the 4 characters isn't so much using their abilities together to solve the puzzles but instead the idea is to solve the same puzzle multiple times (once per available character) using different abilites. This often makes travelling and the puzzles tedious.
- The puzzles are often really easy. I mean REALLY easy. When combining this with the previous con, the puzzles are more often inconvenience than fun.
- One of the characters is specialized in fighting. This is clearly a problem since the game is not an action game which means that all combat is fairly bad. This is not a problem with the 3 other characters since with them the approach should almost always be avoidance and even when it shouldn't the combat is more like a puzzle than actuan action based combat.
- When the world opens to the player, finding the needed things is mainly tedious because the player uses most of their time in running around in areas they have already been in but were missing an item / ability to do something the last time.

The red/black/white aesthetic is interesting, and some of the ship designs are cool, but being able to see where the background is stitched together / mirrored is a bit distracting / takes away from the immersion of the game, The main reason I wouldn't recommend the game is that the controls are pretty bad with a keyboard. The music is well-done. Seemingly random levels and no intial presentation to a storyline make it less immersive, but lend more to an 'arcade' feel. If not for the lack of gamepad support (or if it had customizable controls..) it might be worth checking out, but as-is I would not be deceived into thinking it plays more fluid than what is previewed in the trailer. If you're a big fan of mecha designs or SHMUPs and want to support the developer by purchasing the game, some of the ship designs are cool, and as said before the music is cool, but it's a bit cumbersome to play.

Force Unleashed II fixes all the problems I had with the first game. The gameplay is far more fluid, the controls are simple and easy to remember, the force powers feel useful, there are enough enemies to keep the game interesting, and not too many to overcomplicate things. The menu, while still an obvious console port, works far better, with fast access to your force powers, and a simple menu to change the color of your lightsabers. One noticable change to the game's formula is that now you have two lightsabers instead of one. Also, you'll notice slowdowns whenever you land successive hits on enemies similar to how the God of War series works which I really like as it allows you to more easily plan your next move. Quick time events are unfortutely still very much present. All of the big enemy types that you fight throughout the game have an optional quick time finisher move that got boring to watch so fast, I tried to avoid pressing the quicktime activation button and just finished off the enemy by slashing it instead. One nice addition is the ability to use the force to see where you needed to go next. The first game had a problem with instructing the player on what they were supposed to do next. I also liked the ability to use mind tricks on weak enemies so they would do things like kill themselves or attack their allies.
Now here are the problems with this game. I have never in my life played a shorter game. 4 hours. That's right... 4. There are literally only 3 levels in the game: Kamino, some Cloud City like place, and a spaceship interior. The pacing feels way off, as if I was missing the first 3 levels. After the initial tutorial level, you go to this Cloud City place and fight through room upon room of increasingly difficult waves of enemies until you reach a huge colliseum where you're faced with a gigantic boss. This boss goes on FOREVER. So long, I was afraid I was already facing the end of the game. But no, this is just some overly drawn out filler that takes up a majority of the game. I'm not sure why the developers thought it important to draw this out as it isn't necessarily a fun boss that let's you use your skills to their full potential.
Another major problem is the story. It's not nearly as good as the first one. You barely interact with any of the good characters established in the first game, and your charater's motives are purely to save the damsel in distress this time which just does not feel as powerful as the motive of the first game's character. The storyline overall just feels rather uninspired and doesn't seem to add anything to the overall arch of the Star Wars universe. The cool thing about the first one was that it helped to link the prequel movies and the original trilogy together. Force Unleashed II does no such thing and feels like that awkward straight to DVD movie that nobody ever watches unless they buy it by accident.
The graphics look incredible, especially for a game that's already a couple years old. Very nice lighting, nice soft edges, and some smooth framerates. The cutscenes are also looking fantastic, almost movie quality.
The sound is a big improvement, though the music is still a bit hit/miss. The voice acting of most characters is decent, but not nearly as good as the first game. The main character's voice acting is horrendous this time around, with really awkward pubescent screams when he gets angry that just give you that awkward embarassed feeling. I just want Darth Vader to be like "..whoa.. calm down you big baby."
All-in-all, this game is a better GAME than Force Unleashed I. But Force Unleashed I has a better STORY than Force Unleashed II.

The 'normal' setting in this game provides a really good (but not overwhelming) challenge.  There were a few boss fights where I was continuously dying.   Sometimes I got a bit frustrated at the game not doing what I was wanting it to do (grabbing the wrong item most often).  The controls are pretty difficult..actually, amazingly difficult at times, especially if you're used to simple controlled games.  Still, I'd classify this all as challenges - it wasn't impossible to get through.
The storyline though, I keep going back to that.  The writing was really good, really involved, and this made me want to go find the comics now.  For the story, itself, it's worth it.
Once you beat the game, there's also a 'new game +' mode.  I haven't tried it yet, but I'm not sure I want to.  I know the story well enough now that playing it again isn't really something that interests me.  Maybe in a few months.  I don't think the game kinda 'stands on its own' without the storyline.  The executions seem a bit overdone (honestly wish I could just turn them off), and repetive.  To play the game again, knowing the entire story, just to continue with the 'superpower' thing just isn't there for me.
I do think the game is worth the money.  I'm looking forward to when the 3rd game comes out (which I assume will happen eventually)

Adventurer Manager is a neat concept, but poor execution killed most of my joy. When you name a game "Adventurer Manager," my first thought is that my job would be to outfit the adventurers and let them go on their way.
I didn't do my due diligence before buying this game exactly for that reason.
Instead, most of your time in Adventurer Manager is spent locked in slow turn-based battles or an equipment management system that takes just a little too much effort.
I'd rather be handling diplomacy, town economics, or really anything other than having to do yet another dungeon crawl.
No one likes a micromanager, but Adventurer Manager forces you to be one.
Update following the developer's response:
Hi there,
I appreciate your response. First, I'd like to say that this review is a gut reaction. It's not a mechanical critique of the game.
I admitted that I didn't research the game to drive home the fact that my experience is based entirely around impulse buying your game. I'd read an article on either Rock Paper Shotgun or PC Gamer about Adventurer Manager, saw that it was on Steam, and picked it up without a second thought.
Many reviews come from members of a game's community that either love or hate it. I'm a guy who bought it, played it for a couple of hours, and didn't end up liking it very much.
I'm definitely not accusing you of false advertising. You explain exactly what the game is and what to expect on the store page.  Most of my issues with the game stem from core mechanical problems that can't be expressed through screenshots or gameplay trailers. I'd have had to watch someone play the game to see the stuff that left a sour taste in my mouth.
Having bought the game, though, I've also bought my right to share my opinion about it. Steam only lets me give a game a thumbs up or a thumbs down, but in many cases I'd probably pick a middling option.
I decide by imagining if a friend — someone I know who likes this type of game — asked me what I thought. If I could imagine myself saying "You might like it" at some point, then it's a thumbs up. If I can't imagine myself suggesting it to anyone who I know, then I rate it negatively.
Here are some after-the-fact critiques:
I didn't feel like I was progressing very quickly. Most of why I play these lightweight, casual-ish games is to get the distilled seratonin that can only come with upgrading my dudes.
Tying class unlocks to reputation didn't feel fun. I'd rather just tell my rogue that he's going to be an assassin now.
I did some thinking during my commute this morning about what I actually meant by "slow" turn-based combat.
The auto-adventuring feature is a neat idea, but it's functionally identical to the vast majority of the dungeon crawling gameplay. I think my issue is that I'm only exerting agency over 4 of my 48 adventurers at any given moment.
Let's say that the game took a cue for FFVII's "active" turn-based battle system. The adventurers would handle the fights on their own, but the player's job would be to check in on them and reveal enemy weaknesses, give stat-boosting pep talks, and pull them out if the going gets too tough. The time-based turns combat would then give the player breathing room to swap between adventuring parties on the fly.
These automated parties could adventure simultaneously, and the total number of adventurers you could have in the world at one time would naturally be limited by your ability to multitask between however many parties were adventuring at any given moment.

Story - 8/10
Sniper Elite V2 is a stealth / action based third person shooter developed by Rebellion Developments. The main objective of the game is to hunt and kill the five V2 rocket scientists and stop the V2 rocket launch. There isn't a big number of missions, but they're all really enjoyable and replayable. Over 200 hours in this game and I still love it.
You can decide which tactic you want to use. Stealth or loud is your call and it's fun either way.
There's also co-op in which you and a friend (or stranger) can play the campaign, survival mode, bombing run, or overwatch. There is also DLC and multiplayer which has Capture the Flag, Team Deathmatch, so on.
Storyline Length
I'll be honest, it all depends on how good of a sniper you are. If you're someone who was born to kill, then this game will take you about 3 hours. If you're someone who's just getting into video games, it may take you about 5.
AI / Bots - 6/10
On lower difficulties, the AI is really, REALLY dumb. They can't even shoot in your general direction. They run for cover which, to be honest, shouldn't even count as cover. However, on higher difficulties where gravity and wind direction exists (which really puts your aim to the test), they're stone cold killers. The snipers never miss, the ground soldiers can wipe you out before you can even head for cover. They will use tactics to come and surround you. Despite all I said, they're still a bit dumb anyways.
Experience - 9/10
As if what I said before isn't persuasive enough for you to get the game, then listen up. Each time you get a vital shot (headshot, shot through the heart (and you're to blame), lungs, nuts) then there's an X-Ray camera following the bullet showing what happens to the organ(s) and skeleton because of that shot you made. I know, it does sound really sick and gruesome but actually, it's really satisfying and doesn't really affect you that much.
The game is replayable (and still fun the 5th time playing through it), has many different ways to play through a mission and has a great storyline.
Graphics - 9/10
Cool graphics. While there could be more detail into faces (considering you're a sniper and need to know who your enemy is) it's still playable. There's detail to a lot of tiny things like posters (propaganda), debris, planes and explosions in the air, buildings, so on. They put tons of detail into the X-Ray camera, which adds to the satisfaction of killing in this game. There could be more models of enemies because there do seem to be a lot of "twins".
Sounds - 10/10
Tanks, guns, enemies shouting, grenades all sound realistic. If you had headphones on and closed your eyes, there's a high chance you couldn't tell the difference between this game and actual war footage. The voice acting for Karl is a bit monotone, but that doesn't matter too much. It's a beautiful game.
Controls - 10/10
Very easy to get used to. It's your general shooter game's controls. WASD, 1 2 3 for weapons, B for binoculars, LShift for sprint. Y'know. Easy controls.
Overall - 8.6/10
86/100

Hoy en día es difícil ver shooters de la vieja escuela como Duke Nukem 3D o Doom. Sin embargo, creo que The Darkness II se acerca bastante y, sin perder esa esencia, aplica mejoras y rasgos modernos de esta época. Una dificultad decente, combate frenético y algo caótico, y enemigos bastante cabrones; unido a unos gráficos a la altura, una historia interesante (recordemos que está basado en el cómic homónimo) narrada con pequeñas fases centradas en el diálogo, nuevas mecánicas de juego (como evitar y desactivar focos de luz o luchar junto a tu ayudante), habilidades especiales...
Sí, habilidades especiales. Esto es lo que hace diferente a este juego: dos víboras cubiertas de cuchillas y con muy mala leche que puedes usar a tu favor. Mediante un pequeño árbol de habilidades, podrás dar rienda suelta al potencial de la oscuridad. Cosas como hacerlas devorar los corazones de los enemigos para curarte, rematar salvajemente a los enemigos (hablo de cosas del estilo de empalamiento de torsos, destrozar entrañas metiéndose por el ano y saliendo por la boca, o cortarlos en dos cual ternera en una carnicería), hacerlas agarrar objetos y enemigos para usarlos como escudo, arrojarlos para dañar a los adversarios, o simplemente azotar a los enemigos con ellas para cortarlos en pedazos.
No es ninguna obra maestra, pero creo que es un juego bastante entretenido y que en cierto modo hace sentir ese ambiente de combate intenso y dificilillo que a muchos les puede apetecer recordar. Así que, mientras esté esto presente, sí: lo recomiendo.
(CONSEJO/¡SPOILER!: Sobre el final del juego... no te lo voy a desvelar, pero después de todo el desarrollo de la historia a lo largo del juego, seguramente te esperarás un final dramático y molón... y lo que te encontrarás seguramente te parecerá tremendamente estúpido y seco. Tan sólo ten esto en cuenta para no sorprendente, y no te dejes engañar por este defecto).

The game is in open beta but crashes on a regular basis both loading a match and less often during.
I would have expected this to be fixed as a priority, but adding guns and maps seems to be more important.
This is more of an issue since the numbers on each team were lowered as AFK players cant win matches.
The game is free to play with a premium setting should you choose to spend real money on it.
Premium gives you increased cash and experience from a match. Repair costs and ammo are charged against your earnings. sound familiar?
The game is an arena at present two teams try to eliminate the most enemy or control the resources in a given time. Friendly fire is on. The maps are well thought out and very pretty to see. There are anomalies on these maps that are a hazard or a benefit if you can farm them. At the end of the game you get to loot a stash as a reward this may be anything from an emblem to go on your clothing to money, a gun or gear. As you play you gain character levels giving perks that improve your personal performance. You also gain rep that allows you to buy better gear and weapons with a faction.
You can also mod weapons and gear by spending roubles and parts from items you dismantle.
If you spend gold instead of roubles to mod an item success is a certainty. Mods are randomly determined and of random value between a range of values.
Freeplay and PVE variants have been promised forever but there is not much point picking up the game with an expectation of these modes at present.
Rep Level 0-4 was a blast I had great fun learning the game.
Rep Level 5 and it all changes it gets faster and more aggressive and often you feel out geared and gunned.
I am at rep level 8 and losing an average of 1000 roubles a match. I am not a great player but the chances of progressing without a premium account, buying gold or goodies at this point are slim and slow.
Real money can be spent on gold and on guns. Gold can be spent on guns and gear to help you progress. Golden weapons are generally resented and not only have a reload advantage they gain experience for the user at a higher rate. Gear bought with gold has an experience mod on it as well.

Lots of people putting this game down. I've only got 70 hours in at the time of review, but I've enjoyed the game quite a bit. One warning upfront: you NEED to have a controller for this game. The mouse & keyboard controls are absolutely terrible, I have yet to meet a person that enjoys playing the game that way.
The combat is extremely fun for a quick, straightforward PvP game. This is the bread and butter of the game and I can't stress enough how awesome it is. Each time you think you've learned a character in its entirety you learn a new trick or two. On top of that the way you play has to vary depending on which hero you're fighting and whether or not you're engaged in a 1v1 or a 3v1. It's unlikely that you'll win if you're squaring off against three opponents by yourself, but when you do you feel like a god. It's surprisingly sophisticated for as simple as it seems.
The bots are surprisingly smart. Eventually you get used to fighting them in their varying forms, but even still 70 hours later from time to time a bot will get the upper hand on me and leave me with my jaw dropped. Once you get into higher reputation ranks and you're generally queuing with other experienced people they're definitely not as good as having real players, though - and it can make for some pretty much unwinnable matches if you are unfortunate enough to be stuck on the team with a bot or two.
Their first patch was great. They addressed some major issues with the game - especially bots getting spawned in at full health on player disconnect (people were doing this to troll when they rage quit *all the time*) and elimination / skirmish matchmaking separation. Some people complained about balance issues as a result of the patch, but I don't see it. Their promise to release all DLC to all players at zero cost is awesome and another reason I was willing to dump the initial $60 for the game. If you're not already aware, the season pass will grant you access to the content 7 days early (along with some other in-game perks that I could see making for a handy start-up), but overall this methodology will prevent the community from being split up later down the road and I applaud Ubi for their approach.
I will warn players considering the game that there are huge swathes of the community that are pretty toxic. People rage out quite a bit - especially if you throw them off cliffs / into traps, if you use feats in elimination or skirmish, if you use classes that they think are "unfair," or hell - even if you are reputation rank 4 and and you happened to get matched to someone playing a class that they have significantly lower rank with. I personally find it amusing, but if rage-quitters and the like upset you maybe consider ignoring chat pretty much 100% of the time on 4v4 modes. On the plus side: when playing duels particularly most players seem pretty level-headed and polite.
Single player campaign was okay, but it's nothing to write home about. It wasn't challenging at all, but the storyline was moderately interesting. The co-op element doesn't play into the story itself at all - you just basically have a duplicate played by your friend that comes along on your adventures. The rewards for getting the "collectables" translate to a very healthy start in the multiplayer and allow you to get some good gear for at least a character or two.
The servers are P2P, and I agree for a game priced the way that this one is that is kind of ridiculous. However, outside of some long load times I only rarely encounter any issues - including the disconnects frequently mentioned by other reviewers. Maybe once or twice a day tops, and usually at the end of a match. My Internet is not overly fantastic by any measure, so I can't help but think that some of these reviewers are exaggerating.
Gear is my main beef with this game. I've seen a lot of comments about the game being pay to win, but the best gear you can get is capped by your "prestige ranks" with a class. Not only that but you use your gear to "specialize" your character in certain ways - for every increase you take in one category you are taking a hit in another. It's also fairly easy to gear out a character by buying crates with steel (which is obtained by playing matches) - but I could see the grind being a bit too slow for people that like to play more than 2-3 characters. I have entered matches with no-gear characters and still done *okay*, but a skilled player with high level gear is going to slaughter a skilled player with low level gear pretty much every time.
On top of the above mentioned, matchmaking is in no way "gear aware." The problem with this is that teams frequently end up stacked in favor of one team which can make for some *extremely* one-sided games. Because of this once you have your first rep1 character elimination, skirmish, and dominion game modes are almost not worth playing with any other characters until you've gotten them to rep 1 and obtained a base set of blue gear - which you will have to do by purchasing loot crates with steel if you want to stay competitive and up to par. This gets exponentially worse as you reach higher reputation levels if you favor one character.
Worse-still, matchmaking does not seem to take into account the entirety of the party queued for the match. I had significantly more time to play than my friends when the game launched, and as a result I hit rep 3 with a character pretty quickly. Duel and Brawl are the only game modes that don't apply gear, so they were brand new to the game with no gear on any characters getting matched up against people that had spent the majority of their time playing for the first few days.
Character customization is pretty boring, and when you break into emotes / executions it's entirely too expensive. If you play more than a few characters you will already be struggling to get enough steel to keep them geared up - let alone getting that awesome looking execution you want for each one.
Overall I give the game a solid 7/10.

I missed this game when it first released but had always wanted to give it a go as I heard it was similar to Dungeon Keeper, a much loved game from my early PC gaming days. After seeing it had launched on Steam for a modest price I snagged a copy and am pleasantly surprised by how in depth this hidden gem is, in some ways I actually prefer it to Dungeon Keeper.
The interesting thing about this villainous base builder is that rather than building small lairs and moving from level to level, you only have two islands to build on, one that you access from the start and another that unlocks halfway through. This allows you to expand your HQ over time and it's a rewarding experience to finally see your underground criminal empire begin to flourish. You also have access to a world map screen that allows you to influence the world outside of your base by sending your henchmen to commit crimes or perform espionage in various countries which brings in gold, specialist units and ups your notoriety. But beware, the more influential you become, the more secret agents the governments of the world will send to your island to unravel your insidious schemes. It should be noted that the game's theme is heavily influenced by 60s spy serials and it carries this off with a comedic tone reminiscent of the Austin Powers movies, which I rather enjoyed.
If you're a fan of Dungeon Keeper or looking to get into to the whole base building, overlord style strategy genre, I highly recommend this game. It's a great time sink and it's easy to lose a few hours twiddling your evil moustache and plotting world domination. Just be sure to watch out for that pesky super agent John Steele.

I'm going to recommend this game in spite of all of its flaws if you can get it at a nice discount. I've been playing the game for a few hours and I've found the story fairly engaging and the puzzles fairly decent. Often its flaws are pretty funny too.
I understand the major complaint about this game is that it's a crippled version of a classic game. I didn't play the earlier version, but I find it interesting that in looking through the complaints I have yet to see anybody point out the flaws that hampered the game for me.
1. Navigation is a nightmare. You can't walk freely around. You stand still at points and can look all around you and click on stuff, then you have to click on an arrow in the air to move in a direction to the next point. This is a little awkward, but it might have been okay if it was executed well. It wasn't.
Often, you're facing one point, you click on it, then find yourself facing in a different direction. Sometimes you find yourself facing a wall, other times you find yourself facing in completely the opposite direction that you were facing when you clicked on the point. This means that you will often find yourself circling back on your path when you thought you were heading forward. There's no way around this except to pay very, very close attention to details as you're moving to try and make sure you're turned correctly.
And the points you have to navigate can be very convoluted. Often, you find yourself staring at a point that you want to get to which is fairly close, but there's no arrow pointing to it. Usually, you have to go down a path which takes you farther away from that point, backtracking around until you find a clear path to it even though there was nothing blocking your way.
And sometimes the navigation is just plain weird. Like, for example, you click on an arrow pointing at an open, snowy field only broken in the distance by a line of trees. When you get there you find yourself on a fenced path. How does that make sense?
A mini map would have helped. It would have been simple enough to code.
2. The puzzles often make absolutely no sense. For example, early on we're supposed to distract a guy, then knock him out and throw him into the water, apparently drowning him just so we can get access to his cabin. We find out later that he's apparently one of Dracula's minions... but all we know at the time is that he's really stand-offish. It sems like a rather extreme and counter-intuitive thing to do.
3. They didn't put any effort into animating the characters when you're not interacting with them, not even on the simplest loop of a couple of seconds just to make them seem animated. So as you approach anybody, they look like wax statues, usually paused in mid-action. It's creepy, and not in the way that you want from a creepy horror adventure.
4. When the characters actually are animated, the animation is really bad. This can actually be a little amusing. They seem to have bones made of rubber hoses, the way they swivel and bend in an unnatural, creepy way. When they talk, their mouths don't so much look like they're forming sounds... it's more like their mouths open and their lips waggle around, ambitiously trying to sync with what's being said but failing. Also, everybody's eyes look completely dead... which is creepy and thematically appropriate, but I'm pretty sure it was completely unintended.
I'm tempted to write this off as the limitations of technology when the game was made, but I've seen much better animations from the time.
*
Over all though, I recommend the game because I've been having fun playing it and I think it was worth the drastically dscounted price I paid for it.

I've gotten a lot of hits recently. SOMA blew my mind. It is so good. I actually have the urge to play it again. No game has ever made me think so much about being human. It raises intriguing philosophical questions throughout its story of the mind, humanity, and artificial intelligence. Perhaps my favorite was a religious question. If I could copy my mind, and there existed two (or more) of me, then what happens when any of me ceases to function? If there is a heaven, is there only one spot for me? Or at the moment of awareness, do the copies of me sufficiently diverge to be different people, each with his place? Is living in a simulated environment better or worse or more or less real than eking out an existence with a physical body? A small snippet of why I loved this game and will be thinking about it for a long time to come...
Much of this game is unnerving or disconcerting. The first other character you come across seems to be a machine who thinks he is human. It's unclear at the time exactly what is going on, but you're given the choice to "kill" it or let it "live." It is, by the way, grievously injured and seems to have been crushed by a rock and some other machinery. But it's mentally all there. You can make this choice for several other characters over the course of the game, and make a similar choice in different contexts that feel momentous and weighty indeed. They don't have an effect on the game's outcome or anything, but they sure had an effect on me.
This is the best Frictional game, hands down, and I liked both Amnesia and A Machine for Pigs. SOMA is on another level. Oh, and those creatures scared the hell out of me. AT LEAST 10 times, maybe 15 or 20, I was so anxious that I couldn't even move. I'd just crouch in a corner listening to the creature stalking the nearby rooms hoping that it wouldn't come near me and see me. When I had to run past a creature to get this or that item, the player me would close my eyes and hold forward and shift to sprint because it freaked me out so much knowing that this THING was right behind me about to kill me. And a handful of times I yelled in the apartment as I did so, usually a repetitive string of curse words as I ran for a door and *click click click click* tried to close it behind me before the thing could get to me. The visual and sound effects and the screen tearing really amped up the intensity.
Cannot say enough about this. If you like horror games, if you are in any way interested in thinking about artificial intelligence, philosophizing about humanity, science fiction, and so on, do yourself a favor and pick this up.

The only real gripe I have mechanically is that changing characters is very clunky, and often means just to move from one zone to another, you have to do it four times - once for each main character, since they all discover the totems independantly. This makes traversal sometimes very repetative.
On the performance front, I'm getting wild fluxuations in FPS from 60+ down to below 15, even on the lowest settings.  I can't really figure out why this is, but it just happens in certian zones. When it does happen, the entire game seems to slow down, and this has caused issues with combat or executing actions. This is with a i5-7300HQ and a GTX 1050ti, which while not high-end, is a reasonable performer at the moment.
On top of that, in the 5 hours I've put into the game, I can't count how many major bugs I've seen. Just off the top of my head, I've been caught in walls, fallen into water repeatedly after skating into a zone, or just had my character lock up and freeze in place, all of which requiring me to restart the game. It's very frustrating to get thrown into a wall, and just get stuck there.
I really want to like this game, but the the performance issues and the bugs I've encounted just can't leave me to reccomend it to people.

Shooting down an enemy is one thing, getting back to base in one piece (or at least being able to land) is another. I like the game very much, because more than in any other simulator you spend a lot of time keeping your plane in the air while orientating yourself. If you play it on full realism, that is.
Buy it on sale, it's worth the 23 euros (at the moment). Decide which extra planes you want and buy the DLC that have them included. Every planes behaves differently, and once you fall in love (or already are in love) with a certain plane, you will crash and die a lot with it, while laughing your pants off.

If you love WW1 planes, buy this game with the money you would have spent on food and just live on water and bread for a week. If you're tempted, don't resist. If you hate it, you should ask yourself why you visited the store page of this game, and buy it anyway.

This one probably isn't for everyone, but many will like it a lot, including myself.
It's a third person action-adventure game (Metroidvania?), with a good comparison probably being A Link to the Past amd other top-down Zeldas. There's a continent composed of square regions to explore, and underground areas below almost all of it. You start on a fairly linear path, and have it slowly open up by gaining abilities and new protagonists until the entire continent opens up. Then, of course, it's time to go save it. ;) There are also areas that you'll pass by that become accessible later with new abilities / characters.
Unlike similar games, you have 4 different protagonists (1 at a time), each with different ability sets. So they often have to move through an area in different ways, and some areas and secrets are designed for specific characters. Each character has to reach checkpoints / fast travel points independently to unlock them, so you'll be seeing the same territory several times (but often not in the same way), even above the amout of backtracking usually involved in this sort of game. Some people won't like this, which is why I say the game isn't for everyone. I didn't mind.
The graphics are in the cartoony "Warcrafty" style, which works for this, and they look very nice for the style. The sound is nice but not remarkable, no voice acting. The achievements are for finding individual secrets scattered throughout the game; 100% is quite doable on the first playthrough for diligent explorers. Apparently at some point losing save games was an issue for some, but supposedly it's been addressed and I had no such problems.
TL;DR: if you have a strong opinion (either way) about top-down Zeldas and similar games, expect to feel the same about World to the West. Myself, I liked it a lot.

This is one of the finest flight simulators I have ever played. Been flying sims since I was a kid.
There are a few accessories you should probably have to get the maximum enjoyment out of this title and they aren't cheap.
A head tracking device is almost necessary to get the immersion out of this title. When coupled with headphones, you can hear the nuanced wind sounds as you turn your head in your cockpit, trying to keep a beat on your enemies or just looking around at the gorgeous scenary.
A flight stick is highly recommended, of course. Just like trying to play an FPS title with a controller is alike to eating ice cream with a shovel, trying to play a functional flight sim with a keyboard does not allow you the full spectrum of movement that you should have.
Now, you don't have to have these things, but they are very nice to have. The problem is that these things are expensive, as is this game. I wouldn't say it's "overpriced" because the level of detail makes it evident that there was a lot of work that went into this title. The DLC is also very expensive and it is somewhat harder to excuse this, but the DLC themselves are bundled into packages that at least make sense. For instance, if you buy the package containing bombers, you get mostly bombers.
All things considered, this is a hard game to recommend, unless you fall under the banner of a very niche audience. If you have doubts about this purchase, watch a few videos online and see if this would be for you. It's a beautiful experience, but to get the most enjoyment out of it you have to have a certain set up.

(possible minor/major spoilers ahead) Following on from an amazing game in The Force Unleashed, I came into this with mixed emotions. Given most track records with sequels, and what happened at the end of the first game, I didn't know what to think of this, and yet given how amazing the first game was, I thought they might just pull it off.
However, as much as the gameplay was decent, the story lacked any sort of conviction, or plausability. This was a money sequel, just as I had feared, and added nothing to the first game. I didn't come away feeling any different, the ending of the first game was more than appropriate to answer most questions, about what happens between Star Wars: Episode 3 and Episode 4.
Even though the gameplay was okay, the length of the main storyline is a joke. The first game spanned an epic variety of environments and enemies. Whilst this game I felt like I spent almost all the game just fighting regular Storm Troopers, who are the squishiest of squishies. In the first game, you visit multiple planets, and also revisit them several times, in a star spanning quest. In this, you visit a total of 4 different areas. Almost none of which you spend any meaningful amount of time in, such as 1 planet, where you spend 5 seconds walking around, and then about 2 minutes of cutscene. That's it. The only planet you do spend any reasonable amount of time on, you feel like you're seeing the same thing over and over again, due to how mind numbingly boring and samey the architecture is.
So, if you like the gameplay of the first game, but don't particularly want any sort of meaningful addition to the story, or area design of the first game, then this is the game for you! Otherwise, don't play it.
Edit: Also, about the only redeeming factor of this game, is that it had a first game.

This game falls just above the "no" mark, with subpar graphics and more of the same gameplay as the first. Granted, the glitchiness that everyone saw in the original game no longer is around; the thing can be run on a microwave. Though I still can't get over the fact that this still feels like a poorly done port.
You'll see what I mean when you hear the soundtrack and the fact that it doesn't sound like something from Star Wars at all. It sounds like some kind of orchestrated piece meant for an action movie in space, but not a STAR WARS action movie in space. It's just not all there, something is very much missing and I can't bring myself to forgive the design team for this flaw.
And what the hell was going on when they decided to write the story for this game? This is Star Wars we're talking about, not Star Trek or Battle Star Galatica. Star Wars has a very strong signature when it comes to story telling and anyone who grew up with it knows exactly what I mean. This just doesn't fit the structure at all, and with the strange soundtrack this game seems almost like a parody rather than canon material.
The powers are mostly the same: force push, force pull, force lightning, and mind trick (which I'm not certain was in the first installment). They all feel bland and unpolished, but do add something else to the game which keeps it from getting too reptitive.
Though, repetition is still everywhere and if you've played the first then that's exactly what you can expect from this one. But not everything is bad about that, considering the combat does still flow pretty well and the original cast of voice actors are all back again. Mission wise, it's the same thing over and over again, do not expect it to change. There's little diversity given to what is offered besides fighting enemies or finding an objective. Free roam would actually be a nice change, too bad it wasn't included.
If you're deadset on buying this game, wait until it falls into the single digits during a sale. DO NOT spend over $10, not even if you're a hardcore Star Wars fan. And if you've played the first, know that this one will be the same thing over again but with different (and less) costumes.

Frankenstein: Master of Death is a lovely HOPA flawed by far too many "WTF?!?" moments. The music, voice-overs, and graphics are all excellent, and the video cutscenes are seamlessly integrated into the more static scenes (far more seamlessly than i have seen in any other HOPA). However, again and again i find myself asking "what the hell just happened?" or "why, with a pickaxe, a metal gauntlet, a crowbar, and a knife, am i unable to frighten away one tiny bat who's blocking my access to a widget?" The tons of backtracking is made a non-issue by the ability to warp using the map, but the map is horribly confusing until one realizes that it's larger than the screen and is scrollable (once you realize that, it's no longer confusing, but is notably unconventional for this type of game). i felt compelled to abandon ship after one too many WTFs which just didn't jive with the urgency being presented in the story. (i mean, come on, use your pickaxe or metal gauntlet to break the cabinet's window and grab the thing on the other side, rather than searching the whole island for a key.) Yes, such features are typical of a HOPA, but when urgency is a central part of the story, the protagonist's inability to use a metal gauntlet to break a cabinet window or scare away a bat reveals an inherent dissonance between a story conveying urgency and the OCD personality required of HOPA protagonists. The two do not cooexist well, and that conflict ruins this one for me.

This is the first driving game I've seen that doesn't have pre-made "broken" parts that replace the originals when you crash a car.
That said, the cars don't really drive all that great. Crash simulator is exceptional; handling simulator is not. The game is buggy in some ways, and some of the features could've been done better.
In particular, they tried to get too clever where the camera angles were concerned. The camera tries to turn around and look the way you're facing... whether you've already turned it or not. This means that when you hit reverse, you either leave the camera alone--which means that until it finishes turning on its own, which it won't do when you're not accelerating, you can't see where you're going--or you turn it before you start backing up, which means that as soon as you DO start backing up, it turns AWAY from where you're headed, so you have about two seconds to finish backing up before you can't see and you have to screw with the camera again. Then when you try to go forwards you have to futter with it AGAIN.
Hopefully they'll come up with a better system at some point.
Other than that, this is at least the seed of a really great game. Hard to really enjoy a good crash simulator when you have to manually spawn in every vehicle that you might want to crash into though. Maybe they'll get something like an auto-spawn system in place someday.

At first I was pretty excited for it. I heard some good things about it and I really like stealth games. Now: This game has barely any stealth elements. It is a platformer and NOT a stealth game. Now I like platformers, too, so I kept going. My next complaint is the "dialog". It tries to be like GLaDOS from Portal but it fails spectacularly. Instead of clever jokes and sadistic messages spoken by a sassy computer lady, you get boring text on the wall that is barely related to the situation. And the text mostly consists of generic villain lines like "Please just die!" or some bad joke like "I am gonna miss my favourite TV show like this!". Next on the list: the puzzles. The "puzzles" are not really puzzles. Instead you just do tasks in a specific pre-defined order. You don't even have to think. You just press a button, go through door, press next button, go through next door, jump over a hole and you are done. The only difficulty comes from the enemies and traps but they work on such simple patterns that they barely pose a threat. Another thing I wanted to mention is the bosses, or should I say boss. Yes, every boss is the same exact enemy with a different level around it. I played until the third time I met the boss and then I just gave up on this game. Oh, and don't even get me started on the story. They just copied it from Oddworld: Abe's Odysee!
My verdict: Stealth Inc 2 is a boring generic platformer with streamlined puzzles, an unoriginal story and embarassing dialog. It tried to be the next Portal game and failed spectacularly!

There is almost certainly $10 worth of fun here, but much of it had to have been unintentional.
This game advertises itself as a "meta-RPG" game, and that's true, but it just feels more fun to play a genuine RPG than this. Games like Romancing Saga have features beyond typical RPG fare, which make them awesome to play. This game feels, to me, more like it's stuck between wanting to do a meta-RPG, and a standard RPG, and not presenting either as well as could be done. This game is, at least, quite a bit unique, and that's welcome.
The graphics stand out for their mediocrity: it's presented in a "retro" style, yet even in the era this game styles itself around, these would be considered bad graphics. Not every graphic is bad, and some of them are nice to look at. But there are also graphics to make you question your decision to play this game. Some hilariously bad sound effects; and the just awful, short music rounds out this game. Just mute the sound, if you're going to play this.
Are there good things? Yes. The simplifed pathing through the game makes it easy to play--even if that is held back by pretty bad controls--you feel like you know what to expect, and moving forward happens at a steady pace. Item collecting is presented well: I would love to see such clear representations of what items you find, in other games. In a world without a lot of meta-RPGs, the meta-RPG qualities are welcome. However, these intriguing features are floating on a sea of mediocrity. Is it worth playing this game to see them? Only for the stout-hearted meta-RPG fan.  . . Or someone who only has $10 for a game. It's a pretty good $10 game.

There is largely two factors to this game: The story and the gameplay.
The story is incredible; set detailed fantasy world, but doesn't bore you with too much exposition (if being a lore-nut is your thing, fret not, there's more than enough given to you to read on your own). While the plot itself may be somewhat simple, it's carried to lofty heights with the game's exceptional cast of lovable characters. You'll find yourself taking every chance to interact with them, just to learn more about them and see what they have to say. To me, this is the game's biggest selling point. I want to talk more with Rukey about his family. I want to chat with Jodariel about what she's done in her previous life. I want to hear Sandra's cynicism about... everything.
The other aspect is the gameplay. It's a bit like... NBA Jam? Honestly, the game starts you off pretty easy, and with plenty of time to get the hang of it. Not too long after, you're free to ramp up the difficultly as much as you want. If 'Hard Mode' isn't enough for you then you can give yourself handicaps (True to Supergiant form). Personally, I think it's worthwhile to play on at least 'Hard Mode' just because there's actually a bit of intrege and strategy to the gameplay that you might miss if you're never challenged with the gameplay.
Although vastly different from Bastion and Transistor gameplaywise, Supergiant once again delivers an amazing soundtrack with the game.
If you're not a reader, then this game isn't for you. While there is plenty of rich story, interactions, and lore, its entirely text based. If you don't enjoy reading, then you likely won't enjoy Pyre. The gameplay is simple enough to be fun, yet complicated enough to be intriguing, but it doesn't carry the game by itself.

I missed this game when it first released but had always wanted to give it a go as I heard it was similar to Dungeon Keeper, a much loved game from my early PC gaming days. After seeing it had launched on Steam for a modest price I snagged a copy and am pleasantly surprised by how in depth this hidden gem is, in some ways I actually prefer it to Dungeon Keeper.
The interesting thing about this villainous base builder is that rather than building small lairs and moving from level to level, you only have two islands to build on, one that you access from the start and another that unlocks halfway through. This allows you to expand your HQ over time and it's a rewarding experience to finally see your underground criminal empire begin to flourish. You also have access to a world map screen that allows you to influence the world outside of your base by sending your henchmen to commit crimes or perform espionage in various countries which brings in gold, specialist units and ups your notoriety. But beware, the more influential you become, the more secret agents the governments of the world will send to your island to unravel your insidious schemes. It should be noted that the game's theme is heavily influenced by 60s spy serials and it carries this off with a comedic tone reminiscent of the Austin Powers movies, which I rather enjoyed.
If you're a fan of Dungeon Keeper or looking to get into to the whole base building, overlord style strategy genre, I highly recommend this game. It's a great time sink and it's easy to lose a few hours twiddling your evil moustache and plotting world domination. Just be sure to watch out for that pesky super agent John Steele.

I have a mixed feelings about this game. Certainly its Gothic game only by its name (sure there are monsters which look like exactly from Gothic series and they are named the same like the infamous meatbug for an example).
There is not skill system like they have in example Gothic 1 and 2. When you advance level you get 3 points where you can put into your so called skills such as Mettle, Discipline or Vigour skill lines. Each of these raise your stats in a different ways. Example if you put skill points into Precision skill line you raise your ranged power and mana by 1% every point you add (and when you put enough points into the skill lines you receive abilities such as steady hand which smoothers your aiming so it does not shake so much).
In Gothic 1 and 2 you got 10 LP (Learning Point) each level you advance and you can distribute those how you see fit among various trainers in the game world such as learning archery (in Gothic every point in the archery boosts your accuracy) or black smithing. In ArcaniA you can't raise your strenght or dexterity which is a big shame (in Gothic every weapon has requirements such as strenght for swords and crossbows and dexterity for bows), in ArcaniA you can use every weapon as soon as you find them, buy them or make them.
Gothic has specific crafting places you need to use to produce stuff such as alchemy bench to create potions and an anvil to create weapons. ArcaniA has crafting system also but you can just simple craft what you like (assuming you know the recipe and have items you need) whenever and wherever you want to.
ArcaniA is a pretty game and plays well. Has talented voice actors and good music. But what I miss alot is free roaming in Gothic (among the skill system) where you could immerse yourself into the world, explore it how you wish. ArcaniA certainly doens't feel like an open world rpg.
Fighting system is pretty much mouse button bashing, when you click enough mouse the enemy is dead (certainly this is a step back from the clever fighting system from Gothic 1 and 2.)
At least there is a difficult setting called "Gothic" which gets you a little closer to original Gothic series because we all know when you start as a wimp who gets exhausted easily and can't even kill a simple scavenger (first enemy you counter in G1) and hits like a bloody farmer. I remember my very first experiences with the Gothic games, I used to die so often and had to run to the town enemies hot on my tail for guards to kill. Which comes to the point that in Gothic games when an NPC sees a monster he/she starts to instantly attack it. In ArcaniA you can fight example bloodflys and scavengers near town guards and they just stand there letting you die if you can't handle the monsters yourself. The monsters simply ignore all NPCs and do not pay any attention to them either. I think that this is a huge turn off the NPCs not paying any attention to the monsters in the game world or monsters paying any attention to NPCs.
It is a good game nevertheless. It is not a Gothic game so do not except it to be (even if the name fools you, even if there are NPC characters like Diego and Milten and monsters look the same and have same names) but treat it as its own game and you propably will like it. I was the same like the rest of the players when I first saw that new "Gothic" game is going to be released, hypeted it alot and after it got released and eventually I was crushed, hurt and gravely disappointed. But after some years (I think I last played this 2013) went by and I decided to give it another shot and started to like it when I treated it as an action RPG.
The story is pretty good and there is a small similarity to how Gothic 3 starts like (when you arrive with a boat to the shore).
I would not recommend it for the Gothic fans, or with the full 19,99€ price (I wonder why it is always, 19,99 and not simply just 20 *shrugs*). But I would recommend it for the fans of (action)RPG and when it is on sale lets say 75% off.
Yes it has similarities to original Gothic universe and it tries to pay a homage and fill pretty big shoes but it does not simply fill the need, the void we Gothic fans long for.
In the end it is an okay game (not the best) with its faults and flaws. And it will keep you entertained for a few days and maybe even weeks. Sadly I can't put a neutral review.
UPDATE:
After playing more I remembered why I got bored of this game at the first place. ArcaniA is a good game yes with alot of problems and biggest one which I forgot to mention is its playability. Let's talk about the first island where you eventually arrive after the starting place (which acts like a training area). Each area is divided by high mountains and rockfalls and alike. There is only one route to advance to the next area (and that is usually a bridge for an example or you are given a scroll to clear a bunch of rocks blocking the road) after you have completed few quests in each area you arrive to another area and it is rinse and repeat. So the whole map gets boring pretty quickly and it feels like running from point A to point B and from point B to point C.
Even travelling through these areas feels like to be a chore after a while, yes there are teleports scattered around but they only work when 2 are linked together and suprise suprise those two only work in that area they are assigned to meaning you can't use them to travel from another side of the island to other.  I just spend around 15 minutes to run/teleport from the point where I am to near the point where the island actually starts (and then the same way back) to see if there were any new conversations, any new quests or more items that merchants would like to sell me. Nothing.
I remember why I prefer original Gothic games than this, one of the reasons is that with Gothic 2 for an example as the game progresses more monsters appear, more quests appear to the people you did quests in the past (such as killing some monsters or finding a missing wife). Gothic 2 felt like a living, breathing, progressing world but the truth is that ArcaniA feels pretty dull. Playing is getting to be a chore eventually. But even if it does not offer a replay value (like games with open world do) still when it is on sale it should be considered because it has alot of good things too such as nice music, good voice actors, gorgeous graphics and yes there are those good old Gothic moments when you wander around and suddenly get attacked with a pack of scavengers or bloodflys.
Oh and the character is tied to land only and seems to fear water, there is actually no way to swim in this game which is pretty stupid in my opinion. But hey its not an open world game where you can explore how you wish. You can't even climb a mountain either.
My personal thoughts that if you wonder that should you pick this or games such as Gothic, Risen, Two Worlds, Fallout 3, Fallout New Vegas, Elex, Elder Scroll Series such as Skyrim etc pick one of those with the same money if you do not have those already.
UPDATE2:
In Gothic games it was custom to learn how to "operate" animals; to take their claws, teeth, horns, tongues, hearts and alike. I remember exploring the world and learning the animal abilities from various NPCs. Selling things such as claws were very profitable. Like one NPC told me that if you do not learn the abilties to remove various animal parts the body of an animal just rots away.
In ArcaniA there are no such skills sadly. Of course animals drop things such as meat when you kill them (or stuff such as feathers when you hunt scavengers and stinger when you hunt bloodflys). I miss skinning animals and hear to NPC to tell me how the process works.
UPDATE3:
ArcaniA is clear not build to keep mage class in mind. There are 3 magic skill lines each of them teaching you only one spell and thats pretty much it. In Gothic games (specially 1 and 2) there were plenty of magic scrolls and various spells.

Going back in the past to play a game released in 1993 may seem like a bad idea considering the fact that there are a ton of modern first-person shooters available to play with improved graphics and (presumably) improved gameplay. Although this game may seem simplistic in comparison to newly released first-person shooters part of what makes this game fun is that it is simplistic. Its limitations at the time this game was developed might have actually made this game better than if it were developed by modern video game developers who dominant the FPS market today. Why? Because it doesn't attempt to be realistic (games are not meant to be realistic; they're meant to be fun; realism is boring), it doesn't add in a mediocre, forgettable story because it's expected to be there, you don't walk around at the pace of a normal human being but rather you run with the broken, old era PC game style of running where you run faster than Usain Bolt without ever losing energy AND most importantly it doesn't make you cover behind an object for the majority of the duration of the game. It's just good ol' fast paced, arcade styled fun. Kill the demons, get the keys, find secrets, get new weapons, defeat bosses, beat the game.
Not only is this game a solid recommendation for avid video game players who enjoy seeing the history of revolutionary video games but it is a definite recommendation to even someone who is more of a casual player. Not a good game "for its time", a good game, period. The only real complaint I have about this game is the soundtrack. At the start of a music track the melody sounds nice but then it proceeds to repeat itself for the remainder of its duration and gets annoying to listen to especially since they recycle the tracks for later levels.

The game, though, does have some glitches, such as loot disappearing upon a specific event, and freezing during a specific animation if the autosave occurs. However, despite these flaws, the game is a blast to play. Overall Score- 8.5/10

Do not buy.
Most of the positive reviews of FH came from very early on. And FH can be quite intoxicating, especially early on when you are learning the mechanics, and finally pulling off a hard won duel is truly an epic feeling. So what's wrong?
1. Devs aren't fixing exploits. This might appear to be a "fighting game," but it's actually a Super Saiyan Magic Spells game. The community, which is awful, has discovered how to exploit and abuse a few flawed mechanics. Now everyone does it. No patches, and Ubi rarely mentions any hope of a patch.
2. You'd be incredibly lucky if you fought a match where you swing mideival weapons at each other and block/parry with shields. Unfortunately, that almost never happens anymore in FH. Instead, the enemy will have figured out their ublockable, chainable, cheese combo and just do it over and over and over.... and over and over and over and over. Allegedly, you are supposed to be able to dodge these moves. In reality, they are lightning fast, and it's a p2p game. So everyone always does this now, and you're only hope to win is to do it back. Fun!
3. Magic spells, tactical nukes, etc.: FH has a system called revenge, which long story short means if you've blocked enough or been injured enough, you can go super saiyan when the enemy attacks you and it knocks them down. You can now kill them easily. Does this super saiyan transformation have a cooldown? Nope. Once people figure it out, the entire game is nothing but revenge. There are "feats" (which are spells) you can use in the 4v4 modes. Including a tactical nuke... er sorry I meant "catapult." Again, FH rarely includes sword fights. Mostly it's super saiyans and nukes.
4. Preposterous Ubisoft p2p. Want to play with friends in a group of 4? LOL! It takes us about 20 minutes to figure out who can invite who, and if it will work. Half of the time on player can't join a friend's invite... but if he invites that same friend, the friend can join. Now multiply that by 4. Enjoy spending 20 minutes grouping only to get into a game, which then disconnects, and guess what? It BREAKS UP YOUR GROUP! This is insane.
5. Full priced game, with immediate expensive cash shop plastered all over every aspect of the single worst UI you will ever experience. Insane grind to unlock even the tiniest aesthetics. Normally I don't care about DLC, Season Pass, cash shop, etc. as long as there are some sort of reasonable limits. But once you've paid full price for this game, then immediately see that 99% of the unlockable aesthetics are locked behind A) an expensive cash shop even though you just paid full price for a AAA game, or B) play the game for 500 hours to unlock a paint color for your armor.
For Honor is Ubisoft in a nutshell. The core game idea is good, then they seemingly hired people whose sole mission is to make it as unplayable as humanly possible. The worst UI, matchmaking, stability, exploits, and community of any game in years. I ended up getting FH because even though I know Ubi sucks, R6Siege gave me hope. But that appears to be a one-off. If you buy FH for more than, say, $9.99, you are being stolen from and you will regret it. Back to other, functional games now. Peace out.

Aside from some graphical issues here and there and linear path ( instead of whole open world map )  I quite enjoy my time with Gothic 4. A lot of people hate it but its actually pretty good. Why? Well here's why :
- Combat is actually fluid,fast and there is a little bit of depth ( with combo system and parrying etc. )
I recently played ELEX and I hated it. Combat there was clunky, slow, bad hit boxes and FEEDBACK when you shoot someone with arrow or hit with a mace. Gothic 4 being older game yet it does COMBAT SO MUCH BETTER! You don't feel slow on your feet and when you shoot someone it actually gives nice visual / sound feedback. You can stun enemies and do more damage to the head. Also holding button makes your arrows more powerful! How did they screw up combat in ELEX so hard?!
- Progression. It's fantastic. I never felt like I'm getting my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me by monsters. The balance is just great. You can actually kill harder enemies with this combat. Changing from magic to melee and ranged is super fast and allows great combos. You don't need to visit class trainers and pay lots of dough to learn 1 skill... You just level up and choose whatever you want! It's really simple and great without wasting the time. That being said it is a bit shallow because of the limited abilities you can get. Wish there were more.
- One thing that ELEX does better than Gothic 4 is quests.... Yes they are still stupid fetch quests BUT ELEX actually reminded me of MAss Effect. With Renegade / Paragon system. You could finish the quest in a variety of ways which is great. Gothic 4 feels a bit bare bones in that aspect... Usually you have 1 or 2 choices.
Overall the game is enjoyable thanks to progression and fluid combat with nice meaty feedback when hitting enemies. I actually enjoy this game more than ELEX....

I have put many hours into this game and decided to, finally, review this game. I absolutely love it. With a passion actually. I wasn't here during the beginning sadly, but after watching youtube video's about it, decided to purchase it. Day and night I played this game, learning the in's and out's. I never played during the sandbox times, but after recently getting a taste of it, I can conclude, while it is enjoyable, it gets boring. That said, moving on to progression. It has it's enjoyments as well. Granted, it sucks to die and lose your progress/dinosaur, its also that much more satisfying to reach the Tyrannosaurus, Spinosaurus, etc. and to become top of the food chain. Not to mention, you get to experience other dinosaurs playstyles in the process (if you choose to play bush simulator thats fine too), and the thrill of the hunt is always an exhilarating feeling.
However, with that said, I understand the irritations of megapacks, (formerly, due to recent updates) KOS shants, and all around immature revenge killers, however it doesn't take away the fact this game is a developing masterpiece of its own.
Not to mention, I met my first girlfriend in this game. The Isle is developing an expanding influence, one that I hope brings it justice. Despite all the spiteful, negative review, I for one greatly suggest this game. If you are looking for a good time as your favorite dinosaur quick and easily, go for sandbox (mind the lag lol). If you want an intense experience that keeps you on your toes constantly, try progression.
I will continue to watch The Isle continue to develop, anxiously seeing what the developers have to bring to the table with each update and seeing what's next.

It's been about 100h since I started playing RoF (including non-steam demo). I wanted to wait some time to be able to say something more about it.
At the beggining I must admit I was never a big fan of fly simulators but I've been fan of WWI aviation since I remember. Actually this game "forced" me to buy joystick because previous one was way way to responsive and was cause of many problems due to very light planes. Surprisingly I've never had any problems with DCS World - different kind of planes? I believe that after few years spring in my joystick was to soft at the crucial moments.
Visuals are amazing and runs smooth on I3 3220 and 7870 on high details. I had to turn some of effects off obviously but thats understandable. Sound freeks me out when you diving and can actually feel that speed.
Lots of game modes - career, quick battles, missions, multiplayer. Like I said before - 100h already and I don't even fell that I achieved anything. Multi still alive but unfortunately you'll have to content oneself with FEW servers. When I type few I mean two max three. They're nerver full but It doesn't affect gameplay. All you need is 8-12 planes maybe bit more to have fun and spend some nice quality time with new friends. Because community is so small people are very friendly and happy to help everytime when you need advice. They will cover you, help and make you feel comfy. Lets be honest. Learning curve is very demanding and without internal help you won't be able to be compatitive. Some of them play from release day and there is no chance you will even approach them in combat. They fly on the edge and know every weaknes of your plane. I'm wondering... maybe just because that game is so difficult makes it so rewarding? EVERY single plane shot down in multiplayer makes you happy and smile instantly and you know by the time it's something. It's not a next random kill in FPS game - at least I feel it in that way.
Do I recommend that game? YES. Oh yes. RoF is expensive if you'd like to buy all DLC at once but there is no need to do it. Few monts ago RoF was in some bundle and can be available on steamtrades easily. Even the basic version provide high quality of fun for many hours. What I do is: I just buy on every sale some DLC and improve my gameplay and experience. Spent 30 flying my career with Nieuport 17 and after that time I bought DLC with weapons upgrade. What you can do is install additional guns in your planes to increase firepower. Not only this but thats the main reason. After that change I was exited to spend next 30 or more hours flying the same plane cose it gained new quality.
Hopefully this helps.

I got this game from Humble Monthly, and while it has some rough spots, I ended up satisfied with deciding to play this game.  In World to the West, you play the role of four different characters, each with their own abilities to travel the world with.  Without spoiling anything about the game, this game can be summarized as an exploration game with some relic collection integrated with the main plot.
The game itself isn't difficult to get through once you understand what you need to do, as most of the puzzles aren't hard.  A common issue that seems to effect players at a glance is simply being lost or not 100% sure what to do next.  The game doesn't offer much in the way of assistance other than a waypoint that tells you where the next main objective is.  I had a number of moments where I came to a stop unsure what to do, but persevered and found out I was missing something obvious or overthinking the solution to the problem.  There were definitely questions I had along the way, but they were answered with continued playtime (once again I will not spoil why).
Overall through, I liked the art of the game, some of the music and while the gameplay isn't something I would consider revolutionary, it perfectly fits the bill looking for an adventure exploration game with puzzle elements thrown in as well.  If the art style gets you and you want something that doesn't constantly push you on a one lane track forward to the end, I say go for it.

I just picked this game up during the Winter Sale 2015 for $2.50 USD. I already play a game similar in effort to this, called "Depth" which I'm sure many people here know exists, and this game is markedly different as of right now but not in a bad way.
It's cheap, for one. $2.50 for a game that's still in development is a steal. It's Early Access, so you get to play this game as it evolves into what the developer envisions. The developer regularly interacts and posts replies to community hub posts in regard to the game and questions about it all the time. Go to the community hub and look for yourself... that's pretty nice if you ask me. It shows that the developer is both open to feedback and also probably enjoys helping others enjoy what I'm sure will shape up to be a good game.
Depth is largely finished by now, with the developers just adding more content and DLC here and there like tie-ins and new maps. This game, though, is not. Don't expect it to be. It's very basic and rudimentary at this point - it's humans, who move slowly in these underwater conditions, surviving against waves of sharks rolling in from the outer reaches of the map. It's not exactly a "jumpy" game but it doesn't need to be right now.
I hope this game turns out really well. I don't regret buying it, especially for what I paid, I don't mind supporting developers' efforts to make the game they wanna make, all I ask in return for purchasing is that they finish the game and they make it something cool. This has the potential to be something cool. They've already brought in a co-op survival mode and will be adding an adversary mode soon that lets you control the shark(s) on the map.
It isn't as gorgeous as the new Star Wars game, and it isn't boring like stupid little "retro" 8-bit indie games, but it's a niche game. It's a deathmatch game with SHARKS vs HUMANS. It likely won't get millions of players as a player base in the future but I don't care if it does or doesn't, I only care about whether the game keeps getting better or not and so far it seems like it'll continue to grow and become something of its own.
Pick it up if you can get it for a cheap price like I did, cause I know some people avoid Early Access games out of fear or distrust.
Maybe my review will help someone, maybe it won't. I like the game either way, and I wish it luck cause there really aren't enough DIFFERENT types of shooters out there. The world doesn't need another ♥♥♥♥ing military sim shoot 'em up like Call of Duty anymore.
