I bought this game on sale. It was a little bit over £5. After completing it, I felt like this game should never have existed.
Where to begin?
[THIS REVIEWS CONTAINS SPOILERS FOR THE FIRST STAR WARS: THE FORCE UNLEASHED]
As a very big fan of the Original Force Unleashed game, what made the original game so great for me wasn't it's over the top gameplay, but how it played a role in the Star Wars Expanded Universe. It linked Episode III and Episode IV perfectly, detailing how the last few jedis were killed off, how the rebel leaders initially came together, and ended with a satisfying conclusion that perfectly set up "A New Hope," whilst also being conclusive so you feel satisfied with how it ended. However, the Force Unleashed 2 not only rips open that ending and drags out Starkiller's journey, which should have ended at the seemingly conclusive end of the Force Unleashed 1, but tacks on a story that doesn't add ANYTHING new to the Star Wars mythos.
In the original, you spend half of the game hunting Jedi, which explains how the survivors of order 66 eventually died, and the other half uniting the galaxy against the empire, which explains how the rebel alliance was formed. In the second game, Starkiller spends it finding his lover. That is the whole story. He doesn't set up major plot events in the films; he doesn't even do anything meaningful in his own mythos. He spends the game looking for his girlfriend, and that's it. He even goes out of his way to stay out of any meaningful plot points; when asked to join the rebels and fight the empire, he basically gives them the finger. The only thing that could have added anything to the Star Wars EU is the ending, which obviously sets up a sequel, but that never arrives. As it is, the ending just breaks the entire lore of the Star Wars Universe.
Next, let's look at the game's memorable moments. The original FU had a huge array of great video game and Star Wars moments, something that players and fans would remember for years to come. Hunting rogue jedi, bringing down a Star Destroyer, infiltrating the Death Star, beating the living♥♥♥♥♥♥out of Darth Vader and even fighting the Emperor in a 1 on 1 battle; you did it all. However, the FU2 has a grand total of 1 memorable moment, which is the first boss fight within the first hour and a half of the game. Not even the Final Boss fight against Vader (that’s not really a spoiler, we all knew he would be the boss), the most important part of a game, felt memorable. As it is, for 4 hours, you slice, stab and force your way through the same, (yet granted, interesting) enemies over and over again.
Gameplay is up next. Gameplay is a hard one to talk about. Because, I'm gonna be honest, the gameplay was hella fun. The complaints I'm making against gameplay isn't because gameplay is bad, it's because I personally felt that the first game did it better. The thing is, even though the force powers in the first game were pretty insane, the new ones are even more unrealistic, with the player wielding 2 lightsabers and whizzing about the map firing out lightning and bursts of energy at will. And while it was both fun to and brilliant to behold, it just felt way too flashy and didn’t have any substance to it. There are a few more complaints about gameplay, but nothing worth bickering about; simplistic upgrade system, all combos from first game immediately unlocked, lightsaber duelling revolved around blocking the moment your enemy strikes and then attacking over and over again. In conclusion, it’s fun but too flashy for my liking and not as in depth as the first game.
So, should you buy this game? Buy it if you really do not give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about the story. The gameplay is fun, enemies are samey but there's a lot of different varieties, there's not many levels and it takes about 4 hours to complete, but the gameplay alone is rather fast passed and fun. But if you cared about the original game's story, just forget this exists.
They've recently announced that none of the Star Wars games are canon; however that doesn't mean that you can't have certain SW stories as head canon. So in my eyes, the first game is head canon, and the second game is just a neat little idea of what may have happened if Starkiller continued his journey after the first game, but it's not what truly happens after Starkiller's first game.

Ever wonder what happens when someone plays the Quickman stage of Megaman 2 about 5 too many times, then decides to cram Lemmings and Portal into a blender?  So did I.  Apparently, the result is something like Stealth Inc 2... a platforming puzzle game that rewards quick wit, puzzle solving skills, and reflexes in equal measure.  The single-player campaign is a linear story told in a motion comic style with fairly good writing (especially for a game whose main focus isn't the story).  While the story itself is linear, the levels still allow plenty of room for exploration.  You'll find you can go a lot more places than just the straightest path to the next Test Chamber, though your advancement through the map is gated by puzzles that require a specific gadget to solve, so it's not completely open.
To give you an idea of how addictive this game is... I sat down at about 8 pm last night to play it for "a few hours".  When I finally chanced a glance at the clock, it was 5 am.  9 hours of my life sucked into the struggle to get past the next test or unlock a little mohawk for my clone, and I'd do it again in a heartbeat, much to my boss's chagrin.  Thank goodness for sick days, I guess.

The major drawback is that the main campaign will only last for 5 hours tops (it took me 8 hours with a NG++ game) ,and the vendettas will give you 2-3 more hours.If you decide ofcourse to play the extra campaign or the vendettas with all the charactes (I doubt you will :P ), the time will be multiplied.So here comes the critical question : Are you able/willing to give 30 $ for a game it will only last 12-14 hours tops?Yes the story will be great and Yes the powers and abilities of darkness will be unforgetable but will it worth for the so little time it will last....?In my opinion NO ...buy this game like a did at a steam sale (80%=5$) and you will not regret it.

Icons are huge, and only show the text saying what they are when selected. Hovering over does nothing, so you have to click and drag to make it show the text without selecting, and it will select whatever you're on upon release. All of these things could have been in drastically smaller hotbars/windows. The default controller mapping is okay, but the placement of crouch and interact aren't very optimal for a speedrun focused game like this. There's no controller rebinding, but to be honest that's rare and thus I and many others choose controllers like the DS4 where you have full control map anything anywhere.
The game speed is tied directly to the framerate, and their target was 60. I opened the game and instantly spotted and enjoyed the smoothness of the intro logo animation and menu responsiveness, but when I got in game I knew it was at double speed. Extremely responsive absolutely, but it makes the game drastically harder while also punishing even slightly nonoptimal movements by scaling the timer speed the same. If you drop frames, it will slow down. If you cap at 10 FPS, you could essentially play with tons of time to prefect every step and get flawless times to top the leaderboard, that is if people hadn't already hacked to achieve 0.00s. Capping framerate is bad enough, but tying gamespeed to it is often even worse. Please developers, don't do either.
Taller than 16:9 is letterboxed, while it seems that wider resolutions stretch the hud and just show less of the game vertically.
Interesting puzzles/scenarios, and a nice hub world vs the menu-only level selection of the first game. Many if not seemingly all of the levels include AI companions that play like a co-op game would (very similar to Portal 2), so it's a shame co-op levels weren't included. It's clear the single player levels weren't made for that as there are sometimes multiple companions, they are only around for portions of the levels, and getting them to the exit is a bonus objective. That said, just more levels, even as an expansion, meant for local co-op would be great.
It was a Wii U exclusive for 5 months, and it absolutely shows. The assets were designed for 720P, so all the Menus and HUD scale badly and lose their their sharpness with odd pixelation, as opposed to the blurring you get by setting the whole game to 720 and upscaling. Behind the HUD and Menus, the game itself seems to render at the native resolution, though the 3D character models have aliasing even with 4X MSAA set in the launcher (AA being the only graphical setting in the game).
The music I've heard is very nice, and the overall visual style is there, though the 3D character model's shading contrasts a tad with the levels.
Port issues, but the small scope helps in that respect, and the actual game itself seems engaging and charming, though frustration is sure to kick in if it's anything like the first in the series. Exclusivity for consoles hurts games as evidenced with this games needless 720P target res, and the fact that we still don't have the Ultimate version of the original game in this new engine/style, because it's exclusive to Sony platforms...

Pyre is a great mix of RPG, graphic novel and sports genre. Adding a little bit of each of these genres just in the right amount. The game, as expected from
has deeply written characters and great plot. The player is caught in difficult decisions about the characters fate all the time, having to balance it with the possibility to lose a great character and a good player.
The game is basically a graphic novel, with long (but not dull) dialogues between the characters, often presenting the player with different options to choose from that could affect characters stats in varied ways. Choosing from different pathways or giving credit to one character rather than the other could affect the gamepay at some extend. Although, it didn't feel like it completelly changed the final outcome of the game, it did affect the outcome of the personal journey of each character. Winning or losing in a
also felt like being in control of the story
.
Each character is banned for a reason. This reason is not revealed to you easily. Most of the characters will slowly reveal details of their story to you, depending on your choices during the game. This gives a feel of proximity and intimacy with each character. Each one has their own captivating story to tell. Even adversaries will often make you feel bad for winning a rite.
So, each character has commited a crime and they are now banned from society, being forced to live their lifes in the wastelands of the Downside. From time to time, you are to take part in
. The rites are basically games of basketball with some obstacles on the field. Also, the players have special habilites, being able to ban players form the field for some time, fly, and other RPG-like habilities. The game is in real time and you can control one player at a time. Depending on the difficulty setting, on chosen modifiers and on which team you are facing, you will get more or less action. But you will cheer and celebrate with every dousing of the adversary pyre.
Appart from the Rites mechanics, there is character levelling up and items. Each character, by participating on a rite, gains enlightment (xp). Earn enough of that and you'll be able to choose a nre hability for that character. For each one there are basically 2 hability trees to choose from, each with 4 habilities. There are also items that give the bearer different perks, and these items can also be upgrated to increase the perk they offer.
So, the game mechanics and storytelling are flawless and really keep you interested on the final outcome of the story of each individual character (often asking yourself what will you choose to be the fate of one or another character). But another thing that Supergiant does very well is the art. The game looks entirelly handcrafted and brush-painted. On top of that, there is the
that is, as expected from Supergiant, marvelous. Adding a theme for each character and for each different situation, the combination of art and soundtrack really add up to each moment of the story.
Worth every cent! The campaign is around 20 hours long and it will give you the feels. Also it's a great split-screen game to call your friends in and have some couch fun!

Exceeds even Bastion and Transistor's reputation IMO.
Rules of the game: You have three very differently-statted teammates that you control one at a time. The goal is to douse the enemy team's pyre by throwing the ball into it until it's gone. Characters are out if they get caught in an enemies' attack circle/beam, but return after a (usually) short time. Characters are out for the entire next round if they dive in with the ball rather than throwing it, which saves a lot of time. Characters can't attack while holding the ball, and can pass the ball instantly to any teammate on the field.
Strategy mostly involves understanding your character's strengths and weaknesses, recognizing enemy plays, and developing the board.
Biggest Similarities to Bastion & Transistor:
-Lots of stat customization
-Certain mechanics force you to try out new strategies, rather than sticking to your comfort zone. Not to as high a scale as Transistor, but more than Bastion.
-You have a crazy amount of freedom when it comes to difficulty. After playing it pretty easy in Transistor & Bastion, I really pushed myself playing Pyre. Keep in mind that failing in Pyre doesn't mean a second chance, it means narrative consequences. High difficulty is tense and salty.
-Creative and excellent visuals, sound, and setting
Biggest Differences to Bastion & Transistor:
-No waves of enemies
-You can't permanently kill enemies
-No sprawling levels
-More character-driven
There is a TON of reading in this game. I was worried about this, but was eased in shortly. I'd recommend skipping their sacred text entirely- it doesn't add a whole lot and it isn't necessary. I've noticed that second-person narratives often fail to follow the "show don't tell" rule of fiction writing; this is noticeable in Pyre but isn't true of any of the dialogue, which takes up a great deal of the narrative delivery. The story mostly follows themes of hope and salvation from sin. As I mentioned, it's very character-driven.
Recommended to fans of action games, RPGs, and of Bastion & Transistor (despite it's differences with them).

I don't know any other games that embrace the Spy genre with this much style. Everything about this game, from the music to the characters, is meant to fully immerse you into a world of minions and doomsday devices.
The concept is simple. You are an average Bond villain, and you want to take over the world. In order to do so you need a base of operations (which you have to lay out and build yourself), an army of minions (who live in your base and are trained into better jobs there) and a control room that lets you send your minions across the globe to steal money for you and carry out devious schemes. But this attracts the attention of the 5 superpowers in the world, who will start sending investigators and agents to your base. As your global notoriety climbs, you have to manage your heat or you will become overwhelmed by the number of investigators and soldiers sent to  attack your base.
The game is an incredible lot of fun to play. Although your first base design will inevitably suck, the more you play the better you will get at it. (Also, a minor spoiler: halfway through the game you move to a new base, which lets you fix any mistakes you may have made that playthrough... Only to make a bunch of new ones, of course.)
But I also have two gripes. First of all, you can issue basic orders and give anyone on your island a tag that determines what must be done with them (jailed, dazed or killed), but you cannot directly control your minions. This is understandable - you ARE the mastermind, after all - but can get quite frustrating when all of your minions are busy and you really need something done. Fortunately you can directly control your henchmen, who may not be able to build or do much work around your base, but who are very good at killing, dazing or jailing intruders.
Second of all... The game has a lot of bugs, and most of them are really minor and solved by the Unofficial Patch. Why no such patch was ever brought out officially is beyond me. There are also game breaking bugs: for example, once you place down the conference table in the first island, you may not move or delete it or your evil genius can no longer sit at it. This, of course, halts progression and gets you stuck.
Fortunately these two problems are not extremely big, and have not ruined my fun yet. It's good to be an Evil Genius.

Alright. First off, this game is fantastic, hands down now in my top 10. Great gameplay, fighting system feels forceful and deliberate. The story mode was pretty damn great overall, a bit shallow, but that's fine. I'm not always looking for a piece of artwork in every game, sometimes I just want an action pack war-story thrill ride (it delivers). Customization is pretty nice as well; not ground-breaking but there enough that I feel a bit more unique in my style. Gametypes are seperated well, and there is something for everyone in terms of multiplayer.
Second. No game is without flaw, none. (save for Superman 64, best game ever) This shouldn't come as a surprise but peer-to-peer is /not/ the best way to host multiplayer. This can cause long loading screens and iffy connection issues. That is not saying there are not some benefits to using peer-to-peer, but it comes across feeling lazy and a bit funky (not the good kind of funky). One benefit is overall stability yet we still saw a random black-out early on ( shouldn't happen often using peer-to-peer). This is a minor issue to me, it has rarely affected my time playing the game, and I hardly feel that a random issue here or there should make me as salty as it does to some others.
Finally, to the people who talk so well about a game with only a few complaints (any game), talk about how broken a game that really isn't broken is, or play 20 minutes of a game you just ended not caring for, then spam how awful the game was and "don't recommend"... think first, you may have had a bad experience, maybe your tech isn't up to par or compatible, or maybe you need to learn a 6/10 is a more positive rating. By all means if you /truly/ think a game really isn't worth a purchase ever, if a game is actually broken, and if it isn't just salt then press the "no" button like there is no tomorrow. If not, don't write a review, your reviews are the least helpful. They're either misleading or just in the way of real reviews, negative or positive.

Synergy is one of those little Source mods that can really add a lot of replayability to Half-Life 2. Synergy is simple in what it does - you can play through Half-Life 2 with up to 4(?) friends, but tweaking the maxplayers cvar lets you go up to 16.
But that's not all for Synergy. The community have created all sorts of maps for this little mod, most of them being incredibly difficult co-op minigames or objective maps. There are also physics-based puzzle maps where you have your wits and your gravity gun to complete usually around 20 puzzles per map. All of these custom map types are very fun to play, and take Synergy from a co-op Half-Life 2 experience to virtually it's own game.
Unfortunately, Synergy hasn't aged well - the server list is very sparsely populated, and there are only a few servers remaining that have any sort of active player base.
With that said, if you can get a group of friends together and grab some of the custom-made coop maps, you can have a blast with Synergy. (Quite litteraly, friendly fire is a thing that is toggleable)

I really wanted to like this game.  But when they made it, they forgot to put in the fun.
As a simulation, well, maybe it's great.  Maybe it simulates the Western Front down to Planck-length detail.  I assume it does, and in that respect, well done.  But this awesomeness (if it exists) is hidden behind so many rookie UI screwups and a learning curve so steep, it's a learning wall.  As a game, one you might want to play, it's just terrible.  It feels like it was designed by Skynet: beautiful, accurate, soulless, and with no idea of how actual human beings work.
First off, on loading up, you have to log in.  That's not so bad - except the 'create new account' button was off the bottom of my screen, and moving the task bar didn't help.  A quick visit to the forums told me I had to edit the .cfg file.  Well, I thought, that's a minor lapse, probably something to do with Steam integration.  I could overlook that.
In game, the text looks like it was written by a non-native English speaker: it's stilted and imprecise.   Well, I thought: small indie studio, they take what they can get.  So I overlooked that, and what is literally the worst voice acting I've ever heard in thirty years of gaming - I came to fly, not for the story!
Then I started the training missions.  They are not good.  No, sir, they are not.  If you fail, you have to start again from the top.  They are also timed.  Why is a training mission timed?   Why is there no cue to tell you when you've flown through a ring successfully?  (More than once I was searching for the next ring to fly through, which hadn't appeared yet, because I'd missed the previous ring and thought I'd got it.  And other times I turned around to get a ring I thought, mistakenly, I'd narrowly missed.)
At one point, you need to climb up to a green checkpoint from ground level.  The mission tells you to turn left and climb. But it's almost impossible to do in a straight climb; one veteran player on a forum speculated it was to test your initiative, to see if you were smart enough to turn around and climb in a spiral.  Later on, you're told to throw your plane into a stall - I spent two hours trying, literally, to make my plane fall down in a way that the mission would recognize as doing what it wants.
I thought the point of training scenarios were to help newbies learn.  But I am coming to the conclusion the training missions in Rise of Flight are there to weed out the Insufficiently Faithful.  The attitude is common on the forums - Rise of Flight newbies come in, complain about little things like 'my guns won't fire' (Quick Mission, by default, throws you in without ammunition; you need to tell it specifically you want your guns loaded) and veteran players get snippy because they think knuckledragging arcade jockeys are asking for the game to be dumbed down.  I'm not; I am just asking for the game to suck less.
Of the many UI failures, I'll have to single out the view controls as the worst.  There are several ways of looking around - with the game camera, or with your pilot's head. The game uses multiple head snap modes, with the hat control on the joystick, to look different directions.  But the game doesn't have an indication tell you which head snap mode you are in: you could be in 'look in the direction the hat control is pushed, then back to front when it is released' or 'turn your head roughly in the direction the hat control is pushed, and keep it there' or some other mode - I think there are three, but I'm not sure, because there's no indication on the screen to tell you.
I eventually mastered the view controls (by completely reconfiguring the key and joystick mappings) to the point where they'd only kill me maybe one mission in twenty or so.  (Did I mention that, by default, the mouse controls your view as well?  So if you're playing with a joystick and you maybe perhaps breathe on the mouse a little too hard suddenly you're looking way off up to the left, instead of the big flat green surface rushing towards you from below?)
I turned on the gimp settings (simplied physics, easy controls) and tried to play a couple of non-training scenarios for fun.  But even when I shot down a two-seater, my heart just wasn't in it any more.  The sheer awfulness of Rise of Flight had made the soft gooey accurate-simulation center unappealing.  It felt like hard work, and I'm not even sure whether my opponent crashed because my shooting had a delayed reaction, or because the AI just didn't know how to avoid the ground in a spiralling dogfight at treetop level.
So I can't recommend this game.  I would go so far to as say I hate it.  I hate it because I tried to love it, and it just didn't care.  I wish the developers ill.
A must own for any flight Simulation fan.

The game is all about sneaking around, scrounging for resources while combating and avoiding both man and monster in a post-apocalyptic, moody and tension-filled setting. The game provides players with a strong atmosphere, reminiscent of Metro and STALKER.
The setting may be fantastic, but the gameplay is far from perfect. While gunplay is acceptable, melee combat can only be described as wonky. There’s a fairly well done stealth system, but this does not help you level in any way.
While Nether’s creeping around, looting and shooting down monsters in a post-apocalyptic world sounds good it does not hold up well in practice.
On a technical level, there are a lot of issues both in terms of performance and bugs. Frame rates regularly drop too low to be acceptable, even on a high end rig.
However the biggest problem is the multiply player, no holds-barred, survival experience. Nether was hyped as a co-op experience, but unfortunately that is rarely the case. More often than not you will die at the hands of another player. Sometimes a random player you don't see coming, but also from players you thought were joining in the co-op spirit and who you thought had teamed up with you. They have a habit of backstabbing you and robbing you when you don't expect it. You may say,
but consider this: when you die you re-spawn at a random location with only a knife and have to restart your skill tree from scratch. Yes, every time you die. While I'm sure some people will love this it gets old very quickly.
To make this even worse, just getting out of the spawn area can be a nightmare with other players camping about picking you off when all you have is a knife. Worse is the fact that there seems to be absolutely no control over cheaters. Lots of people using aim-bots and hacks spoil an already marred experience.
The real shame of it is, I think that there is the basis of a really great PVE co-op game here.
Where is the co-op game I was hoping for?

I got this game as part of the November Humble Monthly Bundle and could not be more happy with it.
The soundtrack is fantastic and very upbeat, helping to solidify the welcoming and goofy atmosphere the rest of the game is covered in, all four of the characters you play as are relatively well thought out, with strenghts and weaknesses balanced and individual personalities that while flamboyant and cartoonish, they actually add to the experience. The controls are responsive and I have not encountered any issues playing with my Steam Controller, it runs like butter on my rig and is constantly engaging and fun (even if I missed a really big clue on what to do next and just spent a while running in circles trying to find the next step)
My sole gripe so far, is that the pairing of the characters for the first few chapters was a little counter intuitive. Out of 4 characters there are only 2 that can actually kill and enemy on there own. Which is fine, but the story gives you control of the two more defensive characters together to solve a dungeon before it gives you  the offensive characters. I got through it fine as the game is not that hard, but it would have been nice to not have had to play the first two hours (ish?) with kiting tactics because there is no possible way to kill any enemy I come across.
I highly reccomend this game to anyone looking for something fun, colorful, and not particularily difficult. Those looking for a hardcore moba/diablo like experience should look elsewhere. This game is a more laid back kind of adventure. Great for a break between Rainbow Six matches or after a long raid on ESO or Destiny.
TL;DR Really fun game but not particularily difficult.

I didn't play this game for a long time, so I can't speak to the vast majority of the content. Instead, I'm going to explain why I decided not to continue playing.
This game is aggravating for 2 main reasons:
1) The level design is, in places, poorly thought-out. In particular, I encountered a number of areas early in the game which required more backrtracking than I would have liked. I also went through a memorable area in which a set of especially dangerous enemies were positioned against a background which was almost exactly the same colour as those enemies. Not fun.
2) The game contains a lot of bugs. In my short playtime I managed to die in a way that did not trigger a respawn (ending my session), get trapped in an area that I should not have been able to reach at all, and have a supposedly infinite resource run out (it just stopped spawning).
None of these issues would matter as much if I was having a huge amount of fun in between problems. I suspect that people who really like this genre will be able to look past the rough edges. I just saw no reason to.
I did not receive this game for free, nor did I pay full price. I got it in a Humble Monthly bundle.

Won this through a raffle, but my god, I'd pay for it in a heartbeat to a friend.
Puzzle platformer that reminds me of the old school ways of making it around a map and it doesn't force you to be linear really.
Minor gripe is that each character has to discover a 'save totem pole' before they can insta-teleport there, but honestly as you're looking for all the pieces of the story, you'll guide each character through the entirety of the map. A fair warning to folks who are impatient - they do make you 'meet' all the characters in game before you form your "rpg team", after that, you're pretty free to explore as you gain new abilities and health totems.
If you're more of a speedrunner, you can opt for that as well without really sacrificing anything as there are no real prerequisites for getting from one point to another.
All in all, really well done game that allows some minor frustration with some boss fights (I dig it, but some folks aren't into the 'why does this boss hate me?!) and interesting ways to cross areas that seem impassable.

The first Force Unleashed was by no means a perfect game. On just about every count, Force Unleashed II is worse.
While this game continues to let you play a god-like Jedi who tosses aside armies with a swat of his hand, that's about all it really gets right.
Stiffer and less natural than before, with limited mobility on your character. You can fly through the air, but can't walk faster than a hurried trot. It's been a while since I've played the first one, but in this one my movement felt hamstrung.
Just as in the first game, enemies eventually cope with your god-like powers by being magically immune to some of them (though this is usually less annoying than it is the first time around). I wonder where Vader's armies of secret Force-immune warriors and missile-toting robots went by the beginning of A New Hope.
Boss fights tend to have incredibly simple patterns, and yet drag on endlessly.
There are a few interesting set-pieces in this extremely linear game, but too often the design slows you down with endless and very dull jumping and locking mechanism "puzzles" that really do nothing but delay your progress with pointless tedium.
Overall art direction is OK, with a fair amount of work put into some levels and not so much into others.
Anyone who played the first game knows that the Force Unleashed story is totally ridiculous but serviceable, given that they're just trying to write some kind of plot around the fun gameplay gimmick of being an ultra-powerful Jedi. Despite what a cheesy tie-in it was, it felt epic in its own way.
This time around, though, the writers completely phoned it in. Nothing is explained if you haven't played the first game, and makes little sense even if you did. The plot is extremely lazy--your character doesn't even really talk for the first two levels or so, and there's a lot of pointless cameos. Yoda shows up, says two lines to the protagonist, and then disappears before either character asks the other's name.
In terms of storytelling depth, it feels like a half-baked DLC add-on for the first game at best. That may be a generous assessment. The game is noticeably short, even compared to the fairly short first game.
About the same as before, with an OST consisting of exactly one musical sting for your character. All other music is recycled John Williams score, even if it wouldn't be terribly appropriate for the given moment in the game.
There's still a paper-thin leveling system (your choices here don't really matter). Your lightsaber provides you different bonus stats based on the color, but the advantages from color to color are not terribly significant. There doesn't appear to be much in the way of other cosmetic options.
I could forgive this game's shortcomings if it weren't for the problem that it's a classic example of a bad console port. Most of the graphics settings are completely locked--including the framerate and refresh rate--and it appears that it's impossible to change them. The options menu is clearly blown up from a lower resolution--it looks terrible on 1080. Many users report severe problems on their systems, though I didn't have any.
At $6, I felt like I broke even on this purchase, and I've had a better experience than many, likely due to a computer that can handle this game's overly demanding specs easily. If I paid $50 for this, I would be enraged.

This is the first serious review I am leaving and it is solely because I almost never played it due to the overwhelming negative reviews. Keep in mind this is still my opinion and based on my experiences.
to me is the steep price. At $80 CAD it was a pretty spooky purchase given what I read in the reviews. This is, of course, not including the season pass which will run you up further.
Then there is the premium subscription of champion status which will give you a 25% exp boost, among other things. Furthermore you can buy in-game currency which real money and access some unlocks. This to me was not of much concern. Practising and refining techniques will get you a lot farther than your wallet will and as such "p2w" is of little impact on your gameplay experience.
would be the story mode. If you play games for the single player then this game is not for you. Forgoing the multiplayer will leave you with a very short play through of poorly written Ubisoft garbage and an understandable regret for ever purchasing this game.
Finally there is is the hot topic, P2P and connectivity issues. I went into the game expected some pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥connections and expecting to be kicked out of games repeatedly.
. I started out with a strict NAT type and the matchmaking was pretty unfair but the lag was minimal. After noticing my NAT was strict I did a little googling and found out that forwarding port 3075 UDP changed it to open NAT. Once I had open NAT the connectivity actually is much better than many games WITH dedicated servers. In 14 hours of game time I have not been disconnected once. Not everyone will have to forward any ports, most routers will have UPnP that should take care of it for you. If not then quick searches and small know how will fix your issues. THIS IS STANDARD WITH PC.
The combat is very engaging. If you enjoy duels in fighting games then this should be easy to pickup and learn within a few hours. There is, however, enough depth the combat system that skill ceiling appears to be fairly high and as such should provide with a large amount of game time.
The matchmaking and queue times can be fantastic during peak hours. Playing in the early morning will cause the game to match you with some people that may be far above you in progression or ability.
.
There are probably many other things I could talk about but I felt I had to counter some of the reviews that detail a game play that I am not experiencing. This is not because my router or PC is amazing, as they are both aging and outdated.
All in all I'd be happy to spend the $80 given the opportunity and I intend to put hundreds more hours into it.

In theory this game is an okay effort at making a competitive fighting game. In actuality it's a hastily thrown together mess of a partially finished game. Let's start with characters. Some of them are good enough to play as. Some of them aren't. Some characters physically can't change blocking directions fast enough to deal with certain characters, and move too slow to get away or fight back. If Ubisoft cared about balance, they would all be fun (or at least not tedious) to play. The combat is 90% ganking, which makes the game frustrating and pointless. Not only that, there just isn't enough to do. Since there's no real punishment for ganking, no one plays the game normally. The other biggest annoyance is that tons of people pick a fast blocking character and max out their revenge, which is just as obnoxious and tedious as getting ganked over, and over, and over again with nothing you can do about it. And lastly, we have the connectivity problems. There are some days playing For Honor where I get kicked from or lose connection to at least half the matches I que up for. The game freaks out when anyone leaves the game, sometimes resulting in kicks. This is the result of them using a proven failure of a connectivity system, player to player (just like the old days in COD when the game broke when someone rage-quit). The game feels less than half-finished, and is less balanced than Dark Souls 1 PVP. RIP For Honor, you could have been a good game. I wish I had poured less time into this steaming pile of crap so I could get my hard earned money back.

This is a first kind of review I have ever written, so expect some inconsistenties.
As I write this I have almost 50 hours of gameplay on record. This is only in the finished game, although I also played in the open beta.
Summary:
- Connection ( the elephant in the room)
- gameplay ( the reason you'd buy it in the first place)
- Campaign ( it does exist)
- PvP ( and the supposed unbalance)
- conclusion
--[ Connection]--
The biggest issue with this game is obviously the way it's matchmaking works. You will hear many people complain about connection issues and occasionally lag ( I say occasionally because you have to connect in the first place to experience lag)
For me however, this has not been the case, atleast not of a magnitude of which everybody else seems to be complaining.
And I have dueled with the same person for up to two hours without any form of connection problem whatsoever on multiple occasions.
Guess I have been lucky.
The worst kind of connection issue you can experience is the neverending cycle, as the name suggests it does not end. you will be stuck in the "synchronizing" loop for all eternity until you close the game. not sure if it actually lasts for all eternity but I don't have the patience to find out.
Do not misunderstand me, I am only pointing out potential problems, with emphasis on potential. I cannot guarantee you will experience them, nor can I guarantee that you won't.
--[ Gameplay ]--
to dispel a certain rumor: it is not glorified rock paper scissors.
Quick list:
-----standard-----
- light attacks and heavy attacks
- dashes
- feints/ heavy attack cancels
- three directions
- zone attacks
- parries
- guarbreaks and guarbreak cancel a.k.a. teching
- stamina
- health ( what? did you think I wouldn't state the obvious?)
- executions (soooo bloody satisfying)
-----specific------
- combo's
- unblockables
- uninteruptables
- shoves, throws, bashes, kicks, heatbutts and the occasional impalement ( looking at you lawbringer)
- did somebody really think rock paper scissors covers that all? he must have played that differently from me then
anyhow, every character follows the same rules as stated under "standard". most of these are rather obvious and function as you'd expect.
when you begin the game all of these will be handled in a tutorial after which you can opt to take the advanced tutorial to complete the standard list. (finishing either gives you steel, the in game currency, so highly advised you do)
Every character behaves to a more or lesser degree different from another.
which is good considering there are only 12 as of currently, let's hope the future ones will also live up to that
as a result you can be good with one and bad with the other, but as long as you understand the basics you can use any of them rather well after a small session of training
the best teacher however is simply trying combo's and tricks, this can be done online or against bots.
these bots go from level 0 to 3.
level 2 is probably a good example of the above average player and level 3 is just plain evil.
however, the thing to note is that they are bots, as a result their guard is ussually quite a lot better than that of players.
it is clear that every character is supposed to be balanced and are thus countered by some other character and counter some others themselves, this does not guarantee a win or loss.
win or loss relies on skill a lot but also on luck, only when you are really good at reading your opponent does luck become less of a factor.
--[ Campaign]--
to put it simply, it is a tutorial wrapped in a straightforward but appreciable story. with some added treasure hunting which doubles as worldbuilding through narration.
I believe it serves the game very well.
there are three storylines, or campaigns.
each as one of the three factions.
you get to play as three characters of both the knights and vikings, but only two of the samurai.
the game can be set on easy, normal, hard and realistic
realistic means no UI except for health and stamina, meaning you have to read the moves the ai is telegraphing
I find that to be a rather usefull skill to have online, it does require you to understand the oponents character though
completing the campaign on normal and higher will unlock customizations for certain chars, higher difficulty yields ofcourse more.
--[ PvP ]--
this is where most of your playtime will sink into, unless you have some big love for the campaign (or are hellbent on finding every collectable)

honor is truly great, but vengeance is a great substitute.
now that that rant is over:
you will have people of different character levels against one another.
in the event you have three level 5 on your team against 4 prestige 5's ( level 101 till 120), it does not neccesarily mean they are more skilled than your teammates.
levels are tied to characters, as a result your teammates can be higher leveled at other chars while the enemy has only played that specific char since release.
have seen people of level 2 drill people of prestige 4 (level 81 to 100) into the ground and everyone else on their team too.
what it does affect in the teamgames is gearstats, these can be altered through customization. this alters some of your stats. can cause the infamous revenge spam.

Rise of Flight is a World War 1 flight sim that is a game made for flight sim enthusiast's, thus the game tenders to a small audience and genre. The game upon start-up is a tad confusing for someone who has never really had a flight sim, but being a normal gamer I ventured into the unknown playing a quick match. After taking awhile to find the "Start Mission" button I was off.
The game is visually stunning, even for me with a relatively old gaming rig. The detail to the airplane is stunning and really helps capture the feel of playing in one of these vintage aircraft, from the seat to the gunsight everything seems authentic and comes alive as you fly around and if you have any interest in airplanes this game takes you right in.
For controls it really depends, the only thing I can say specifically is that you NEED a joystick. Its required to play unless you want to spend hours assigning controls to your mouse. Anyways, each plane has its own play style and handles differently. Some planes require more mastery of the controls to play than others. I found that for noobs the best planes to play are German, I found they were easier to control over the British and French planes.
The Game has a couple of different modes, obviously a multi-player mode but it also has a campaign, quick match and Career mode. In Multi-player I feel as though everyone should know how it works but if not: All servers have their own maps and rules with differing difficulties meaning only so much help is given to you via onscreen gauges and auto managed engine controls. Usually the objective is to kill the enemy. Pretty basic. The campaign is (from what I gathered) just a bunch of missions with varying objectives, from intercept enemy fighters to attacking their bases. Finally my favourite mode: Career mode. In Career mode you get to choose from either Belgian, French, British or German careers (When you pick a side you are just picking a squadron from that nationality). Once you've selected what side you want to play for, you can change the date (Between September 1916, to December 1918) to get the aircraft you want, because they are available only during the time they were available during the war. Once you've done that you pick your name, age and background (E.G: I was a fisherman from New Foundland). Finally you get to play the game, the Career mode is connected to a server so you get to see leaderboards for overall scores, and people in your squadrons score. I personally like the feature, adds a bit more of a goal and sort of drives you a bit. The game also gives you a newspaper every week and its actually pretty fun to see the progression of the war in-game and on the right it has the top 50 aces and its cool to see how some keep passing the other. In Career mode you start off as the low of the low, a grunt pilot who gets assigned missions and you do em, but you get a bit of an option. In my first Career mode I decided that doing the missions were not eventful enough so I broke away from my flight and went off on my own to hunt down some Germans, I found 3 and killed them. Returning to base and finishing the flight I got awarded a Victoria Cross and a Military Cross, it was kinda cool to be awarded medals. Makes the game have even more of a goal. After a month of playing I now have him pretty high on the leaderboards. Sadly, the career mode allows for restarting the mission so I doubt many people in the top 100 have played fairly.
One thing that is very angering is the selection of planes, there are around 8-10 base planes. I assume since the game isnt very popular, the dev's made it so that to get any more planes you have to pay for the packs. It wouldnt even be that bad if the packs didnt cost $25-$30. And you only get like 4 planes, a rip off but what can you do? I would personally like to be able to make my own combination of 4 planes and pay like $15. Seems more reasonable. The base planes are among the most popular like the "Sopwith Camel" and the "Albatros" so atleast you dont have to be at a disadvantage in multiplayer because they are good fighters, just sucks there is barely any variety.
The learning curve for this game is not that bad, obviously its there and pretty hard but compared to DCS or IL2 its alot better because the planes are relatively simple, and if you really cant stand all the realistic settings you can switch em off which makes it much easier for people who could care less about learning the game and just want to shoot other planes. It caters to hardcore flight sim players and people just interested in World War 1 aviation.
A couple of personal notes that I want to discuss: Multiplayer with friends is absolutely a ton of fun, playing seriously or just messing around; Its a ton of fun. The game allows for players to be in the same plane so you and a couple friends can all be in a bomber just having the laughs of your life or actually trying to win it for the team, either way its awesome. Although, the game as a lone wolf is a bit depressing. Even when trying my hardest the enemy always seems to best me in turning or diving, and no one ever really trys to back you up. Obviously some games people coordinate the team but most times its just Call Of Duty World War 1 planes.
My final verdict is 8.5/10. The game looks amazing, has a pretty wide variety of missions and career mode is endless fun, Multiplayer can be hit or miss with some people and the lack of a variety with the planes kinda sucks. The core mechanics are solid and fluid and the game can be switched from super realistic to arcade style.

Stealth inc 2 is a platformer which means its gameplay only focuses on two things highscore and speed running.
(
pace of the game depends on the type of processor you have. those who with i3 or Amd equivalent will feel this game is slow paced. Although that in no way impacts your score/time.)
There are only 3 options in the video menu when you fire up this game, Resolution settings, MSAA and Fullscreen on & off. Visually this game feels C-3PO having sex without lube, choppy and joyless  even more so if you try to run it on fullscreen mode with the highest resolution your monitor can support. And the MSAA doesnt seem to do much either as it only goes as far as 4x.
Some sequences in the game do feel nice with ivory lights casting their dark shadows. It helps to some extent to set a tone which quickly fades when you  pass through them.
The game offers around 47 different soundtracks which switch ramdomly, although being assigned to maps. Ranging from melodies snatched from a party with raging alcoholics to calm and plesent ones. They seem to work well with the gameplay trying to sound different and interesting. Definately memorable at that.
The gameplay offers nothing new. It carries its gameplay mechanics from various other games in the market like  the Portal series and Dustforce. All you do is run around in a test facility consisting of 6 maps with 8 levels in each,  clearing test segments something like the game  Dustfroce which are suppose to add a non-linear feal. You mostly find yourself evading and/or tricking sensors that trigger traps (more so often they are lasers) or some moving with laser or sensors on it. All this  with a few gadgets at your disposal that you get every new map you advance.
The thing with games like these is that they are ment to be repetative but given the situation with this, it starts becoming more of a chore.
The game does try to keep it fresh by letting you make your own map and upload it to its community right from the game application itself. Which others would then play and rate.
You are a clone in a test facility that finds you more disposable than paper cups. Helping as many of your fellow clones as possible you must now try to escape this wretched place of effective  laser traps! All this while you are kinda being provoked by the antagonist as he wants to watch you fall/fail/die trying  so he can win 'Employee of the month'.
And well, finally,  the game was ported to pc from Wii U. Maybe thats whats wrong with this game, that affects its visuals which keep you from enjoying it. At the end of the day, you don't have that feeling to come back for more which derives me to the  conclusion buy it on sale if you must.

I've gotten this game since the patch came out so I haven't had any problems getting matches and I've been able to play them with no lag at all. I have honestly had the most fun playing as a counselor trying to escape rather than playing as Jason himself. However there are a few things that concern me and is sort of ruining the gameplay experience for me. I'll try and explain them in the best way that I can.
1.  Glitching to win:
There are several glitches in the game currently that are making the game tedius when exploited. For example there is a glitch that will allow you to run while in combat mode as a counselor and while doing so you get walk as fast as you would if you were sprinting and if your stealth stat is high enough you can quickly traverse the map undetected.
Another glitch that I have seen while playing the game is similar to the bear trap glitch that will be patched soon. This glitch allows counselors to glitch into the walls completely out of Jason's reach. The game heavily favors Jason winning and I get how annoying that is but there's nothing more annoying then having to wait the full 10 and sometimes 15 minutes for Jason to tirelessly swing and attempt to grab them whil they're stuck in the wall. I've recently played in a match where a counselor glitched into the door and ended up just above the door frame. Jason was able to kill him by just hitting the door but for some reason the game didn't register him as being dead and with all the counselors dead the game just sat there for the remaining 10 minutes anyway.
2. Jason:
As I've stated in the previous paragraph Jason is meant to be so strong that winning is in his favor but there are a few things about Jason that are simply unfair and if not changed then it could cause some people to steer away from the game.
For starters Jason is able to hit your through walls, doors and windows. I don't know why this is the case but if Jason is chasing you and you run into a cabin and shut the door, while your'e locking the door behind you he can swing through the door and hit you. Not only does he hit you but he also does damage to the door reducing the hits needed to knock it down.
In the same instance if you should go through a window the animation for diving through is so long that he can hit you as you hit the floor by swinging through the window. I have lost quite a few matches this way. Where I would go through the window and Jason's weapon would clip through the window and still hit me. With the ability to just walk through any baracade while in rage mode it just seems unfair that he should be able to swing through a door or a wall and be able to hit you as well.
The most annoying thing about Jason is his ability to grab you. I have not played Jason enough times to know how his grab feature works completely (Yes after playing 27 hours in the game I've only played as Jason maybe 10 times...), but some of his grabs literally take less than a second to pull off. So unless you have a pocket knife or a friend with good aim, you're going to die no matter how fast you tap the button mapped to escape his grip.
Aside from his grap kills and their short time windows, the biggest problem with Jason's grab is that it's immunte to everything. Here are some examples of his grab being completely OP that I have seen.
A. I have seen plenty of Jason's grab a counselor as their shotgun blast goes off allowing Jason to completely ignore the dameage and stun state.
B. I have seen Jason players grab counselors who are in the middle of swinging a weapon at them. This completely nigates the use of weapons in the game as you'll never be able to hit Jason with them. It doesn't matter if you wait around the corner or wait in the next room for an ambush. If he sees you swinging, he can grab you right out of it. The only time I've seen weapons used effectively is when Jason is still in a swinging animation from knocking down a baracaded door.
C. Jason's grab makes the victim part of his body. What I mean by this is I've seen times where Jason would grab a counselor and one of their friends would come to their aid and hit Jason with a weapon but at the same time kill their friend. Now this is obvious with the shotgun as the spread would hit both people. But I have seen this happen with a baseball bat, a sword and even the wrench. While Jason is in the grab state, a counselor would hit him from behind and the player would drop dead as Jason goes into the stun animation. And the death explanation would say "Betrayed"
D. Jason is able to grab counselors out of the window as they're climbing through. I know that this seems like a perfectly legit thing to have for Jason but what makes it unfair to me is that the counselor has to go through an animation in order to get through the window that they can not cancel should Jason be nearby. And there have been times where he has grabbed them after they've made it inside cabin. Though this can be contributed to latency issues, I feel like it's happened way too many times to just be lag.
3. Hiding:
There is a mechanic in the game that allows counselors to hide in closets and under beds. There are even maps that allow you to hide in tents. However this entire feature is useless and should be removed because Jason's Sense ability allows him to see exactly where you are hiding. This is more evident when he is in rage mode. So the counselors should have the ability to hide removed and replaced with something more useful as I have never seen a situation where hiding was beneficial. For some reason, even while hiding counselors generate enough fear to appear in Jason's Sense ability.
4. Counselor stats:
And finally the biggest issue I see with the game so far that is ruining it for me is the counselors in general. In my opinion, there's absolutely no reason to pick a male counselor in this game unless you're trying to kill Jason that run. The male counselors in the game are so underpowerwed that I have found myself picking female counselors so that I don't die within the first 10 seconds of the match. Granted some of those deaths were just me spawning by cars and spawning in the telephone cabin(which are common places that Jason players check first) but there have been several times where I would start out as a male counselor and do nothing but walk or crawl as soon as I spawn and Jason will instantly teleport to me and kill me after chasing me for nearly 4 to 6 minutes. The only two possibilities that I can think of for this is either the Jason players have a hack that lets them see exactly where you are or males make enough noise while walking and crawling to get Jason's attention. Stats included the female counselors have the highest stats across the board saving the strength stat. And the only male counselor worth playing is Tommy Jarvis. It's been my experience that walking and crawling don't matter at all for male counselors.  If you do decide to play the male characters be prepared to find yourself running from Jason withing the first 2 or so minutes of the game. Whereas I believe there's only one female character out of the bunch that can't freely job around the map undetected.
Despite this I have had tons of fun with the game so far. I haven't been bothered by only having three maps though I do hope they add more and the myth of this game only being fun in a lobby with friends isn't really true in my opinion. I've played it solo now since I've had it and there's only been one guy that I can think of that was a terrible person to most people in the lobby. I have enjoyed playing the game and sometimes turning on my mic to talk to people and work together. If this game were 59.99 I would say wait. And at 39.99 you should only buy it if you like this genre of game. It will not be for everyone and sometimes not even for fans at its current price. I can say for myself though that I haven't regretted my purchase yet.

I really, really hate to say this but I am sorely disappointed in this game's state.
I love Friday The 13th as a franchise and I was more than hyped to follow this game as it changed from "Slasher Vol 1: Summer Camp" to the Friday The 13th game it is today. At this point, probably the only enjoyment I can maybe find in this game is just seeing Jason in it in familiar locations.
I stopped playing this game for months because of game-ruining bugs such as key items for escaping getting stuck in the ground, completely rendering the counselor players helpless. It was upsetting with the fact that almost every game these things would happen. Granted now some bugs have been ironed out, I kept up with patch notes and all that fun stuff and was feeling happy and hopeful to where the game was headed.
So now I'm changing my review to this for all the right reasons. My FIRST GAME in MONTHS, we start out in the rainy Jarvis House map. Right off the bat, framerate is basically dead. Not just for me, but for my friends with high-end computers as well. But, this might be a misunderstanding since my card was set to integrated in my Nvidia control panel for whatever reason. BUT the friends on higher end PC's were still having drops. Optimization seems to kinda hit the fan a tad bit with this new lighting system that appears to be implemented (correct me if I'm wrong but I'm pretty sure I may be right) and rain may need some optimization as well. But, just as instant, what happens this time? My friend spawned in to have his camera literally placed on the ground viewing the grass which was only fixed by our friend also luckily being Jason. Otherwise, he'd have been killed and that'd have been it for him. And after I had died, I closed the game to check which graphics card it was running on and then it LITERALLY DRAGGED EVERYONE IN MY PARTY OUT OF THE GAME WHICH HAS NEVER HAPPENED BEFORE. Which brings me to my next point.
Bug fixes. This game's got a lot of bugs. And there's a page dedicated to reporting them. But the big problem is not necessarily the bugs being here but the fact that this game literally went at the very least *two whole months* without an update. According to research I just did, it got TWO updates in the span of FOUR months. One being little fixes and some DLC and then the other being the bigger, important update of more well-needed fixes. The time between these things is so ridiculous and most certainly not good for the game's rep and lifespan.
I honestly want nothing more than to see this game succeed, believe me. But I know deep down no matter how much I reassure myself, I can't help but feel like it won't. The playerbase seems to have fallen in the numbers by a ton and with how frequent fixes and updates are, which is not frequent AT ALL, I can't see anything happening.
Then there's pricing which at the moment is wayyy too much than what you get when you pay for it. Wait for a sale. Or wait til the game's content, which hopefully DLC is purely cosmetic and the rest for free, is plentiful enough to make it worth the whole $40. Which will probably be awhile.
In conclusion, maybe you might enjoy it if you're a die-hard fan and just don't give a flying♥♥♥♥♥♥about buggyness or stability. But more than likely, fan or not, you probably won't for any of the reasons I listed prior. More love and care was put in to attention and detail than anything else and it's the one thing I appreciate the most in this product. I'll keep my eye on changes and fixes and all other kinds of nonsense but at this point, there's really no fixing the utter disappointment I feel right now and I'm sorry to say it, I truly am.

"World to the West" is an Indie-RPG made by the Norwegian game studio Rain Games.
Me and my class was lucky enough to meet the team and visit their studio in Bergen, in October 2016. They let us play-test a demo of the game, and give constructive feedback to help them improve the game even further.
Pros (+):
+ Great story
+ The characters are charming, well-developed and looks good (my personal favourite must be Lord Clonington)
+ Magnificent graphics, awesome art-wise
+ The game has about 20-25 hours of gameplay (If you're a completionist like me, hunting for achievements)
+ Tons of exploration, not just limited to the main story
+ Big map
+ Price is not too big, nor too small, got it on Steam's Summer Sale though
+ Superb, original and neat soundtrack
Cons (-):
- Story is a bit too short, in my opinion
- I still don't like the font (told the developers I didn't like it too)
- Combat system can be a bit... "buggy" at times
- I got stuck some places, due to the lack of pin-pointers on where to go next
- A bit annoying having to lead one character to a saving place, then switch character and lead another one to the same saving place (A bit repetitive in that way)
So if you like RPGs, Indie-games, tons of exploration and a neat story, I'd recommend buying "World to the West".

As a huge fan of Teslagrad to the point where I became a significant member of its speedrunning community, I was looking forward to playing World to the West more than most people. Does it live up to the hype? Here's my review.
The number one question of Teslagrad fans is, how does this compare to Teslagrad?
Number one, it is much brighter and lighter than the dark themes that Teslagrad held. It is fully in 3D with very vivid, cartoony graphics. Some beautiful hand-painted scenes appear in some places as well.
Number two, there are still puzzle platform mechanics, but it should be viewed more as an homage to Legend of Zelda in that you will frequently need certain items and different character abilities to navigate the terrain and the main objective areas.
Number three, the game opens up as a fully dialouged, storylined action adventure akin to Secret of Mana, not at all like the wordless pictoral storytelling that Teslagrad did. The map is large and double layered, with a bright overworld and a spooky underground littered with tunnels and caves. There is a bustling town where you can talk to nearly everyone, and a crazy old lady drives the main plot. The overall game is much longer, slower, and more storied than Teslagrad, which is a turn-off to a speedrunner's mindset.
Number four, however, is that the game will frequently remind you that you are in the same universe as Teslagrad. You have a Teslamancer as one of the four main playable characters, with familiar abilities. While you are no longer in Electropia, you find people from the neighboring countries, Mesmer and Motorland, and get to see how they interact and what they think of Teslamancers. Jørn Lavoll delivers a superb soundtrack, which includes many references to music from Teslagrad. And of course, we can't forget the hidden scroll collecting. Many reminders from Teslagrad wait to be discovered and appreciated.
Now, the next question. How does this fare as a standalone game for people who have never seen Teslagrad?
Overall, you can't help but compare it to Legend of Zelda. It feels very much like it, but is still quite fun in its own way. Since it is from a small Norwegian indie game developer, you can't expect it to be as huge as Breath of the Wild. But it's also one-quarter of the price.
The opening chapters of the game introduce you to the main characters one by one, occasionally crossing paths, until late game when they all converge together and you are then allowed to freely roam. Until that point, the game feels a bit constrained and scripted. At first the characters are physically constrained from roaming, with obstacles they can't clear until acquiring special items later on. And even then, at one particular point after acquiring a new item and attempting to go back and explore with it, I was annoyed at the old lady literally stopping me and saying "No, you can't explore yet, go do your quest first."
Another point some people may not like is that there are checkpoints throughout the world where you can teleport from point to point, but each character cannot teleport to a checkpoint unless they have personally visited it already, so there's quiite a bit of travel needed because you essentially need to traverse the world four times, once with each character, to acquire a sufficient set of checkpoints for each one. The main objective areas require the combined might of all four characters, so hauling each one to each area is a bit of a slog, but it can also be treated as a challenging puzzle because each character needs to take a slightly different path governed by their ability to circumvent obstacles. So there are often times when you see a shiny thingy you want to reach, and say to yourself, "Well, only that character can reach it. Now how do I get them all the way over here?"
Overall I give World to the West a big thumbs up. To me, Teslagrad is Rain's Hobbit, and World to the West is their Lord of the Rings. A heavily expanded and richer gaming experience. I can't wait to see what's next.

In theory this game is an okay effort at making a competitive fighting game. In actuality it's a hastily thrown together mess of a partially finished game. Let's start with characters. Some of them are good enough to play as. Some of them aren't. Some characters physically can't change blocking directions fast enough to deal with certain characters, and move too slow to get away or fight back. If Ubisoft cared about balance, they would all be fun (or at least not tedious) to play. The combat is 90% ganking, which makes the game frustrating and pointless. Not only that, there just isn't enough to do. Since there's no real punishment for ganking, no one plays the game normally. The other biggest annoyance is that tons of people pick a fast blocking character and max out their revenge, which is just as obnoxious and tedious as getting ganked over, and over, and over again with nothing you can do about it. And lastly, we have the connectivity problems. There are some days playing For Honor where I get kicked from or lose connection to at least half the matches I que up for. The game freaks out when anyone leaves the game, sometimes resulting in kicks. This is the result of them using a proven failure of a connectivity system, player to player (just like the old days in COD when the game broke when someone rage-quit). The game feels less than half-finished, and is less balanced than Dark Souls 1 PVP. RIP For Honor, you could have been a good game. I wish I had poured less time into this steaming pile of crap so I could get my hard earned money back.

This is a first kind of review I have ever written, so expect some inconsistenties.
As I write this I have almost 50 hours of gameplay on record. This is only in the finished game, although I also played in the open beta.
Summary:
- Connection ( the elephant in the room)
- gameplay ( the reason you'd buy it in the first place)
- Campaign ( it does exist)
- PvP ( and the supposed unbalance)
- conclusion
--[ Connection]--
The biggest issue with this game is obviously the way it's matchmaking works. You will hear many people complain about connection issues and occasionally lag ( I say occasionally because you have to connect in the first place to experience lag)
For me however, this has not been the case, atleast not of a magnitude of which everybody else seems to be complaining.
And I have dueled with the same person for up to two hours without any form of connection problem whatsoever on multiple occasions.
Guess I have been lucky.
The worst kind of connection issue you can experience is the neverending cycle, as the name suggests it does not end. you will be stuck in the "synchronizing" loop for all eternity until you close the game. not sure if it actually lasts for all eternity but I don't have the patience to find out.
Do not misunderstand me, I am only pointing out potential problems, with emphasis on potential. I cannot guarantee you will experience them, nor can I guarantee that you won't.
--[ Gameplay ]--
to dispel a certain rumor: it is not glorified rock paper scissors.
Quick list:
-----standard-----
- light attacks and heavy attacks
- dashes
- feints/ heavy attack cancels
- three directions
- zone attacks
- parries
- guarbreaks and guarbreak cancel a.k.a. teching
- stamina
- health ( what? did you think I wouldn't state the obvious?)
- executions (soooo bloody satisfying)
-----specific------
- combo's
- unblockables
- uninteruptables
- shoves, throws, bashes, kicks, heatbutts and the occasional impalement ( looking at you lawbringer)
- did somebody really think rock paper scissors covers that all? he must have played that differently from me then
anyhow, every character follows the same rules as stated under "standard". most of these are rather obvious and function as you'd expect.
when you begin the game all of these will be handled in a tutorial after which you can opt to take the advanced tutorial to complete the standard list. (finishing either gives you steel, the in game currency, so highly advised you do)
Every character behaves to a more or lesser degree different from another.
which is good considering there are only 12 as of currently, let's hope the future ones will also live up to that
as a result you can be good with one and bad with the other, but as long as you understand the basics you can use any of them rather well after a small session of training
the best teacher however is simply trying combo's and tricks, this can be done online or against bots.
these bots go from level 0 to 3.
level 2 is probably a good example of the above average player and level 3 is just plain evil.
however, the thing to note is that they are bots, as a result their guard is ussually quite a lot better than that of players.
it is clear that every character is supposed to be balanced and are thus countered by some other character and counter some others themselves, this does not guarantee a win or loss.
win or loss relies on skill a lot but also on luck, only when you are really good at reading your opponent does luck become less of a factor.
--[ Campaign]--
to put it simply, it is a tutorial wrapped in a straightforward but appreciable story. with some added treasure hunting which doubles as worldbuilding through narration.
I believe it serves the game very well.
there are three storylines, or campaigns.
each as one of the three factions.
you get to play as three characters of both the knights and vikings, but only two of the samurai.
the game can be set on easy, normal, hard and realistic
realistic means no UI except for health and stamina, meaning you have to read the moves the ai is telegraphing
I find that to be a rather usefull skill to have online, it does require you to understand the oponents character though
completing the campaign on normal and higher will unlock customizations for certain chars, higher difficulty yields ofcourse more.
--[ PvP ]--
this is where most of your playtime will sink into, unless you have some big love for the campaign (or are hellbent on finding every collectable)
Most important piece of note: Honor is a choice made by players
since when have online players ever been consistently honorable in a game?
just because the game is called For Honor people will not suddenly change
especially in teammatches honor is something you should not expect your enemy or your team to have
however, some of the best moments in the game have been when either or both were honorable.
If the enemy however is not honorable, by all means feel free to throw them of a cliff.
honor is truly great, but vengeance is a great substitute.
now that that rant is over:
you will have people of different character levels against one another.
in the event you have three level 5 on your team against 4 prestige 5's ( level 101 till 120), it does not neccesarily mean they are more skilled than your teammates.
levels are tied to characters, as a result your teammates can be higher leveled at other chars while the enemy has only played that specific char since release.
have seen people of level 2 drill people of prestige 4 (level 81 to 100) into the ground and everyone else on their team too.
what it does affect in the teamgames is gearstats, these can be altered through customization. this alters some of your stats. can cause the infamous revenge spam.
--[conclusion]--
is it a good game?
yes, its gameplay is solid and satisfying.
is it time consuming?
matchtimes depend on the gametype but in general it is really addicting
I believe you can always improve on every aspect of the gameplay
does it have issues?
connection for some
are there rage factors?
connection for some and certain chars ( I do so badly want to shove that spear down your throat nobushi)
is it worth your money?
if you like its gameplay and can thus allow time to slip between your fingers while playing, then sure
as a piece of advise, if you do get bored, go try to master another character, it helps a lot
in the end, the core of the game is solid and it is that which is worth your money.
The connection issues can only become less while its core can not.
if you are sceptic, but gaben blesses you during a sale with a discount on the game, I suggest you buy it
I hereby end my review

Pyre is a weird game and hard to recommend. Compared to other Supergiant releases, it's longer and has more content and a more developed setting, but the combat which is at the center of the gameplay can be infuriating and gate plot information. It's hard to tell wheter it was infuriating because I was invested into the plot and didn't want certain outcomes or because it's genuinely annoying.
In principle the combat is very novel and interesting but some characters don't feel very responsive or fluid and really do their part to extinguish that feeling of fast paced tactical back-and-forth.
The plot and its accompanying artistic assets guarded by the combat sequences are, I suspect, the reason everyone praises Pyre. The storyline follows a qualitatively diverse cast of characters that are well written and superbly illustrated, although said illustrations are scarce and subtler implications are hidden in tooltips and subtexts rather than perceptible on the portraits.
Visually, the crisp portraits contrast with the colourful compositions that make up the landscapes of the world map. It's a very weird mixture but not unpleasant, especially when you start to take notice of all the little elements that are related to the lore, or when you're told about the epic events of the past that shaped the land.
The soundtrack is another Supergiant masterpiece but this time denser with lore and more dependent on the context of the game, which I suspect will make it harder to listen to on its own, unlike Transistor's and Bastion's.
One of the main concerns people voice about Supergiant Games' releases is that the games are very short, however, Pyre proves to be an improvement considering it has a fair amount of replayability and lore locked behind different decisions, as well as a Versus mode.
I've just finished playing the Standard Campaign, which, without counting breaks, took 14 hours, reading all the lore and interacting with everything I could.
It's a hard recommendation because the plot is what drives the player forward, but it can feel very wide yet shallow until some later elements are introduced or events take place. It tackles the broad subject of freedom and the understanding of freedom but lacks a proper exploration of the subject, focusing instead on the struggle of certain hard decisions, leaving untied ends in previous topics and ultimately not making you reflect about the implied main topic at all.
That said, it's still a very nice piece of art tied up as a video game, which is what I get Supergiant Games' stuff for.
