Pyre is... a game. Certainly, it is a very different game from Supergiant's previous games, Bastion and Transistor, which were themselves different from each other. Unlike them, Pyre is not really an action game, yet like them Pyre has a heavy emphasis on its story, if not heavier than either - for once, what's going on is a lot clearer than it was in either of Supergiant's previous games.
It is hard to describe what kind of game Pyre actually is - you could call it a sports game involving a fantasy sport, because that's a large part of the game. Or a Visual Novel, because that's also a part of the game. And I'm not even sure what to call the part of the game that connects the aforementioned two parts together - it's definitely unique.
Let's describe the gameplay first, a radical departure from the more action-based gameplay of Bastion and Transistor. You pick three exiles at the start of a Rite, each with different abilities, but can only control one at a time, and your goal is to extinguish your enemy team's Pyre using the orb, usally starting at 100 with each Exile doing a certain amount of damage, usually 15, 20, or 30. You can also banish exiles on the enemy team by casting one of your exile's auras at them or running into them with an exile with a larger aura - or any exile if they have the orb, since having the orb takes away your aura. You can also fling the orb, which may not do as much damage to a pyre as simply jumping into it but won't banish your exile. Early on, this is fairly easy to win, since your opponents won't be quite as aggresssive, but later on it get quite tough when you start facing enemy teams with their own items and abilities or teams with exiles that can temporarily hover. You can also make it harder by using Titan Stars, Pyre's equivalent of Bastion's Shrine and Transistor's Limiters, though Titan Stars come halfway unless you're on True Nightwings mode, and with Titan Stars rites can become very, very difficult. There's also Scribe Trials, Pyre's equivalent of Bastion's Proving Grounds and Transistor's Tests, each one dedicated to a different exile and will give you a special talisman for that exile only when completed successfully, and they tend to be very powerful. In terms of length, it is by far Supergiant's longest game.
As previously stated, Pyre has a much clearer story than Bastion or Transistor, and on top of that, it is a lot more focused on individual characters than either of them were, particularly the band of exiles that make up the Nightwings and the leaders of enemy teams, and a few others as well. The basic premise of the story is clear: you were exiled from the Commonwealth, as was everyone you come across, and you desire to return by proving yourself in the Rites. Everyone wants to return, and that's the reason for the gameplay of the Rites. On top of all this, Pyre has a bit more worldbuilding than Bastion or Transistor - the Book of Rites will reveal more pages of itself as you go through the game, and tell you more about the world, as well as what the characters themselves will tell you at times. I can't really speak much more of the story, since Pyre is definitely a little more based on its story than Supergiant's previous games.
It wouldn't be a Supergiant game if it didn't have a lot of emphasis on its music, and Pyre definitely delivers on that. I would say that Pyre's soundtrack hops around a bit more between genres, especially for the themes of enemy teams. Where it becomes really good though are two certain songs, which I would say blow anything from Bastion or Transistor out of the water - and it's hard to express what I want to say about them without actually spoiling why they're great.
Pyre is a good game, but it's also radically different from Supergiant's previous games, and it's easy to understand why people might be unsure how to feel about it. But I'd say to give it a chance, even if you feel unsure.

I love Stealth ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. I played the hell out of the original free version, made a dozen levels, played the hell out of the deluxe version, made more levels. The anticipation for this one was big.
So, how does it hold up comparing to its predecessors? Not amazingly well, unfortunately. But still a great game nonetheless.
One difference, which I must say is not better nor worse but probably worth mentioning, is the stealth aspect of the gameplay suffered a big blow. The level design emphasizes platforming, the vision cone of the enemies is not as reliable as it used to and you can't easily tell where the shadows are just by looking at the screen. What makes this dead clear is that not once while playing this game I looked at my visibility meter, I completely forgot it existed. It's almost irrelevant now.
I always thought the level designers working on stealth ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ were brilliant! Well, that is absolutely still there. Very clever, fluid and challenging. It is a rare thing for me to stop while playing a game to admire the amazing cleverness of the level in front of me and this happens frequently here.
Now for the big problem I have with the game: open world map with metroidvania elements. Why, why must I witness game after game making the same exact mistake. Any game that contains puzzle elements, like complex platforming, stealth or old plain box pushing have the same limitation: no immediate replay value. Once you solved the puzzle, giving it to you to solve again will not bring any new experience, satisfaction or challenge. Backtracking through a door you already know the combination is not a challenge but a chore. That's why it didn't work on Fez, that's why it didn't work on Thief 3 and Thief 4 and that is why it didn't work on Stealth Inc 2.
At first I was keeping an open mind about it. They have great level designers, maybe they figured a way to keep the nonlinear map an interesting aspect of the game. For a while it did, navigation was easy, one part led to another, stealth elements were rightfully kept to a minimum and so on. But inevitably the player will take a wrong turn and get lost on a map of solved puzzles and that's when the tediousness strikes. I kept desperately clicking on the map screen hoping there was a warp-to feature, so I can finally get to the next test room, the part of the game that is worth my time.
Anyway, if you can swallow this annoying aspect of the game, the test rooms are a blast! Precision platforming with interesting new mechanics being added as the game progresses all designed masterfully. There are also additional challenges as usual for replay value.

A hybrid between point and click mystery and hidden object, this one isn't that bad. For what it's worth, it will keep you casually entertained for a while. The point and click part is rather typical, and I have to say most of the puzzles are quite logical. It's not outstanding, but if you catch it on a good sale, you can go for it, maybe for kids or for a couple of hours of mental rest.
PROS:
+ Simple, straight-forward, good within its genre.
+ No ludicrous inventory combinations -mostly.
NEITHER/NOR:
# Story was... kind of like in porn, a forced excuse for the puzzles and the hidden object scenes, but not that awful.
# Voice acting was poor, but within the "cartoon-esque" style of most hidden object games.
CONS:
- The backtracking lost all logical sense after a while, destroying immersion.
Example: you get to a room where a very dramatic situation is happening, and you need to act quickly... BUT you also need to go back to room #4 to pick up that piece of XXX, then combine it with the item in room #7 at the other end of the place, then cross a river and catch a plane, then finally go back to your... emergency? Made no sense at all.
- The "oh I need a special shaped key" became annoying after a while and took over any hint of story.

Generic hidden object game, you move around the rooms solving puzzles, collecting keys and interacting with various objects in order to advance to the next room, sometimes you have to click on certain items in a screen filled with a variety of objects. The plot, your character receives a mysterious letter by his close friend Victor Frankenstein who is asking him for help in some urgent matter.
The Pros
Interesting plot even if you can predict what is going to happen from the first few moments.
Cool cutscenes filled with flipping medical sketches and brownish notepads. I really liked them.
Nice locations and backgrounds, a lot of rooms.
Low price.
The Cons
The game’s difficulty is a joke, there is no time restriction or anything like that. I solved some of the puzzles in less than twenty seconds on the hardest difficulty (there are two difficulty settings) and I waited to see if the second part of the puzzle would be harder but there wasn’t one.
The backtracking in this game is ridiculous, you travel back and forth between the rooms collecting keys, every key consist of two or three similarly shaped objects scattered around in different locations. You will have to collect at least forty key pieces throughout the game , there is a navigation menu for quick traveling around the rooms but advancing to the next location quickly becomes a chore .
The menus are too close to some puzzle interface buttons so you might open them by mistake.
Some locations are completely bizarre, why does Frankenstein have a carrousel in his front yard? How does a pirate ship end up in the middle of a lake on top of a mountain? Stuff like that.
Conclusion , It is not that bad of a game but there are better ways of prolonging the game’s duration instead of scattering two million keys around the rooms  and locking them behind meaningless (because of the low difficulty ) puzzles . The game felt too much of a chore for me to enjoy compared with other games of the same genre and the plot slowed down to a crawl for most of its duration because of the same reasons . Buy it if you like running around and collecting things .

My main gripe with this game is how it's structured. I'm sure a lot of people really like how there's 4 characters that each have different abilities, but personally I didn't like it that much. In Zelda, you just have Link, and an area you can't access means "come back later when you have the hookshot", for example. In this, an area you can't access means "come back later as a different character." That is fine, and all, except you end up exploring the same world as different characters who traverse it only a little differently from each other. You can't use totems you unlock on one character, as another one. Scarf girl finds a totem, and only she can teleport to it.
And the first few hours of the game, at least, are populated with "get these two characters from point A to point B", except they might only barely help each other solve puzzles if at all. It's just "here's one puzzle, solve it twice". Now maybe, later in the game, the puzzles get more complex, and require teamwork, but I wasn't really enjoying the game enough to justify sitting through it until that point.
I'd also prefer if the totems did not exist as anything other than save points, and you could just swap between available characters on the fly. It's kind of a huge pain to run around with each character to unlock the totem for them. But I realized that if that were the case, there would be no real reason to even keep 4 seperate characters at all.
Anyway, the game looks nice, and connects to Teslagrad, which is cool, so totally go for it if you think you'll like it. I didn't, though.
Also I loaded a save and lost a solid hour of progress, so that sucked.

World to the West is the successor to Teslagrad, a game which takes inspiration from the old Zelda titles. World to the West puts you in the shoes of four odd characters who have different abilities. They all have individual storylines at the start but after a customary introduction, they all somehow end up in the company of each other.
For example, the game starts off with Lumina’s story who is trailing with her father and comes across a field which requires her to use the blink ability of hers to cross gaps. A little later she is teleported into a different world and the game basically starts there. Other characters Teri, Knaus and Lord Clonington are similarly introduced with their own character motivations and skills.
Teri is a mindbender and can bend the will of her enemies to make them do her bidding and solve other puzzles while Knaus can dig into ground and reach the opposite sections of the blockades. He can also stealth away from the enemies by using this ability of his. Lord Clonington is a brawler with a wide arsenal of fighting skills and the ability to smash rocks and climb ledges.
World to the West features a large map and leaves to your own for figuring out which character will be suitable for the puzzles and blockades found on the map. In a metroidvania style of gameplay, there will be roadblocks which you can’t unlock unless you come back with unlocked abilities.
There are fast travel points present throughout the map in the form of totem poles. These also act as checkpoints in the game and you respawn at these points if you die at the path ahead. The same checkpoints also act as a character swapper as the characters do not move together.
This leads to a fair amount of backtracking and takes more time to figure out some puzzles than it should. The option to change characters on the fly would have been more appreciated in this sort of a game. Another gripe for me is the fact that unlocking a fast travel point with one character doesn’t unlock it for the others. These small issues make the game feel somewhat more repetitive than it actually is.
The combat in World to the West is simple and very easy. The enemies mostly feel harmless and are only useful in increasing the difficulty of some puzzles. The bosses are also easy to beat with the simple combat system. While the combat is not the strength of World to the West, its exploration certainly is.
There are a number of collectibles dotted around the map and unlike something like Assassin’s creed, these collectibles do not have markers or you cannot place markers to remind you of these. You need to keep in mind where you found the location of these while switching to another character. While most of these are optional stuff and mostly gives an increment to the health bars, the game requires you to collect a certain number of these to reach the final area.
The game’s story while not much interesting is genuinely funny and you can be assured to have a few chuckles throughout the journey. The way the characters interact with the environments and side characters and the manner in which they comment on it ensures that the game feels fresh. The game also does not overstay its welcome and ends around a 9-hour mark. Your mileage on this may vary.
World to the West sports a very unique and visually pleasing aesthetic.  The environments are nicely designed and there is a lot of detail present in every frame. Things like leaving footprints adds some nice visual flavour.
There are a lot of colors popping out here and there without making it look crowded on the screen. World to the West is nothing groundbreaking in terms of its visuals but it is a delight to look at.
Excellent sound design is present throughout the game. The soundtrack is brilliant and adds to the environment beautifully. A couple of tracks here and there felt out of place sometimes but it does a great job of looping them in at the correct times.
World to the West is a very enjoyable exploration game. Go into this not for the combat but the exploration aspects of it. There are some solid puzzles, some genuinely funny moments, good character building and a neat visual aesthetic. There are few nitpicks here and there but it does not take away from the overall experience of the game. It might be steep for some people but if you like this sort of games, World to the West is going to be right up your alley.

World to the West is a game I've been looking forward to for years, ever since I first played Teslagrad in 2015, and I'd say it lived up to my hype reasonably well. Though it plays nothing at all like its prequel - it's in 3D, for a start, and takes place in an open world with vastly different mechanics - it takes place in the same fantasy realm and has quite a few callbacks to the original game.
For a 3D game, it runs very well on my low-end computer, although the hitboxes can be a little bit problematic at times, particularly when fighting. That being said, however, the movement is smooth and the controls are learnable if not intuitive.
The plot of the game isn't strong by any means, but it's acceptable, I suppose. It was mostly an excuse to get me to explore different areas, which was naturally delicious and ate up my time quite nicely. The dialogue, however, is extremely amusing. 10/10 would recommend that dialogue.
"I'll give you one thing, young lady: you have spirit."
"That's what old people say when they can't say anything nice."
Mechanics are where the game really shines. It can best be described as a co-op game for one player, and the varying mechanics of the four different, interchangeable characters are used primarily to help the others progress. With so many skills, it took me quite a while to figure out some of the puzzles - they're not Teslagrad good, but they're clever nonetheless. It really isn't something I've played before, and for that I salute Rain Games.

NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
World to the West is the follow-up game to the popular indie 'Metroidvania' platformer, Teslagrad, from developer Rain Games.
In World to the West, you alternately play four unlikely heroes: Lumina, a young girl with the ability to teleport short distances; Knaus, a small young boy who is able to crawl through tight spaces and dig tunnels underground; Miss Teri, a renowned adventurer with a very useful scarf; and Clonington, a cloned strong man with the ability to, well, punch things really hard. These four heroes are brought together by a mysterious old woman whom everyone calls "Auntie", who shows them all their own carved faces on a series of magic totems positioned about the game world.
Graphics - World to the West features cartoonish 3D graphics with basic textures and a somewhat dated look. The characters are colourful and unique, with their individual personalities suiting their character models and animations well. The creatures you encounter are mostly well done, too. But sometimes the world looks rather bland, with limited variation within similar areas, and the simple textures doing little to bring the world to life. This is especially true of some of the dingy underground sections.
The exceptions to this are the dynamic lighting, which looks really rather nice, the shadows, some special effects, and some of the outdoor water sections, which look quite lovely. The water, especially, doesn't really fit in with the rest of the simple, cartoon-style graphics, however.
There are also some issues with hit detection against platforms, and I've been caught out by invisible platform sections along walls, and other visible sections of rock that would let me fall straight through them. There are some sections where I became stuck on walls or objects, too, though I managed to wriggle my way free eventually each time.
Graphics options are limited to antialiasing and shadow settings, as well as the baseline resolution, windowed/full-screen mode, and vsync.
Sound - The title music is lovely and a nice introduction to the game. The in-game music is good, too, and somewhat typical of the genre. For some reason much of it reminded me of good ol' Spyro on PSX.
Sound effects are fine -- nothing jaw dropping, but also nothing terrible. There is no speech.
Gameplay - Unlike its predecessor, World to the West is a 3D puzzle platformer through and through. You must use the unique abilities of each of the four different characters at your disposal in order to progress through the game, with each of the characters being best suited for particular puzzle types.
The game begins slowly, gradually introducing you to the four heroes one at a time, and also introducing them to each other. The plot is revealed slowly, too, with each character having his or her own individual goals. Characterisation of the heroes is one of the game's strong points; if you're like me you'll find yourself looking forward to playing one of the characters over the others, as they all have different personalities and play styles.
The objective of the game is basically one of exploration. The game is divided into above and below ground levels, each broken up into smallish areas with one or more paths available to travel to other areas. Many areas have a range of puzzles, most of which can only be solved by a particular hero's abilities. Some have encounters with creatures or other enemies, who can often be avoided, but not always. In some areas you'll also find magical totems on which the heroes' faces are portrayed. These are save points that restore some of your health, and also allow you to teleport to any other totems that the current hero has previously visited.
And this leads me to what is probably the most frustrating part of the game: characters can only teleport to totems that they have visited themselves, leading to a considerable amount of backtracking over ground already explored by other characters in order to reach a totem with a different character in order to solve a nearby puzzle. This needless repetitiveness could have been easily avoided, too, by allowing all characters to teleport to any totem that has been unlocked by any of them.
Combat, too, when unavoidable, is rather repetitive and definitely not one of the game's strong points. Once I began play with Clonington, the 'tough' of the group, my interest in the game rapidly decreased, as fighting one after another of the same two creature types wasn't really my idea of fun. I did persevere, though, and things became more interesting again after he'd solved his first individual quest.
Often in the 3D platform genre, the controls can make or break a game, and I'm happy to say that using a controller with World to the West works extremely well, like a good console platformer should. It was good enough that I didn't even try with keyboard and mouse. Characters went where I told them and did what I wanted them to do every time (except for the graphical issues mentioned above).
The game is often quite slow to progress, so I found I had to be in the right frame of mind to focus on the puzzles and enjoy the relaxed pace. Finding a new item that grants a character a new ability was always a great way to reinvigorate my interest, too, but these were a bit too few and far between to hang out for them.

Cons:

- Graphics are a bit lacking in some areas
- Moves a bit too slowly in parts
- Not inexpensive
World to the West is a competent 3D puzzle platformer with a mildly interesting plot, good characterisation, and a fair whack of content. Some of the pointless backtracking across already-explored locations to get new characters to totems gets a bit wearing, as does the mindless combat, and the graphics look a bit dated and bland in some sections, letting down the game a little bit. And at its retail price, it's not exactly cheap for the genre, either.
Still, if 3D puzzle platform games are your thing, then you should give World to the West a try.

Ages ago, I wrote a review about the first game I picked up from Supergiant: Transistor, a game that I strongly considered one of the greatest I had ever played. Solid in soundtrack, gameplay, artistic direction and just about anything else you could name, it quickly convinced me to keep an eye on Supergiant (whom I had not heard of prior to picking the game up). Lo and behold, one day I jump on Steam to see Pyre made by the same folks who blew my mind with their previous title. Naturally, considering the pedestal I had put Transistor on, I couldn't help but pick up Pyre. Silly me, I thought I was prepared for the next Transistor. But Pyre is anything but the next Transistor - and I'm all the more pleased by that.
Unlike its linear predecessors, Pyre is a game all about decisions. Hard decisions. Agonizingly difficult choices that can change the end result a fair amount. We're talking things you really have to weigh out before committing to them. You, the Reader, are exiled for the crime of being able to read - a punishment that often leads to death. But you, Reader, are fortunate enough to run across three masked, robe-wearing people who save your life. In exchange? They ask you to read a book THEY have -  the Book of Rites, as it is - which happens to be the key to freedom from the Downside. The catch? Only so many can go free. The biggest choice for you, Reader, is who the freed will be.
And boy, do they make the choices hurt. The game plays as a mix between a sort of choose your own adventure book and a 3-on-3 sport thing that I can't really describe with any accuracy. The pain is during the liberation rites - send home your worthy opponent by throwing the match? Send home your favorite character and lose your best competitor in the Rites? Send home someone you care less about but risk never having the chance to send your favorites back? Send the best for the revolution, or the most deserving in your eyes? These choices plague you the entire game, and the weight of these decisions is definitely a highlight of the game's writing: Supergiant creates true beings, characters that all have their own stories and personalities, all with their own reasons to be sent home. At the same time, many of your opponents also have very real reasons to go home. Everyone has a struggle, and your play and choices will decide who is freed from it. The game covers it at the end as well, informing you of what happened to who was freed and who was not. It makes your decisions crucial.
The soundtrack is something else. Back when I reviewed Transistor, I said I doubted another soundtrack would come close to matching it. Here I am now, eating my words, because Darren Korb and Ashley Barrett AGAIN managed to make something just as good if not better. Each team has its own music, the pieces during travels are incredible, and the credits song (Bound Together) might have actually taken my favorite song spot from The Spine off Transistor's soundtrack. Flawless sound design brings this world to life in a way that is tough to explain, but better off experienced.
All in all, this is another exquisite entry into the Supergiant library of games. Great gameplay (and they weren't afraid to do something MASSIVELY different, which deserves respect in a time when most companies play it safe), a soundtrack to move even the most stoic listener, and terrific worldbuilding with lifelike characters.
My only complaint is that I still don't have a goddamn Ti'Zo plushie. Supergiant, just saying...it's around the holidays...it'd be realllllllllllll cool to have one.

Got this on sale for 50 cents, so I can't really complain, but for $5 this game would be a big disappointment. Think of all the things that tend to be tedious about hidden object adventure games: lots of pointless back-and-forth between locations, stiff 3D animated cut scenes, tasks that demand exactly the right tool even though you have plenty of stuff that should be able to solve the problem... this game had it all.
That last issue was especially aggravating in this game. It's annoying when you use an item and it vanishes from your inventory when any rational person would keep it around, and that happens here with a torch and a bucket, both of which would come in handy later. You do get to keep quite a few items for most of the game, like a knife, a crowbar, and a screwdriver.
But for example, when you find a cabinet with a missing handle and a cracked glass door, you can't use your crowbar to shatter the already broken glass to get the fishing pole you can clearly see in reach. You have to run around for ten minutes until you find that missing handle. At one point I was confronted with boards nailed across a doorway. I couldn't use the crowbar because the boards were nailed from the other side, which is dumb enough, but I also couldn't use the hacksaw in my inventory to saw through the boards. No explanation for that. The game forced me to wait until I found an ax before I could get through those boards.
That kind of thing happened over and over again. Along with another pet peeve of mine that shows up in too many of these games: you're supposedly racing to rescue your friends, but your character is too squeamish to touch cobwebs or coal with his bare hands, so you have to go find gloves and tools. It breaks any suspension of disbelief the story managed to work up.
I play this type of game partly to admire the illustrations, and this had nice art. But in some little areas, the second I clicked on the items to add them to my inventory, the scene vanished, and I wasn't able to click on it and see it again, which seems like a waste after they went to the trouble to illustrate those areas.
The story for some reason makes Igor out to be the villain rather than Viktor, but this change doesn't seem to amount to much. It appears to be set in the original story's time period, but there are weird anachronisms-- at one point, you find and search a Volkswagon Beetle! The hidden object scenes and puzzles were very easy.
For one or two bucks this game would be okay, but I think anyone who pays more than that would be disappointed.

2. The game is stupendously short. You can reach the end in two and a half hours on normal if you've played spectacle brawlers with platforming elements before. No, I'm not kidding: two and a half hours. Even for £5 on sale it's an absolute ripoff.
There are a variety of other issues with the game, including:
- Story being non-existent. It really does feel like a cash-in. No thought was put into it at all. Using the already lame clone excuse in order to pull the player in for another full-priced ride that has poorer combat and lasts only 20% of time it took to beat the original game is incredibly ♥♥♥♥♥♥ of the publisher and dev.
- Repetitive enemies. Each enemy type has a particular way to beat them; a single weakness the game tells you the moment you meet them. The rest of the level is then you exploiting that weakness and meeting the same enemies again... And again... And again.
- You meet Yoda. At one time I thought this would have been cool... Now it just feels forced. "Look how Star Wars we are! We're part of the universe!" Not to mention, the 'level' you meet Yoda in (yes, it's counted as one of nine levels) involves jumping up a cliff then running into a cave. There's no combat whatsoever. It's basically a five minute cutscene.
- Plot holes and inconsistencies; general lack of an attempt to flesh out the narrative. They could have done a hell of a lot with clone Starkiller, but they didn't. They just used it as an excuse to bring him back for a sequel.
However, if you really don't care about any of the above problems and don't mind the price and/or are a big fan of the first game, it might be worth picking up solely based on the cool-factor of a boss fight against an alien 1000x your size while plummeting towards a planet surface. That's about the only cool thing I found in this, though.

Thoroughly enjoyed my first experience of this game. I had never heard of it before, but I have been looking for a game just like this for a long time.
Although it is an old game (11+ years), this does not feel old in anyway, and if you told me it was released this year, I wouldn't be able to tell you otherwise without seeing the date.
It is a great spin on the save the world nonsense that has been milked by companies for years (like the Quantum of Solace game that is just repackaged Goldeneye, (but lets not travel that rabbit hole)), and allows you to do the exact opposite, like setting traps for inspectors, interrogating prisoners, building a beautiful underground lair :) and just allowing yourself to be a generally bad guy.
Once you get involved in building that beautiful lair and your nefarious empire it becomes extremely hard to stop (see that time played of 8 and a half hours, that was just on the first night). I consider replayability (its a word) to be one of the greatest measures of a game, especially on PC and this is one that will be in my library for the long haul, up there with Sins of a Solar Empire, Duke Nukem, AOE 2, C&C RA2, etc. You know those games where you may not play them for a while, but you always find yourself coming back to reinstall and play them.. well this is no doubt one of those.
I am (like the rest of the community) hoping rebellion brings out a second at some stage, but to be honest, if that day never comes I don't think il be overly disappointed because this is such a great game and its aged like a fine wine.
The other bonus to age is that prices drop, and even without a sale this bad boy is a bargain.

You may not like this game if (these are not intended to be negatives):

3. ...you prefer a gun/weapon in your hand(s) to clear obstacles.

6. ...you don't like exploring / prefer action.

I'll start off by saying that this game could've been really good, but unfortunetly it's just not.
I wanted to like this game (and I tried really hard to) but I spend most of my time getting irritated by the unbalanced classes and really stupid things in the fightingsystem.
Extremly unbalanced,♥♥♥♥♥♥p2p, Bad matchmaking and gear has too much impact on gameplay. Guardbreaking and deflecting is broken. Getting caught by guardbreak leads to getting thrown 10 meters and off a cliff which leads to instant death even though you have been winning the duel. Characters like Shugoki or Raider are at a huge disadvantage which is why you usually face 4 agility classes in a game with the exception of some warchiefs and a few nobushi. Since any agilityclass can parry or deflect a shugoki Heavy attack (Which leads the shugoki to lose ALL their stamina on one attack.) without any real difficulty you basicly just have to dodge untill that attack comes to completly cripple the shugoki class. It's also real interesting how a tiny 50kg agilityhero can easily guardbreak and throw a sumowrestler or norse giant 5 meters off of a cliff. To top things off you can't by yourself fall to your death which actually leaves you the option of combatrolling towards a ledge, somehow that still counts as dodging an attack even though you didn't move from your original position. Dodging also works when you're just rolling into a wall.
To balance things they could've made guardpenetrating attacks unparryable, which still leaves regular heavy attacks for the parry but forces them to dodge and create distance when the special attack comes.
Agilityclasses should not be able to throw heavy classes like they're big bags of air, instead the throw could've changed into a short stun.
If you force someone into a corner or lead them to a ledge that should actually lead to you having the advantage in the fight, THEY SHOULD NOT BE ABLE TO ROLL INTO THE WALL AND SOMEHOW STILL DODGE. and if you're stupid enough to roll down a cliff YOU SHOULD DIE. I bought Gothic when it came out originally, it ran badly on my pc back then but i loved the environment, characters, quests, everything, when Gothic 2 came out it again ran kinda badly on my pc (the teleport rune to the port brough all PCs down) and Gothic 3 was too much for a small team and a publisher that released a game to early. After that we had an add-on developed by somebody in india and a new game by Spellbound. That company never made an RPG, being more famous for their Airline Tycoon game as well as Desperados and Robin Hood, Tycoon and Strategy games, they had no experience with RPGs and it shows.
Even if you remove the "Gothic!" stigma from the game (and that's hard considering you still encounter the same characters and they sometimes (like Lester) act like they know you from long before) you have a very mediocre "by the numbers" rpg with the same old "go there and get this" and "go there and kill this guy" quests, with caves that usually go in a circle with the objective to get being right there at the start high above on a ledge.
Gothic always also had a world that was crafted with unique places, surprises, even up to Gothic 3, there were lots of great places, no town looked the same, there was a lot to discover and Arcania fails in all categories. There's no open world, just small places/islands you work your way through, caves follow the same "run in a circle" motion mostly, it's even worse than in Skyrim.
The AI is non existant either. Back even in the first Gothic if you draw your sword all NPCs reacted telling you to put down your weapon and when you dragged a whole lot of enemies behind you, NPCs would come to your aid, fighting them. That was in 2001. A decade later we have Arcania were nobody gives a ♥♥♥♥ about what is going on. You can lure monsters to a town and nobody cares. You can fight (mild spoiler) an orc boss with 6 orcs sitting close by and thow orcs never care, they just sit there without any animation. In the Gothic games when you looted a chest, when you tried to rob somebody, when you anything, the npc's reacted, they acted and reacted depending on their nature and how they thought what was right or wrong.
Arcania is a linear, easy (even on the highest difficulty setting that laughably is called "Gothic") game that more resembles Diablo 2 than Gothic. Go there, kill that, the Quests you fullfill easily along the way since most of the time you act in a bubble of a worl and not an "open world" like Gothic 3.
Fighting is also equally bad. Roll around, strike, roll, hit, roll, hit, or load up your big hit to make some big damage. There's nothing that makes fighting challenging or interesting. Enemies just attack you, run into you and again, Gothic 1 made that better, the blood flies in gothic 1 would fly around you and hit you, in Arcania they fly in one place and shoot something at you that doesn't do a lot of damage. You also level up to fast, enemies level with you (in Gothic 1-2 there wer areas you only could enter after a certain level, making the whole "exploring" worthwhile) and after you become a master you breeze through the game at ease.
The only 2 good things and really only good not exceptional or awesome are the graphics (steam version has a lot of problems though) and the music which tries to recreate old gothic themes and it sounds kinda nice but it's nowhere near Kai Rosenkranz' stuff for Gothic 1-3 and the Risen games.
Something to go for if you are looking for something new

Played through it because I had some spare time on my hands. However, would not play through again. The story-telling is bad, characters lack any kind of depth (*) and the main hero always sounds like he's in a hurry and irritated.
(*)Example: I found a dead soldier and went back to his fiance:
- me: "Your fiance is dead, unfortunately"
- her: "Really? *sobs* This cannot be.." *next text line, still her* "What are you going to do now?" (sadness suddenly vanished out of her voice).
You cannot get rid of the impression that the (german) voice actors have read each line one by one without having the slightess clue of what the next line will say.
Map progression is linear to the point that I missed a quest hub completely because I went another way that lead straight through a mountaint to the other side of the map. To get back I would have had to walk around have the map again (mountain was a one-way road), because there's "no way" of fast traveling (only to a certain amount). I decided not to go back and have no idea what I missed. Nothing apparently, because I was able the finish the story anyway.
All the old NPC's from Gothic 1 - 3 were planning some "secret mission" at one point, but they would not tell me about it. I thought they will tell me later... I just realize they didnt at all...
Last quest area (major city) was a clusterf*** of alleys blocked with barricades and alike. Which fitted the plot, but is irritating af when you simply want to reach different parts of the city, which you have to for the main quest. You get several "choices" on how to progress your story, which do not matter at all, because there's no alternative. Do whatever you find the easiest without any consequences.
Skill tree is pretty straight forward. Each "class" (melee, range, mage) has 2 - 3 talent choices which you simply skill until maxed out. Played as a mage, which is basically kiting your enemy while using your fire, frost or lightning spell (yes, there's exactly one for each affiliation with updates on dmg and AoE-capability) until it drops dead. Got 2 hitted occassionally, but basically no difficulty at all (hard difficulty).
All in all: Would not recommend.

Well too bad, you'll have to buy separate DLC for that. But what is included in the game is excellent. Much better than the outdated Sniper Elite original game.
SE V2 is a combination stealth/sniper simulator game where you play an American sniper infiltrated into Berlin in 1945, as the Russians are closing in to capture the city. Your mission is to rescue a German scientist wanting to defect to the Allies and give them information about the German V2 rocket program that he worked on.
Stealth gameplay is fairly standard fare and what you would expect if you are familiar with games like Far Cry or MGS. You can throw rocks to distract enemies. You can time your shots like Jude Law in Enemy at the Gates to take advantage of loud noises from airplanes or artillery strikes and mask your gunshots. Compared to Sniper Elite 3, this game significantly lacks in player control, but it is a great game regardless. You can also melee enemies to death, and you come equipped with 3 weapons at all times - ranging from bolt action rifles to semi-autos, SMGs and rifles like the STG44, to AT launchers and pistols (silenced Welrod included).
You can also set traps using explosives like land mines and tripwires. However, these don't work at all on vehicles. Also, the only way to kill a vehicle in most levels is to shoot its gas tank, resulting in some Michael Bay goodness.  Last but not least, there is of course the bullet time. You get to watch your bullets fly through the air, go through enemies heads or balls or wherever you choose to shoot them, and even see these ridiculous Michael Bay explosions where shooting a gas cap on a fuel tank blows up a Tiger.
The game features co op, pvp multiplayer, and a few hours of single player/co-op DLC. The difficulty curve is also real, as Sniper Elite significantly changes ballistics, introduces windage, removes the ability to tag enemies for easy tracking, and increases enemy difficutly.
Easily one of the best stealth and sniping games on the market.

Sniper Elite V2 was a fun game. The campaign was relatively short (see playtime) and the story was nothing special, but this game seems like a sniper-focused version of Wolfenstein. Who cares what's going on in the narrative? Let's blow the skulls off some Nazis (and sometimes Russians) in full 3D, X-Ray, zoomed-in glory. The levels in the game steadily increase in difficulty such that it's still enjoyable throughout.
I do have some gripes with the game, and I'm giving this a recommend more as an 'action' title than a proper stealth, sniper title.
Chief problem is the enemy spawn-in mechanic, and the general encounter-based set pieces of the game. Instead of having the whole level be your sniper playground, you have to eliminate one set piece. When you move forward (often out of a good position), poof! Enemies appear. You can even catch them popping into existence. Then onto the next encounter. I don't think this does the game any favours. Although I am not asking for a full open world like Crysis 1, if the entire level had the enemies spawned in, that would have been much better. Combine that with squad-based AI and reinforcement mechanics, and it really could have changed the whole game to a more sniper feel.
Not much side stuff or progression. You do get small sniper rifle upgrades, but they really are small. No skills or anything. You shoot some skulls, and you shoot some more skulls. That's all. Not a terrible thing, just simple. No side missions. There's two types of rather pointless collectibles that are just a chore.
It's a few years old now, and the environment, terrain, etc are not aging the best. If that's something that bugs you, perhaps the more recent Sniper Elite 3 would be better.
The game also has co-op missions and a multiplayer mode. I did not try these. Allegedly, there is no X-Ray killcam in the co-op mode, which... That's the main selling point gone right there!

In its current state I would highly recommend anyone who is remotely interested in the game to wait until the final release. The Game's a very hollow shell when it comes to combat, most fights in the game usually boils down to either killing/killed in 1 shots against smaller/larger dinosaurs respectably, or standing still facing one another spamming left clicks until one of you drops dead. Some of the play styles of the players can be  very toxic like with Kosers(Kill On Sight Not For Food) and Care Bears(People who protect others while they progress) I don't have much of a problem with Care Bears since they help easy the games unforgiving progression, but they also destroy The Isles food chain to a point were Ive seen other players ask if someone from that group would sacrifice themselves to prevent other players from starving to death. I know this isn't much of the games fault, its more of the fault of this games community but since you may decide to purchase the game I'm letting you know this is the kind of thing your about to head into. Progression mode is the only game mode at the moment but is almost unenjoyable with the way it handles death. I'll be using the example of a carnivore progression from a Velociraptor to a Giganatosaurus, that progression being Velo<Herra<Allo<Acro<Giga.
Now for those of you who don't know, in progression you always start a game as a Velociraptor and must survive long enough to evolve(progress) into a stronger dinosaur. You earn 1 progression point every minute your alive and then spend an accumulated amount of points to progress. In order to change from a Velociraptor to a Herrasaur you require 30 points(minutes) and each progression increases the amount needed to progress by 8x,
(0)<(30)<(120)<(120)<(120).
Meaning in order to progress from a Velo to a Giga you must survive for 6 hours and 30 minutes. Now the time needed to progress isn't the issue, the isle is definitely not a game to be enjoyed in 1 sitting. The Problem arises with the way death is handled, if you die as a Herra or higher, you HAVE TO RESTART AS A VELOCIRAPTOR! Which means if you are an Acro with only 10 minutes needed to progress to Giga and a much larger dinosaur kills you, you must restart at the beginning. Meaning those 6 hours and 20 minutes of playing the game were wasted and you must spend another 6 hours and 20 minutes to get back to where you were at. Now an easy way for you developers to fix this if you are reading would be to have the player respawn on death as the previous progression. An example would be if you die as a Acro you respawn as a Allo, and if you are killed again as a Allo you respawn as a Herra. This would definitely fix the problem people have with "Kosers", since from what I can tell the hatred people have for them steams from the time needed to catch back up. As for "Care Bears", simply adding A.I Dinosaurs and B.O.T.S for other players to hunt would improve this situation by a country mile. But besides the measurable time investment this game has what else seems to be the problem? Well, the game is mostly...Boring.
Now the majority of game time you will spend in the game will be lying down, in a bush, next to a water source, for hours. The Nickname "AFK Simulator 2017" really describes the early and mid-game sections of The Isle. Instead of stalking, hunting and exploring the Isle's Beautiful maps and environments you instead spend your time by the pool side of a pond. This problem comes from the fact that players REFUSE to leave a nearby water supply, and as such the inner areas of the island are devoid of life (save for Velociraptors and Dryosaurs dying of Dehydration). A way for the developers to fix this would be to either lower the hydration drain significantly or give players a valid reason to explore. Maybe for example add RIVERS to the map to help herd players toward different sections of the island, or add hard to find COLLECTABLES that add progression points or customizability to your dinosaur, the Blue plants the herbivores have is a step in the right direction but its not enough.
In my opinion I still see a HUGE amount of POTENTIAL for this game going forward. But if you are more interested in playing the game and not face these problems above? I say WAIT. Wait for the developers to put more meat into this game and put some shine on these rusty mechanics. I recommend checking back sometime in 2018 or at the most 2019 to see if some measurable progress has been made on the game. Again I really think this game has potential but I really hope THE ISLE doesn't become another THE STOMPING LANDS.

The darkness 2 was overall an excellent and satisfying experience. The game-play is great with a balanced skill system, great AI, and an engaging story. I would definitely recommend it as the game's notable combat mechanics and versatility, fun boss battles, and great characters and story make it a very enjoyable experience from beginning to end. However, the game is still very short and possible to beat in about 4 hours running straight through, and also has a rather frustrating cliffhanger ending. I only encountered about two or three minor bugs and a few camera issues in a small section towards the end throughout my play-through but nothing game breaking or that might deteriorate the experience, the game is very stable overall. The online vendetta mode is also entertaining allowing for 4 player co-op missions with friends, but the highlight of the game is still the campaign mode which you will want to play multiple times in the regular and new game+. Overall I would give The Darkness II a try, if you don't want to pay the full $29.99 for such a short game I recommend waiting for a sale or buying it now during the Halloween sale, you will be glad you did. Also if you are still undecided on whether you would like the game I would suggest playing the free demo since it provides a preview to the game's content.

Great for the DOOM.wad file. The vast majority of my experience with the Doom games (Ultimate Doom, Doom II, and Final Doom) has been running the .wad files from the CD ROMs via ZDoom. So don't let my Steam stats throw you off.
The Ultimate Doom includes all the episodes, including "Thy Flesh Consumed". The Steam release runs via DOSbox (just like the
release), which is admittedly inferior to ZDoom in every way. Fortunately, the .wad file included in the Steam release works with ZDoom/GZDoom AND the Brutal Doom/Project Brutality mods. Legally obtaining the .wad file to play all the Ultimate Doom episodes via ZDoom is justification enough for the $5 (USD) price tag.
Get ZDoom or GZDoom here:
Get Project Brutality here:
Right click Ultimate Doom, click LOCAL FILES, and skim down to the DOOM.wad. Copy the DOOM.wad and paste it in the zdoom or gzdoom folder. Launch zdoom or gzdoom and enjoy!

A modern hack 'n loot with a retro twist. A lot of features have been implemented so far and for an Early Access title it's definitely got some punch, but a few things still need some attention. The user interface, while reasonably complete, still feels a bit kludgy:
-When dealing with sixteen or more characters at the same time some ease of use functionality like a 'Next' and 'Previous' button for sliding between them would make life much nicer instead of having to repeatedly back in and out of menus to deal with them.
-On the subject of characters, two words: Party Management. The ability to group them out and sort them manually instead of the game's auto sort process which is a constant hindrance to things like University training and gearing them out. Some fashion of control over the list at the very least would go a long ways.
-A way to speed the crafting process (read:salvaging, which is super speedy with greens and greys but takes aeons with yellows and purples) would be dandy. Perhaps a 'Salvage All' option with a confirmation box to make sure you don't accidentally torch something you wanted?
-On the subject of confirmation boxes one would certainly be welcome with castle upgrades, I can't tell you how many times I've accidentally torched a section because the game's mouse settings don't align with my system's setting.
Again, I realize we're still in Early Access but these are definitely things that need addressing.
That said I've gotten a lot of entertainment out of this one and consider it well worth the five or six bucks spent, and with 1.0 in the not too distant future I've hope that what is all ready entertaining will become even more so. Definitely recommended.

A story of my first harrowing minutes:
I had just gotten out of training. The boat left, and I was down there in the blue. There was an old Russian sub, and it gave me the willies.
As I swam, I saw shapes in the darkness. Big ones. I start to panic.
Rocks. They were rocks.
One thing they don't teach you in training: it's quiet down there. You see, they train us all at once, so we get used to the noise.
But it's quiet. So quiet, you can hear your heartbeat. And your thoughts echo in your head. But you can't speak; you've got scuba gear on, and furthermore, if you speak, you know that THEY will hear you.
Then I saw moving shapes. No, scratch that; I HEARD them way before I saw them. When everything is still, the tinest movement is audible.
They were indistinct, far away. I didn't dare move; I just watched.
Manta Rays. Two kind old Mantas, out for a swim. I relaxed.
And then I felt something pass me.
It was monstrous. Its skin was black and scarred with harpoon-marks and shark-tooth scars. Its shadow blocked out the distant, indistinct, iridescent sun.
A shark.
I raised my harpoon gun confidently, despite my terror; this thing was HUGE, but that meant it was a big target.
I dodged it, effortlessly; it was big, lethargic, and not-too-aggressive. I killed it.
Something darted between my legs. I could feel my heartbeat begin to race; like an infernal pump in my ears. Thump thump, thump thump, thump thump.
It bit me. I blinked and reeled from the pain, spinning to see what had attacked me.
It was a Mako.
And it wasn't alone.
I began to swim up. That's when I learned it.
I'm afraid of heights. I'm afraid of submarines. I'm afraid of big, indistinct shapes in the distance of that savage, silent deep.
And I'm afraid of sharks.
I neared the surface and saw the magnitude of my predicament; Six Makos and a Tiger shark had followed me, circling gleefully. They could taste my blood.
I screamed. I begged the sky for help.
But the sky has no reach in the Deep. That's Death's dominion.

As a big fan of Teslagrad, I was excited to see this new story crafted by Rain Games. I am not disappointed.
The world feels so rich! No matter where you go, it feels in place. You can go from a very cheerful, bright section into a dark gloomy dungeon, and it feels natural. It's wonderfully crafted, each screen being unique, it entices you to adventure and explore as you go through the game. The level design is fantastic. General travel is simple, and each screen offers small challenges or puzzles to achieve upgrades and money. Every dungeon introduces you to a new mechanic, challenging the way you think. I've had a few moments already where I began to feel a little lost, but realized that I was just forgetting one of the mechanics that was available to me. I've never felt like I couldn't complete or accomplish something.
The characters are incredibly charming, every one of them. I've laughed countless times reading their dialogue, and they're all incredibly unique. As I played further into the game, and began to know the characters more, I've loved every single one. The design is really great, very enjoyable, and makes you interested to learn more about them.
The music in this game is INCREDIBLE! As soon as I launched it, a big smile appeared on my face and I began bobbing my head. As I progressed, I was constantly surprised at just how fitting the music was in each area. How lovely it sounded, how catchy it was, and how my desire to own the OST continued to grow. It's very well designed and it's pleasant to listen to (Even over and over if you're on a screen or in a town/dungeon for a while). It really enriches the world.
The gameplay itself is rather intuitive. Controls feel fluid and natural, they're very easy to learn, and even easier to implement. Rain Games did an excellent job ensuring that anyone could pick up the game, and feel like they know how to play it.
Over all, World to the Rest is a beautifully and carefully crafted game with a compelling story, beautiful art design, amazing sound track, and fun mechanics. I haven't picked up a game that felt this well polished AND rich in story in years.

Plot is set on Southern Isles, which are ravaged by war led by King Rhobar III in his effort to unite rest of the kingdom under his rule. The new nameless hero inhabits one of these islands and after his village has been burned down, his goal is to find those, who are responsible for it.
Even though the game is from 2010, I have to say graphics is great. Wilderness, monsters, weapons, armors, lights,     shadows etc. everything is nicely done. Only thing that was irritating me where faces. Looks like designers created about five faces and those are repeating over and over on different characters slightly changed with hair, beard, hats etc.
Game is poorly optimized. Only thing you can do is to set different values in configuration files. According to default    settings, game is supposed to run only on one processor core, which is nonsense. Considering release date in 2010,    most games were optimalized to run on multiple cores by then.
This game has one of the worst voice acting I've ever heard. Most voice actors are simply exaggerating and final result is implausible, which really breaks the immersion.
In hand to hand with voice acting comes dialogues. Dialogues in this game are poorly written. I can't believe a mature person would write something like this. Example: "What kind of mystery?" "Mysterious mystery." "What mysterious mystery?" "That my friend is a mystery."
I mean, who the hell would write something like this?
RPG elements are non-existent. You cannot interact with most things which are not related to quests. Character development is very simplified to leveling up certain abilities.
Combat is very easy. You either dodge attacks by rolling, or it is simple click-fest (which is easier since you stunlock your oponents). Trying to achieve certain combos is needless since click-fest is more efficient.
Quests in Arcania are similar to those from most mmo games. Go there, and either gather X items or kill X enemies and come back for reward.
I really wanted to like this game while playing. At start I had really huge problems with everything, but as I progressed through the game I either got used to it, or things started to get better. But the ending made my decision easier. It was simply cut off from game and released in so called expansion.

This game is an obvious port from a console yet it doesn't support gamepads (unless it's a wired xbox 360 controller, which is stupid). The controls are crap on the PC and hardly work. The camera is taken over much of the time by the game which points you in a specific direction and doesn't let you look away so it hinders your combat. Many times during fights (especially boss fights) you'll get stuck facing one specific direction and can't turn around so you can't fight any storm troopers or anything that are shooting at you.
I definitely DO NOT recommend this game to anyone. Do not waste your money buying this for PC. If you want, try it out on a console, but stay away from the PC version.

Pros:

Cons:

I feel like for a casual hidden object game, this game takes concepts into absolute extremes, and it ruins the experience.
The good:
- Scenes (normal and hidden object) look beautiful.
- The story has a Re-Animator vibe to it, kind of dark for a game of this nature and pretty cool.
- Hidden Object Scenes often have puzzles integrated into them directly that you must solve to collect an item. These are similar puzzles to what you see in other HOGs, but I enjoyed that slight twist. It also has standalone puzzles that are sometimes similar to what's in the HOG scene.
The bad:
- The game itself is very short (achieved 100% with 2.7 hours), and
- the majority of that time is spent collecting excessive amounts of tools and items, and backtracking through scenes to use them. I know this is a common tactic in many HOGs, but the in this game, it seems like for every one item or tool you use to unlock a chest or new area, you discover two to three new ones.
- Because it requires so many items to complete, it does get overwhelming trying to remember the exact location of every single interactive object in each scene. Probably not too difficult on Easy difficulty, but if you're playing on Expert, you will probably be missing destructible walls and lost items left and right. Often times you'll wind up advancing five or six scenes to collect an object, and then spend ten or more minutes trying to remember and then find the location that it's to be used.
- That's confounded by the fact that the game's locations become a blur. You can theoretically divide it up between three main indoor areas (which are subsequently each divided up between three to six sub-rooms), and then linear outdoor areas that conjoin them. While it's fairly easy to keep track of the outdoor areas, I would find myself oftentimes wandering around one house for several minutes just to realize the object I was looking for was actually in a different house altogether.
- Finally, the puzzles themselves are just way too easy and require very little thought.
Overall, although it starts off on a strong foot, it quickly devolves into an extremely repetitive (and oft frustrating) experience that became a chore to finish.
I would recommend any number of other HOGs before this one.

Adventurer Manager is an entertaining and promising mix of retro-style RPG and city manager. Yes, some elements feel redundant and grind-y after a while, but the game, even as it stands, contains plenty of other features to play with if boredom kicks in. The gear-forging system is fun, and the mad lib-style generation of auto-quests and character bios is a cute touch. I also enjoy the way skill points are distributed. Rather than gaining a tree of progressively awesome skills, you're allowed a certain number of skills to drop points into as you please. The number of skills allowed (as well as proficiency in those skills) progresses with level. It isn't without flaws; the gold-earning system is a little unbalanced, and as others have mentioned, the combat gets repetitive pretty quickly. However, considering the depth of the game in its current unfinished state, I'm excited to see how it develops.

This is a great little game that can be played in small chunks that quickly ramp up if you have a taste for roguelikes, old school jrpg dungeon fighting, and outrageous humor.  This isn't a game that takes itself seriously, and yet endears itself in many ways.  Every adventurer has his/her own bio that is completely randomized (and I do mean randomized.  You may laugh at some of the combinations that crop up).  The automatic questing system is a bit slow, but it's meant to be used alongside the manual dungeons where you can control toons actually fighting your foes, picking and choosing from dozens of abilities to win each fight.
There is much to do here besides dungeon fighting.  You can meltdown gear you find, crafting the leftovers along with gems to tailor the optimum suit for your adventurers.  You can build your castle up with a handful of improvements, send adventurers to University to earn dozens of powerups, and when they are ready to collapse, let them rest up for more forced dungeoneering.
If paper-dolling is your thing, you may enjoy this game for that reason.  In addition to a ruler/adventurer barbershop, there's a great variety of different items to dress up your adventurers, along with several races that become available who have their own distinctive appearance.  The different graphics that each tier of equipment brings to the equation really sells the idea of progression, and you might feel proud of your little pixel people as they go from rags to weapons and armor of mass destruction.  Of course, the graphical style is pixelized, but the art style is consistent as far as I can tell, and will hearken back to the golden age of console rpgs, and yet this is more than a good, old-fashioned rpg.  The management aspect of the game is very present, with the ability to send your characters on random adventures which will see them slogging through some menial task on autopilot, while you either fast forward, fight off invasions, or go manually dungeon delving.
Since release, I've yet to delve into the game as much as I'd like to, but there is much depth promised as the level cap is set to fifty, and if you play on ironman mode like me, it might be a while before you actually complete all of the content.  As of release, or shortly before, they added the feature of character aging, which sells the progression aspect of it even more.  It's an interesting idea to have your mortal adventurers retire, although I've yet to play enough to reach the stage where I'm incilned to retire them.  Just the idea that your beloved pixel people might die really bursts with intrinsic story, even while it tries to be as silly as possible, it can't help but create its own story as heroes rise, age as the seasons pass, and eventually fall.
You can visit your adventurers who've fallen in battle in the graveyard, resurrecting them if playing normal mode. I'm unfamiliar with this feature as of post release, but I'm hearing that there's some sort of debuff that's applied when you resurrect them.  Otherwise, you can strip them of their gear if you wish to dishonor them, or leave the gear, and engrave a tear-soaked epitaph that's sure to induce a fit of sorrow.
Overall, if you like pixelized, old-fashioned rpgs or manager simulators, or just wacked out humor and are in need of a few hyucks, you'll probably find something to like about this game.  There's a story filled with humor and over-the-top silliness, but more than that, there's some juicy gameplay.

An old favorite of mine. I distinctly remember just seeing this on an EB Games shelf when I was 14. I loved the box art at first glance and upon further inspection, I discovered that this game involved the building of a secret island lair, from which countless dastardly schemes could be unleashed upon the world. "Perfect," said young Myself. The only reason I really remember this experience was because the oldest woman I have ever seen working at a video game store tried to get me to show her some form of ID because it was rated Teen. I told her I was fourteen years old and I didn't know of any kids my age who had IDs who weren't sheltered because I didn't know any of these kids because they were sheltered and sat at home playing games about learning and stuff and living life like an inspirational poster, only to dream secretly at night of escape and perhaps even breasts or♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥or whatever body parts they learned to like.
Anyway, I bought this game, took it home and installed it and it ran horribly on my Compaq from the dark ages. I had what fun I could with it barely functioning, but ultimately it got tossed aside for a while UNTIL I GOT A DESKTOP THAT DIDN'T HAVE WINDOWS ME ON IT. I spent days installing games that I once thought were meant to run with the in-game models either upside down or simply invisible for the first time in double digit frames and with all of their visual effects present. I made my way through the pile and then suddenly arrived at this little gem from the past. I reinstalled it and away I went into my second world domination career.
My apologies for the story. Moving onto the game, you are tasked with the objective of constructing a hidden lair somewhere on some unknown island (where bumbling tourists and slightly less bumbling secret agents happen to wander to) with the intent of world domination. You must start smaller, however, and your options slowly unfold for you as you progress. It's pretty much Dungeon Keeper in a Bond movie setting. Over time you will research new rooms and equipment to further your schemes. Unfortunately, over time your enemies will become much less forgiving as well. You will eventually have to build a front, an island hotel to lure tourists in until they grow bored and leave. You will have to capture skilled individuals to train specialized minions. But most importantly, you will carry out evil deeds from your control center.
This brings us to the world domination portion of the game. This is basically a view of the globe on which you will place minion pieces used for stealing cash for your lair, plotting new heists and whatnot, and carrying out said shenanigans. These plots range from stealing the Eifel Tower to clubbing seals and to obliterating the city of Nashville, Tennessee, thus eliminating country music from the world; your singular act of goodwill throughout the course of the game. It's bursting with humor, much of it slapstick or parodic of spy fiction in general. If that's not your thing, you may not enjoy the game so much, but me? I can't get enough of it. I will say, however, that this is probably where the game struggles most. Playing from this sort of board game-like perspective can become pretty monotonous at times and you ultimately just spend a lot of time waiting. You have to keep a near constant check on it near the end of the game and this becomes nerve-wrecking once you're being bombarded by meddlesome agents at your home base at all hours of the day. Something in the interface to show a sort of minimized view of the information this screen provides during base construction/defense would have been nice.
The game is pretty tricky to figure out and will probably take a few practice runs to get the hang of before you can really start progressing. I'd say the first half or so of the game is learning all the intricacies where the second half is more of a "here's an island, go wild and work towards this ultimate goal" sort of thing. This is an objective-based game and there isn't much point to just letting your base idly run without moving forward in the story a bit. In that aspect, it's not particularly open-ended and this actually does restrict it quite a bit. Don't go in expecting any sort of free mode. There will be none of that. Of course, if you want, you can totally give yourself all the items and a ton of cash and just make your island into an insane deathtrap for incoming agents.
Which brings me to one of the game's strongest features: its base construction. You have a limited space in which to build your island stronghold and there isn't really one way you have to go about it. This is where the game most certainly gives you the most freedom. You can opt to have a very open base, with all of your rooms sort of running into one another for easy maneuvering. Or you can take the route of twisting, tight corridors chock full of traps both deadly and confusing to the enemy (or even your own minions if they're not careful). Your goal in base construction is more or less to keep your heat-generating rooms as far away from the entrance as possible, while keeping things like minion barracks and mess halls towards the front. Or you can always just fill the entrance corridor with flame pits and slaughter every intruder before they even get a chance to step through the door. The AI is just smart enough to keep you on your toes, yet dumb enough to get themselves into some silly predicaments fairly often. About the AI, though, it should be noted that your minions are not directly controllable while in your base (apart from your avatar and your handful of main henchmen), and this can lead to some awkward situations, often involving their unnecessary deaths or dismemberment.
I could ramble about this game for a good while, but that's all I can think of off the top of my head that's worth mentioning. I would like to lay out some pros and cons, I suppose:
+Wonderful base building; again, traps are a load of fun to play with
+Great art direction and style; TF2 reminded me of this when I first saw it
+Superb music
+Lots of humor, though this is always subjective
+Tough, but very satisfying to succeed at
+Polish, polish, polish. I don't know of very many glaring bugs in the game
-World domination feels kind of like playing a board game, which may not be what you'd expect from this and is also fairly monotonous/stressful as it almost always eats away your minions
-Fairly steep learning curve. Some objectives are relatively unclear in their descriptions
-Minion AI often leaves a lot to be desired. There is a henchman that will more or less destroy your base if he enters combat
Would I recommend it? You bet. Almost every flaw present here can be looked past pretty easily. I know fun is a bad word, but at the end of the day, this game supplies loads of it.

Very fun game.
It's not perfect though, but people tend to overreact about their grievances.
It could definitely benefit from dedicated servers instead of their peer-to-peer network and an actual competitive mode or two would be great. These are my biggest complaints whereas some of my lesser complaints are that the dev's seem to be making some questionable balance changes.
Overall it's an incredibly fun game with gameplay that is very rewarding. The class diversity is unreal (12 characters that all play completely different from each other). The microtransaction system seems offputting at first, but with only two and a half weeks of gameplay I have earned enough of the in game currency to purchase roughly 1 and a half of the most expensive cosmetic sets.
There are plenty of quests to do for extra credits and you get a fair amount for completing the story mode too.
One thing to note for new players. Yes, all the classes are "locked" when first start, but this only means that you cannot earn random drops of loot after fights with those classes. Fear not though, because completing the beginner and advanced tutorials grants enough credits to unlock 10 of the 12 classes. Then just complete three to five daily quests to get the rest.
This is a good game with solid mechanics that's tarnished only by it devolper's choice to use peer-to-peer and is worth a shot. Don't buy into the salt from people who were mad about a single afternoon when the network crashed.

I recommend this game although not whole-heartedly. If you are a flight-sim air combat fan what can I say, the sim part is great. So much so that I went and picked up a set of rudder pedals as the twist on my joystick was a bit off.
That being said, you do need the hardware to play and you need quite a bit of it to play online and still compete. Joystick is a sheer minimum, I would also recommend the flight pedals, possibly a throttle control and for the ultimate, TrackIR (I'm not sure if any VR goggles work or work well).
That's one of the two "irks" with this game: in addition to the big price tag for the base game as well as the additional planes, you could easily shell out $400 for a flight sim rig (joystick, rudder control, throttle control and head movement control), so be told!
The second irk is the "Career Mode" which is currently in Beta, but (as of this writing) is busted. It's what I play flight sims for, a bit of role playing along with my air combat. The developers have had downtime and a big patch and the issue wasn't addressed (and may be the cause according to the developer forums). At a higher level it looks like the developers are very, very passionate on modeling flight and combat, but could use a bit of help in developing a game: the learning curve is pretty much vertical (which I expect in a flight sim) but there are very few in-game assets in getting new pilots up to speed.
In all, I'd say if you are a fan of realistic flight combat sims (not arcade ones), already have the hardware, and are willing to wait for a good sale (especially for the extra airplanes), have at it. If you are looking for something with a slightly shallower learning curve, there are other, better options for you.
Now if you will excuse me, I need to price out a new HOTAS rig. And possibly a flight chair.

If I play this on my low-spec laptop, the game runs in slow-motion, with sounds playing normally but the game taking ages to move. I play it on my PC, and the game runs at unplayable extremely fast speeds. There is no VSync option anywhere to be found, so I can barely play. You have a 144hz monitor? The you're out of luck. And although this hasn't affected me, many players have had problems running the game in the first place.
It's really disappointing because mechanics like the Inflate-a-Mate look really interesting to experiment with, but the moment I uninstall this game everything I've done will be lost as they didn't add Steam Cloud support. It's like they threw it out on Steam, added some achievements and left it.
If you enjoyed the original Stealth ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, then get this on a sale. If you haven't played Stealth B-astard Deluxe (or the original free version), then try that instead. This is not a proper sequel.
