The Darkness II is an excellent game.  You play Jackie Estacado, head of a crime family and host to a parasitic entity older than humankind called 'The Darkness'.  It's based on a comic book series called 'The Darkness'.  The storylines between the two are different, but similar.  This is also the sequel of a 2007 game called 'The Darkness', but it does differ in a number of ways from it's predecessor, which was produced by a different developer.  It has a new graphical style (think comic book), quad-weilding of weapons, better multiplayer, shorter main campaign, and a generally more polished presentation with smoother combat.
The graphics are gorgeous, striking a nice balance between realism and art, and utilizing a cel-shading technique to simulate a comic book feel.  The overall effect is beautiful.  The game world is highly polished and very well fleshed out.  Locales are believable and easy on the eyes.  The characters are all very well animated, and individual characters often have their own personal touches.  The attention paid to all the little details is impressive.  One locale, for instance, is gorgeous, but a major gun fight ruins almost everything.  Repeat visits following the fight find it in various stages of repair.  It's a really nice touch.  A lazier developer would have left in ruins or just never revisited that location.
At this point, when talking about graphics and attention to detail, something should be said about the gore; this game is bloody.  Very bloody.  Your powers enable you to rend enemies into pieces.  I can't count the number of different kill animations, but it's ALOT.  Using your dark tendrils you can slice a person in two, cut off their head, pick them up and tear them apart like a wishbone, crush them horribly, impale them, rip out their spinal column, tear open their chest and take out their hearts, gouge out their eyes,...  ugh... the list goes on.  This is not a cupcake with sprinkles kind of game.
The games narrative is one of it's strongest suits and certainly what kept me playing, though you will hear the word "♥♥♥♥" way more then you would think possible.  Major characters include roughly a dozen or so mob of your own henchmen, each with their own personality, your Aunt Sara - your last living family (apparently), Johnny Powell - a neurotic expert on The Darkness and occult things in general, and a Darkling with a British accent who calls you "Monkey".  Many other characters besides, but I don't want to spoil anything.  As I said, the narrative is very strong in this game - there's alot of exposition in monologues, dialogues, cutscenes, and even in some read items.  There is a decent, well-written story with plot twists in it.  If you decide to use a walkthrough, understand you will be spoiling half the fun of this game.
The sound in this game is also very nice.  The voice-acting, in particular, is amazing.  They hired top-notch voice actors.  One of the most familiar would be Mike Patton, of 'Faith No More', returning to voice 'The Darkness'.  Some have noted that character of 'The Darkness' doesn't sound exactly the same as the previous game.  End credits reveal that Brian Bloom, who voices Jackie, shares billing with Mike Patton for the character of 'The Darkness'.  The music is good, without being distracting, and the sound effects all hit the right mark.  If there were a negative to be mentioned it would be that certain dialogue is heard repeatedly - The British Darkling has only a few different lines he uses when he's bored waiting for you to continue moving forward in a mission (and he bores quickly).  The enemies will often, likewise, repeat much of the same dialogue when encountering them in fights.
The combat in the game is fluid, fun, and provides a healthy challenge without being impossibly hard.  You have control of two demoic tendrils - one that grabs objects, enemies, and devours enemy's hearts, while the other can slash vertically and horizontally.  Each of your hands can also weild a weapon (all guns), though if you single weild a gun you can improve your aim by using the iron sights on the weapon.  Weapon variety....  in most of the game you will be limited to the choice of a shotgun, handgun, uzi, or carbine... but other weapons do present themselves.
During the course of the game you can find relics (up to 29), which will add to something called 'essence'.  These items have dark essence and owning them provides you with an additional 300 essence.  killing enemies also provides you with essence.  Essence is used throughout the game to purchase abilities from one of four different skill sets on a wheel.  I made it through the game using only half of those skills, so there were unique abilities I never even tried.
The campaign is not long.  It can be completed in 6 or so hours, though they pack alot into it.  If you dally or hunt carefully for every relic, it will take a little longer.  Then there is Vendettas, which can be played co-op with up to four people, or singleplayer offline.  Vendettas played as a campaign allows you to play as one of four Dark essence users, people who have powers of Darkness, but without the tendrils.  They each have their own unique personality, weapons, and skills.  The campaign follows a story that runs parallel with the main game and is rich with the same colorful voice-acting you're treated to in the main game.  There is alot more humor in the Vendettas campaign.
Great game.  Totally worth it!

I have to admit that this game is waaaay more fun that I imagined and I got addicted to it.
The good things:
I really like the idea of being a king that rules over a little army of heroes that have to loot dungeons for me while I sit on my comfortable throne and plan my revenge on the evil guy, wich works actually pretty good, as far as I have played it now. (3 groups of heroes around lvl 12-14).
The dungeon crawling itself is done well enough. Most enemies have a weakness against certain attacks or elements and sometimes have special effects or buffs like vampirism or things like that. The loot from chests and monsters is motivating for more and the fact that every class has  it's own skill tree offer different strategies to make the dungeon runs more interesting.
Auto save- a lot of early access games and betas that I have played until now suffered of bugs that made the games crash a lot...and they did not automatically save the progress, so I was often thrown back many hours, which is god damn frustrating. Not with this game, It may crash from time to time and it has its bugs...but I never lost much because of that.
I also really like the humor of the game.
The not so good/bad things:
The game in its current state is not really pretty, but the Ui does it job and the gameplay can make up for it.
The crafting system does not seem really that interesting, same with the vendors because I almost always find equipment in
the dungeons that are way better than the things that I can buy or craft.
Bugs:
At the moment the game still suffers from a lot of bugs, which is probably to be expected from an early access game.
For example, I once entered a dungeon and the navigation buttons on the Ui just disappeared, so I could not move through the dungeon, nor could I escape it - a restart fixed it and it only happend once and almost no progress was lost thanks to the autosave option.
Another bug that appears more frequently is that sometimes when a hero has had a level up, the game is not showing the stat points that I had already invested or the bonuses from the current equipment, which made it appear as if the character was completely broken and useless - which is luckely not the case, a computer restart always helped and sometimes it's just enough to enter a dungeon and teleport back to the city.
------------------
Aside from those points, I really like and appreciate the information that the developers are giving potential customers on the steam page before buying the game.
They make it absolutely clear, that the game itself is still very far from being complete and they also make clear which features are already working and what they still want to add. Also, the game seems to be updated frequently. That is sadly not as common as one might think it should be with Early Access games, so well done devs.
TL;DR
To be perfectly honest, when I bought this game I was not really expecting much of it, it was more like a "it's only 5 euro, it won't hurt me that much"- decision.
But, until now I have not regretted it. The game delivered everything the devs promised and I really want to dive into more dungeons, grab loot and level up my characters and I really want to see the game getting big, because it has a lot of potential and can already be quite entertaining.
5.5-6 out of 10 for the game for now, because it still needs work to make the dungeons less repetitive and for the grafics.
EDIT:
I forgot to mention some bugs that I have found.
For once, sometimes when I revived a hero from the graveyard, the message that pops up won't dissapear. If I hit escape the menu will pop up behind that message and I have to restart the game (the hero will still be alive after doing that)
You can actually put four heroes into a group and can save that group in one of 4 slots, so you don't have to make a new group before entering a dungeon over and over again. BUT the game allways overwrites all my save slots with the last group that I have saved, which is annoying because of if you have almost 30 heroes things get really confusing.
Which brings me to my last point, the Ui in the Adventurer menu really needs something to filter the hero list for level, classes or maybe equipment. My suggestion would, to let the player put their heroes in groups on the main/map screen. I think that would help a lot.

It's not straightforward to recommend this game. On the gameplay front it does many things poorly, several in game factors collaborate to frustrate the player. Stupid minions running one by one into their deaths, while you can only watch their folly. Pesky invulnerable super agents destroying your base. Traps being somewhat poorly balanced. There's no way to turn off just the announcer's warnings - you'd have to turn off all sounds. The pacing is very slow at the beginning. There are only two islands on which to construct your bases - no random maps, no skirmish mode. Specialist science minions and social minions have little to do. Acts of infamy provide little tangible benefit...
How can the game be any good then?
Because of the things it does good, it does really well. And there are very few games similar to this (Dungeon Keeper being the closest).
It's all style over substance. The art direction, themes and music (particularly title soundtracks) are just spot on and so perfectly captures the idea of playing Bond-film like villain, constructing a secret base in order to take over the world! The animations are superbly done, cartoony, but appropriately so. Thus even though the game is 10 years old, it still manages to look alright.
If the theme and management style in any way appeals to you give this game a try, but if you enjoyed Dungeon Keeper this is almost a must-play in my opinion.

Okay, when I bought this game it was not perfect, but it was very good, you see you start out you create a ruler, and you hire adventurers from the Inn, and basically send them out on random adventures, and sometimes, when you take on more story essential quests you actually get to control whatever party you have and what they do, at this point I would say it is between the games Tribal Wars and Classic Ultima from the Graphics stand point to classic FF from the turn and skills stand point when you do manual adventures. You get to manage your parties of adventurers (Up to 4) giving them equipment, deciding what skills they have, and pumping up their stats, and it all sounds good so far right. Well there is some down sides, and a lot happened after the current update.
First: Before the update you used to pick adventures from the signs in town, and you would get information from how many encounters your party would get, to how dangerous the adeventure was, and then you would get the time limits of said adventure and rewards there of once your adventurers had said number of encounters.  Now they have added a Endurance bar, they have put all the adventures that is automated on a menu that shows up in the center of your screen, and they give you info on how much gold  and experience you'll get from each encounter., and as you form your party you get told the difficulty of said adventurers, However, while this all sounds good and everything, you do not have the ability to leave the game and let the adventurers do their thing when your not controling them(well you do but you'll see what happens if you do so if you continue reading) manually, in addition you notice how I didn't say the number of encounters are now shown, that is because essentially since they put the Endurance bar in, and saying you have so many encounters, so much award(Gold wise), and it costs so much Endurance, they went with a system, in which you have to tell your adventurers when to stop the adventure, before your party comes home, and then you have to rest them, improve their stats, give them new equipment etc. Now I understand this is a management game and all, but let's be honset folks, if you hired workers to build your porch, left for the day, and came back to find they built your porch, tore down part of your fence, tore through your neighbors yard,  and basically your the proud owner of the great porch of China, complete with exhausted  workers ready to collapse all around, all because you weren't there to tell them to stop(Your adveturers stats get sapped when their endurance goes down to a certain level, and can actually hit zero, in which you have to rest them to get their stats back up.) You would be very upset with all the problems this would cause along with the sheer incompetence of not knowing the job well enough to know when to stop, you would be very upset. indeed, and after making sure they are taken care of you probably would not hire them again, but alas, while you can fire the adventurers and never have to hire them again, the people you replace them with will do the very same thing and cause you the same problems(well in this game they would anyway.)  While this can be worked around,  with enough time and patience, it basically took what should be a click and forget game and turned it  into something you have to stay on and at times feels like you have to dredge through.  Of course this is all the management side of things.
Second: It seems there is a lot of things that have changed, the skill tree for instance only has a total of nine skills, down from twelve, not major, and the game is more refined for it, so that is basically a good thing, However it seems the adventures have gotten harder on your party as well, also good equipment pops up a lot more rarely now, of course these factors can be good or bad, pending on how you look at it, but the worse thing is, there seems to be a few more bugs then before, and this is the reason for my  ultimate conclusion at the end.
Is this game good, yes if you like management games, and you have a lot of patience, you'll get hours and hours of gameplay already, and this is still a incomplete game, but for 5 bucks it is well worth it. If your a classic role playing fan, it is a iffy call, you might like parts of the management, but might get frustrated with it in it's current form, but you will like the manual adventures , the skills and the classes, though they are basic for this kind of game.  Overall it is a enjoyable little game and well worth the check out at 5 bucks, but be warned, your mileage may very.
Overall I give this a 7 out of 10. It's not perfect, but it is good enough for me to recommend.

An atmospheric horror game with a narrative that questions the existence of existing, life. afterlife and death.
The story revolves around a naive man that came in for a brain scan, only to end up in an underground water faciilty. He attempts to find a way to escape but ends up finding things much more complicated and completely disturbed by the truth and mystery of the facility and its current and former residents.
To be frank, there's nothing much for me to say except that the story and mysteries are quite immersive that its one of the few games I remembered for having the most memorable story and ending.
As a horror game, it's okay if you're just running away from monsters. It plays out well as a psychological horror however.
The game is incredibly suspenseful with a gameplay that you do little with the mechanics by using your brain with basic controls. The game can occasionally be quite draining if you are constantly pursued by the monster or always waiting for it to go away.
The audio and scenic visuals are quite good. As the sound effects feels quite realistic and the voice acting quite natural.
The location, landscape and level design for the areas you visit are either scenic or just different that it feels or looks good.
This is how I feel about the game and it truely comes to my highest recommendation for narrative, back stories and exploration of the underwater environment and its facilities.

Different negative take on the game here besides the latency and connection issues.
Besides the massive bugs and latency issues, the game is overly complicated for what it sells. Personally, I was looking for a more chivarly-type game and that's how this game came off to be but it's totally not. This game is parallel to a fancy combat fighting game such as Tekken or Mortal Kombat and just add swords and spears and take away the fluidness and also add more cheese.

The attack and defense combinations are borderline unnessacarily difficult for my taste; attempting to duel is atrociously imbalanced as the game rewards triteness and you just get people rushing to push you off a ledge every duel. Additionally, the combat itself is mundanely mind boggling and is rather a game of deception than a game of combat skill. The defensive manuevers are too rigid in my mind for it to be a somewhat realistic combat scenario. One wrong sidestep gets you killed in this game of musical chairs of who can take advantage of the rigid (Three) guard stances and character counters (Which shouldn't exist.) I can settle with the combat combinations despite their absurdity in executing them however it is the forced and constrained character movement that stops me from playing this game.
The majority of combat is attempting to get past your opponents guard and execute an unblockable attack or a cheesy stun that renders your guy futile from either poison or fatigue. Moving in this game reminds me of playing the first resident evil where you can only strafe in 90 degree angles W,A,S,D. (I wouldn't be surprised if they got their idea from such)
If the game had moved more torward the direction of non-explosive signature attacks and less towards musical chairs combat with dynamic movement it'd sell for me.

Gameplay-wise, this game is great. It actually made me go back to playing all the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. games because I remembered how great they are. This game handles about as well as to be expected from a low budget, arena shooter, so don't expect absolute accuracy, or good response times. I've found that this game is really entertaining to jump into for a hour or so to kill time but there's huge problem with that; the way matchmaking works as well as because of the low player population, it takes forever to find a match. Seriously, have a book on hand so you can get some reading in for 5-10 minutes while you wait to find a game.
The major, unforgiveable fault with this game is the balance. There absolutely isn't any. At all. There are different factions that have different fighting styles, or at least so they claim. I chose Scavengers, which supposedly favor long range combat, yet so far I've only unlocked one extra bolt action rifle, and that doesn't even have a scope. I'm on the 4th level set of this faction. But hey, I've unlocked a couple SMGs and a shotgun so that should be good for balance right? Wrong. The scavengers get light but highly mobile armor, which is to be expected. But all the other factions get much better armor. Armor that makes a player capable of taking 3 rifle shots, which are normally a one shot kill to the torso or head. Diving in further, this game suffers the most from the free-to-play game stigma, Pay-To-Win. The premium currency is gold (how f'ing original), and with that you can buy armor, weapons and etc. that are far better than what you could buy with the standard currency. We're talking one shot, semi-auto, box mag shotguns. Scoped, one shot rifles. Armor that makes you next to impossible to kill. Not to mention the XP boosts and so on that allow you to improve a variety of stats.
I experienced many fun games until I got stuck faced against a premium player, then it was just miserable and I only stayed in the game so I could complain about the player in the end. Watching him charge into our spawn to wipe out 10+ at a time before we could do anything, and when we'd finally kill him, he'd come running right back. One shotting everything in his way. His armor making him a tank, his guns making him OP.
So, before writing this review, I had another one of those games, with yet another Pay-To-Win player, so I guess you could say I'm a little salty and hyper-critical right now. The in game moderators that loiter in the general chat have nothing useful to say, mostly they just sit there and brag about how their gear has 4 different +10% modifiers (Normal gear can only have 3, and none go that high. Plus upgrading has a very low chance to actually work. Most of the time, you'll lose an upgrade when you try to upgrade to level 2, and then you'll be back at square one) and how they have all the top tier gear..
This game should be marketed as a Pay-To-Win game. At least that way, people would understand what they are getting into. Or at least separate the Pay-To-Win players from the Free-To-Play players. Because nobody wants the one guy with a golden machine gun to show up at a BB gun fight.

- Fighting dinosaurs has problems.  You often either bite through someone or you bite miles away and they die.  Also dinosaurs have some balance problems, although they seem okay in general.
- A more minor gripe, but the in-game UI is a bit unclear.  It does the Gears of War-esque red screen for damage which doesn't really help much.  Atm there is a debug menu that shows health/stamina/coords etc but it's not a permanent fix.  Joining and leaving groups is a bit odd and I tended to stay away from it.
- Limited Developer Feedback.  Updates are frequent, but there isn't much saying they're listening to the community's problems.  As it is Early Access, systems that struggle are to be expected, but devs need to be clear that they see the problems and are working on it.
Pros:
- Art assets are stellar!  Best part of the game imo.  The models look very nice, fantastic skin textures and the animations give the dinos a good sense of weight which is often sorely missed.  With a good computer, the last couple of maps have looked very good.
- Steady-ish servers that hold up to 100 people.  If the server goes down, you don't lose progress which is very nice!
- Relatively active community.  Not had a day very often where there wasn't a mostly full server and most of the community is alright.

The Darkness II is an excellent game.  You play Jackie Estacado, head of a crime family and host to a parasitic entity older than humankind called 'The Darkness'.  It's based on a comic book series called 'The Darkness'.  The storylines between the two are different, but similar.  This is also the sequel of a 2007 game called 'The Darkness', but it does differ in a number of ways from it's predecessor, which was produced by a different developer.  It has a new graphical style (think comic book), quad-weilding of weapons, better multiplayer, shorter main campaign, and a generally more polished presentation with smoother combat.
The graphics are gorgeous, striking a nice balance between realism and art, and utilizing a cel-shading technique to simulate a comic book feel.  The overall effect is beautiful.  The game world is highly polished and very well fleshed out.  Locales are believable and easy on the eyes.  The characters are all very well animated, and individual characters often have their own personal touches.  The attention paid to all the little details is impressive.  One locale, for instance, is gorgeous, but a major gun fight ruins almost everything.  Repeat visits following the fight find it in various stages of repair.  It's a really nice touch.  A lazier developer would have left in ruins or just never revisited that location.
At this point, when talking about graphics and attention to detail, something should be said about the gore; this game is bloody.  Very bloody.  Your powers enable you to rend enemies into pieces.  I can't count the number of different kill animations, but it's ALOT.  Using your dark tendrils you can slice a person in two, cut off their head, pick them up and tear them apart like a wishbone, crush them horribly, impale them, rip out their spinal column, tear open their chest and take out their hearts, gouge out their eyes,...  ugh... the list goes on.  This is not a cupcake with sprinkles kind of game.
The games narrative is one of it's strongest suits and certainly what kept me playing, though you will hear the word "♥♥♥♥" way more then you would think possible.  Major characters include roughly a dozen or so mob of your own henchmen, each with their own personality, your Aunt Sara - your last living family (apparently), Johnny Powell - a neurotic expert on The Darkness and occult things in general, and a Darkling with a British accent who calls you "Monkey".  Many other characters besides, but I don't want to spoil anything.  As I said, the narrative is very strong in this game - there's alot of exposition in monologues, dialogues, cutscenes, and even in some read items.  There is a decent, well-written story with plot twists in it.  If you decide to use a walkthrough, understand you will be spoiling half the fun of this game.
The sound in this game is also very nice.  The voice-acting, in particular, is amazing.  They hired top-notch voice actors.  One of the most familiar would be Mike Patton, of 'Faith No More', returning to voice 'The Darkness'.  Some have noted that character of 'The Darkness' doesn't sound exactly the same as the previous game.  End credits reveal that Brian Bloom, who voices Jackie, shares billing with Mike Patton for the character of 'The Darkness'.  The music is good, without being distracting, and the sound effects all hit the right mark.  If there were a negative to be mentioned it would be that certain dialogue is heard repeatedly - The British Darkling has only a few different lines he uses when he's bored waiting for you to continue moving forward in a mission (and he bores quickly).  The enemies will often, likewise, repeat much of the same dialogue when encountering them in fights.
The combat in the game is fluid, fun, and provides a healthy challenge without being impossibly hard.  You have control of two demoic tendrils - one that grabs objects, enemies, and devours enemy's hearts, while the other can slash vertically and horizontally.  Each of your hands can also weild a weapon (all guns), though if you single weild a gun you can improve your aim by using the iron sights on the weapon.  Weapon variety....  in most of the game you will be limited to the choice of a shotgun, handgun, uzi, or carbine... but other weapons do present themselves.
During the course of the game you can find relics (up to 29), which will add to something called 'essence'.  These items have dark essence and owning them provides you with an additional 300 essence.  killing enemies also provides you with essence.  Essence is used throughout the game to purchase abilities from one of four different skill sets on a wheel.  I made it through the game using only half of those skills, so there were unique abilities I never even tried.
The campaign is not long.  It can be completed in 6 or so hours, though they pack alot into it.  If you dally or hunt carefully for every relic, it will take a little longer.  Then there is Vendettas, which can be played co-op with up to four people, or singleplayer offline.  Vendettas played as a campaign allows you to play as one of four Dark essence users, people who have powers of Darkness, but without the tendrils.  They each have their own unique personality, weapons, and skills.  The campaign follows a story that runs parallel with the main game and is rich with the same colorful voice-acting you're treated to in the main game.  There is alot more humor in the Vendettas campaign.

Fan of the Gothic series?  Splendid.  You should be.
Want a more immersive experience playing what many feel to be a sub-par RPG?  Why wouldn't you?
Do yourself a favor: turn off Quest Markers, Health Bars, Overhead Feedback, Enemy Captions, and Feedback Bar.  This will improve the experience and make the journey feel pretty close to past Gothic games.  Thank you, Spellbound, for giving us the option to turn off these hand-holding aberrations.
Oh yeah, play the game on Hard difficulty, at least.
Now, a few good points:
- A meaty feel to combat (I went two-handed + bow & arrow), including excellent sound design reflecting type of weapon impacting "flesh" type of enemy.  Hitting a golem with a sword or warhammer will produce distinct sounds, hitting a wolf with a sword or axe will produce distinct sounds
- Great soundtrack, as has always been the case with the Gothic Series
- Lots of armor sets, a ton of weapons, an absurd amount of items to craft of each type (foodstuffs, potions, weapons, armor, amulets, etc.)
- UI-friendly inventory
- Meaningless interactibles:  you can take short naps, saw tree trunks, watch Nameless play goblin drums, pray, rotate rotisseries, take bong hits, and more
- Good story... at times odd, quirky dialogue, decent voice acting, and, of course...seeing old friends
A few bad points:
- Clones, clones, yeah....clones
- Fetch quests, lots of them
- The "world" can feel empty at times
- Crafting can be done anytime/anywhere.  You're no longer required to be at an Alchemy Table to brew potions, no longer need to be at a stove or campfire to cook, no longer need to do any blacksmithing
- Skill tree is underwhelming
- The last few hours of the game are a tedious and total slaughterfest
In closing, ArcaniA can still feel like Gothic, if you let it.  I did, and I enjoyed the 39 hours I put into this game.  Recommended.

Ever fancied being eaten by a shark every two to three minutes?  How about dying from lack of oxygen on a semi-regular basis (in spite of the fact that the ocean is apparently teeming with many a full, diverless air-tank)?  And most importantly of all, do you enjoy the frustration of wasting tonnes of harpoon gun ammo TRYING to shoot sharks at close range and completely failing?  If you answered "yes" to at least two of the above, Shark Attack Deathmatch 2 may be just the game you've been waiting for.

I am, of course, just being a bitter ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, so in acknowledgement of the fact that there's maybe a few people out there talented enough to actually stay alive longer than five to ten minutes in this hard-as-all-♥♥♥♥ ♥♥♥♥er of a game, I'll mention some of its good features.  The graphics are awesome, the maps are genuinely interesting - hell, even occasionally inspired (sunken New York, anyone?) - and the sound is awesome, too.  On the whole, the atmosphere is absolutely fantastic and the underwater worlds perfectly immersive.  The problem?  Well, maybe there isn't one.  Or more to the point, maybe the problem is ME.

Rival game Depth at least attempted to be SLIGHTLY more than a "deathmatch", but true enough to its title, that's literally all this one seems to be. Well, that and a "survival mode", which as we all know is just gamer lingo for "single-player deathmatch".  Man, I so badly want someone to make one of these first-person, scary shark games with a STORY.  If you make a game like that, and make it as GOOD as this and Depth admittedly manage to be, I WILL MARRY YOU AND HAVE YOUR BABIES.  Even if you're a dude.  Hell, I'll even be the woman, if such a compromise has to be made.
What the ♥♥♥♥ is with the uber-popularity of all these multiplayer games, anyway?  Don't any of you people like YOURSELVES?  Or do you just not have any REAL-WORLD FRIENDS?  WHY CAN'T SOMEONE MAKE A TOTALLY ♥♥♥♥ING AWESOME SINGLE-PLAYER SHARK GAME?!  I love games.  I love sharks (well, okay, only in a they-totally-scare-the-bejesus-out-of-me way, but you know what I mean).  I WANT A SCARY, TENSE SHARK GAME WHICH ISN'T A DEATHMATCH.

Oh, and before all you clever♥♥♥♥♥♥♥start asking me why I bought a game with "deathmatch" in the title just to write a review complaining that the game IS a deathmatch, for the record, a friend gifted me this.  And even after the semi-disappointment of Depth, I was still excited to start 'er up.  But upon finding that this was considerably HARDER than Depth, and attempting to consolidate this with the equally indisputable fact that I'm basically pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥at video games, I have to say that I'm going to declare Depth my favourite of the two games.  If for no reason other than the fact that I actually managed to KILL some sharks in that one.  Which is a pretty cool thing to be able to do in a shark-killing game, right?
And yeah yeah yeah, I know that's just a cue for all you smart ♥♥♥♥ers to point out that if I only exercised a little patience, or failing that simply (and not to mention magically) "get gud" at the game, I might achieve my holy grail and actually KILL A ♥♥♥♥ING SHARK.  But you know what?  Right now I really couldn't be ♥♥♥♥ed.  And I'm on mutha♥♥♥♥in' HOLIDAYS at the moment, so that's surely gotta be sayin' somethin'...

In conclusion, definitely recommended to anyone who fancies themselves any good at these kinds of games, or indeed to anyone who just fancies a quick, immersive dive into a truly believable underwater kingdom before being unceremoniously "murdered by a shark" (the game's words, not mine).  With little doubt, the best shark-feeding simulator liable to be released on Steam this year.
Oh, and PS...good luck finding a multiplayer game to actually JOIN.  I think I managed to CREATE such a game, but alas, I was the only thing remotely resembling a HUMAN BEING in it.  But I guess it is only in Early Access, so with a little luck we'll see that particular comment of mine become null-and-void in the near future.  I have a suspicion I will revisit these waters, sooner or later, but for now the ♥♥♥♥ing sharks can just go hungry.  FINNED, FISHY ♥♥♥♥ERS.

So last week I wrote my review on Force Unleashed 1. I was impressed with the story and how well it fit in the Star Wars universe and the only major complaint I had was that the controls sometimes felt clunky, that the game could have been a LITTLE bit more than it was.
I finally got around to playing this, and it feels like my opinions flipped. You play as Starkiller again, and the introduction gives a good start to WHY you are there. If you didn't play the first game before this I recommend you do, otherwise you will be totally lost. Anyway, I'll go through each section.
Story: 5/10
The only reason the story is this high is because the first game did a magnificent job setting things up. You know your story from the first, although the Starkiller in this game doesn't remember much about his past (minor spoiler, don't worry you find this out in the openning cutscene, Vader tells you that you are a clone). You basically spend the game trying to get back to your beloved Juno's arms, that's about it. No major plot development like in the first one, nothing that helps you define yourself as a Sith or Jedi. In fact, Starkiller feels a little bit less of a badass and a bit more angsty than I would have liked.
Graphics & Sound: 8/10
The sound is easy, they did a good job with music, it fit in well, and the whole Star Wars lightsaber/force sound effects are amazing, exactly what you expect. The graphics are polished and the cutscenes are really well done from what I could tell. There are 2 very major reasons why I don't give this game a 10/10 (keeping in mind that the game was released over 3 years ago). First of all, most of the cutscenes actually involve your character model, thus including your dual lightsabers and the crystal color you chose, which is good. The problem? The fully CGI cutscenes that are videos, they just had him with dual red lightsabers. It felt really lazy and removed me from the experience a little bit. Other games make sure their full cutscenes include the specialized weapon and armor you are wearing, don't switch me back to the original, it is really annoying. I took 1 point off for that. The second thing, while the game looks great and everything, the characters look different than from the first. General Kota and Juno specifically, and Starkiller as well but not to the same extent. They just LOOK like different people with similar features. That bothered me slightly, yes they are WAY MORE polished than before, but it detracted from their original look.
Gameplay: 9/10
Gameplay is magnificent in this. They changed the combat system and leveling system, the menus are more fluid, fighting is more fluid, FORCE POWERS ARE MORE FLUID. This was my problem in the first game, not so in here. You basically have most of your kit from the first game, and as you gain experience you unlock more force powers along with being able to upgrade them up to a maximum level of 3. This is beautiful, and being able to rapid fire Force Push (even though I never used it) is amazing. Also, put a point into Jedi Mindtrick, it is the most fun part of this game. The game felt more fluid, and I died maybe a few times to mis-timed jumps, but never because the camera screwed me or things not being responsive.
Overall: 8/10
The story was kind of lame, and it was the only thing to take away from it. The game is short, it took me 6 hours (theres like 8 levels) and I didn't feel like it took forever. The action was amazing and the fights were fun. Everything else aside, I enjoyed this A LOT more than the first game.

Would I recommend this game? Yes. But not at full price, or at the very least, not until they fix server stability.
+ Fun gameplay. Something new -- maybe the closest thing to it is Chivalry Online's combat, except far less complicated. I feel like it's a cross between that and a fighting game, since when you start learning the harder-to-master mechanics and begin playing against smarter people, it's all about them mind games -- performing a lot of feints and mixups to trick your opponent while reading their own attacks and movements. At least, thats how I see it, and thats mostly where I enjoy it.
+ Free seasonal content. Apparently the future of the game plans to introduce new heroes, game modes, maps, etc. upon the completion of every season. It will all be free of charge and accessible to all players, at least according to stuff online. Season pass only lets you have all that about a week early before the rest. So at least they're not trying to make a quick buck off that.
- Abysmal server connections. You don't need to read my say on this to hear about how bad it gets. If they AT LEAST fix this, then the game would be worth buying -- on sale. Full price ehhh, but only if you really really REALLY want it.
- Strange gear system. New gear will have stats that increase (and decrease) certain aspects of your heroes -- These can be purchased in bulk via CS. People will and have cried it's P2W, and tbh they're kinda right. You can avoid this if you just play 1v1 duel games like I do, where gear stats aren't accounted for. IMO, putting in stats on gear was a terrible mistake anyway -- ALL gear should have just been COSMETIC purchases if they wanted to make money from it. Instead, they're just now trying to balance gear stats because of 'unforseen results' from the P2Winners.
- Terrible community. Literally the same rhetoric from Soulsborne and fighting games, the salt is just as bad, if not worse. There's a lot of bitterness and trash talk in open channels, and people will cry "no honor" and "♥♥♥♥ing 1v2" in FOUR VS. FOUR Dominion/Elimination gametypes. If they want a 1v1 so badly, queue for the goddamn 1v1 gametype! I can bet you those mfers are probably too ♥♥♥♥♥ to play the 1v1 duels. Players also tend to RQ when they get their♥♥♥♥♥whooped and currently theres no penalty system in place to stop that. And when that happens to the whole opposing team, you're kicked to the menu for lacking player numbers. As if finding a game wasn't hard enough as is. GG.
- Few game modes. The current ones can get p stale too. I'm a little reserved on this one since they're apparently going to introduce more gametypes, so we'll see. Currently, the best game types are 1v1's and maybe 2v2's. When it's *that* focused, that's where it really shines (them mind games I mentioned. super fun). 4v4 gametypes just tend to be too chaotic to really enjoy all the mechanics and combos -- i tend to be on the defensive in a 1v4 more often than I am trying to outflourish another player..

Cons:

Survarium — это free2play MMO-шутер от первого лица(MMOFPS), действие которого разворачивается в недалеком будущем. События игры построены вокруг масштабной экологической катастрофы на Земле, причины которой достоверно неизвестны.
Ядро
Игра разрабатывается на новой собственной технологии Vostok Engine, выходцами из разогнанной GSC Game World. Основав новую студию под незатейливым названием Vostok Games, они решились повторить собственный успех, да только на поприще онлайновых развлечений. Собственно, так и появился Survarium.
Режим игры
В Survarium три игровых режима, каждый из которых — фактически отдельная игра. Режим командной игры ближе к классическим сетевым шутерам, где две команды игроков сражаются друг с другом, кооператив — это сюжетная кампания на нескольких человек, а режим свободной игры — это как раз та MMO в стиле S.T.A.L.K.E.R.
На момент старта открытого бета-теста смысл всего происходящего достаточно прост: проводим сессионные матчи в целях прокачки, заработка ресурсов и экипировки. Повторяем, пока не надоест. Проще говоря, формула World of Tanks перекочевала и сюда, только с присущими жанру FPS поправками.
Подготовка к игре
В игре присутствует магазин, в котором приобретается необходимое снаряжение, т.е. оружие, экипировка, патроны, и спецсредства. Также в игре присутствует великий рандом: по окончанию игры вам, возможно, повезет и выпадет какая-нибудь вещь, причем это может быть что угодно!
Все вещи имеют свой класс и характеристики и различаются по уровням- чем выше уровень надетого снаряжения, тем выше будет уровень боя, для соблюдения баланса. Представлены все виды стрелкового оружия, начиная с пистолетов, заканчивая ручными пулеметами и снайперскими винтовками.
Соответственно экипировка бойца состоит из множества вещей, начиная со шлема, заканчивая рюкзаком. Все эти ништяки можно купить за игровую валюту, заработанную в боях, либо, как уже было сказано, получить из рандома. Система монетизации пока- что построена так, что вкладывая в игру свои реальные деньги, вы не получаете особых преимуществ. Вы можете купить премиум- аккаунт, увеличивающий ваш доход, приобрести камуфляж любой расцветки для своей экипировки, купить премиум- вещь а также, к примеру, быстро починить свое оружие. Но тем не менее, игровой баланс продуман очень хорошо и «Pay to win» здесь не работает.
У всех вещей в игре есть свои характеристики, например каждая надетая вещь дает определенное количество брони, а у каждого оружия свой определенный урон. Помимо этого некоторые вещи добавляют слоты под патроны либо под спецсредства. У всех вещей есть свой вес, и чем больше и тяжелее на вас снаряжение, тем труднее бойцу передвигаться. От этого напрямую зависят показатели выносливости и скорости бега.
Умения
Чтобы повысить свои характеристики и боевую эффективность, в нашем распоряжении есть умения. Их пока только две ветки из пяти. Можно например увеличить скорость перезарядки, грузоподъемность или выносливость. Иными словами, собрать героя под свой вкус.
Геймплей
Если же говорить о геймплее, отличительной чертой проекта стало то, что личные достижения далеко не всегда означают результат. Дабы победить, необходимо таскать на базу и складировать ящики с микросхемами. По окончании срабатывает всем знакомое правило: у кого больше, тот и победил. Данная схема позволяет превратить присущий большинству сетевых шутеров хаос в некое подобие осмысленной партии, где побеждают лишь прикрывая и помогая друг другу. Ко всему прочему в игре присутствует деление на кланы и принадлежности- еще одна классическая составляющая современных онлайн игр.
Итог
Survarium представляет собой неплохую MMOFPS и выделяется из общей массы своей сталкерской атмосферой. Все-же игра пока что в открытом бета- тесте, и имеют место быть баги, неудобности и недоработки. Мы уверены, что когда игра будет доработана до конца так, как задумано, то в нее будут играть огромная масса любителей этого жанра. Это достойная внимания игра, которой хочется пожелать успехов в разработке. Ведь все мы уже давно соскучились по аномалиям, артефактам и выживанию в условиях повышенной радиации, которыми был полон знаменитый S.T.A.L.K.E.R.

I'm rating "Hook" at Not Recommended because of its inability to handle large, widescreen formats (in my case, a 34" monitor with 3440x1440 resolution).  It starts out fine, but within a few levels, elements start running off the screen until the puzzle cannot be worked.  According to some forum posts, hitting ALT-ENTER to switch between full and windowed mode should work around that.  In my case, all it did was give me a windowed mode game in which I couldn't see all the elements.  I ended up right-clicking on the executable (Hook.exe), selecting Properties then Compatibility and telling it to run in 640x480 resolution.  It let me finish the game, but looked pretty bad.
OTOH, if you don't have a large, widescreen monitor, the game is acceptable.  There are 50 fairly simple levels that took me a total of 89 minutes to finish.  That doesn't sound like much, but for the $0,84 I paid for it, it's right in line with my "dollar an hour" metric.  I have three minor issues (besides the widescreen problem):
- There's no volume control.  The only way to adjust (or turn off) the music/sound is do so at the OS level.
- The ESC key pops you IMMEDIATELY out of the game.  There's no confirmation that you really want to do that.
- There's absolutely no explanation of the game elements.  It's not tough to figure things out.  But, there really should be a blurb describing something the first time it's used.
Those are pretty trivial issues.  So, if you don't have a large, widescreen monitor, go ahead and give it a try.  If you do have a large, widescreen monitor, don't bother.

-Attempting to shoot Jason but instead murdering a fellow teammate who was in Jason's grip or behind Jason. This is probably the most common bug I've witnessed, and it can be quite frustrating when one loses XP due to unnecessary collateral damage.

This bug and others that disrupt potential escape oppurtunities are probably the worst ones for the game. TL:DR-This game is ultimately a fun experience (which is amplified by party play) that has certain bugs that don't ruin the experience, but definitely decrease the functionality of certain crucial game mechanics.

SUMMARY:
- Excellent squad based multiplayer FPS

I've played this a lot pre steam so don't pay attention to the /played above. I am from the hardcore crowd.
Survarium is not your typical project. It's not S.T.A.L.K.E.R 2, but it clearly appeals to the people who want a S.T.A.L.K.E.R 2. It has more or less the same kind of gear, of maps, of atmosphere, anomalies... But it's a multiplayer squad game (8vs8 battles, 15 min time limit with matchmaking) and it's Free to Play. There's a reciep for bitterness here so get your anticipations under a tight leash :P. Later, they'll have the freemode, which will not be S.T.A.L.K.E.R 2 either but will be closer to it, and is a very exciting prospect, but it's not anytime soon.
Survarium as it is now, then. Well good news, it's pretty great at what it does. It's one of the very few game of its genre with a real atmosphere. It's (very) pretty, the sound is amazing and the weapon feel is just as good as weapon feel gets in an FPS. Map design is also excellent, very strong vista, easy to understand terrain but lots to learn in practice, although quite a few imbalance (most maps are asymetrical). Also despite the inevitable "it's pay 2 win" rant that just every F2P gets, it's actually not at all P2W. To the point that if you consider buying stuff, I'd suggest you to focus on  premium rather than getting the golden weapon (although some can be an option for faster leveling). Weapons are statistically balanced. By "statistically" I mean it's not my opinion but what post match data show. Mostly all weapon are used, with no predominance.
That being said, the game has its problem, which mostly revolve on "lack of player for NA and to a lesser extent, EU". While they had open servers in NA there simply wasn't enough player for matchmaking to work there so right now it's merged with EU. Bottom line, if you're from the Americas, expect subpar ping. Clearly some deal with it (at the right hour, at least you only face ppl with subpar pings as well) but it's a big big cons. Even if you're from EU matchmaking can be a bit long (2-3 min) although it remains acceptable... The issue is more than when the player pool is low you end up meeting people far away from your league, both in term of skill and gear. From there you take a very painful beating. The game gives a few advantages (short invuln, respawn close to action) to base camped team but expect to rage fighting a brutal yet laughing robocop with a gun as big as you while you run at him in your sportswear and a water pistol. Even when it's not that extreme expect a lot of situation where you'll feel powerless.
Which is not to say you'll actually be that powerless. Most people beaten by a guy with better gear don't realise they're mostly outskilled because better gear also mean way more experience in the game. If you set your mind on learning (what could I have done better) you'll see that while the gear difference is real, everyone die fast in that game and there's always something you can do.
To sum it up it's a pretty hardcore squad based experience. To some extent it looks like COD with much better gun play, superb post apocalyptic atmosphere and a few interesting and original modes such has "find and bring back the batteries". It also has a few signatures element:
- constant grass amount: no matter the quality setting, visibility is the same for all. As a result, hiding is essential and force you to work on your peripheral vision, notice small moves at a distance at the border of the screen etc.
- anomalies: odd piece of.... thingy that developp on the map during the game. They're toxic and can kill you and block path but with proper gear you can also collect them for buffs
- bullet physics: bullet go through lesser material or bounce or both. They also slightly fall at long range.

Woa this one is a bit hard to review. It's an old game from an old distant galaxy in the olden times...
Fast review: If it's 10$ or less, you can buy it, over that go buy starforce 2 instead! Much better in everyway!!!
Now for the detailed review:
- Space strategy 4x game realtime with pause and adjustable speed. Colonize planets, develop them, build ships, conquer
- There ain't much graphics in this game. An old windows xp can run this game fine. Ship battle are kinda 2D boring affair.
- There is far too much bass in the background music! I had to turn it off after a few minutes, i was THAT annoyed by it.
- The gui is unpolished. It's not buggy, but it's not intuitive. It takes quite a while to find out where everything is and how it works. Because it's not a big AAA game, there ain't much information either in forums or elsewhere. It's pretty sparse. But on the other hand, if you stick with it, the learning curve is not that bad. Nothing compared to Distant Universe for example.
- The ship design is unique compared to any game i've played. Designing a dreadnought or a cruiser is the same, only the amount of armor and the hull choice seems to decide what amount of HP the ship has, but they both will have the same amount of components. A bit dull if you ask me. Clunky too. But, god it's complicated at first with something like 20 stats that you can affect with the components you include. Example: Amount of ammo your ship has, the amount he will spend by second, the amount of fuel, amount of fuel spent by second, amount of energy generated and on and on. I think it's a bit too much detail, but you can design your ship to your heart content! Also, all ships pretty much looks the same, only difference is size (which you can also set. If you want a fighter bigger looking than your dreadnought, you can do that too!).
- The research graph is interesting and kinda fun. I like it. It's also one of the few part of the game that is intuitive and easy to understand and use.
- The zoom and map movement is pretty horrible. It made me think of the first 3D game i've ever played where they had not yet mastered how to move the camera in 3D. Haven't found a good way yet to move around my empire except by planet name. And the funny part is that the game may look like 3D, but you actually move only in 2D. HAHAHA!
- The amount of ships you are going to lose because of them reaching empty fuel is pretty crazy. You need tankers everywhere and in large numbers. Yeah if a ship or fighter reach zero fuel, they die and can't be 'revived' except maybe with boarding ships.
On the other hand, there are no cash and no ship maintenance in this game. So if you want a fleet with 1 million ships, you can go ahead and do it. You seem to only be limited by the amount of ore that is on planets and asteroids.
- You can automate each ship with pretty detailed orders, but you can also shoot yourself in the foot repeatedly with a bad automated order. It does not always act like you think it does. And there are no explaination anywhere about them. So go go experiment.
- Everything in the game will improve with the appropriate tek researched. Every building on planets, every component on a ship including armor and hull. There are a lot of research fields.
- You can retrofit ships as long as you kept the same design name. For example, 'Carrier' blueprint. If you changed the name, then it is not considered the same class of ship and no retrofit for you. So you keep the starting design from start to end game. Does not matter that you completely change a ship vocation and components, as long as the design name is the same you can retrofit it.
- You will make millions of ships. Eventually, you won't even bother and you will put your planets on repeat order so they crank out the same ships forever. And you send them attacking the frontier. You can have a biiiiiiiig empire. A bit hard to manage properly thought.
- They kept the physics in the game as newtoninan as possible with even ship mass and thruster power. Depending on mass, a ship can take awhile before changing speed or even direction! It sure is pretty realistic, but i don't think it makes for very fun battles. The amount of errors you will make in your designs before you get them just right is going to be huge.
- I've looked at the starforce 2 game and it seemed much better than this one. They kept the same concept, but graphics are loads better, the gui too is a lot more friendly with nice icons that do what they look like, spying and improved diplomacy to do dirty trics and the design of ships seems much more interesting and fun. Also, unlimited galaxy that you can generate! You decide the shape of the map and how many stars there is and they generate it for you! You are only limited by the speed of your computer! So you can 'in theory' generate a billion star map! It won't play well but you can do it!
- Diplomacy is pretty bare bone and pointless. Enemy ai don't seem too challenging either after you master the game. Everything looks a bit bland. Once you played one game to completion, you don't really want to play another one.

The Darkness II is (obviously) the sequel to The Darkness. Unlike the orignal, The Darkness II has a bright and comic-like graphic style. This is a bit odd seeing as how the game is called "The Darkness", and that it's kind of hard to tell if you're actually in a dark spot or are under a light. (Don't get me wrong, the game flat out makes it obvious that you're in light because it makes both Jackie and the darkness itself flinch. It's a little annoying, honestly.) The game has great voice acting and a decent story, and both the aiming and darkness mechanics are a huge improvement from the first game. Also, unlike the orignal game, you're no longer wandering back and forth in a "free-roam" type of style, instead you're lead on a linear path. As much as I like the beautifully colorful art style in this game, I miss the dark and dreadful style of the first one. But, all in all, The Darkness II is a wonderful game and a must-buy if you enjoyed the first game.

The promising sequel to a fantastic XBL indie arcade game.
If you're new to this game, congratulations, you're in for a treat. Take an FPS, put it at the bottom of the ocean, fill the arena with viscious sharks, and this is what you get. It's a unique experience that I can't say I've really had anywhere else. Moving through 3D space adds a new level of depth to your actions. You don't have to worry about an enemy hiding behind cover on top of a building, you have to worry about an enemy floating over your head. While 3D movements might not be new in the space shooter genre, it is a unique addition to the FPS realm.
Currently the game consists of a deathmatch mode, and a solo-survival mode. In survival you have to battle it out for as long as you can against hordes of sharks. At the time of my writing this I have been informed that co-op survival will be out soon, and I can assure you that's going to be a new level of fun.
Lastly, if you're the type of person who likes to support cool indie devs, this is definitely something you want to get behind. Just look at the fourms; the devs are always interacting with, and taking feedback from, the community. I've even played a handful of games with the devs myself.
P.S. If you'd like to try this game out before dropping money on it, I highly recommend grabbing the demo or paying $1 for the first game on your 360. It will give you a good feel for how this game plays.

* Non-gimmicky combat dynamics
* Surreal, dark atmosphere
* Rewarding skill trees that encourage dynamic play styles
* Sound effects and voice acting are crisp and realistic
* Varied enemies and unique combat situations
* Story was lame and overly-climactic
* Far too short
* The post-endgame gamemodes don't add much replay value
* Optical focus issues during gameplay (solvable by restart)
* Exploration utilises quick-time events too often
An enjoyable game with unique, creative combat situations and isn't bogged down by cinematics, etc. Thus it makes for a good (albeit short-lived) pick-up-and-play, if not for the dishearteningly short story.

Its hard today to keep an unbiased opinion on early release games when the Steam Store in flooded with them.
A good example of this is a survivalist, first-person shoot-em-up known as Nether. Although Nether is pretty standard in its game mechanics and resembles most of the styles of DayZ. Which is a game almost everyone has heard of, and or played. DayZ originally (was) a free client-side mod for Arma 2 which is now currently $30 on the steam store. Arma 2 was a very dull, hyper-realistic military shooting game that was as fun as watching paint dry.
The summary of Nether is that you spawn in the games variety of safezones or in the open world. Scavange to find various resources to get the edge on other players, all the while trying to grasp your manhood after running from most, if not all of the creatures in the game.
Earlier you might have noticed that I compared this game to DayZ frequently. That my friends is because this is practically is DayZ with updated graphics, smaller world design, and more content. One of the most prominent features being the player on player interaction of this game which consists of three basic principles.
1.) Do not ever trust anyone you do not know.
2.)You will encounter bandits who have a insane advantage over you and will imediately shoot you on sight.
3.)Newbie players who you will kill in order to blow off some steam from constantly getting killed.
In my honest opinion I am against games that are Early-access which cost money. However, to the games credit it did have a large variety of weapon choices and it would seem to be fun to play with your friends. Another positive outlook that I have, is that compared to most Early-access games, the developers do a great job of updating the game. My final word is that Nether is a hit and miss type of game that will either fully immerse you in its world, or have you deleting it from your steam library a couple days later.
I can not recomend this game to everyone. If you like survival type games then go for it cause for the games credit. It was extremely fun to play at times.

First of all, ignore the time played counter, it is not reflective of the amount of hours I spent playing ArcaniA. Because of technical issues, I had to constantly switch between the Steam version and a retail version. A more accurate game time would be around 20-21 hours.
At it's core, AcraniA is a failed experiment. After Pirahana Bytes washed its hands of the series after the publisher, JoWooD, forced Gothic 3 out the door before it was ready, Spellbound Entertainment (who is most notable for Desperados) was given the reins. However, Spellbound was a studio that didn't have any prior experience in the type of RPG that Gothic was, and it shows. ArcaniA's intended purpose was simple: To reboot the Gothic series and turn it into a more accessible, console-friendly experience. This idea was misguided at best and while there is nothing at all wrong with making formerly very hardcore franchises into more welcoming ones (Deus Ex, System Shock, Hitman, etc), ArcaniA completely fails to understand what worked about Gothic as a series. The property is simply misused here, and the additions to the mythology and world of Gothic only serve to undermine it. The much beloved freedom the previous games had is also sacrificed in order to have a more linear experience that exists in an unhappy middle-ground between Fable and Oblivion.
The story takes place on an unexplored island that has not been represented in any Gothic game before and features a new protagonist. After Gothic 3/FG, The Nameless Hero was crowned Rhobar III and has embarked on a campaign of conquest with the goal to unify all of humanity under one banner. This campaign comes at the cost of many lives, however, including your hometown and your (immediately killed off and fridged minutes after introduction) fiance, which is razed to the ground with you as the only survivor. The story continues from there and characters from the other Gothic games make appearances as crucial characters in the story, with each getting redesigned from the ground up. Examples would be that now Diego is a swarthy, vaguely Spanish-ish, pirate and Gorn loves violence and fighting. To be fair, the Gothic games didn't have the strongest of characters to begin with, so this can be excused.
What can't be excused is how the plot ultimately progresses into nonsense. Not the fun kind of nonsense that developers like Quantic Dream deliver, but the confusing, irritating nonsense of a story that was written in a hurry and poorly translated. Even at the end, I still didn't know anything beyond a surface level understanding of the events that are taking place.
ArcaniA also ditches the Genome Gaming Engine that powered Gothic 3 for the Vison 7 engine and at times, the game can look quite nice. There are some nice lighting effects and the view distance is quite good as well. However, that is about all the nice things I can say about the tech that drive this game. While Genome was buggy and unoptimized, I would have very much preferred it during my time with ArcaniA. The Steam version in particular is currently broken on the highest settings, with lighting and shadow rendering being miscast onto characters faces, to name one problem. The framerate/framepacing was also abysmal on hardware from 2016, with an incredibly bad play feel. Eventually I googled the problems I was having and discovered that the best way to play is with a patched up retail copy. So I ended up buying this game twice in order to play through it because of the lack of maintenance on the Steam version. However, the retail version is also very broken, with textures and shadows sometimes completely failing to load, 2D elements such as the HUD and map/mini-map becoming corrupt and video cutscenes refusing to play. In order to experience ArcaniA in the best possible way, I ended up having to constantly switch between the retail version and the steam version.
The overall aesthetic of the game is also quite plain. Spellbound was clearly 'inspired' by the success of other console-focused western RPG's, especially Oblivion, and attempted to replicate that look. So expect lots of European looking castles, farms, inns and the like. There are also some snowy temples, a giant magical tree surrounded by swamp, but it's mostly castles and villages. The most interesting looking area, which had a very Arabian look to it, was blocked off in the game and you only ever see the front facade of it, along with the skyline. Nothing about the art style is notable or exceptional in any way.
The combat and RPG systems of Gothic have also been left behind in favor of a very basic combat and leveling up system. The core gameplay loop is indistinguishable from most RPG's where you see an enemy, kill the enemy, get xp, repeat. Not to say that Gothic didn't reinvent the wheel with combat, but it felt far more interesting then it does in ArcaniA The interesting Learning Points system is replaced with a menu-driven perk system, which is, again, very plain.
Overall, ArcaniA dosen't succeed in it's mission. The game didn't sell well, Spellbound went under with JoWooD, who was already in dire fiancial straits, and history moved on. I can't even recommend this game as a curiosity for fans of the series or a simple timesink because the game is so plain and mediocre as well as bug-ridden and glitchy.

The only part I had trouble with (and this seems to be a common sentiment) is the gameplay of the rites themselves. The difficulty curve is... really weird, to put it mildly, and certain characters are far easier to work with than others, which adds another layer of strategy to the liberation rites. Do you send a character away because you think it will have the best effect on the story, or just so that you don't have to use them any more?
For me, the parts of this game that I enjoyed far outweigh the parts that I found frustrating and I would definitely recommend this for anyone who enjoys a story with a great ensemble cast.

I don't feel this game deserves all the hate that it receives but I will admit that it is objectively a bad game. With that, you can still find some enjoyability and I just-barely recommend it for at least one playthrough if you've beaten your other action RPGs. Some quick thoughts after beating it...
Pros:
*Good visuals.
*Easy to pick up and learn.
*Ability to choose between melee, archery, or mage paths.
*Main voice actor does a decent job.
*Story is just interesting enough to keep you interested at times.
Cons:
*Most of the voice actors are garbage.
*Character development is really shallow.
*Pace of the game is agonizingly slow at times if you explore everywhere.
*Story is a fairly typical revenge story. A shepherd becomes a god (figuratively).
*Linear game progression. (This didn't realy bother me, though)
*Combat is fairly basic. Ranged playstyles are basically easy mode while melee can have a really hard time on the harder difficulties.
Conclusion: If it's on sale, give it a shot. You can rush it if you like. If you focus on the experience and don't try to find things to hate, you may even like it a little bit.

I barely write reviews. This game is quite different to the other Games by Supergiant Games (Bastion and the absolutely amazing Transistor). I somehow expected to be disappointed, because I was in total awe from Transistor and had just played it for the first time a couple of weeks before Pyre came out. So I was totally pumped, but also worried.
But, from the moment I started the game I was sucked into the strange world and it's fascinating characters and lore. I absolutely enjoyed the various characters, their interaction and the story that was told. Indeed, again Supergiant Games managed to create a fascinating and not-yet-seen fantasy world, something that most games lack today. It shows that it's still possible to create something truely fantastic (creative, new, special).
I read some critique about the "game in the game" and that it doesn't quite stand up to it's predecessors, but I must really disagree! It's quite different, which I like, and I could definately feel Supergiants magic touch. It is not a fight with weapons and no murder, granted. But that's very interesting for a change!
I find it deeply satisfying and oddly tactical. It's really something that fits quite well in the whole story and like the fights in Transistor, it doesn't get old due to a lot of possible upgrades and player combinations and the fact that I as the player could learn and progress myself aswell. At the same time, it gives the game meaning and winning a game (losing is part of it, too!) feels really good, especially when your characters needed the point!
So to make it short, I love the game, it's very creative and has a really rich and interesting story, great characters (and beautiful ART and MUSIC!!) and a special way to resolve the classic "fighting" with a high-paced, satisfying gameplay.
Strongly Recommended!

A worthy sequel. After the first set of test chambers, each successive set (at least so far--I just finished the third) introduces a new gadget. Along with new robots, this enables a wider variety of puzzles compared to the first game where using gadgets was just for fun (except for the Teleporter Chambers, of course). In fact, that's probably the best way to imagine the test chambers in this game--like the teleporter DLC from the first game but more variety.
The next big change is the overworld--all of the test chambers are connected via a Metroidvania style overworld. After each set of test chambers that features a gadget, you get to use that gadget in the overworld, opening up passage to the next area as well as to numerous secrets and challenges.
My only real complaint so far is that it's not as clear as in most Metroidvania games when you are missing the right item to proceed, or when you simply haven't figured out the puzzle. This is somewhat due to the nature of the gadgets--there isn't a really obvious obstacle like a different color door, for example. On the first playthrough you have no idea what the upcoming gadgets are so you can't realize, "Oh, I will be able to come back here when I unlock gadget X."
This is a very minor complaint and I figured out my error with a bit of Googling (someone else had the exact same confusion) so it is very easy for me to recommend this game to both fans of the first Stealth ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥/Stealth Inc. game, and to anyone looking for a Metroidvania puzzle game.

I would not recommend this game.  However, it wasn't bad, but I got the game for $1 and got my money's worth out of it.
Anyways... Tutorial was terrible and could be skipped past without any problems.  The asteroid level/minigame in the beginning I absolutely hated, but I can see where it's needed for story (if the game has any) and I wish you could skip passed it at will (you can skip it if you fail too many times).
Once you get to the game I enjoyed building the houses and doing quests to gain colonists.  The most difficult part is figuring out how to tell them what to do.  For one, someone has to plant trees and another cut when I feel like that should be one job, because the wheat planter also harvests.  Your max inventory is limited to 5 item types with 16 being the max per stack.  I could live with that since, but end up making a lot of stockpiles that only hold one type of item.
Finally, it feels unfinished still: I found a few bugs and there is one resource I never found a use for that you have to mine from rocks.  You can cook wheat to make bread, you can make flower out of wheat, and cook wheat into bread.  Either way you make break you still end up with the same amount of bread per wheat and the colonists don't know how to cook flour so it's a useless resource.  You can put the crafting bench, furnace and a stockpile in the houses, but I was only ever able to place a workbench and nothing else.  I did get lucky a few times; I was able to place the furnace instead of a workbench and also place a stockpile in one house and that house also happened to have a workbench in it.  I encountered a bug were if you gather over the 16 stack size in your inventory without unloading it, that resource vanishes into thin air.  I found it because I was mining rock to build the big house which needs 16 stone.  I mined over 16 and it disappeared.  I just dismissed it as a fluke but it happened a second time too.  After that I was very careful to never overload my character with resources.
Worth a few good spooks, really good story as well.

I'll write this review from my point of view as a long time high level player of SB.
The core changes in Stealth Inc 2 can be summed up as such
The new equipment requires that you aim manually using your mouse (for mouse and keyboard players). Using teleporters from SBD as the reference point, the new control scheme requires far more dexterity as you need to specifically aim your throw. Unlike the original where you only have 3 static paths to choose from (high, middle, low), you now have the freedom of adjusting your throw arc according to your mouse position. They also introduced throw strength (e.g. single click to drop the equipment next to you, long clicks to do maximum distance throws). The most annoying thing about this is aiming while the camera moves as the throw arc changes with the camera perspective. Note that just as in SBD, the lines indicating the throw path are ultimately just guides, the actual path is actually slightly different.
In case you're wondering, yes you can remap the key bindings.
In Stealth Inc 2, the graphics have been overhauled and it's now a 2.5D experience. However, this change is one I actually dislike as I prefer the faster response of SBD. Subjectively, I find that the movement of the player character is somewhat different from SBD. Basically, there's a stronger sense of inertia now which makes it such that changing directions when you're running is slower. When changing directions quickly, you will sometimes notice that you're moving in the opposite direction that you're facing (e.g. moving left but facing right).
There are
graphical options apart from Resolution, Anti-Aliasing and Fullscreen/Windowed mode.
The sound isn't exactly catchy but it also isn't something you'll end up turning off. It's very similar to the original games given that it's done by the same person, Ricky Honmong. =)

Eh, I don't play this anymore really at all vanilla, too many excellent mods (aka most anything not brutal doom) supersede the vanilla experience. But let's review this nevertheless for the sake of doing it.
- Setting. Game might be about blasting monsters mindlessly, but there is definitely a pretty solid lore in there. A mega-corporation with low morals. Space marines. Risky scientific endeavors. So put shortly, UAC conducts teleportation tests between two sites built in Phobos and Deimos. Surely enough demons, bored, decide to pour in both facilites in masses after noticing the convenient wormhole made by UAC's teleportation test. Phobos quickly gets overrun, same happens to Deimos facilities but even more unpleasantly The whole damn moon disappears from Mars's orbit to someplace else entirely..so you are now alone, in Phobos's hangar. Only way out is through the masses of those foul creatures. Angry demon slaying ensues.
- Protagonist, while he suffers from the classic problem of FPS-protagonist wordlessness, there definitely is a lot of character to him. Seriously. A lone marine armed with weapons and his hatred for demons goes through the 2 overrun UAC sites and lastly goes through Hell and is at the end teleported back to Earth..only to discover an unpleasant revelation. Is able to withstand a strength enhancing drug that allows to punch humanoids to a bloody mess in a single hit, while for an average fit person the drug can be fatal. He is also good guy material, he refused to attack innocent civilians when his superior ordered so.
- Weapons. Standard FPS guns, for weapons 1-5 there is the pistol, pump shotgun, hilariously slow firing gatling gun and a rocket launcher that fires hilariously fast. Last 2 weapons are plasma ordnances, a rifle and then the BFG that can clear a room of baddies in a single shot's blast.
- Gunplay. Not bad for '93. Super shotgun, rocket launcher, plasma gun and BFG got great sounds.
- Enemy designs. Simply iconic foes. And by mechanics side too good design although the enemies lose out to Build engine games' enemies in threat level.
- Atmosphere. There seriously is that. First episode, you romp through the Phobos base, consisting of a high tech theme.
Then, deimos base, which has from first level off, been modified by demons, there starts to be marble, wood and holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ even flesh as building materials. So yeah episode 2 is a cool sickening combination of human tech and demonic architecture.
Lastly, blast through the vicious hordes in Hell itself. Diabolic undertones aplenty. And gore. Tortured to death humans are seen every level.
- Thrash metal soundtrack. There are however more ambient pieces too which are just as memorable. I recommend to use Virtualmidisynth and a proper soundfont to maximize musical greatness.
The bad:
- This release doesn't come with an option to launch either in dosbox emulation or to use a source port..come on.
And lastly for some mod recommendations (not all of these are complete yet) Hotline UAC, PSX Doom conversion, Demonsteele, Zharkov goes to the store, DoomZ, Knee Deep in Zdoom, Russian Overkill. Not gonna include Brutal Doom here since that mod has gone way too complex and overall in many ways inferior to version 11-16. And it never was a mod as magical as people make it out to be.
