In preparation for the imminent release of Adventurer Manager I thought I would add this review based on my experience with the game as an active Alpha Tester - some may call my review biased given my tester status so I should point out that I'm just a normal guy who stumbled upon Adventurer Manager a few months ago and leapt at the opportunity to get a hands on look at this great game. If you find my review a little one sided, then just put it down to me loving AM! :)
Firstly what is Adventurer Manager?
To sum it up in a nutshell AM is a retro style RPG with a traditional 80's / 90's feel JRPG combat system with a heavy emphasis on humor, customisation and dungeon grinding, loot finding goodness.
The game is still in it's alpha stage so a large quantity of what the developers still have planned has yet to make it to release, but it is clear that when it's all in AM will lack for nothing and will be in my opinion one of the most content rich and fun to play games of it's genre.
Dont believe me? Want to check out what the developers has in store? Head on over to the VA Studios forum and have a look  - I think you'll agree...it's gonna be large! ;)
Dialogue, NPC's and Story:
There has been a large amount of effort into scripting and designing some of the most hilarious NPC's and random quests and I take my hat off to the devs for still making me chuckle every time I get smited with a paperclip upon completeing a quest. Seriously...The Baker anyone?  :D
Graphics and Sound:
Whilst the 8-Bit retro feel isn't to everyones liking  I personally find the design of the game to be top class - The amount of detail and effort into making each piece of gear, each mob (be it standard or boss) and each dungeon unique and well crafted is extraordinary. In so many other games of it's type you end up seeing a large number of 'pallet swaps', but not so in AM. Every element has a vibrant and chunky feel to it. There are still missing pieces to some of the art (mostly with regards to skills/spells), but these will be upcoming and I'm confident they'll be just as good as what is currently completed.
The same with the sound and music - There are some missing sound effects in the game, and one or two of the tracks are a little short before they loop to beginning however, the music itself is addicting, well composed and well implemented. A few of the tracks have that 'sticks in your head' side to them so all in all I'd definately rate the audio.
Gameplay:
So far  lvl range 1-21 is unlocked, 3 races and 5 classes to choose from and a host of skills for each class to play around with. The customisation at the moment is limited as the developers primary focus was to get the UI and dungeon, loot and combat mechanics in place however considering the alpha status of the game it will still take many, many, many hours of grinding and getting slaughtered by boss's to 'finish' the current content and with the amount of things on the cards I couldn't want for more! Each update and new feature that gets added is exciting  and I constantly look forward to seeing what is round the corner.
Whilst in a lot of games grinding can be repetative and dull I think this game has captured well that diabloesque feel to it. Each time I go through a dungeon and find that legendary or unique class piece of loot I get that 'OOOoooo shiny!' feel and I still don't get tired of slaughtering pixelated bats by the thousand lol.
Production and the development team:
It's not often a reviewer would add something about the guys making the game, but my alpha testing has given me the opportunity to speak to the developers via chat/forums and I can say unreservedly that the team itself is one of the friendliest, open, and passionate about their game teams I have encountered. I strongly recommend any who like the idea of being part of Early Access to head over to the VA Studios website, sign up to their forums and get involved with the AM community :)

Take over an island lair, recruit and train your minions, then use them to commit acts of infamy around the world.  You'll need to carefully balance accessibility for your minions and traps and defenses for the spies that are soon to come poking around, recruit henchmen and level them up, and finally make sure that your minions' needs are met so they don't lose loyalty to your organization!
It's a ton of fun, and the only reason I can think of that it hasn't been done again is that the bar's set too high. This is seriously my favorite game of all time, and one of the best base-builders I've ever played.
The theme is great and really fitting, and very reminiscent of a lot of super-villain based movies. The diversity of your minions is also awesome (in terms of minions, you've got the smart, the social, and the strong). The mechanics are really simplistic in a lot of ways but feel really deep - like the stats system in the game. It all works out to really reduce the amount of micro-management you typically have to do in a base-building game.
The AI is something special in EG. In a lot of games, the AI just sort of knows where everything is and just rushes your face until either they're dead or you're dead. In EG, enemy agents that come to your island have literally no idea where anything is, where and traps are or anything at all really. They have to explore your island themselves, and they'll do their best to spot out any obvious traps you leave for them and break into every area they think is suspicious. It's also cool to sometimes see your own minions patrol around the base on their own when they're bored and have nothing else to do, taking the occasional smoke break (usually in the freezer, no idea why).
EG's an amazing game, and I really wish they'd make a sequel instead of Facebook games and stuff. Maybe one day, but for now this is a great pick-up. It goes on sale all the time, and it's an absolute bargin for $2.50 when it's -75% off. Buy it.

Linear action FPS game with a lot of violence, blood and vulgarity. Basically it's like playing a horror game but
What I love most about this game is the story-telling, the narrative of the game. All the characters in this game have their own personality, even the crazy ones! The person who voiced Johnny Powell is a genius!
There is a multiplayer mode called the "Vandette". It has a number of co-op missions that you can play solo or play with up to 4 players online. Each playable characters have their own personality and their own dialogues as well! The multiplayer campaign fills in the holes in the single player story very well.
The artsy graphics adds a lot of nostalgic feel to the game environment. This type of graphics rendering method also brilliantly mask away a lot of disgust from the bloody violence where it would be gross if rendered too realistically.
If you are the reading type and like to understand as much of the game world as possible, you can learn a lot from reading the relics origin. The game universe is based a lot closely to our real world religions, with a little fictional element added into it. And it makes a lot of sense! (On top of that, it has the funny narration from the crazy genius!)
Once you are done with the single player campaign, you can replay the campaign with new game plus to learn more about the game setting and to hunt for collectibles. But it's only worth 2-3 playthrus before it gets repetitive. Multiplayer have quite a number of maps but since multiplayer characters have very limited skillset, it gets repetitive very soon.
My Score: 10/10 (Highly recommended!)

Overall this game has almost everything most first person shooters come out today forget about: a good story, a sense of pacing, diverse combat, and color pallete with more than just a few shades of brown.

Sniper Elite V2 is a fun sniping orientated 3rd person shooter. In this game you play as a generic American White male with no backstory sent to single handedly take out hundreds of nazis. Bullet ballistics can be tweaked to be affected by wind, gravity, or nothing for a casual experience. The game does allow you to equip a secondary SMG and pistol but close quarters combat is usually not the correct play because you die very easily in this game. Enemy AI is competent enough to try to flank you while a sniper or mg nest pins you down.
The shooting feels and sounds great. Also the by now iconic gore kill cams of the series are of course present and do a good job at breaking up the monotony of the otherwise very basic combat. There's nothing like seeing the same bullet enter the heart of one enemy and exit out te testicles of another. :) The kill cam can be turned off or lessened.
Stealth is by far the most fun and effective way to play this game. However this is where the game's greatest issue surfaces. While the original sniper elite was about open levels where stealth was incredibly encouraged, Sniper Elite V2's levels feel like guided linear corridors in comparison. Stealth is also just not always an option sometimes which is frustrating.
Enemy AI is for the most part decent. However, one annoyance was that if you are detected by one enemy soldier, for some reason literally all other enemies in the vicinity will immediately know your exact location.
The game also has co-op missions/hoard mode which has no one playing it atm and multiplayer which is still active with a very small community. That being said as someone in US WEST, the closest server to me had a ping of over 500.
Overall the base game is great fun but even for the somewhat low base price of 20 USD I say perhaps wait for a sale unless you really love sniping games. I usually take my time with games but for this game the main campaign literally took me only 6 hours to beat on the "medium" difficulty.
As for the DLC, Neudorf features an open map that shows that the majority of the main game's maps should've been like. Aka decent sized maps where you can choose how to tackle the objective and use stealth. Landwehr is the hardest one by far which 100% requires stealth or you will lose. St. Pierre is extremely mediocre. All the mentioned DLC take about an hour each to beat which honestly isn't enough content for full price. Kill Hitler might seem cool at first... that is until you realize that you are paying 8 USD for a mission that is literally 20 minutes long.

Well, I don't really see where some of these bad reviews come from. I'll admit I'm only 16 hours into this game, However, I've been thoroughly enjoying this game. Visually, It's quite fun to look at it, Extremely beautiful. However there's a lot of reused sprites, and voices which can be a flaw to some (It is slightly annoying, but not a minus for me) I actually enjoy the story so far, I think the combat is alright with really three main ways of playing, Mage, Melee weapon or Bows/Crossbows. There's a lot of crafting you can do(Like making weapons) and a bit of alchemy to do(Like making your own potions, These potions vary from adding to your health regen to increasing your overall stats temporarily)
I will say this though, This game is a bit buggy. You can get stuck in poorly rendered areas or just jumping where you aren't suppose to go, The cut-scenes will make you crash from time to time as well, However you can easily watch the cut scenes from within the Arcania folder if you do crash and just skip them in game. Does this make the game unplayable? For me, No it doesn't. It can be annoying to crash during a cutscene and have to rewatch it again, But it's no big deal for the most part.
I'll also say this, I had a lot more problems running this game off an FX-8150 CPU than I do with my current i7 3770k(Graphics card is a 7970 for those wondering), Whether this game doesn't like AMD or something along those lines I can't say for sure, But my system isn't a slouch by any means. I feel like this game might run better on older systems then newer systems, For instance my laptop running an old first gen i7 at 1.73GHz and a 1GB ATI card(I think 5850) seems to run it without any cut scene errors or crashes.
But in the end, I really do enjoy this game, The main story keeps me interested, I feel the combat is alright for the style of game that it is, and despite some minor things here and there, I would recommend this game when it's on sale. I personally feel it's worth it's $20 price tag that it wears now. If you see it on sale and you read the reviews and thought "Well, Now I'm not too sure..." I would take the chance to try it out. I can't vouch for the other games in the series as I've never played them, But please, Give this one a chance!
Edit: I've now completed the game with 26 hours played, I'm definitely going to be playing through it one more time, And possibly might buy the DLC as well. I took my time for the most part playing through this and had all but one quest finished(finding 30 belier artifacts), So I'll assume you can get around 25 30 hours on average for this game's full completion. The ending was a tad disappointing in terms of the fight, However I feel the story was still enjoyable despite this. Combined with the great visuals, and a decent combat system, I think this game was well worth picking up if you enjoy RPGs. There is quite a bit of walking, Like most RPGs but it never once bothered me.
There is a huge amount of potions you can create, A handful of decent weapons, and a couple decent armors. The best items you can craft obviously don't come till later on in the game. The weapons you can make don't come until you're about half way 3/4ths of the way done with the game, When you're able to create Steel Ingots. Some boss fights are underwhelming, Especially when you play the game at normal difficulty or lower, Some bosses will drop some decent weapons however. I strongly recommend following the "Kill everything you see" tactic, Unless you run into mobs that you have difficulty taking down, As each mob will drop a certain item that is special to it. That's it for what I have to say, Enjoy!

-graphics; dynamic and unique, this game looks like a CGI cinematic during gameplay.
-combat. Feels refined, no odd glitches or overpowered abilities or enemies.
-Story. The constant pursuit to rescue Juno keeps the pace of the game quick.
The Bad
-variety. Not the largest variety of enemies. Trying to keep enemies in-line with the franchise is challenging, but is also restrictive.
-quicktime events. Overdone and finishes off tough enemies quickly and easily.

I hadn't read or known anything about this game before I played it, and I ended up being completely blown away.  I played this with a friend, and after each play session, we'd find ourselves in deep conversations about some of the game's themes/ideas/questions.  It was incredibly haunting, even if I didn't realize it fully while playing it.
Besides the themes, the gameplay itself was awesome.  It was the right amount of scary, the right amount of mystery, and the story was gripping.  The enemies were varried, and even though the environments seemed similar, we found them different enough to still be fun.
My only complaints (SPOILERS): Huge decions/choices didn't really matter in the end.  The online community was quick to point out that these questions were meant to affect the actual player (which they absolutely, did to this day), but it still would have been nice to have it swing the story somehow. This also would have increased replayability.  My second complaint is that I also kept waiting for a big twist or surprise-- even until the very end. Just don't bother, guys. This title had a ton of potential, but it just fails as a game. The only thing it has going for it is its production values, with pretty decent cinematics and at least some good voice acting. But the actual gameplay is what we buy it for, and that part is frankly broken. Way too much backtracking (made worse by the lack of a map or other fast travel option), increasingly absurd "keys" and other such cliched inanity, and far, far, FAR too many times - even for a game like this - when a simple solution (like just smashing that thin pane of glass with any of the several suitable tools in my inventory) was rejected as "impossible" in favor of yet another of the far too numerous "special" access items or actions. In fact, while I know these are a staple of the genre, never have I seen them so blatantly and nonsensically overused throughout every segment of game - they absolutely saturate it. Thankfully, the ordeal will be over in under two hours, assuming you're a genre veteran.
Even the Hidden Object scenes are far too easy for any but the youngest players (and some darkness in the story undermines the game's suitability for that particular audience), and if you keep the UI locked to the screen (as many of us prefer to do), you WILL have blocked objects in almost every HO scene - a cardinal sin of HO design. And in the rest of the game, progression is frequently obscured by unintuitive action requirements. The nail in the coffin? A glitch kept a late-game item from entering my inventory when I found it, instead resetting its little vignette and keeping me from activating it again - translation: I couldn't finish the last minutes of the game. For you developers out there, that's not really what we'd call acceptable.

EDIT: It's been a few months so I decided to come back to 'The Isle' to see how it had changed since I last played. The progression system has been streamlined a lot since then, it is now a pretty good mix of eating and time spent in game giving you progression points. It doesn't feel as slow or as desperate. Survival mode now adds something to the game instead of limiting it too much.
Mod support has been added, allowing the community to change the game however they wish. So far, there are a few new maps and some mods that allow differing rules and conditions within the game. It has added a lot of power to the community, allowing the devs to persue their end goal without us losing out on features or game modes.
Overall the game has come a long way since I last played and the community in-game is still just as strong and friendly as I remember. Given the ability to have heavily customised servers, the future of the game looks very promising. I was wrong when I said that the game wouldn't return to something I would want to play, it has, and well done to the devs for listening to the community and giving back the sandbox mode everyone loved. I have to say though, the survival mode is just as fun now. This is a game I can now recommend, I hope it stays that way.

You could be a wide range of awesome looking dinosaurs, roaming the plains and forests, using in game sounds and gestures to communicate with each other. Then the game started getting updates which weren't ready for public servers, things like leg breaking, which meant you couldn't step over a small rock or run at all without risking broken leg and 10-30mins of sitting, waiting for it to heal. It took months before this was addressed and then the progression system hit. Sandbox mode was turned off so that progression would be tested properly. I think they did this because they knew no one would play it otherwise. It's terribly punishing and makes very little sense, the fun fell out of the bottom of the game overnight and the community became sour. The devs hit back with bans and insults and things got progressively worse. I stopped playing when I realised their vision of the game was far removed from what they had sold and I very much doubt that the game will ever return to anything I would like to play.
Before you buy, my advise is to watch some recent youtube footage or twitch streams and make sure you know what the devs are planning on making. They don't see the community as paying customers at all, we are all wrong and have no good ideas or say on anything.

This game could have been very, very good. It has a very unique, well-presented concept : you get to play as a James Bond villain, complete with the stupid minions, eight-feet tall bodyguards and shark-filled traps. The art and concept teams did a great job, creating very interesting characters and buildings that makes you want to unlock everything and to find out what the game has to offer.
The one problem this game has is its pace, and it's, sadly, a crippling issue. No matter how well optimized your base is, you will spend most of the game waiting endlessly for minions to be recruited, trained and outfitted so you can attempt missions. Those "missions" only require you to have the right number of henchmen, to click on a button and to wait (and hope) until the mission succeeds or fails. That's it. You don't get to do anything else, you don't get to command your soldiers as they attempt to steal a german satellite or whatever you sent them out to do. Clicking "Start mission" and waiting. That's all there is to this game besides base building and it's a little underwhelming.
Then again, it would all work perfectly if you did not have to wait for dozens of minutes for your henchmen to be recruited and trained for missions. The worst part is that you always have to choose between waiting less or playing efficiently : recruiting minions faster costs money, so if you want to use your money carefully (and you will), you need to wait even longer. Same goes for your missions : you need to send henchmen away from your base so they can steal money... which makes your missions' progress even slower, because the henchmen you're using to steal money can't go on missions. There is no way to increase the game's speed either. It's like the developers really wanted the player to choose between waiting for long, unproductive minutes or to use his hard-earned funds to actually keep playing the game. It's not rewarding at all and makes the whole game feel like a grind.
I have played about twenty hours because every once in a while, I tried giving the game another chance, reinstalled it and started another playthrough, only to get tired of it at the same point, after five or six hours, every time. It's just so terribly slow, so full of waiting and almost devoid of actual gameplay besides the base building that is also very, very slow once you spent your initial funds (because earning money in this game is also very slow and difficult). To me, Evil Genius will always be the game that could have been, and that never will be.

Although Doom is has an amazing legacy as the first really mainstream first person shooter and all modern fps games stem from the absolute classic that is Doom, if you were to strip away all of it's history and nostalgia thus viewing it from the lens of modern gaming (albeit a bit open-mindedly) and all that it's progressed.....it's still an amazing game that you absolutely should really pick up.
So, what stops Doom from being just "a game that you should play because you probably like FPS games and this is an old FPS so you should get it became it's old."? What sets this game apart from modern FPS' like halo or cod and even other retro shooters? Well, I'll tell you:
Doom is all about speed! Because of all of the demons, zombies and projectiles constantly being thrown at you, staying still and behind cover even for an instant means death. This central mechanic keeps the combat tense and fun. Having to stay constantly on the run is a mechanic that I haven't seen used by many other shooters, don't get me wrong. I love more cover based games like Half-Life or Uncharted but they usually have you just pushing from point A to point B so nothing quite compares to the at times bullet-hell like action found in Doom as you sprint and shoot your way around the well designed levels. That's another thing id sure did know what they were doing with levels. All cleverly designed maps, just maze like enough to encourage exploration but not enough that you'd get lost, with plenty of land marks and a few rest zones.
One thing that had me wary of buying Doom was the possible lack of a story. While for me story isn't everything in a game it is certainly a big part and it's what mainly helps me stick around till the end. IE, fun gameplay: I'll play it for a while and probably get board after a while, Good story: I'll play till the end to see where it was going and to help the characters.
And while it's barely ever mentioned Doom does have a rather compelling plot (no really. read the story section in the manual for more) that developers as you finish each chapter (set of levels).
(The plot/ setup.)
While later entries into the doom series have changed this around, expanded, retconed it, this is all you need to know for now.
In the near future, you play as a Marine who was sent (as punishment for attacking your superior who ordered you to shoot innocent civilians) to a top-secret and shady lab built on mars and it's two moons owned by the UAC. With nothing much to guard from except Mars sand you spent all day watching movies and goofing off while the scientists experimented with supernaturally powered teleportation technology. Everything teleports fine from facility to facility on the planet and it's moons until on day the stuff they send over start to mysteriously explode except for people to turn insane and then explode. Soon after one of the moons and all the people just disappear. All attempts to contact them or find out they're current location and the other moon calls for Immediate backup. It seems the UAC experiments accidentally opened portals to hell where demons and other creatures managed to come through. Your squad flies over to the first moon to help and possibly find out what happened to the other missing moon, while you are told to guard the perimeter outside. After a bit you start hearing loud screams and then nothing. Did they manage to kill your squad? Either way you are now stranded with the only way out being through a teleporter that led to the missing moon on the complete other side of the facility.
Ah well. at least now you get to kill a few demons....armed with only a pistol because your squad took all other heavy guns.
So grab your iconic green doom armor, a broomstick and shells, your strangely yellow chain saw, a BFG and get ready to rip and tear through hell and back. Can you survive The UAC's mess?

After putting over 50 hours into this game, I think that I can reliably say what is good and bad about this game -
The good:
-Unique fighting style with multiple combos and defenses.
-Solid target system
-Beautiful graphics
-Balanced level design
-Lots of customization and gear
The bad:
-Connections issues. These are still a major issue.
-Input lag. This may be a localized phenomenon, but I seem to have lag between button pushes that can be up to 3 seconds. It's a little ridiculous, because it's instantly noticable once I go to multiplayer.
-Gear stats. In almost all the game types, gear stats are activated. This can make it hard to find a suitable match for a beginner, because of the gear imbalance.
-Matchmaking. This just straight sucks. I am often put into matches with players who are rep 3 and higher, often with max gear score. This stems from the fact that you pick you hero AFTER you have found a match.
-Salty players. The Salt is REAL in this game. I get it, some things suck when they happen the way they do, but some people can not just let it go.
All in all, I do really enjoy the game. I would recommend that you get it, because knowing how ubisoft works, their launches are dumb and not that great, but they fix the game well given enough time. I think that given its flaws, with a good polish it will be absolutely phenomenal.

is an RTS 4X of theoretically limitless scale and great strategic depth. A game could include over a thousand star systems if it's running on high-end hardware.
Unsurprisingly, nothing too amazing (though the planets actually look pretty nice), but then at the scale most games of
run, it should be considered something of a small miracle that there are as many objects rendered as there are. The UI is mainly just functional, nothing too pretty; it's not as intuitive as it could be and it can be hard to figure out what's going on even if you read the necessary literature, but it's nothing that can't be gotten used to.
Pretty standard space game fare. The soundtrack is decent enough, though a little light on tracks. Some notification sounds can be easy to miss or sound too much like other notifications.
This game has as deep a ship design element as one could hope for (like the creation of ships the size of star systems that shoot planet-sized asteroids, if one so wishes and has the means) as well as an interesting approach to tech trees which adds an element of chance to breakthroughs and branching. Unfortunately, the gameplay is usually too fast-paced to take full advantage of the ship design features and the pace of the game also negatively impacts the management of planets as well (an element that seemed fairly well done at first). Additionally, there seems to be an unresolved bug regarding energy weapons never cooling down, so avoiding those is recommended. Overall, however, the gameplay of
feels a bit like
or
on the scale of a galactic 4X, albeit with a good deal more of untapped depth.
The Galactic Armoury mod adds a fair amount of content to the game and is highly recommended. If I recall correctly, the developers themselves helped with the mod, so it's sort of an "official" expansion.

The Darkness II is a fast-moving and violent FPS set in an interesting universe. You play as Jackie Estacado, the current Don of a mafia crime family who has always had a dark secret to him (Though you don't need to play the first Darkness game to understand this. It's pretty well covered in the first few missions). Wracked with grief over the death of his girlfriend and the sudden stress of having some underworld illuminati-esque organization trying to kill him... Jackie unleashes the beast.
Jackie has the demon known as the Darkness residing in him, which manifests itself in a Dr. Octopus meets Satan crossover. While you can run around and shoot people, you also have the ability to slash, stab, Impale, execute, blind and slaughter enemies with these tendrils of pure evil that are shooting from your shoulder. A pseudo-Deus ex skill tree allows you to upgrade yourself into being a run-n-gun tank, a magical hit and run fighter, a stealthy executioner or what have you. The story is a tad boring, with Jackie's constant lamentations, but it also has it's interesting bits you can read into (such as the history of the Darkness as told by your tweaker buddy).
Without giving too much away, the two endings are sort of... disappointing. But the Darkness II isn't some highly artistic, thoughtful puzzle platformer. It's about 8 or 9 hours of gutting mobsters alive with xenomorph Slayer fans on your shoulders and throwing around a little British Imp that pees on dead bodies.
Looking for a few days worth of casual shooting? Give it a try.

Tennis is a sport that receives woefully little attention from game developers, and yet it is a wonderfully gripping sport. Not all of us want to play ridiculously Hollywood-esque "first person simulations" where graphics and endorsement by, say, the world's top ten players only are traditionally considered to be essential elements of the game mix. And here is a game that takes a very different view, illustrating brilliantly that there are STACKS of very good players, thousands of tournaments and that to get to the top it is a LONG HARD STRUGGLE
To me it doesn't matter that the players did not endorse this, I think all the top 100 and more are based on real players anyway and it can be quite fun to work out who is who (pretty sure I saw Mark Venus in there, so the knowledge of the sport from the developer is top class)
What makes this game so much fun is that it is unashamedly full of little details which can become crucial (for example if your player stops practising an element of his/her game he/she will actually get worse at it over time.
I would be delighted if enough people invested in this so that one day perhaps there could be a version with the option of viewing matches in a slightly more hi-res format but it doesn't actually matter that much. If the players found out about the game and eventually endorsed it that would be fab too

Two thumbs down on this one. The UI is nearly impenetreable and there is no tutorial at all. It just throws you in and assumes you'll be able to figure things out. The diplomacy system makes no sense and 9 times out of 10 you won't even be aware people are trying to give you "diplomatic missions" until you get the alert that your time is up. The system for setting up trade routes and supply runs to even out resources in your empire is so convoluted that even after a *long* time trying to figure it out I simply threw my hands in the air and gave up, usually with over half of my planets completely unable to make anything because they're missing some critical resource that, no matter how much I try, I can't seem to ship in from other worlds that have excess.
The battles are basically just giant zerg rushes and frequently cause massive drops in FPS because the computer just builds up huge-massive fleets and sends them all over the place, thanks to there being no unit cap. And a player that isn't aware of the size scaling issues can very easily set the scale too large only to discover later in the game that when they *thought* they were doing well it turns out that the computer made a fleet of like 1000 super ships the size of several star systems.
TLDR- The game isn't very fun, it's got a near impossible learning curve, there's no tutorials or explanations for the vast majority of in game functions and the ship designing does not pause the game, meaning every time you need to upgrade or change around ships you're wasting time that you *should* have been spending micro-managing your empire. Which, unfortunately, is required because without constant attention everything just falls apart.

Pyre, the latest title from Supergiant Games, is - at first glance, at least - a departure from their previous titles. Gone is the action, world traversing adventure of Bastion and Transistor and in is node-based world maps and a caravan devliering you to matches of will and skill - a sports meets RPG combat setting to prove your will to return to your homeland.
Underneath that though is Supergiant's trademark style - the beautiful art, Darren Korb's amazing soundtrack work, interesting characters and world building, difficulty modifiers, and most importantly - a story about differences and trying to enact change.
Pyre is fantastic fun and a great $20 spent.

Edit 10/08/2017: It's been nearly a year since I last reviewed Isle's progress. As such I have decided to update my review (as anyone reviewing an early access game should) once again..
If you don't want to read through the full version, you can find a simplified "Pro's & Cons" version at the bottom.
------------------------------------------------------------Long Version--------------------------------------------------------------
1). The Developers: I honestly don't even know what to say about them anymore that isn't already being said by others. They're pretty much just as bi-polar as the community. One minute they're doing fine and getting along with everyone, the next they're tearing people down faster than a lion tears into a monkey. When it comes to development, it doesn't even feel like they're all that invested in the game anymore. They neglect to fix glaring issues like antiquated dinosaur stats that go back several months (seriously, how long as Acro been nerfed? Or Shant been a Rex killer? Bet most vets of the game don't even remember) and would rather continue to tinker with experiments that don't go far. We don't need a totally new map every few months with variants that cause even a GTX 1070 to seize up just for them to be completely abandoned and deleted a few months later, we need core game improvements. Something the devs don't seem to understand.
2).Gameplay:Oy. Where to begin. Let's start with an obvious one: Players are still very unpredictable, some follow you, others pretend to be friendly only to kill you while you're stuck in an animation, some think it's dinosaur Call of Duty and kill because they can, and others will protect you with their lives.
With the new gender system the devs have implemented since my last review, all variety is gone. Aside from the dinosaurs themselves, there are only two skins each to choose from as opposed to the varitable rainbow to choose from before: Male and Female. That's it. Most of them aren't even slightly camouflaged. Heck half of them have more bright tan-desert type skins or even near-white that stick out like orange Christmas lights against the dark green environment of the current map. The stats of quite a few dinosaurs are incredibly unbalanced. Acro was nerfed several months ago and was never fixed. It's the fourth biggest carnivore yet has the healing ability of one of the smallest dinosaurs in the game (+50hp around every 5 seconds. With 4790 health that's garbage, most everything in the game heals much faster than that), Shantungosaurus was given a major health, damage resistance, and damage output buff to help it deal with Hypo Rex (a boss creature) but was never rebalanced once Dondi pulled Hypo from public servers, so almost nothing can kill it short of a group of rexes and even *they* might not walk away. Rex has been babied by the devs since day one and only recently got a slight nerf that hardly changed how Rex is played: Kill everything in 3 bites or less. I could go on but honestly this part is already getting a little long for my liking.
3). The Community: The Isle's community will never change, that much is obvious. As countless reviews will tell you, the community on Isle is extremely bi-polar and overall a pain. You'll either meet people you'll hang out with nearly every time you play, or you'll get trolled constantly and/or insulted for not bowing at the devs' feet and praising them for putting out a patch that changes file pathing which has no effect on the game at all. Obviously this example is an exaggeration... but I wouldn't be surprised if people have experienced this first-hand
Love it or hate it, this is my honest-to-God review of The Isle and why with this itteration of my review., the lack of balancing that's allowed to continue for so long, the community being the way it always has been, and the overall lack of direction the game currently has, I'm leaning more towards the negative. This game has real potential, but time and time again the ball ends up being dropped. Is my review likely to change? Probably, we'll see.
Did I miss anything? Feel free to comment. Keep it game-related though. No one needs to hear that The Isle can't run on your laptop's Intel HD graphics card or something.
------------------------------------------------------------Short Version-------------------------------------------------------------
----------Pros----------
-Amazing graphics.
-The mechanics are solid... ish.
-Models are; while not being 100% scientifically accurate, amazing.
-Entertaining with friends.
-Some mods are well-done and add interesting content.
----------Cons----------
-Balancing isn't really a thing. Most stats a dinosaur have don't reflect the creature well at all.
-Devs are incredibly impatient and downright rude at times.
-Beginning to lack direction, feels like it's going nowhere fast these days.
-Sandbox is really the only mode left that offers anything. Other gamemodes are rare as Progression is being dropped for Survival which itself only has two dinosaurs (Rex and Carnotarus).
-Other players tend to be a real headache.
The core feature takes some getting used to, but the story of music are as enjoyable as always.

Truly a game worth playing and having some real fun. Friday 13th goes back to the times of old horror films we use to watch in our CRT (big back) Tv sets. We would all gather around the family couch and have fun watching it, However, it was more of a fear than humor. This game started out for me as a fear, Fear that Jason would get to me, he'd stalk me, and kill me as he is designed to do. Until after 1 week of playing I’ve become immune to this feeling and has become more of a challenge, rush and not to forget humor!! When you first begin the game as a Councilor (Human Player) my advice to you is Start of with Stealth actions, seeing as your first character will be Venessa Jones she's naturally louder at running and moving around so be sure to crouch (CLTR) and get the knowing’s of how things work, Eg: opening and closing doors, finding items, loot that's resourceful and ones that aren't. Take a moment and explore don't rush or run, Use that trusted (X) key on the keyboard to activate a mild jug and take it from there. Always remember to take your time but don't stay one place, keep moving! Jason has a bunch of cool abilities to find you. One of his main features is Sense, he can sense when you're in a house or outside once you're in his proximity (Range) this allows him to hunt and kill.  Try your best to stay with others or slowly get to the others. This works great if he's not aware of your location and you've kept hidden during that time. If he knows your location and is coming after for you press your SHIFT Key and run! Run like you've never run before, pay attention to your stamina as it runs out quickly when sprinting.  If you stop or crouch you can build it back up slowly. Later on, you can use Perks to help fasten this process. This is a great game with great initiative. For $40.00 on Steam it's worth every buck! Important: This game has bugs, many. It's a work in progress and will be updated in the days to come. We can only hope they provide many updates, free DLC's and a few other achievements in the days to come.

where to start.
the isle, where you can play as a herbivorous or carnivouros dinosaur and live out your lifespan.  ive clocked 32 hours on this game and im still having fun, however there are some points i must bring to light for future prospective buyers.
- dinosaurs
-the map is huge and takes a while to explore, which is nice if you are a large dinosaur wandering aimlessly.
-communication is simple with sounds that you can make to other players to tell them how your feeling (for example i was looking after some baby miasaura and a spinosaurus came a little too close for my liking, i gave a threataning toot to him and he backed down and moved away.  im a good mumma)
- you can choose to "nest" and come in at a higher tier dinosaur as soon as you get an invite, which is alot of fun to do.
-the dinosaur skings and walking animations are so gorgeous.  plenty of love has gone into them.
-progressing to the next tier to be a better dinosaur.  you get randomly spawned to a completely new part of the map, and sometimes that is litteraly a death sentence. ive had many a playthrough where i have progressed into a shantungosaurus and have died due to not being able to find food or water nearby, thus meaning i have to start that climb all over agin to be the top herbivore.
- no maps, so if you dont know where food and water is from memory or have never played the game, HA your dead. start again.
- food.  you can never eat enough food to fill your belly as a large herbivore.  and i got so over hearing the munch munch for the 400th time as i futiley ate every plant i saw.  i realise thats the point of this game, to be as realistic as possible, but man its not fun to spend 4 hours real time just eating plants in the game.
-the learning curve of this game is huge.  theres no room for error as a first time player, and your constantly dying.  i even got to the point of nearly giving up and getting my money back because i just kept dying because a map was half finished.
-bugs bugs bugs.  falling through the map and dying, cant eat, stuck on corpses etc.  simple to fix stuff but hasnt been addressed.
-if your in a group with other players and you progress, good luck finding them again.  you can spawn on the opposite side of the map to them and spend a good hour in real time trying to get back to them.  you should spawn at the nearest spawn site to them so you can keep herds together, like real dinosaurs did.
all in all i give this game a 6/10.  controls are good, gamplay is nice for an early access, and those models are divine!  sadly however there are too many cons at the moment that need to be addressed asap, rather than adding in more dinosaurs the developers definetly need to look at the bugs and fix the little stuff with each creature in game, rather than mashing more into the pot.
EDIT 20/6/2017
whoo boi! since my last review mods have been added thus allowing for the community to add more maps.  i might even say i take back my previous negative on the modding!!
such love has gone into this game and i am most impressed.  still a few frame rate issues bt that would honestly be me playing on a laptop.
updates almost daily and i feel that this game is starting to get back on track.

Your friend Victor has reached out to you asking for help, but he has done so in a vague way. You must find out what ails your friend so you quickly go to where he is. You are to be met by the love of his life Elizabeth, but upon arrival a monster pulsing with electricity takes off with her, and closes the gate behind it. You will now have to find your way through this and many more puzzles as you try to unravel the mysteries surrounding not only this place but what your friend has been up to.
Maybe I'm getting better at these type of games, but I felt like this one was pretty short. After two hour and a half I saw the credits rolling, the rest are spent on getting the rest of the achievement and of course once again a twist right at the end. I wonder if any of these games will actually have a sequel? One of the few things I dislike about this game is when there were some items that seemed pretty important at the time that were one and done, but there were other items that definitely could have different uses that you just kept in your inventory forever. At the same time you would get to a point in the game where you are still toting around a lot of the reusable stuff that you have now gotten used to and magically it would disappear after you hit the limit or the usefulness was magically up.
Although the game was short I did enjoy the puzzle solving, and the different puzzles that were put in my way. I did notice that there were quite a few times where I felt like I was going between the exact two places to unlock something or retrieve an item. I know that you don't want to just have a room that is done one time through, but it seemed odd that to unlock this room you had to go to another room and then go back, unlock something, and then go back to that other room to unlock something there in turn.
At the end of the day this game definitely allows you to dip your foot into something that can definitely keep you occupied, and for the most part entertained. Is this a must have game, no, but its not a terrible game either. So if you're a fan of the genre, you might want to get it while it's on sale.
EDIT: Almost forgot to mention that right off the bat I ran into a problem where the game was crashed for no reason. And after doing some investigating, turned out the problem was on my end (thanks ESET!). Thankfully that was the last time I see it though.

What is Frankenstein: Master of Death? Apart from a fierce name, that is?
Frankenstein: Master of Death is one of those casual adventure games that contain some hidden object search. The story of this game is based on the famous novel by Mary Shelley: You play as the hero who needs to help Frankenstein in containing a monster that his assistand Igor created.
The game is completely controlled with the mouse. I'm not sure in how far it is a typical hidden object game, so I'd like to elaborate how it plays:
You go through a number of screens, always being able to return to every previous screen. Those screens contain points of interest that for the most time have a puzzle or keyhole you need to interact with. In a few cases, those points aren't shown by a "navigation" tool that shows the possible interactions - I think there are three points like this in the game where you have to use an object on a piece of wall to advance -, but usually they are shown. So when you interact with them, you might have to use one of your items in the inventory, you might just collect something, a puzzle comes up or a keyhole shows. If a puzzle comes, it could be a hidden object game where you have the additional task of assembling three items before you can collect them, sometimes including easy minigames. Other puzzles are visual puzzles where you for example slide pieces around, or at one point even a tangram that took me the longest of all to figure out. In the case of a keyhole, you can open it with the fitting items if you found them earlier, such as a flower key or some ornaments. In addition, solving a puzzle might be required.
And that is pretty much all that happens, essentially it is a classical adventure but with lots of casual puzzles thrown in. Now in theory you can skip puzzles after a while, but this is never necessary (except maybe at the tangram) and locks you out of one achievement if you do so. Talking about achievements, there are 20, all which can be gotten with a single playthrough on the "hard" difficulty mode. Since everything is still easy, the "easy" mode is probably a complete no-brainer. Apart from the three hidden walls you can open. There is a hint system, which to my knowledge does not invalidate any achievements. Achievement hunters still should face no challenge here, as the missable achievements only require to not skip anything - including cutscenes and dialogue - and play on the hardest difficulty.
The story is not completely uninteresting, but doesn't add much to the original. Which is a shame since the thoroughly interesting ethical issues of a Frankenstein machine are only addressed briefly. The music is good, but forgettable, the sounds are fitting.
So what remains is a game that kept me entertained for three and a half hours, I played through it in one go with losing interest at one point but not enough to stop playing since the progression is nicely paced. There is often a wonderful flow, leading you to get one item and remembering from an earlier scene that you can try it there to open a locked passage or container. Can I recommend this then? Well, the main strength of being nicely paced and short here works against it in matters of playtime, so I can recommend it if you get it on a sale or are generally interested in the genre.

The blizzard swarmed the offices of Ironclad Games Corp. Snow was common enough in Vancouver, but no one in British Columbia had quite seen a storm like this. Sheepish developers were busy prototyping a fresh reboot of "Sins of a Solar Empire", while loved ones called in, urging workers to stay off the road and bunker down at the office.  There were no races with defined playstyles, histories, or specific mechanics. No one had spent much time iterating anything but the most serviceable art assets, statistics, and tools for generating vast universes of orbiting planets and stars. The heroes and villains were essentially a blank page. The scope and ambition of mechanics bristled in the minds of developers, like the hail bearing down. It was this moment that "Star Ruler" would briefly blink into existence.
Let's talk about Star Ruler. This is a game made by fans of realtime space 4x games, which looked at cheesy sci-fi, and said "why not?" You start off creating Snailigons, the mad race of starfarers you dreamed up, and then a random galaxy of stars to rule. You decided that while whatever lessor races were getting up to, Snailigons were perfecting production, Communism, and Hard metallurgy- from a mish mash of racial and political perks. Snailigons soon outbreed the comfy confines of Orbos III, to colonize the neighboring Orbos II, and strip-mine everything else in the Orbos System.
Snailtopia would cover the stars in Orbos fashion, or that was the plan anyway. You "found intelligent life", or rather invaded a colony of spacefaring meatbags. Humans declared war, and sent a cute fleet of flak firing fighters. Your hardshell cruisers tore the never-ending stream of fighters apart with lasers, for about 2 years. Then they adapted with pesky "shields" and "rockets". Snailtopia would need to respond- it had to adapt. Thankfully, every ship can be micro-designed via technologies uncovered in your sprawling random tech tree; from scale, to crew size, weaponry, propulsion, tools, and defenses.
Clearly, Snailigons would create one unstoppable, planet sized destroyer, scorching the offending human systems into obliv... into your care. It works right up till the discovery of a second race, which promptly rips through the SA-43 Molluscan, like butter- salty butter. Now you, Star Ruler, are managing trade, adaptive war, politics, and survival across multiple systems, and it starts to feel a little heavy. You know there are more stars to manage, and who knows what opposing intelligences lie in wait there. You probably should have made a smaller galaxy to play in, and with 3 species instead of 30 to inhabit it. You know, Snailtopia's leader had a good run, but it's time to retire.

Pyre kind of defies description, it's a combination of visual novel and sports game, but perhaps the best description of it would be that it is a Supergiant game: The music is brilliant, the art is gorgeous and the story is deep and engrossing. Darren Korb's magnificent score is perhaps the most intricate he's ever created, with multiple versions of each track and music for every character and team and an ending theme that changes based on what choices you made in the story.
And what a story it is, perhaps missing the emotional core of Transistor, although there are many heartfelt moments to be found, Pyre's story is about as unique as everything else, set in a grim land full of criminals and vagabonds, where the only hope of escape is fantasy basketball, Pyre tells the story of a ragtag group of heroes who must compete to earn their freedom and overthrow the totalitarian regime responsible for their exile. Each character is different and interesting and each has a story to slowly uncover as you journey through the world. But the unique selling point here is that you get to choose which characters get to leave and which stick around. Towards the end as time begins to run out, these choices become harder and harder to make and you'll soon find yourself agonizing over whether or not you made the right decision.
The art in Pyre is, in my humble opinion, the best supergiant has ever created. Rich, detailed and colourful, the art design is some of the best I've ever seen. Each character, object and background is lovingly rendered and, despite being still images most of the time, convey a lot of life and emotion. It's the little details that really make Pyre for me, the way text highlights slightly as you hover over it, the knick knacks you collect in your wagon that you can mess with in various ways, much like Hearthstone's game boards. These make Pyre, along with the branching story that has so many possible outcomes, one of best visual novels you'll play this year.
The gameplay, though, is perhaps where I think Pyre falters a bit, the core mechanics are interesting and each playing field and enemy type varies the gameplay in significant ways but more often than not Pyre's fantasy basketball felt as if it lacked a certain depth. There are lots of modifiers you can use to change characters and the game as a whole, but when all is said and done, they often feel like they've made little impact to the game. More often than not I found myself using the same tactics to win 99% of matches and while each character type had different attributes and counters, at the end of the day, rushing the enemy's "basket" (or pyre) was the best way to go about a match. The only positive I got out of playing this way was that when it came time to decide which characters should gain their freedom, balancing whether or not I wanted that character to be free versus whether I wanted to lose a key player in my team made the decision all that much harder to make.
All in all, Pyre is one of the most unique and interesting gaming experiences you'll have this year, just don't expect a wealth of mechanics.

I played Nidhogg 1 and liked it, so I was interested to see how the developers built on the success of the first game now that presumably they had more support, resources and experience.
I can say that Nidhogg 2 general improves on its art design, certain game mechanics such as the introduction of different weapons, the sound has been improved and more locations have been added. And that’s where the improvements end and the game falls short of delivering a sequel that I though was worth my time
The only mode this game has is 1v1, and unless you have lots of friends who all play this game then you are limited by the number of opponents you can fight. I was never able to find an opponent through its online matchmaking system even though I tried multiple times (a problem I with Nidhogg 1). Without being able to find an opponent, I was only able to play against one friend who purchased the game with me. As for single player, it’s not much fun playing 1v1 against AI. aside from being stupid, they are predictable and easy to beat.
Lack of opponents and additional game modes are what killed this game for me. Why is the matchmaking so poor? Why didn’t they introduce alternate game mechanics such as sudden death mode, or add additional enemies so it’s not always 1v1, why not 2v2, or 1v2. Why am I even trying to come up with these ideas? Where is the CREATIVE approach from the developer on this game? Nidhogg 1 was a success because the gameplay was fun and a unique concept to many. But even then, it suffered from replay ability. Nidhogg is essentially the same game repackaged. After about 4 hrs of gameplay it will be over. Only pick this game up if you are an avid Nidhogg diehard fan.
Note: I don’t have time to go sifting through community pages to find others to play with. That should be included in matchmaking.

Equipped with a sniper rifle, your protagonist must traverse through various WW II locales to eliminate high-ranking Nazi officials. The story gets interesting when you find out one of the officials is actually a traitor who has vital information as to what the Nazis are preparing for in their desperate attempt to turn the tides.
This game is the epitome of long-range warfare! Sniping enemies has never been more fun! The Ghost Warrior games are nowhere near as exciting as Sniper Elite. The game regularly awards your long-distance, deadly shots with a slow-motion cutscene during which you can see the gory (and glorious) results of your doing. Quite often you get to see how the bones and organs are crushed within the enemies' bodies. Seeing how the heart of an MP40 wielding soldier explodes can be quite disgusting but also quite invigorating!
Unfortunately, while the titular activity in this game is very well carried out everything else in the combat is quite mediocre. Close-combat fight can be quite difficult - it is next to impossible to get a headshot with an MP40 or a Thompson. It is as if the creators deliberately weakened all the other weapons just to force you to use the sniper rifle at all times. Not the mention the amount of bullets you have at your disposal - you will almost never run out of bullets while sniping. I get their point - still, a more refined system could have been put in place.
I heard completing a major part of the game is possible via stealth gameplay - some of the achievements can only be obtained by taking this route. Still, I did not find the insta-kills interesting enough - I had several failed attempts due to the clunky movement of our character. Setting traps is also possible; we have tripmines, landmines and dynamites. Too bad it is quite rarely a must during the roughly 8-hour long campaign.
Those of you who've already read my Nazi Zombie Army reviews must know how much I hate both games. I hate that you have an excellent idea but the execution is just horrible. Connecting to a host took ages and drops from the multiplayer game were frequent. With Sniper Elite V2's campaign I hate them even more as I can now see what levels the creators recycled to get their campaign ready. And now that I've mentioned the DLC titles I can confirm I did not find any cooperative / multiplayer sessions, at all. I expected this, though.
Putting aside the non-existing online gameplay sessions Sniper Elite V2 offers a rather lengthy and great campaign. I do not know what can be more fun than taking out a tank by hitting its fuel tank with a well-aimed shot! This game is THE sniping game. Period!

Welcome to Disconnect Simulator 2017!
Oh? You're about to finish a match? It would be a shame if someone were to... DISCONNECT YOU!
Oh? You're in the middle of a story mode mission alone? It would be a shame if someone were to... KICK YOU BACK TO TITLE SCREEN!
Oh? You're about to start a match... Lol, you thought.
Oh? You have a nice team? Let me... DISCONNECT HALF OF THEM AND REPLACE THEM WITH BAD BOTS!
Oh? You want a balanced match? Let me put all the people who've dumped a lot of hours into this game on one team, and all the newbies on the other.
Oh? You want an honorable match? Let me introduce you to the toxic side of the community!
Seriously. When someone friends you because they say it's difficult to find people non-toxic in the community, there's an issue. Maybe me and that guy just have bad luck, who knows. But here we go.
I just want to finish a match to finish my order, and apparently that is not chill. It comes bundled with endless rage, the inability to play without internet, and even then the possibility of getting disconnected even if you're playing by yourself (does not matter if you're in the middle of a story mission or not, get ready to get disconnected), and maybe, if you're lucky, a good match that you can finish by the skin of your teeth!
In all seriousness, 80% (maybe an overestimate but whatever, it’s still way too much) of the time I've spent in this game (outside of the story) has been spent in "matchmaking" (which it really doesn't feel like matchmaking, more like throw them where you can fit them) or being disconnected. I was going to refrain from writing a review, because the gameplay is nice and the customization is nice, but oh. my. god. UBISOFT. The troubles of this game make me want to punch them in their collective genitalia. The story is mediocre, super stereotypical, which would be forgivable, if their multiplayer worked reliably and consistently. I want to like this game. But the aggravation it brings. Makes me regret spending $70 on it. That was my stupidity. I read the reviews and went "Oh nahhhh, it can't be that bad, I'm sure its worth it." Jokes on me. I cannot in good faith recommend this game due to the just overall stupid laziness that the devs have shown. Plus, it’s a tossup if you deal with the toxic side of the community or the non-toxic. My luck, I've dealt more with the toxic (really, you'd think in a game called "For Honor" people would be a bit more honorable, but nah). I rarely get the non-toxic side of the community, and when I do, it’s very nice. It makes me happy. But that's so rare at this point, I don't know if it's worth it.
So, if you read this far, thank you for reading my little rant. Try not to make the same mistake I did, but if you do, don't say I didn't warn you.
Oh? You still want to get the game? I hope you have good internet and ethernet cables. Do yourself a favor, if you insist, start out in duels after you finish the story mode on normal at least. I would recommend at least playing part of it on hard. Fight some AIs to find your class, then just play that over and over to level up enough to hold your own. Frankenstein: Master of Death is a hidden objects game where after receiving a letter of Victor Frankenstein, an old friend and a brilliant scientist that has managed to resurrect the dead you travel to his home to reveal a secret.
There are different kind of puzzles, mini games and tasks to find many objects from a list in the screen. In these ones, sometimes you must combine objects of the scene with objects of the inventory, so it adds a plus of difficulty in this kind of puzzles.
You can choose the difficulty between: easy and difficult but there is no difficult instead.
There is a hint button in a corner to help you. Depending on the level of difficulty, it refills quickest and tells you which are your next step.
You move around the different places using icon arrows on the screen. There is a map that indicates if there are things to do or there is nothing to do in these locations. It also teleports you to one location if you click on it, so its easy to move around and solve puzzles.
The different locations are drawn in high resolution and characters are well modeled in 3D. There are a lot of animations that helps to explain the story and pre rendered cut scenes
Music is quite good and enviroment sound are normal.
The game has achivements and trading cards and you could finish the game in few hours obtaning all of them.
These guys have learnt of their last games, and they are improved the overall quality of their new game.
As all these kind of games, it is a great entertainmentto play during an evening.

Use Gzdoom, or any other source port, also "Wadsmoosh" if you own most Doom classics, it's  awesome.
Having said that, What hasn't really been said about Doom and the ammount of influence/impact it had in the gaming industry as a whole if not only in the first person shooter genre?
The game single handendly  place first person shooter as a category in other developers minds at the time, and even more than 20 years after it's release people are not only still talking about the game in itself, but also creating content, and playing the game, fact that probably can state more than any words can in regards towards the type of significance the game held, and still holds to this day.
With the right reason too, I can remember the game way back when it came out, even into the late 90's it was the type of game everyone needed, or had, installed in their machines, alternatively you had a series of people like me that simply were oblivious to it, but I remember Doom being my first experience playing a first person shooter, my uncle presented it to me as something incredible, but forbidden as he escorted me towards his pc with my parents in the same room while they were not looking, then the guy set the game on the hardest difficulty (nightmare)...
I couldn't even get past the first level of the game, principally because I couldn't really even understand what I was watching, I had so many questions:
Why is there a hand in the middle of the screen?
Whose face is that?
Am I looking at a marine upside down?
I can remember vividly how I asked those question to myself, in my head.
Then after a very long time nothing really happened, Doom became a memory of the past that I never really remembered up until one day I looked at an image of Doom on the internet.
I didn't felt interested in playing the game however, 10 years had gotten by if not more from my first experience with the game and I didn't felt the need, nor did I had the means through which obtain the game, or so I thought, after a while I played the game after purchasing it through xbox live arcade, I felt dissapointed and didn't play the game after a while, I guess I just wasn't in a good state of mind to enjoy the game, at the time I was more into Left 4 Dead, and Call of Duty, than I was into anything resembling the rightly called, "godfather" of first person shooters.
This was around 2009.
Then 2010 came and went, and finally around 2011 Modern Warfare 3 came out, it was named the best selling game, and naturally after playing it I felt in love with it, as much tho as I felt frustrated with it, I really got into "competitive" gaming at the time, and the experience that I had when I finished playing Modern Warfare 3 around the ending of 2012 or so was bad, I couldn't really get into many games after it, I hated Call of Duty after my experience with Modern Warfare 3 I saw it as a pointless competitive game that didn't serve any other purpose than to lure insecure people like me with grand desires to feel superior while achieving something arbitrary through absurd, and ridiculous means.
You couldn't really win, Call of Duty Modern Warfare 3 had an undebatable impact in the release of future games, between 2012 as well as 2013 every single "triple A" game needed to have one element from that game, or another, whether it was to try and replicate it's campaign "expectacular" set-pieces, or alternatively add some element from first person shooters, or the military, if not both.
Not everything was bad, but on the other hand not necessarily bad games needed to have a lot of their aspects "streamlined" in other to appeal as many consumers as possible, there were also a lot of first person shooter games around that time simply trying to replicate an old formula from another game.
I felt overwhelmed, in a way I wanted to quit games and move away from them, in another I liked some of the stuff that started coming out, in between them, Doom 3 Bfg came out, wanting to play a first person shooter that deviate from the "norm" that Call of Duty Modern Warfare 3 had set in its influence as a whole, I started to play the classic Doom games, that some might say they're the "antiphysis" of the, then, "modern" first person shooters.
I fell in love with the games, principally because everything in them seemed to have a purpose of some kind, the weapon placement, the enemy placement, the difficulty curves in between each setting, the general aesthetic, the music, the secrets, the levels, even the sounds of weapons, or pickups.
Everything in Doom, seemed to me, and still seems to me, as if it was tested before being added into the game, but in an exhaustive manner, plus the games had uniqueness, and individuality set in so many different aspects of it's design, it wasn't until then when I could see the brillance of this games.
At the time I just had consoles, I didn't had a pc.
After a while, Doom became my Call of Duty, it would be the only game I played, and thought about when wanting to play.
Then TotalBiscuit released a video detailing a popular mod called "Brutal Doom"
It seemed amazing and according to him, easy to install, plus it also seemed to make the game a lot more violent, which I was curious to see.
Then, just having a mac for a laptop, and old one at that, I invested myself for about 2 hours or so that same night after I watched, said, video, in order to install Doom, not knowing about natively supported source ports, nor knowing about Steam, I simply downloaded some demo that I found in a website, created a wrapper, and then proceeded to install everything in one place, it took a while to run, but it was worth it.
For it was the subsequent experience that I had what made me not only fall in love with Doom, even more than I was already, but also propelled me into saving money for a pc.
It was a different game, similar to the one I played on my ps3, but I wondered.
If Doom, a 20 year old game, can play, run, and look this way on a macbook that isn't even made to run this game natively, Then how can other games look, run, and play?
Truly an act worth more than a thousand words speaking in tone for the amazing level of quality to come to expect while playing this game.
And as for my time played... Ignore it, I played this game easily more than a hundred hours, it wasn't until earlier today when I finally found out how to install the game on Steam to play, let's see how many hours i'll sink till the end of the year.

First person shooter games tend to be rather straight forward, and many would argue that is how they should remain. On occasion we run into something diversified, such as Natural Selection 1&2, F.E.A.R., Crysis, and so forth but generally the use of non-standard guns and bullets usually delivers an undercooked concept, better in theory than execution.
Darkness II sets itself apart from its peers, wherein the use of secondary skills (beyond aim and shoot) as not only a gimic, quirk or occasional use but an intergral part of gameplay. The use of the "Darkness" power is both creative an intuitive, allow variety of different situation uses, from hurling debris to stun enemies, impalments, but also utilizing plate shaped items from the field as mobile cover, disarming enemies, aquiring out-of-reach ammo and health from behind cover, and so forth.
This gameplay is best combined with a gamepad, allowing a very intuitive use of left and right shoulders for powers in uninterrupted use of left and right trigger for either two hand, single hand or duo weilding guns.
In summary, Darkness II combines the best aspects of First Person Shooting and Melee Hack&Slash in a seemless uninterrupted co-existance offering a very unique take on the FPS genre nad delivering a fresh dose of gameplay.

Pyre is Super Giant’s third game, and is probably the biggest departure from what you could call “their norm” yet.  That is to say, the game isn’t an isometric action RPG where you have a single character whose actions are being narrated by someone in the game, like Bastion or Transistor.  Instead they’ve created something that almost defies classification.  Pyre is a sort of party based, sports RPG with visual novel elements, and, as mismatched as it is, Supergiant pulls it off.
As mentioned, Pyre, is new ground for Supergiant Game, primarily because the gameplay and story are heavily segregated from one another.  The game starts off much like a visual novel, with the player being introduced to the cast of characters and how the game is going to play itself out.  After this, there is a bit of an abrupt shift into the gameplay mode.  The rituals, as they’re called, play out in a 3v3 competition that’s similar to fantasy basketball.  An orb spawns in the middle of the playing field and each time tries to run into the enemy’s pyre (read: goal) while holding the orb.  In order to steal the orb, you must hit the carrier with your aura.  Each character exudes aura passively, so long as they are not holding the orb, the size of which is determined by what clan they are from.  Characters can also use their aura offensively, the most common usage being a straight line wave.  While holding the orb, characters lose their aura and become unable to cast it offensively.  Even the orb carrier can still sprint and jump over enemy auras, leaving them able to avoid the enemy offense.  The carrier can also throw the orb (regaining their aura and possibly causing a foe to lose their’s), or pass it to a teammate.
It is through these mechanics that Pyre attempts to create the coveted “easy to learn, but hard to master” gameplay style.  Personally, I think they succeed.  The game plays in a very intuitive manner, but when you dig deep, there’s lots of little tricks that can be exploited in the mechanics themselves.  The only downside to this is the lack of online multiplayer to find people willing to dive into the mechanics and have some excellent matches.  While I understand why a small team such as Supergiant shied away from including online play, it’s lack of presence is definitely felt.
Outside of the rites, the game basically unveils the story in front of you, with you making minor decisions here and there, with the occasional major decision cropping up.  The main conceit of the game is the characters attempting to win their freedom from banishment by partaking in the rites.  The player’s choices come into effect at the end of a season (I guess you can call it that, since this game is practically a sports game), wherein they decide which character they’ll attempt to free.  This also plays into the other big effect that the rites have on the story; the game keeps going whether you win or lose a rite, and the story goes on accordingly as well.  Supergiant chooses to focus their narrative efforts on the characters and their interactions, which allows this highly variable approach to work, while looking deceptively more complicated than it is.  All that changes is character dialogue and who is available for the player to use during the rites, so it’s tough to feel like you’re missing out on anything.  This web of character interactions ends up creating an engaging and interesting narrative, though most of it comes from the world in which the game takes place.
While the story is engaging and interesting, watching it unfold can get a bit tiring.  Outside of the rites the gameplay is limited to selecting choices off a menu and reading dialogue.  Unlike most RPGs, where your characters actions and decisions are what drive the plot forward, the text is the vehicle that moves Pyre’s story forward, with choices being interspersed to give the illusion of gameplay.  I stuck with this game for the story and the gameplay of the rites, but I don’t think I’ll be revisiting it any time soon, as the amount of things to do in between gameplay moments doesn’t justify a second look.  Supergiant’s previous two games had seamlessly merged these two facets together, but this experiment seems to have sacrificed this in order to make gains in other areas.
Pyre takes place in the Downside, a strange, inhospitable place littered with the corpses of fallen titans, otherworldly monstrous beasts whose very existence warped the Downside into the twisted place it is when the game begins.  The characters are, for the most part, from the Commonwealth, an enigmatic civilization that is only mentioned in oblique references, making it somewhat difficult to paint an accurate picture.  The Downside, on the other hand, is a gorgeous, almost alien landscape, with colors everywhere, naturally occurring plants and rock formations grow beyond their normal scope and in otherworldly shapes.  As often as it is described as inhospitable, the visuals of the game supplement the description perfectly.  Pyre’s world is one that is begging to be explored, and revisited, just to see the beautiful artwork that Supergiant has created.  The Downside deserves to be in another game, a game where the player gets to interact with it more directly rather than be told what it’s like to be living there.
I’d feel remiss if I didn’t mention the music, this is another Darren Korb composed soundtrack after all.  Once again, it’s a very excellent soundtrack, it accurately fits the tone and themes established by the game.  It’s clear to see why Supergiant and Darren Korb keep working together, they know how to weave their works together.  While the soundtrack is still excellent, it does sound a bit reminiscent of his work for Bastion, but if the worst I have to say about it is that it sounds too similar in tone to some of his older work, it’s still a phenomenal bit of music.
Pyre is a game that is worthy of your attention.  Fans of the Bastion and Transistor may feel a little left out in the cold, as this game shares almost nothing in common with them on the surface.  Stick with it, and Pyre will show you some good story, and fast, fun mechanics that for the right player could be everything.
