Pyre is a truly ambitious game, and it accomplishes everything it set out to do.
The Rites are fairly intuitive and exhilarating and very few of the matches are a cakewalk outside of the tutorial.
The characters are interesting, engaging, and, well, full of character. All of them are just trying to survive and get back home.
The landscapes are beautiful and highly varied. I was always excited to move on to the next Rite to see where it took place.
The lore of the game and the writing in general is fantastic. I spent perhaps half of my time playing reading the in-game history book and interacting with the characters, and I regret none of it.
Finally the music; just like the other Supergiant games, the soundtrack is fantastic. I bought it even before I had heard it because I knew that Darren Korb would deliver on making some sick jams. Having listened all the way through it, I was not disappointed.
Perhaps the only reason I would list to not buy the game is if you don't like reading or visual novels, this game's maybe not for you. If you're okay with some literature though, I give this game a hearty reccommendation.

The isle... Now that's a game that's been on my mind a lot as of recent. With one year of game development complete last december, I feel that now is my time to give my two cents on how it's been going so far.
So, the first time I saw the isle on steam was a bit over a year ago. Having been fond of dinosaurs for as long as I can remember, I instantly started digging for my wallet to go purchase some funds for my account. I purchased my game, started it up, and was greeted by what in my eyes was the perfect dinosaur game. Even with all it's flaws at the time, it consumed multiple hours of my daily routine and I just couldn't get enough of it.
Since then alot has changed, for better or worse. Development progressed at a good pace, new dinosaurs being added every month and new mechanics being introduced constantly. The first 'big' change to the game arrived when the first instance of progression came out. Now, to be perfectly honest, it was terrible. You'd spend what back then seemed like an outrageously long amount of time getting your dinosaurs, only to be chomped down by a horde of herreras. Nevertheless, I collected my patience and waited for them to improve on it. Shortly after, they released a new mechanic known as 'weight classes', and while it was a rough mechanic with lots of flaws, it did the trick. I quickly got back to enjoying the isle daily.
Development kept going forward at a steady pace from that point, a few dinosaurs added here and there, and a huge new map for us to play around in.
Around this time I started to notice, that Dondi, the head developer of the game, was disliked among players. I started doing research on the forums and ended up in their discord. After this point I learned more about the development team and the game, and mainly where they're aiming to go. And boy, I had no idea what I had gotten myself into; While many players complained that Dondi, the man in control, actively ignored their suggestions for improving the game, I realized that I may very well be getting much much more than what I initually paid for. I started to realize, that from the get go, this game had a goal it was striving to reach and a team of developers that had the enthusiasm to reach that goal. What amazes me, is that even though the community tends to give the developers hate when gamechanging updates are introduced to bring the game towards it's end goal, the team just keeps going. The whole team had clearly been picked with special care to assure a high quality dinosaur survival game, one that would have much more to offer in the future.
The game, in it's current form still has flaws. Ones concerning the unbalanced shantungosaurus, the unrealistic weights of some dinosaurs and the difficulty of the progression system, have been brought up multiple times on the offical discord, and to my surprise, while none of the suggestions for fixing these 'issues' have gotten through, Dondi has actually been directly replying to these complaints on their discord, and while he is sometimes 'mean' to the person he replies to, he clearly has his plan for an ideal game, and he trusts on it working out. As it stands I would give the game a 7/10, there are some big flaws affecting the enjoyability of gameplay, but it still manages to keep me busy to the late hours almost every day. They're clearly doing something right here. If they reach what they strive to become, however, this game is easily a 10/10 to me, and I sincerely hope they do, even if much of the community might be ignorant about why Dondi does things the way he does them, and keeps giving him hate for it.

First off, I love this game.  I've been playing it almost since it was first released and continue to come back to it time after time.  Granted... in that amount of time, I've never once reached the end.  Oh, I've gotten close.... so very very close.... only to end up falling victim to the bugs/glitches of the game, computer crashes, reformats, etc etc.
The ability to play as a Evil Genius in a James Bond/Archer/Austin Powers type world is actually a great concept and really done well here.  You can build your own evil volcano lair while attempting to take over the world... I'll say it again, a evil volcano lair... Why I steeple my fingers just thinking about it.
Building and maintaining your evil lair of evilness can be a blast and way more through provoking than it should be.  The same can be said for trap placement and layout for your hotel.
There is enough humor to keep you tickled the whole time you play.  Just reading the mission text should give you at least a giggle and nothing can beat watching a super agent go through a series of traps you cleverly set for them.
Gaining henchmen is done rather well and they do have special abilities all their own.  Which can be helpful... unless you go with Red Ivan.  Why would anyone use a bazooka inside your bosses base?
The options to torture those that have chosen wrongly to stand in your way of total victory are plentiful.  Seriously, take some time to look around for things to use.  You'll be surprised by the options... like the the messes blender.
Having said all that...
There are bugs... oh... is there ever and after a little while of playing you start to notice the lack of certain options.  Why can't I build a hallway thats one square wide?  Really?  Why?  Also... why can't I hide the entrance to my evil volcano lair?  Shouldn't that be like, I don't know, the first chapter in Evil Genius 101?  Could use one of those huts all camouflage like....
This is one of those games that I pray gets a sequel that it deserves and one that isn't as buggy.  After all, it is a wonderful game with plenty of tongue in cheek humor.

Back in the '90s, first-person shooters were not actually called FPSs, but Doom Clones.  That should tell you something about how much Doom changed the face of gaming when it came out in 1995.
Whether you're a first-person veteran or a total noob like me, Doom is a wonderfully playable, shockingly entertaining game.  Don't be fooled by its age; none of the clunky awkwardness you may have experienced in some other '90s games is here in this classic game.
Levels are non-linear, meaning they require exploration and some thinking to complete on top of the intense combat.
The controls are simple, but beautifully so.  There's no ducking, reloading, or regenerating health.  You must keep moving if you want to survive ("circle-strafing", as it's affectionately known by the community).  It's pretty easy to catch on to.
The game's combat can be very easy or nightmarishly hard depending on the difficulty, meaning Doom has a lot to offer both gaming newbies and gods.  I'm playing on the second-easiest diffuculty, and it provided a good challenge for me (a noob) while I learned the ropes, and now I'm ready for the next level.  And no matter what difficulty you play, you feel like a badass as you single-handedly mow down the legions of Hell with fists, shotguns, chainguns, rocket launchers, and the legendary BFG.
Visually, Doom is not only a huge milestone in the history of gaming, but is still a good-looking game today.  The graphics may be old, but the aesthetics (what really matter) hold up extremely well.  Levels are fun to explore and look at, important items are easy to recognize, and the variety of landscapes from moon bases to Hell itself are extremely creative, and perfectly give off that demonic vibe that makes it clear just how horrible a demonic invasion is.
You need to try this game out.  It's as essential as Portal for the modern gamer.  Even if you don't normally like FPSs, give this one a shot if you see it on sale.  You won't be disappointed.

I just finished this game...including nearly all sidequests. I really wanted to like this, but I just can't. The problem is not, that this is not Gothic anymore. I knew that already when I bought it (Even thou it tries to be Gothic by having the name in its title). The Problem is, even seeing it as a single game, without the series, its just not a good game. However I'll try to make a list of pros and cons here and you'll see for yourself if you want to play it or not:
Pros:
-Graphics + Design of the enviroment
-Easy controls
-Very easy, its pretty hard to die in the beginning, it slowly gets harder, but you never get to the point where you need more than 2-3 tries to kill an enemie, which makes it a good game for people, who don't often play RPG's and/or want quick and fast progress
-It's not hard to find your way, they're all pretty obvious, there are no long walking parts
-You meet some NPC's from the Gothic games (however meeting some of them makes no sense, because of the end of Gothic 3)
-(Bandages are food ;b)
Cons:
-Voice actors in german and english (didn't try others) are terrible. You just can't take them seriously
-The only thing you need gold for is potions, weapons/armor are free, which gives you nearly no reason to explore your enviroment -> if you do so, you'll find nothing better anyways
-There are no real choices and the few choices you make have no influence
-Combat is pretty much clicking, clicking, clicking...and rolling now and then
-The story is linear, you visit one part of your map after the other, there is no need to go back and what happens next is obvious all the time, every possible cliché is used
-Skill tree...is not a tree, more like skill lines, good thing is you can't do anything wrong here and your skills don't have influence on what weapons/armor you wear. Magic skill lines will upgrade your spell, there are only 3 spells in total for the whole game
-Lots of quest items only spawn after you got the quest...one more reason to not look into caves as long as noone tells you to do so
-The graphics are good in general, but you'll find lots of glitches/textures
-Invisible walls everywhere
-No reason to play it again, you'll see everything there is in one playthrough
-Some small bugs (NPC's not willing to talk to you unless you reload your last save, enemies getting stuck)

Pros: Still one of the most ambitious rts games I have ever played, Star ruler makes up for bare-minimum graphics with mind boggling scale and complexity. Will your strategy involve fleets of ai controlled drones? Or a handful of superdestroyers? Perhaps you prefer to send carriers full of small, manned bombers? The ability to customize your strategy to your tastes is easily the best part of the game, followed by a galaxy generation system limited only by your hardware. Its the little details that make the ship building mechanic shine. Your free to design whatever ship you want, but you'd better pay attention! The game will hold your hand just enough to complete the ship design, but be sure to add enough fuel! I only needed to build one expensive fleet of ships that drifted into black nothing with empty tanks before I knew to check fuel specs EVERY time I designed a ship. Ammo consuption, power levels, life support, net acceleration- all important variables in your design. A ship that suffers a power outage every time it fires its main weapon will be an expensive coffin when the fighting starts. You get the idea.
Cons: Its certainly rough around the edges; Its a game that doesn't really know if it wants you to micro manage every little detail, or let its automated systems do the heavy lifting. It often feels like big complex mechanics were put in place and then made irrelevant in order to keep the game playable. Examples include an entire resource (luxuries) that in all my 80 hours of gameplay I didn't worry about once. There is also a system for how happy your populace is thats supposed to affect how fast they build things, but it never seemed to cause problems. Theres an entire game buried in the social and economic aspects of star ruler, but its like the devs realized no one wanted to be bothered with luxuries when a galactic war was on and painted over it.
I've had so much fun with this game that I have to recommend it. At the same time, its difficult not to wish the developers had focused more on their design; cutting away the pointless bits, defining the core mechanics. . . Its a great game that could have been better, but I love it all the same.

TL;DR - This game is superbly gorgeous visually, but lacks vision and boils down to a very linear, and repetitive gameplay. The combat is just button mashing, and the story is boring. However, if you are a hardcore RPG fan, I recommend this game, as it still offers a new experience, and the world is fun to traverse. If you're looking for a Skyrim or Dragon Age experience, LOOK ELSEWHERE. This is an odd game.
In depth review -
This is game is... Interesting, to say the least. Now I can't necessarily say it's horrible, and I can't really say it's good, either. This game is a weird anomaly of a game, and has an interesting combination of good, and horrible, mechanics and features.
To be honest, I have never had the pleasure of playing any of the original Gothic series, so going into this game, I didn't have any knowledge prior of some sort of bar this game had to meet. However, going in, I did get that "Weird RPG feel." You know the one. The feel you get when you launch a game from the Risen series, or the first Witcher game. It just has a weird feel to it, and I can't explain it, unless you've experienced it.
Anyways, let's start with the basics of the game, and what's not good or good about those. First off, I'd like to mention the first thing I disliked; the voice acting. Good lord. It's like something out of the Arma franchise. So much overacting, or there's complete lack of enthusiasm with these people. You'll go straight from a stereotypical, high-pitched, screetching witch, to a bored, complaining footsoldier who is in mid-combat. Appropriate. It's just very bad, and very... jarring. It takes you way out of the immersion, and that's not a word I like to use.
Next on the list is the aesthetic appeal of the game, and to be honest, for a game that's 5 years old, it looks great. The colors are fantastic, the sceneries are incredible, and the lighting effects, down to some of the tiniest details is great. Just wait til you get to the point where you fight some flaming stone golems, and you'll see exactly what I mean. Adding to this point as well, there is a GREAT variety of environments. You have everything from starting with a sandy, lush beach island, to a volcanic cliffside, rain forests, and green moderate forests with plenty of rain, and lakes to enjoy. Adding to this again, the world is quite nice. It's not overwhelmingly huge, but they did a good job not making it too linear, even though it has more of that path system. The only thing I'll add that I didn't like about aesthetics were the character models. They weren't BAD persay, but they all tend to look VERY similar, which tends to be a problem with these larger RPGs, especially the older they are.
The next thing is the gameplay. Really, to be honest, there isn't any. It's trying to be The Witcher, or Dragon Age, with dialogue options and in depth combat, but what it boils down to is just click, click, and click some more. No need to dodge, or even look at what dialogue you're selecting. It all will do the same thing; you win. I have not had a problem ever with the difficulty. I HAVE been playing on normal, but I didn't die til about 6 hours in. Just keeping clicking that sword around, OR just run away. That's always an option, unless the quest specifically orders something to be killed.
The dialogue is just dumb, just look at what I said about voice acting.
Now, here is where my BIGGEST problem is with this game; ♥♥♥♥ THE QUESTS. Oh my god. I have never seen a more roundabout way to keep a game's playtime up. Jesus, these people milked the ♥♥♥♥ out of these quests. Get ready to fight some goblins, because that 99.9% of your problems. Not your friends and wife-to-be being murdered, NO, your biggest problem will be goblins. Need to prove yourself to someone? Kill goblins. Need to return the kings standard? Goblins took it. Need to help an herbalist get his stuff back? Goblins took that♥♥♥♥♥♥too. Need to ANYTHING in a cave? GOBLINS ARE IN THAT ♥♥♥♥ING CAVE! And believe me, there are way too many quests that involve going into a cave with goblins. I would easily say that 70-80% take place in a cave. I'm not making that up. That's my honest guestimate. The other problem with the quests is this; they drag them the ♥♥♥♥ out so long. One of the quests you need to go find a king or something that was taken prisoner. Ok, easy enough right? Wrong. You go talk to the orc who's guarding the gate of the camp, hoping you can just kill, or run your way through. Wrong again, you have to talk to this guy. He wants some booze from a shaman who brews the stuff in a forest nearby. Ok, easy enough again, right? WRONG AGAIN. Guess what, this guy won't give you the booze (which is called skabooze, by the way, real imaginative, right?), until you find his nephew somewhere in the forest who ran off. EASY ENOUGH RIGHT?? ♥♥♥♥ING WRONG YOU ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, BECAUSE GUESS WHAT? YOU NEED TO GO FIND THIS GUYS AMULET THAT ANOTHER SHAMAN TOOK! At this point you want to just kill everybody, and what doesn't help is that your character acknowledges along the way that all of this stuff is redundant, and stupid. He constantly gets impatient and makes sarcastic remarks about having to go do menial and boring stuff, and then later, he EXPECTS it. So the DEVs KNEW this♥♥♥♥♥♥was redundant and menial, but still willingly put it in the game. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. Anyways, the Shaman that took that other orcs amulet, that you need to get booze, that you need to get into a gate, that you need to get the prisoner? Guess what? After you fight him, YOU HAVE TO GO INTO A ♥♥♥♥ING CAVE THAT HE HID IT IN ON THE OTHER SIDE OF THE FOREST, FILLED WITH ♥♥♥♥ING GOBLINS AGAIN!!!!! So all of that♥♥♥♥♥♥ and guess what? YOU JUST KILL THE ORCS INSIDE ANYWAYS, SO WHY WASTE THE TIME GETTING THAT ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ HIS BOOZE TO BEGIN WITH?!?!
Whatever. Beyond that, there's something about this that I can't explain that's rather appealing. The skill trees are ok. Combat works, even though it's just button mashing. The areas are rather gorgeous at times, and the music is just on par. The dialogue is complete crap, and story is uninspired, but at the same time, I get enjoyment from this game, and will probably end up playing the original Gothic games. Those are supposed to be the really good ones. So if this one works for me somewhow, I'm sure those will too.
Overall, it's a 5/10 for me, but I still recommend it to the hardcore RPG fan. Give it a shot, you might enjoy it if you're into those weird RPGs. But remember, it ain't no Dragon Age, or Skyrim.

I had a mixed feeling about rating this game good/bad.
Its a classic DOS game from the 90s and it was very good at that time.
Sadly the port to linux is simply letting it run in dosbox (simulating DOS), so it seems the developers did not put much time in it.
For its normal price of E9,99 it is definitely not worth it, but with a discount of 75% I got it for E2,49, which is fine.
It also has some bug issues:
- when run for a long time.. the game update gets very slow, so you need to save the current state, quit and restart the game again.
- Sometimes the path seek algorithm seems to hang, but the rest of the GUI does not. As workaround I load the previous saved state and continue from there again.
The resolution seems to be just 320x200, but scaled a bit to something like 640x480 running with a black border on a 1900x1080 display. But I found that via a config file you can tell dosbox to use a 3xhq scale wich reduces the border and increases the details slightly.
It is sad the developers did not put the effort of running it in a higher resolution. Now I am looking at a tiny overview of an area in which to move the soldiers, so I must move my view window all over the place to see what is going on. There is a full sector overview, in which each tile seems drawn in a 2x2 pixel, but then the details are gone.. so its hard to put your soldiers behind trees.
About the game storyline and features.. it is really good.
You hire a team of max 8 soldier and in a turn-based manner you scan an sector of the map for enemies and shoot them. When they are all dead, the sector is yours and you can put guards and workers (to get money) in and move on. With more money you can hire better soldiers and you can find weapons/items in each sector, which helps you to get the next sector.
This sounds simple enough.. but the game has some nasty events thrown back at you to make it very hard to accomplish your tasks:
-  The soldiers often miss their target (even a high skilled 91% sharp shooter),  the enemy however seem to miss rarely.. so I try to move my soldiers as close as possible to the enemy to get a higher chance of a hit. The enemy however can shoot you from a great distance (even ofscreen) and hit you.
- The trees/bushes should provide a cover so the enemy can not hit you (and you can not hit them). However sometimes the bullet can get through and still hit.. so you are never sure if the cover really works.. it seems random.
- So often your soldiers get wounded and need a medic to stop bleeding, but even when healed they will perform badly for that day.
- They can only heal/rest fully when not used for a day, but then you have less soldiers that day to accomplish your task.
- You can fire them and hire new ones, but new soldiers notice this and might not follow you or ask for double pay. Soldiers might hate eachother or leave you.
- Booby traps over the map can kill you.. even though for a 97% explosion expert.
- While your busy in one sector the enemy (3 soldiers) can take over another sector and kill 8 guards (the max possible) and this in easy mode!
- Your weapons can be jammed when you try to fire.. costing your "action points" and making it useless for a next time.. so now I bring atleast two guns for each highly skilled soldier.
- You might try to start with better skilled (but expensive) soldiers, but then you run out of money quickly.. I myself choose the cheapest best mark (good shooters), two cheap medics and a repair guy (to open locked doors and repair items) and one very good shooter (Ivan marks=91%).
During gameplay I replace the cheaper ones with better ones.. but this can not be done often
- I suggest reading the manual carefully as a lot of features were not clear to me from what the GUI shows:
- the medic can become a doctor.. but it must have a medic box in its hand to do so.
- the repair man can repair items at the base (must hold toolbox).. but can not repair items when on duty,  so it seems useless to let him bring the toolbox every mission.
- you might find items that seem useless (eg oil, cloth, glass, fuelcan), but when you place one item in the main hand and place another in the extra slot below it, it might merge to a new item.
- the soldiers you hire have their own skillset, but some of the soldiers seem to have an useless skillset or another with the same skillset is cheaper.. so why are they in the game.. just to confuse you?
Above makes the game interesting and I was surprised how much effort was done in a game of the 90s. A lot of voice acting has been done for each certain event a soldier might experience, which is nice and funny.
However for me it is also frustrating.. all events together are just too random and I keep on saving and loading to be able to continue, hoping that each time the situation differs a bit.
But saving during the "day" gameplay has just one slot.. so if you make a mistake and save it and want to redo it, you need to redo the entire day. Oh.. and they made an option that you can play without the save option, but that seems for hardcore players only.
You have another save possibilty for multiple slots in the main menu of the game, but this can only be used after a "day" is finished.
You can play the game in easy/normal/hard mode and on youtube I see players play this on hard.
I myself have trouble enough just playing it on easy mode.. :(
So my conclusion is a "No":
I feel the game reacts too much random.. making it hard/impossible to predict the outcome of each action. It is difficult enough already just to spend the "action points" wisely and create a strategy,
but now the gameplay is merely following the steps:
1. save current state
2. try something
3. if failed, reload and goto step 2
4. if really sure current state has a new advantage, goto step 1
5. goto 2
At that rate it takes a long time to finish the game.. but it is not much fun.

The father of the king of turn-based squad-sized tactical games – the predecessor of Jagged Alliance 2. This release contains an original game, a campaign about capturing Metavira island from the forces of bad scientist in favor of good scientist… and standalone add-on Deadly Games, which is not holding a story, being just a list of separate missions. Although the challenge of those missions in the Deadly Games makes it a very good tactical game on its own.
What is more, Steam now releasing just the same version of the game as GOG – with DosBox, and everything polished and tuned up to the perfect condition. Funny thing is that the game I’m calling the king, the second Jagged Alliance, in gold edition, that Steam sells now… requires quite a bit of fixing, after you’ll install it, but the first game, aged 21 years now, running smoothly out-of-the-box.
Some basic info: in the Jagged Alliance you’re settled as the mercenaries commander and entrepreneur, who hires them from some agency via personal notebook, trains them, hones them…  And sending them to death, to capture some sectors of the God-forgotten island somewhere in the Pacific ocean, where inhabits some unique medical panacea plant, which can’t be find anywhere else in the world. Game combines turn-based tactical warfare of little squads of mercs with strategical elements, where you planning your budget, since we’re all know that for every war you need money, money and even more money. Every merc you can hire have some personality, strong and weak points, and stats, which can be trained or dropped, considering your gaming experience. Mercs are calculating your actions, and follow you only when you’re good both with paychecks and strategy on the battlefield.
What I’m trying to say there is that even in the first Jagged Alliance we can see many of the elements still considering a highest insignia of top-notch tactical games where you’re operating the small unit of soldiers. I can call the Valkyria Chronicles as an example there, its fun was builded on the same base of interactions between team-mates.
Yet… With all good points we see in this game, like interesting and deep mechanic of controlling warfare, resource gathering and interpersonal relationships altogether -  it is really hard to actually recommend buying this game now to anyone not familiar with it already. Even if you are good with the given genre, it might be a very hard experience, considering the fact it is real old-school, without tutorials or playgrounds. Well, in case you are really want to see how things were settling in the game’s GUI 20 years back, or if you’re up to some kind of pilgrimage to the roots of one of the best-game’s-mechanics-ever-made  – OK, give it a shot.

Jagged Alliance has been one of my most beloved game series for some twenty years now. But I feel most sentiment towards the oldest one, the original JA. Yes, the graphics looks ancient today. Its mechanics lacks a lot of things that were addressed in Deadly Games and later in JA2 and a few things can be quite frustrating. Yet I like it more than JA:DG - because it has story, more tactical choices and gives you much more freedom in the way how you'd like to make your way through the game.
I guess it has very little potential to attract new generation of gamers and the only ones to purchase this game will be antediluvians such as myself, who have spent hundreds hours playing it  twenty years ago, but it is a pity, because only a handful of games are so memorable... and can be played over and over again and lose little of their appeal decades after their first release.
JA:DG are much more straightforward, they add multiplayer (sort of), level and campaign editor, Mickey the weapons dealer with the most stereotypical Irish accent I've ever heard... Game mechanics are a wee bit more polished y'know, but the missions are in the order Gus Tarballs lays them for you, one per day and that's that... Don't get me wrong, it's not worse game than the original JA, in some ways it's better and I spent probably hundreds of hours playing it as well... Yer it lacks some charm of its predecessor, at least for me.
TL;DR:
If you're under thirty, don't buy it, you probably won't like it.
If you're old enough to remember its first release and enjoyed it then, get it on sale, for 2,49€ it's a bargain and the game is still as much fun as it once was - and you get both JA and Deadly games.
It runs in DOSBox, so it works even on Win10 and machines built in 21st century ;-)

DARIUSBURST Chronicle Saviours is the latest entry in Taito's long running Darius franchise.  If you're unfamiliar with the series, it's characterized by sea-life based enemies and awesome soundtracks scored by Zuntata.  I was interested in the game for a long time, but like many I held off on purchasing due to its considerable price point.  Although I like it now, I must admit the “Freedom” song from the trailer was initially a turn off as well.  It took a while, but I'm glad I was eventually able to play DBCS because it's quite good.
This title contains a port of the arcade game Dariusburst Another Chronicle EX, and a specially created single player campaign called CS Mode.  In case you don't know, the arcade game is originally played on a fairly large screen.  This means the arcade port will likely be letter-boxed to fit the shape of your monitor.  This can initially be a little jarring, but I didn't have any issues getting used to it.  I don't have the equipment to test it myself, but it does have dual monitor support.  There is also something called Chronicle Mode, which I believe to be an online campaign similar to CS mode.  I don't have any experience with Chronicle Mode, so further information about it will not be contained within this review.  The arcade port is set up similarly to other Darius games.
Original Mode contains zones A-L and Original EX has zones O-Z.  As you play through the game you choose a three letter route.  Letters farther into the alphabet represent higher difficulty stages.  Route ADH is considered to be the easiest route, and QUZ is the hardest.  The game also allows the player to choose between a one credit entry and unlimited credit entry.  Choosing unlimited credits will not record a score.  The credit option combined with the flexibility of routes allows the player to make the game as easy or as difficult as they wish.  There are nine playable ships to choose from, though one of them only appears in CS Mode.
The abilities of each ship vary extensively.  Most of them have a burst weapon that can be utilized with proper timing to counter enemy bursts.  Two ships don't need need to time counterbursts, and a few of them lack the ability to burst entirely.  Several have fixed bursts (essentially a detachable burst drone) that can be aimed to form bullet blocking barriers.  As you fly through each stage there will occasionally be enemies that will drop orbs corresponding to the color of the enemy.  The red ones will upgrade the weapons system, the green ones will upgrade bombs/missiles, and blue ones are for ARM/shields.  Unlike the typical one hit deaths often seen in STGs, you're able to take hits until the ship runs out of shielding.  I don't know what the exact hitbox dimensions are, but it's close to the entire size of your ship.  To compensate for this, the bullet patterns aren't as dense as danmaku style shooters.  The types of enhancements obtainable vary from ship to ship.  Some of them are easier to use than others, and they have different scoring multipliers to compensate.  In order to get more points you'll want to destroy all the enemies in each wave, use your burst frequently (if there is one), and kill bosses by counterbursting.  It may all seem a little overwhelming at first, but fortunately there is a great way to learn how to use each ship effectively.
CS Mode consists of well over one hundred unique missions (specifically 186 according to one source I found).  I'm unable to confirm the exact number of missions myself, despite the fact that the bulk of playtime consists of playing this mode.  Regardless of the exact number, I can confidently say there is enough content there to keep most players busy for a very long time.  The missions heavily vary in difficulty and length.  Most of them simply require winning, but a few do have alternate objectives such as obtaining a certain score and finishing within a time limit.  Each mission has a preset ship which is the intended way to play, however if a mission is too challenging the player can use in game currency (earned from completing missions) to buy a heavily upgraded custom ship for the mission.  I enjoyed using the presets, and found it to be a great way to learn how to play effectively with each ship.  As I grew more experienced I found that some of the ships I initially disliked eventually became my favorites.  You will fight many of the same bosses over and over, but I found there to be more than enough variety to keep me entertained.  CS Mode sports music from many Darius games and playing it made me a fan of Zuntata's work.  I've found myself listening to the tracks outside of the game multiple times.  I enjoy many of the songs, but if I could only suggest a few I'd say that “Olga Breeze”, “Hinder One”, and “Good-bye my earth” are worth listening to even if you don't buy this game.
DARIUSBURST Chronicle Saviours is an excellent STG.  Between the arcade modes and CS Mode there is a ton of great content.  I only have two criticisms of this game.  First and foremost the backgrounds for boss fights can sometimes be a little drab, although you probably won't spend much time looking at them.  My second criticism is the lack of a practice mode.  CS Mode acts as sort of a substitute, but an actual practice mode would have been much appreciated.   Although I believe DBCS would be a great first shmup, the full price cost is probably a little prohibitive for those wanting to dip their feet into the genre.  If you're the type of person that enjoys playing for 1ccs and high scores though, you shouldn't have any trouble getting a good value out of the game. If you don't play many hidden object games, it might shock you to learn there's a huge amount of variance between them. Frankenstein is an excellent example of this, having a solid engine and slick visuals married to absolutely brain-dead gameplay. And that's not even that much of a knock against it, considering the trappings of the genre.
Frankenstein is, unsurprisingly, a re-telling of Mary Shelley's classic tale of science gone awry, just with more crests and crossbows to click on. In a strange twist (yes I am going to spoil the plot of a hidden object game, brace yourselves), Frankenstein is actually the hero, compelled to complete his heinous experiments by his partner and patron Igor. You play his friend, firmly invested in saving him from Igor and his monster, who looks remarkably like Raziel from Soul Reaver pre-jaw loss. The cutscenes are pretty well animated and the game actually has dynamic 3D models for many of the characters and creatures, which is a huge step up from its peers.
The gameplay is the customary hidden object scenes and simple puzzles, but taken to an infantile extreme. The hidden object scenes are absolutely huge, with some objects to find being nearly a quarter of the screen. Seriously, you could click at random and find all but the multi-part items, which usually just require pushing a button, using a knife on a rope, or assembling something. The challenge here is way, way down from other hidden object games, and is brought back up in aggravating fashion by tons of backtracking and an absurd number of crests. Seriously, I think there are maybe three keys in the game compared to the three dozen crests you have to collect to open up all the rooms of the mansion.
It's a very clean-looking product, with no technical hitches and all the quality-of-life elements of a modern hidden object game. It's just not very engaging, mostly because of the poor difficulty balance. If you got it for pennies like I did it's worth a try, but I can hardly recommend it at full price.

This review covers the original 4 DOOM releases including: Ultimate DOOM, DOOM II: Hell on Earth, Master Levels for DOOM II and Final DOOM as the games are very similar in style, release date (early-mid 90's) and due to me not wanting to make 4 reviews of essentially the same thing.
Here stands the original game that sparked controversy worldwide. Now who wouldn't want to play that?
What appears to be watered down compared to todays' games the classic DOOM series is still one of the most well-known releases of all time. In regards to being a classic, it stands next to many other popular FPS's of the time including Wolfenstein 3D, Duke Nukem 3D and the original Shadow Warrior just to name a few. The game was violent, hellish, gory and played sick metal midis while you fight through hordes of cyborg demons. Included in this purchase (and the other 3 games) are some newer expansions that have been added since the original, which was a nice touch. I recommend buying the old DOOM(s) if you're a retro enthusiast, don't mind a lack of graphics and/or if you wish to see the birthplace of the FPS genre. And of course there is a huge mod community on the interwebs to enhance your experience or overhaul the game into something entirely new.
Side note: On sale, the DOOM Classic Complete bundle was $7.49 USD and includes the 4 previously mentioned games; a pretty reasonable tribute for an inspiration into the world’s most popular genre.

How To Like - Frankenstein: Master of Death - Review
Short Version:
- Maybe Buy it On Sale & Only Play it On Hard Mode (as the game itself recommends)
- Expect a fun and short (couple of hours long) interactive Puzzle-play experience.
- Don't expect great story or characters you'll care to remember
- Seemingly illogical at times, but kept me enjoyably engaged until I finished the game - in one go.
Long Version:
WHEN MUST YOU PLAY THIS GAME -
I recommend - you play it - WHEN you're in the mood to take a break from long, intensive & content-heavy-games (which we love and must always go back to), and you're in the mood to play something just for fun - that'll massage your brain, in that almost-challenging-kind-of-way...
Also, while the Game is a HOG, the entire game isn't about finding hidden objects, in fact the HOG part of the game appears in the form of minigames within the game, absent which you're usually solving puzzles or collecting objects and putting them to use, which according to me was really fun - as it kept the game from becoming monotonous...Since the only other HOG i've played is Criminal Cases on FACEBOOK - I embarassingly admit - I'm fully aware of how quickly such games risk tiring you out...
WHEN MUST YOU NOT PLAY THIS GAME -
If you're expecting a story-driven experience - Do not play this game then! Because the story just feels like it's there for the sake of being there, flimsily attempting to hold the game together. Not meaning to be harsh, but I just felt like the backdrop and the base story - "Visit Frankenstein who manages to resurrect the dead" - just had so much potential to make for an interesting plot and memorable characters.
WHAT COULD HAVE BEEN! -
Instead of playing an investigating friend that's trying to puzzle out how to save your friend from the resulting dangers of his experiments with death, the story could have been intelligently woven around Frankenstein himself. In other words a HOG that had the player traverse "the fragile border between life and death," carrying out puzzling experiments and collecting important ingredients and samples - to concuct the solution for eternal life. If it had a solid story and a loveable character, it could have even been as something I'd love to see and gladly buy - when released as episodes.

ALL IN ALL THOUGH -
It's definitely a fun experience worth playing, or atleast a game you should give a shot - if on discount. It's a relatively short game that provides an experience which you'll enjoy, but not one which will stay with you after you'ved played it.
But I'll say this though, eventhough you'll scoff and complain at a few instances in the game, if you're into it - the game can keep you hooked and it's a fun experience to watch unravel. I was playing it with a friend by my side and even as a spectator - it kept him engaged to the end as well, just watching and shouting suggestions and ideas for solving the puzzles and obstacles the game presented, all the way till we finished it.
It also helps that the game has mini-cutscenes that show you actually using your objects from your inventory, on the objects to which their uses correspond to. Although couldn't help but raise an eyebrow, when I could break open a box with a crowbar which I had, but had to go through various obstacles to find a handle to use in order to open a glass cabinet.
... AAAAAND If I don't stop blabbering now, this review may just extend to being longer than this game. Forgive the dry humour - it's in good taste, eventhough if funny tasted good - that joke would taste like crap.
...Urrr so yea! I Totally recommend playing this game as not being a bad idea. I'm glad I did!
Disclaimer - This Review is subject to my fallible judgement & limited knowledge.
- Saad Merchant

Wow! Just finished the game on the 'Hitman' (Hard) difficulty in about 6 hours and absolutely loved every minute of it!
It was a lot better than I expected. You play the character of an American mobster boss with a super natural power called The Darkness. This power manifests itself in the form of two 'Demon Arms'. The fact that you can combine these tentacles of mass destruction with your regular fire arms gives a very interesting twist to the FPS gameplay.
You can use your demon arms to smack enemies around, throw random objects at them or grab and then brutally execute them. The darkness is not just a gimmick, you really need to use it throughout the game to make progress and stay alive. For instance, use your tentacle to rip the door off a car and use it as a shield to make your way through an army of gunmen; when you are done, split the last enemy in half by throwing the door at him. Fun!
You also have a British demonic little helper that looks like he walked straight out of Overlord (he even has the same schenanigans), who can distract an enemy and make it an easy target for you to finish off.
There's a skilltree that lets you invest your soul essences (that you gather by collecting relics and harvesting the hearts of your enemies) in ammo upgrades and some additional powers. The game is pretty well balanced. Only the massive Black Hole that evaporates a room full of enemies faster than you can say 'fogeddaboutit' seems a little overpowered (but it's still a lot of fun :D).
Overall, a great game with refreshing gameplay for an FPS; Nice graphics, animations, voice acting; BUT - it's a little short.

I saw this on sale, saw the gameplay, and thought 'yes'. Easily a very quick £4 spent for me.
And I must say, I wasn't disappointed.
Welcome to the Mafia. You're introduced to Jackie, a Mafia boss, who is very good at what he does - killing people. Because why not.
He is in mourning over his dead wife/girlfriends/I can't remember, and when he gets a hit on him, and almost dies, two octopus arms tear out of his back.
Now I know what you're thinking - "How is he alive?" "Isn't his back in incredible pain?" "Will this turn into hentai?"
The answer to all of these will (not) be answered, except for the first, maybe.
Now onto the actual review of the game, which I did at Hitman level (hard?). Everyone likes bad news first, so I'll do it that way.
Cons:
Story is a bit 'meh' in my opinion.
The characters don't develop a massive amount, except the main character a tiny bit.
The multiplayer part removes the most awesome part, quad-wielding.
The Campaign and the Multiplayer are both quite short.
Pros:
Awesome, brutal combat and kills
QUAD-WIELDING! Most innovative part of the game, and makes it a lot more attention focusing. You'll need to keep track of 2 guns, a heart eating arm and a whip arm.
Enemies require more than just a few bullets in the later parts, and you may need to come up with a battle strategy. Lol no just whip 'em with your tentacle.
Multiplayer is fun with friends, and requires you to work together rather than spray-and-pray.
Overall I give this a 6/10. People think 6s are bad, but in comparison to some games *coughsonic06cough* which are at 1 or 2,  it's actually a good game. Because it's short, it's not worth £20. Because the multiplayer removes the best part, it's not worth £15. Because there isn't a huge amount of replay value, aside from collectables and relevelling your character to max out your perks, It'd be worth around £10/$15. If you can get at these prices, or in a bundle for some odd reason, go right ahead. But don't shell out full price, as it isn't worth that much. There are people out there willing to sell cheaper than full price, but I can't say here because that's probably illegal or something.
Some people will disagree, and that's fine, this will be better to others than it was to me. I recommend playing it on Hitman difficulty, as the ones before are too easy and the one after is for a second run.

Star Ruler is a very open-ended game. This supports modding very nicely and there are some wonderful mods out there for it, such as Galactic Armory. The blueprint design system lets you stop worrying about exactly how the ship is going to be put together and worry more about exactly what types of systems you want to install, and how much of them. There is almost no limit to how big a ship's scale can be, and everything is done on a beautifully simple relative ratio allowing you to take any ship design and rescale it easily. Research is well handled, while simple, it is also complicated with the possibility of randomizing links between different fields, resulting in completely unique paths to the future technologies per play. Unfortunately the game's multiplayer support is not up to snuff, so is difficult to play with others over the internet. LAN games appear to work fine however. One thing to note: Star ruler 2 is allready in development, so this game is pretty much solidly locked as it is. The original promises of expansion and update have come to fruit to a degree, and it's a wonderful game overall, but don't buy it for multiplayer unless you're going to game on a LAN.

Star Ruler is the perfect example of an indie diamond in the rough. The core realtime 4x gameplay gives you a ton of freedom and ship design is fun and open, while the game progresses to eventually become really hectic. The customization and stuff isn't overdone to the point of being spergy like in some of these types of games. However, the game is pretty graphically poor, there being only two visually distinct sets of ship designs and everything being sort of par for the course budget indie space game graphics. The studio seems tiny though so can't really fault em that. A bigger issue is that the gameplay tends to degenerate into walling off a section of the map well enough that the AI can't bust through easily, and then beelining a ship of such a large scale none of the AIs can deal with it as it blows up planet and sun after planet and sun. The basic resource gameplay is realtime resource chain management sort of similar to Anno games, at which the AI has perfect micro - the difficulty setting seems to be what bonuses they get, and I couldn't find a difficulty at which I could have a back-and-forth fight with the AIs. Either I would crush them outright, fight them to a stalemate then win after two hours of turtling like outlined above, or get totally♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ This game seems to have a lot of potential for multiplayer but there ain't nobody playin this obscure♥♥♥♥♥indie pile lol. With more dynamic and varied AI this could be great. The sequel will be something to look forward to, though I gotta say an expansion fixing some of this would be better, first.
It's a recommend if you dig stuff like Endless Space and Sins of a Solar Empire with a dash of Anno and a pinch of autism mixed in, then all the polish knocked off

It is completely clear playing this that the makers never played the original 3 games by Piranha Bytes and did not care at all about the actual story. The read the synopsis of the originals, the list of characters and they make up their own story that has nothing to do with the rest of the series.
In short, the reason I cannot recommend this game as a fan of the Gothic series is that this game is simply does not belong in the series and was a grab on the IP recognition of it alone. It should have been written as an original game.

SOMA is the culmination of everything that Frictional Games have learned during the development of Penumbra and Amnesia.
Like both games before, the story is a deep venture into some sophisticated issues. This time - personality, uniqueness and consciousness.
What seperates SOMA from the previous games is that the main character is voiced now and all the voice acting is on a whole new level, which the devs have acknowledged as something that took away a fair portion of the budget. It helps immensely as it conveys character's emotions so much better and the performances are top notch.
Gameplay is pretty much the same as with previous titles, however the areas feel bigger now. You also get the occasional area where a monster is patrolling and you have to hide and sneak around which worked in Penumbra and Amnesia especially but here it detracts from the amazing story and feels a bit frustrating. I do understand their reasoning for including it, however.
Visually it is a leap over Amnesia. Textures are crisp and the lighting especially is beautiful and enhances the atmosphere of each location.
Overall it is a great game and I personally enjoyed it more than Amnesia or Penumbra simply because it felt more grounded and believable and I particularly like the themes the story portrays.

The most irritating part of the entire game for me was climbing up to a snipe spot and having laid down a half dozen traps on my way up (assuming I was going to have a huge fight coming down) only to find the enemy spawned past all my traps.

I know exactly what you are thinking "A shoot 'em up for $50, that's ridiculous."  Yes, that would be ridiculous for your average schmup.  First thing you should know about Darius Burst Chronicles is that it has content, in spades.  The main arcade mode is a branching path where you play three levels in a row.  You can mix and match the levels in quite a few ways.  It also had 10 unique bosses.  Then there is Chronicle Savior mode with hundreds of levels and various challenge.  You will not play everything in this game, you just won't.  The original arcade machine was meant to be unlocked by everyone at the arcade.
The great thing about DB:CS is that it balances the difficulty quite well for most gamers.  It doesn't go to the extreme lengths a lot of modern bullet hell schmups go to.  Thus it is more approachable by your average gamer.  However, it can still offer a healthy challenge.
The game also has a rich scoring system for you to rack up a multiplier and tactically kill your enemies with your beam for more points.  You get the most points by scoring the deathblow on a boss with a counterbeam.  So there is depth there if you want it.
If you like Shoot 'em ups, this game you will probably enjoy this game.  Now the $50 price is steep, but I feel they can also justify it with the amount of content they give you.  If you don't want to spend that much, an entirely reasonable position, this can make a great game to pick up on sale.  At $20 it would be a no brainer.

So, the game is currently just a barebones survival game, where you play as a dino.. So what got my to 84 hours without regrets?
Simply put: The gameplay, as is, is good. Sure its barebones, and thers plenty of salty moments, but its good. And you can feel that the game is getting improved, even by minor updates.
So, lets look at the bad stuff first, which is what you would most likely be absolutely furious about at first.
1: Carnivore progression is slow and tedious, it takes a long time to reach apex, and until you do, your basicly either a scavenger, or have to get lucky finding a smaller dino to prey on.
2: Certain dinos are broken right now, as i write this. This includes the Puerta, spino is overpowered due to massive HP pool and fast attacks, as well as high dmg. The Shanty is extremely powerful as well. I wont say any names, but certain carnivores are basicly unable to hunt since bleed was removed.
3: Toxic players, KOS (Kill On Sight), and general sloughter. These are things you have to deal with on a regular basis on some servers.
So.. Thats some really bad things right? Well, half can be avoided and dealt with, so lets look at the positives.
1: Community, on certain servers, are absolutely amazing, making the progression and waiting an actual joy.
2: Some servers have rules which somehow managed to balance the playing field, making smaller carnivores viable again.
3: The KOS and general sloughters provide two things: You learn how to hide, sneak, and scavenge effectively.
4: The game grows on you over time, as you learn where to go, when, and as what. And once you have died several times after hours of waiting to progress.. Well, once you realise its not so bad, it grows more and more bearable.
5: The devs are pretty good, we get regular updates, both on what they work on but also patches.
6: Almost all servers have a discord community running, which makes it really easy to find people to play with, news, server rules, and so on.
Now, if you look at pro's and cons, it evens out somewhat. But one thing i really like about the game developers is that they actually pulled the entire combat system out, so they could refine and improve it. They already brought breaking bones from falls, and fall damage in general back in. So it is just a matter of time before the game see some major changes.
So, in all honesty, i would not recommend this to everyone. It is far from a game that every player would like. But for those who give it time to grow on you, become active in their servers community, and learn the game. Yeah, i do recommend it to people who are willing to give it a fair chance.
And heres a little warning: most people probally will only try it 2 hours to get a refund, you wont like it after the first 2 hours. You will most likely hate it. The game is rough, and punishes you for making mistakes. I had to reach around the 20 hour mark before i truly enjoyed it.
I hope this helps, and i will probally rewrite the review when the game changes again.

I have never played a game before in the Gothica series, so in regards to the reviews towards the game's story and depth I did not hold much creed in.  Because I had no basis of comparison from this series specifically, I dismissed those criticisms as associative and wanted to play the game on it's own merits.
Graphically, this game is quite impressive for a title from it's time.  The bitmaps, many of the object models, and foliage and water all look impressive and would be comparable to a game from today.  Environmental sounds are also quite good.  Character models however are showing their age; all males and females share the same basic physique, and the character model used is pretty simplistic.  The player character looks like he's got a bird's nest growing on his scalp.  His hair is detailed but does not move; the hair spray in the Gothica universe must use super glue as it's base.
The writing and voice acting in this game are jarringly bad and repeatedly wreck the process of immersion.  For example, at the beginning of the game, you need to acquire a bangle so that you can propose to your girlfriend.  Despite just previously completing a quest that had me wipe out a camp of goblins (thus having gold from corpses and weapons to sell going into this quest), here I see my character rationalizing having to do a retrieval quest for the bangle because he 'has no gold', which was clearly and obviously incorrect.
The dialogue 'tree' in this game is flat-out nonsense.  You rarely have any actual options, and after a couple of hours, I stopped caring about what lore they may reveal and just wanted to move on to questing.  A couple of hours after that, I no longer wanted to play.
Despite the fact that this game was also made for consoles, this version does not have a functioning inventory while using the controller.  I found this to be an unacceptable technical oversight when compiled with the other problems I had playing this game.
I can't recommend a game that I have no desire to finish.  I don't know how this game compares to other games in the Gothica series, but I generally don't think this is even a good RPG.

So, I'd never played a Darius game but wanted to and this was the only one... so I grimaced and paid the $60 (well, ended up being $80 after I came back for DLC... but the DLC gets its own mode and is entirely stand-alone, so don't worry too much about it).
On first starting up, I didn't know what was happening... did I want AC or CS mode?! What are all these other choices within each one? How do I get to the 3K levels they're talking about? I played through the game a few times (you can set infinite continues) and thought myself a chump for dishing out top-dollar... then I started goofing around in the menus and I was really happy.
The game takes a bit of menu-spelunking to get to all the goodies. But you can play (AC Mode) the core game in a whole bunch of ships from the Darius series-- and they're all reasonably unique. Chronicle Mode (CS Mode) lets you fly through increasingly-hard branches of the game against different end-bosses. Some of the end bosses are derivative of each other (i.e. all the "... Wheels" are more or less visually the same with different colors, weapons, and attacks). In AC Mode, there's ALSO a Chronicle Mode which is different-- you choose a planet, then an area where each area is a permutation... sorta like Chronicle Mode in CS mode, but less linear. It's worth calling out that AC Mode is a port of the arcade game, which is somewhat-famously played across a REALLY wide three-monitor setup. This is such a direct port, the game warns you to watch your head when leaving the arcade chair.
DLC Mode gives you special ships based off Sega and Taito games. Choose a ship and a region and fly off. You can also just use regular Darius ships here, too. It's Darius's answer to arena-style games. Personally, I like playing this when my attention is divided or I've had a long day and need to blow stuff up.
All this mode stuff gives you plenty to explore. The high score list is like a textbook of your legendary accomplishments. All this is why the game is why the game is worth $60.
So... after you finally choose a mode that suits how you're feeling today, how is the gameplay? Well, friggin' amazing, of course! The 3D models seem a little dated to me... the 3D models aren't weighed down by crazy shaders like most games of late. But, then, the game throws hundreds of them on the screen at a time. Enemies come from both sides of the screen in places. Some of the ray attacks are REALLY gorgeous. If you see Violent Ruler, you'll know what I'm talking about. The levels themselves range really wildly from stupidly easy to amazingly hard. Like a good arcade game, the first levels are pretty easy and the final levels are blindingly tough. In the first levels of the Chronicle modes, the main levels themselves are pretty easy, but the boss battles get tough and you really need to learn how to defeat each one.
Lastly, I wanna say something about the Darius franchise. The game itself is well documented at the game's website (
) as well as a fan-made Wikia page (
). It's been around forever. The fans are loyal, and playing and falling in love with this game is like entering into a community.

There are worse HOGs than Frankenstein: Master of Death, but it still isn't very good.  The English translation is mostly passable, but frequently stilted, and some of the voice actors are less than convincing.  The gameplay is very linear; despite a few forks in the map, you will work through each puzzle and unlock each gate in exactly the designed order -- you will never have a few potential options.  The HO scenes are brief and not particularly challenging.
The pseudo-historical setting is even more anachronistic than usual.  Your character arrives on the scene in a horse-drawn carriage, but later uncovers a Volkswagen Beetle... presumably just because the creators already had an HO scene set in a car that they wanted to use.  The Frankenstein mythos is predictably abused as well.  The original book is completely lost, and the game refers more to the various film adaptations, but with Igor the lab assistant transformed from a deformed wretch into a power-mad nobleman with a penchant for moustache-twirling villainous monologues.
This might satisfy the itch to play an HO game, but there are plenty of superior options out there.

When I first fought my way to the Nidhogg, I was in utter amazement. Two people fencing with each other in a realm of nothing but possibility with crisp, definitive animation and the most simplistic looking characters one could ever have built, one yellow, one orange. The only thing the game was missing was an effective and useful matchmaking system with proper netcode. Yeah, playing online with your friends was damn near impossible, but, for local play, Nidhogg is king.
Nidhogg was simple, if you start on the left, move all the way to the right through multiple screens while fending off attacks from the man on the right, or, if you’re on the right, move all the way to the left through multiple screens while fending off attacks from the man on the left. It’s tug of war with swords, and you have to score a kill to advance through screens. SUPER basic, but very fun.
So, how does one make something objectively less fun by adding to it? I have two major reasons.
1.
There’s nothing really wrong with adding new options to a game, provided you can turn them off. The major issue with Nidhogg 2’s weapon system is that every time you respawn, you respawn with a new weapon in your hands, starting with the original rapier, then a broadsword, a dagger, and finally a bow & arrow.
None of this by itself would be a huge issue if they were useful in any way except the broadsword.
f we got to choose our weapon of choice at the beginning of the round, that would be cool, or, while respawning, hit a face button to choose a weapon, if you wanted to be able to change it up situationally. Right now, you’re likely to respawn with a bow & arrow while your opponent is running as fast as possible towards you and can gut you before you can even fire a shot.
2.
I actually really enjoy the level design of the second game, sure, there are moving platforms and stuff like that, but, there was in the first game too. Heck, it’s all graphically coherent and looks decent, but, where it really fails in my mind is that everything looks goofy, and so when you get to the end and get eaten by a giant worm, it’s just… expected at that point. It’s like hearing a joke but already knowing the punchline. The game before looked like something potentially serious and you’re fighting over who gets eaten by a giant worm. I know, it’s nothing spectacular or amazing, but it was so surprising the first time I played. Everything is so cartoony in the second game that it’s missing the major “wow” factor it had the first time – and, I’m not talking about it being unexpected (as it was the first time I played Nidhogg), I just mean, that it so clearly changes the fundamentals of the world our characters our dueling in. Even the character animations feel more goofy now. They camped up the game that seems like the original was unintentionally campy.
All in all, Nidhogg 2 is NOT a bad game, it’s really quite fun. The updated netcode is a work of art, and on my dollar store internet, even I could fight with randoms from across planet earth who just wanted to stab me and get eaten first. If they update the weapon system somehow, letting you choose what weapons you want before a round starts, or possibly adding an option for just a duel with single weapons, that would be amazing.
It won’t ever be the Nidhogg 2 I hoped it was going to be, but, it’s clever and fun, and still a fun game in it’s own right, it just feels less when they’ve added so much more.
Graphically, the game is much different. It’s a clever style, but it doesn’t feel Nidhogg to me. I understand that telling an artist his graphics aren’t what my mind imagined in his first game is entirely wrong, and enjoyment of graphics are nothing if not subjective (except when it comes to cluttered Uis, cheaply thrown together assets with different resolutions, and other obvious problems) but, there are plenty of people who agree with that opinion. If you like the new artwork, support this guy. If you like the new weapons, support this guy. Heck, if you like Nidhogg 1, leave a message in the comments on his game that even though you disagree with the direction Nidhogg 2 went in, you want to support him because you were a fan of the first game, don’t let me detract from you supporting an indie developer because I disagree with the direction he went with his game.
I am just not a huge fan of Nidhogg 2’s gameplay or graphic style in general when compared to Nidhogg 1. Dive kicks knock both players down. No cartwheel thrusts. All of the old, effective strategies are removed and you’re stuck holding a bow and arrow that makes you feel like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.

Rather unique playstyle and very unique game idea. Real time strategy base builder, the game is restricted to two maps that change throughout the storyline. Micromanage every inch of your evil lair in combination with uncontrolled simulated minions, as well as tourists who tend to wander in the wrong places and forces of justice from 5 different world powers that send out varied agents that disrupt your activities.
Full of witty and occasionally dark humor this game offers a very fresh experience not often available in the gaming market. Although following a linear progression to 'World Domination' the game is suprisingly flexible, as your Evil lair is extremely customizeable ranging from the creation of room shapes, varied room types based on function, large and varied asortment of equipment to use for each function as well as the ability to demonlish sections and start over allows for the creation of large open areas full of equipment or snakey corridors ful of small very specific cubicles. Combine that with varied minions, stolen objects, Agents of Justice, Henchmen and traps creates for a very replayable expereince despite the linear storyline. The downside however is that it is an older game from a smaller studio reflected in some limitations as well as the very occasional bugs.

You'll have a blast killing your friends while breaking down doors, throwing people through windows, and using Jason's many supernatural abilities to scare people and keep them on their toes. I'm not much a writer these days so this isn't going to be the most polished review but I'll try to be to the point.
Negative reviews tend to be by people who lack an understanding of how much work is required to make a good game and are clueless about the difference between development stage and finished product or by people who don't care enough to research the games they review. Not every negative review is going to be inept and I respect someone's right not to like a game.
While this game has problems they do not make this game a bad one. There are bugs (some brand new) that pop up, some of which are extremely annoying but not game breaking. Most guns do real damage in the game. While some guns need some tweaking (being more accurate than their real world counterparts) I hesitate to say any gun is truly OP. The premium guns are not P2W (extra ammo in a clip being the very minor exception). IMO all guns should be killers. So if anything, some guns are under powered. Pistol seem a bit weak, for instance.
The maps are mostly just the right size for P2P shooter.  They should create a spawn zone so that bullets cannot do damage either coming in or going out of the protected zone.  At least they have a small safety period when you spawn so you can't be shot. It's my opinion that a team that works together can defend the spawn and push the enemy back. Hence the importance of squads and voip in this game.
After reading up on the future plans for this game I must say that the devs are very thoughtful about what they are trying to do. I hope they get around to improving the graphics in this game as it looks like an older game sometimes. I"m sure it's on their minds. They really seem care about this game and the people who play it. They also respond to my support tickets when a response is warranted.  I'm amazed at how patient they are with angry players, sometimes diffusing a player's anger with polite and honest answers.
As for hacks and cheats, every well known MP game is going to be under attack. I've personally seen at least one that I'm certain of.  VG doesn't make you jump thru hoops to report problem players; they consider reports seriously and take care of the offenders quickly, unlike some Devs who take weeks or months (if at all) to deal with reported cheaters and other problem players. I've experienced this personally.

This game is an absolute classic and is still just as good as ever. I would fully recommend this to anyone who is interested in Turn-Based Strategy, and have played the original X-COM games or older Turn-Based games. This is not for those who don't like difficulty or challenge in their video games, and it sure in Hell isn't for those who don't like older games.
Jagged Alliance Gold is intuitive and has better design and features than 99% of games that are made today. Things like unit exhaustion, explosives turning out to be duds or not going off when they're supposed to, and mercenaries who not only have certain strengths and weaknesses outside of stats, but have their own personalities and will voice their opinion when they feel like. Something as simple as having your band of mercs have their own wants and needs is something that most games two decades later can't achieve with 100x the budget and you really have to ask yourself why that is.
Overall I'd give Jagged Alliance Gold a 10/10. There's a reason why it's considered the Great-Granddaddy of all Turn-Based Strategy, and it still shows even to this day.

I have never really been a person for third-person shooters but I got this game on sale because it looked really good and had good reviews. Overall I am really pleased with my purchase but do not think it is worth the full £22.99, however if you can get this game whilst it is on sale then do, you won't regret it.
First, the story has unexpected twists in it and each mission I have found actually contains a lot of replay-ability, especially for achievement hunters.
Secondly, the shooting mechanic in this game is second to none with Arma 3 being a possible equal for sniping. It allows you to change the difficulty settings with presets or create your own difficulty so you can replay missions on a harder difficulty for that extra little challenge. When enemies hide behind burnt out cars you can still shoot them through the gap in the windows which actually not many games include, the meshes and hit boxes for enemies are amazing
Third, although I have not really played multiplayer due to a slow internet connection the option is there in this game which allows you to pit yourself against friends and fellow players in a bid to see who is the best sniper in the world.
Overall this game is fantastic with good mechanics and well designed missions, however it does have its drawbacks:
-The covering sounds are really obviously made to trigger in the presence of the player, understandeable but it ruins the immersion when you move to a different area but still within hearing range of the other repetitive cover but you can't hear it, just the new one. This isn't too much of a problem but it could be the sound only works as a cover if you are within a certain distance of the source but the sound continues anyway, just to add to the immersion.
-The enemy AI snipers on elite difficulty can apparently see through walls if you are close to a doorway or hole in a wall etc, often if they are facing a different way they can still target you even though there is no physical way they should be able to. I'm all for difficult enemies but it seems a little too hard.
- DLC achievements are frowned upon by many, myself included, but at least the DLC is relatively cheap in comparison to say Dawnguard and Dragonborn for Skyrim.
- The game is pricey if you only play through the once on easy to medium difficulty because you will not get the play time out of it.
In conclusion, I would give this game about 9/10 purely because of a few problems that could be worked out with one or two updates. I would definitely recommend trying the demo first if you don't normally play this style of game, or pick it up on sale.

If there was ever a love letter towards it's fanbase, DARIUSBURST Chronicle Saviours is that towards the Arcade players who have done this type of gaming for nearly 30 years ongoing.
Taito's flagship title, next towards Space Invaders and Bubble Bobble, back in 1987 set the world on fire with it's multi-screen ( 3 in fact! ) set up and large display with vividly colorful planets and massive bosses with destructable parts. Since then the series has evolved in a number of ways and different playing styles, but the astetic of shooting down large robotic fish and water wild life 'swimming' in space has always stuck firm and made it stand out in an ever growing crowd. Fast forward towards 2009, nearly 12 years since the last Darius, G-Darius released, when we would at last return towards the Tuna Sashimi killing spree we all missed, with quite an overhaul at that.
Darius Burst main gameplay trick comes about with the Burst Beam function. By dealing damage and cancling bullets, you build up the Burst Bar, allowing you to use the Burst Beam, a powerful tool that can ether travel with your ship, or you can deploy it at a location and angle of your choice to fire and cut down waves of foes or null streams of bullets. With this in mind, the game has little fear in tossing foes at every angle and side of you, forcing you to learn how to make the best use of this tool both to shoot them all down, and to keep yourself alive doing the large scale boss battles, that return in full force.
Now, 6 years later after a number of revisions, arcade releases and content updates, we now stand at Darius Burst Chronicle Saviours and it's such a jam packed package it's hard to find any single point to begin. For starters, this release comes with the Arcade release of the game, Another Chronicle, in perfect emulation. Another Chronicle worked by unlocking new ships and features based on both playtime, and success rating of people playing on it, inclduing in its  Chronicle mode, a large network of 'planet' like hubs, each one with a massive assortment of challenges and objectives that would take any single person a lifetime to obtain, but was made to be worked on as a group. For the steam release, this carrys over with the 'Arcade Cabnet' feature, 180 emulated Online cabnits via steam allow you to pick one and work on these yourself JUST as if you where in the arcades! Of course you can always pick one of the one's already completed, and see how the game is with everything unlocked as well just the same.
On the note of unlockables, this game offers 8 different ships to make use of, 4 of them made just for Darius Burst, while the other 4 are outright callbacks towards the previous games, being Darius, Darius II/Twin, Darius Gaiden, and G-Darius. Each one has thier shot type and weapons based off of their title gameplay ( outside of the G-Darius, that loses the Capture system in place for earning Options, and using those for the Alpha Beam ) and offers an utterly freash experance towards the game as a result. It's also wonderful to be able to use the older styles in a newer setting, letting oldschool fans take great glee in using fan favs.
With that, comes the real killer app of this package, Chronicle Saviours mode. This mode alone is the thing that is the real love letter, the thing that wishes to go "Thank you for sticking with us for so long." In essance, it's Darius Burst answer towards a 'Story Mode' for a STG, breaking it up into different sigments, each one with it's own assortment of stages and the like, give tell of Darius and it's colony planets fought vs the Belser Army's ever growing and advancing numbers.The real notable part of this is using the noted ships from previous games changes the music towards that as well, more less covers each game's story in some way to at last perhaps reach an ever conclusive ending towards the entire series as a hole. The only other game to give out such a swan song in such way was R-Type Final.
Overall, this package is beefy, and if you've ever loved the series in the past, it's about time to come back and give it's last hurrah a good playing.
