Also the powerups that float across the screen can be grabbed by everyone as long as they get it before it fades.  Other reviewers have touched on gameplay already so I won't get into that.  If you really want to see gameplay, I highly suggest watching some videos - you get a good feel for how the mechanics work and most likely if you think it looks really fun to play just from watching alone, it will be an even better experience when you're the one behind the wheel.
Now, is this worth the pricetag?  I've logged 24 hours so far and that's just from playing AC mode.  I barely touched Chronicle and haven't played EX at all aside from just messing around for a few minutes to see what it was.  There is so much replayability in this game due to the different ships, routes, and modes, that you will be entertained for a very long time.  If you are a min/maxer and/or completionist, I imagine you could easily sink over 100 hours playing this game.  If you love shmups and think this game looks fun, I personally think the price is worth it.  I have sunk much more than $50 playing this game in arcades alone so for me this is a bargain, lol.
As for difficulty, the nice thing about this game is you can personalize your difficulty setting.  There are 3 starting zones (easy, medium, hard) and from there they branch into 2 zones each (easy-bottom and medium-top zones overlap, as do medium-bottom and hard-top), and those into another 2 zones (zones overlap again), etc.
Top zones are always easier than bottoms ones, so it follows that if you always choose the top zone then you are choosing the easiest route, and if you always choose bottom zones then you are choosing the hardest route.  So if you start off in the medium zone but think it's too difficult, at the next zone you can choose the top zone which will bring you back into the easy route.  That being said, I can 1credit this game on the hardest path until the last boss, but I have yet to get past the stage 4 opening boss in ikaruga on the easiest difficulty, lol...

I don't normally do this so I apologize in advanced. I will try to be as nice as possible....
1) Game looks pretty nice, cap ships look cool and at first I thought "wow this is gonna be cool!"
2) Hotas support is a real pain. I don't want to go into too much detail here but it took me hours to setup. I gave up trying honestly cuz I bought this game a few days after release. Now finally today I dedicated another 3 hours to trying to to setup my Hotas. I have CH fighterstick and CH pro throttle. It is SOOOO complicated with about 40 different axis choices and it doesn't sense any axis so you must do this manually. Would be easy without the maybe 15 or so subcategories for axis. I have never seen anything this complicated and I have played many space sims. Feels like they just threw HOTAS support in for us and said "you figure it out!". In the end of a 3 hour setup run I finally stopped trying to designate my throttle and rolls to any axis. I just shut them off and found out how to designate those controls to the keyboard. In other words, old school 90s wing commander style play from here out, Stick and keyboard. Still, I was determined to give this an honest try.
3) Sounds Really rough here. When overheating you hear a loud "ping!". Thought I could turn that effect down by turning sound fx down and leaving music and master volume up but nope. Just turns down other sounds but that damn ping sound stays loud as hell! The weapon sounds are also really bad here. No real gun sounds and no real missile sounds. One good thing I will say is the voice acting is pretty cool. Well done in that department.
4) Gameplay. Really simple, boring fighting. Made it 10 missions in. Only way you can tell you are being attacked is a red color in the corner of your ship. No feel of impact or sound effects to help you know. Also on the flipside it's hard as hell to tell you are hitting the enemy ship other than they visually take damage. Even after all the HOTAS nightmares the joystick randomly rolls while making fast movements. The CH Fighterstick CANNOT ROLL so this is a software problem with the game. This never happened in any space sims I ever played before. Very annoying. Also everytime to fire your guns the whole screen blurs up and shakes like crazy. Not cool man....
5) Summary Guys, I thank you for trying to make a fun single player space combat game. I miss these types of games dearly as a big fan of the glory days of Wing Commander, Freespace, X Wing and Tie Fighter. However, this time...mission not accomplished. I am very sorry to write a review like this. But the fact that I paid money for this game is a damn shame. I have played fan made mods of Wing Commander and Freespace games that are honestly 10 times as good as this. Those were made by non pros. Examples would be Wing Commander Saga, Wing Commander Standoff, and about a dozen Freespace mods. I do however hope you guys try again sometime soon. But you need to take your time and make a good game. Make the game interesting. Instead of just checkpoints all the time give us real destinations. The guns need to feel like guns. Missles need to be improved greatly. The art style you guys used was awesome. IT LOOKS SWEET!! Also, next time you build a space combat game, make it with the HOTAS in mind from the beginning. Don't just tack in on after the fact. Space combat games died with Freelancer and I think a big part of that was the fact that this is the beginning of mouse space combat games. Alright, that's all I have to say. Once again, I'm really sorry to the creators if this sounds harsh......but it's all the truth. I respect you a lot for trying but this has been a terrible gaming experience for me.

- Okay this ones pretty big: I REALLY wanted sirens. Everytime I turned on a car light strip-thing I wished for sound. And so I turned to a somewhat shady mod called the "Siren and Horn Mod AND MORE" to get the sounds for the sirens. Here's what happened: I installed the mod (was pretty hard to install, not usual, as mod installations are easy; just drop the zip into the BeamNG.drive folder in your documents), and then I hoped. When I spawned a vehicle, it would say "Fatal vehicle error. Please respawn the vehicle." Well, long story short, the mod broke my game. The game prompted me to file a support ticket, which I did, even with the knowlege the devolopers can't help with mods. So, they wrote back to me and, as I had expected, said they couldn't help. The next day, I opened my game (I had to uninstall and reinstall), and low and behold, and update was prompted. I clicked install, waited and started to play the game. I got in a cop car, turned on the lights, pressed the key for the lights again (to turn it off), and I heard a siren sound. Yep, they added a siren after I had filed a support ticket. Basicly what I'm trying to say is, EXCELLENT support.
- Easy mod installation (as I said above)
CONS:
- I wish there was a steam workshop
-Driving is hard, but it's better with a controller
OVERALL:
Great game, and you should totally get it.

So, I got this game from a friend a while ago, and I decided to write my first review on this one.

At the beginning I found this game amazing. I enjoyed it a lot, even if it was a bit boring sometimes. You had to walk ages and ages to find something, most of the time you'd just starve or die of thirst because lakes and eatable plants/other dinosaurs were so far away.
But then, all of a sudden, the devs decided to go nuts and completely wrecked the cool concept of this game. They removed the sandbox setting.
Now you have to play for hours and hours to be the dinosaur you want to be. And that is simply not fun. The devs themselves don't seem to care for their community at all. They're just doing their thing, even if their players clearly don't like it. I have to say, the devs made a good job at coming up with this game, they really try to maintain it well and keep it updated, but they fail. Heavily.
The game also seems to not work for a lot of people, I myself have had problems with it with a pc that has quite a bit more than the recommended specs say. And the devs simply don't seem to care or be able to fix it. Welp. It's their problem in the end if they lose all of their community.
So, to sum it all up:
~Pro~
- graphics
- dinosaurs!!
- cool animations
- cool sound design
- nice idea overall
~contra~
- the devs
- bad spawn points
- no sandbox (hasn't been readded afaik, haven't been playing for a while)
- painfully slow paced and boring at the beginning
- you can die a lot
- insanely buggy and glitchy at times
- updates always seem to bring more problems
~CONCLUSION~

Long story short: addictive shooter with great immersion. At this point, repetitive and somehow frustrating. There's a very good idea behind the game, but it has to be deeply improved. Nice experience for a couple of hours. Ridiculously cheap if you try to feel a S.T.A.L.K.E.R experience: this is a different game.
Pros:
-Addictive. I don't know what it is, but it gets you coming back. Controls feel nice. Shooting is good. You want to keep playing, getting better gear, learning every piece of the map and trying different approaches. Killing enemies feels very satisfying.
-Fast gameplay. Don't expect to plan thorough tactics here. If you go with a team and microphone, level design allows a certain degree of it. But if you play every now and then, you have to use the map to your advantage and be in constant motion. Kill, move, hide, run, kill, flank, etc. Overall, terrific feeling: gets you focused.
-Beautiful art design, fantastic immersion. It is the strongest virtue of the game. For some people like me —even though we're aware this is not a S.T.A.L.K.E.R game— due to the excellent sound design, aesthetics and decrepit environments, sometimes you feel nostalgia. It evokes GSC franchise. And for those who don't played the S.T.A.L.K.E.R franchise, Survarium simply feels different, surrounding, alive. Anomalies and devastated post-apocaliptic scenarios are well-executed and depicted.
-Free to play. Think about it. Again. Feels good, right?
Cons:
-Crashes. Very common. VG fixes problems with every patch, buy unfortunately, this is not the common case. Maybe once a month. They work slowly given their many limitations as a small company. Yesterday, for instance, I couldn't play for a whole match. Crashed after five minutes and kept throwing me to the desktop. It gets irritating when you just want to play a quick game.
-Non satisfying loot system. This is very personal —as the rest of the review, anyways— but I feel it doesn't keep you hooked. I can play 5 hours in a row on my free days and don't get anything interesting nor useful. Sometimes, you think playing the game is a  vast waste of time, since you are expecting some sort of reward, especially when you make a good match score. Sadly, the chances that you get a helpful weapon or armor are very, very low.
-Balancing matches. This is totally ♥♥♥♥ed up —and pardon me the expression—. I've recently read VK are working on it. Should be better addressed by next patch. At this point, you get involved in matches where people are too good or too bad. You feel utterly♥♥♥♥♥♥♥or under the skin of a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ depending on the case. It gets unspeakably irritating when you cannot enjoy the experience because of campers. Sometimes you can't even walk out of your base —even with the protection bonus they give you for a couple of seconds— without dying. I guess everyone has a different way of enjoying a game, but for me, it ruins the immersion and experience. I like players with skill, killing me legitimately. It's way more fun in the opponents recognition than just blocking your base and don't let you play.
-Updates. I personally know how harsh it is to work without resources or as a small team. Every decision counts and looks critical. I get it. And it is very frustrating because there are awesome ideas amongst people, but funds don't allow neither the time nor the possibility to make them all real. That said, they really have to put effort in major changes. They have to bring a colossal patch with huge improvements and additions. Make community feel they are going forward, although slowly. I'll wait more if needed be, but take a big step and make some noise. I really want this game to work and VK to have a great life as developers. For me that is For Honor in a nutshell. The game has so much potential. But I feel like peer to peer connection has completely destroyed the game. This was my first game on Steam. I even pre ordered it. But I feel like Ubi has cheated us again. The betas were even more stable than the full game (I played both of the betas). Micro transactions are kind of like the final killing blow. Not only that but also you have to buy steel packs to activate your season pass (My friend used it. His season pass was activated just after buying a steel pack). This goes the basic faults of the game
Single player: Though the single player is more of a complimentary to the multiplayer, I feel like they could've done something more with this. Single player was really boring. There was not any plot twist in there. There was almost nothing in the single player. "Just go and kill some dude"-this kind of stuff. They did not even bother to give the playable characters their own name let alone give their own unique faces (The Raider's face was a bit showed but that did not satisfy me). There was not any backstory of Apollyon. We don't know why she started this war and why she craves it so much. There was not any defining or unique moments in the game. Even the speaking of the characters seemed funny. For example when the raider confronts the female Berserker, it seemed like she was talking in slow motion. Another example is the fight between the Raider and General Tong or something (I don't really remember his name. He is the Orochi with the golden outfit). He kept saying continuously "You are a raider. Legendary!" This was really irritating. I loved the horse race and the elephant mission in the game. But that's just it. More irritating is that they restricted the game size to 31 GB on release. They really should've added more content in the single player. There wasn't even any background music. Just a cold dead game.
Multiplayer: This game is more of a muliplayer based game. So the multiplayer experience of this game is more refined and enjoyable than the single player. The duels and fights are so much tense! I mean... MAN! I love this game's multiplayer! Timing is so crucial! It really gets your heart pumping. Buuuut.... "Advanced" peer to peer has left this game completely broken. There are almost constant network errors. They kick you out of multiplayer sessions if your internet can't cope up with other people's internet. And the most annoying problem is that players just kind of teleports behind you all on a sudden. Because of peer to peer connection. If your internet's connection is poor, you have 0% chance of surviving the multiplayer. No dedicated servers. Greedy Ubi just keeps cheating us again and again.

Where to begin with this... well, for starters "Everyday Shooter" isn't.  The basic gameplay mechanic is similar to the twin-stick shooting mayhem of Geometry Wars, but the devil is in the details.  Each level is different from the last and part of the game is learning how the rules permutate as you go.  Shooting certain things allows you to make progress, others build up point multipliers, and others cause chain reactions which release mass tokens that can buy game upgrades.  The upgrade system is pretty neat in that it could almost be called "buying cheats" but not really since the upgrades help to give you better access to the later levels rather than forcing you to grind your way through the early parts if you're tired of them.  In addition to all this you have an interactive musical score with guitar effects that are synchronized with the onscreen action providing an amusing jolt to your activity.  The visuals are pretty abstract and trippy.  A little slight, but fun.  I like it.

Writing this review having never played any other Frictional Games© video game, nothing said here will be weighed against
to which
is often compared.
As I first began to play
, I was initially put off by the rudimentary graphics and cartoonish art style it often employed (notibly in regards to pictures within the game), but I came to be mesmerized with the game's plot.  The writers at Frictional Games© managed to create an effective and well-told story regarding philosophical questions about identity and consciousness, as well as one of the best video game endings I've ever played.
does a good job in allowing the player to step into the protagonist Simon Jarrett, having him learn about the story alongside the player, often pontificating about the twists that the plot takes.  With this said, the game features one major shortcoming in immersion, and that's it's inability to allow the player to come to their own moral conclusions about events which unfold.
The most glaring issue which stood out with
was it being released by a software developer which has carved a niche for itself within the survival-horror genre.

might have been improved if it did away with it's horror element and focused instead on the exploring and puzzle-solving.
Regardless of the game's shortcomings, it's easily one of the best games I've played in the past few years, and it's plot and attention to detail should be commended.

Let me tell you a story.
The Terran Empire had been expanding for thousands of years, and met an empire that surpassed even theirs. With nearly every planet colonized, it was only a matter of time until a war for galactic domination ensued. The Terran Empire had one advantage: They had developed advanced jump drives that let them move their ships anywhere in the galaxy within seconds. When war was declared, massive alien fleets steamrolled through every system, each fleet equivalent to the entire Terran navy. The Terrans, using their strategic maneuverability edge, worked to group their whole navy up, and destroy each steamrolling enemy fleet one at a time. That was the plan. However, significant losses after the first battle made the Terran fleet unable to do more than token resistance as their race was exterminated.
So, I reloaded the save.
This time, at war's declaration, the Terrans sacrificed all their systems along their borders, and split up their fleet into dozens of small strike forces. Jumping them all deep all over the enemy empire, they caused havoc, able to destroy multiple systems each in the time it took the steamrollers to take out one. A war of strategic attrition ensued, as it was a race to see who could conquer the other faster in order to gain the technological and economic edge. The tide of battle started to turn in the Terrans favor. A critical system lay in the path of the enemy: A shipyard system, powered by the resources of a hundred worlds, frantically pushing out huge state of the art warships. The system was switched over to defenses, and soon became a fortress bristling with artillery. As the enemy arrived, they were met with fierce railgun and artillery fire, but they pushed in. fleets were scrambled from around the galaxy and hundreds of ships arrived, firing salvoes as they jumped in, and the enemy fleet was vanquished. From then on, the Terrans struck where they chose, and destroyed fleet after enemy fleet, until the galaxy was theirs.
Sound epic? This was my afternoon. Star Ruler is an amazingly rewarding game, where basically anything you can think of can be done with the simple ship creation and AI tools. Huge mining carrier ships producing fleets on their own? check. stick engines and guns on planets and fly them around? check. Create a ship literally the size of the galaxy? check.
Downsides: There are a few reasons why Star Ruler isn't the best game ever. 1) Because there are no galaxy size or ship size or fleet size caps, you can have literally thousands of ships. This requires a powerful computer. For many people this isn't a problem, but it may be for you. 2) The game is basically all macro and very little micro. It doesn't matter so much how your fleets tactically engage the enemy, so much as how many fleets you have and where they are strategically. Again, if you're just looking for macro gameplay, this isn't an issue. 3) The diplomacy is shallow at best, just serving as "the thing that is happening when you aren't at war". If you're playing star ruler you're probably not looking for diplomacy however, so this is probably negligible.
Incredible and deep story, simply a masterpiece!

Hello. Are you interested in buying this game ? Let me tell you about this game. This game is not worth your time and money. This game starts you off as a shepherd (not THE shepherd) and has you trying to woo your girlfriend on some island. This game will then do what any game does to ruin the good mood and send you away on a journey for revenge.
All the story progress in this game is just for the sake of getting your revenge. Remember that, when you slug through the chapters, hoping for a cool story.
This game lets you decide on how to play it by offering you all the options : Melee, Ranged and Magic. The overly simplistic and lame skill-tree requires tough decision making from you. +1% mana and +1% mana regen or rather +1% stamina and +1% stamina regen...or maybe +1% ranged damage and +1% mana regen ? The choices...Eventually you might also reach one of the maybe 10 new skills..I say new, but in the end they just change the skill you already have to something better, like giving you a power bash or letting you combo more attacks...meh.
This game is kinda separated into different hubs, where the actual chapter is being played. As soon as you finish one, you basically move onward to the next hub area. This game is technically an open world game, but you don't have any necessity to ever venture back to the places you've already been to and instead keep following a linear route to your goal. This game sports acceptable environmental graphics, but butt-ugly character models. This game also features some of the most laid back casual combat ever. This game is hardly a challenge on normal difficulty and at least your progress will be steady..combat wise..
This game however does have a major flaw, which will most likely make you quit rather sooner than later :
THIS GAME HAS NO QUEST MARKERS. This game will just tell you to find an item/person in the east/west/north/south of where you accept the quest and then has you run around the place trying to find the item/person without any sort of indication. Even worse, this game often has the habit of only spawning the item/person you are looking for once you accepted the quest to do so. That means you can run all over the map in advance, explore everything possible and then have to do it all over again after accepting some random "HEY, FIND THIS CHEST IN THAT CAVE WHICH NOW EXISTS BUT DIDN'T BEFORE". This game will then commence laughing at you, until you open google after an hour to just look up where the item/person is, that you're looking for.
This game incorporates very boring and bland dialogue as well, which often makes you feel as if you're just playing some random mmo. Nothing in this game will make you feel involved with the world, mostly because the world itself is such a boring, empty yet quite spacy place..still very empty though..too empty even..way too empty..not enemy wise..quite a few enemies...but otherwise very empty.
This game has no redeeming qualities at all. Even the lockpicking system is really irritating with its required timing. This game does allow you to craft, but thats just reading a recipe, press "C" , select the thing and click the "craft" button.
This review is already way too long for this game, so let me tell you once again that this game is really not worth it.
This game, which I have played for 10 hours, is not recommended :P

Why you should buy SR:
Scale: You can play with a 2 system galaxy for a quick and brutal fight, or a 9000+ system galaxy for a epic game.
Customisability: Most ships you're going to be using will be designed by yourself. The ship design system is good. you're not just swapping out weapons on hardpoints, you're designing ships from scratch. You place subsystems, including life support, crew quarters, bridge, power generator, engines, etc on a grid to your liking. Where you place a subsystem matters. Got a big gun at the front? It'll be taking hits first.
There's a wide range of weapons and utility subsystems to research too. Different weapons are good at different things. Raw DPS doesn't always win battles.
Depth: Every planet has its own economy. It's not super deep on a single planet scale, but it's there, and when you consider how many planets there are... You can exploit weaknesses to your advantage. Kill farm planets to starve enemies population.

Key points:
For those of you who are confused by the virtual cabinet system, I'll explain why it exists and how it works. On the actual
arcade game, Chronicle mode progress is stored in the arcade cabinet itself, allowing different players who play on that cabinet to work together to complete and unlock levels as well as compete with each other to see who can complete the most levels. To replicate this experience with the home version of the game, a series of virtual cabinets is provided, and players around the world share these cabinets, each with its own Chronicle mode progress, just as if they were playing on the same physical arcade cabinets. You may either play on the randomly-selected cabinet, or choose any one of the (128 as of this writing) virtual cabinets to play on.
The price tag may seem a bit high even with the large amount of content, but if you're a fan of arcade shmups and have been waiting for something new, this is the game you're looking for.

It has the right level of difficulty, some parts can be easy, some levels and bosses can be tough, its enough to engage you, with only 2 rediculous boss types.
The ships are numerous, about 9 of them, and of those 9, 8 of them are fun There is a good variety there as well. Each ship, though they mostly have pretty similar missiles/bombs, and basic shots, they differ with their burst beam mechanics which is hard to explain in text.
There are a total of 16 different boss types, and each boss type can have 1-3 variants on average, with the exception of the "jaw" boss, which has about 5 variants. Each boss type can be similar or very different from each other, the game manages to stay fresh with this kind of variety.
The level design can range from moving around empty space, to going through enemy bases which requires menuvering through tight spaces. Its kind of odd to explain, but while the game manages to throw a large variety of different levels at you(and sometimes the exact same ones), each level is modular in its design. Expect it to be a little repetative, though the game will always occasionally give you a new level type. In CS mode, each zone is basically a set of levels and bosses, the "area select" screen shot above shows an example, you will have 2 leves, a boss, a level, then the last boss of that zone. there are 185 different zones in CS mode. (possibly more, the more you beat the more you unlock)
It is also worth noting that the game also comes with the Arcade version, Another Chronicle, which if you have duel monitors the game is in ultra wide screen. Well with a sequal announced and after another lengthy divethrough, its time once more to review the game. I will begin with a summary, and progress to a list.
Summary: This is a management game in which you play the titular Evil Genius. You have three choices, a short man who's good at research, a woman who makes your minions never leave you, and a tall man who has "connections". Your biggest goal is to stick humanity a collective new one and ruin most life on the planet in the funniest way possible. You do this by building a base inside a mountain and completing acts of infamy around the world, in order to expand your base and allow you to progress towards your goal. This takes a long time, and the forces of justice will stop at nothing to end your madness, eventually sending several super secret agent stereotypes to kill you. Story aside, your view will be fixed upon your secret base. Naturally you are too luxoriously evil to work yourself so you get minions to do your dirty work for you. There are military, scientific, social, and construction minions who shall aid you, along with some special henchmen who's power matches that of a dozen minions. You use the world map in order to send your minions on missions to get you money and powerful artifacts, naturally your illustrious Evil Genius has not the time to participate on these missions or watch them. Although some of what I said may sound negative, I love the game. It is great fun, but it does have a great deal of grind. If you want a goofy alternative to top down strategy where you get to quote James Bond villans, this is probably your only option, you rather specific tasted fellow. And now, some other points.
#1: Don't mess with traps on your first playthrough. In my experience they cost more than they are worth, both figureatively and literally. Literally as in they cost valuable money, and won't see much use without some in depth thinking and figuratively as in often minions may just step into them. I may be remembering it wrong.
#2: There is a realatively low minion population cap, so don't get 20 of every type of minion.
#3: Henchmen are a very rare comodity, only get the ones that will REALLY work for you.
#4: Don't get to much heat, do this by hypnotizing and distracting agents. Flat out killing them will make the agencies send more, better armed ones. When you get a bunch of nuclear reactors in your power station and an agent sets one off, it will be a poop and a half to deal with.
#5: Tourists are your worst enemey. They are everywhere and will continually raise heat if they manage to get home after seeing your schemes.
#6: Super agents will begin to invade your base after a period of growth. They are invincible unless defeated in a certain way, and they are able to carve a bloody canyon through your minions and henchmen. Only capture and bring them into your base if you have the way to permenantly beat them, if not prepare for canyon carving. Mild spoils ahead, but I'd like to at least give you some context. This is your last chance to exit the review, nothing else is going to be said. I will give you one last chance.

Got this game when it was 97% off, so I only spent $0.16. Good thing too, because it was not as I expected. The game had good reviews, so I expected a more challenging game. More or less my own fault for not checking the game description and tags properly before buying it.
If you want a casual game, as it tagged as one, go for it, it's a nice, very simple game. Otherwise, it's just a point-and-click puzzle game, where the puzzles are not that hard, and where most of the game consist of "find the new key to open this new door". Took me less than  two hours to finish on hard.
Below are the reasons why I didn't like the game.
***Spoiler Alert***
Even though I was playing on hard, by just clicking on some objects to get information about them, you get the answer to the problem directly (e.g: click on object to inspect it - text box appears: "I need to use the crowbar on this.")
"Face terrible monsters", it says. You cannot directly perform a single shred of action against the only monster in this game (not counting the reanimated mouse, which is in a cage, and the reanimated tiger, which you put to sleep in a few clicks). You can find the TOOLS to fight monsters, but all the fighting happens in the cut scenes.
2K resolution is wasted on this game. You don't even see it. You could have designed the same game in the 90s.
On the other hand, considering that's it's an indie game, and not a game developped by a big company, it's very nicely done.
Overall: It's not a masterpiece, but if you have $0.16 to waste, it will entertain you for two hours. Maybe four if you want to get all achievements.

Bit Planet has done some very cool things with this game.
Normally, I would hit the good points first, but I want to get my complaints out of the way.
On the plot side, the characterizations of the different pilots can be pretty cartoony, to the point of things becoming unbelievable. Lieutenants have an alarming tendency to order captains (and even generals) around, and it's done with complete impunity. It was hard for me to suspend my disbelief in that area. Further, there is an outsized amount of profanity used by a particular pilot, and it seems to be gratuitous rather than character establishing. (Maybe it's just me.)
Speaking technically, the game does have some nagging, but mercifully un-fatal bugs. The first is that the Ingress/ hacking loop still delivers invalid codes in some situations. It's incredibly frustrating to select what should be the right code, only to have it fail...and be taking fire from a number of turrets at the same time. Also, there's an occasional graphics glitch where a "sun" overlay gets plastered all over the center of your screen. (The problem can be quickly fixed by selecting a different screen resolution, and then reverting.)
Every once in a while, a rough edge in overall experience design makes a glaring appearance. The most notable of these was a mission where you have to save some transports that are dropping through atmosphere. The success/ fail conditions for the mission are not at all clear at first, although the success condition is so low that I suppose you can shrug your shoulders a bit.
My final negative point is that "jinking" in a tough dogfight doesn't seem to be possible. If an enemy fighter succeeds in getting you "zeroed," you either have afterburners available for escape, or you're in big trouble. The only turning option you have seems to be heading directly toward your attacker, which lets them hammer you several more times before they overshoot. Hopefully, you're not in a crowd.
But the above paragraph leads me into what's really, really good about the game:
Energy management.
Really.
There are lots of other space sims that give you the ability to transfer energy amongst three systems, such as shields, weapons, and afterburner. In every other such game that I've played, that energy management is fairly secondary. In "Battle Of Sol," it's front and center in a very neat and satisfyingly challenging way. Especially when flying the Hades(?), each energy reserve is pretty shallow. You have to keep your head in the ETS game, or you will be in enormous trouble. This lends a nice boost to the tension of combat, especially because the basic dogfighting isn't all that hard.
The criticality of the energy management also helps to create noticeable differentiation between the Hades and the Arrow fighters. Arrows don't let you manage energy transfer manually, and the afterburners are "all or nothing," but the regen time is fast...for two out of three systems. The bugbear you get to wrestle with is that shield regeneration isn't under your control - you have to escape from combat almost entirely if your Arrow gets mangled. This "personality difference" really keeps you on your toes, and is a great way to add variety where a whole bunch of different ships aren't a gameplay option.
Another great choice by the developers is the need to master the "slide" mechanic. In other games, the ability to keep your heading while changing your orientation is handy, if not necessarily required. In this game, you'll either get it or get torn to shreds. Giving thought to your heading and then engaging a slide is the only thing that will keep you effective against gun platforms and capital ships. Once you do get it, you'll feel very much more like an ace pilot, especially since you'll actually be able to do some good.
Another thing I like was the (seeming) overall homage to the reimagined "Battlestar Galactica." The UCS missions often feature percussion-heavy music that would fit right in with BSG, and the Hades guns seem to behave - and sound - very much like what you would find on a Colonial Viper. Maybe this was all intentional, and maybe it wasn't...but it's fun either way, and made me smile.
Bit Planet has really done some fine work here, and I think they could build a real challenger to Wing Commander and Freespace if they keep iterating and extending what they've got already. This particular game isn't an instant classic, mosty because it's not deep enough for that, but the seeds do seem to be there.

I would love to recommend this game. I personally found this game really fun... when I had the time to dedicate to playing it.
The developers have the right to design what they want, and prioritise what they want. From time to time, these developments fall in line with what players suggest, ask for or point out would be useful. Other times, they seem to be a thousand miles off base. But arguably the worst part, I find, is the attitude I've seen. There is an attitude of entitlement that feels unnecessarily aggressive, and in turn it's bred a horrible attitude throughout the player base too, making this one of the most divisive games I've ever seen.
And
is why I can't recommend this game.
I can't in good conscience recommend a game that has the sandbox mode removed, and when people ask for it to return (because not all of us can work at home and dedicate several
every day to progress just one or two dinosaur stages, only to wind up losing it every time servers need to reset or every time that we die) there is an overtone of threat from the developers themselves. "Shut up or it's never coming back." This, in turn, then leads the playerbase to be equally split - those who continue to point out that we
don't have time for such an extreme progression system but
the survival aspect of the game and
would love to play - and those who tell people to effectively sod off and find a different game if they don't like the survival system.
Here's the thing: I love the survival aspect of this game. I adore it. I
to love the notion of a progression system. But it has been made incredibly obvious that the progression system will
work out for me, with my time schedule. I won't ever reach a top tier dinosaur (not that I particularly want to, to be honest) and I'll be lucky to enjoy mid-tier dinosaurs for any length of time. And to clarify: I've never asked for the sandbox to come back, and I appreciate that the devs need people to play the progression system so they can test it.
But the
of the developers, and in turn the attitude it has bred in players, is ultimately what seals my non-recommendation for me. I can't recommend a game where the developing team behind it has an attitude of "Sod off" and they let that same attitude run rampant in their playerbase, because then they don't have to look like the guilty party by saying it themselves any more. I don't want to recommend a game where it's so easy to die and lose the progression you work hard for because important systems - like a scent system to help guide players to water in maps where there are
landmarks - and people will write off your critique of the system as you being some "carebear baby who can't play survival" when the reality is that, mechanically, the game is lacking and the odds stacked against you.
I want to recommend this game. I want to be able to change this review one day and say that the proper mechanics exist, that the progression system isn't so
because of several other missing mechanics that make survival so hard. I want to be able to say that the developers listen, take suggestions and regard feedback with a level head. Maybe one day, I'll be able to. But right now, I certainly can't, and as much as I want to love Isle, I can't recommend it to any who would be interested in purchasing it. Unless you enjoy grinds more frustrating than Korean MMOs that take just as long - except with the added bonus of losing all the progress you ever made.

EDIT 8/13/15: After this latest update (.30), I can't help but say I've almost entirely lost faith in this game. In one patch we went from a decent game with plenty of potential, to "COD with health kits". So yeah, I think I'm leaving my recommendation status at "no" until they get this game sorted out.
I'm honestly on the fence about this one, because it has some really fun moments, and then it has some really, really bad moments. I mean, I just got an Uzi from a post-game loot drop, and it said it was in poor condition and I had to fix. Guess what it said after I paid the 500 ruble fee? I have to wait TWELVE hours before it's fixed. I'm still waiting as I type this (I can't attach a screenshot, so you're gonna have to take my word for it). But seriously now? This is literally iPhone game tier bullcrap, and I really hope there aren't any more inconvenient surprises waiting for me down the road, like watching a guy in premium armor tank a 7.62 to the chest (oh wait, that already happened. On several occasions).
But for all the angering moments that this game has, it can be SUPER exciting, trust me. One of my highlights from today was when I was playing a match of research on Bridge. We were losing initially, but I managed to get a lucky frag onto point B and got a triple kill with it, then managed to gun down 2 other dudes with my Kiparis, eventually leading to a victory for us. If that's not the tightest thing you've ever seen then get the hell out of my face. Unfortunately, the North American servers are down at the moment, meaning that my/your gameplay is gonna be rather inconsistent if you live in the US of A. But again, it's really worth the price of $0.00. Oh, and speaking of pricing, I have to admit that the graphics look STELLAR. I can run the game at a silky smooth 60 FPS on ultra with no stutters, CTDs, or even general bugs. That's pretty impressive for a F2P game that's been in Steam EA for a month.
Character customization is a really neat touch. Currently my main loadout is a WW2 Russian soldier, complete with Paratrooper helmet, leather jacket, and Moist Nugget. Speaking of moist nuggets, the guns in this game sound D-O-P-E. Better than Insurgency, even. They sound incredibly loud and incredibly aggressive, like you feel like you can take down a jet with your Mosin. Definitely not something I was expecting out of an F2P, especially considering that the guns in Rainbow Six Siege (a $60 AAA game) sound like airsoft guns.
As far as content goes, there's a wealth of (mostly Eastern European) guns, 2 or 3 maps, and 3 game modes. There's TDM (do I seriously have to explain this one?), Battery Retrieval (like Blood Money from Battlefield Hardline, but with batteries), and Research (just like Control Points from TF2). You can upgrade your guns by giving them stat boosts (no silencers and scopes, unfortunately, not unless you're using a sniper rifle), as well as get various decals for your clothing.
Coming back to the problems I initially spoke of at the top, this game can feel rather P2W at times. Yes, it's a low budget Ukrainian developer, but that's hardly an excuse, because it's everywhere. Want to your repair your gun? That'll be $1, unless you're fine with waiting half a day. Want to get an extra loadout slot? That'll be $.50 a day for premium. You want an SMG that doesn't fire egregiously slowly? Well, you can pony up $5 now for a decent premium gun, or you can grind for 50 more hours until you rank up enough to buy one. No hurry. Not to mention that the Steam DLC packs have atrocious pricing. $25 for 2 guns, some goodies, and $10 worth of gold? Bootyful. $50 for 3 guns, $15 worth of gold, and some goodies? FULL JEWISH.
If you're looking for a free game that looks good, sounds good, and plays good, then I honestly think there is some enjoyment to be had in Survarium. Currently there's only PVP modes, but the devs promise free roam, PVE, and more. Still, the wallet bait is strong with this one, and frankly the current lack of American servers is a bit of a chub killer. But hey, if you want high quality shooting, why not?

Hook is a relatively simple and especially cheap puzzle game. It uses basic "electric current" mechanics to move gates around in order to complete the level. As the game progresses on, the levels get harder to complete, along with introductions to movable joints. It puts a new spin on the classic pipe games, where you have to direct a flow of some liquid to an ending point, by removing the ending point all together, and replacing it with the disolving gates and wires that make up the level.
While for only 50 levels, and one achievement, .99 USD, is a relatively good price for a game that may take multiple hours to complete. The games graphics and sounds are appealing and almost trance-like. The gameplay mechanics is certainly an orginal twist on the aforementioned pipe games, which in all is relatively simple. However, the game is increasingly complex, as the levels progress, making you complete it in a determined amount of steps. The only limiting factor is the amount of lives that you have, which reset after each level.
If you can't complete the game in one sitting, it automatically picks up where you left off upon relaunch. The game defenitly is well-polished off, however, I would like to see more levels added, especially as once you complete the game, their is no additional gratification that can be achieved.
So in all, I would personally rate this game 8/10, due to the disappointing lack of extra-content after you complete the game.

A simple relaxing puzzle game. Each stage presents you with a series of "hooks", and each hook is connected to a button, which retracts the hook it's connected to when clicked. The goal is to clear the board by retracting all the hooks. The trick is though, that if a hook hits another hook while it's retracting, it stops, and you have to start all over. The challenge lies in figuring out what order to retract the hooks.
The game starts out simple enough, with only buttons and hooks, so all you have to do is press the correct buttons. However, then they start throwing curve balls, such as rotating connectors that change which hooks are connecting to which buttons, buttons that connect to more than one hook and other complications. Eventually, the game turns into a twisted form of jenga where not only are you trying to figure out which hook to retract, but also trying to make sure that you aren't retracting any other hooks.
The game is simple to pick up. There are no instructions, so you're expected to learn new mechanics as they appear (think Portal, except without naration by a murderous AI). However, it's easy to intuit what everything does.
The only real gripe I have about this game is that it's short. You can clear through all the stages in about an hour. I kinda wish there were more stages to play because this game was so fun. If you're looking for a short puzzle game to fill the hour though, I highly recomend this game.

Firstly I am a big fan of Supergiant Games and this one is no exception. Pyre is very different to their other games, it dares to differentiate and does it perfectly. If you were waiting for a new Bastion this is not it.
Focusing heavily on text based story telling you can experience a wide variety of diverse character that you will eventually begin to care. There is a lot of reading in this game if you don't like reading then I would suggest having a look at the core game-play namely the Rites.
The Rites is a 3 vs 3 battle arena where you take the characters that join your party in the story mode and battle them against different factions that you meet in the game. The object of the Rite is to douse the Pyre (Fire Pit) of the enemy by dunking an energy orb into it by either throwing it or jumping your character with it into the flames.
Every character faction you meet has different abilities that can be used in the Rites which compliments a wide variety of play styles. From fast moving and big slow moving characters to even flying characters.
Pyre is a game you really should experience for yourself, if you are looking for something truly innovative this year.

TL:DR – Did you like Freespace? Do you like or even prefer narrative based space combat games? Do you understand that a team of 6 developers are not going to give you the experience of a AAA game? If you’ve just answered yes to those questions you will get something out of the around 5 hours of campaign available in this game.
I felt compelled to write a review on The Battle of Sol. At the time of writing it is sitting with a mixed rating and that seems rather unfair IMO. I’ll be honest, there are so many games on Steam that if a game has a mixed rating or less I very rarely add it to my account, even if I got it in a bundle, and I definitely wouldn’t buy it. Such is the nature of a swamped marketplace. For this game that makes me a little sad that others almost certainly take a similar life’s too short approach and will be skipping this. There are so few games in the narrative space combat genre and this game is a decent game in its own right.
First to what this isn’t, this isn’t indie Star Citizen or indie Elite, there is no open world. If you ever played Freespace that is the most similar experience, all be it stripped down in many ways, it is an indie game after all. It is a narrative experience played out over a series of combat missions, if that doesn’t appeal then this game probably isn’t for you. If you’re like me and grew up playing Freespace and its sequel and loved them, then there is something for you hear.
I’m just going to reiterate, this is indie Freespace, be under no illusions of that. Freespace may have been years ago but the golden age of Interplay was created with a sizeable budget and development team at that time. Technology may have moved on but the dev team appears to be only 6 in size for this game which is not going to create the content equivalent to a AAA title even many years later.
The story is ok, certainly not ground-breaking but not appalling. The acting isn’t going to win awards but it’s not annoying either, to be fair I’ve heard a lot worse in games with much higher budgets. It’s not short IMO for an indie narrative game, but neither is it that long, you can complete it in around 5 hours if you are playing at a challenging setting. The missions range from great to ok, for me the game started strongly after the tutorial but tailed away towards the end as the focus was taken off dogfighting, which was a mistake IMO. You only get to fly two fighters, you don’t get to choose your weapon load out and most dogfighting you generally rely on guns anyway which is fine by me. However the controls are decent and again should be familiar to anyone who liked Freespace, just with less options for management, although you do get to give orders to wingmen at times. It plays fine with a 360 controller if, like me, you no longer bother getting the flightstick out for casual games, but I’m lead to believe there is joystick support. The graphics are ok and at 144 FPS maxed out it looks good enough but nothing special, it certainly won’t be giving Star Citizen any headaches in the art department, but luckily it’s a genre that doesn’t need awesome graphics to succeed. There is the option to replay any mission from the menu once you have unlocked it in the campaign and a number of achievements to unlock if you are that way inclined.
The Devs are very active with little fixes and very responsive to bugs and issues. My one major criticism would be that it seems to have left early access slightly too early. The devs were literally patching bugs as I played, but you can now play the game from start to finish without encountering a major game breaking bug and I saw very little glitches or minor bugs.
If you don’t go in expecting AAA quality there is a lot of enjoyment to be had from the around 5 hours of campaign. If you are a genre fan you should pick this up, if you’re not a genre fan it is still a fun game and better than others I have played on Steam with much higher review scores. If it’s in a bundle it’s a no brainer.

Evil genius puts you in the position of the leader of an emerging evil organisation - an Evil Genius. You start with money and basic rooms to start your fledgling base, and will gradually gain access to more rooms and minions as you carry out missions.
Pros -
- The game is relatively easy to learn, with a quick tutorial to show you the basics, as well as a detailed glossary for every room and item.
- The game is challenging enough to almost always keep you occurpied and thinking.
- There is quite a bit of detail in the game, especially in minion animation and such.
- Agent AI is acceptable, with them snooping around your entire base, unless you stop them with traps.
- The game visual and audio assets are quite nice. The terrain is quite low-res and undetailed, but the models look colourful. Audio is also acceptable. Overall, aesthetically, pretty good for 2004.
Cons -
- The game is very slow, and requires you to play for hours if you want to complete it. This is nice for some people, but boring for others, and you can sometimes be waiting for minutes to get funds so you can build something. There is also no time speed setting.
- Although the game has enough features to make it fun, I feel that there could be more. There are only two ways of making money - The world domination screen, where you send out minions to provinces and tell them to steal, and stealing from tourists (something I haven't been able to figure out yet).
- Pathfinding for the minions is mediocre. You will often find groups of 3 or 4 just standing by a door for a few seconds before continuing on their way.
- Revising your base design to fit new rooms closer ot the entrace, for example, can be difficult. For a new player, who doesn't know what rooms they will get later may fill up any space, then have to destroy rooms/make rooms smaller etc. The problem is that building/removing/destroying rooms and objects takes time, which can be detrimental if your base is crawling with enemy agents.
Despite the cons, I still find this game enjoyable.

As a long serving Shmup fan, I was flabbergasted to see not only a PC conversion of DB:CS, but also in the depth of the content specifically designed for home users, and a stunning arcade conversion too.
The visuals are crisp and, in my opinion, sensational. Smoothness without fault, it just feels like this has been nurtured and cared for on build and post release. Indeed, good to see fixes for the PC edition coming regularly and little updates here and there; another sign this is a product that is deeply loved by the developers. Having the 32:9 display is a great feature too and is still impressive and imposing on a single screen of decent size in arcade mode.
Indeed, when going into the big game content and playing the massive story mode, the resolution fills the screen - and comes as quite a shock (unless you're fortunate enough to actually have 2 x 16:9 displays at work - which are natively catered for as well, don't you know!). Awesome.
As a result, it is a game that should be loved by players too. Side scrolling shooters don't come along with this scale of content and abundance of quality often (if at all, and particularly on PC).
Sound is also truly fantastic; do yourselves a favour and treat yourself to a listen at high volume, with a serious sound system. Incredible quality, music and sound effects abound; just the initial menu ambience is enough to get the pulse racing before jumping in to a game with some exquisite soundtracks, great effects only to have your seat soiled by the WOAH! BOSS COMING WARNING SOUND!!! Dramatic in style, dazzling in quality, beautifully paced and executed. A crowning achievement.
DB:CS is a truly sensational experience for one; chaotic, tactical and exciting in local multiplayer as well (up to 4!). Different ships provide different abilities, plenty to suit all sorts of players with pickups that need careful consideration in places too. Tactical play on pickups for multiplayer scenarios is required as there is a finite time limit on each pickup once the first player collects. Again, an extra dimension to a challenging game and format.
Really great fun, excellent difficulty curve too and with a great swathe of bosses and enemy patterns, this is a game that should be picked up and loved - and I, for one, absolutely love it.
Simply put, I can't recommend it enough. Now, I'm just going to have one more go...

The presentation is top-notch. Transitions, particles, animations, models are all greatly done and the game runs at 60+ FPS. It still looks like a PS3 game and it's not something you would call not something you would call "current generation", but you don't play shoot'em'ups for "cutting edge graphics developments and ultra realistic shaders".
It's also very well optimized, no framerate drops and some people say they can play it on old laptops.
I absolutely love it. The music is probably why Dariusburst regarded as an "offbeat" shooter, because truth to be said, that's the main thing which distinguishes it from thousands of other shooters. Avantgardish upbeat jazzy tunes with a touch of bizarre vocals, ambientish piece with opera-like female vocals, etc. One of the levels even had the original track from an early SNES Darius game, in all its 16-bit glory.
Some of tracks really stick with you. Worth listening to outside of the game, that's for sure.
What story?
The movement of your ship is very fluid, controls are responsive, bullets on the screen have different colors, shapes and overall are recognizable. More details in the mode reviews below.
I couldn't play this mode for long because of the aspect ratio on a single monitor. It really hurts the experience for me and distracts from gameplay (and the text becomes barely readable).
All I can say from what I've seen that it's a port of an arcade game, classic Darius campaign with multiple routes for you to choose from. The enemies and levels are the same ones you see in CS mode. It features three modes in itself and has local co-op support (up to 4 players). It worth noting that there's an option for Unlimited Lives right from the start, very useful for people who play shoot'em'ups rather casually and want to see all content in the game or players who just gave up on trying to beat it.
If you have a dual monitor setup, go for it. It looks fantastic:
Loading screen with boss fight hints wasn't translated at all. Overall it feels like a very direct port from arcade. As the result, you can make a dedicated “arcade like” cabinet just for this game (if you a hardcore fan).
You're given a special preset for your ship before you start a level. Instead of "coins", you have a number of hits you can take before it's Game Over. I believe the number changes with the ship preset, but it's about 30 for the standard one. 26 hits for Life 1, and then 3-4 hits for the rest of them (you usually have 3-4 lives per area).
First levels are a walk in the park, but just by Level 5 or so the difficulty goes up and by Levels 9 and 10 it's already pretty tough and requires many thing to memorize.
Don't let these first levels fool you, Dariusburst Chronicles is a hardcore and tough game.
“3000+ levels” is listed as the main feature of the game, but for me it's a one huge fault.
Everything feels like it was randomly generated, no zone has its own face. What's worse, is what bosses are also always the same and they repeat all the time. You complete one level, beat the boss and then you meet the same boss on the very next one. And then again. And again, and again and again. They all have different variations which change their attack patterns a bit, but they still all the same and have the same battle music.
Standard enemy appearances are no different, you see the same patterns with the same enemies, same obstacles, same “surprise” enemy attacks. You almost cry in happiness when you see something new in the next area you play, be it a new music track or just a different background. It's recycled to no end and this is what made me to leave the game without willing to play it further. It should be noted that people who say “wow, it's so full of content, hundreds of  levels” are the same ones who enjoy endless grinding in JRPGs because “wow, I spent so many time on these battles, this 1000+ hour RPG is a great value for my money and developers surely didn't use any cheap tricks to make the game longer!”
But hey, there's still the AC mode. I just wish to have a dual monitor setup to play it properly.
The price of 50$ is pretty high, especially since it's a digital release. Lowering it to 20-25$ would be a better solution, in my opinion.

To start off this game has A LOT of stages to play, there is no lacking of content here. There are two modes to choose from at the start menu. Then there's CS Mode, Chronicle Saviors, where you play through a single player campaign.
I really like the music in this game, it has a very interesting and unique sound sometimes. The graphics in AC Mode are ok and then in CS Mode they are really improved. The controls are alright as well, but I prefer playing with my controller instead of hitting z, x, c, and v on my keyboard.
I'm disappointed that the loading screens are in another language since I'm sure there's some useful information on there I just can't read it. Another thing that's a bit annoying is that in Chronicle Mode it is really hard to read the objectives for the areas. There's also no multi-player and some of those objectives require four players so you'll have to find some friends and controllers if you want to do those.
I do wish there was an actual tutorial you can select that'll tell you everything, but if you leave it on the AC Mode title screen for about 30 seconds you'll get a random short video that'll tell you a couple useful tips.

A fun and addicting game, but very, very buggy. The bugs will ruin some of your games, especially when you are Jason.
My biggest problem with the game currently is survivor play. It's too random. There is no clear objective or win condition. You either get lucky or you don't.
Calling the police is the easiest way to escape, but getting them called is not all that common since the phone fuse is either difficult to find, or in many situations can disappear if the player holding the fuse is killed.
In some rounds, you will get stuck trying to fix a car, but if Jason catches on and kills most of the survivors (and especially if the fuse is already missing), you are screwed. There is no way to win other than hiding in a corner and hoping Jason doesn't find you until the excessive 20 minute round timer runs out.
As Jason, the game is more focused, because there are 7 elusive objectives running around the map. While difficulty may vary based on how may tools the survivors have managed to randomly uncover, the outcome is far more in your own control.
If the many glitches are addressed and survivor gameplay is made more "gamey" and less based on chance, I think this could be a great game. As it is, it's just a fun game.

It's a fun game, for the six or so hours that the campaign lasts. And I played it on hard.
You play as a generic mafioso who, after the tutorial, reveals that he's the host for The Darkness, a malevolent entity which gleefully kills people in a bunch of horrifically fun ways. About halfway through the plot your character is killed and is then resurrected by The Darkness, which makes you realize that dying during gameplay really shouldn't be that big a deal if your inner demon can just bring you back to life following the subtle plot twist of getting shotgunned in the face.
I have some minor gripes with the controls; you'll want to remap them or else your attempts to aim, shoot, and flail around with your demon arms basically results in you stumbling and haphazardly firing your guns into the ceiling and walls like a drunken redneck.
There is a variety of enemies to encounter who make the combat a lot of fun and interesting.
The plot and it's overall theme of sanity and evil versus absolute evil were quite enjoyable, and I liked that the game had at least two different endings.
I haven't played the 'vendetta' content yet, but considering the "Main Story" lasted less than six hours I feel justified reviewing the game without playing all of its content.

"I love this game, but ♥♥♥♥ this game sometimes" - the last line in my original review, in which I tentatively gave the game a thumbs up. More time playing and learning about further Ubi-community interactions made me change my mind.
Before struggling through this text-dump of mine, or more likely just looking at yet another thumbs down and moving on, I recommend reading this
review. It basically summed up the major issues with this game while also being entertaining to read.
This is a good game, don't get me wrong. Well, it could be a good game. The fighting mechanics that form the core of this game and make it fun are great, and it's by far the most in-depth melee combat system I've personally ever come across in a game. The game has the potential to be a long-lasting hit, but the problem is this:
Ubisoft
The release of this game is honestly worse than that of Rainbow Six Siege, and while R6S did eventually struggle its way to freeing itself from the chains that initially caused it to have such a bad release, it's taken a year of constant communication between the devs and the community, and in For Honor's case, the devs not only seem unwilling to listen to the playerbase, but bent on actively mocking them. It seemed like the game would be great on release, but then some♥♥♥♥♥♥for-brains idiot at Ubi decided to cut server hosting and instead use P2P. After relentless complaint from millions of players from day 1 onward, Ubisoft eventually decided to do... nothing.
Aside from the massive security problems facing players because of the P2P system, (Your IP address is basically sitting on a tassled plinth waiting for any random small-scale hacker to take and use to ♥♥♥♥ you over), the connection is terrible, and if just one player in a match of 8 has an internet connection that is anything short of... well, slightly above average, but still, then EVERYBODY in the match suffers, and it's almost guaranteed that all will be kicked due to "server" errors from either this or the bugs one could normally expect from a new game. The in-game currency system is massively shrewd, and unlocking a single effect for a single character can sometimes require weeks of farming in almost all of one's free time, unless you're willing to shell out upwards of 50 dollars.
These are all annoying, but the thing that really killed this game for me is the aforementioned lack of communication between the devs and the playerbase. For a while now some devs had been doing a weekly stream detailing upcoming changes and releases, and they worked to release a new batch of content, even if it is just some emotes or ornaments for characters' helmets, every week.
This week they decided that even that was too much work, and instead one poor guy working for Ubi had to basically just say the dev's intentions on a Reddit post, and then suffer the full brunt of the community's backlash. "That's not bad at all" you say, and yes, this and even the next bit aren't that important, but they are symptoms of Ubisoft's complete lack of respect for the customers that keep their corporation alive. They ignored the constant requests of the community to fix massive game-breaking problems, and instead said something along the lines of 'we will be accepting community artwork to use as marketing material for the game.'
Those submitting artwork might not get recognition, and they certainly won't get paid for their art, and even ownership of it will likely be transferred to Ubi, meaning that someone's passion project made to honor (pardon the pun) this game that they liked so much would be stripped from their possesion and displayed in front of millions of people without any compensation or payment, and likely no recognition.
Basically Ubisoft's just saying "We don't care about listening to you and fixing the problems that ruin the game for a large majority of you, but hey, we'll take your stuff and use it as our own, so yay everybody's happy now!"
It's not a bad game, but the publisher seems to be actively attempting to kill it through scummy mechanics in-game and a lack of even attempts to work with the community, and because of this, many players, myself included, have stopped playing the game, maybe forever, and want nothing more to do with it. If it's on sale, then maybe get the cheapest "edition" (none of that "deluxe edition + season pass" ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t), but otherwise take your business elsewhere.

If you are a fan of puzzle games then Hook is a must for your library.  There are 50 stages in all and it will take you about an hour to play through them all.
The early stages introduce you to the basic mechanism and each stage gets progressively more complicated to solve.  The main premise of the puzzle is to extract a series of hooks from a weave.  The hooks interlock together in ways that require you to remove them in the correct order.  You press buttons to initiate pulls on wires that connect to the hooks.  There are contactors between the buttons and the hooks that you can rotate to control which wires connect to the button and consequently which hooks are withdrawn.  Choose the wrong wires and the hooks will bind against each other.
This game has very clever concept and I really enjoyed playing it.  I paid a dollar for it and I think I got very good value for my money.  My congratulations to the developer on a job well done.

Soma is not a horror game that solely relies on its dark claustrophobic environments and terrifying encounters. At it's core is  a question about existence and what does it mean to be truly human? This is where the game truly sets itself apart from Amnesia. Whereas Amnesia was more like a traditional scary story, Soma is the horror story that probes your beliefs about existence. Coming into this game, I steered clear of any spoilers and was pleasantly surprised by the choices they give you in this game. At points in the game you can decide whether people or robots you encounter will live or die. Other choices include deleting data and answering questions about a certain virtual reality machine. Regardless of what you choose, the most impact these choices are going to have is making you think about the reprecussions that could occur or probing your moral beliefs.
Besides the philosophical horror department, SOMA handles other aspects of its game fairly well. Audio is definitely a huge plus and plays big into what scares you as well as how you may handle your choices (hearing people scream after I do something is horror itself). The underwater environment is superb at giving a feeling of claustrophobia though don't expect getting lost so easily as you won't be meandering in the dark alone the whole time. Eerie lights in the distance and the occasional weird (or hostile) creature may greet you. For gameplay, SOMA is similar in how it handles this to Amnesia which is no brainer since it's made by the same people. Puzzles exist but you can tell they're not made for players to focus on for more than just a few minutes. If I remember, puzzles were a bit more difficult in Amnesia though I care not for this change. It's mostly better since this makes it feel like you're not doing fetch quests and allows the story to flow smoothly without interruption. Speaking of story, it's great! It very much entwined into what I've said earlier about SOMA's existential questions. The main character, Simon, is one of the mouthpieces in the game for these questions. There's one section in the game where it's a long elevator down the ocean floor and Simon and another character, Catherine, ponder about their unique situations and comfort themselves. It's a powerful calm scene and a needed one especially after such heavy sequence beforehand. Both main characters, Simon and Catherine are quite likeable though at a few parts Simon seems blissfully unaware (or maybe it's intentional to show his blind hope?) of one important plot point. Overall he comes out as the usual good guy character though one that's forced into a dreadful existential situation.  Catherine is a colder person though you warms up to you later and you will grow to like her. She's a more pragmatic than Simon. As is usual of Frictional Games, one can choose to explore side sections to reveal more background info to add onto the main plot. I highly recommend doing so as it enhances the experience. It definitely hooked me onto the story a lot more.
Overall, SOMA is a welcome iteration into Frictional Games' line up. Some may argue that it's not as scary as Amnesia but as I've repeated, it is not a horror game that relies solely on its usual horror tropes.

Nidhogg 2 is the sequel to the hit 2014 game, where you fence your opponents to become a sacrifice to a massive Wurm (the aforementioned Nidhogg).
Story:
Nidhogg 2 doesn’t really have a story mode. The single player campaign is really just levels where you try to get to the end of the level and that’s about it.
The basic plot is that there is a tournament where you fight against people to become a sacrifice to a giant worm or a wurm as the game calls it, as there can only be one sacrifice. If you want a story Nidhogg 2 is not a place to look for one.
Graphics:
Apparently a lot of people are not happy with the new art style. The first Nidhogg was a pixel art style game, but the sequel however is a lot more detailed graphically and brings on an entirely new art style.
Personally, I find this new art style to be absolutely amazing. The characters have different features like different hair styles, clothes and other things, unlike in the first game where the only difference in sprites were their colors.
Each environment is incredibly detailed and it’s actually a joy to actually gaze upon how great everything looks and how much detail is in the background and the actual map.
Audio:
The audio is also a lot better than it was in the first title. The soundtrack in the first game was nothing special and rather forgettable (in my opinion), but the soundtrack in Nidhogg 2 is actually really good. It ranges from a relaxing tune to a track that really gets you pumped up.
Other sound effects like stabbing and blood splatters all make a come back and they are better than ever. Let me tell you: when you stab your enemy and hear him die ( as morbid as this will sound) it’s incredibly satisfying and will keep you going and wanting to fight more and more.
Gameplay:
Gameplay in Nidhogg 2 is pretty much the same, but with some new additions. For newcomers I’ll give a brief rundown on how everything works. You are put into a 2D arena and have a sword which you can point down, middle and up; and then you stab your enemy or try to disarm them. Once you kill your opponent you need to proceed to the right side and get to the final screen to get consumed by the wurm.
The gameplay in Nidhogg 2 is incredibly simple, which makes it quite addictive to just pick up and get to slicing. But as stated, the sequel brings on new additions, like new weapons. First of all there are different swords which all have different stats, and now there is also a crossbow. Apart from these minor additions the gameplay is pretty much the same and it works just as well in Nidhogg 2.
One of the other new additions to the game is a character creation feature. Unlike the first game where you have a preset model and all the other characters are just different colors, this game has different features which you can use of to craft a unique character. Even though this feature is pretty limited, it’s still a very nice addition to the game.
Verdict:
Nidhogg 2 is an incredibly fun game. The new art style, amazing soundtrack and the incredibly fun gameplay make it a must own. Even though the single player is short, the multiplayer is enough of a reason to keep playing and I see myself spending a lot more time with this game in the future.
Final Rating:
8/10
Pros:
+Fun combat
+Great visuals
Cons:
-Short campaign
