Nidhogg 2 is the sequel to the fun little sword fencing game Nidhogg. This game is a very fast paced and intense tug of war battle. It's a 1v1 fighting game and death can occur almost instantaneously when you spawn, keeping you on your toes the whole time. This fun and fair fighting game is unfortunately dragged down by networking issues, but the single player and local aspect is impeccable.
When you start, you'll have a nice variety of customisation options to choose from, ranging from your character's colour to accessories. You and your opponent will spawn with a random weapon out of 4 possibilities, which are a broadsword, rapier, dagger, and bow. Each weapon is different and takes time to master, although I find the bow to be the hardest to use. Once the fight has initiated, it's balls to the walls action from here on out.
Each character starts on an opposite side of the screen. The goal of each character is to make it to the opposing side of the level. Say my character started on the left, my goal is to make it to the far right of the map. There's an invisible wall at the edge of the screen and I can only proceed should I kill my opponent. But if I die, then the opponent can push back and make their way back towards the other way. This continues until someone eventually makes it to their winning side of the map which then results in the victor being suddenly consumed by a giant wurm. This game while intense and gruesome, is lighthearted and humorous fun.
There's a singleplayer campaign that pits you against an AI and takes place through all 10 stages 1 by 1. This gives you good practise of the game and lets you learn the mechanics and develop your strategies, but the AI isn't particularly great. Every stage is unique though, visually and mechanically. There's an ice level with icebergs that oscillate vertically, and levels with multiple paths and doorways. There's also conveyer belts and flowing lava which push towards a certain direction. There's a really good variety in level design and each level is graphically gorgeous. Accompanying each level is an amazing soundtrack. I loved the music, it's practically an earworm generator. I'd definitely recommend picking up the OST along with the game.
I ran into issues when duelling online against a friend. There's visible input delay which makes it impossible for precise sword fighting, and thus button mashing is what I had to resort to. In a game that requires quick reflexes and precision, having lag is not a very good thing. Latency is not such an issue in other games, I can reach up to 300 ping and still not experience perceptible lag. Another issue that only occurred online was slowdown. Absolutely abhorrently abysmal slowdown. On one of the levels when there was lots of fire in the background (the castle or volcano map) the FPS dropped to an unbearable single digit and we both had to give up. With overseas online being unplayable, we're left with same-region online, local co-op and the singleplayer campaign. Fortunately, if you have friends, it is enough for this game to be worth the money.
Overall, Nidhogg 2 is a very worthy successor of it's predecessor. The new weapons, art style and hilarious fun keep this game entertaining, but sadly the online aspect is not so good.

Being a fan of SuperGiant's past works of Bastion and Transistor, I was excited to play Pyre. One of the first things I noticed, however, was that Pyre was not like Bastion or Transistor. If you've heard anything about the game, its probably that it is hard to describe. The out-of-combat experience is similar to a visual novel in that you talk to characters and make some choices by selecting from a list of options. In-combat, the game plays similarly to a three on three sports game. This gameplay is probably the biggest departure from SuperGiant's past works. Also the narrator that was so prevelant in the other two is not nearly as central. He is still there, but not as much as previous games. In short this is not a game you should pick up just because you liked Bastion and Transistor, because it is not those games.
However, this isn't a bad thing. The game does some great things. The biggest one to me was the cast of characters. All of the playable characters and all of the leaders of opposing team are memorable with unique stories and motivations. To me, learning more about these characters was the best part of this game. Without spoiling anything, there was a point in the game where I started a match and immediately paused the game becuase of who my opponent was. I had to stop and think to myself, "Should I purposely lose this match so my opponent can win?". This happened twice during the match and in the end I decided to purposely lose. The fact that this happened should show you how great the characters are.
The game itself was something I wasn't initally fond of, but after playing with it for a while I enjoy it. Every character plays differently and the different team combinations you can and play aganst make the matches very interesting. The mechanic of having whoever scored the last point be temporarily unplayable really keeps the games dynamic and prevents the spamming of one strategy. The upgrade system gives boosts that are actually meaningful and majorly change how you use that character. Its not just upgrades like "+1 strength".
And of course, it is still made by SuperGiant, so the music and visuals are amazing.
TL;DR: This isn't Bastion or Transistor. It is more focused on a cast of characters rather than one and the combat resembles a sports game. The characters are compelling and interesting and there is a lot of depth to the combat through varied characters and a good upgrade system. The visuals and music are stunning.
Worth a bit of fun and gore. Meh story and level. Fun shooting though.

*Note: This review is strictly based off of my opinions and experiences with the following game.*
If you're a diehard fan of The Isle, or if you've been stalking the reviews for a while, you might recognize this review format. That's because I reviewed this game a long time ago when it first started gaining some popularity, and back when it was a lot newer to steam. I decided after a while that it was time to revisit, and see if I enjoyed it more than the last time.
- Survival mode. It's brand new, and currently only has two playable dinosaurs, but it's so much better than progression. Instead of having to waste hours of your life slowly climbing a ladder of creatures you probably don't enjoy, or have already been stuck on for who knows how long, you get to pick the dinosaur you want as soon as you join the server. However, unlike sandbox, you spawn in as a juvenile. This really keeps the thrill and spark of the game alive - you don't just start off almighty and powerful. You still have to work, and put effort in. While you're small, you have to hide, hunt smaller prey, scavenge, and slowly grow until you can face your rivals. This game mode really works well, and I look forward to seeing where it will go when everything else is added.
- The game provides plenty of experiences with different types of modes and servers. Don’t enjoy the grind of progression? Go to sandbox. Want to still work towards something? Try survival. Want to roleplay or have a more immersive setting? Try realism.
- The dev team updates regularly.
- The models, sounds, and most of the animations are absolutely stunning.
- The map design has improved a lot. No longer must you constantly worry about water - all the lakes work properly, there's some scattered all around the map, and they're quite easy to find. Other players usually make their way to them as well, so finding food or friends is easier.
- Future content is looking better than ever, leaving a ton of potential for this game.
- To this day, the community is still one of my least favorite things about this game. Regardless of which server you go to, you can never escape it. On most servers, you'll find what everybody has called "KOSers," which is basically an annoying player who finds great joy in killing absolutely everything it comes across as soon as it sees it. It will usually leave a giant trail of bodies in its path, slightly breaking gameplay by leaving so much food around to be devoured, removing the need for most predators to hunt... I mean, why should they when they can scavenge? Unless they'd like to kill for sport, which just leads to more KOSing and ecosystem breaking. It also breaks any sort of immersion you might've had, seeing as you just stumbled into a graveyard full of fifty rex corpses.
(Did I mention that some KOSers aren't even carnivores? Oh yes, even your everyday herbivore can turn into the next serial killer of the map. Simply become a shant. Silent, fast, extremely powerful, and easy to progress to. To be honest, I think I've been killed by more shants than all the apexes combined.)
Carebears are... well, yet another annoying type of player. They're the type of players that simply hate the survival aspect of the game it seems, as they protect literally everything, even if it's outside of their species. I've seen carnivores protect herbivores, and vice versa. It doesn't really make sense to me, and it's extremely annoying when you're hungry and they won't let you even come close to their precious friend group. I've even had them corpse guard before.
And finally, you have the people that form mega packs. Don't get me wrong, forming a pack of twenty rexes is awesome both in theory and quite literally. The sight alone is breathtaking. But then a couple hours pass, and that fun fades away. Nothing can stop a force that large (currently), except other mega packs. But it becomes less a game about surviving and more of a really pathetic game of turf wars. "I bet I can kill more of your offspring before they grow than you can to mine!" You hunt a few things, fill up, drink, lay down, wait for an hour or so, repeat x100,000. You don't really have to worry, the thrill of having hatchlings isn't really there because so many people are protecting them... It just becomes bleh. But to some people, it never gets boring. So mega packs are created over and over again, leading to an unbalanced ecosystem full of apexes. If you're something outside of that pack, you might as well kiss your shiny new dino goodbye, because you're going to become chow for their ten billion babies soon. Half of the server is going to be looking for you like you're fresh steak.
- Official servers are terrible. No need to hunt when literally every corner you turn, it looks like world war III just occurred. The alternative is no bodies at all and hardly any players online. They're still on Progression Mode, the amount of points you need is actually ridiculous, and the people are even more unfriendly then they are on unofficial.
- Some of the dinosaurs seem to be rather unbalanced compared to others? Obviously, with the game still in EA, things are bound to change, but it can get annoying from time to time. For example, the lower tier dinosaurs. Now, you'd think that medium sized carnivores would hunt medium/small sized prey. Well, only half of that is true. Let's say you play as an allo. Most of the herbivore branch will be untouchable. And even stuff close to your size will most likely break your legs like twigs. Meaning most of your food will come from scavenging, picking off the smallest prey possible, or... you know, hunting carnivores your size. The fact that it's ten times easier to kill a carnivore your exact size or a tiny bit smaller, but it's near impossible to kill the mid-tier herbivores makes no sense to me. Another example would be the trike and shant. Both of them are pretty much tanks. I've seen apexes being chased across the map by those things.
- Still no map, you have to learn the landmarks of each map. </3

Survarium is a Survival FPS game that offers a variety landscape, with graphics to match.
First going into this game, you'd want to try out the Multiplayer, which is probably the
thing that has gotten this game so many bad reviews (2000 or so positive, 2000 or so negative)
throwing it into the mixed zone.
I've tried it myself, when the servers weren't being shut off for some oblivious reason, and
from what I've read I wasn't surprised to see that the comments section for this game were
correct.
Unfair gameplay that makes you want to tear the hair out of your head, the usual generic tid
bits that upset players such as Spawn Camping, which I'm quite unbiased about because Its going to
happen anyway whether you complain or review about it or not. Then you get to the whole "Punishment"
system. Players walking into their own traps, causing point deductions for your own team, mostly done
on purpose. It also doesn't help that the game is trying to throw DLC at you for obnoxious prices in an
early access game, which is only supposed to be for players testing out your game, and not for pulling off
an EA stunt. So far, you're probably disgusted by what this game has to offer from what I've said so far, but
it gets much, much, worse. Bullet physics are a a joke, mediocre but not even at best, damage is so bad, that
you'd expect certain weapons to do more damage than others, but for some reason an assault rifle 1 hit kills you
over a headshot to the face. Most of the game revolves around Team Killing, and most of the people that'd played
this game would probably agree with me. This whole game is just trying to throw DLC down your throat, and expect you
to wait for the full game to release. US Servers are a laughing stock, and US players are forced to play on the EU servers due
to the incompetence of the developers. I've seen some pretty shameful games, reviewed some pretty shameful games, but this one
has got to be the WORST one I've reviewed so far this year.
It's infuriating, It's unsettling, It's just sad how the developers find it alright to do this with their game.
The Physics are down right awful when it comes to being useful in any way, along with the lag that comes with the servers, it
doesn't help that the game won't work correctly and you're jumping all over the place.
If the developers ever decide to fix this game, I'll still not want anything to do with this poor excuse of a release.
They try to bring in more people by sponging out S.T.A.L.K.E.R for a fanbase to work off of, but here It just doesn't work, It never would've worked, and to me It never will.
S.T.A.L.K.E.R was a very great game, to others it was alright, it was good, or they didn't like it. That's all fine and dandy, but this title is just a mockery of that franchise.
There's plenty of more choices, most are even out of Early Access and have little to no problems matching with this games, so
It'd be best if you check those out instead with a quick search of the Steam Store, Google, and so forth.
In honor of all of this, Survarium gets the first ever NaN Ops Award this year, so congratulations!
You're receiving this award for:
Forcing DLC in an early access game that is obnoxiously priced;
Having a horribly broken game, that may still be playable, but is a big heaping pile of mess as it stands;
And for even releasing the game in this state at all.
Survarium, you are awarded with the Worst Game of 2015 award, until another one comes to take your title!
Congratulations!
Now of course, for the review table.
All reviews are scored from 1 (Meaning stay away from this game), to 10 (Most likely won't happen since no game is perfect)
Would I recommend this game?
No. And I can firmly say that without a doubt.
Until the Developers can get off their butts and fix what needs to be fixed, there's no replayability, no fun (for the most part), or anything like that to get out of this game.
Not to mention the shameless DLC thats being shoved down the players throats for 40.00? That's not bad, that's just completely rubbish.
You'd think after update 0.28 the game would get better, but It failed to even do that at all.

"I love this game, but ♥♥♥♥ this game sometimes" - the last line in my original review, in which I tentatively gave the game a thumbs up. More time playing and learning about further Ubi-community interactions made me change my mind.
Before struggling through this text-dump of mine, or more likely just looking at yet another thumbs down and moving on, I recommend reading this
review. It basically summed up the major issues with this game while also being entertaining to read.
This is a good game, don't get me wrong. Well, it could be a good game. The fighting mechanics that form the core of this game and make it fun are great, and it's by far the most in-depth melee combat system I've personally ever come across in a game. The game has the potential to be a long-lasting hit, but the problem is this:
Ubisoft
The release of this game is honestly worse than that of Rainbow Six Siege, and while R6S did eventually struggle its way to freeing itself from the chains that initially caused it to have such a bad release, it's taken a year of constant communication between the devs and the community, and in For Honor's case, the devs not only seem unwilling to listen to the playerbase, but bent on actively mocking them. It seemed like the game would be great on release, but then some♥♥♥♥♥♥for-brains idiot at Ubi decided to cut server hosting and instead use P2P. After relentless complaint from millions of players from day 1 onward, Ubisoft eventually decided to do... nothing.
Aside from the massive security problems facing players because of the P2P system, (Your IP address is basically sitting on a tassled plinth waiting for any random small-scale hacker to take and use to ♥♥♥♥ you over), the connection is terrible, and if just one player in a match of 8 has an internet connection that is anything short of... well, slightly above average, but still, then EVERYBODY in the match suffers, and it's almost guaranteed that all will be kicked due to "server" errors from either this or the bugs one could normally expect from a new game. The in-game currency system is massively shrewd, and unlocking a single effect for a single character can sometimes require weeks of farming in almost all of one's free time, unless you're willing to shell out upwards of 50 dollars.
These are all annoying, but the thing that really killed this game for me is the aforementioned lack of communication between the devs and the playerbase. For a while now some devs had been doing a weekly stream detailing upcoming changes and releases, and they worked to release a new batch of content, even if it is just some emotes or ornaments for characters' helmets, every week.
This week they decided that even that was too much work, and instead one poor guy working for Ubi had to basically just say the dev's intentions on a Reddit post, and then suffer the full brunt of the community's backlash. "That's not bad at all" you say, and yes, this and even the next bit aren't that important, but they are symptoms of Ubisoft's complete lack of respect for the customers that keep their corporation alive. They ignored the constant requests of the community to fix massive game-breaking problems, and instead said something along the lines of 'we will be accepting community artwork to use as marketing material for the game.'
Those submitting artwork might not get recognition, and they certainly won't get paid for their art, and even ownership of it will likely be transferred to Ubi, meaning that someone's passion project made to honor (pardon the pun) this game that they liked so much would be stripped from their possesion and displayed in front of millions of people without any compensation or payment, and likely no recognition.
Basically Ubisoft's just saying "We don't care about listening to you and fixing the problems that ruin the game for a large majority of you, but hey, we'll take your stuff and use it as our own, so yay everybody's happy now!"
It's not a bad game, but the publisher seems to be actively attempting to kill it through scummy mechanics in-game and a lack of even attempts to work with the community, and because of this, many players, myself included, have stopped playing the game, maybe forever, and want nothing more to do with it. If it's on sale, then maybe get the cheapest "edition" (none of that "deluxe edition + season pass" ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t), but otherwise take your business elsewhere.

Soma is not a horror game that solely relies on its dark claustrophobic environments and terrifying encounters. At it's core is  a question about existence and what does it mean to be truly human? This is where the game truly sets itself apart from Amnesia. Whereas Amnesia was more like a traditional scary story, Soma is the horror story that probes your beliefs about existence. Coming into this game, I steered clear of any spoilers and was pleasantly surprised by the choices they give you in this game. At points in the game you can decide whether people or robots you encounter will live or die. Other choices include deleting data and answering questions about a certain virtual reality machine. Regardless of what you choose, the most impact these choices are going to have is making you think about the reprecussions that could occur or probing your moral beliefs.
Besides the philosophical horror department, SOMA handles other aspects of its game fairly well. Audio is definitely a huge plus and plays big into what scares you as well as how you may handle your choices (hearing people scream after I do something is horror itself). The underwater environment is superb at giving a feeling of claustrophobia though don't expect getting lost so easily as you won't be meandering in the dark alone the whole time. Eerie lights in the distance and the occasional weird (or hostile) creature may greet you. For gameplay, SOMA is similar in how it handles this to Amnesia which is no brainer since it's made by the same people. Puzzles exist but you can tell they're not made for players to focus on for more than just a few minutes. If I remember, puzzles were a bit more difficult in Amnesia though I care not for this change. It's mostly better since this makes it feel like you're not doing fetch quests and allows the story to flow smoothly without interruption. Speaking of story, it's great! It very much entwined into what I've said earlier about SOMA's existential questions. The main character, Simon, is one of the mouthpieces in the game for these questions. There's one section in the game where it's a long elevator down the ocean floor and Simon and another character, Catherine, ponder about their unique situations and comfort themselves. It's a powerful calm scene and a needed one especially after such heavy sequence beforehand. Both main characters, Simon and Catherine are quite likeable though at a few parts Simon seems blissfully unaware (or maybe it's intentional to show his blind hope?) of one important plot point. Overall he comes out as the usual good guy character though one that's forced into a dreadful existential situation.  Catherine is a colder person though you warms up to you later and you will grow to like her. She's a more pragmatic than Simon. As is usual of Frictional Games, one can choose to explore side sections to reveal more background info to add onto the main plot. I highly recommend doing so as it enhances the experience. It definitely hooked me onto the story a lot more.
Overall, SOMA is a welcome iteration into Frictional Games' line up. Some may argue that it's not as scary as Amnesia but as I've repeated, it is not a horror game that relies solely on its usual horror tropes.

Firstly I was never a super fan of the re-imagined TV series. So look at this as someone who tolerated that show rather than a BSG2 super fan. I recommend this game.
As a space ship tactical battle game it does very well. The WEGO system is well suited to large unit command. You and your opponent (game AI or multiplayer) have time to think of orders, where to move, make corrections to arrange a set of movement and fire. The battle then runs for a cycle. There will be times the enemy tactics surprise you. Times you wish you had thought they might do that, espically if they volley missiles. I find after a fleet battle it has been 20+ minutes and I feel mentally tired from the solid challenge. Espically as I try to not get my ships killed.
The strategy side has been diverse enough that I haven't gotten bored with mandatory mission repeats. Just don't rush down the storyline missions. Play a few other battles each chapter. Getting an officer to have a larger fleet is a big game changer.
The ships individually seem a bit simple. The point of a fleet game is that there are many ships. Thats how things get complicated. I could wish for a few more commands which I are candidates for submission to the forums.
I'm sure there are some battle methods that will repeat. That though is true of most sims or real life.
For example put your fighters on defense, sail the fleet away from the enemy, keep firing missiles every 4 turns they need to cycle and see if you kill more than you lose. Turn when engaged with guns. If you think of modern naval ships with their missiles that is kinda what they do to: exchange long range missile fire under defenses for as long as possible.
The tactical and strategic game mechanic seem well suited to be used to other non-Newtonian space settings like Star Wars other franchises. Having the ships named lets you get a hope or loss feeling as they enter dangerous situations. You can edit the names so I give them penant numbers. In turn this gives me some idea how long a ship has survived the campaign.

NidHogg 2, the sequel to NidHogg, is created and published by Messhof. It is a casual action, fighting game, that is available on Steam or on PS4. It has several different game modes, Arcade, which is the games story mode in which you fight a computer on all the different levels, this is also something that you can speed run. The next game mode is Local play, in which you can play with your friends with one computer in an either quickplay, which is 2 player, or tournament, which is 3-8 players. You can do this by either using one keyboard, using a keyboard and controller or just plugging in 2 controllers. Another game mode is online in which you can do ranked or unranked. You can select how far your opponent can be away from you to reduce lag, but the lower distance you go the harder it is to find a game.
Nidhogg 2 has great fighting mechanics with it using 3 different layers your weapons can be, so you can either aim for the head, chest or legs. If you are on the same level as the opposing player and they attack this blocks their attack. It also uses very easy to learn controls, but it uses weird uncomfortable keys for those controls. Another thing that can be annoying is the place the player spawns, it often spawns them quite close to the enemy and with no invulnerability so you can either spawn with a bow at short range or have the enemy through there weapon killing you without you having time to get ready. One more thing, some certain weapons are more ‘op’ then others with one, being able to disarm swords and being the longest, so people with smaller swords like daggers will be stabbed before they can stab back.
The progression system is well designed. Once you’re or your any kills you they can move in the direction they must get to the ned stage. And as stated before, they use different stages or rooms, that once you kill the enemy and get to the edge of it, you walk through a door or opening and move to the next stage. The way you win is also a great idea, with it making you the winner once you finally past the final stage. If you are players of equal skill you can be going back and forth through the stages going on for ages, adding extra time while it still being fun and intense.
The story, or arcade mode, of NidHogg 2 isn’t really a story, its more just a whole bunch of levels played with a computer. It progresses through the levels which have different feature, but these are all the multiplayer maps as well. It is a great way to learn the game and have a bit of fun, or to speed run. But if you wanted an actual story, this game doesn’t have it, it just has a group of levels you play with bots. Also the length of these is quite short, I completed all them in one sitting, it took me, a  beginner and being someone who didn’t play the original game, only 30 minutes to complete. Even though this game isn’t a story based game and is more designed around 1v1 combat, I would have at least liked a longer arcade mode and more levels, lasting for around an hour.
The graphical design to NidHogg 2 is very different to the pixel art NidHogg. It has proper sprites, while still being pixilated, showing more details and making it look better in my opinion, all though the character sprites do look a bit silly.
All the levels and backgrounds look very well designed, graphically wise. It still sticks with the pixel theme but uses lots of different colour and incorporates lots of detail with the colours, sprites and look of the levels changing to the theme of each level, like sewers, and a beach map. All this looks visually pleasing even though it was done by a small team. Though sometimes when there is a lot of things going on, it makes the game lag and slows down the actual game.
The sound design is this game is very well done. It uses great sound affects for all the different little things that happen and incorporates different types of music depending on the map and the looks of it. It also uses great music that can sound like its blended into the game when you’re playing certain maps. The music changes the feeling of the game, from calm and relaxed to tense. The music and the sound are incorporated perfectly into this game to make it even more enjoyable.
+Great sound effects and music
+Fun, intuitive fighting mechanics
+Great graphics
-Game slows down while lagging
-lack of story, and short arcade mode

This game is definitely more of a casual RPG, but it's a lot of fun. There isn't a whole ton of places you can go outside of where they want you to go, but they do a great job making you feel like the world is semi-open, and there are definitely choices you can make.
The graphics are pretty sweet, the gameplay is decently fun but not overly complicated (the game play is sort of like FPS diablo you can't really do much besides attack or block or roll out of the way). The sound and music is quite good, and the voice over acting is also quite decent. Yes, certain NPC character models are recycled and same with voices, but it's not a big deal. I think the land is beautiful and the levels are very well designed. I would love to see this title evolve into a modern engine in 2015, with similar gameplay but maybe a little more difficulty.
I'd recommend this for some casual RPG play. The skills system is interesting and can provide for maybe 3-4 different builds of characters: warrior, archer, mage, alchemist. It'd take some elaborating but creative games could play the game a few times through I think. I've not finished the game yet but I think I will eventually.
It would be great if there were some mods that would make this game a little more hardcore; like there is no encumberance or weight to the inventory so you can literally just pick up hundreds of everything without consequence. The pace in which the main character moves makes me grateful for this. Also, jumping and colision detection is kind of goofy you can jump like off of a small hill and sustain some damage from that height. It feels like jumping physics are a little weird with the gravity too. There are invisible walls that can't be traversed (and that's OK IMO, even Skyrim has this kind of thing) the weird thing here in this game is the way the character is like caught on the wall, and skies invisibly like floating/skating away from the wall (to prevent him from getting stuck)? It's a little weird and it ruins the immersive feeling of the rest of the game which is pretty decent.
I'm playing an archer/melee guy (leveling my Precision first then I'll do Discipline) and it's fun, I find the balance to be pretty decent. The main issue I have with the difficulty is that the game is almost too generous with healing items, I have over a hundred things in my inventory right now at level 9 that can heal me almost completely in addition to items I've got equipped that boost my time lapsed health regeneration. This is where the casual side comes in.
The issue is that casual would be a little more acceptable if the story was better, but the story is just fair. The main character has a decent plot line and the idea that we're going to stop a war and save the country eventually is kind of plain but fun to play through. But the game doesn't have enough meat on it's bones in between the main plot points. The side missions are fun, and I really enjoy my time playing through all the various quests just grinding. Others might not though.
Anyway I'd recommend this game to people who would enjoy a casual RPG-esque adventure through a beautifully rendered world who don't thrive on difficult game engines and are in for more of a Choose Your Own Adventure++ FPS with some RPG bits thrown in. It's definitely worth the money I paid and I'm glad I bought the game.
I'm really interested to see what this developer could do with a modern RPG.
It's no Skyrim, but it's worth playing if you approach it knowing it won't wow you but give you sufficient entertainment and a steady pace to make you feel heroic even if being a little too easy.

If you're a fan of classic shmups, this game is worth it.
The price tag is pretty high, but most of the previews and quick looks of the gameplay don't do justice in showing how much content is included. There's the typical Darius arcade mode with branching stages, then there's the mission-based chronicle mode. Missions are just series of stages and bosses, with occasional rules or limitations or preset ship designs. But they aren't kidding when they say there are well over a thousand of these.
The virtual arcade cabinets are an interesting design choice for online play. Each cabinet shares the unlocked stages across all players, so cabinet 0001 would probably be a good one to compete for global high scores or just access the fully-unlocked Chronicle mode, while you (and friends) could probably pick a later cabinet if you want one to yourself. There's also a CS mode which is basically a combination of Chronicle mode and the story-based arcade stages.
Mechanically, this game is as tight as any other Darius. Sometimes you're crushing waves of enemies, but when you do enter bullet hell with depleted shields, it can get harrowing. Ships operate based on the game they originated from, which is a nice touch.
I won't lie; this is an expensive game for the genre. But the developers really made the extra effort to create a true-to-life port of the arcade game you would get from buying the thousand-dollar cabinet. My only knocks against it are the lack of online co-op and the catch-22 of trying to emulate the arcade screen resolution if you aren't using multiple monitors. But there's always room for updates.

First of all, I should say that I'm a huge fan of Darius series and Taito games in general so I might be a liiiittle biased here.
Now that I got that out of the way, let's move on to our main topic here, the game, DARIUSBURST Chronicle Saviours. Oh wow, where do I start?
You might have looked at the price point and went, "oh my god, that's high!” Believe me, I was like you too when I found out about it. I mainly bought this for its Arcade port of DARIUSBURST Another Chronicle, considering how hard it is to find the real cabinet version of the arcade game plus tons of new added content, I’d say it’s a really good buy.
The game is fun, it’s separated into two parts, CS Mode which is the new single player content made exclusively for this game and AC Mode, which is the arcade port of Another Chronicle. You have 9 (or was it 8?) different ships to choose from and some of them are from the older Darius games which was a pleasant surprise for me. (They even changes the music to older Darius music if you play as them in CS Mode, neat). The boss fights are great and the game boasts a pretty darn awesome soundtrack too, but I think a lot of us can agree the “freedom” song on the trailer is kinda meh.
The amount of levels you can play in this game is hugeeeeee! Mainly in CS Mode and Chronicle Mode in AC Mode. But a little warning. Sure, the game has tons of content but there's some repetition here and there and maybe some tweaks between the levels. Something like, "beat these levels and bosses with this ship". I think that might also be the case with Chronicle mode in AC Mode but I haven't really touched it yet during the time this review was written. But still, I enjoyed every second of it. And it really helps to get better for beating AC mode with 1 credit. Hey, on the bright sight, most of other shmups just have around 5 or 6 levels and this one have waaaay more than that. Fun!
If you’re a shmup fan, you definitely should get this but maybe when it's on sale, because honestly I still think it's a little bit pricey. But either way, this is the biggest shmup game I’ve ever played and I had a lot of fun with it, I hope when you bought this, you too will have fun with it :3

A surprising gem. Gunplay is solid, if a little uninspired. Story was gripping throughout and very well paced: people have complained about the length, but I felt I got more than my money's worth. This game is lovely to look at, and despite its age, still holds a candle to any modern shooter thanks to its expertly rendered cell-shading, which maintains a perfect comic book vibe throughout, and allows the graphics to remain essentially timeless.
Two places the game falls down, to differing extent are the atmosphere and level design.
Atmosphere is largely absent from this game unfortunately, despite offering a mythos that could easily be exploited for spine-tingling vibes. The soundtrack is completely forgettable and generic, and the ambient sound design extremely lacking. While we're on the topic of the mythos, I found myself not caring much. The game makes many attempts to engage you with the mythos, but such attempts felt only about three-quarter♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Perhaps this is a problem with the source material, I'm unsure. I normally dive into mythos pretty heavily, but despite my best efforts, I couldn't engage with this game's beyond the initial veneer. Something was lacking.
As to level design, while I wouldn't say it was atrocious, or even bad, it was thoroughly uninspired. One often has the sensation of moving from room to room, both figuratively and literally. Not only is the design linear, but it offers little opportunity to exploit level features to one's advantage. With that said, many of the sets look goregous, although just as many are enither here nor there.
I've begun rambling here, so I'll just say, if you can get this game for $5 you'll have gotten more than your money's worth, and I'd even happily drop a tenner on it. At the time of this review, full price is $40, and there's simply no way this game is worth that when one considers what else is available for that kind of price, however it regularly goes on sale for large discounts. I regularly see it at ~80% off, so if you can get it at that kind of discount (and you can if you're patient) I recommend it.

A strongly tactical and immersive game of turn based vessel warefare - with cinematic level combat action. The strategic level is less strong, it doesn't quite succeed in setting a framework in which the battles take on extra meaning.  However, Scripted story missions appear in sequence at various places, and times.  These succeed in adding the flavour of the conflicted politics and personality from the BSG backstory/cannon.  Such missions are pitched to be a little more challenging, and unlock "requisition Points" that can be used to unlock technology.
But, it's the tactical depth of the ship battles that this game is really about:  3 dimensions of combat, distinct weapon system technologies, maneuverability, speed, directional armour thickness, fields of fire, green-on-green hits and you can ram.
However - it's got a few bugs (battle playback being the main running issue) - and needs additional content to justify the £30 price (it should be £20).
9/10 (ignoring the price).

Oh, DARIUSBURST. You come so close, and yet you falter mere steps away from the finish line.
Many people will look at the price tag and think twice about it, but if your concern is lack of content, you shouldn't worry. DARIUSBURST is a game that is absolutely stuffed to the gills. There's a full recreation of the Arcade mode in 32:9 (with dual-monitor support!), including Original (choose three stages from a total of twelve in the traditional Darius split map), Original EX (Original but harder), Chronicle (thousands of stages, unlocked collaboratively with other players), and Event (currently unused). There's also a new mode, similar to Chronicle meant for home play on a 16:9 monitor by a single player. There are dozens of enemies and bosses, most if not all of the latter having one or more variants with different attacks. There are eight ships to choose from in arcade and a ninth in CS, all of which have dramatically differing capabilities.
As far as actually playing it goes, DARIUSBURST doesn't disappoint either. The controls are responsive, the ships don't feel too fast or slow as you dodge between volleys of fire and take down enemies, and the battles are all delightfully flashy and impressive in a way that makes it fun to watch despite the average graphics. It's really a great game.
And yet, there's a big red thumbs down at the top of this review. And it's there for a reason. DARIUSBURST doesn't lack for content, and it doesn't lack for gameplay, but that's not all that's important to a game. What DARIUSBURST is ultimately missing to make it woth the full price tag is polish. It's an overall gread experience, that is nonetheless missing things - both minor little pleasantries and arguably key features.
There's no replay functionality whatsoever.
There's no stage practice option beyond finding a Chronicle course that starts with the stage you want to practice.
When playing AC mode on a single monitor, it's letterboxed... with bland black rectangles, as opposed to some of the series' gorgeous art assets.
Without multiple controllers, there's no way to pick the color of your ship.
There's no online multiplayer, when many of the stages in Chronicle cannot be entered at all without a team of two or more.
The arcade loading screens, meant to inform the player about their ship and the bosses, are inexplicably left untranslated from Japanese.
Those are all features that other shmups, cheaper shmups, have provided in the past. Yet DARIUSBURST, a fully-priced retail release, lacks them.
And that's why, ultimately, I cannot click the "Yes" button and recommend it. If there were a Mixed option in addition to Yes and No, I'd cheerfully pick that one, because there's a lot here to like. But if it's got to be one of the two...
DARIUSBURST would be worthwhile at $30. It'd be a bargain at $20. But at $50, I can't recommend it to anyone who would be on the fence and decide to read some reviews. Wait for a good sale, and THEN get it and have a great time.

A great package for any shooting game enthusiast, filled with more variety, options, and modes than just about any other release in recent memory. In contrast to more traditional "five stages and done" arcade games, the original arcade release of Dariusburst: Another Chronicle EX (DBCS's "AC Mode") contains 24 stages ranging from very easy to very hard, eight unique player ships, and a separate "Chronicle Mode" where players can collaboratively chip away at a massive selection of thousands of stages.
This alone would be enough to keep a player occupied for a very long time, especially one who was interested in delving into the game's scoring system with each of the eight different ships, each of which generally plays much differently than the rest. However, Chronicle Saviours also includes a completely separate "CS Mode" which, while somewhat similar to Chronicle Mode, more or less functions as the game's "story mode." CS Mode includes a variety of special challenges, stages, and bosses not found in the original arcade release, and with a map of over 200 stages to unlock, it will keep you busy for quite a while if you're interested in fully completing it.
Graphically, it's not likely to knock anyone's socks off on a technical level, but the audiovisual presentation still manages to impress from time to time. Many of the bosses -- especially the largest ones -- create quite a spectacle, and the game's soundtrack is generally excellent. There are still a handful of noticeable flaws: controller mapping is a bit inflexible, and "AC Mode" is a straight port with no added functionality -- meaning no practice mode, no replay functionality, and no extras like an "all stages" mode.
While I would recommend this game without hesitation to fans of the shooter genre who are able to get lasting enjoyment out of these games, it may obviously be a bit of a harder sell for a casual player who's just looking for a couple evenings' worth of credit feeding. Even then, though, four-player co-op with friends on a super-widescreen setup can still be a recipe for a pretty good time.

DARIUSBURST CS marks the return of the Darius series to the PC. Yes, Darius Gaiden and G-Darius had actual PC ports so I'm hoping that maybe one day we'll see those also showing up on Steam.
With that cleared, let's take a look at the game: quantity seems to be the keyword here (and with the asking price, no wonder!) The game features the full arcade version (with Original and Original EX modes as well as the MASSIVE Chronicle mode with planets and areas to liberate in a networking effort with other players across the world) and with its original aspect ratio.
On top of all the arcade goodness, there is also a more console-styled mode called Chronicle Saviours, featuring a full blown galaxy map full of planets and missions. This mode fits in one screen but unfortunately looks considerably worse than the arcade counterpart. It's also a fairly grindy mode compared to the arcade version, with over 200 stages but only so many different bosses (I think it's 40 bosses but that includes their variations, some of them pretty notable).
Graphics-wise, the game looks nice but it's not a powerhouse by any means. On the bright side, you can run this even on a toaster of a laptop and it'll still run fine.
Overall music, presentation, ship variety, boss design and mechanics are fantastic, although the "counterburst"/burst mechanic timings are incredibly hard to master but so rewarding when you manage to pull them off. (Thankfully, Chronicle Saviours mode has the Murakumo and Genesis ships, which allow you to counterburst at will!) The one big complaint I have is that mastering the no damage art is going to be beyond the skills of most.
To wrap things up, it's paradise time for shmup fans and unbelievable that such a title made it to PC. At the same time, a testimony of future proofing so I can't wait to see this running on dual monster 80" screens or something.
This is going to be a title you can come back every once in a while years on for "just a couple more shots"!
Edit: the addition of DLC packs with even more stages and ships has pretty much increased even MORE its content. Even more recommended than before!

24 years old and still an intense and difficult experience that will give you hours of demon killing, blood splattered fun. This game is a classic, and rightfully so. It would go on to define everything a shooter strives to be and still remains quite fun.
Story: You are the only surviving person on a remote, demon infested base on Mars. Now pick up some guns, and go kill the demons. The story is meant to be minimal and is (as you've probably heard countless times) not that important. It fits in pretty well with the typical Nintendo game stories of the times. The game has three basic phases, one on Mars, one in upper Hell, and one in Lower Hell, each with its distinct objective that spans the entire episode. There is a fourth episode, but it doesn't have anything to do with the original trilogy and is in all honesty, not much fun to play through unless your a huge masochist. Despite the story being minimal, it is still quite compelling due to its simplicity and the lack of BS dialogue appearing every five minutes.
Overall Score for Story: 9/10
Gameplay: Despite not having a y-axis, the shooting remains fast paced and intense. There is a huge collection of destructive weapons and unlike many modern shooters, each has a distinct purpose (besides the pistol). The shotgun is great for clustered, weak enemies, the chain gun is good for staggering, the BFG for taking out large groups of strong foes, etc. There is also a huge cast of enemies that, just like the weapons, also serve distinct purposes. The possessed marines are the weak infantry made to slowly eat away at your health, the Imps the standard enemies that are deadly at any range, the Pinkies the bullet sponge "chargers" that attempt to close the distance and melee you, the Barons of Hell the towering, seemingly invincible, yet slow moving leaders that kill you with just a few hits, etc. The combinations of the diverse armory and enemies make this game somewhat strategic as you try to figure out which weapon to blow apart which demons with. Progressing isn't too difficult, you move room to room killing everything that moves while collecting keys that allow you to enter new areas. This simple formula makes for some great times and the game has great replay value due to the secret areas and endless amount of mods available.
Overall Score for Gameplay: 10/10
Characters: The characters are pretty basic yet unforgettable. There's Doomguy who doesn't talk but makes some memorable faces and kinky grunting noises when he takes damage. There are a few bosses but they don't talk and you know nothing about them except that their evil and need to die. Still, works pretty well though and I doubt you'll really care.
Overall Score for Characters: 8/10
Graphics: For its time, the graphics were a big deal and though extremely outdated now, they are charming and work perfectly with the game. If you really don't like them, there are plenty of mods you can install to make the game look good.
Overall Score for Graphics: 9/10
Sound: The sound design in this game is also very charming and works well. The monsters all have unique and recognizable growls, the weapons still pack a punch, and other objects have satisfying sounds as you pick them up or interact with them.
Overall Score for Sound: 8/10
Soundtrack: The soundtrack is very recognizable and memorable. Although basic, it truly sets the mood of each level and each is very different from the last.
Overall Score for Soundtrack: 9/10
So there you have it. This game is awesome and still provides plenty of awesome content. The mod support is phenomenal and if your into modding yourself than this game should provide an easy canvas for you to mess around on. If your looking into getting something story intensive than this is not it but the gameplay is still extremely fun to play. To any fan of first person shooters, this game is a must play as it is the grand daddy that started it all (besides Wolfenstein 3D).
Overall Score for Game: 9.1/10

Overall a very good game, nothing particularlly new here but everything is well executed* the story is interesting enough to keep you engaged and the gameplay is solid. The art style is the real winner here. The first The Darkness suffered from poor visuals and blockly looks along with a light mechanic that was cool in concept but not so much in gameplay. The fluidity of the combat is very impressive as well, you'll go from shooting guys in the face to disembowling them with your claws to ripping car doors off of cars for cover all without missing a beat. There is great attention paid to detail in the level design and non consequential objects placed around the levels. Voice acting is surprisingly good. The length of the main campaign is maybe a little short for $30, but if you catch it on sale for $25 or less I'd say you'll get your money's worth.
Overall a very enjoyable time was had playing and I'll probably fork over a couple of bucks for DLC if and when it hits, assuming it's single player content.

It doesn't happen often, but it sucks you right out of the game when it does.

When I had first heard about this game, I was intrigued mainly because I did enjoy the cheesy slasher films during the 80's and 90's. Pre-loaded the game and was unable to play it for the first three days while the developers fixed server-related issues which prevented my connection. Poor planning on their part ruined the launch of this game. However, since they've fixed that issue, I've had a ton of fun with this game. The game has some issues, just like any piece of software does (sorry folks, bug-free software simply does not exist).
Pro's
- Definitely captures that Friday The 13th atmosphere with the spot on music and game design.
- Playing as a counselor is where the fun is at.
- Jason's kills look pretty gruesome
- Strategy and teamwork are the keys to surviving.
Con's
- Playing as Jason can be...boring.
- Near impossible to hide from Jason
- Car-driving mechanics need some fine-tuning
- Some exploits still exist which prevent you as Jason from locating counselors.
Overall, the game is a blast and I'd definitely recommend it to anyone. That being said, you really should gather a group of friends and play together as that's where the fun really is at. Don't get me wrong, I love to solo it up as well but, communication is totally the key here for surviving Jason. You need to work together, gather items and outwork Jason. Playing as the counselor is more entertaining for me as there's more strategy involved in order to win.
Don't hesitate, spend the 40.00. Enjoy!

I was utterly impressed at the quality of this game. I got it for a dollar from a humble bundle and, honestly, didn't expect much from it. If you like shooters, I would recommend this game.
-Story: 8/10
The story was surprisingly good. I figured it was just a "mc has x. you kill people. people die." kinda story, but it actually has quite a bit of depth and made me think about it. There are essentially 2 possibilities to what the story could be and I could hardly tell which was the real story up until the end of the game. I won't go any more in-depth for spoiler reasons.
-Gameplay: 8.5/10
It was plain fun. There are a good amount of weapons and a ton of items around the area that you can throw at people along with your little serpent tentacle♥♥♥♥♥♥arm things. There is also a talent tree to focus more on weapons, executions, tentacle rapey arms, and a mix between tentacle rapey arms and weapons.
-Difficulty: 7/10
The game was difficult if played on the highest difficulty. It's hard to say if it's because I was using a controller and I suck♥♥♥♥♥♥at controllers on shooters, or because of the gimmicks. I would give the difficulty a 9 because of how many times I died, but most of the times I died it was just because I would turn a corner and would almost instantly die from an ambush. It seems that it was more of a horde of enemies difficulty scale rather than challenging fights, mini-bosses, or bosses. The bosses themselves were generally pretty easy. Shoot them until they die, more or less.
Quick pros/cons list:
Pros:
+Fun and interesting combat
+Great story
+Variety of weapons and playstyles are allowed
+Controller Support
+Co-op (I have not tried co-op and will most likely not, so I cannot say how good it is.)
+Choices, though limited, there are choices.
+Talent trees
+Comic book-like graphics
Cons:
-Not many choices
-Talent trees
-Difficulty scales with being overwhelmed
-Bosses were a bit of a push-over
-Not many boss fights
-Comic book-like graphics

Firstly, this choosing between recommending and not recommending this game was hard. I finally settled on no after things quickly devolved in to ceaseless key hunts. Ultimately, this game played out like a late-nineties to early-two-thousands "I Spy" game, but with much more work put in to the art side of things.
I was unable to watch a lot, if not all of, the cutscenes, as playback stuttered horribly to the point of not functioning.
In terms of artwork, the game is really an 8/10, with two points off for the somewhat low-quality pre-rendered parts that were presented in an obviously different resolution and aspect ratio from their surroundings (this is noticeable when video crossfades back to the game), and for some of the models (the cat next to the basement door) having a disengagingly low polygon count and/or bizarre texturing issues (the bat looked like one big smear of the same texture).
In terms of script, things hold up pretty well; however, I noticed some glaring grammatical mistakes characteristic of non-native english speakers and some serious misnaming of objects, for instance:
* Nail Clippers are called "Foreceps"
* A Gazzelle Head is called a "Cow"
* A musket or flare gun is called a "Revolver" (regardless, it has a single-round chamber -- not a revolving chamber).
* A trowel is referred to as a "Spatula"
* Vaccuum tubes are referred to as "Bulbs"
* A suspended cable car is referred to as a "Funicular" (a Funicular is slanted trolley that travels on a slanted track).
in addition to many more.
Furthermore, there are some absolutely bizzarre anachronisms:
* Glue in a foil tube with 70s-era labeling
* Fire extinguisher in modern style
* A reel-to-reel tape player makes an appearance in a time when wire recording was just beginning to appear
* Toy Robot
* Early-40's vintage aeroplane
* Bizarre cyborg robot thing
* A vinyl record which, to add insult to injury, is then played back on a record player clearly intended for shellac records
and I could go on.

The tutorial and in-game help files are only so useful -- Knowing that a ship component has certain capabilities is different than knowing how it should be applied.
That being said, after playing a few times I have a much better grasp of the game.  Ship blueprinting is IMMENSELY detailed and a lot of fun if you're someone who likes to puzzle through building them to do what you want.  The AI is kind of bad in that you can get it accept and it will often propose horrendously bad deals.  There is functional multiplayer, but the game isn't quite designed for it because of timescaling.
Not bad for $5 if you dont mind the complexity.

I really want to like Evil Genius. The Bond-villain style of the game is really fun and funny, and the idea of building your island lair up from scratch has some real appeal to it. But in the end this game simply is far too shallow and repetitive to be enjoyable in the long term.
The art design is charming, and so are the animations and sounds, but the meat and potatoes of the gameplay simply loses its appeal far too quickly.
The base building mechanics are solid and the traps are fun to build and use, but there is no differentiation between islands, and you are often restricted in the size of base you can build. Research can grant you more expensive but more space efficient versions of existing technology, but deleting old building plans within the confines of limited space and starting over is a real pain.
The minion AI is atrocious, which I suppose is intentional, but it is also lazy developing. Your minions will constantly die in your own traps, and minions make no distinction between themselves as far as their role goes. Your ever so valuable third tier minions are just as likely to stumble into the gas pit attempting to kill an intruder in hand to hand combat and die as a plain worker is. I don't even want to start talking about how repetitive the evil missions are.
These are just a sampling of the problems with the game. Overall, I would say it is a fun little game that is not worth more than a couple dollars.

I think the joy and fun of the first Nidhogg title lies in its simplicity. The fact that there was a minimalist tone to everything, faceless characters, one-track sound design, and the general feeling of a gameplay focus rather than a world-building / detail focus made the game incredibly unique, and made it easier to focus on your opponent and filling the maps with their orange or yellow blood.
That unique feeling of running through a tiny pixelated man as they burst into a cloud of paint is no longer truly present. The addition of multiple sword variants is welcome and spices up the gameplay, but I feel that the bow and arrows, although an occasional welcome challenge in a match, just clutter what was originally such a beautifully simple concept. The pixel art, while done very well, gives the game more of a comedic / campy feel rather than the dark, hilariously sadistic vibe of the first game.
All of this certainly does not make Nidhogg 2 a bad game. The mechanics are well developed and fleshed out, the maps are very well created and set up, the controls are tight and the soundtrack is enthralling. The game, while good, is not what I would specifically call Nidhogg. It doesn't have the same spirit or vibe as the original, but change can be good, I suppose. I played enough time to get about halfway through the arcade mode, after which point I discovered I needed a little more practice before taking on the incredibly smart and difficult mid-to-late stage A.I. I did, however, have a lot of fun in the short time I was able to enjoy, and I'm sure my friends that used to frequently come over to enjoy the local play of the original Nidhogg will have quite a bit of fun with this sequel as well. While I do really like this game so far, but I will always be a little bit sad that the simplistic majesty of the original isn't around anymore.

Let me first mention, I didn't like this game back in the day, however this "resurrected" version is something I enjoy more. Although it is an apocalyptic world, not something I particularly enjoy(this is only due to how I prefer RPG games), this game is actually pretty well done.

Let me just say, if you enjoyed Killing Floor, you'll probably enjoy this if you join the PvE servers, otherwise you'll have to deal with the PvP scenario which I don't recall being in Killing Floor.
Although the game is pretty good to play, there are issues with it.
I think a major problem about these games is it is just oddly built for me, this is a separate issue, but it makes most survival games seem generic, in similarity to how I find most MMOs generic which causes me to get bored and leave the game in due time. This survival game has that odd mechanic to it, but plays out in a way to where it's actually playable and I tend to ignore it. Anyhow, here are the actual issues or things I think they should address in the game:

My ultimate problem, and this is coming from someone who loves both this game and Battlestar Galactica, is that the fleets too heavily mirror one another and that the game is worse off for it.
This game has a lot going for it, and is very fun--that's no lie--I purchased and hardly ever played Battlefleet Gothic. But after deciding to rewatch the miniseries, I think I've nailed down the issues I personally have with the game.
The Colonial Fleet and Cylon Armada both rely on guns, missiles, and fighters. And that's all well and fine, but ultimately there should be a difference between the two of them, a much greater difference as we can see in the show. The Cylons relied primarily on two things there: fighters and missiles, and lots and lots of both. In the game, while this does take place nearly half a century earlier, the Cylons are deploying battleships and gunboats that can rival a battlestar's gunnage and that just doesn't feel right. When I use a battlestar, I should feel like I have the beefiest, tankiest, ship on the field. It carries an entire wing of fighters, it has enough guns to lay down a screen of weapons fire to blot out the sun.
Or it should.
Instead, I get a ship that melts to Cylon gunfire in seconds, whether it's in the middle or the edge of combat, and one that can deploy a field of fire, but can choose to either do that or target enemy vessels. When targetting an enemy vessel, the broadside turrets on the flight pods are too low on their damage to even matter. The artillery guns on a battlestar's back? They'll miss on nearly every shot that isn't targetting a basestar, and that's not right. I expect to be able to dish out damage and deal damage at the same time, the flak screen to be a natural product of a battlestar's firing solution. Instead, I get to block missiles while an enemy's guns still continue to shred me in the minute or so it takes a fully armored battlestar to melt. It isn't right.
The Cylons should be focusing on four primary things: boarding, hacking, missiles, and fighters. The Colonials would be at home focusing on fighters, armor, and guns. Instead, we have two mirrored fleets and not nearly enough diversity of playstyle. This is not to even mention that during the campaign mode, the difficulty jumps to a nearly impossible level where Cylon fleets start numbering at nearly a dozen, all of them large, while you've barely even started to construct anything able to fight them. By the time you do, you realize that not only are your fleets weaker, but that whenever you do fight your command ship and officer are always targetted and lost first, leading to a cascading failure of your entire campaign. And this occurs because a battlestar is less than half of what it should be, guns and armor and all.
I want to love this game. I love what it does have going for it. The models are great, the combat and visuals are fun and exciting, the music and replay feature are a blast, and the gameplay is fun too! But it has glaring issues that, until fixed, render me unable to honestly enjoy it.

Oh man I wanted to like this game so much.  It has a lot going for it, and it does a good job of capturing the BSG vibe, in fact I really, immediately felt comfortable with the aesthetic and the story. It has a very innovative and cleverly designed tactical layer, the ship movement and positioning, the turn-based combat, and the actual fighting are well executed.
The strategy layer leaves much to be desired, for a simple enough interface it's inelegant; and I understand that the low-high tech aspect of BSG is well represented, the interface doesn't feel the slightest bit substantial.  The nested menus are uncomfortable and awkward to navigate, as is the strategy map.  This is nitpicking though, as the actual game itself shouldn't be judged by poor design choices.  The real problem is the game balance and the cylon ai.
In the early game, your most potent weapon is suiciding your fast moving ships in ramming attacks against the toughest cylon ships, followed closely by mass missile barrages.  There's no real strategic competence required, just focus one ship until it is destroyed then move on to the next one, while counting on the RNG of your ships' accuracy to deal sufficient damage to give you a numerical advantage.  The Enemy very predictably targets whichever ship your officer is placed on, allowing you to execute the same strategy over and over again. None of the fights seem like fair pitched battles after the early game, you're either very easily disposing of an enemy force, or the cylons are suddenly OP and slicing through your ships with ease.
The linear tech tree makes for limited customization, while you do have a simple slider in game to divert power to offense or defense, your ability to actually adapt to challenges is limited to what ships you choose to employ in your actions; rather than the expected 4x staple of modifying or designing ships, which is a missed opportunity.
I really wanted to get into this game, but it's frustratingly limited and although it has real potential, it feels like playing a tech demo or a proof-of-concept offering rather than a finished game.  I'm hoping that updates and mods improve the UI, Customization options, and enemy AI; because this game does have a ton of potential. That being said, I'll still recommend the game because I think it's worth supporting it's further development and I hope the developers continue to improve the game.

When you play ArcaniA aka Gothic 4, it seems to be very important how the game is compared to it's predecessors. And there's a lot to live up to because the first 2 games were considered sort of icons of the genre. Here’s a list of remarks made while playing:
Game mechanics:
+ Looting is fast and simple.
+ One of the coolest looking minimaps I've seen.
+ Main quest conversations trigger automatically when approaching the right npc. This prevents fruitless dialogues with npc's who don't really have anything to say.
+ Health regenerates
+ Interesting lock picking system
+ Game creates savegames itself in important places. Don't remember the previous ones doing that.
- If the quest location stays out of the range of the minimap then the minimap doesn't show you the direction towards the location.
- Minor bugs with characters getting stuck behind invisible obstacles.
- The question weather it is open world or not. Fans of Gothic say that ArcaniA is not open world like the other Gothic games were. I ask: was Gothic 1 open world? They say 'yes, but a really small open world'. I say: well, there you have it. Arcania has those small areas, bigger than in Witcher, but it's not open in the same way Gothic 3, Skyrim and GTA were. I bring it up because it has been noted as a flaw.
- Levelling up badly balanced. The game is way too generous in helping you max your stats. By the time I was through two thirds of the game I had maxed out everything I needed.
Design:
+ Beautiful textures, highly improved compared to Gothic 3 BUT they blend together horribly.
+ Weirdly the game get's better designwise as the it advances. Looks like they created the first chapter just to learn how to do the job.
- The guy who created the 3D models didn't have a clue about human anatomy.
- Like so often in games the main character looks like some fancy-pants out of a men's magazine.
- In game written material is in some kind of modern comic font which doesn’t blend with the rest of the game at all.
- During dialogues, when the characters are zoomed in, armor stretches and bends as if it was part of flesh and muscle.
- Insanely few character models. The orcs, for example, look all the same.
Game flow:
+ ArcaniA’s best feature: they've come up with a helpful, easy-to-use dodging system. My experience with other games (Elder Scrolls, Assassin's Creed, Gothic) is that going in for the kill is more profitable that starting to dodge/ block, which in most cases is hard and pointless. ArcaniA nailed it and I give them huge credit for it.
+ Npc's with quests are marked with an exclamation mark.
+ Auto-aim enemies in malee battle (like in Assassin’s Creed) . In ArcaniA you come across places where you fight off 8 enemies or so at once. The auto trigger feature makes the battle in such occasions more fluent and faster overall.
Atmosphere:
+ The protagonist actually talks when you trigger a dialogue. Games these days (Skyrim, Half-Life etc.) have taken the silent protagonist approach which in my opinion closes some potent doors.
+ Diego and Gorn are the coolest they've ever been during the whole series.
+ The character is a charming fellow with good spirit. It contrasts highly with the previous nameless hero who at least in Gothic 3: Forsaken Gods was a war mongering bloody dictator who went after some small tribes that wanted to live their own way).
+ Goblins do whatever goblins might do before you arrive, they don't just stand there idly. They have a tribal look and seem a little more sophisticated than those poor bare guys in Gothic 3. AND they carry cool names like ''Warrior of the bugeater tribe'.
+ There's actually an epic story behind the whole thing with twists and drama.
- To the end it doesn't develop that true Gothic atmosphere that made the previous games popular.
- Voice acting is terribly overdramatized, doesn't sound like natural speech at all.
- In the whole there's not much to explore, the world feels empty.
A remark about Gothic: some ancient cultures belived that your spirit is immune to harm if your enemy didn't know your real name. The idea is used in both fantasy books and occult rituals. You have to know the name of the demon to summon him. Knowing the name bends the demon to your will. This allegory now comes to mind as I think of the former nameless hero, now Rhobar III who has been attacked by a demon. While he was nameless, he was mighty, but once he got a name, he became subject to harm. The game unconciously plays with this idea.
The verdict:
Try the game. Never mind the old Gothic games, they had their flaws as well. Arcania had both good and bad sides.

Initially extremely interesting, the game quickly devolves into a subpar NBA Jam minigame glued together by slices of pretentious visual novel. The RPG mechanics can be completely ignored, there's no strategy to the minigame (simply give the ball to the faster teammate and run rings around the enemy) and the whole thing comes off like a pretty sketch for a more fleshed out game. It looks and sounds great but becomes tedious very quickly. A turn based affair where you could coordinate with your teammates effectively to play passes and set up throws would have been interesting. Instead imagine trying to play basketball where only one person from each team is allowed to move at once - not fun. Whereas Transistor suffered from being a turnbased game which should have been realtime, this suffers the opposite problem.

Arcania is a good beginers entry to rpg games.  It has been stripped and dumbed down from other gothic titles to appeal to a lighter crowd. What you have here is a streamlined story with minimal side quests, terrible voices, repetative character models and mediocre combat.  Most enemies have timed power attacks easily avoided with a roll and almost everyone can be killed by backing up while firing arrows.  The graphics are better than older gothic games of course but arent anything special.  The amount of armour and weapons is extremely limited with a pathetic crafting system.
On a plus note the game is easy to play if your not familiar with or are intimidated by advanced rpg games.  The games npc's occasionally offer a bit of adult humour if your patient enough to listen to there awful voices.

I don't know where to start. And I don't like that I can't give a thumbs up AND thumbs down. But this will be a long review.
First, for a game billed as a strategy game, there is but one strategy. And that is to build enough ships to make seven ship fleets to protect each of the four quadrants of your map. This is not difficult with the exception that you play on the highest of three difficulty modes. Once you figure this out, this is where my biggest problems comes into play
1) This is not a strategic game. It's a reactive game because the Cylons always have the initiative. They will attack your fleet or your planets and you simply react to the attacks - the entire campaign, until the very end.
2) The game becomes repetitive and ultimately boring. The AI becomes predictable. AI will set up the enemy ships in one of three directions relative to you, left, right and forward. Elevation of these fleets are either slightly higher, lower or even with yours. The enemy fleets are cookie cutter fleets.
3) For a game with the namesake of the most famous Battlestar in existence, you don't need a Battlestar to complete the game. And as far as I'm concerned, a Battlestar slows your fleet down.
4) The ships:
A) The Manticore corvette is pretty good for very early game, but it become weak and actually uses up a space in your fleet better utilized by another ship.
B) The Adamant frigate will be your workhorse and fleets of seven Adamants can be used through the campaign to the end, thereby rendering the next three ships fairly useless.
C) The Ranger missile cruiser is fairly useless because of the low hitting power of its missiles, even though it will fire every other turn. The  battles are short enough that you will rarely get more than 3 or 4 salvos off. The AI will focus fire this ship.
D) The Minotaur gunship is not a good ship. Like the Ranger, the AI seems to focus fire this ship. And this ship really needs to get fairly close to the enemy for it to really work. And it is slow.
E) The Atlas carrier carries two squadrons of Vipers, your WWII equivalent fighters. While the Adamant carries one squadron of Vipers, a Battlestar carries two squadrons and your shipyard also carries two squadrons, I never saw the need to use the Atlas.
F) The Battlestar. Well, you get a taste of this ship in the second or third mission you play, which is part of the tutorial. You won't see another Battlestar for quite some time thereafter. I find the namesake of the series lackluster. It has a missle launcher and carries two squadrons of Vipers. It also uses the unique concept of FlaK. This creates a FlaK field on either side or all around the ship that will simply shred anything that comes in contact with it...including your own Vipers, missiles or ships, so one must be careful when setting off your FlaK defenses.
But, the Battlestar is low. You may know the old addage saying A fleet is only as fast as its slowest ship. This is true in this case. While its maneuverability is exceptional, like the Minotaur, it simply can't keep up with the rest of the fleet. And this, from a physics POV doesn't make a lot of sense when you factor out friction and most gravity and factor in humungous engines. The ship is not that powerful in weapons, other than its Vipers. The AI will focus fire it if it doesn't have another ship such as the Ranger or Minotaur to focus first.
This ship, with its guns and firing arcs should lay waste in short order any Cylon ship smaller than their large carriers.
Before I wrap this review up, I'm going to say that within the first 50 hours of play, I was bored with the game. There simply isn't anything in the game that would want to make you play for hours and hours and hours. There is nothing new to unlock once you have all the ships, special weapons and whatnot. The Resource missions are all the same. And in my opinion, the campaign was much to short.
But you may ask..."Why did you play 250 hours if you were bored with it?" Well, Through that time I played with the three different difficulty settings. While did this, I kept wondering if anything different or special would pop up or unlock. Maybe a hidden mission, or a once per campaign ship or something like that. But no, the game is a straight through campaign.
But do I recommend the game? I'm going to say Yes. And that's only because the Devs and Slitherine say there will be added content in the future. Is it worth $40? Well, I can go to the shooting range and blow through $40 worth of ammo (depending on the gun I take) within 3 minutes. Or I can go to 2 two hour movies with my family with popcorn and drinks for $40. So I leave the question of worth up to the individual reading this review.
So have fun with this game and then shelve it to wait on further content.
